description: Tensors and Dynamic neural networks in Python with strong GPU acceleration
content:
---------------------------------------- PyTorch is a Python package that provides two high-level features: - Tensor computation (like NumPy) with strong GPU acceleration - Deep neural networks built on a tape-based autograd system You can reuse your favorite Python packages such as NumPy, SciPy, and Cython to extend PyTorch when needed. Our trunk health (Continuous Integration signals) can be found at [hud.pytorch.org](). - [More About PyTorch](#more-about-pytorch) - [A GPU-Ready Tensor Library](#a-gpu-ready-tensor-library) - [Dynamic Neural Networks: Tape-Based Autograd](#dynamic-neural-networks-tape-based-autograd) - [Python First](#python-first) - [Imperative Experiences](#imperative-experiences) - [Fast and Lean](#fast-and-lean) - [Extensions Without Pain](#extensions-without-pain) - [Installation](#installation) - [Binaries](#binaries) - [NVIDIA Jetson Platforms](#nvidia-jetson-platforms) - [From Source](#from-source) - [Prerequisites](#prerequisites) - [NVIDIA CUDA Support](#nvidia-cuda-support) - [AMD ROCm Support](#amd-rocm-support) - [Intel GPU Support](#intel-gpu-support) - [Get the PyTorch Source](#get-the-pytorch-source) - [Install Dependencies](#install-dependencies) - [Install PyTorch](#install-pytorch) - [Adjust Build Options (Optional)](#adjust-build-options-optional) - [Docker Image](#docker-image) - [Using pre-built images](#using-pre-built-images) - [Building the image yourself](#building-the-image-yourself) - [Previous Versions](#previous-versions) - [Getting Started](#getting-started) - [Resources](#resources) - [Communication](#communication) - [Releases and Contributing](#releases-and-contributing) - [The Team](#the-team) - [License](#license) ## More About PyTorch [Learn the basics of PyTorch]() At a granular level, PyTorch is a library that consists of the following components: | Component | Description | | ---- | --- | | [**torch**]() | A Tensor library like NumPy, with strong GPU support | | [**torch.autograd**]() | A tape-based automatic differentiation library that supports all differentiable Tensor operations in torch | | [**torch.nn**]() | A neural networks library deeply integrated with autograd designed for maximum flexibility | | [**torch.multiprocessing**]() | Python multiprocessing, but with magical memory sharing of torch Tensors across processes. Useful for data loading and Hogwild training | | [**torch.utils**]() | DataLoader and other utility functions for convenience | Usually, PyTorch is used either as: - A replacement for NumPy to use the power of GPUs. - A deep learning research platform that provides maximum flexibility and speed. Elaborating Further: ### A GPU-Ready Tensor Library If you use NumPy, then you have used Tensors (a.k.a. ndarray). ![Tensor illustration]() PyTorch provides Tensors that can live either on the CPU or the GPU and accelerates the computation by a huge amount. We provide a wide variety of tensor routines to accelerate and fit your scientific computation needs such as slicing, indexing, mathematical operations, linear algebra, reductions. And they are fast! ### Dynamic Neural Networks: Tape-Based Autograd PyTorch has a unique way of building neural networks: using and replaying a tape recorder. Most frameworks such as TensorFlow, Theano, Caffe, and CNTK have a static view of the world. One has to build a neural network and reuse the same structure again and again. Changing the way the network behaves means that one has to start from scratch. With PyTorch, we use a technique called reverse-mode auto-differentiation, which allows you to change the way your network behaves arbitrarily with zero lag or overhead. Our inspiration comes from several research papers on this topic, as well as current and past work such as [torch-autograd](), [autograd](), [Chainer](), etc. While this technique is not unique to PyTorch, it's one of the fastest implementations of it to date. You get the best of speed and flexibility for your crazy research. ![Dynamic graph]() ### Python First PyTorch is not a Python binding into a monolithic C++ framework. It is built to be deeply integrated into Python. You can use it naturally like you would use [NumPy]() / [SciPy]() / [scikit-learn]() etc. You can write your new neural network layers in Python itself, using your favorite libraries and use packages such as [Cython]() and [Numba](). Our goal is to not reinvent the wheel where appropriate. ### Imperative Experiences PyTorch is designed to be intuitive, linear in thought, and easy to use. When you execute a line of code, it gets executed. There isn't an asynchronous view of the world. When you drop into a debugger or receive error messages and stack traces, understanding them is straightforward. The stack trace points to exactly where your code was defined. We hope you never spend hours debugging your code because of bad stack traces or asynchronous and opaque execution engines. ### Fast and Lean PyTorch has minimal framework overhead. We integrate acceleration libraries such as [Intel MKL]() and NVIDIA ([cuDNN](), [NCCL]()) to maximize speed. At the core, its CPU and GPU Tensor and neural network backends are mature and have been tested for years. Hence, PyTorch is quite fast — whether you run small or large neural networks. The memory usage in PyTorch is extremely efficient compared to Torch or some of the alternatives. We've written custom memory allocators for the GPU to make sure that your deep learning models are maximally memory efficient. This enables you to train bigger deep learning models than before. ### Extensions Without Pain Writing new neural network modules, or interfacing with PyTorch's Tensor API, was designed to be straightforward and with minimal abstractions. You can write new neural network layers in Python using the torch API [or your favorite NumPy-based libraries such as SciPy](). If you want to write your layers in C/C++, we provide a convenient extension API that is efficient and with minimal boilerplate. No wrapper code needs to be written. You can see [a tutorial here]() and [an example here](). ## Installation ### Binaries Commands to install binaries via Conda or pip wheels are on our website: []() #### NVIDIA Jetson Platforms Python wheels for NVIDIA's Jetson Nano, Jetson TX1/TX2, Jetson Xavier NX/AGX, and Jetson AGX Orin are provided [here]() and the L4T container is published [here]() They require JetPack 4.2 and above, and [@dusty-nv]() and [@ptrblck]() are maintaining them. ### From Source #### Prerequisites If you are installing from source, you will need: - Python 3.11 or later - A compiler that fully supports C++20, such as clang or gcc (gcc 11.3.0 or newer is required, on Linux) - Visual Studio or Visual Studio Build Tool (Windows only) - At least 10 GB of free disk space - 30-60 minutes for the initial build (subsequent rebuilds are much faster) \* PyTorch CI uses Visual C++ BuildTools, which come with Visual Studio Enterprise, Professional, or Community Editions. You can also install the build tools from The build tools *do not* come with Visual Studio Code by default. An example of environment setup is shown below: * Linux: ```bash $ source /bin/activate $ conda create -y -n $ conda activate ``` * Windows: ```bash $ source \Scripts\activate.bat $ conda create -y -n $ conda activate $ call "C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\\Community\VC\Auxiliary\Build\vcvarsall.bat" x64 ``` A conda environment is not required. You can also do a PyTorch build in a standard virtual environment, e.g., created with tools like `uv`, provided your system has installed all the necessary dependencies unavailable as pip packages (e.g., CUDA, MKL.) ##### NVIDIA CUDA Support If you want to compile with CUDA support, [select a supported version of CUDA from our support matrix](), then install the following: - [NVIDIA CUDA]() - [NVIDIA cuDNN]() v9.0 or above - [Compiler]() compatible with CUDA Note: You could refer to the [cuDNN Support Matrix]() for cuDNN versions with the various supported CUDA, CUDA driver, and NVIDIA hardware. If you want to disable CUDA support, export the environment variable `USE_CUDA=0`. Other potentially useful environment variables are documented in [`cmake/EnvVarForwarding.cmake`](./cmake/EnvVarForwarding.cmake). If CUDA is installed in a non-standard location, set PATH so that the nvcc you want to use can be found (e.g., `export PATH=/usr/local/cuda-12.8/bin:$PATH`). If you are building for NVIDIA's Jetson platforms (Jetson Nano, TX1, TX2, AGX Xavier), Instructions to install PyTorch for Jetson Nano are [available here]() ##### AMD ROCm Support If you want to compile with ROCm support, install - [AMD ROCm]() 4.0 and above installation - ROCm is currently supported only for Linux systems. By default the build system expects ROCm to be installed in `/opt/rocm`. If ROCm is installed in a different directory, the `ROCM_PATH` environment variable must be set to the ROCm installation directory. The build system automatically detects the AMD GPU architecture. Optionally, the AMD GPU architecture can be explicitly set with the `PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH` environment variable [AMD GPU architecture]() If you want to disable ROCm support, export the environment variable `USE_ROCM=0`. Other potentially useful environment variables are documented in [`cmake/EnvVarForwarding.cmake`](./cmake/EnvVarForwarding.cmake). ##### Intel GPU Support If you want to compile with Intel GPU support, follow these - [PyTorch Prerequisites for Intel GPUs]() instructions. - Intel GPU is supported for Linux and Windows. If you want to disable Intel GPU support, export the environment variable `USE_XPU=0`. Other potentially useful environment variables are documented in [`cmake/EnvVarForwarding.cmake`](./cmake/EnvVarForwarding.cmake). #### Get the PyTorch Source ```bash git clone cd pytorch # if you are updating an existing checkout git submodule sync git submodule update --init --recursive ``` #### Install Dependencies **Common** ```bash # Run this command from the PyTorch directory after cloning the source code using the “Get the PyTorch Source“ section above pip install --group dev ``` **On Linux** ```bash pip install mkl-static mkl-include # CUDA only: Add LAPACK support for the GPU if needed # magma installation: run with active conda environment. specify CUDA version to install .ci/docker/common/install_magma_conda.sh 12.4 # (optional) If using torch.compile with inductor/triton, install the matching version of triton # Run from the pytorch directory after cloning # For Intel GPU support, please explicitly `export USE_XPU=1` before running command. make triton ``` **On Windows** ```bash pip install mkl-static mkl-include # Add these packages if torch.distributed is needed. # Distributed package support on Windows is a prototype feature and is subject to changes. conda install -c conda-forge libuv=1.51 ``` #### Install PyTorch **On Linux** If you're compiling for AMD ROCm then first run this command: ```bash # Only run this if you're compiling for ROCm python tools/amd_build/build_amd.py ``` Install PyTorch ```bash # the CMake prefix for conda environment export CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="${CONDA_PREFIX:-'$(dirname $(which conda))/../'}:${CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH}" python -m pip install --no-build-isolation -v -e . # the CMake prefix for non-conda environment, e.g. Python venv # call following after activating the venv export CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="${VIRTUAL_ENV}:${CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH}" ``` **On macOS** ```bash python -m pip install --no-build-isolation -v -e . ``` **On Windows** If you want to build legacy python code, please refer to [Building on legacy code and CUDA]() **CPU-only builds** In this mode PyTorch computations will run on your CPU, not your GPU. ```cmd python -m pip install --no-build-isolation -v -e . ``` Note on OpenMP: The desired OpenMP implementation is Intel OpenMP (iomp). In order to link against iomp, you'll need to manually download the library and set up the building environment by tweaking `CMAKE_INCLUDE_PATH` and `LIB`. The instruction [here]() is an example for setting up both MKL and Intel OpenMP. Without these configurations for CMake, Microsoft Visual C OpenMP runtime (vcomp) will be used. **CUDA based build** In this mode PyTorch computations will leverage your GPU via CUDA for faster number crunching [NVTX]() is needed to build PyTorch with CUDA. NVTX is a part of CUDA distributive, where it is called "Nsight Compute". To install it onto an already installed CUDA run CUDA installation once again and check the corresponding checkbox. Make sure that CUDA with Nsight Compute is installed after Visual Studio. Currently, VS 2017 / 2019, and Ninja are supported as the generator of CMake. If `ninja.exe` is detected in `PATH`, then Ninja will be used as the default generator, otherwise, it will use VS 2017 / 2019.
If Ninja is selected as the generator, the latest MSVC will get selected as the underlying toolchain. Additional libraries such as [Magma](), [oneDNN, a.k.a. MKLDNN or DNNL](), and [Sccache]() are often needed. Please refer to the [installation-helper]() to install them. You can refer to the [build_pytorch.bat]() script for some other environment variables configurations ```cmd cmd :: Set the environment variables after you have downloaded and unzipped the mkl package, :: else CMake would throw an error as `Could NOT find OpenMP`. set CMAKE_INCLUDE_PATH={Your directory}\mkl\include set LIB={Your directory}\mkl\lib;%LIB% :: Read the content in the previous section carefully before you proceed. :: [Optional] If you want to override the underlying toolset used by Ninja and Visual Studio with CUDA, please run the following script block. :: "Visual Studio 2019 Developer Command Prompt" will be run automatically. :: Make sure you have CMake >= 3.12 before you do this when you use the Visual Studio generator. set CMAKE_GENERATOR_TOOLSET_VERSION=14.27 set DISTUTILS_USE_SDK=1 for /f "usebackq tokens=*" %i in (`"%ProgramFiles(x86)%\Microsoft Visual Studio\Installer\vswhere.exe" -version [15^,17^) -products * -latest -property installationPath`) do call "%i\VC\Auxiliary\Build\vcvarsall.bat" x64 -vcvars_ver=%CMAKE_GENERATOR_TOOLSET_VERSION% :: [Optional] If you want to override the CUDA host compiler set CUDAHOSTCXX=C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\2019\Community\VC\Tools\MSVC\14.27.29110\bin\HostX64\x64\cl.exe python -m pip install --no-build-isolation -v -e . ``` **Intel GPU builds** In this mode PyTorch with Intel GPU support will be built. Please make sure [the common prerequisites](#prerequisites) as well as [the prerequisites for Intel GPU](#intel-gpu-support) are properly installed and the environment variables are configured prior to starting the build. For build tool support, `Visual Studio 2022` is required. Then PyTorch can be built with the command: ```cmd :: CMD Commands: :: Set the CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH to help find corresponding packages :: %CONDA_PREFIX% only works after `conda activate custom_env` if defined CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH ( set "CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=%CONDA_PREFIX%\Library;%CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH%" ) else ( set "CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=%CONDA_PREFIX%\Library" ) python -m pip install --no-build-isolation -v -e . ``` ##### Adjust Build Options (Optional) You can adjust the configuration of CMake variables through environment variables, which the build forwards to CMake (see [`cmake/EnvVarForwarding.cmake`](./cmake/EnvVarForwarding.cmake) for the full list). For example, pointing the build at a specific Conda prefix, CuDNN, or BLAS: On Linux ```bash export CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="${CONDA_PREFIX:-'$(dirname $(which conda))/../'}:${CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH}" spin develop ``` On macOS ```bash export CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="${CONDA_PREFIX:-'$(dirname $(which conda))/../'}:${CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH}" MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=11.0 spin develop ``` After a first `spin develop`, you can inspect or adjust the CMake cache interactively with `ccmake build` (or `cmake-gui build`) and rebuild with `spin develop`; your edits persist, because reconfiguration does not use `--fresh` and environment variables only seed cache entries that are not already set. The corollary: once a variable is in the cache, changing its environment variable no longer affects it -- edit the cache directly (or delete `build/CMakeCache.txt`) to change it. The build type and compiler are the exception; the build always re-applies them. ### Docker Image #### Using pre-built images You can also pull a pre-built docker image from Docker Hub and run with docker v23.0+ ```bash docker run --gpus all --rm -ti --ipc=host pytorch/pytorch:latest ``` Please note that PyTorch uses shared memory to share data between processes, so if torch multiprocessing is used (e.g. for multithreaded data loaders) the default shared memory segment size that container runs with is not enough, and you should increase shared memory size either with `--ipc=host` or `--shm-size` command line options to `nvidia-docker run`. #### Building the image yourself **NOTE:** Must be built with a Docker version >= 23.0 The Dockerfile is supplied to build images with CUDA 12.6 support and cuDNN v9. You can pass `PYTHON_VERSION=x.y` make variable to specify which Python version is to be used by Miniconda, or leave it unset to use the default, as the Dockerfile uses system Python. ```bash make -f docker.Makefile # images are tagged as docker.io/${your_docker_username}/pytorch ``` You can also pass the `CMAKE_VARS="..."` environment variable to specify additional CMake variables to be passed to CMake during the build. See [`cmake/EnvVarForwarding.cmake`](./cmake/EnvVarForwarding.cmake) for the list of available variables. ```bash make -f docker.Makefile ``` ### Previous Versions Installation instructions and binaries for previous PyTorch versions may be found on [our website](). ## Getting Started Pointers to get you started: - [Tutorials: get you started with understanding and using PyTorch]() - [Examples: easy to understand PyTorch code across all domains]() - [The API Reference]() - [Glossary]() ## Resources * [PyTorch.org]() * [PyTorch Tutorials]() * [PyTorch Examples]() * [PyTorch Models]() * [Intro to Deep Learning with PyTorch from Udacity]() * [Intro to Machine Learning with PyTorch from Udacity]() * [Deep Neural Networks with PyTorch from Coursera]() * [PyTorch Twitter]() * [PyTorch Blog]() * [PyTorch YouTube]() ## Communication * Forums: Discuss implementations, research, etc. * GitHub Issues: Bug reports, feature requests, install issues, RFCs, thoughts, etc. See the [issue lifecycle](CONTRIBUTING.md#issue-lifecycle) for how they are handled. * Slack: The [PyTorch Slack]() hosts a primary audience of moderate to experienced PyTorch users and developers for general chat, online discussions, collaboration, etc. * Facebook Page: Important announcements about PyTorch. * For brand guidelines, please visit our website at [pytorch.org]() ## Releases and Contributing To report issues or contribute changes to PyTorch, see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). title: [MPS] test_output_grad_match_combinations_mps_float16 fails because MPS sums fp16 grads in a different order than CPU
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`TestConsistencyMPS.test_output_grad_match_combinations_mps_float16` fails on every run on main (b0e48e7b450) on an M4 Pro with macOS 27.0.1. In CI it has been disabled as flaky since July (#188985).

```
python test/test_mps.py TestConsistencyMPS.test_output_grad_match_combinations_mps_float16
```

```
AssertionError: Tensor-likes are not close!

Mismatched elements: 1 / 2 (50.0%)
Greatest absolute difference: 0.0078125 at index (1,) (up to 1e-05 allowed)
Greatest relative difference: 0.0013418197631835938 at index (1,) (up to 0.001 allowed)

The failure occurred for item [0]

Caused by sample input at index 11: SampleInput(input=Tensor[size=(2,), device="mps:0", dtype=torch.float16], args=(), kwargs={'r': '4', 'with_replacement': 'True'}, broadcasts_input=False, name='')
```

**Why.** The forward of `combinations` is plain indexing, so its backward is `IndexBackward0`, i.e. `index_put(accumulate=True)`, which sums the fp16 gradients of repeated elements:

<url>

MPS sums them in a different order than CPU, and not in the same order from run to run, so the two round differently. In the failing sample, each of the 2 input elements appears 10 times in the output, so each grad is a sum of 10 fp16 values, and CPU and MPS end up 2 ULP apart. Over 9000 random cases (500 seeds of the 18 OpInfo samples), repeated over several runs:

- CPU and MPS are equally accurate against a float64 reference: at most 3.7 and 4.0 ULP off, with a mean of 0.19 ULP for both.
- They differ from each other by up to 4e-3 relative, and 3.6% to 3.8% of the cases fail the default fp16 tolerance (rtol=1e-3).

**Proposed fix.** Add `combinations` to `FP16_LOW_PRECISION_LIST` (atol=2e-2, rtol=1e-2). `_unsafe_masked_index_put_accumulate`, which uses the same accumulating `index_put`, is already there for the same reason:

<url>

All 9000 cases pass with it in every run. The forward is exact, so the looser tolerance hides nothing there. A tighter per-op tolerance like the one `nansum` has (atol=rtol=5e-3) also passes, but with only about 25% headroom over the worst case.

This issue will resolve the issue mentioned in in <url>

### Versions

Is debug build: False

Libc version: N/A

Python version: 3.12.15 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Oct 1 2026, 20:11:32) [Clang 20.1.8 ] (64-bit runtime)
Python platform: macOS-27.0.1-arm64-arm-64bit
Is CUDA available: False
CUDA runtime version: No CUDA

title: [MPS] Small-input CPU fallback in torch.linalg.eigh causes a performance cliff
body:
I think we should re-consider this small-input CPU specialization, which causes GPU -> CPU -> GPU roundtrips.

# AI-generated report reviewed and edited by me

## Describe the issue

On an Apple M3 Max with PyTorch 2.15.0, `torch.linalg.eigh` on an MPS tensor becomes substantially faster when the batch grows from 11 to 12 matrices of size 32×32.
The larger batch does more work but takes about 2.26× less time.

The [MPS implementation](<url>) routes `batch * n * n < 12288` through CPU.
For 32×32 matrices, batch 11 is below this threshold and batch 12 reaches it.
This is explicit routing inside the operator, so disabling optional fallback with `PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=0` does not remove it.

My use case is complex-valued tensor-network training with small unitary projections.
This also affects `torch.linalg.polar` backward, which [calls `linalg_eigh(H)`](<url>), including for 4×4 matrices.

## Minimal speed test

Save the following as `benchmark_eigh_threshold.py` and run it with `python benchmark_eigh_threshold.py` in an environment with PyTorch 2.15 and MPS available.

The same seeded Hermitian matrix is repeated into each batch.
Inputs are created before timing; correctness checks and ten warmup calls per shape also run outside the timed region.
Each timing block contains twenty calls, with MPS synchronization before and after the block.
The script reports total time per completed batch call, with seven rounds in alternating shape order.

```python
"""Stock-PyTorch threshold probe; larger batches do more work, not equal work."""
import platform
import statistics
import subprocess
import time

import torch

assert torch.backends.mps.is_available(), "This reproducer requires MPS."
print(f"torch={torch.__version__}, git={torch.version.git_version}")
print(f"python={platform.python_version()}, os={platform.platform()}")
chip = subprocess.check_output(["sysctl", "-n", "machdep.cpu.brand_string"], text=True).strip()
print(f"chip={chip}, threads={torch.get_num_threads()}, interop={torch.get_num_interop_threads()}")
torch.manual_seed(2026)
a = torch.randn(32, 32, dtype=torch.complex64)
h = (a + a.mH) / 2
reference = torch.linalg.eigvalsh(h)
inputs = {b: h.repeat(b, 1, 1).to("mps") for b in (11, 12, 13)}
samples = {b: [] for b in inputs}

# Check correctness and warm each shape outside the timed region.
for b, x in inputs.items():
  values, vectors = torch.linalg.eigh(x)
  values, vectors = values.cpu(), vectors.cpu()
  expected = h.expand(b, -1, -1)
  residual = ((vectors * values.unsqueeze(-2)) @ vectors.mH - expected).norm() / expected.norm()
  spectrum_error = (values - reference).norm() / reference.expand(b, -1).norm()
  assert residual < 1e-4 and spectrum_error < 1e-4
  print(f"batch={b}: reconstruction={residual.item():.3e}, spectrum={spectrum_error.item():.3e}")
  for _ in range(10):
  torch.linalg.eigh(x)
torch.mps.synchronize()

# Seven rounds, alternating shape order; 20 calls per synchronized timing block.
for round_id in range(7):
  order = (11, 12, 13) if round_id % 2 == 0 else (13, 12, 11)
  for b in order:
  torch.mps.synchronize()
  start = time.perf_counter_ns()
  for _ in range(20):
  torch.linalg.eigh(inputs[b])
  torch.mps.synchronize()
  samples[b].append((time.perf_counter_ns() - start) / 20 / 1000)

print("Completed-call us: median [min, max] across 7 blocks of 20 calls")
for b, times in samples.items():
  print(f"batch={b}, elements={b*32*32}: {statistics.median(times):.2f} [{min(times):.2f}, {max(times):.2f}]")
  print("  block_us=" + ", ".join(f"{t:.2f}" for t in times))
print("This probes a routing discontinuity; different batch sizes are not equal-work controls.")
```

## Observed results

Measured on 2026-10-31:

| Batch | Input elements | Route in PyTorch 2.15.0 | Median µs per call | Min–max across blocks, µs |
|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|
| 11 | 11,264 | Internal CPU fallback | 1,306.00 | 1,276.16–1,438.21 |
| 12 | 12,288 | Native MPS | 579.11 | 568.13–597.05 |
| 13 | 13,312 | Native MPS | 538.80 | 528.51–561.30 |

All reconstruction and eigenvalue checks passed; the largest relative reconstruction error was `6.44e-6`.
These measurements show a discontinuity at the routing threshold.
Because the batches contain different amounts of work, this minimal test does not measure a same-input before/after speedup from removing the threshold.

## Expected behavior and proposed scope

Please revisit the small-input CPU-routing heuristic and consider removing `too_small` from this condition, while retaining the unsupported-dtype and threadgroup-memory checks.
A same-input comparison of the existing C++ implementation and a version with only this threshold removed would validate the change directly.
The performance question is the cost of routing an MPS operation through CPU and back; computation whose inputs and outputs remain on CPU is a separate case.

The analogous SVD threshold was removed in [#195950](<url>), then included in the 2.14.1 backport [#198394](<url>).
The small-input `eigh` threshold remains in 2.15.0.

### `benchmark.py`

```python
"""Same-work CPU/MPS routing microbenchmarks; no project imports.

Run with PyTorch 2.15.0; JSON results are written beside this script.
Use --profile separately: profiler logging is never enabled during timing.
CPU thread counts are left at the PyTorch defaults.
"""

import argparse
import gc
import json
import math
import os
import platform
import random
import statistics
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

os.environ.setdefault("PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK", "0")

import torch

if torch.__version__.split("+", 1)[0] != "2.15.0":
  raise RuntimeError("This comparison requires PyTorch 2.15.0 and its matching Metal source.")
if not torch.backends.mps.is_available():
  raise RuntimeError("This comparison requires an available MPS device.")

OUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def stats(values):
  ordered = sorted(values)
  return {
  "median_us": statistics.median(values),
  "min_us": min(values),
  "max_us": max(values),
  "p25_us": ordered[len(ordered) // 4],
  "p75_us": ordered[3 * len(ordered) // 4],
  "samples_us": values,
  }


def sync():
  torch.mps.synchronize()


def matrix(n, batch, dtype, hermitian=False):
  gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1729 + n + batch)
  shape = (n, n) if batch == 1 else (batch, n, n)
  a = torch.randn(shape, dtype=dtype, generator=gen) / math.sqrt(n)
  if hermitian:
  a = (a + a.mH) / 2
  return a + 2 * torch.eye(n, dtype=dtype)


def operation(a, op):
  if op == "svd":
  return torch.linalg.svd(a, full_matrices=False)
  if op == "eigh":
  return torch.linalg.eigh(a)
  if op == "polar":
  return torch.linalg.polar(a)
  raise ValueError(op)


def make_fn(base, op, route, producer, backward=False):
  device = "cpu" if route == "cpu_only" else "mps"
  x = base.to(device).requires_grad_(backward)
  shift = torch.eye(base.shape[-1], dtype=base.dtype, device=device) * 0.0001
  target = torch.eye(base.shape[-1], dtype=base.dtype, device=device)

  def run():
  a = x + shift if producer else x
  if route == "cpu_roundtrip":
  parts = tuple(v.to("mps") for v in operation(a.cpu(), op))
  else:
  parts = operation(a, op)
  if backward:
  unitary = parts[0] @ parts[2] if op == "svd" else parts[0]
  loss = (unitary - target).abs().square().sum()
  return torch.autograd.grad(loss, x)[0]
  return parts

  return run


def measure_group(functions, rounds):
  # Warm every exact shape/path first. Interleave routes each round.
  for fn in functions.values():
  for _ in range(12):
  fn()
  sync()
  latency = {key: [] for key in functions}
  throughput = {key: [] for key in functions}
  count = {}
  for key, fn in functions.items():
  sync()
  start = time.perf_counter_ns()
  for _ in range(5):
  fn()
  sync()
  elapsed = (time.perf_counter_ns() - start) / 1e9 / 5
  count[key] = max(5, min(500, math.ceil(0.020 / elapsed)))
  rng = random.Random(91)
  gc.disable()
  try:
  for _ in range(rounds):
  order = list(functions)
  rng.shuffle(order)
  for key in order:
  fn = functions[key]
  for _ in range(5):
  sync()
  start = time.perf_counter_ns()
  fn()
  if key != "cpu_only":
  sync()
  latency[key].append((time.perf_counter_ns() - start) / 1000)
  sync()
  start = time.perf_counter_ns()
  for _ in range(count[key]):
  fn()
  if key != "cpu_only":
  sync()
  throughput[key].append((time.perf_counter_ns() - start) / 1000 / count[key])
  finally:
  gc.enable()
  return {
  key: {
  "latency": stats(latency[key]),
  "throughput": stats(throughput[key]),
  "calls_per_throughput_block": count[key],
  }
  for key in functions
  }


def validate(base, op):
  rows = {}
  for route in ("cpu_only", "mps_builtin", "cpu_roundtrip"):
  result = make_fn(base, op, route, False)()
  sync()
  parts = [part.detach().cpu() for part in result]
  if op == "svd":
  u, s, vh = parts
  reconstructed = (u * s.unsqueeze(-2)) @ vh
  values = s
  else:
  values, vectors = parts
  reconstructed = (vectors * values.unsqueeze(-2)) @ vectors.mH
  residual = float((reconstructed - base).norm() / base.norm())
  rows[route] = {"relative_reconstruction_residual": residual}
  if route == "cpu_only":
  reference = values
  else:
  spectrum_error = float((values - reference).norm() / reference.norm())
  rows[route]["relative_spectrum_error_vs_cpu"] = spectrum_error
  if not math.isfinite(spectrum_error) or spectrum_error > 1e-4:
  raise RuntimeError(f"Failed spectrum validation: {op} {route} error={spectrum_error}")
  if not math.isfinite(residual) or residual > 1e-4:
  raise RuntimeError(f"Failed correctness validation: {op} {route} residual={residual}")
  return rows


def metadata():
  return {
  "torch": torch.__version__,
  "torch_git": torch.version.git_version,
  "python": sys.version,
  "platform": platform.platform(),
  "hardware": subprocess.check_output(["sysctl", "-n", "machdep.cpu.brand_string"], text=True).strip(),
  "cpu_threads": torch.get_num_threads(),
  "interop_threads": torch.get_num_interop_threads(),
  "environment": {key: os.environ[key] for key in ("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS", "MKL_NUM_THREADS", "PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK", "PYTORCH_MPS_FAST_MATH", "PYTORCH_MPS_PREFER_METAL") if key in os.environ},
  "torch_build": torch.__config__.show(),
  "timing": "perf_counter_ns; warm 12 calls/path; randomized path order per round; 5 separately synchronized calls/round; throughput 5..500 calls/block targeting 20ms, synchronized before/after; no thread overrides; default eager execution; resident input or explicit pending input x+1e-4*I; CPU-only timing excludes MPS sync; GPU pre-sync occurs before clock starts",
  "roundtrip": "public Python equivalent of CPU decomposition with input .cpu() and every output .to('mps'); not exact historical C++ fallback overhead",
  }


def profile():
  from torch.profiler import ProfilerActivity, profile as torch_profile
  rows = []
  for op, n, batch in (("svd", 4, 1), ("svd", 32, 12), ("eigh", 4, 1), ("eigh", 4, 767), ("eigh", 4, 768), ("eigh", 32, 11), ("eigh", 32, 12)):
  for dtype in (torch.float32, torch.complex64):
  fn = make_fn(matrix(n, batch, dtype, op == "eigh"), op, "mps_builtin", False)
  fn()
  sync()
  with torch_profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU], record_shapes=True) as prof:
  fn()
  sync()
  key = f"{op}-{str(dtype).split('.')[-1]}-{n}-{batch}"
  prof.export_chrome_trace(str(OUT / f"trace-{torch.__version__}-{key}.json"))
  events = [{"name": e.key, "count": e.count} for e in prof.key_averages() if "linalg" in e.key or e.key in ("aten::to", "aten::_to_copy", "aten::copy_")]
  rows.append({"case": key, "events": events})
  print(json.dumps(rows[-1]), flush=True)
  (OUT / f"profile-{torch.__version__}.json").write_text(json.dumps({"metadata": metadata(), "cases": rows}, indent=2))


def main():
  parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
  parser.add_argument("--profile", action="store_true")
  parser.add_argument("--rounds", type=int, default=7)
  parser.add_argument("--quick", action="store_true")
  parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path)
  args = parser.parse_args()
  if args.profile:
  return profile()
  path = args.output or OUT / f"results-{torch.__version__}.json"
  result = {"metadata": metadata(), "rounds": args.rounds, "cases": []}
  # At n=4,16,32, eigh changes routes at B=768,48,12 respectively.
  shapes = [(4, 1), (4, 16), (4, 256), (4, 767), (4, 768), (4, 769), (16, 1), (16, 16), (16, 47), (16, 48), (16, 49), (32, 1), (32, 4), (32, 11), (32, 12), (32, 13)]
  if args.quick:
  shapes = [(4, 1), (16, 1), (32, 1), (32, 11), (32, 12), (32, 13)]
  for op in ("svd", "eigh"):
  for dtype in (torch.float32, torch.complex64):
  for n, batch in shapes:
  base = matrix(n, batch, dtype, op == "eigh")
  # Both input states for single matrices; pending state for batches.
  for producer in ((False, True) if batch == 1 else (True,)):
  case = {"op": op, "dtype": str(dtype), "n": n, "batch": batch, "pending_producer": producer, "backward": False, "mps_route_by_2_15_source": "internal_cpu" if op == "eigh" and batch*n*n < 12288 else "native_gpu", "validation": validate(base, op)}
  functions = {route: make_fn(base, op, route, producer) for route in ("cpu_only", "mps_builtin", "cpu_roundtrip")}
  case["timings"] = measure_group(functions, args.rounds)
  result["cases"].append(case)
  path.write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
  print(json.dumps({k: v for k, v in case.items() if k not in ("validation", "timings")} | {"latency_us": {k: round(v["latency"]["median_us"], 2) for k, v in case["timings"].items()}, "throughput_us": {k: round(v["throughput"]["median_us"], 2) for k, v in case["timings"].items()}}), flush=True)
  for op in ("svd", "polar"):
  for dtype in (torch.float32, torch.complex64):
  for n, batch in ((4, 1), (16, 1), (32, 1)):
  base = matrix(n, batch, dtype)
  functions = {route: make_fn(base, op, route, True, backward=True) for route in ("cpu_only", "mps_builtin", "cpu_roundtrip")}
  # Check gradient equivalence at generic full-rank inputs, away from repeated spectrum.
  gradients = {key: fn().detach().cpu() for key, fn in functions.items()}
  errors = {key: float((value-gradients["cpu_only"]).norm()/gradients["cpu_only"].norm()) for key,value in gradients.items()}
  if not all(math.isfinite(v) and v < 1e-3 for v in errors.values()):
  raise RuntimeError(f"Gradient mismatch {op} {dtype} {n}: {errors}")
  case = {"op": op, "dtype": str(dtype), "n": n, "batch": batch, "pending_producer": True, "backward": True, "gradient_relative_error_vs_cpu": errors, "timings": measure_group(functions, args.rounds)}
  result["cases"].append(case)
  path.write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
  print(json.dumps({k: v for k, v in case.items() if k != "timings"} | {"latency_us": {k: round(v["latency"]["median_us"], 2) for k, v in case["timings"].items()}, "throughput_us": {k: round(v["throughput"]["median_us"], 2) for k, v in case["timings"].items()}}), flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
  main()
```

### 🐛 Describe the bug

When computing gradients for torch.logit(x, eps=...) on CPU with an eps value provided, NaN values in the input tensor x produce a gradient of 0.0 instead of NaN. This is inconsistent with the same operation on CUDA, which returns NaN gradients for NaN inputs.

title: MPS: conv2d silently returns uninitialized memory when batch > 65536 (2.11 through main)
body:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

`F.conv2d` on MPS **silently returns uninitialized memory** for most of the output when the batch dimension exceeds 65536 (2^16). There is no error, no warning, no NaN in fp32: the affected output region is simply never written by the kernel, so it reads as zeros on freshly allocated buffers and as stale allocator contents otherwise. In `half`/`bfloat16` the affected region contains NaN/Inf.

Measured boundary on M4 / macOS 27.2 (pip wheels):

- `kernel=3, stride=2` and `kernel=1, stride=1`: batch ≤ 65536 correct; **batch ≥ 65537 → every output element with batch index ≥ 65536 is never written**.
- `kernel=3, stride=1`: **batch = 65536 → the entire output is never written**; batch ≥ 65537 → only the first `N mod 65536` samples are written, the remaining 65536 are not (verified with an identity-coding probe; e.g. at N=66000 exactly samples 0..463 are computed correctly, 464..65999 are untouched).

`conv1d` had the same failure through 2.14.1 and was fixed in 2.15.0 by the new conv1d Metal kernels. The 4-D conv2d path still routes to `MPSGraphConvolution2DOp` and still fails on 2.15.0 and on main.

This is a nasty silent-corruption bug for real workloads: any large-batch training/eval step or large inference batch on Apple Silicon gets plausible-looking garbage with no signal.

## Code snippet

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
N = 66000  # 2^16 + 464
x = torch.randn(N, 32, 8, 8)
w = torch.randn(64, 32, 3, 3) * 0.1

ref = F.conv2d(x, w, stride=2)
out = F.conv2d(x.to("mps"), w.to("mps"), stride=2).cpu()

d = (out - ref).abs()
print(d[:65536].max().item())  # ~9e-06  (clean)
print(d[65536:].max().item())  # ~9.4  (garbage; should be ~1e-05)

# Proof that the affected outputs are never written:
buf = torch.full((N, 64, 3, 3), 777.0, device="mps")  # warm the MPS allocator
del buf
torch.mps.synchronize()
out2 = F.conv2d(x.to("mps"), w.to("mps"), stride=2).cpu()
print((out2[65536:] == 777.0).all())  # True on 2.15.0 and main
```

The "never written" claim comes from the sentinel above (267,264/267,264 elements exactly 777.0 on 2.15.0) and from an identity-coding probe (input coded `x[n,c,h,w] = 1000 + n + c/100`, single one-hot weight tap, large per-channel bias): each output decodes to the (sample, channel) that produced it, and every affected output decodes as "no contribution at all".

## Error messages

None — that is the problem. For comparison, on macOS < 15.1 there is a `TORCH_CHECK_NOT_IMPLEMENTED` guard for *output channels* > 2^16 in the same function; the batch dimension has no guard.

## Versions measured (M4, macOS 27.2, python 3.14, pip wheels / nightly index)

| torch  | conv1d, N > 65536 | conv2d, N > 65536 |
|---------------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| 2.11.0  | broken  | broken  |
| 2.12.1  | broken  | broken  |
| 2.13.0  | broken  | broken  |
| 2.14.1  | broken  | broken  |
| 2.15.0  | fixed  | **broken**  |
| 2.16.0.dev20261030 (main) | fixed  | **broken**  |

Not affected (all verified on 2.15.0 at the same sizes): plain `mm`/`bmm` with M/B > 65536, and `F.conv3d` with D = 1 up to N = 131073. PyTorch's own Metal conv kernels (`conv3d_mpp` / `conv3d_simd`, int64 addressing) are fine at these batch sizes; the failure is specific to the `MPSGraphConvolution2DOp` path that 4-D convs take.

## Diagnosis

4-D convs reach `MPSGraphConvolution2DOp` in `_mps_convolution_impl` (`aten/src/ATen/native/mps/operations/Convolution.mm`). The new conv1d picker added for 2.15.0 in the same file already documents a sibling of this limitation for Apple's matrix ops:

```cpp
// matmul2d on M1/M2 misreads operands whose row stride exceeds this many elements.
constexpr int64_t kPreApple9MppMaxStride = std::numeric_limits<uint16_t>::max();
```

This looks like the same Apple-side 16-bit limitation family — on the batch/grid dimension instead of the row stride — and, unlike the row-stride case (guarded only for pre-Apple-9 GPUs), it **does** reproduce on M4.

## Suggested fix (validated locally)

In `_mps_convolution_impl`, when `input_t.dim() == 4 && input_t.size(0) > 65535`, route to `conv3d_metal_forward` via `unsqueeze(2)` — the same precedent the conv1d path already uses in that file. Measured correct on 2.15.0 for N up to 131073 (max diff ~1e-05 vs CPU). I'm happy to open a PR with a regression test if the approach sounds right.

## Workaround

Chunk the batch to ≤ 65535 samples per conv call.

title: [inductor] is_big_gpu() and get_max_num_sms() assume a CUDA device and raise on npu-only builds
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch/_inductor/utils.py:get_gpu_type()` returns `"cuda"` whenever no device in `GPU_TYPES` reports itself available:

```python
avail_gpus = [gpu for gpu in GPU_TYPES if _device_is_available(gpu)]

if not avail_gpus:
  return "cuda"
```

`is_big_gpu()` (no explicit device) and `get_max_num_sms()` both resolve the device through it, so on a torch build without CUDA they end up in `torch.cuda.*` and raise. NPU users run exactly that setup: the official CPU wheel plus torch_npu.

On Ascend 910B4 (torch 2.16.0.dev20261029+cpu, torch_npu master `32b8dec`):

```
GPU_TYPES: ['cuda', 'xpu', 'mtia', 'mps']
get_gpu_type() -> 'cuda'
is_big_gpu()  -> AssertionError: Torch not compiled with CUDA enabled
get_max_num_sms() -> AssertionError: Torch not compiled with CUDA enabled
```

The accelerator is there and fully usable — `torch.accelerator.current_accelerator(check_available=True)` reports `npu`, and `DeviceProperties.create(torch.device("npu", 0))` returns `multi_processor_count=40` — it just never lands in `GPU_TYPES`, because an out-of-tree backend does not necessarily claim `DeviceInterface.is_gpu()`.

Second, related problem: even when a caller passes the device explicitly, the SM heuristic is CUDA-flavoured:

```python
min_sms = min_sms_override
if min_sms is None:
  min_sms = 16 if device.type == "xpu" else 68  # 3080
avail_sms = prop.multi_processor_count
if avail_sms < min_sms:
  log.warning("Not enough SMs to use max_autotune_gemm mode", ...)
  return False
```

so `is_big_gpu(torch.device("npu", 0))` returns `False` for a 40-core Ascend part, and `max-autotune` stays disabled on npu until the harness overrides `config.max_autotune_gemm_min_sms` by hand. That override is precisely what a determinism suite on npu has to carry today:

```python
inductor_config.max_autotune_gemm_min_sms = 40  # 910B4 AI cores
```

### Suggested fix

- `get_gpu_type()`: when no GPU-type device is registered, fall back to `torch.accelerator.current_accelerator(check_available=True)` before `"cuda"`, so the helpers resolve the device that exists instead of crashing.
- `get_max_num_sms()`: read `multi_processor_count` through `DeviceProperties.create(...)` rather than `torch.cuda.get_device_properties("cuda")` (identical value on CUDA).
- `_is_big_gpu()`: keep the 68-SM default for CUDA and use the lower 16 bar for other accelerators (xpu already does), so devices that count cores differently are not rejected outright.

PR forthcoming.

### Versions

- PyTorch version: 2.16.0.dev20261029+cpu (commit 45f9fe1c9c9997a94cd6e2afd5b93920427b566b, nightly wheel; same code present on main @ 9933f275f857)
- CPU: aarch64 (Kunpeng), Linux
- GPU model and configuration: Ascend 910B4 x8 via torch_npu 2.16.0.dev20261029+git32b8dec (PrivateUse1)
- triton-ascend 3.6.0+git0cfb1708, CANN 9.2.0

title: [inductor] Dynamic-shape staged sub-parent epilogue plans split into two kernels or compute wrong values
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Staged sub-parent epilogue fusion (`NestedReduction.sub_parent_epilogue_plan`) does not produce a single fused kernel for dynamic-shape parents. On Ascend NPU (`triton_experimental` backend, NestedReduction is enabled for the device) 8 cases of the upstream `test/inductor/test_nested_reduction.py` fail — persistent and non-persistent variants of:

- `test_multi_op_prologue_and_epilogue`
- `test_pointwise_producer_standalone_sub_parent_epilogue[dynamic_axis0]`
- `test_pointwise_producer_standalone_sub_parent_epilogue[dynamic_axis_batch]`
- `test_pointwise_producer_standalone_sub_parent_epilogue[dynamic_axis_feature]`

Symptom:

```
E  AssertionError: Expected 1 but got 2.
  # metrics.codegen_nested_reduction
```

and for the `dynamic_axis_batch` / `dynamic_axis_feature` variants the result is also numerically wrong (relative/absolute difference) — i.e. the compile splits into two nested kernels and one of them computes a different value.

### Root cause

The plan is built from symbolic access relations. Three proof paths assume the reindexed access keeps a form the symbolic checker can simplify directly, and give up (return `None`) or return a non-affine form when the parent extent is a symbolic size:

1. **`MemoryDep.normalize_with_ranges`** cannot split `(4, s77)` into `(s77 // 16, 16)`; in other cases it "succeeds" with a result mixing `FloorDiv`/`ModularIndexing` over the *target* coordinates, which the downstream lane/equality proofs cannot relate to the split forms. The canonical affine reindex is the row-major ordinal `x * rnumel + r`; it is usable whenever the generic result is missing or non-affine, but generic normalization must still run first because it collapses size-1 axes (B=1 must stay collapsed).
2. **Multiple parent accesses to the same storage** in different symbolic forms (the displaced producer's ordinal write vs the reduction body's split read) currently return `None` from `_try_get_sub_parent_access_relations`. The equivalence needs integer facts on synthetic coordinate symbols, which `statically_known_equals` cannot decide; comparing affine coefficients (they only contain shape-env symbols) does.
3. **`SIMDKernel._split_iteration_ranges` / `add_range`** reject a divisible size when the divisor is itself a symbolic quotient (`s77 == 16 * (s77 // 16)` is guard-backed but not chained into `(4*s77) % (4*(s77//16)) == 0`). Proving the quotient instead of the multiple-of relation is sufficient.

In addition, a pointwise producer emitted **before the first reduction node** in the final parent order is a *displaced* producer: it runs inside the reduction loop and its output is not a live sub-parent source, so the epilogue must reload it instead of asking the value resolver to preserve a loop-local CSE value. Such a producer has to be ordered before the reduction body and exempted from the "leading node may not feed a final node" and "node1 must go before node2" gates, while the plan and the cross-domain proof still authorize the pair.

### Reproduce

```bash
source /usr/local/Ascend/ascend-toolkit/set_env.sh
export TORCH_NPU_USE_COMPATIBLE_IMPL=1 TORCHINDUCTOR_NPU_BACKEND=triton_experimental
export TORCHINDUCTOR_COORDINATE_DESCENT_TUNING=0 ASCEND_RT_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0
export TORCHINDUCTOR_WORKER_START=subprocess
cd /tmp
python -m pytest /home/zhoushaowen/nested_test/test_nested_reduction.py \
  -k "test_pointwise_producer_standalone_sub_parent_epilogue or test_multi_op_prologue_and_epilogue" \
  -q -o addopts= --rootdir=/tmp --tb=short
```

### Versions

| item | value |
|---|---|
| PyTorch | `2.16.0.dev20261007+cpu` (commit `7f758944`) |
| torch_npu | `2.16.0.dev20261007+git72b9c1a` (`triton_experimental` backend) |
| triton-ascend | `3.6.0+git0cfb1708` (CANN 9.2.0) |
| Device | Ascend 910B4, NPU-only (no CUDA) |
| Python | 3.12.13 |

The same plan/proof code is device neutral; the NPU backend is only where the non-linearized tile model exposes it.

title: [dynamo] `except` around `torch.linalg.inv` is not taken when the error comes from the data (singular matrix)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

A `try/except` that falls back from `torch.linalg.inv` to `torch.linalg.pinv` works in eager, but under `torch.compile` the `LinAlgError` for a singular input is raised out of the compiled function and the handler never runs.

```python
import torch


def f(x):
  try:
  return torch.linalg.inv(x)
  except RuntimeError:
  return torch.linalg.pinv(x)


x = torch.zeros(2, 2)
print(f(x))  # pinv result
print(torch.compile(f, backend="eager")(x))  # fails
```

Same with `except torch.linalg.LinAlgError`, and with `torch.linalg.cholesky` on a non positive-definite matrix. Errors that fake tensors can detect are handled correctly: for a non-square input (`torch.randn(2, 3)`) the compiled function takes the `except` branch.

```
  [0., 0.]])

  result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
```

title: [meta] `bool_tensor >> 1` works in eager but fails under `torch.compile`: "rshift: Expected input tensor to have an integral dtype"
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`t >> 1` and `t << 1` on a bool tensor work in eager (the result is promoted to int64), but fail under `torch.compile` during fake tensor propagation. `torch.bitwise_right_shift(t, 1)` compiles fine.

```python
import torch


def f(t):
  return t >> 1


t = torch.tensor([True, False])
print(f(t))  # tensor([0, 0])
print(torch.bitwise_right_shift(t, 1))  # tensor([0, 0])
print(torch.compile(torch.bitwise_right_shift, backend="eager")(t, 1))  # works
print(torch.compile(f, backend="eager")(t))  # fails
```

Possibly `shift_dtype_check` in the meta for `__rshift__` / `__lshift__` rejects `torch.bool`, while the eager kernel promotes it to `int64`.

### Error logs

```
tensor([0, 0])
tensor([0, 0])
tensor([0, 0])
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "repro.py", line 12, in <module>
  print(torch.compile(f, backend="eager")(t))  # fails
  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
[...]
  File ".../site-packages/torch/_dynamo/utils.py", line 4484, in _get_fake_value_impl
  raise FakeTensorObservedException(msg, real_stack=e.real_stack) from None
torch._dynamo.exc.TorchRuntimeError: RuntimeError when making fake tensor call
  Explanation: Dynamo failed to run FX node with fake tensors: call_function <built-in function rshift>(*(FakeTensor(..., size=(2,), dtype=torch.bool), 1), **{}): got RuntimeError('rshift: Expected input tensor to have an integral dtype. Got torch.bool')

from user code:
  File "repro.py", line 5, in f
  return t >> 1
  ~~^^~~
```

### Versions

title: [inductor] argmax_with_value combine emits a 1-bit ugt (ops.gt on i1) that non-CUDA Triton backends cannot lower
body:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.max(x, dim=0)` (NaN-propagation semantics) lowers through
`get_reduction_combine_fn` for `argmax_with_value` in
`torch/_inductor/ir.py`. The floating-point branch builds a NaN-aware
comparison over two `i1` (bool) operands:

```python
a_isnan = ops.ne(a, a)
b_isnan = ops.ne(b, b)
mask = ops.logical_or(mask, ops.gt(a_isnan, b_isnan))
```

`ops.gt(a_isnan, b_isnan)` emits a 1-bit `>` (`ugt`). CUDA's LLVM backend
lowers 1-bit `ugt` to `icmp`, so this is invisible on CUDA; but third-party
Triton backends (here triton-ascend, `bishengir-compile` / hfusion→HiVM) have
no `CompareFn` mapping for this mode, so every config — including the
small-block fallback — fails at MLIR compile time. This is a code-level issue
(the combine is emitted on bool operands with `>`), not a backend config or
autotune issue.

## Minimal repro

```python
import torch

def f(x):
  return torch.max(x, dim=0)

x = torch.randn(8, 8, device="cuda")
torch.compile(f)(x)
```

On CUDA this passes. Compiling the same graph for an out-of-tree Triton
backend without a 1-bit `ugt` lowering (e.g. Ascend NPU / PrivateUse1 +
triton-ascend) raises:

```text
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: RuntimeError: Failed to run autotuning code block: No valid triton configs. All configs failed compilation (including small-block fallback). Last error: MLIRCompilationError:
///------------------[ERROR][Triton][BEG]------------------
[ConvertLinalgIRToBinary] encounters error:
LLVM ERROR: mapCompareModeHFusionToHiVM: unsupported hfusion::CompareFn
PLEASE submit a bug report to <url> and include the crash backtrace.
Stack dump:
0.  Program arguments: /opt/ascend/cann-9.1.0/bin/bishengir-compile /tmp/tmpbbk46u8y/kernel.mlir --target=Ascend910B3 --enable-auto-multi-buffer=False --enable-auto-bind-sub-block=True --enable-auto-blockify-loop --enable-hfusion-compile=true --enable-hivm-compile=true --enable-triton-kernel-compile=true --mlir-print-ir-after-failure --mlir-print-stacktrace-on-diagnostic -o /tmp/tmpbbk46u8y/kernel
///------------------[ERROR][Triton][END]------------------
```

The offending comparison is the `>` on two `i1` operands (the NaN-aware
`ops.gt(a_isnan, b_isnan)` emitted by `get_reduction_combine_fn`); triton-ascend
has no `hfusion::CompareFn` mapping for a 1-bit compare.

## Expected behavior

The reduction combine should not emit a 1-bit `>` on bool operands; it should
use an equivalent boolean expression that any backend with `logical_and` /
`logical_not` can lower.

## Suggested fix

In `torch/_inductor/ir.py` `get_reduction_combine_fn`, replace the i1 `>` with
the equivalent 1-bit form (`a > b` on 1-bit values is `a & ~b`):

```python
mask = ops.logical_or(mask, ops.logical_and(a_isnan, ops.logical_not(b_isnan)))
```

`logical_and` / `logical_not` already exist on the upstream `OpsHandler` and
Triton handler, so this is backend-agnostic and numerically identical.

```python
  return t.real * 2


t = torch.randn(3).as_subclass(Sub)

print(torch.compile(f, backend="eager")(t))  # fails
```

Compiling a function whose input is `.real` (or `.imag`) of a complex wrapper subclass fails while fakifying the input. The same works for a plain complex tensor, and for the subclass itself.

```python

from torch.testing._internal.two_tensor import TwoTensor


def f(r):
  return r * 2


x = TwoTensor(torch.tensor([3 + 1j]), torch.tensor([5 + 2j]))
print(torch.compile(f, backend="eager")(x))  # works
```

title: [MPS] scaled_dot_product_attention raises NotImplementedError for dropout_p > 0 under torch.no_grad()
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


Python Snippet:
```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

q = torch.randn(2, 4, 8, 16, device="mps", requires_grad=True)
F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, q, q, dropout_p=0.1)  # works

with torch.no_grad():
  F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, q, q, dropout_p=0.1)  # raises
```

On MPS, the math backend sends calls that don't need grad to _scaled_dot_product_attention_math_for_mps ([attention.cpp#L896](<url>)), which rejects any dropout ([Attention.mm#L760](<url>)). That condition doesn't look at dropout_p. Calling torch.ops.aten._scaled_dot_product_attention_math directly on MPS under no_grad with dropout_p=0.5 works and applies dropout, so checking dropout_p == 0 in that condition would route these calls to the general path.

title: [dynamo] Unpacking a 0-dim tensor raises an internal AssertionError instead of TypeError, so `except TypeError` is skipped

### 🐛 Describe the bug

In eager, unpacking or iterating a 0-dim tensor raises `TypeError: iteration over a 0-d tensor`. Under `torch.compile`, Dynamo raises `AssertionError: Can't unpack scalar tensors.` instead, which escapes the user's `try/except` and fails compilation.

```python
import torch


def f(x):
  try:
  a, b = x
  except TypeError:
  return x * 2
  return a + b


x = torch.tensor(3.0)
print(f(x))  # tensor(6.)
print(torch.compile(f, backend="eager")(x))  # fails
```

The same happens with `except Exception`, with `list(x)`, and with `dict(t)` on a 1-d tensor (eager: `TypeError: cannot convert dictionary update sequence element #0 to a sequence`). Without `try/except`, the compiled function raises `AssertionError` where eager raises `TypeError`.

title: [inductor] pad_mm pass breaks on NPU builds: device whitelist rejects NPU, bf16 path queries torch.cuda without CUDA
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

The pad_mm shape-padding family (`torch/_inductor/fx_passes/pad_mm.py`) is unusable on NPU builds (torch_npu / PrivateUse1):

1. **Device whitelist**: `check_device()` only accepts cuda/xpu tensors, so the pass never fires on NPU.

2. **Hard crash without CUDA**: `is_mm_compute_bound()`'s bf16 special case queries `torch.cuda.get_device_capability()`:

```python
if (
  dtype is torch.bfloat16
  and K > M
  and K > N
  and (torch.xpu.is_available() or torch.cuda.get_device_capability() < (9, 0))
):  # doesn't repro on h100s:
  return True
```

On a torch build without CUDA (e.g. the official CPU wheel used together with torch_npu, which is how NPU users run inductor), `torch.cuda.get_device_capability()` raises `AssertionError: Torch not compiled with CUDA enabled`, and the whole compilation fails with `BackendCompilerFailed`. Only bfloat16 mms with `K > M and K > N` enter this branch, so float16/float32/amp never expose it — but every `*training_bfloat16*` variant of a 24-variant run2run determinism suite (3 HF models × training/inference × 4 precisions) fails with `fail_to_run`.

Full traceback (Ascend 910B4, CANN 9.2.0, torch 2.16.0.dev20261029+cpu, torch_npu 2.16.0.dev20261029+git32b8dec):

```
File ".../torch/_inductor/compile_fx.py", line 763, in _recursive_joint_graph_passes
  out_gm = joint_graph_passes(gm, input_device)
File ".../torch/_inductor/fx_passes/joint_graph.py", line 853, in joint_graph_passes
  ).apply_graph_pass(patterns.apply)
File ".../torch/_inductor/pattern_matcher.py", line 2880, in apply
  if is_match(m) and guard_or_false(entry.extra_check(m)):
File ".../torch/_inductor/fx_passes/pad_mm.py", line 832, in should_pad_mm
  return should_pad(match, mat1, mat2, torch.ops.aten.mm)
File ".../torch/_inductor/fx_passes/pad_mm.py", line 559, in _should_pad
  if not is_mm_compute_bound(m_concrete, k_concrete, n_concrete, mat1.dtype):
File ".../torch/_inductor/fx_passes/pad_mm.py", line 305, in is_mm_compute_bound
  and (torch.xpu.is_available() or torch.cuda.get_device_capability() < (9, 0))

AssertionError: Torch not compiled with CUDA enabled
```

### Suggested fix

- `check_device`: accept NPU tensors (mirror the xpu treatment);
- `is_mm_compute_bound`: skip the bf16 special case on NPU — Ascend 910B-series is bf16-native, the same family the "doesn't repro on h100s" (cap >= 9.0) comment targets — and fall through to the machine_balance estimate.

PR forthcoming.

title: [Inductor] Ensure consistent device selection in CppWrapperGpu
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

When integrating an out-of-tree accelerator backend with Inductor's C++ wrapper, we subclass `CppWrapperGpu`. However, `CppWrapperGpu.__init__()` unconditionally sets `self.device` using `get_gpu_type()`, overwriting any device type explicitly selected by the subclass.

Notably, `CppWrapperGpu` inherits from `CppWrapperCpu`, whose initializer already preserves an existing `self.device` and defaults to `"cpu"` only when it is not set. This allows `CppWrapperGpu` to specify its device before reusing the parent's initialization, but the same pattern cannot be used by subclasses of `CppWrapperGpu`.

We would like the C++ wrapper to consistently honor the selected target device throughout initialization and subsequent code generation, while preserving the existing default behavior.

This would allow out-of-tree backends to reuse the complete parent initialization through `super().__init__()` without duplicating internal initialization logic that may change across PyTorch versions.

### Alternatives

We considered inheriting directly from `CppWrapperCpu`, but the backend relies on GPU-specific kernel invocation and code generation logic provided by `CppWrapperGpu`, as well as its initialization.

### Additional context

The backend registers its own C++ wrapper through `register_backend_for_device`. This example illustrates the **current limitation**, not the calling convention of a proposed API. It assumes the NPU runtime, device overrides, and active graph-lowering context have already been initialized:

```python
class NpuCppWrapper(CppWrapperGpu):
  def __init__(self):
  self.device = "npu"
  super().__init__()
```

The GPU initializer replaces the subclass's selected device with `get_gpu_type()`. This matters when global detection differs from the intended target; it does not imply that every invocation fails. The request is to let a registered device wrapper complete its parent initialization while consistently using its selected target. It does not require preserving this exact preset-attribute calling pattern as the eventual interface.

In addition to the constructor, `DeferredTritonCallWrapper._generate_lazy_scratch()` also uses `get_gpu_type()` to determine the scratch allocation device. This can cause the generated allocation device to differ from the wrapper's selected device. The intended behavior is to consistently use the selected target device throughout wrapper initialization and code generation.

In a local, host-side code generation test using a prototype with explicit XPU selection, lazy scratch still emitted a CUDA allocation when global detection returned CUDA. This demonstrates a device-selection inconsistency in generated code; end-to-end device execution has not yet been validated.

Source at `888a0a8f05f7`:

- [`GraphLowering.init_wrapper_code`](<url>) selects the registered wrapper using the graph's device type.
- [`CppWrapperGpu.__init__`](<url>) uses global detection before selecting codegen overrides.
- [`CppWrapperCpu.__init__`](<url>) preserves an existing `self.device`.
- [`DeferredTritonCallWrapper._generate_lazy_scratch`](<url>) performs global detection again for scratch allocation.

title: @torch.autocast decorator leaks autocast state across overlapping calls
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Bug Description (minimal examples generated by ChatGPT)

Hello there! I ran into this issue when a main thread and a sidecar thread could both call the same function decorated with `@torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)`. It seems that the autocast state in the main thread could be changed by calls from the sidecar thread.

After looking into it, I think the problem is that the decorator reuses the same `autocast` instance across calls. Its `__enter__` and `__exit__` methods store and restore the previous autocast state through instance attributes, which can be overwritten by another call.

The issue can be reproduced on CPU:

```python
import threading
import torch

@torch.autocast("cpu", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
def f():
  if threading.current_thread() is threading.main_thread():
  worker = threading.Thread(target=f)
  worker.start()
  worker.join()

with torch.autocast("cpu", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
  print("Before:", torch.is_autocast_enabled("cpu"))
  f()
  print("After: ", torch.is_autocast_enabled("cpu"))
```

In my expectation, the main thread is still inside the outer autocast context, so its autocast state should remain enabled, and the output should be
```text
Before: True
After:  True
```
But in fact, the output is
```text
Before: True
After:  False
```

It turns out this issue can be reproduced using a single thread. Recursively calling the same decorated function also causes state leakage:

```python
import torch

@torch.autocast("cpu", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
def f(n):
  if n > 0:
  f(n - 1)

print("Before:", torch.is_autocast_enabled("cpu"))
f(1)
print("After: ", torch.is_autocast_enabled("cpu"))
```

Output:

```text
Before: False
After:  True
```

Expected:

```text
Before: False
After:  False
```

### Likely cause (Analysis assisted by ChatGPT)

In `torch/amp/autocast_mode.py`, `autocast_decorator` uses:

```python
def decorate_autocast(*args, **kwargs):
  with autocast_instance:
  return func(*args, **kwargs)
```

The same `autocast_instance` is reused for every invocation of the decorated function.

Meanwhile, `autocast.__enter__` saves the previous thread-local state into instance attributes such as `self.prev`, `self.prev_fastdtype`, and `self.prev_cache_enabled`. These attributes are then read by `__exit__` to restore the state.

When two invocations overlap, the second `__enter__` overwrites the values saved by the first. The first invocation can then restore the wrong state when it exits.

Using a fresh `with torch.autocast(...)` context inside the function avoids this issue.

title: index_select / index_add_ CUDA kernels truncate int64 indices before the bounds assert (silent wrong rows)
body:
### Description

Three CUDA kernels in aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Indexing.cu load an int64 index as `IndexType` (`unsigned int`, the 32-bit offset type) *before* their bounds assert, so indices in `[2**32, 2**32 + dim_size)` truncate to a small in-range value and the assert never fires:

```cpp
IndexType dstIndex = indices.data[...];
CUDA_KERNEL_ASSERT(dstIndex < dstAddDimSize);
```

- `indexSelectSmallIndex` (used by `index_select` for <= 3072 indices, and through advanced indexing `tensor[idx]`): silently returns the wrapped row.
- `indexFuncSmallIndex` / `indexFuncLargeIndex` (the legacy path for `index_add_` when alpha != 1, complex/bool dtypes, dim != 0, or CUDA < 12.8 builds, and for `index_reduce_` ops other than amin/amax on half/bfloat16): silently accumulates into the wrapped row.

Negative indices are rejected only because their low 32 bits wrap to huge values; an assert placed after the truncation can never catch the wrap.

For `index_select` the large-index path (> 3072 indices) dispatches to `gather`, whose kernel validates the full int64 value — so the same index either asserts or silently corrupts depending on how many indices are passed. CPU raises `IndexError` for all of these.

### Repro

```python
import torch

src = torch.arange(30, device="cuda").reshape(10, 3)
idx = torch.tensor([2**32 + 3, 2**32], device="cuda")
print(torch.index_select(src, 0, idx))
# tensor([[ 9., 10., 11.],  <- row 3, wrapped silently
#  [ 0.,  1.,  2.]])  <- row 0, wrapped silently
# CPU: IndexError: index out of range in self

x = torch.zeros(10, device="cuda")
x.index_add_(0, torch.tensor([2**32 + 7], device="cuda"), torch.ones(1, device="cuda"), alpha=2)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(torch.nonzero(x).flatten().tolist())
# [7]  <- silently accumulated into row 7; alpha=2 forces the indexFunc path
```

### Expected behavior

The assert should check the original index value before the narrowing cast, as the `gather` kernel already does.

### Versions

torch 2.16.0a0+git4df2ac4, CUDA 12.8, RTX 4060 Ti (sm_89)

## Agent details

An AI assistant (Claude Code) wrote the text of this issue; the bug, repro, and analysis were driven and verified by cainiao33 on a local CUDA 12.8 build.

title: embedding_dense_backward on CUDA silently corrupts grad_weight or hits an IMA for out-of-range indices
body:
### Description

`embedding_dense_backward` on CUDA does not validate the index tensor. With out-of-range int64 indices it either silently corrupts a valid row or triggers an illegal memory access, depending on the number of indices:

- **n <= 3072 without `scale_grad_by_freq`** (`embedding_backward_feature_kernel`, `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Embedding.cu`): the kernel stages indices in shared memory as `int`, narrowing each int64 value. An index of `2**32 + 3` narrows to `3`, passes the (nonexistent) bounds check, and its gradient is silently accumulated into row 3 of `grad_weight`.
- **n > 3072 or `scale_grad_by_freq=True`** (the sorted path, `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/EmbeddingBackwardKernel.cu`): `sum_and_scatter` and `compute_grad_weight_atomic_accumulate` write `grad_weight[target_row * stride + f]` with no bounds check, so the same index computes an address tens of GB out of bounds and produces an illegal memory access.

CPU by comparison silently skips out-of-range indices in the default path (a side effect of the chunked accumulation; its `scale_grad_by_freq` path additionally indexes `counts[indices[i]]` out of bounds on the heap).

### Repro

```python
import torch

num_weights, D = 10, 3

# silent wrong write: n <= 3072 and no scale_grad_by_freq
indices = torch.zeros(4, dtype=torch.int64, device="cuda")
indices[1] = 2**32 + 3
grad = torch.randn(4, D, device="cuda")
grad_weight = torch.ops.aten.embedding_dense_backward(grad, indices, num_weights, -1, False)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(grad_weight[3])  # nonzero: the gradient meant for the invalid index landed on row 3

# illegal memory access: n > 3072, or scale_grad_by_freq=True with any n
indices = torch.zeros(4096, dtype=torch.int64, device="cuda")
indices[1] = 2**32 + 3
grad = torch.randn(4096, D, device="cuda")
grad_weight = torch.ops.aten.embedding_dense_backward(grad, indices, num_weights, -1, False)
torch.cuda.synchronize()  # CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered
```

### Expected behavior

The backward kernels should raise a device-side assertion for out-of-range indices, as `_embedding_bag_per_sample_weights_backward_kernel` already does (#192445), instead of corrupting memory or writing wrong results.

### Versions

torch 2.16.0a0+git4df2ac4, CUDA 12.8, RTX 4060 Ti (sm_89)

## Agent details

An AI assistant (Claude Code) wrote the text of this issue; the bug, repro, and analysis were driven and verified by cainiao33 on a local CUDA 12.8 build.

title: [inductor][cpp_wrapper] Generated C++ wrapper build time regression on gcc 15
body:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.compile(inductor, cpp_wrapper=True)` produces a single generated C++ wrapper file. Compiling that file takes **~9x longer with GCC 15.2 than with GCC 11.4** — 17:07 vs 1:53 for the wrapper of `Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B` int4 weight-only (1024→128 tokens, batch 1). GCC 15 spend 94% of the compile in `dominator optimization`; GCC 11/12/13 are unaffected.

## Reproducer

```bash
# gcc 11
TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=./cache-gcc11 CXX=/usr/bin/g++-11 CC=/usr/bin/gcc-11 python repro.py
# gcc 15
TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=./cache-gcc15 CXX=/usr/bin/g++-15 CC=/usr/bin/gcc-15 python repro.py
```

Each run regenerates the identical `main.cpp` (both runs produce the same cpp wrapper) and compiles it with the chosen compiler. The wrapper compile wall is the `main.cpp` → `main.so` mtime gap inside the cache:

```python
# repro.py
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from torchao.quantization.quant_api import quantize_, Int4WeightOnlyConfig
from torchao.quantization.quantize_.workflows.int4.int4_packing_format import (
  Int4PackingFormat,
)
from torch._functorch._aot_autograd.subclass_parametrization import (
  unwrap_tensor_subclass_parameters,
)

torch._inductor.config.cpp_wrapper = True

MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B"
INPUT_TOKENS = 1024
MAX_NEW_TOKENS = 128

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
  MODEL_ID, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda"
)
quantize_(
  model,
  Int4WeightOnlyConfig(int4_packing_format=Int4PackingFormat.TILE_PACKED_TO_4D),
)
unwrap_tensor_subclass_parameters(model)
model.forward = torch.compile(model.forward)

ids = tok("The capital of France is", return_tensors="pt").input_ids
ids = ids[:, :1].repeat(1, INPUT_TOKENS)
inputs = {"input_ids": ids.to("cuda"), "attention_mask": torch.ones_like(ids).to("cuda")}
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=MAX_NEW_TOKENS, use_cache=True,
  do_sample=False)
```

| compiler | wrapper compile time (s) | E2E `python repro.py` |
|---|---|---|
| gcc 11.4.0 | 112.79 (1:53) | 11:16.85 |
| gcc 15.2.0 | 982.86 (16:23) | 25:08.72 |
| **ratio** | **8.71x** | |

(compile wall = `main.cpp`→`main.so` mtime gap inside each `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR`; the same wrapper content is compiled in both runs. These in-process numbers match the standalone g++ compile times of the attached wrapper, 1:53 vs 17:07.)

title: [ROCm][MI200] `linear_cross_entropy` FP16 backward recomputation uses alternate GEMM path, causing test failures
body:
## Summary

Three FP16 `linear_cross_entropy` tests consistently fail on MI200 (gfx90a) with reduction='none' and accumulation policies `auto`, `balanced`, and `compact`.

My investigation suggests that the failures are caused by forward-logit re-computation during backward inheriting the ROCm backward-only FP16 alternate GEMM behavior.

## Root Cause Analysis

In the `reduction='none'` backward path, `linear_cross_entropy` recomputes the forward logits while `ROCmBackwardPassGuard` is active.

Consequently, the re-computation GEMM is treated as a backward GEMM and uses `rocblas_gemm_flags_fp16_alt_impl`, producing slightly different numerical results from the original forward computation.

These differences propagate to the weight gradient, causing the tests to exceed the 3 * eps tolerance.

## Validation

Disabling the alternate FP16 implementation:

  `ROCBLAS_INTERNAL_FP16_ALT_IMPL=0`

makes all three failing tests pass.

This suggests that the failures are associated with PyTorch's use of the alternate FP16 GEMM path during forward-logit re-computation, rather than an incorrect `rocBLAS` or `hipBLASLt` kernel.

## Expected Behavior

Forward-logit re-computation during backward should maintain numerical consistency with the original forward computation, or otherwise satisfy the expected gradient accuracy.

Could the PyTorch maintainers advise whether this re-computation should bypass `ROCmBackwardPassGuard` or whether another fix would be more appropriate?

## References

* Detailed investigation: <url>

title: [dynamo] After `t.numel()` on a `__torch_function__` subclass, every later `t.<attr>` evaluates to the numel
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

For a `__torch_function__` subclass that defines `__init__`, constructed inside the compiled function and passed through `F.linear`, every attribute or method of the result accessed after `t.numel()` returns the numel. There is no error, so code that branches on `t.is_complex()` / `t.dim()` silently takes the wrong branch.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


class Sub(torch.Tensor):
  def __init__(self, data):
  super().__init__()

  @classmethod
  def __torch_function__(cls, func, types, args=(), kwargs=None):
  return super().__torch_function__(func, types, args, kwargs or {})


W = torch.randn(3, 4)


def f(x):
  t = F.linear(Sub(x), W)
  return t.numel(), t.dtype, t.dim(), t.is_complex()


x = torch.randn(2, 4)
print(f(x))  # (6, torch.float32, 2, False)
print(torch.compile(f, backend="eager")(x))  # (6, 6, 6, 6)
```

It is the same with `nn.Linear` and `t @ W.T`. It does not happen without `__init__` on the subclass, with `x.as_subclass(Sub)` instead of `Sub(x)`, with `torch.relu` / `t + 1` instead of `F.linear`, or when `t.dim()` / `t.is_complex()` is called before `t.numel()`. Calling the methods through `getattr(t, "numel")()` also gives the right values.

title: [nested] as_nested_tensor(layout=torch.jagged) picks the ragged dim from the data; equal-length inputs silently get dim 1
body:
AI assistance was used to draft this text. I checked the facts below against the linked sources and the public wheel contents.

### Description

`torch.nested.as_nested_tensor(tensors, layout=torch.jagged)` chooses the ragged dimension from the input shapes. In `torch/nested/_internal/nested_tensor.py` the ragged index is taken from the first dimension in which the tensors differ and falls back to 1 when none differ. There is no argument to choose it (`torch.nested.nested_tensor_from_jagged` does have `jagged_dim`). For a list of equal-shaped `(C, L)` tensors the result therefore has the component axis as the ragged one, while the same data with unequal `L` has the length axis as the ragged one.

### Reproduction (CPU)

```python
import torch
C = 4
for lens in ([5, 7, 9], [7, 7, 7], [7]):
  nt = torch.nested.as_nested_tensor(
  [torch.arange(C * l).reshape(C, l) for l in lens], layout=torch.jagged
  )
  print(lens, tuple(nt.shape), nt._ragged_idx, tuple(nt.values().shape), nt.offsets().tolist())
```

Output on torch 2.13.0:

```
[5, 7, 9] (3, 4, j1) 2 (4, 21) [0, 5, 12, 21]
[7, 7, 7] (3, j2, 7) 1 (12, 7) [0, 4, 8, 12]
[7]  (1, j3, 7) 1 (4, 7)  [0, 4]
```

Downstream code that assumes the length axis is ragged and relabels `_ragged_idx = 2` then fails on the second and third layouts (for example, verl issue #7899 with multi-component position ids).

### Request

Either document the inference rule in `as_nested_tensor`, or accept an explicit jagged dimension so callers with equal-length batches can state it. I searched open and closed issues for this and found none.

### Versions

torch 2.13.0, CPU, Python 3.12, macOS.

title: [ROCm] varlen_attn with an explicit causal window (-1, 0) aligns the mask top-left when seqlen_q != seqlen_k
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On ROCm, an explicit causal window `(-1, 0)` in `varlen_attn` (and in `_flash_attention_forward` / `_flash_attention_backward`) aligns the causal mask to the **top left** when `seqlen_q != seqlen_k`. CUDA FlashAttention, and the ROCm `is_causal` path without a window, align it to the **bottom right**. KV-cache decoding hits this directly: one query against N cached keys sees only the first key, so generation turns to garbage after the first token.

Repro:

```python
import torch
from torch.nn.attention.varlen import varlen_attn

torch.manual_seed(0)
dev, dt = "cuda", torch.bfloat16
h, d, k_len = 8, 128, 64
q = torch.randn(1, h, d, device=dev, dtype=dt)  # one decode query
k = torch.randn(k_len, h, d, device=dev, dtype=dt)
v = torch.randn(k_len, h, d, device=dev, dtype=dt)
cu_q = torch.tensor([0, 1], device=dev, dtype=torch.int32)
cu_k = torch.tensor([0, k_len], device=dev, dtype=torch.int32)

out = varlen_attn(q, k, v, cu_q, cu_k, 1, k_len, window_size=(-1, 0))

# bottom-right causal: the single query attends to all k_len keys
p = torch.softmax(torch.einsum("qhd,khd->hqk", q.float(), k.float()) * d**-0.5, -1)
ref = torch.einsum("hqk,khd->qhd", p, v.float())
print("max abs diff vs bottom-right causal:", (out.float() - ref).abs().max().item())
```

On MI350X with PyTorch 2.12.0+rocm10.0.0 this prints `max abs diff vs bottom-right causal: 3.71`; a bottom-right causal mask would leave only bf16 rounding differences.

The cause is `calculate_swa()` in `aten/src/ATen/native/transformers/hip/flash_attn/aot/mha_all_aot.hip`: it replaces the bottom-right sentinels with the raw explicit window, and AOTriton measures numeric windows from the top-left diagonal.

Found through vLLM's ROCm CI: the HF reference for `domyn/Domyn-Edge-Base`, whose remote code decodes through `varlen_attn`, produces nonsense on MI355 while the same model with `use_cache=False` is correct.

Fix proposed in #201930.

### Versions

PyTorch 2.12.0+rocm10.0.0 (also reproduced on a source build of main), ROCm 10.0, MI350X (gfx950).
