title: [ROCm][kineto] Wait for in-flight kernel dispatch records when stopping
body:
## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Fixes #200903
Fixes #200382
Fixes #200246
Fixes #200383
Fixes #200401
Fixes #199891
Fixes #199893

Supported by @jeffdaily

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

The torch.profiler for ROCm was sometimes missing GPU kernel events because it wasn't waiting for them to arrive when stopping profiling.

## Agent details (if applicable)

My agent came up with this analysis, but I've read and approved it.

**Problem.** Short `torch.profiler` sessions on ROCm often come back with no GPU kernel events. This is what fails the copy-dispatch tests in `test_torch.py` (the DISABLED issues above), and it also hits CUDA-graph replays. Root cause and reproducer: ROCm/TheRock#9008.

**Cause.** rocprofiler-sdk writes the KERNEL_DISPATCH buffer record from its HSA completion handler, which can run after `hipDeviceSynchronize()` has returned. `RocprofLogger::stopLogging()` flushed once without waiting, so the record arrived in the next session's flush and was dropped there as out of range. rocprofiler-sdk 1.4.2 makes this much more frequent (ROCm/rocm-systems#14378), but it also happens with 1.4.1 under load.

**Change.** A KERNEL_DISPATCH callback tracing service (ENQUEUE operation) records the `dispatch_id` of every kernel dispatched while the session is active, including each kernel of a graph launch and runtime-internal blits; `buffer_callback` removes it when the dispatch record arrives. `stopLogging()` re-flushes every 50 us until none are pending, bounded by the new kineto config key `ROCPROF_DISPATCH_RECORD_WAIT_MSECS` (default 20; 0 restores the old behaviour), and warns how many records it gave up on (for the first 10 stops in a process). The bound matters because a kernel still running at stop never yields a usable record: its end time is past the session window, and if its record arrives during the next session it is dropped there as before. The pending set is cleared at `startLogging()`. pytorch/kineto#1564's drain-until-stable approach was not used: it adds at least 30 ms to every stop.

**Test plan.** gfx90a (MI250X), ROCm 10.1, A/B on one build via the config key. Misses of 64 profiled sessions, three runs each; the copy sessions run inside `test_torch.py`'s own harness, and the graph sessions replay a 5-kernel `torch.cuda.CUDAGraph` under the same load:

| rocprofiler-sdk | copy tests, wait=20 | copy tests, wait=0 | graph replay, wait=20 | graph replay, wait=0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.4.1 | 0, 0, 0 | 7, 10, 9 | 0, 0, 0 | 6, 9, 5 |
| 1.4.2 | 0, 0, 0 | 21, 19, 16 | 0, 0, 0 | 8, 9, 6 |

- `python test/test_torch.py -k test_copy_strided_chunk -k test_copy_transpose_tiled -k test_zero_strided_emits_fill_kernel -k test_zero_dense`: passes 3/3. These copy-dispatch tests, re-enabled when the DISABLED issues above close, are the regression tests for the race.
- Stop and enqueue cost, compared with the unpatched build: no measurable difference (stop median about 0.2 ms, `g.replay()` + sync about 0.064 ms either way).
- Kernel still running at stop: stop returns at the cap (about 20.5 ms), one warning, next session records normally.
- Sessions that capture a CUDA graph do not wait (nothing is dispatched during capture): stop 0.2 to 0.4 ms, no warning.
- gfx1100 (W7800): the race did not reproduce there even with wait=0, so it shows no regression only: 64/64 graph-replay sessions with all 5 kernels, same stop cost, cap holds.

title: [Opsmate Oncall Operator] Run test_conv_bias_no_extra_cast_for_fp32 with TF32 off
body:
Summary:
<url>
Please use Accept, not Accept and Ship: after you accept, Oncall Operator's auto-lander attempts the land. Shipping it yourself can make you the commit's pusher, and Phabricator won't let a pusher close its post-land owner review.

---

## The issue
- `test_conv_bias_no_extra_cast_for_fp32` (added in D127808162, pytorch#201713) compares compiled vs eager fp32 conv grads at atol/rtol=1e-5 but leaves cuDNN TF32 on (the default). On some GPUs the TF32 conv backward differs between the two runs by ~1e-3, so the test fails on A100 MIG slices (14 SMs, cc=80) in the mixed `gpu-remote-execution` pool and passes on full GPUs. That is why the same revision both passes and fails in TestX (T295767744).
- Measured on the same MIG worker in one process: TF32 on gives an x-grad max diff of 9.124e-04 (the exact TestX failure value) and a w-grad max diff of 1.708e-03; TF32 off gives 1.907e-06 and 7.629e-06. Forward output diff is 3.8e-06 either way. This is cuDNN conv precision, not an Inductor lowering bug: both runs call the aten conv, and the x-grad strides are identical.

## The fix
- Decorate the test with `with_tf32_off`, the existing `common_cuda` helper for tests that use convs but are not testing conv precision. The test still checks fp32 numerics against eager and that no `.to(tl.bfloat16/float16)` cast is emitted. The fbcode and xplat copies are kept identical.
- Alternatives not taken: loosening the tolerance would weaken the fp32 "unchanged numerics" check, and pinning the target to `A100-exclusive` (`TESTS_WITHOUT_MIG`) would move the whole `cuda_repro` suite off MIG to hide a precision mode issue.

Test Plan:
## How we tested
- Before (unmodified test, GPU RE, worker reported `DeviceProperties(multi_processor_count=14, cc=80)`): FAIL, 563/98304 mismatched, greatest abs diff 9.124e-04, matching TestX. <url>
- Diagnostic plus fix (same 14-SM MIG slice): TF32 on x-grad diff 9.124e-04, TF32 off 1.907e-06; the decorated test PASSED. <url>
- After (final patch, 14-SM MIG slice): `buck2 test fbcode//mode/opt fbcode//caffe2/test/inductor:cuda_repro -- --regex test_conv_bias --print-passing-details --env TORCH_LOGS=output_code`: 16/16 `test_conv_bias*` PASS. <url>

title: [Inductor] Lower aten._to_dtype_rounded
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #202755
* #202754
* #202753
* #202752

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

<!-- TODO -->

## BC-breaking?

<!-- TODO -->

## Summary (human written only)

<!-- TODO -->

## Agent details

_Written by Claude Code (AI assistant)._

Inductor now generates code for `Tensor.to(..., round=...)` instead of falling back to the eager kernel, so the conversion fuses with surrounding ops.

- The lowering emits a new ops-handler method, `ops.to_dtype_rounded(x, dtype, src_dtype, rounding)`, rather than extending `ops.to_dtype`, so existing `to_dtype` call sites, CSE keys and the C++ backend's dtype-convert cache stay untouched.
- Triton on CUDA uses the same instructions as the eager kernel, as inline PTX, since Triton's own conversions can differ (e.g. libdevice honors Inductor's flush-to-zero mode). As in eager, the directed float8 modes round to nearest and correct the result; since the mode is known at codegen time, each kernel only contains its own mode's logic.
- Elsewhere (ROCm, XPU, older GPUs, e8m0 `to_nearest_even`), Triton uses `triton_helpers.round_float32_to_bits`, a port of `c10::convert_with_rounding`.
- The C++ backend calls `c10::convert_with_rounding` (now included in `cpp_prefix.h`). These kernels are not vectorized, because `CppVecKernel`'s scalar fallback assumes equal input and output vector widths.
- Other backends, float8 dtypes Triton cannot store, and float64 sources on non-CUDA Triton fall back to eager. float8_e8m0fnu outputs are allowed for this op in `unsupported_input_tensor`.

### Test plan

`test/inductor/test_rounded_conversion.py` checks bitwise equality of compiled and eager results for every dtype pair and mode on CPU and CUDA, asserts on the emitted instructions, checks that an MX-style e8m0 scale + float8 quantization graph compiles without fallbacks, and runs the Triton software helper directly against eager. For float8_e4m3fn and float8_e5m2, compiled and eager were also compared on every float32 input in all modes (ad hoc). On a GB200:

```
python -m pytest test/inductor/test_rounded_conversion.py -n 16
python -m pytest test/test_rounded_conversion.py test/inductor/test_fp8.py -n 24 -k "e8m0 or E8M0 or rounded or Rounded"
python -m pytest test/inductor/test_op_completeness.py
python -m pytest test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py test/inductor/test_cpu_repro.py -n 32 -k "to_dtype or convert or dtype_conv or float8 or fp8 or bfloat16 or half"
```

All pass except `test_index_propagation_to_dtype_inf_cpu`, which also fails without this change on this aarch64 machine.

title: Use CUDA conversion instructions for Tensor.to(..., round=...)
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* #202755
* __->__ #202754
* #202753
* #202752

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

<!-- TODO -->

## BC-breaking?

<!-- TODO -->

## Summary (human written only)

<!-- TODO -->

## Agent details

_Written by Claude Code (AI assistant)._

The CUDA kernel of `_to_dtype_rounded` now uses hardware conversions where they exist, and `c10::convert_with_rounding` otherwise (and on ROCm):

| Conversion | Hardware path |
|---|---|
| float → float16 | `__float2half_r{n,z,u,d}` (`cvt.r*.f16.f32`) |
| float → bfloat16 | `__float2bfloat16_r{n,z,u,d}` (`cvt.rn/rz.bf16.f32` from sm_80, `cvt.rp/rm` from sm_90) |
| float → e4m3fn / e5m2 | `__nv_fp8_e4m3` / `__nv_fp8_e5m2` (`cvt.rn.satfinite.*x2.f32`) from sm_89 |
| float → e8m0fnu | `__nv_cvt_float_to_e8m0(..., __NV_NOSAT, ...)` (`cvt.rz/rp.ue8m0x2.f32`) on sm_100a and similar |
| double → float / float16 | `__double2float_r*` / `cvt.r*.f16.f64` |
| double → bfloat16 | `cvt.r*.bf16.f64` from sm_90 |
| other double sources | round to odd into float in PTX, then the float paths |

Notes:
- The float8 instruction only rounds to nearest, saturating. For e5m2, overflow to infinity is fixed up afterwards; `__NV_NOSAT` would do that itself, but it is a ~2x slower software emulation (see #177870). The directed modes decode the rounded result (also in hardware) and step it by one encoding toward x when it is on the wrong side, without branches; for e5m2 that step overflows to infinity by itself.
- float → e4m3fn with `to_nearest_even` is a single `F2FP.SATFINITE.E4M3.F32` per element, and runs at copy bandwidth (7.4 TB/s on GB200).
- Round to odd is exact enough because float has more than two extra bits and covers the range of every narrower dtype. float16/bfloat16 sources widen to float exactly.
- The e8m0 instructions only exist for arch-specific targets, so `RoundedConversion.cu` is also built for `100a;103a;110a;120a;121a` via `_BUILD_FOR_ADDITIONAL_ARCHS`.
- The mode stays a runtime argument: as a template parameter it only sped up the directed float8 modes by a further ~17%, and made the object 2.7x larger.

### Test plan

The oracle tests now exercise the hardware paths, and a new slow test compares the device with the CPU on every float32 input for float16, bfloat16, float8_e4m3fn, float8_e5m2 and float8_e8m0fnu in all four modes. SASS was checked with `cuobjdump` for sm_80, sm_89, sm_90 and sm_100a. On a GB200 (sm_100, CUDA 12.8):

```
python -m pytest test/test_rounded_conversion.py -n 16
PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_SLOW=1 python -m pytest test/test_rounded_conversion.py -k test_exhaustive_float32
```

title: Add round= to Tensor.to for narrowing float conversions
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* #202755
* #202754
* __->__ #202753
* #202752

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

<!-- TODO -->

## BC-breaking?

<!-- TODO -->

## Summary (human written only)

<!-- TODO -->

## Agent details

_Written by Claude Code (AI assistant)._

`x.to(dtype, round=...)` selects the IEEE 754 rounding direction of a conversion to a narrower floating-point dtype: `"to_nearest_even"`, `"toward_zero"`, `"toward_positive"` or `"toward_negative"`. It is allowed only from float64/float32/float16/bfloat16 to a dtype that cannot represent every source value (float32, float16, bfloat16, float8), and raises otherwise. The motivating case is float32 → float8_e8m0fnu rounded up, for MX scales.

Semantics (documented in `Tensor.to`, implemented by `c10::convert_with_rounding` from the previous commit):
- The exact value is rounded once, including for float64 sources, so `"to_nearest_even"` matches the default conversion.
- On overflow, results rounded toward zero become the largest finite value; the others become infinity or, for dtypes without infinity, what the default conversion produces (saturation for e4m3fn, NaN for fnuz and e8m0).
- e8m0 rounds the magnitude, clamps to 2^-127 below it, and rounds nearest-even ties up. This matches PTX `cvt.rz/rp.ue8m0x2.f32` (non-satfinite).

Implementation:
- The four `to.*` overloads gain a trailing kwarg-only `str? round=None`, backed by a new op `_to_dtype_rounded(Tensor self, ScalarType dtype, str round, *, MemoryFormat? memory_format=None)`. Its out variant is the TensorIterator kernel (CPU, CUDA, Meta); the functional variant allocates like `_to_copy` (shared helper) and calls it, so changing the memory format costs no extra kernel. Device changes compose with `_to_copy`, rounding on the accelerator.
- A new op rather than a new `_to_copy` argument: out-of-tree `_to_copy` kernels would break, and Python handlers on `aten._to_copy` (nested, DTensor, subclasses, ...) would silently drop the argument. A separate op fails loudly instead.
- Plumbing: Python parsing (through `parse_to_conversion`, like `copy` and `memory_format`; `nn.Module.to` rejects `round`), autograd (identity gradient), vmap, refs, stubs, docs, Dynamo trace rules.
- TorchScript consumers of the `to.*` schemas: static runtime, NNC (refuses a non-None `round`), shape registries, and the TorchScript ONNX exporter (exports `to_nearest_even`, rejects the directed modes).

The new `to.*` schemas pass `is_backward_compatible_with` and `check_forward_compatible_with` against the old ones.

### Test plan

`test/test_rounded_conversion.py` compares every mode on CPU and CUDA with the oracle from the previous commit, and covers errors, overloads, memory formats, autograd, meta/FakeTensor, vmap, `torch.compile`, export, TorchScript and cross-device calls. NNC fusion and TorchScript ONNX export were checked ad hoc.

```

python -m pytest test/test_decomp.py -k HasDecomp
python -m pytest test/dynamo/test_trace_rules.py test/test_overrides.py -n 16
python -m pytest test/jit/test_symbolic_shape_analysis.py test/test_static_runtime.py -n 16
python -m pytest test/test_ops.py test/test_fake_tensor.py test/test_legacy_vmap.py -n 24 -k "_refs_to or _refs__to or test_to or to_copy or _to_ or .to_"
python -m pytest test/export/test_export.py test/test_torch.py test/test_tensor_creation_ops.py -n 24 -k "to_ or _to or test_to"
```

All pass except two distributed export tests, because this build has `USE_DISTRIBUTED=0`.

title: Add c10::convert_with_rounding and fix two narrowing-conversion rounding bugs
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* #202755
* #202754
* #202753
* __->__ #202752

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

<!-- TODO -->

## BC-breaking?

<!-- TODO -->

## Summary (human written only)

<!-- TODO -->

## Agent details

_Written by Claude Code (AI assistant)._

`c10/util/FloatRounding.h` adds `c10::convert_with_rounding<Dst>(x, mode)`: it converts a float or double to float32, float16, bfloat16 or any float8 dtype with an explicit IEEE 754 rounding direction (to nearest even, toward zero, toward positive, toward negative). It is header-only integer arithmetic, so it runs on host and device and handles the non-IEEE float8 formats. Formats are described by their `std::numeric_limits`, plus one policy trait, `detail::Saturates` (true only for float8_e4m3fn). It defines the semantics of the upcoming `Tensor.to(..., round=...)`.

This commit uses its round-to-nearest-even mode to fix two bugs in the default conversions:
- float64 → float16/bfloat16/float8 rounded twice, through float32: e.g. `1 + 2**-11 + 2**-40` became `1.0` in float16 instead of `1 + 2**-10`. The CPU and CUDA copy kernels (`Tensor.to`, `copy_`) now convert these pairs directly. Other casts through `c10::convert` (Scalar, TensorIterator dynamic casts) still round twice, as the TODO in `TypeCast.h` notes.
- float32 → float8_e8m0fnu rounded subnormals in (2^-127, 1.5·2^-127) up to 2^-126 instead of to the nearer 2^-127. Fixed in `fp8e8m0fnu_from_fp32_value`; the emulation in `test_float8_e8m0fnu_rne_rounding` encoded the old behavior.

Both change results only for inputs that were rounded incorrectly. Single-threaded CPU float64 → float16 becomes ~1.3x slower (110 vs ~85 ms per 16M elements on Grace); CUDA is memory-bound and unchanged.

Also, the float8 `numeric_limits` specializations now declare `has_denorm` as a `std::float_denorm_style`, like float, Half and BFloat16, instead of a `bool`.

### Test plan

`test/test_rounded_conversion.py` checks the default conversions from every float source to every narrower float dtype, on CPU and CUDA, against an independent oracle built from a table of the destination's values: all float16/bfloat16 inputs; for float32/float64, every destination value, midpoint and their neighbors, plus random and special values. The old double-rounding path fails it (~190k mismatches for float64 → float16). The helper was also checked standalone against an oracle on ~1e9 inputs in all four modes, against the legacy converters on all 2^32 float32 inputs, under UBSan, and on device vs host.

```
python -m pytest test/test_rounded_conversion.py -n 16
python -m pytest test/quantization/core/experimental/test_floatx.py -n 16
python -m pytest test/test_torch.py test/test_type_promotion.py test/test_tensor_creation_ops.py test/test_type_info.py -n 32 -k "finfo or copy or _to or to_ or half or float8 or bfloat16 or cast"
python -m pytest test/test_ops.py test/test_unary_ufuncs.py -n 32 -k "_refs_to or _refs__to or to_copy or e8m0 or float8 or test_to"
python -m pytest test/inductor/test_fp8.py -n 16 -k e8m0
```

title: [inductor] Resolve the accelerator in the SM-count helpers instead of assuming CUDA
body:
`get_gpu_type()` returns `"cuda"` when no GPU-type device is registered, so on a torch build without CUDA (the CPU wheel plus torch_npu is how NPU users run inductor) both `is_big_gpu()` and `get_max_num_sms()` raise `AssertionError: Torch not compiled with CUDA enabled` even though a fully usable accelerator is present. The npu backend is registered and `torch.accelerator` reports it, it just never shows up in `GPU_TYPES` because out-of-tree backends need not claim `DeviceInterface.is_gpu()`.

This change makes the three helpers device-agnostic:

- `get_gpu_type()`: fall back to `torch.accelerator.current_accelerator(check_available=True)` before `"cuda"`;
- `get_max_num_sms()`: read `multi_processor_count` via `DeviceProperties.create(...)` instead of `torch.cuda.get_device_properties("cuda")`;
- `_is_big_gpu()`: keep 68 SMs as the CUDA default and use the lower 16 bar for the other accelerators (xpu already did), so a 40-core Ascend part is not classified as "Not enough SMs to use max_autotune_gemm mode".

With this, max-autotune works on npu without the test harness hand-setting `config.max_autotune_gemm_min_sms`.

Fixes #202740

### Validation

Ascend 910B4, CANN 9.2.0, triton-ascend 3.6.0, torch 2.16.0.dev20261029+cpu + torch_npu master `32b8dec`:

| call | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `get_gpu_type()` | `'cuda'` | `'npu'` |
| `get_max_num_sms()` | `AssertionError` | `40` |
| `is_big_gpu()` | `AssertionError` | `True` |

- `test/inductor/test_deterministic.py::DeterministicTest.test_max_autotune_deterministic_False`: `Ran 1 test in 25.089s — OK` on npu **without** the harness override of `config.max_autotune_gemm_min_sms` (max-autotune really runs: `AUTOTUNE ... 7 choices`, counters asserted).
- CUDA behaviour is unchanged by construction (`get_gpu_type()` still resolves `"cuda"` when it is the only available entry in `GPU_TYPES`; `DeviceProperties.create` reports the same `multi_processor_count`; `min_sms` stays 68). This machine has no CUDA device, so the CUDA path itself was not exercised.

title: [inductor] support dynamic-shape staged sub-parent epilogue fusion
body:
Fixes #202736.

Stacked on #201737: that PR's scheduler hunk (demote the live-source requirement for the producers that run before the first reduction node) is included here unchanged, because this fix builds on it and the stack should apply cleanly. If #201737 lands first, that hunk drops out on rebase — please review the rest.

Staged sub-parent epilogue plans are built from symbolic access relations. Three proof paths assumed the reindexed access keeps a form the checker can simplify directly, and either gave up or returned a form the lane/equality proofs could not relate when the parent extent is a symbolic size:

| area | change |
|---|---|
| `scheduler.py` — `normalized_source_accesses` | if `normalize_with_ranges` returns `None`, or a result that is not affine in the target coordinates (`FloorDiv`/`ModularIndexing` over the target vars), fall back to the row-major ordinal reindex `x * rnumel + r`. Generic normalization still runs first so size-1 axes stay collapsed (B=1). |
| `scheduler.py` — `_try_get_sub_parent_access_relations` | a source may be reached by multiple parent accesses in different symbolic forms (the displaced producer's ordinal write vs the reduction body's split read). Select the split form independent of node order and prove equality by comparing affine coefficients — they only contain shape-env symbols, so `statically_known_equals` decides them; also retry the lane proof after expanding `ModularIndexing(u, 1, B) = u - B * FloorDiv(u, B)`. |
| `scheduler.py` — `_pointwise_node_matches_domain` / `_sub_parent_access_preserves_x_boundary` / `deps_match_normalized` | total-element-equality and flat-cover fallbacks: when the flat element counts match, the node covers the parent domain exactly once, so the symbolic split proof (which cannot divide `(s77, 512)` into `(s77 * 32, 16)`) is not required. |
| `scheduler.py` — ordering/fusion gates | a pointwise producer emitted before the first reduction node is a *displaced* producer: it runs inside the reduction loop, so its output is not a live sub-parent source and the epilogue reloads it. Order it before the reduction body, exempt it from the "leading node may not feed a final node" and "node1 must go before node2" gates, and add the staged-group channels (reverse pair + Path 5 + displaced frame read) that the existing plan/proof authorize. |
| `codegen/simd.py` — `_split_iteration_ranges` / `add_range` / `fits_in_main_body` | prove the quotient when the divisor is itself a symbolic quotient (`s77 == 16 * (s77 // 16)` is guard-backed but not chained into a multiple-of check); compare dynamic shapes with `statically_known_equals` instead of `==`. |
| `choices.py` — `can_fuse` / `can_fuse_horizontal` | a staged sub-parent fusion carries its producer into the kernel, so "no shared data" / low memory score is not a valid rejection signal when the backend returns a sub-parent epilogue plan. |

Graphs without a displaced producer are unchanged: the displaced set is empty, source relations pass through untouched, and the ordinal fallback only triggers when generic normalization is missing or non-affine.

### Test plan

Ascend 910B4 (NPU-only, no CUDA), CANN 9.2.0, torch `2.16.0.dev20261007+cpu`, torch_npu `2.16.0.dev20261007+git72b9c1a`, triton-ascend `3.6.0+git0cfb1708`:

```bash
export TORCH_NPU_USE_COMPATIBLE_IMPL=1 TORCHINDUCTOR_NPU_BACKEND=triton_experimental
export TORCHINDUCTOR_COORDINATE_DESCENT_TUNING=0 TORCHINDUCTOR_WORKER_START=subprocess
cd /tmp
python -m pytest /home/zhoushaowen/nested_test/test_nested_reduction.py \
  -k "test_pointwise_producer_standalone_sub_parent_epilogue or test_multi_op_prologue_and_epilogue" \
  -q -o addopts= --rootdir=/tmp
```

| | result |
|---|---|
| before | 8 failed: `Expected 1 but got 2` (`metrics.codegen_nested_reduction`) + numeric mismatch on `dynamic_axis_batch/feature` |
| after | 14-item subset (the 8 + B=1 regression guards + dynamic bonus) **14 passed** in 376.90s |
| full file | **364 passed / 58 failed / 8 skipped**; remaining failures are CUDA-only inline asm (24), the backend's persistent-reduction capability gap (16), AOTI (2), backend gaps (4) and fusion-decision differences (10) |

body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):

* #202737
* #201754

CPU, CUDA and MPS each spelled out the same adaptive average pooling checks by hand, and the copies had drifted: only the 2D CPU backward and MPS backward checked the input rank and the `grad_input` dtype, 2D CUDA forward never checked the `out` dtype, and the 3D CUDA forward accepted a 1-element `output_size` it then indexed out of bounds. Behavior changes are limited to error paths, except that the non-empty check now covers only the pooled dims for 3D as it already did for 2D (matching the meta functions and decompositions), so a 5D input with zero channels returns an empty output instead of raising; both CPU and CUDA 3D kernels already early-out or loop zero times on empty outputs. Error messages are now prefixed with the op name consistently, and the regexes used by OpInfo error inputs still match.

## BC-breaking?

No.

## Summary (human written only)

When integrating an out-of-tree accelerator backend with Inductor's C++ wrapper, we subclass `CppWrapperGpu`. However, `CppWrapperGpu.__init__()` unconditionally sets `self.device` using `get_gpu_type()`, overwriting any device type explicitly selected by the subclass.

title: [inductor] Support NPU tensors in pad_mm device gates
body:
The pad_mm shape-padding family is unusable on NPU builds:

- `check_device()` whitelists only cuda/xpu, so NPU tensors are always rejected and the pass never fires;
- `is_mm_compute_bound()`'s bf16 special case queries `torch.cuda.get_device_capability()`, which raises `AssertionError: Torch not compiled with CUDA enabled` on torch builds without CUDA (e.g. a CPU-only wheel used together with torch_npu), failing compilation outright on every bfloat16 K-dominant mm in training graphs.

This PR treats NPU like the existing device families:

- `check_device` accepts NPU tensors (mirroring the xpu treatment);
- `is_mm_compute_bound` skips the bf16 special case on NPU — Ascend 910B-series is bf16-native, the same family the `doesn't repro on h100s` comment targets — and falls through to the machine_balance estimate.

title: Fix KeyError in collect_env when xpu-smi lists GPUs without device_name
body:
## Summary

`get_intel_gpu_onboard()` in `torch/utils/collect_env.py` indexed every entry of `xpu-smi discovery -j`'s `device_list` with `device["device_name"]`. The surrounding `except (ValueError, TypeError)` was written for JSON decode failures and does not catch `KeyError`, so a single entry without a `device_name` aborted `get_pretty_env_info()` — which is the entire body of `test/test_utils.py::TestCollectEnv::test_smoke`.

Under xpu-smi 1.x this never triggered because the tool filtered `device_list` by `ZE_AFFINITY_MASK` and only returned fully-described, visible GPUs. xpu-smi 2.x enumerates all onboard GPUs regardless of the mask and reports each masked one as `{"device_id": N, "device_state": "survivability mode", ...}` with no `device_name`. Intel GPU CI pins one GPU per test worker via `ZE_AFFINITY_MASK`, so env collection crashes there.

The fix reads `device_name` with a `device_state` fallback (and a final `"N/A"`), so a masked device still occupies one line in the report instead of raising, keeping the device count honest.

Fixes intel/torch-xpu-ops#5944

## Test Plan

```bash
python test/test_utils.py -k TestCollectEnv
ZE_AFFINITY_MASK=0 python test/test_utils.py -k TestCollectEnv.test_smoke
```

A new regression test (`test_intel_gpu_onboard_without_device_name`) uses a mocked `run_lambda`, since the real failure requires a multi-GPU host plus xpu-smi 2.x.

title: [Inductor][AOTI] Build template host-side TMA descriptors in the C++ wrapper, including dynamic sizes
body:
Summary:
X-link: <url>

Template kernels mark their host-side TMA operands in `host_tma_descriptor_args`; the Python launchers build those descriptors, and D128252177 lets them read dynamic sizes (a symbolic M such as `ks0`) at launch. The C++ wrapper (AOTInductor's) never could: a template's TMA operand reaches the kernel's call wrapper as its tensor, but the wrapper expected a `StableTMADescriptor`, which only user-defined kernels pass. So the TLX Hopper templates turned host-side TMA off under `cpp_wrapper`, and under AOTI every TLX GEMM built its descriptors on the device, costing every CTA a descriptor write and fence before its first load (1.1-2.1 us per kernel under a dynamic M, per D128252177).

- `cpp_wrapper_gpu.py`: for each template TMA formal, the call wrapper takes the tensor (`<name>_tma_tensor_`) and builds the `StableTMADescriptor` from it: the address from the tensor, the shape and strides from the template's descriptor dims, which are ints or integer expressions over the kernel's args (`ks0` is already a parameter of the wrapper), read at launch. The existing initializer then encodes the CUtensorMap from Triton's final metadata, and the launch unpacks it as before. The descriptor helpers are emitted with the first such wrapper, since call wrappers are generated after the header. `HOST_TMA_TEMPLATE_DESCRIPTORS = True` lets templates detect the support.
- `triton_heuristics.py`: the compile step rewrites a host-side TMA operand's signature to `tensordesc<>`, but `save_gpu_kernel` stored the pre-compile `triton_meta`, so the C++ wrapper launched pointers into a kernel compiled for descriptors ("CUDA driver error: invalid argument"). The launcher now keeps the compiled signature, and the saved `triton_meta` takes its `tensordesc<>` rewrites.
- TLX `registry.py`: under `cpp_wrapper`, the Hopper templates use host-side TMA (static and dynamic dims) when the C++ wrapper supports it and kernels are autotuned at compile time (AOTI's default). The lazy-compile wrapper still cannot take a template's host-side descriptor, so there both operands stay device-side.

The lazy-compile path (`autotune_at_compile_time=False`) is unchanged.

Test Plan:
On H100 (fbcode//caffe2/test/inductor/fb/tlx:test_templates, triton beta):
- New `TestHopperMMTemplate.test_dynamic_m_cpp_wrapper` (WS and small-K templates x mm/addmm x compile-time/lazy autotune): with compile-time autotune, the generated C++ builds A's descriptor with `global_shape[0] = ks0` and neither descriptor is built on the device; outputs match at M = 706 and then M = 300 through the same compiled code. With lazy compile, both stay device-side.
- `-r 'TestHopperMMTemplate.*test_dynamic_m'`: 12 tests OK.
- `-r 'TestHopperMMTemplate|cpp_wrapper'`: 81 tests OK.
- arc lint clean.

title: [Inductor] Prevent input mutation from buffer reuse across cond branches
body:
## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Fixes #202514

## BC-breaking?

No.

## Summary (human written only)

Compiling `torch.cond`/`torch.switch` with an identity-like branch (`t + 0.0`,
`t - 0.0`, `t * 1.0`, `t / 1.0`) silently overwrote one of the caller's input
tensors. See #202514 for the reproducer and the generated code.

Root cause: Inductor folds the identity branch back to its operand, so the
branch's graph output is that operand's `InputBuffer` and the cond output
aliases the input's storage. `GraphLowering` only turns an output back into a
copy when an input was *mutated*, not for this pure-identity case, so nothing
marks the output non-reusable and a later pointwise op reuses that buffer in
place. Eager/`aot_eager` are unaffected because there the identity body is a
real op returning a fresh tensor (and `cond` forbids a branch output aliasing an
input).

The fix copies any branch output that aliases an operand in `Switch.create`
(the same `ExternKernel.copy_input` de-aliasing `WhileLoop._clone_aliased_inputs`
already uses), so each cond/switch output owns its storage. Only identity-like
outputs pay a copy; ordinary branches, `t.clone()`, and the non-taken branch are
unchanged.

## Checklist

- [ ] Passes lint (`spin fixlint`) — not run in the author's local environment; relying on CI lint.
- [x] Added/updated tests — `test/inductor/test_control_flow.py`.
- [ ] Updated documentation — not applicable.
- [ ] Included benchmark results — not applicable (a copy is added only for the rare identity-branch case).

## Agent details (if applicable)

This PR was prepared with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic), an AI coding
assistant, and is opened as a **draft pending the author's review**.

How it was validated (by the AI assistant, reported for transparency):

- On a CPU nightly wheel (`torch 2.16.0.dev20261029`) with the fix applied to

title: [MTIA][Inductor] Add runtime bridge and C++ support preamble for JIT wrappers
body:
Summary:
> Part 2 of 4 splitting the MTIA JIT C++ wrapper launch path; see [D125061388](<url>) for the end-to-end wrapper codegen.

This diff adds what a generated MTIA C++ wrapper needs to compile and link against the runtime, without generating any kernel calls yet.

- **Real header, no copy.** The runtime header `inductor_runtime.h` ships with the Python package. `get_inductor_runtime_compile_flags()` copies it into the Inductor cache under a content-based name and passes it as `-include <header>`, so generated code uses the real structs and function declarations. This also works for fbcode remote compiles, which only see files passed on the command line.
- **Link target.** `inductor_runtime_bridge` is a small extension that generated wrappers link against. Generated code calls the `torch_inductor_mtia_*` functions directly. In link-grouped binaries a runtime function is visible to the wrapper only when a linked module references it (`link_whole` does not change this), so the bridge keeps a `[[gnu::used, gnu::retain]]` table of every entry point. `test_every_runtime_function_resolves_in_generated_wrapper` reads every exported function from the header and fails if one is missing from that table.
- **Support code.** `MTIACppWrapperCodeGen._write_mtia_runtime_support` emits helpers: status checking, checked integer narrowing, current-stream lookup, and an `MTIAInductorKernel` that loads a fatbin file. A generated wrapper checks `TORCH_INDUCTOR_MTIA_RUNTIME_ABI_VERSION` from the header against the loaded runtime before creating its first kernel, so a wrapper replayed from the Inductor cache against a newer runtime fails clearly instead of misreading data.
- **Device guard.** The MTIA `DeviceOpOverrides` map the AOTI device/stream guards to `MTIAInductorDeviceGuard` and the ATen device type to `at::kMTIA`; `write_header` defines `MTIAInductorDeviceGuard` for every MTIA wrapper, so graphs that emit a device guard without a Triton launch still compile.

body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #202707
* #201769
* #201768
* #201767
* #201766

Split out of #201766 on review: this is observability for the pre-existing
runtime-failure path and is independent of nearest match and borrowed
recording.

A tuned solution that fails at runtime returns a non-OK status from `Call()`;
every caller -- gemm, bgemm, gemm-and-bias and scaled gemm -- already reads that
as "use my own non-tunable path", so the failure surfaces as a caller-side
fallback to default rather than an error. Behaviour is unchanged: this adds a
`TUNABLE_LOG2` line and returns the same status as before. Without it the
fallback is silent and the failing candidate is never named.

The signatures are hoisted out of the resolve block because TUNABLE_LOG
evaluates its arguments before checking the level, so the log reuses them rather
than recomputing them. They stay empty while TunableOp is disabled, which is
what the `!op_sig.empty()` guard tests: there is no resolved solution to name.

Level 2, like the other per-call messages in the same function -- a solution
that keeps failing would otherwise log on every GEMM at verbosity 1.

The failure is deliberately not cached: unlike a borrow, a tuned entry that
fails is a real defect and should stay visible rather than be masked after the
first call. There is no retry on Default either, since every caller already
falls back, so retrying here would duplicate that and hide which candidate
failed.

title: [Checkpoint] Preserve device RNG state for keyword tensor inputs
body:
## Summary

Fixes #202549.

Non-reentrant checkpoint forwards kwargs to the checkpointed function, but only traverses args when inferring the device type and saving device RNG states. Consequently, CUDA tensors passed only through kwargs can be omitted from RNG preservation. For a function such as `x * torch.rand_like(x)`, backward then recomputes with different random values and produces incorrect gradients.

Pass `(args, kwargs)` to both `_infer_device_type` and `get_device_states`, so their existing pytree traversal also includes nested keyword inputs. Updating device inference alone is insufficient: the corresponding device IDs and RNG states must also be collected.

The reentrant path and existing CPU RNG and device-type selection behavior are unchanged.

## Test plan

Built main at `888a0a8f05f7` with this patch and tested on 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs with CUDA 12.9:

```bash
pip install -e . -v --no-build-isolation
python test/test_utils.py -k TestCheckpoint -v
```

- Build succeeded; 38 tests passed and 4 CPU instances of accelerator-only tests were skipped.
- Added regression coverage for positional, keyword-only, mixed, nested, and multi-device inputs, with `preserve_rng_state` both enabled and disabled.
- On the original implementation, keyword-only inputs produced incorrect gradients and advanced CUDA RNG during backward on all 8 GPUs. With the fix, all 24 comparison cases passed.
- The keyword-only regression test fails without the fix and passes with it.

title: [AOTI] Check constant dtypes
body:
## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Fixes #202017

## BC-breaking?

No. Stricter validation of inputs that were already undefined behaviour. A tensor whose dtype differs from the exported constant's dtype (including same-byte-size reinterpretations such as int32 values for an fp32 constant) is now rejected instead of being treated as raw bytes.

## Summary (human written only)

`update_constant_buffer` validated that a constant was present and on the expected device type. The copy path memcpy'd the caller's storage size into the blob slot and rebuilt the tensor with the exported dtype, so a bf16 tensor supplied for an fp32 constant gave silently wrong outputs (the issue's 0.5 outputs), and a larger dtype would copy past the slot.

This adds a dtype comparison (`aoti_torch_get_dtype` against `model.constant_dtype`) in the existing validation loop, before any allocation or copy, so it covers the active, inactive, user-managed and from-CPU update paths. The error names the constant and both dtype codes, in the same shape as the device-type message. The test rejects an all-fp16 map on the inactive, active and user-managed paths, shows the active output is unchanged, then shows a map mixing one valid changed constant with one wrong-dtype constant (both visit orders) is rejected without partially writing. I have no local source build: I ran the test against a 2.16.0.dev20261029 CPU nightly wheel with the patched header copied into site-packages (the header is compiled in). It fails before and passes after. Dtype names, shape checks and rethrowing the message text through the runner are left out on purpose.

## Agent details (if applicable)

This change was prepared with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code; an independent model review was run on the diff). The assistant located the validation loop, wrote the dtype check and the test, and verified them against a wheel. I reviewed the diff and the test before opening the PR.

title: [AOTInductor][Windows] Pin the MSVC OpenMP runtime to prevent teardown crashes
body:
## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Fixes #198205

## BC-breaking?

No public API or ABI changes. Existing compiled models and packages must
be recompiled to include this fix.

## Summary (human written only)

I've reviewed and tested this PR locally and discussed it with my colleague @xieofxie. Any feedback or suggestions are welcome!

## Agent details (if applicable)

The implementation and tests were prepared with AI assistance.
This section is AI-generated; validation results below summarize
agent-reported runs.

### Problem and approach

On native Windows, destroying an OpenMP-enabled AOTInductor runner
immediately after execution can crash the process with an access
violation (`0xC0000005`).

This change pins the MSVC OpenMP runtime for the lifetime of the process,
while allowing individual model DLLs to unload. It identifies the runtime
from `&omp_get_max_threads` and uses `GetModuleHandleExW` with
`GET_MODULE_HANDLE_EX_FLAG_FROM_ADDRESS | GET_MODULE_HANDLE_EX_FLAG_PIN`,
rather than relying on a hardcoded, versioned DLL name.

The native MSVC `omp.h` import declaration ensures that the address
identifies the runtime rather than a model-local import thunk. Pinning
failures report the immediately captured `GetLastError()` value.

The address-based approach follows @xieofxie's suggestion.

### Lifetime tradeoff

This version trades a small process-lifetime runtime footprint for safe
model unloading.

- Benefit: model DLLs and their embedded data can be reclaimed, and the
  model DLL files become deletable after runner destruction.
- Cost: the OpenMP runtime remains loaded until process exit. Its retained
  workers and associated resources are not reclaimed per model.
- Conservative scope: models compiled with OpenMP enabled also pin the
  runtime even when their generated kernels contain no parallel regions.

This is a runtime-lifetime workaround, not an OpenMP worker-shutdown
mechanism. It does not establish a bound on thread or handle growth,
or resolve package-extraction cleanup issues.

The change is restricted to native MSVC OpenMP builds on Windows.
Clang and LLVM OpenMP are explicitly excluded.

### Regression coverage

The regression covers:
- Nonparallel and parallel kernels.
- Raw model DLLs and explicitly extracted packages loaded by directory.
- Sequential and concurrent runners.

Each configuration checks 16 independent model DLLs for actual unloading,
file deletion, and output correctness after runner destruction. Isolated
child processes have bounded timeouts and process-tree cleanup.

### Validation (agent-reported)

Native Windows x64 CPU, Python 3.14.7, MSVC 19.44.35229,
VCOMP 14.50.35719.0, and torch 2.16.0.dev20261018+cpu.

- Original reproduction matrix: two teardown crashes before the fix;
  all nine cases pass afterward.
- Regression matrix: all four parallel-kernel configurations crash
  before the fix; all eight configurations pass afterward, with no skips.
- Address-ownership and unload/delete probes confirm that the runtime,
  not the model DLL, is pinned.
- A negative control without the import declaration detects accidental
  model pinning and fails model deletion as expected.

Validation used the stock wheel with the reviewed header changes applied 
and freshly compiled models, not a full framework build. Package
temporary-directory cleanup warnings remain. Targeted lint and formatting
checks passed, but a clean full lintrunner result is not claimed;
CLANGTIDY, CUDA, and other platforms/toolchains were not validated.

title: [Testcase Refactoring][PrivateUse1] Add hw_classification to test_ren…
body:
## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Part of #185590

## BC-breaking?

No. Metadata-only addition; no runtime behaviour change when `--hw-classification` is
not passed.

## Summary (human written only)

Annotate `TestRenamePrivateuseoneToExistingBackend` in
`test/test_rename_privateuse1_to_existing_device.py` with
`hw_classification = HardwareClassification.GENERIC`, as part of the test case
refactoring effort tracked in #185590.

This is a metadata-only change (+8/-1, of which 7 added lines are an import block
reformat). It lets CI and out-of-tree accelerator backends schedule this test class
through `--hw-classification`. No test semantics, no test count and no device
placement changes.

## Why no device decoupling is needed

`TestRenamePrivateuseoneToExistingBackend` holds 1 test,
`test_external_module_register_with_existing_backend`, which verifies the
`privateuse1` backend rename mechanism: renaming to an already-existing backend name,
the one-shot semantics of `torch.utils.rename_privateuse1_backend()`, the difference
in AMP behaviour before and after `torch._register_device_module()`, and index
resolution in `torch._utils._get_device_index()`. Reviewed case by case, the class has
no hardware coupling:

1. No hard-coded `cuda` string or device instance, no `.cuda()` / `torch.cuda.*`.
2. No CUDA-only decorators and no device branching. The only decorator is
  `@skipIfTorchDynamo`, which is hardware-agnostic.
3. No pytest `is_cuda` parameterization.
4. No `device` parameter and no `instantiate_device_type_tests` registration.
5. No tensors are created and no operators are invoked at all — the test drives
  framework-level registration state only.

Every test belongs to one hardware category, so there is no mixed category to split
and no class rename is required.

The `"maia"` string in the test is the object under test — the target name passed to
`torch.utils.rename_privateuse1_backend()` — and is not a hardware coupling point.
`DummyPrivateUse1Module` is a stub module constructed inside the test to simulate
custom backend registration. Both are deliberately left untouched.

## Changes

Only `test/test_rename_privateuse1_to_existing_device.py` is touched (+8/-1):

- Import `HardwareClassification` from `torch.testing._internal.common_utils`; the
  import block is split across lines and sorted case-sensitively per isort, which
  accounts for the bulk of the added lines.
- Add `hw_classification = HardwareClassification.GENERIC` as a class attribute of
  `TestRenamePrivateuseoneToExistingBackend`.

## Validation

**Local build.** Not applicable — test-only change, nothing to compile.

**Unit tests.** The file runs on CPU (the default device for this test, as it creates
no tensors):

- `pytest --collect-only -q` reports the same collected node id before and after the
  change (1 collected, identical fully-qualified name).
- Running the file without `--hw-classification` gives the identical per-test outcome
  before and after the change (1 passed).
- `--hw-classification GENERIC`: `total=1, passed=1, unclassified=0, mismatched=0` —
  1 test executes, 0 failures.
- `--hw-classification ACCELERATOR`: `total=1, passed=0, mismatched=1` — 0 tests
  execute (negative control).

**CUDA / accelerator.** Not applicable and unchanged from upstream: this file
exercises the `privateuse1` registration mechanism only and has no CUDA code path.

**Lint.** `isort --check-only`, `ruff` and `flake8` report no issues on the changed
file.

## Risk

None. Metadata-only change that does not affect test logic or compatibility.

## Agent details (if applicable)

AI-assisted analysis produced the per-test breakdown and the local verification
commands listed under `Validation`. The commands were executed by the submitter, who
confirms the reported results. The patch is an additive change and the full file has
been reviewed by the submitter.

title: [CPP FakeTensor] Treat the C++ FakeTensorMode as the FAKE dispatch mode
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* #200139
* __->__ #202701
* #202700
* #202699
* #200435
* #200146
* #199942
* #200349
* #200144
* #200129
* #200128
* #202287

A C++ FakeTensorMode is installed in FakeTensorModeTLS, together with the Fake
dispatch key, rather than in the FAKE infra mode slot that holds a Python
FakeTensorMode. Code that enters, suspends or looks for "the fake mode" goes
through that slot: FakeTensorMode.__enter__ unsets any previous fake mode,
unset_fake_temporarily suspends it, and callers such as proxy_tensor and
_functional_collectives check it with _get_dispatch_mode(FAKE).

_set_dispatch_mode, _get_dispatch_mode and _unset_dispatch_mode now treat an
installed C++ mode as the FAKE mode whenever no Python FakeTensorMode holds the
slot. _set_dispatch_mode(wrapper) installs wrapper._cpp_mode with the Fake key
on, _unset_dispatch_mode(FAKE) clears both and returns the wrapper, and
_get_dispatch_mode(FAKE) returns it. So a C++ mode is entered, suspended and
restored through the same calls as a Python FakeTensorMode, and the existing
callers above handle it unchanged; CppFakeTensorMode.__enter__/__exit__ (later
in this stack) mirror FakeTensorMode's. Restoring turns the Fake key on rather
than restoring its previous value, which is equivalent because
FakeTensorModeTLS keeps the key included exactly when a mode is installed. As
with FakeTensorMode's enter_stack, what to restore is kept on the Python mode,
so entering one mode on two threads at once is not supported.

Test Plan:

```
python test/test_fake_tensor.py -k CppFakeTensorModeBindingsTest
```

test_fake_dispatch_mode_slot checks installing, reading and suspending a C++
mode through the slot against the Fake key, and that entering a Python
FakeTensorMode suspends the C++ mode until it exits.

Authored with an AI assistant.

A Python FakeTensor has no real data, so FakeTensor.__new__ marks its storage
to warn on mutable data pointer access, or to throw when
torch._functorch.config.fake_tensor_allow_unsafe_data_ptr_access is False.
Dynamo and export set that config to False while tracing so that reading a
fake's data pointer is an error rather than silently returning a meaningless
pointer.

C++ fakes now do the same. c10::FakeTensorMode gets
allow_unsafe_data_ptr_access_, read from the config when the mode is created
and exposed read-write on _CppFakeTensorMode, and set_fake_tensor_mode applies
it to the fake's storage.

```
python test/test_fake_tensor.py -k CppFakeTensorModeBindingsTest
```

fake of a mode with unsafe access disallowed raises on data_ptr().

_from_meta_and_device(meta, device, mode) turns a meta tensor into a C++ fake
of mode, in place, like Python's FakeTensorConverter.from_meta_and_device. The
Python CppFakeTensorMode's converter (later in this stack) builds C++ fakes with
it. It checks that the input is meta-backed rather than is_meta(), since a C++

tensor is modified, and like a fresh Python FakeTensor, the result shadows no
real tensor.

_maybe_get_fake_mode(t) returns the Python wrapper of a C++ fake's mode, or

title: [inductor] Pass 0-dim CPU expressions to GPU kernels by value
body:
## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Fixes #199676

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

The issue was related to how `torch.compile` handled CPU scalar tensors when they were used with GPU tensors. Instead of passing the actual value from CPU memory to the GPU, the compiler was passing its memory address, and the program crashed with a CUDA driver error saying `invalid argument`. To fix this issue, I made a change in `maybe_copy_cpu_scalar` inside `torch/_inductor/lowering.py`: now, when the GPU operation needs a small scalar value stored on the CPU, the compiler handles that value on the CPU first and passes the actual value to the GPU. I also made sure that this change only applies to the problematic cases, so operations that were already working correctly don't introduce unnecessary overhead. I added three tests in `test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py` to verify the fix.

## Agent details (if applicable)

> The following was produced by Claude Code (AI assistant) and reviewed by me.
>
> **Root cause.** Eager passes a 0-dim CPU operand of a CUDA op to the kernel by value. Inductor handles 0-dim CPU graph inputs (`is_unspec_arg`) and realized 0-dim CPU buffers (`Scheduler.update_zero_dim_cpu_tensor`), and `maybe_copy_cpu_scalar` handles `ReinterpretView` operands. An *unrealized* 0-dim CPU expression computed from a non-0-dim CPU tensor slips past all three. Examples are `(1.0 - lr.to(torch.float32).squeeze()) * 2.5` from the issue and `lr[0] * 3`, with `lr` of shape `[1]`; the second is not in the report. The expression is fused into the Triton kernel, which is then handed `lr`'s CPU pointer.
>
> **Fix.** In `maybe_copy_cpu_scalar`, a non-`ReinterpretView` 0-dim CPU operand of a non-CPU op is realized when it reads a CPU tensor that is not 0-dim. It becomes a 0-dim CPU buffer, which the scheduler already passes by value (`.item()`). This follows the approach suggested in the issue. I narrowed it after finding that an unconditional `realize()` added a CPU kernel to graphs that already worked, such as expressions over 0-dim inputs from Dynamo-unspecialized Python scalars (1 -> 2 kernels). With the narrowing those stay at 1 kernel, and the third test locks that in.
>
> **Tests** (in `test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py`, next to `test_cpu_scalar_with_gpu_tensor`):
> - `test_cpu_scalar_expr_with_gpu_tensor`: the graph-input repro from the issue plus `b[0] * 3`, static and dynamic shapes.
> - `test_cpu_scalar_expr_from_custom_op_with_gpu_tensor`: the custom-op repro from the issue.
> - `test_cpu_scalar_expr_from_0d_cpu_tensor_with_gpu_tensor`: a 0-dim CPU input expression still compiles to one GPU kernel.
>
> The first two fail without the `lowering.py` change and pass with it.
>
> ```
> python -m pytest test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py -k cpu_scalar_expr
> ```
>
> **Regression check.** I ran these with and without the change; both runs had the same 18 failures. 17 need `CUDA_HOME` (C++ wrapper / AOTI; no CUDA toolkit locally), and `test_conv_bias_no_extra_cast_for_fp32` also fails without the change.
>
> ```
> python -m pytest test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py::GPUTests -k "scalar or cpu or device or unspec or item or mixed or copy_ or lerp or addcmul or where or clamp"
> python -m pytest test/inductor/test_cudagraph_trees.py -k "cpu or scalar"
> python -m pytest test/inductor/test_cuda_repro.py
> ```
>
> Run on an RTX 4050 Laptop GPU (WSL2) with the `2.16.0.dev20261029+cu134` nightly and Triton 3.9.
>
> **Not covered.** As the issue notes, this only fixes lowerings that go through `transform_args`.

title: [XPU][Inductor] Fix FlexAttention TMA pointer-load assertions
body:
## Summary

Fix FlexAttention TMA pointer-load assertions that fail after Triton kernels are defined at module level by default.

Fixes #201710
Fixes #201711

## Root Cause

PR #200502 changed Inductor to define Triton kernels at module level by default. In this mode, top-level `@triton.jit` helpers are renamed with a kernel-specific suffix to avoid naming conflicts.

As a result, the generated helper call changes from `load_checked_2d(Q, ...)` to `load_checked_2d_<kernel_name>(Q, ...)`, causing the existing regex in `_pointer_load_pattern()` to fail.

The generated kernel behavior is correct; only the test assertion needs to be updated.

## Fix

Update `_pointer_load_pattern()` to accept the kernel-specific suffix by adding `\w*` after `load_checked_2d`.

The pattern still requires an operand-qualified call (`Q`, `K`, or `V`), ensuring that it matches the actual pointer-load fallback rather than the helper definition.

## Validation

- Reproduced the original failure with module-level Triton kernels enabled.
- Verified that both `TRITON` and `TRITON_DECODE` test variants pass after the fix.
- Confirmed that the tests also pass with module-level Triton kernels disabled.
- Confirmed that the updated regex does not incorrectly match the TMA descriptor path.

title: [inductor] Pin torch.cond/switch operands to the strides the branches were compiled for
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* #202768
* #202767
* __->__ #202692

## Human Note

This seems like a severe silent incorrectness bug specific to torch.cond, the fix PR is quite short and plausible though I don't claim to understand all the subtleties

## Agent note

`Switch.create` lowers each branch against the operands' FakeTensor
strides, but it passes the realized operand buffers to the branches with
whatever layout Inductor picked for them. These can differ:

- An operand Inductor lays out in a different order than eager does, e.g.
  `a.t() + b` with a row-major `b`. Eager follows `a.t()` (column-major),
  Inductor follows `b`.
- A buffer that gets stride padding, e.g. `a.t().relu()` where `a` has 8261
  columns, on GPU: Inductor pads the leading stride from 8261 to 8288.
- An operand whose layout was already fixed differently, e.g. a convolution
  output that layout optimization made channels-last.
- An expanded operand whose base has a different layout.

With `size_asserts` on, the branch's input check fails at runtime
(`expected size 8261==8261, stride 19==1 at dim=0`). With it off, the
branch kernels index the buffer with the wrong strides and silently return
wrong values. Plain `torch.compile` of a `torch.cond` hits this.

The fix pins every tensor operand to its fake strides with
`require_exact_strides` before creating the node. `InvokeSubgraph` and
`WhileLoop` already do the same for their operands. For a `FlexibleLayout`
producer this just fixes its layout, so the common case adds no copy; a
buffer already laid out differently gets a copy. Strides of size-1 dims are
ignored as usual. Padding is not allowed, because the branches index with
the unpadded strides. Each operand goes in as a `TensorBox`, as in
`WhileLoop`, because the path of `require_strides` that keeps an expand
slices its input.

Under `no_grad`, a branch may mutate an operand in place. If that operand
was pinned through a copy, the branch mutates the copy, so the fix copies
it back into the original buffer after the node (`copy_`). Without that the
mutation would be silently lost, e.g. a branch doing `y.mul_(2)` on a
channels-last conv output.

This came up while prototyping an always-on, single-compile version of Meta's
intermediate logging (per-tensor statistics logged from inside compiled
models), which wraps each logging site in `torch.cond` on a runtime flag.
More context (Meta-only):
<url>

Authored with an AI assistant (Claude).

## Test Plan

```
python test/inductor/test_control_flow.py -k test_cond_operand_strides -k test_switch_operand_strides
python test/inductor/test_control_flow.py
```

- `test_cond_operand_strides` and `test_switch_operand_strides` cover the
  order, padding and expand cases on CPU and CUDA, with static and dynamic
  shapes.
- `test_cond_operand_strides_copy` covers the copy case (a channels-last
  conv output under `force_layout_optimization`), with and without a branch
  that mutates the operand.

All of them fail without the fix, under both the Python and C++ wrappers,
and pass with it. The mutating copy case also fails with the pinning alone,
without the copy back.

title: [mergebot] Check the ciflow runs above a stack that test the PRs being landed
body:
**Impact:** the merge command (pytorchbot merge) on PRs in a ghstack or GitHub stack, plus a short paragraph in CONTRIBUTING.md.
**Risk:** medium

## What
Some landing PRs need a ciflow label they do not carry, because the PR above them runs it for the stack. Before landing, the merge bot now checks that run: it refuses the merge if the run failed, and waits while it is still running.

## Why
Issue: <url>

CI hardware availability is the bottleneck. Every PR of a large stack that carries a `ciflow/` label runs that workflow on every rebase. Those runs consume the macOS, A10G, ROCm and other scarce runners, which delays jobs on main and holds up viable/strict updates.

The approach is to run each path-based `ciflow/` workflow only on the top-most PR of the stack that needs it. That PR's head contains every PR below it, so one run tests them all.
- **Merges stay safe:** before landing a stack, the merge bot verifies the run on the PR above that stands in for the PRs below it.
- **Failures stay easy to troubleshoot:** Dr.CI shows a failing run at both ends. On the PR that ran it, a note names the lower PRs it also tests. On each of those lower PRs, the comment shows the failures.

Moving the labels up removes the signal the merge bot got from each PR's own run. A lower PR could then land on its own, or under the PR that carries the label for the stack, without that run ever having to pass. This change makes the run above count:
- **The right run:** it is matched by its ciflow tag, so runs of other labels and pull_request runs never count. The PR above must contain the landing commit, so a stale stack cannot pass on an old run.
- **Failures and waits:** a failure that Dr.CI does not clear refuses the merge. A run that is still going, or has not started yet, makes the merge wait.
- **Nothing runs the label:** if the PR being merged needs a label, has PRs above it, and nothing above runs that label on its current changes, the merge is refused with how to fix it.
- **Unchanged cases:** lower landing PRs with no run above them, and PRs at the top of their stack, are not blocked, as today.
- **Flags:** `-f` skips the check; `-i` ignores the failures present when the merge starts.

# Notes
- The labeler and Dr.CI side is the pytorch/test-infra stack pytorch/test-infra#9275 to pytorch/test-infra#9281. Land this PR first.
- Labeler globs are matched the way the bot's minimatch matches them, checked against every labeler.yml glob and every file in the repo.
- When nothing runs a needed label, the merge is refused rather than adding the label and waiting, as the merge command does with `ciflow/trunk`. Switching to that is easy.

title: [ROCm] Add a check for hipBLASLt handles shared across streams (#202679)
body:
Summary:

Overlapping launches on one hipBLASLt handle from two streams can hang split-K GEMMs (see the previous diff). The pool now orders the handles it hands between threads, but other code can still use one handle on two streams. This adds a check, off by default, that finds where that happens.

With `TORCH_HIPBLASLT_CHECK_HANDLE_STREAMS=1`, each hipBLASLt launch through ATen records the handle's stream, device and thread. A launch on a different stream or device, while the handle's previous stream still has queued work, logs a warning with both streams, both threads and a backtrace. It reports two kinds of launch:
- The previous thread has exited, and this thread got the handle from the pool for its stream. The pool moves a handle between threads only when its owner exits, so this is a handover, which the pool orders. Each launching thread holds a thread-local token that the launch history keeps a weak reference to, so the check sees the exit even after the thread's id is reused.
- Anything else, reported as unexplained sharing.

Each kind logs at most 20 times per process. A fence that fails to order a launch has its own budget of 20, so repeated sharing cannot silence a failure. With `=fence`, unexplained sharing also makes the new stream wait for the previous stream's work. The fence is recorded on the device of the previous stream and waited on from the current device, so it also orders a handle that a caller carried to another device.

The check never fails the launch it checks. It clears any CUDA error it hits instead of throwing, and if the fence cannot be set up, the warning says so and the launch goes ahead unordered.

`checkCublasLtHandleStream` runs before each ROCm `cublasLtMatmul` in `CUDABlas.cpp` and before `hipblasLtMatmul` in TunableOp. When the check is off, it costs one static load per launch. It skips capturing streams. It never touches a previous stream that c10 does not own, since its owner may have destroyed it and HIP crashes on a destroyed stream (see the previous diff), so sharing that involves such a stream goes unreported.

Test Plan:
On MI300X, same setup as the previous diff, on one-GPU workers and a two-GPU worker (`resource_units = 2`), 5 runs each, plus 3 on the final code:
- `cuda_cublas_handle_pool_test`: `main()` now sets `TORCH_HIPBLASLT_CHECK_HANDLE_STREAMS=fence` before any test runs, so the check's tests run wherever the binary runs. 14 pass, 2 skip on one GPU; 15 pass, 1 skip on two. The skips are `CachedWorkspaceLeavesHandleUserOwned` and, on one GPU, the cross-device test. The previous diff's tests never launch a GEMM, so the check does not touch them. The check's tests:
  - `LtHandleStreamCheckOrdersCrossStreamLaunch` (0.3 s): one thread on two streams, so the check reports unexplained sharing and orders the launch. It waits for the launch, then checks that the work queued before it has finished.
  - `LtHandleStreamCheckOrdersCrossDeviceLaunch` (two GPUs, 0.5-0.6 s): the same as the handle moves from a pool stream on device 0 to device 1's default stream, then to device 0's default stream. Both default streams are the null stream, so with V1's stream-only comparison the second hop goes unchecked and fails, 3/3. Earlier variants failed it as well: V0.4 waited on device 0's default stream when going to device 1, and recording on device 1's stream the event created on device 0 failed with `invalid resource handle`, so the event is recreated when the device changes. The test launches on both default streams first, because a first launch on device 1 took longer than the sleep and let a broken hop pass.
- E2E: the scratch handoff test from the previous diff, run with `=1`, completes 5/5 and logs the handover. The new thread got the same `std::thread::id` as the exited one, and the token still saw that the old thread had exited:
```
W1030 10:29:50.232107 772854 CublasHandlePool.cpp:1215] hipBLASLt handle 0x7fb93d804600 launched on stream 0x7fb93d841380 (device 0) by thread 140433376151104 (aten_handoff_wa) while stream 0x7fb93d841000 (device 0), where thread 140433376151104 (aten_handoff_wa, exited) last launched it, still has queued work. The pool handed the handle over when that thread exited and orders this stream after that work.
```
and the cross-device fence test logs both hops:
```
W1030 10:29:48.974419 837777 CublasHandlePool.cpp:1215] hipBLASLt handle 0x7ffeeecbb9bc launched on stream 0 (device 1) by thread 140587392189760 (aten_pool_fence) while stream 0x7fdcedaac180 (device 0), where thread 140587392189760 (aten_pool_fence) last launched it, still has queued work. No pool handover explains this; overlapping launches on one handle can hang hipBLASLt split-K GEMMs. Ordered this launch after that work.
W1030 10:29:49.070636 837777 CublasHandlePool.cpp:1215] hipBLASLt handle 0x7ffeeecbb9bc launched on stream 0 (device 0) by thread 140587392189760 (aten_pool_fence) while stream 0 (device 1), where thread 140587392189760 (aten_pool_fence) last launched it, still has queued work. No pool handover explains this; overlapping launches on one handle can hang hipBLASLt split-K GEMMs. Ordered this launch after that work.
```
- The "Could not order this launch" path ran only in the pre-fix variants above. No test makes the final code's fence fail, so the failure budget has not run.
- No test covers skipping a previous stream that c10 does not own. A test that destroyed the previous stream also passed against V1, 3/3: the capture query on the destroyed stream reads freed memory, and there it did not reach the `hipStreamQuery` that crashes in the previous diff's probe.

title: [ROCm] Order a reused per-stream handle after its last owner's work (#202678)
body:
Summary:

On ROCm, `getCurrentCUDABlasLtHandle` gives each (thread, device, stream) its own hipBLASLt handle (<url>). A handle owns device state that cannot serve two streams at once: the synchronizer flags that hipBLASLt's single-kernel split-K solutions (`GSUAMBSK`) signal and spin on.

When a thread exits, its `PoolWindow` pushes its handles back to the free list right away, even while GEMMs it queued are still running. The next thread to reserve a handle on that device pops the same handle (LIFO) for its own stream. Both streams then run split-K GEMMs on one synchronizer. A consumer workgroup can find its flag consumed by the other launch and spin forever, which stalls the HIP queue and every host thread waiting on it.

This came from a production stall on MI300X (ROCm 7.0, hipBLASLt 1.2.70002). A rocm-debug-agent wave dump showed the split-1 workgroups of a GSU=2 `GSUAMBSK` fp16 GEMM spinning on flags that read 0, after every split-0 workgroup had finished. A standalone hipBLASLt repro with that kernel and shape hangs every time two in-flight launches share a handle on two streams, and never with one handle per stream.

This diff makes the ROCm stream-keyed path of `DeviceThreadHandlePool` order every handover:
- When a thread exits, record an event on the stream each of its handles last ran on.
- When another thread takes such a handle for its stream, make that stream wait on the event.

A capturing stream cannot wait on work outside its capture, and its kernels run whenever the graph is replayed. So when the stream that takes a handle is capturing, as when an autograd worker runs its first GEMM in a captured backward, the host waits on the event instead, in relaxed capture mode. It waits without the pool mutex, because the work it waits for may itself wait on a thread that has yet to take a handle. If the wait throws, the handle goes back to the pool still fenced. A handle released while its stream is capturing gets no event. A handle whose event cannot be recorded goes back unordered, with a one-time warning.

Only streams that c10 never destroys get an event: the default stream and pool streams. The owner of any other stream may destroy it before the thread that used it exits. On ROCm 7.0, `hipEventRecord` and `hipStreamQuery` on a destroyed stream abort the process (`pure virtual method called`), while `hipStreamIsCapturing` returns `hipSuccess` and the next stream created reuses the address, so no error check can catch it. A handle released from such a stream goes back unordered, as before this diff. The new `c10::cuda::isStreamFromPool` matches pool streams by address, so a pool stream that AOTInductor wraps with `getStreamFromExternal` still gets an event; the production stall above ran on such streams.

This covers both pools that key handles by stream:
- hipBLASLt handles, for the synchronizer above.
- Public rocBLAS handles. Each keeps the workspace bound at its creation, so the same handover can let two streams' rocBLAS kernels use one workspace at once.

CUDA builds and the per-device pools are unchanged.

Test Plan:
On MI300X, RE `amd-gpu`/`MI300`, `fbcode//mode/opt-amd-gpu -c fbcode.rocm_arch=mi300 -c fbcode.enable_gpu_sections=true`. caffe2's own ATen CUDA test targets land on RE workers without an AMD GPU, where every test returns at `at::cuda::is_available()`, so these ran from scratch targets that build the same hipified sources on MI300 workers.

- `cuda_cublas_handle_pool_test`, 5 runs: this diff's 13 pass, `CachedWorkspaceLeavesHandleUserOwned` skips (needs `TORCH_CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CACHE=1`). The new tests:
  - `LtHandleFromExitedThreadWaitsForItsStream` (0.3 s) and `PublicHandleFromExitedThreadWaitsForItsStream` (4.1-4.5 s, mostly rocBLAS handle creation): once the event the next thread records on its stream completes, the event the exited thread recorded after its sleep has completed too. V1 instead checked that the next thread's event was still pending while the sleep ran, which failed 1 of 6 runs on a loaded worker.
  - `LtHandleFromExitedThreadWaitsForItsStreamUnderCapture` (0.3-0.5 s): a worker takes the exited thread's handle on a stream the main thread is capturing in global mode. Against V0.2 of this diff, which skipped the wait under capture, it fails: the exited thread's sleep is still running when the worker gets the handle. With the host wait it passes, and the capture still ends with `hipSuccess`.
  - `LtHandleFromExitedThreadWaitsForItsWrappedPoolStream` (0.3 s): the same with the exited thread's pool stream wrapped by `getStreamFromExternal`, as AOTInductor runs it.
  - `LtHandleHostWaitLetsOtherThreadsTakeHandles` (0.3 s): the exited thread's stream waits on the GPU (`hipStreamWaitValue64`) for a value that the test writes only after another thread has taken a handle, while a worker takes the exited thread's handle on a capturing stream. Against V2, which waited while holding the pool mutex, it fails 3/3: the other thread stays blocked until the test gives up after 30 s.
  - `LtHandleReturnSkipsDestroyedExternalStream` (0.2-0.3 s): a thread takes a handle on an external stream, destroys the stream and exits, and the handle goes back to the pool. Against V2, the thread exit aborts the process 3/3 (`pure virtual method called`).
- `cuda_stream_test`, 5 runs each on a one-GPU and a two-GPU worker: `IsStreamFromPoolTest` and the 17 existing tests pass. The scratch targets build it with `-Wno-unused-value`, because ROCm 7 marks `hipError_t` nodiscard and the existing tests ignore it.
- E2E, scratch test not in this diff: the GEMM from the production hang (fp16 `at::mm` of [130, 3536] x [128, 3536]^T), 2000 per thread. A thread queues them on one stream and exits; the pool gives its handle to a thread that queues them on another stream. Both streams wait on one event, so their GEMMs start together.
  - before: hangs 4/4 (`same_handle=1`, then the 60 s watchdog fires)
  - after: completes 3/3 in 2.6-2.8 s (`same_handle=1 gate_closed_after_launches=1`, then `DONE`), outputs match a reference. These runs included the next diff with its check off. With this version (and the next diff's), it completes 5/5 in 2.5-2.8 s with the check off and 5/5 with it in warn mode.
- No test makes the event fail to record, so the warning has not fired.

title: [Inductor] Fix ceil-mode average pooling backward divisors, including 3D
body:
## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Fixes #198119

## BC-breaking?

No.

## Summary (human written only)

Fix incorrect backward divisors for average pooling with `ceil_mode=True`, including 3D. Add regression tests, verified on an RTX 3080.

## Agent details (if applicable)

With `ceil_mode=True`, the last pooling window can extend beyond the padded input. Inductor's backward lowering still used the full kernel volume when `count_include_pad=True`, producing incorrect gradients. For an input of length 6, kernel size 3, stride 2, and no padding, the final window needs divisor 2 rather than 3.

The 2D and 3D lowerings now clip each window's divisor to the padded input bounds. This also fixes 1D through its 2D decomposition. Explicit `divisor_override` values retain precedence, and windows that do not require a varying divisor keep the existing constant-divisor path.

Related prior work: [mottopanikeiku's commit](<url>) contains an equivalent 2D/3D fix. Additional coverage here includes mixed-axis shapes and reuse of a dynamically compiled function across input sizes 6, 8, and 7.

Tests compare compiled outputs and gradients with eager execution on CPU and CUDA, covering 1D/2D/3D, padding, mixed axis sizes, dynamic shapes, floor mode, and divisor overrides. The 3D tests exercise this backward lowering even when the forward operation falls back to ATen.

Validated on main `611154b` with CUDA 13.3 and an RTX 3080. Before the fix, 22 of the 34 new tests failed. After the fix, all 34 new tests and 16 existing pooling-backward tests pass. Lint also passes.

```bash
python test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py TestAvgPoolBackwardCPU TestAvgPoolBackwardCUDA -v
python test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py CpuTests GPUTests -k '*avg_pool*d_backward*' -v

```

title: [transport] Replace new_transport_rank with Transport.connect_rank
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* #202534
* __->__ #202670
* #202536
* #202535

new_transport_rank only connects a newly constructed transport to one peer. With multi-peer endpoints (parent change), one transport needs to connect to many ranks through a Store.

Transport.connect_rank(peer_rank, *, store=None, rank=None, tag="default", timeout=None) is a base-class method built on bind() and connect(), so it works with every backend. It takes a per-pair attempt counter in the Store, binds, swaps endpoints and connects. `timeout=None` uses the transport's default timeout (NIXL: its constructor `timeout`). Calls pair in order per rank pair and tag; a distinct tag separates several transports connecting the same pair. To connect several peers, call in a consistent order on all ranks or use threads with one Store client each (`store.clone()`). The Store must be trusted: bind() bytes may describe registered memory. Each peer deletes the endpoint bytes it reads, best effort; attempt counters, and bytes left unread by a failed or timed-out call, persist.

BC: removes new_transport_rank (#198889, shipped in 2.15.0) from the private, experimental torch.distributed._transport. GitHub code search finds no users outside PyTorch. Migration: `t = new_transport(backend, device, **kwargs); t.connect_rank(peer_rank, store=store, rank=rank, tag=backend.lower(), timeout=bootstrap_timeout)`; `tag=backend.lower()` keeps the old per-backend pairing. Unlike new_transport_rank, a failed connect_rank does not close the transport.

Implementation +107/-104, docs +2/-2, tests +297/-104.

Summary:
> For a description of the overall stack, see the top diff of this stack.

Lets a backend decide, at the fusion commit point, whether a `MultiTemplateBuffer` fuses with a candidate epilogue or producer and which template choice it is finalized to, instead of the default benchmark comparison in `Scheduler.speedup_by_fusion` (a lone fused kernel against lone-kernel timings plus the epilogue). MTIA needs complete-workload costs for this decision.

- `choices.py`: frozen dataclass `MultiTemplateFusionDecision(fuse, choice=None)` and `InductorChoices.multi_template_fusion_decision(scheduler, multi_node, other_nodes, epilogue)`. The default returns `None`, which keeps the current behavior.
- `scheduler.py`: `Scheduler._multi_template_fusion_decision`, consulted in `speedup_by_fusion` for MultiTemplateBuffer pairs after the atomic-add guard and not when `config.multi_kernel_hints` is set. `None` keeps the benchmark path; `fuse=False` declines.
- An accepted decision still passes the benchmark path's legality checks: `_has_layout_conflict_for_template`, no atomic-add producer, and producer-fusion support of the chosen template (`_producer_fusion_enabled_inputs` for that choice equals the buffer's). It needs a template: `choice` must be a `TritonTemplateCaller` among this buffer's choices with the buffer's size and stride; without `choice`, the buffer must already be finalized to a Triton template, which is reused. Otherwise the fusion is declined (logged via `WhyNoFuse`) and nothing is finalized.
- Decisions are immediate only: `_try_fusion_pairs` commits an accepted immediate fusion right away, so finalization coincides with the commit. Hook decisions do not take part in pending (competing) template fusions.
