title: [pr-review] Give re-reviews the interdiff since the last automated review
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #202667
* #202634

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Part of pytorch/test-infra#9243

## BC-breaking?

No.

## Summary (human written only)

Pass the differences between PR after addressing some previous review feedback

## Agent details (if applicable)

The previous PR in this stack tells re-reviews to settle their earlier findings and review what changed since the last review, reading `/tmp/pr-interdiff.txt` when present. This provides that file. Without it the review sees only the PR's full diff against its base, which does not say which lines are new since its last review, so a re-review reviews all of them again.

- `fetch_pr_comments.py` adds `previous_review_sha` to its output: the commit the latest automated review saw (`commit_id` of the review it already selects), empty without one. A re-run on the same commit gets a "nothing changed" note.
- `prepare` passes it on as an output, validated as a 40-hex SHA or empty, together with that commit's merge base with the PR's base, resolved by the compare endpoint on complete history like this run's merge base (empty if the commit is gone).
- A new `review` step, after the size gate and before any credential, fetches those two commits (depth 1, as for the merge base) and runs the new `scripts/pr_review/interdiff.py` from the trusted checkout, which writes `/tmp/pr-interdiff.txt`. Diffing the earlier commit against HEAD would show a rebase's upstream changes to the PR's files as the author's, and ghstack PRs are rebased often. So the script replays the earlier version onto this run's merge base with `git merge-tree` (explicit merge base, no checkout, no shared history needed) and diffs HEAD against that, so upstream changes cancel out. A file the replay cannot merge changed both upstream and in the PR; it gets the plain diff under a heading saying it includes upstream changes. No earlier review, an unavailable commit, no changed files, any failure or a result over `MAX_DIFF_BYTES` give a one-line note instead, so the model's read rule always resolves and the review never fails for this file. File names are literal pathspecs and are decoded losslessly, so a non-UTF-8 name cannot fail the step. `interdiff.py` is part of the prompt hash, like `fetch_pr_comments.py`.
- Stage A may read the file (`Read(//tmp/pr-interdiff.txt)`), and the Offline prompt names it.

The contract tests pin the new read rule, list `interdiff.py` among the trusted programs the review job runs, and model `PREVIOUS_REVIEW_SHA` and `PREVIOUS_MERGE_BASE_SHA` as plain values, like `MERGE_BASE_SHA`. `test_interdiff.py` covers a rebase (upstream changes left out), a file changed on both sides, no rebase, a re-run on the same commit, the notes, an unexpected failure, the size cap, pathspec-like file names (the test fails without `--literal-pathspecs`) and a non-UTF-8 file name. Renames since the last review show up as new files; detecting them is a follow-up.

Evaluation: replaying #199555 rounds 9-11 locally (3 runs each), re-reviews given an interdiff and the previous PR's skill raised 0 new and 0 previously non-blocking blocking findings in round 11, against 1 new with today's skill (see the previous PR). The step was also run on that PR's real commits. Round 10 -> 11 was a rebase: a plain diff of the two commits showed 10 changed lines in 5 files, all of them changes the base made; the rebase-aware interdiff shows none of those, plus the one file both sides changed (965 bytes instead of 9 KB). It wrote notes for no earlier review and an unavailable commit, and failed on a malformed SHA.

Test plan:

```
python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts/pr_review -t .
lintrunner -a .github/workflows/hardened-pr-review-run.yml scripts/pr_review/*.py
```

title: [ROCm][kineto] Fix segfault at exit with a profiler session still open
body:
## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Related: #199973 (found while testing it)

Supported by @jeffdaily

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

The torch.profiler for ROCm could segfault at process exit if a profiling session was still running, because it used thread-local state that had already been destroyed.

## Agent details (if applicable)

My agent came up with this analysis, but I've read and approved it.

**Problem.** A process that exits while a `torch.profiler` session with GPU activity is still running can segfault on ROCm. On gfx90a with hipBLASLt it crashes on every exit; on other archs and on the rocBLAS path it depends on what is left in freed memory (`MALLOC_PERTURB_=165` makes those crash too).

**Cause.** `exit()` destroys the main thread's thread_locals before the static destructors of rocBLAS and hipBLASLt run. Those destructors call `hipModuleUnload`, which rocprofiler-sdk still traces, so `RocprofLogger::api_callback` indexes its destroyed `thread_local` timestamp map. Per-thread-buffer mode and the correlation-id stacks touch destroyed thread_locals the same way.

**Change.** `api_callback` keeps the ENTER timestamp in the SDK's per-call `user_data`, which rocprofiler-sdk retains from the ENTER to the EXIT phase of one call, so the map is gone (and with it a hash insert and erase per traced HIP call). The remaining per-thread state (correlation-id stacks and the per-thread buffer) moves into one `thread_local ThreadState` whose destructor sets a trivially destructible `t_threadExiting` flag before its members are destroyed; once set, `api_callback` and the correlation push/pop return early and rows go to the shared buffer. The HIP calls dropped this way are those a thread makes after its kineto state is gone: for the main thread that is inside `exit()`, where no session can collect them; a worker thread exiting during a session loses its last such calls, which were undefined behaviour before. The new `test_profiler_left_running_at_exit_cuda` exits a subprocess with the profiler running under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=165`.

**Test plan.**

gfx90a (MI250X) and gfx1100 (W7800), TheRock ROCm 10.1 (rocprofiler-sdk 1.4.1), on main 9c0fed78773, A/B by reverting `RocprofLogger.cpp`. Exit codes of a script that starts a CPU+CUDA profile, runs a matmul and exits without stopping (139 = SIGSEGV):

| BLAS path | env | gfx90a without fix | gfx1100 without fix | with fix (both GPUs) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| hipBLASLt | plain | 139 x3 | 139 x3 | 0 x15 |
| hipBLASLt | `MALLOC_PERTURB_=165` | 139 x3 | 139 x3 | 0 x15 |
| rocBLAS | plain | 0 x3 | 0 x3 | 0 x15 |
| rocBLAS | `MALLOC_PERTURB_=165` | 139 x3 | 139 x3 | 0 x15 |

The backtrace without the fix is `api_callback` -> destroyed `thread_local` map, called from `hipModuleUnload` in hipBLASLt's or rocBLAS's `TensileHost` destructor inside `exit()`.

```
python test/profiler/test_profiler.py -k test_profiler_left_running_at_exit_cuda
python test/profiler/test_profiler.py
python test/profiler/test_kineto.py
python test/profiler/test_profiler_tree.py
```

- The new test fails 6/6 without the fix (`Expected 0 but got -11`) and passes 6/6 with it on both GPUs, with hipBLASLt and with `TORCH_BLAS_PREFER_HIPBLASLT=0`.
- With the fix, `KINETO_USE_DAEMON=1` and per-thread buffers (`ROCPROF_PER_THREAD_BUFFER_ENABLED=true`, confirmed active) also exit 0 under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=165`.
- `test_profiler.py`, `test_kineto.py`, `test_profiler_tree.py`: no new failures (the two `TestMetadataJsonFormatCUDA` `grid` failures fail the same way without the fix).

[VecLib] SVE: compute `VecBool<T>::zero_mask()` without the stack
body:
Summary:
`SveVecBool<T>::zero_mask()` expanded the predicate to a `Vectorized<T>`, which `Vectorized<T>::zero_mask()` then compared against zero, stored to a stack array and looped over lane by lane.

It now stays in registers. The false lanes (`~p`, which keeps the bits that belong to no lane clear) are packed to one predicate bit per byte with `UZP1` against an all-false predicate, and expanded to 0/1 bytes. Multiplying each 64-bit element by `0x0102040810204080` gathers its 8 bytes into the top byte (byte k lands on bit 56+k; the lower partial products add up to less than 2^56, so they never carry into it). A `TBL` with indices 7, 15, ..., 63 moves those top bytes into the low 64 bits, which are returned. With the constants hoisted, that is `not`, up to three `uzp1`, `mov #1`, `mul`, `tbl` and `fmov`. It needs 8 bytes per 64-bit element, so it holds for vectors of up to 512 bits (`static_assert(VECTOR_WIDTH <= 64)`); SVE256 is 256.

SVE2.1 `PMOV` would make the move a single instruction, but it is not available on the targeted cores. A store and reload is what this replaces.

`Vectorized<T>::zero_mask()` in `vec_float.h`, `vec_double.h` and `vec_bfloat16.h` still goes through the stack; it could become a comparison followed by this.

This diff was authored with an AI assistant (Claude Code).

Test Plan:
The `zero_mask()` body, extracted verbatim from the edited header into a freestanding harness, against a scalar reference for 8-, 16-, 32- and 64-bit lanes, 20000 predicates each (random, all-true and all-false), built from `svcmpne` as comparisons build them. Run under QEMU user mode at a 256-bit vector length, built for both SVE (predicated `mul`) and SVE2 (unpredicated `mul`):
```
clang++ --target=aarch64-linux-gnu -march=armv8.2-a+sve -msve-vector-bits=256 -std=c++17 -O2 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -static -fuse-ld=lld -Wl,--no-dynamic-linker run.cc -o run
/opt/fb-qemu-user/bin/qemu-aarch64 -cpu max,sve-default-vector-length=32 ./run  # 0 failures
# same with -march=armv9-a+sve2  # 0 failures
```
A copy with a wrong `TBL` index fails for every lane size, so the harness catches mistakes.

Compile check of the real headers: a scratch `cpp_library` (not included in this diff) that instantiates `(a == b).zero_mask()` for float, double, BFloat16 and int8..int64 with `-march=armv8.2-a+sve+bf16 -msve-vector-bits=256 -DCPU_CAPABILITY_SVE -DCPU_CAPABILITY_SVE256 -DCPU_CAPABILITY=SVE256 -DHAVE_SVE_CPU_DEFINITION`:
```

```

title: [VecLib] Add `Vectorized<T>::orNanIf`
body:
Summary:
mathlib's `Vec<T>` has an `orNanIf(p)` member that `single.h` uses to force NaN into lanes where a predicate holds (domain errors, NaN inputs). `Vectorized<T>` has no equivalent, which blocks moving `single.h` from `//mathlib` onto ATen's veclib.

`orNanIf(mask)` returns all bits set (a NaN) in every lane where `mask` is true and leaves the other lanes untouched. It is added for `float` and `double` on AVX2, AVX512, NEON and SVE, plus the generic `vec_base.h` fallback:
- AVX2/AVX512/NEON: one bitwise OR of the value with the mask, the same instruction each file's `operator|` uses.
- SVE: `mask` is a `VecBool<T>` predicate, so it is one `svsel` against an all-ones vector, which avoids materialising the predicate as a vector first.
- Generic: `*this | mask`.

Test Plan:
Standalone probe (`agent_space/ornan/t.cc`) that checks, for `float` and `double`, that true lanes come back as all-ones bits and false lanes are bit-identical to the input.

NEON, native, clang and gcc:
```
clang++ / g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -DFBCODE_CAFFE2 ... t.cc && ./a.out  # PASS
```
SVE: the devserver's vector length is 128 bits, so it runs on a copy of the headers with `VECTOR_WIDTH` set to 16; the real headers at 256 bits are compile-only:
```
clang++ / g++ -march=armv8.2-a+sve -msve-vector-bits=128 -DCPU_CAPABILITY_SVE256 -DCPU_CAPABILITY_SVE -DCPU_CAPABILITY=SVE256 ... t.cc  # PASS with both

## Summary (human written only)

> "let's put the samples in the suite then" - mlazos

## BC-breaking?

> No.

## Agent details (AI generated)

Authored with an AI assistant at mlazos's request; submitted as a draft for human review.

### Problem

Raw-bit sweeps do not guarantee particular FP32 formula boundaries or parameter/input combinations. Random upstream gradients also miss most subnormal encodings. Add explicit cases that CI must compare bit for bit.

### Architecture

Add forward/backward edge tests in test/inductor/test_strict_numerics.py, reusing the strict configuration, raw-byte comparison, leaf-gradient checks, and compiled-kernel requirement. Existing broad sweeps and mismatch ledgers are retained; the new tests add no expected mismatches.

The generator covers 28 op names: 24 fixed-boundary unary operations, plus lerp, logit, softplus, and clamp. Supported FP16/BF16/FP32/FP64 cases include adjacent representable boundary values, signed zeros, subnormal/normal transitions, infinities, and signed NaN payloads, constructed in their own dtype on CPU before CUDA transfer. Parameter cases cover scalar/tensor lerp weights, logit's eps bounds after native precision conversion, exactly representable softplus crossings, and scalar/tensor clamp bounds. Backward crosses each input tuple with all 22 incoming-gradient encodings and checks every floating input leaf without broadcast reductions. Unexpected eager errors in added backward cases fail.

### Examples

FP16 lerp now explicitly tests weights 0.499755859375 (0x37ff), 0.5 (0x3800), and 0.50048828125 (0x3801), crossed with cancellation and signed-zero endpoints. Tensor weights get start, end, and weight gradient comparisons.

FP32 log_ndtr tests 0xbf800001, 0xbf800000, and 0xbf7fffff around -1. Every boundary input is paired with gradients including +/-0, smallest/second/largest subnormals, smallest normal, +/-1, infinities, and signed NaNs. Logit also tests negative eps that rounds to -0 in FP32, eps above 0.5, and NaN eps.

### Test Plan

Source-extracted current generators and sweep methods passed native CUDA contract checks on the existing PyTorch 2.16.0a0+git42b6894 build (CUDA 12.9/Triton 3.5, H100): 94 supported op/dtype pairs, 202 forward calls, and 200 native gradient calls. Operand encodings and gradient crossings were verified.

```bash
# From agent_space/strict_reference_delivery:
/home/mlazos/.conda/envs/pytorch-3.12/bin/python edge_sample_validation.py
# From the new test worktree:
lintrunner -a --revision HEAD --take RUFF,PYFMT,NEWLINE,SPACES,TABS,TESTOWNERS,TEST_HAS_MAIN
git diff --check
```

An older-build compiled probe with all strict flags explicitly enabled passed ReLU forward/backward and exposed sqrt/log1p forward/backward mismatches. No tolerance or ledger exception was added. A current-source decomposition check also confirms FP64 logit backward gaps exposed here: x=-1, eps=-1, incoming gradient 1 gives native NaN vs decomposition -0.5; x=0.5, eps=NaN gives native 4 vs decomposition 0. These existing compiler gaps remain enforced by the new tests. The full current worktree is unbuilt; CUDA 13.2/Triton 3.9 numerical validation will run in CI.

This is a test-only addition atop the numerical reference stack. Coverage of all OpInfos, complex backward, arbitrary fusion/layout graphs, and all binary/ternary combinations remains separate work. Existing no-kernel cases report skips.

Adds an `inductor_huggingface_tp` job to inductor-periodic on a four-A10G runner. For prefill and decode with `--tp-size=2` and full-graph compilation, it checks accuracy and graph breaks against new expected CSVs and measures performance. It also runs the process-launching TP tests with `PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_SLOW=1`. check_accuracy.py gains `--require-complete`, which requires exactly one result for every expected model: the TP job is unsharded, and a missing model would otherwise pass. update_expected.py reads the TP job's artifacts.

perf_cli.py parses the TP performance CSV names (`..._tp<N>_<phase>`), selects a baseline periodic run with a successful TP job on the same runner hardware, and pairs results only for the same hardware, phase, TP degree, model, and workload dimensions. On timeout, the driver sends SIGTERM to torchrun, which forwards it to its workers and kills them after a grace period, instead of killing torchrun and orphaning workers blocked in collectives.

title: [pr-review] Re-reviews converge: settle earlier findings, don't move the goalposts
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* #202667
* __->__ #202634

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Part of pytorch/test-infra#9243

## BC-breaking?

No.

## Summary (human written only)

Everytime the review agent is running, it introduces some new blockers regardless of what has been ficed and what has been asked by the author to ignore.

## Agent details (if applicable)

On a re-review, the pr-review skill re-reviews the whole PR from scratch, and "Everything is a must-fix" turns every new observation into a blocker, so a PR whose author fixes each round's findings can still collect new blockers every round (pytorch/test-infra#9243; on #199555 the production review raised 1, 2, 2, 5, 6, 5, 4, 7, 5, 6, 7, 7, 6, 6, 7, 5 blocking findings over 16 rounds).

This adds "Re-reviews converge" to "Earlier Automated Findings": settle the earlier blocking findings first (report one still present again as a continuing finding, drop one fixed or convincingly answered); review what changed since the last review in full; on code the last review covered and that has not changed since, raise a new blocking finding only for a defect with a concrete failure and say why it was not raised before; keep earlier non-blocking points non-blocking unless the code got worse or the concrete failure that rule requires can now be shown.

Supporting changes in the same file:
- The commit the last review saw comes from its body header ("Automated review of <sha>"), which every review has; `/tmp/pr-interdiff.txt` holds the changes since then when present, and modes with git can run `git diff <sha> HEAD`. Code whose change status the reviewer cannot tell is reviewed as changed, so a missing interdiff costs convergence, not recall.
- "Covered" excludes files an earlier review named as not reviewed (early posts under the Time Budget) and code whose earlier findings were left out (`truncated`, or a body that says some findings did not fit); those get a first review, and so does the whole PR when the reviewer cannot tell which code an omitted finding was about.
- An unaddressed maintainer comment still always blocks, whatever code it is on.
- "Everything is a must-fix" now says exceptions are marked where they apply (runner naming and workflow REVIEW.md advisories already are) and names re-reviews among them, and the skill says to write "non-blocking" in such points, keep them out of the Recommendation's justification, and not recommend Request Changes when only non-blocking points remain. Without that, stage B and post_review.py post every finding as blocking under a Request Changes verdict.

Evaluation: local replays of #199555 rounds 9-11 with production's prompts and models, 3 runs each, every round given the previous round's findings from the same run, as production gives them. Blocking findings in rounds 10 and 11, compared with that run's previous review (matched by an LLM judge):

| | Round 10 (author added code) | Round 11 (10 changed lines) |
|---|---|---|
| Today's skill | 7: 2 new, 2 previously non-blocking | 7: 1 new, on unchanged code |
| This change, with an interdiff | 8: 4 new, all on the code added in that round | 8: 0 new, 0 previously non-blocking |

The hardened workflow does not provide `/tmp/pr-interdiff.txt` yet; without it the skill compares the earlier findings' code with HEAD. Providing it is a follow-up. One PR and three runs: a signal, not a measurement.

Test plan:

```
python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts/pr_review -t .
lintrunner -a .agents/skills/pr-review/SKILL.md
```

title: [Inductor] Benchmark epilogue fusion for templates selected with input_gen_fns
body:
Templates selected with `input_gen_fns` never got a `MultiTemplateBuffer`, because the scheduler benchmarks fused kernels on random inputs, and random grouped MM offsets can cause illegal memory accesses. As a result, epilogue fusion for grouped MM was always taken without checking whether fusion is actually faster.. This PR keeps `input_gen_fns` on the `MultiTemplateBuffer` and passes the generated tensors, by buffer name, to the fused-kernel benchmark.

The change is opt-in, and only the grouped MM lowerings opt in. The generated tensor has to be a valid value for the input buffer itself, which doesn't hold for the other `input_gen_fns` users: flex attention templates mutate their inputs, which `MultiTemplateBuffer` doesn't support, `custom_op` needs the winning choice right away, and `flex_gemm` generators return views that don't match the argument buffer.

To test:
```sh
pytest test/inductor/test_benchmark_fusion.py -k BenchmarkMultiTemplateFusionGpuTest
pytest test/inductor/test_max_autotune.py -k grouped_mm
```

## Agent Report

Dependabot already opens security updates for .ci/docker/requirements-ci.txt,
one PR per package, but nothing proposes ordinary new releases, so the `==`
pins there only move when someone bumps them by hand. This adds a weekly
version-update entry for /.ci/docker. Minor and patch bumps are grouped into
one PR, so the image is rebuilt and tested once a week instead of once per

different version per Python version with environment markers are ignored:
Dependabot evaluates markers for a single Python version and would bump only
the matching line, so those are bumped by hand. With

lower bounds and unpinned entries alone. A 7-day cooldown (Dependabot's default is 3)
keeps a release out of the PR until it has been public for a week, so a
compromised or broken release is more likely to be yanked first; security
updates are not delayed.

title: [mobile] Bounds-check operator index in applyUpgrader
body:
## Author Notes

Small security improvement that shouldn't really matter for anything

## Agent Notes

> This section was generated by an AI assistant (Claude Code).

`applyUpgrader()` (torch/csrc/jit/mobile/parse_bytecode.cpp) indexed `code.op_names_[inst.X]` for every OP instruction without checking `X`. Both the ZIP loader and the FlatBuffer loader call it during model loading whenever the model's operator version is older than `kProducedFileFormatVersion`. Instruction operands and the operator table come independently from the serialized file and nothing validates one against the other before this point, so a malformed model with a negative or oversized operator index caused an out-of-bounds heap read before interpreter validation. This adds a `TORCH_CHECK` in the shared helper that rejects out-of-range indices with a `c10::Error`, leaving valid lookups and the OP-to-CALL rewrite unchanged. New tests call `applyUpgrader()` directly (-1, size, INT32_MAX, 0 with an empty table, plus the last valid index with and without an applicable upgrader) and load the existing operator-version-2 div fixtures (`.ptl` and `.ptl.ff`) with every OP operand rewritten to 1000, checking that loading fails with the new message.

BC-breaking: No. Built locally (release, CPU-only) and `spin lint` is clean; the C++ tests were not built or run locally (`BUILD_TEST=0`) and rely on CI. Untested configurations: `DISABLE_UPGRADER` builds and `FB_XPLAT_BUILD`.

title: [Profiler] Decide Kineto GPU tracing per session, not per process
body:
**Problem**

If the first profiler session in a process requests only CPU activity, every later CUDA session silently records no device events and no CUDA runtime events. The legacy torch.autograd.profiler.profile() default triggers it, as do torch.profiler._utils._init_for_cuda_graphs() and Inductor's TorchProfilerBenchmarker, which then fails with "'_CALLABLE' CUDA event not found".

libkineto is set up once per process, by the first session, and the cpuOnly flag it receives is fixed for the life of the process. #186036 changed that flag from "a device is present" to "this session requested a device activity", so the first session's answer sticks for every later one. The reverse order leaks too: once a CUDA session has run, later CPU-only sessions arm CUPTI and record CUDA runtime events. #186970 and #198209 worked around the first problem by priming Kineto with a CUDA session in three test modules.

#186036's goal still stands: a session that requests no device activity must not touch CUPTI, which Cuspy may own.

**Fix**

Split the flag in two. libkineto is again registered with GPU support whenever a device is present. Registration touches no CUPTI, because Kineto subscribes only when a trace enables GPU tracing. Each trace then decides whether to arm the GPU tracer through a new libkineto config key, GPU_TRACING_ENABLED, which kineto_shim sets from the session's requested activities. GenericActivityProfiler::shouldTraceGpu() gates every per-trace GPU path on it, and the XPU child profiler honors it too. The key defaults to true, so on-demand traces behave as before.

The alternative was to register CPU-only and upgrade on the first device session. After the upgrade, CPU-only sessions would arm CUPTI again, and the upgrade would need new APIs to change state on the live proxy, controller, and profiler.

_init_for_cuda_graphs now uses torch.profiler.profile(), whose default activities include CUDA, so it initializes CUPTI as intended. The test priming and its helper are removed. test_cuspy.py inherited its priming from test_profiler.py; every in-process session there is a Cuspy session, which Kineto sees as CPU-only.

Review the libkineto gate first (Config, GenericActivityProfiler), then the PyTorch side (kineto_shim.cpp, profiler_kineto.cpp), then the tests.

**Test Plan**

test_device_tracing_decided_per_session runs CPU, CPU+CUDA, and CPU sessions in a fresh process. It checks that only the CUDA session records device and CUDA runtime events, and it fails before this change.
GpuTracingFollowsEachTraceConfig checks the libkineto gate with a mock GPU profiler. test_cudagraph_profiling_workaround now asserts that its CUDA session captured device events; before, it passed without capturing any.

```
python test/profiler/test_profiler.py -k test_device_tracing_decided_per_session -k test_cudagraph_profiling_workaround
for b in build/bin/kineto/*; do $b --gtest_shuffle --gtest_repeat=3; done
python test/profiler/test_profiler.py
python test/test_linalg.py -k test_norm_fused_type_promotion -k test_matmul_folds_viewable_size_one_dim -k test_addmm_out_distinct_c_and_d -k test_rowwise_scaled_gemm_numerics_tunableop
python test/profiler/test_cuspy.py
```

title: [hardened-pr-review] Upload the review's inputs to S3
body:
✴️ iz2: Each automated review run already records its verdict row and model transcripts, but not the inputs the model was handed. Those can only be partly rebuilt from GitHub later: comments get edited or deleted, and heads that were force-pushed away are not guaranteed to survive. This PR stores the inputs so a run can be replayed or turned into an eval case.

A new step in the `review` job uploads to `s3://ossci-raw-job-status/pr_review_traces/<repo>/<run_id>_<attempt>_input/`:
- `pr-diff.txt`: the merge-base..head diff the review read
- `pr-files.txt`: the list of changed files
- `pr-comments.json`: the title, body and filtered PR conversation the review was shown
- `manifest.json`: `head_sha`, `base_sha`, `merge_base_sha`

The step runs right after the PR conversation is written, before the model stages, and only if the job's AWS credentials step succeeded, so the too-large path skips it. The files go under `pr_review_traces/` because that is the only prefix the review job's role may write, and that prefix is not publicly readable. Existing trace keys are unchanged. The step is best-effort: a staging or upload failure, or an upload that runs past its 120 s timeout, becomes a warning and the review continues.

`test_workflow_contract.py` gains `TestTheReviewInputsAreKept`. It checks that every S3 write in the review job goes under `pr_review_traces/`, and it pins the step's gate and its position. It also runs the step against a stub `aws` to check what gets uploaded, what happens with a missing input, and that a failed upload only warns.

Test plan: `python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts/pr_review -t .` runs 548 tests, all passing. The first live run after merge should show the `_input/` objects beside that run's trace.

> Part of #154444. Depends on #202611.
> 
> Ports the int8 convolution entry points that `quantized/cpu/qconv.cpp` uses from ideep (`ideep::convolution_forward`) into `aten/src/ATen/native/mkldnn/detail/Conv.{h,cpp}` (namespace `at::native::mkldnn`). The port is line-for-line and changes no behavior: it still takes `ideep::tensor` / `ideep::attr_t` and uses ideep's engine, stream and primitive cache.
> 
> ### Ported
> Public (`detail/Conv.h`), each with ideep's comments:
> - `convolution_forward_prepare`: ideep's int8 `prepare` (with bias, without the `is_channels_last` argument).
> - `convolution_forward_compute<reorder_src, reorder_weight>(const convolution_forward_params&, ...)`: compute with pre-prepared params. Explicitly instantiated for `<false, false>`.
> - `convolution_forward_compute<reorder_src, reorder_weight>(src, weights, bias, ..., scales, zero points, ...)`: ideep's int8 2-in-1 compute. qconv uses it when its primitive cache misses. Explicitly instantiated for `<true, true>`. ideep's comment on this function says "without bias", but it takes a bias tensor; the comment is kept verbatim.
> 
> File-local (`detail/Conv.cpp`):
> - `do_prepare<with_bias>`: ideep's int8 overload.
> 
> These reuse the int8 `prepare_parameters` and the scales/zero-points `compute_dispatch` from #<13/N>, and `get_primitive_desc` / `do_compute` from #201224.
> 
> ### Type change
> - `convolution_forward_params`, already ported, moves unchanged from `Conv.cpp`'s anonymous namespace into `Conv.h`. `OnednnUtils.h` now defines `using ConvParams = at::native::mkldnn::convolution_forward_params;`. qconv only reads `params.pd`, and stores and copies the struct in `ConvPrimitiveCache`, which works the same with the moved struct.
> 
> ### Call sites switched
> - `quantized/cpu/qconv.cpp`, in `PackedConvWeightsOnednn::apply_impl`:
>  - `prepare` on the cache fill
>  - `compute<false, false>(params, ...)` on a cache hit
>  - the int8 2-in-1 `compute` on a cache miss
> - `quantized/cpu/qconv.cpp`, in `_quantized_convolution_onednn`: `prepare` / `compute<false, false>`. These sit in the `#else` of `IDEEP_PREREQ(3, 1, 0, 0)`, which is never compiled with oneDNN 3.x; they are switched for consistency.
> 
> The `ideep::engine::cpu_engine()` argument is dropped from each call; it equals the default.
> 
> Still on ideep: quantized deconvolution in `qconv.cpp` (next PR), and `t_store().clear()` in `IDeepRegistration.cpp`.
> 
> ### Dropped
> - The `engine` parameters, as in the earlier ports.
> - In the 2-in-1 compute: ideep computes a local `is_channels_last` and never uses it (it passes `true` to `compute_dispatch`). The unused local is removed; it fails `-Werror=unused-variable` builds outside ideep's system-header include.

title: Fix LogXMLReruns.node_reporter() KeyError on pytest >= 9.2.0
body:
## Human Note
cross-ref #202385 (pytest 9.2.0 breakage was observed there and pytest was pinned to 9.1.1 in the inductor-benchmarks images as a stopgap; that PR's own description flags "making the conftest override compatible with pytest 9.2 is a separate follow-up"). This PR is that follow-up, and reverts the pin so CI actually exercises pytest 9.2.0+ end-to-end -- if it passes, pytorch is compatible with the latest pytest again.

## Agent Report
### Problem

`test/conftest.py`'s `LogXMLReruns` (a subclass of pytest's `junitxml.LogXML` that adds `<rerun>`/`<skipped>` reporting) overrides `node_reporter()` to key `self.node_reporters` by the plain `report.nodeid` string. pytest 9.2.0 changed the base class's own `node_reporter()`/`finalize()` to key by a new structured `report.id` (a `NodeId` dataclass) instead (PyTest Change: <url>). `LogXMLReruns` doesn't override `finalize()`, so the inherited `finalize()` always pops using `report.id` -- a key this override never wrote under -- so every pytest session that uses `--junit-xml-reruns` together with `pytest-rerunfailures` crashes:

```
INTERNALERROR>  File ".../_pytest/junitxml.py", line 544, in finalize
INTERNALERROR>  reporter = self.node_reporters.pop((node_id, workernode))
INTERNALERROR> KeyError: (NodeId(...), None)
```

This matches the crash #202385 pinned around (same traceback shape, same file/line). It reproduces with `pytest-rerunfailures` installed (even with `--reruns=0`) on a single trivial passing test -- no GPU or distributed test infrastructure needed, since the crash is purely in junitxml bookkeeping.

### Fix

Two commits:

1. **Delegate key derivation to `LogXML.node_reporter()` via `super()`** instead of recomputing it, then reclass the returned `_NodeReporter` to `_NodeReporterReruns` in place (safe: `_NodeReporterReruns` adds no new `__init__` state over `_NodeReporter`, and neither class uses `__slots__`). This tracks whatever key scheme the installed pytest version actually uses on either side of the 9.2 boundary, instead of hardcoding pre-9.2 behavior that will keep drifting on future pytest releases.

  ```diff
  def node_reporter(self, report: TestReport | str) -> _NodeReporterReruns:
  -  nodeid: str | TestReport = getattr(report, "nodeid", report)
  -  # Local hack to handle xdist report order.
  -  workernode = getattr(report, "node", None)
  -
  -  key = nodeid, workernode
  -
  -  if key in self.node_reporters:
  -  # TODO: breaks for --dist=each
  -  return self.node_reporters[key]
  -
  -  reporter = _NodeReporterReruns(nodeid, self)
  -
  -  self.node_reporters[key] = reporter
  -  self.node_reporters_ordered.append(reporter)
  -
  +  reporter = super().node_reporter(report)
  +  if reporter.__class__ is not _NodeReporterReruns:
  +  reporter.__class__ = _NodeReporterReruns
  return reporter
  ```

2. **Revert #202385's pin** (`pip_install 'pytest==9.1.1'` in `install_inductor_benchmark_deps.sh`) so the inductor-benchmarks images go back to whatever pytest TorchBench's unpinned `requirements.txt` resolves (9.2.0+ as of this writing), letting CI actually prove the fix holds under the real failure conditions rather than just locally.

13-line diff in `test/conftest.py`, 5-line revert in the docker script.

### Validation

Verified locally with `pytest==9.2.0` and `pytest-rerunfailures==16.7` installed:

- A minimal repro -- a single `def test_trivial(): assert True` run as `pytest test/trivial_test.py --junit-xml-reruns=... -p no:xdist --reruns=0` -- previously hit `INTERNALERROR` on every run; passes clean after this fix, with correct, well-formed junit XML (`<testsuite ...><testcase .../></testsuite>`).
- A second repro exercising all three report-outcome paths `LogXMLReruns` customizes at once (a test that fails on first attempt and passes on rerun under `--reruns=2`, an intentional `pytest.skip()`, and an intentional failure): no `INTERNALERROR`, and the generated XML's `<rerun message="...">` and `<skipped type="pytest.skip" message="...">` elements both render correctly through the reclassed reporter -- confirming the `__class__` swap doesn't silently break `append_rerun()`/`append_skipped()`.
- Re-ran both repros against `pytest==9.1.1` (the version this code originally targeted, and the version #202385 pinned to) to confirm no regression on the pre-9.2 path.

```bash
python -m pytest test/trivial_test.py --junit-xml-reruns=/tmp/out.xml -v -p no:xdist --reruns=0
python -m pytest test/flaky_test.py --junit-xml-reruns=/tmp/out2.xml -v -p no:xdist --reruns=2

title: [Inductor][Host-side TMA] Build host TMA descriptors from dynamic sizes read at launch
body:
Summary:
Host-side TMA descriptors recorded by templates (`tma_descriptor()` with `HOST_SIDE_TMA`) are built by the launcher, but `_resolve_dims` only accepted integer dims. A dynamic size, e.g. M under a dynamic batch, renders as the kernel's size arg (`ks0`), so the descriptor was skipped and the template had to build it on the device instead: every CTA writes and fences a descriptor before its first TMA load. On H100 that costs the TLX Hopper GEMM templates 1.1-2.1 us per kernel under a dynamic M, enough to lose short GEMMs to the pointer-based Triton template.

The launcher already receives every kernel arg by name, including the size args, so it can read them at launch, as cuBLAS does with its runtime sizes:
- Scope: only template descriptors registered through `tma_descriptor()` take launch-time dims; it marks them with `launch_dims`, except under `cpp_wrapper`, whose C++ launcher builds descriptors from integer dims only (C++ wrapper support is D128275486). Pointwise/reduction host-TMA descriptors still resolve to integers only.
- Validation: a dim is accepted if it parses (`ast.parse(..., mode="eval")`) as integer arithmetic over the kernel's integer args passed at launch (signature `i32`/`i64`/`u32`/`u64`, not constexpr): int literals, those names, `+ - * //`, unary `-`. The launcher gets `ast.unparse` of it. True division, calls, attributes, tensor args and anything else do not resolve, so the descriptor stays in-kernel as before.
- One decision: `_create_compile_meta` decides which args are compiled as `tensordesc<>` and records their resolved dims in `compile_meta["host_tma_descriptors"]`; both launchers (`TensorDescriptor` per launch, and the static launcher's cached expander) build exactly those, and raise if a launch-time dim names an arg the launcher does not receive instead of passing a raw tensor. Compile results cached before this resolve integer dims as before.
- Cache: the static launcher's descriptor cache keys on (address, shape, strides), since with launch-time dims the same buffer can come back with a different shape, and keeps the last 4 encodings per descriptor position (LRU), so alternating sizes do not re-encode every launch.
- `HOST_TMA_SYMBOLIC_DIMS = True` lets template authors detect the support.

TLX Hopper template time measured by Inductor max-autotune under a dynamic M (H100, us):

| GEMM | static M | dynamic M, device descriptors | dynamic M, this change |
|---|---|---|---|
| addmm 600x256->256 | 6.8 | 8.2 | 6.9 |
| addmm 220x256->256 | 6.8 | 8.0 | 6.8 |
| addmm 600x128->3536 | 9.1 | 10.4 | 9.3 |
| addmm 600x2048->2048 | 18.4 | 20.5 | 19.0 |
| addmm 600x2560->1280 | 18.1 | 19.2 | 18.1 |
| addmm 600x2048->256 | 11.6 | 13.2 | 11.9 |
| addmm 600x960->256 | 9.5 | 10.8 | 9.8 |

Test Plan:
Tests in `TritonHostSideTMATestCUDA`:
- `test_host_tma_template_dynamic_dim` (static and Python launchers): a minimal `TritonTemplate` that TMA-loads an input through `tma_descriptor()` with `HOST_SIDE_TMA`, M marked dynamic; two sizes run through one compiled kernel, numerics match, and the launcher builds the descriptor from `[ks0, 128]`.
- `test_host_tma_resolve_launch_dims`: integer arithmetic over int args resolves; `ks0 / 2`, `2ks0`, `ks0(ks1)`, `ks0.bit_length()`, `ks0 ** 2`, a tensor arg, an unknown name, a newline and `__import__` do not.
- `test_host_tma_launchers_reuse_compile_decision`: both launchers emit the compile-time dims as code, and raise when a launch-time dim's arg is missing.
- `test_host_tma_descriptor_cache_keys_on_shape`: a new shape re-encodes, alternating shapes reuse their encodings, and the least recently used is evicted past 4.

```
buck2 test mode/opt -c fbcode.nvcc_arch=h100a fbcode//caffe2/test/inductor:torchinductor_strided_blocks -- --regex TritonHostSideTMATestCUDA
```
H100: Pass 113, Fail 2. The two failures (`test_reduction_padded_output_tiling_cuda`, `test_3d_reduction_with_broadcast_cuda`) fail the same way without this change.

End to end through the TLX Hopper templates (`test_torchtlx_templates.py -r test_dynamic_m`, mm/addmm with M marked dynamic, a second M through the same compiled kernel, A's descriptor built on the host with shape `['ks0', ...]`): Ran 4, OK.

## Agent details (if applicable)
Developed with assistance from Claude Opus 5.5.

> Part of #154444. Depends on #201224.
> 
> Ports ideep's **deprecated** `convolution_forward::compute_v2` into `aten/src/ATen/native/mkldnn/detail/Conv.{h,cpp}` (namespace `at::native::mkldnn`). Its only caller is `ConvPrepack.cpp`, which backs the `mkldnn_prepacked::conv2d_*` ops used by the TorchScript TensorExpr fuser. The port is line-for-line and changes no behavior: it still takes `ideep::tensor` / `ideep::attr_t` and uses ideep's engine, stream and primitive cache.
> 
> This is the third of three convolution PRs (split for size). It adds to the forward port's `detail/Conv.{h,cpp}`.
> 
> ### Ported
> Public (`detail/Conv.h`), each with ideep's `// DEPRECATED` comment:
> - `convolution_forward_compute_v2`: with and without bias.
> 
> File-local (`detail/Conv.cpp`), same names as in ideep:
> - `conv_deconv_utils::prepare_parameters`: the quantization overload (scales and zero points).
> - `compute_dispatch`: the scales/zero-points overload.
> 
> ideep routes `compute_v2` through these int8-capable functions even for fp32. `ConvPrepack` always passes empty scales and zero points, so only their fp32 branches run today. They are kept line-for-line and will be reused by the quantized-conv port. The call chain is the same as ideep's: `compute_v2` → scales/zero-points `compute_dispatch<with_bias, true, true>` → int8 `prepare_parameters` → `get_primitive_desc` / `do_compute`. The last two come from the forward PR.
> 
> ### Call sites switched
> - `mkldnn/ConvPrepack.cpp`: `compute_v2` with and without bias.
> 
> ### Dropped (no ATen callers / unused)
> - `compute_v2`'s `algorithm`, `prop_kind`, `lowp_kind` and `engine` parameters. ATen never passes them; the internal `compute_dispatch` defaults, identical to ideep's, apply.
> - The unused local `weights_zero_point` in the int8 `prepare_parameters`. ideep has it unused too; it is hidden there because ideep's headers are included as system headers, but here it fails `WERROR` builds.
> 
> ### Other changes
> - `IDEEP_ENFORCE` becomes a debug-only `dnnl::error::wrap_c_api(...)` under `#ifndef NDEBUG`, as in ideep.
> - Called directly from ideep for now: `ideep::utils::get_compatible_dilates`, `ideep::utils::group_dims`, `ideep::utils::tensor_scale_mask`, `ideep::utils::tensor_zp_mask`, `ideep::utils::conv_weight_scale_mask`, `ideep::IDEEP_DEF_SCALE`.
> 
> ### Testing
> - **Coverage:** `test_mkldnn_fusion.py` and `test_freezing.py -k mkldnn` call the ported `compute_v2` 40 times (20 with bias, 20 without). I checked this with temporary instrumentation, which is not part of the PR.
> - **oneDNN verbose logs** (`ONEDNN_VERBOSE=1`, timings stripped, sorted counts) are identical before and after:

>  - `quantization/core/test_quantized_op.py -k "qconv and pt2e and not fp8"`: 257 distinct lines.
>

title: [CUDA] Fix dropout Philox offset under-reservation for vectorized kernels
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #202606

Fixes #202370

`dropout_cuda` reserved Philox offset assuming each thread draws 4 random values per 4 elements. Two vectorized paths of `fused_dropout_kernel_vec` drew more, so the next RNG call reused values this call had consumed.

Below, `T` is the total number of threads launched (capped at what fits on the GPU at once).

`VEC=8`: contiguous half/bf16 inputs with a 16-byte-aligned data pointer and numel divisible by 8 (CUDA since #145746; ROCm before that). Each iteration draws 8 values, but `4 * ceil(numel / 4T)` were reserved, which falls short whenever `ceil(numel / 4T)` is odd, e.g. any `numel <= 4T`. The reservation is now computed after the vector width is chosen, using `max(vec_size, 4)` values per `vec_size * T` elements.

`VEC=2`: contiguous fp64 inputs, fp32 aligned to 8 but not 16 bytes, half/bf16 aligned to 4 but not 8 bytes, or numel divisible by 2 but not 4. The `gridxvec_loop_state` toggle was meant to share one `curand_uniform4` across two iterations, but it was only flipped inside the branch that requires it set, so every iteration drew 4 values for 2 elements, overrunning the reservation whenever `numel > 2T`.

Fix for both is a refactor of the vectorized dropout kernel that handles varying vectorization sizes in a straightforward way.

**NB: For a given seed, we have the following behavior changes post-fix:**

```
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Path  │  This call's mask  │  Generator offset advance  │
  │  │  │  (affects later random ops)  │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Unvectorized, VEC=4  │ unchanged  │ unchanged  │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ VEC=8 (aligned half/bf16; CUDA  │ unchanged  │ changes only when ⌈numel/4T⌉ is │
  │ and ROCm)  │  │  odd (+4 per call)  │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ VEC=2 (fp64, misaligned, numel  │ changes only when numel > 2T, │  │
  │ ≡ 2 mod 4)  │  and only elements past the  │ unchanged  │
  │  │ first 2T  │  │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ VEC=16 (ROCm, 1-byte dtypes;  │  │ changes unless ⌈numel/4T⌉ is a  │
  │ not currently reachable for  │ unchanged  │ multiple of 4 (+4, +8 or +12  │
  │ dropout)  │  │ per call)  │
  └─────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘
```

title: [hub] Lock the cache when downloading checkpoints and repos
body:
---

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Fixes #68320

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

The issue was that when multiple processes tried to download the same model weights or GitHub repository at the same time, they could download the same files multiple times or interfere with each other, causing errors. I fixed this by adding `FileLock` in both download functions, so only one process downloads the files while the others wait and reuse the downloaded files. I also added concurrent tests to verify that only one download happens and the files are stored correctly.

## Agent details (if applicable)

> The following was produced by Claude Code (AI assistant) and reviewed by me.
>
> **Root cause.** `load_state_dict_from_url` and `_get_cache_or_reload` check `os.path.exists` and then populate the cache with no coordination, so every process sharing the cache downloads. For repos each process also `_remove_if_exists`es the shared zip, the extracted directory and `repo_dir` while others use them, and `shutil.move` into an already-created `repo_dir` nests the repo inside it. On Windows the checkpoint `shutil.move` falls back to a non-atomic copy over a file another process may be reading.
>
> **Fix.** Both functions take `torch.utils._filelock.FileLock` on `<cache entry>.lock` and re-check the cache after acquiring it. The cached fast path never touches the lock. An OS lock (`flock`/`msvcrt`) was chosen over `FileBaton` because it is released when the holding process dies.
>
> **Tests.** Two offline tests in `test/test_hub.py` (`file://` URLs, 4 threads, slowed-down `download_url_to_file`) assert a single download and a correct `repo_dir` layout. Both fail without the `torch/hub.py` change and pass with it. Across 4 spawned processes, a local repro went from 4 downloads to 1.
>
> ```
> python -m pytest test/test_hub.py -k concurrent -v  # 2 passed
> python -m pytest test/test_hub.py  # 20 passed, 5 skipped (network/torchvision/stdin, unrelated)
> ruff check / ruff format --check / mypy torch/hub.py  # clean
> ```
>
> **Related.** The open docs-only PR #195294 documents the rank-0 workaround; this PR fixes the underlying race.
>
> **Out of scope.** The repo zip is still named after the branch only (`<hub_dir>/main.zip`), so two *different* repos on the same branch populating the cache at the same instant could still collide. That's a separate, pre-existing issue.

title: Fix use-after-free in clone_symvec when sizes/strides alias the destination
body:
Fixes #202604

Fixes a heap-use-after-free in `c10::clone_symvec()` when the source aliases the destination.

### Problem

`TensorImpl::set_sizes_and_strides(SymIntArrayRef sizes, SymIntArrayRef strides, ...)` copies the new symbolic sizes/strides with `clone_symvec(src, dst)`, which calls `dst.clear()` before reading `src`. If `src` aliases `dst`, i.e. a tensor's own `sym_sizes()`/`sym_strides()` are passed back in, `clear()` destroys the `SymInt`s that `src` still refers to.

`squeeze_(Tensor& self, int64_t dim)` does exactly this when the squeezed dim isn't 1:

```cpp
self.as_strided__symint(self.sym_sizes(), self.sym_strides());
```

So `squeeze_(dim)` on a tensor with symbolic sizes (e.g. a FakeTensor under a `ShapeEnv`, as in `torch.compile` with dynamic shapes) reads freed memory and segfaults in practice:

```
c10::clone_symvec()
c10::TensorImpl::set_sizes_and_strides()
at::native::setStrided<>()
at::native::as_strided__symint()
...
at::native::squeeze_()
```

### Fix

`clone_symvec()` now clones into a temporary `SymDimVector` and then move-assigns it into `dst`, so it is safe when `src` aliases `dst`. This fixes all such callers, not just `squeeze_`.

### Test

Adds `SymIntTest.SetSymbolicSizesAndStridesFromOwnSizesAndStrides` to `c10/test/core/SymInt_test.cpp`: it sets symbolic sizes/strides on a `TensorImpl` (which holds the only references to the `SymNode`s), calls `set_sizes_and_strides(impl->sym_sizes(), impl->sym_strides())`, and checks the sizes/strides are preserved. Without the fix, the test fails under ASan with `heap-use-after-free` in `c10::clone_symvec`; with the fix it passes. We found and verified this in Google's internal build of PyTorch, where in-place `squeeze_` on FakeTensors with symbolic dims crashed.

title: [ROCm] Re-evaluate the addmm Lt disable on every call
body:
## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Fixes #186873

Supported by @jeffdaily

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

On ROCm, whether addmm uses hipBLASLt depends on the preferred BLAS backend, which can be changed at runtime, but that decision was cached on the first addmm call. A process whose first addmm ran under hipBLAS never used hipBLASLt for addmm again, even after switching the preferred backend to hipBLASLt. The decision is now made on every call.

## Agent details (if applicable)

Problem: on ROCm, if the first addmm in a process runs while the preferred BLAS backend is rocBLAS (or CK, or on a device without hipBLASLt), later addmm calls never take the Lt path, even after `torch.backends.cuda.preferred_blas_library("cublaslt")`. In CI this makes `test_mm_submatrix_offline_tunableop` record 8 GEMMs instead of 10 whenever an earlier test in the shard ran matmul under cublas (#186873).

Cause: `addmm_out_cuda_impl` caches `isGloballyDisabledAddmmCudaLt()` in a function-local static. On ROCm that function depends on the device and on the preferred backend. The existing ROCm re-check is OR-ed into the cached value, so it can add a disable but never clear a latched one.

Change: evaluate `isGloballyDisabledAddmmCudaLt()` on every call and drop the static and the ROCm re-check. On CUDA the function only compares an env var that it already reads once into its own static, so the result is unchanged. New ROCm-only test `test_addmm_lt_follows_blas_backend_switch` runs linear+bias under cublas, switches to cublaslt, and checks with TunableOp that the GemmAndBias path ran; it uses a subprocess so that its addmm is the first in the process, and skips on devices where hipBLASLt is unsupported.

Test plan (done with Claude, MI355X): the new test fails before and passes after; `test_mm_submatrix_offline_tunableop` fails with "Expected 10 but got 8" after `test_matmul_small_brute_force_1d_Nd` before the fix and passes after; the tunableop and addmm tests pass (43, 559 and 917).
```
python test/test_linalg.py -k test_addmm_lt_follows_blas_backend_switch
python test/test_linalg.py -k test_matmul_small_brute_force_1d_Nd_cuda_float32 -k test_mm_submatrix_offline_tunableop_cuda_float32
python test/test_linalg.py -k tunableop
python test/test_linalg.py -k addmm

```

title: [ROCm] Use wall_clock64 for torch.cuda._sleep on gfx12
body:
## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Supported by @jeffdaily 

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

spin_kernel uses wall_clock64() on gfx11 and clock64() on other AMD GPUs. On gfx1250, clock64() reads the shader cycle counter of the CU that runs the wave. These counters are not synchronized across CUs and their rate follows the shader clock, so the spin length is wrong when the wave resumes on another CU or the clock changes. On gfx1250, 100 ms sleeps took 13 to 368 ms. Use wall_clock64() on gfx12 too. This also switches gfx1200/gfx1201 (RDNA4), where clock64() also follows the shader clock (#197541); not tested on RDNA4. get_cycles_per_ms() calibrates with the same kernel, so callers that use it need no change. Hard-coded cycle counts now sleep longer on gfx12, as they already do on gfx11.

title: [PyObject dispatch] Reuse DispatchKeySet objects across calls
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #202588
* #202587
* #202586

* #202583

* #202571
* #202570
* #202569
* #202568
* #202567
* #202566

PyObject dispatch builds a new Python DispatchKeySet (a pybind11 instance) on
every call that hands a key set to Python: every call into a Python kernel
registered with_keyset, and every redispatch fallback to the C++ entry point.
Creating and destroying that instance costs ~0.5 us on its own, and ~1.5 us
inside a custom_op's grad path. Every custom_op call with an input that
requires grad pays it, because its Autograd kernel takes the key set.

Python can't change a DispatchKeySet: its operators, add and remove all
return new ones, and the class allows no new attributes. So calls with the
same key set can share an object. A new helper
(pyobject_dispatch_key_set_object) keeps a 4-entry per-thread cache from raw
key set value to Python object, replaced round-robin, and both places use
it. A thread sees few distinct key sets at a time; the Autograd kernel of an
op called repeatedly almost always gets the same one. The cached objects are
deliberately never released at thread exit, as a thread can outlive the
interpreter.

Test Plan:

```
python -m pytest test/test_custom_ops.py -k test_pyobject_dispatch_passes_keyset_to_python_kernel
python -m pytest test/test_custom_ops.py -n 8
python -m pytest test/test_python_dispatch.py
python -m pytest test/test_overrides.py -n 16

title: [PyObject dispatch] Record calls for the profiler without leaving the fast path
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* #202588
* __->__ #202587
* #202586
* #202585
* #202584

* #202570
* #202569
* #202568
* #202567
* #202566

While any RecordFunction callback is registered, every call that could take
the PyObject dispatch fast path goes through the C++ Dispatcher instead.
That includes a running profiler and an always-on sampled observer. A no-op
custom_op then costs ~3.7 us instead of ~1.3 us, because only
Dispatcher::callBoxed records calls. An earlier commit in this stack made the
fast path hand such calls over, checking with at::hasCallbacks() so that
callBoxed samples each call exactly once.

The fast path now records calls itself, as callBoxed does:
- It samples the callbacks (at::getStepCallbacksUnlessEmpty) once it has
  taken the call: after normalizing the arguments and computing the key set.
  Calls it hands to the C++ Dispatcher are sampled once, there: a
  __torch_function__ handoff, the skip flag, and arguments it can't
  normalize.
- When a sample hits and the op is observed, it records around the dispatch
  with Dispatcher::runRecordFunction, which this makes public. "Observed"
  comes from c10::ObservedOperators, as OperatorEntry computes it. Inputs
  are converted to IValues only when a callback asks for them, and outputs
  likewise.
- The direct call into C++ kernels now uses OperatorHandle::redispatchBoxed
  with the key set the fast path computed. callBoxed would record the call a
  second time, and this also skips recomputing the key set.

One difference from the C++ Dispatcher path: callbacks run with the GIL held.
The C++ entry point releases it before callBoxed.

Alternative: copying runRecordFunction's two lines into python_dispatch.cpp
would keep the Dispatcher's API as it is. But it would duplicate the rule
for which sequence number ties a call to its autograd node.

Test Plan:

```
python -m pytest test/test_custom_ops.py -k "test_pyobject_dispatch_samples_callbacks_once or test_pyobject_dispatch_records_profiler_events"

title: [custom_op] Don't pass Metadata through autograd.Function.apply
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* #202588
* #202587
* __->__ #202586
* #202585
* #202584
* #202583
* #202582
* #202581
* #202580
* #202579
* #202578
* #202577
* #202576
* #202575
* #202574
* #202573
* #202572
* #202571
* #202570
* #202569
* #202568
* #202567
* #202566

On the grad path, a custom_op's autograd kernel passes its autograd.Function
(Generated) one extra, non-Tensor input: a Metadata object holding the
dispatch keyset and the keyword-only arguments. forward needs both, and it
only gets what's passed to apply, which turns kwargs into positional inputs
too. Autograd then treats Metadata as a real input, and custom_op pays to
build it and to hide it again:
- forward builds a dataclass (~160 ns) and splits it back off the args;
- apply and the autograd engine handle one more input;
- backward hides the extra input: it slices it off ctx.needs_input_grad and
  restores it in a finally (~200 ns), and pads every result with a None.
In a training-style forward+backward loop, a custom op costs ~15 us more than
an equivalent hand-written autograd.Function, and this is ~3 us of it.

The autograd kernel now pushes (keyset, keyword_only_args) onto a per-thread
stack (_forward_inputs) and calls Generated.apply with only the op's
arguments; forward pops the entry first thing. Generated's inputs are now
exactly the op's, so backward no longer adjusts needs_input_grad or pads its
result; it keeps the checks on how many gradients the formula returned.

It's per-thread because custom ops can run on several threads at once. It's
a stack because code between the push and forward could call custom ops
itself; those push and pop their own entries before forward pops this one.
If apply raises before forward runs, the kernel removes its entry in a
finally, so no later forward can take it. That happens under torch.func
transforms today: apply raises "must override the setup_context
staticmethod" there, before calling forward, as it did before this change.
An order where entries cross would need a task switch on one thread between
the push and forward (e.g. greenlets).

Alternative: keeping Metadata as an input and generating a fixed-arity
backward wrapper per op would save part of the backward cost without the
handoff, but none of forward's.

body:

Every custom_op call spends ~420 ns in OpOverload.__call__ before it
reaches the PyObject dispatch fast path. The cost is a Python frame
forwarding *args/**kwargs, plus a call to
torch._C._peek_should_skip_torch_function() (~100 ns). That check sends the
call to the C++ entry point when a __torch_function__ handler has set the
one-hop flag to skip __torch_function__. CustomOpDef.__call__ adds its own
frame on top. Every other OpOverload whose op uses the fast path pays for
the same check.

The fast path now checks the flag itself, first thing, and routes such
calls to the C++ entry point as OpOverload.__call__ did. Its own handling of
the flag further on (removing the Python key, consuming the flag) was dead
on this path, since OpOverload.__call__ never let such calls reach it. That
handling is gone from pyobject_dispatch_vectorcall; the redispatch path
keeps it.

OpOverload.__call__ is now just `return self._op(*args, **kwargs)`. Both
versions of CustomOpDef.__call__, the generated one and the generic one,
call `self._opoverload._op(...)` directly.

Dynamo traces CustomOpDef.__call__, and treated the `_op` call as an
unsupported method call, which is a graph break. TorchInGraphFunctionVariable
now treats calling `_op` on an OpOverload as calling the op, which is all
that OpOverload.__call__ does. A comment there says it has to stay that
way.

Once this was in, clang-tidy flagged a possible null `kwnames` in
pyobject_dispatch_handle_torch_function. It can't be null when there are
kwargs, but the code now checks.

Alternative: CustomOpDef.__call__ could keep calling the OpOverload and
branch on torch.compiler.is_compiling(), which would avoid the Dynamo change.
But that call costs ~80-100 ns per call in eager, about a quarter of what
this saves.

body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):

A custom_op that mutates any of its arguments costs ~5.3 us per call,
against ~1.7 us for a functional one. The difference is its ADInplaceOrView
kernel, a Python function (adinplaceorview_impl). On every call:
- PyObject dispatch builds a pybind DispatchKeySet to pass to it;
- it bumps each mutated argument's version counter through Python helpers;
- it masks the keyset with a pybind `&`;
- it calls OpOverload.redispatch to continue.
The generic C++ kernel for that key, autogradNotImplementedInplaceOrViewFallback,
can't replace it: it only bumps mutated returns, not mutated inputs.

For a mutable op that returns no views, custom_op now registers a C++
kernel, MutationVersionBumpKernel, through a new private Library binding
(register_mutation_version_bump). It bumps the version counter of each
mutated Tensor, including those in a Tensor[] or Tensor?[]. Like
torch.autograd.graph.increment_version, it skips None and inference
tensors, which have no version counter. Then it redispatches past
ADInplaceOrView, as the Python kernel did.

PyObject dispatch recognizes the kernel, as it does PythonKernelHolder's
Autograd skip. It does the same bumps on its PyObject arguments, instead of
handing the call to the C++ Dispatcher. Mutable view ops keep the Python
kernel, which relies on the generic fallback's view handling.

Alternative: keeping the Python kernel and making its pieces cheaper, as
was done for the Autograd kernel's redispatch, would still pay for a call
into Python and a keyset object on every call.

```

of mutated Tensor, Tensor?, Tensor[] and Tensor?[] arguments (with a None
element), with PyObject dispatch on and off. With it off, the C++ kernel does
the bumps. The existing test_mutated* tests cover the version bumps of real
mutating kernels. I also checked by hand, on both paths, two more things:
autograd still raises when an op mutates a tensor saved for backward, and

body:

With a TorchFunctionMode active, every custom_op call costs ~6 us instead of
~1.7 us. torch.set_default_device() is one common way to get there: it
installs DeviceContext. The mode itself is cheap (~0.2-0.4 us); the cost is
the route to it.

The PyObject dispatch fast path hands any call that needs __torch_function__
handling to the C++ entry point, the pybind11 binding from
_get_operation_overload. That route does a lot before it reaches the
handlers:
- it converts the arguments into py::args and py::kwargs;
- it builds std::strings for the namespace, op and overload names;
- _maybe_handle_torch_function looks the OpOverload up again, through
  `import torch` and four attribute lookups;
- only then does it call handle_torch_function_no_python_arg_parser.
The whole handoff costs ~4.3 us for a custom op, against ~1.8 us for an aten
op like torch.neg.

The fast path now calls handle_torch_function_no_python_arg_parser itself.
It collects the overloaded arguments with the same helpers, in the same
order, as _maybe_handle_torch_function. It builds the args tuple and kwargs
dict from its vectorcall arguments. Handlers get the OpOverload as func, so
the fast-path object keeps a weak reference to it, passed in by
_enable_pyobj_dispatch; a strong one would be a cycle, since the OpOverload
holds the fast-path object.

In two cases the call still goes to the C++ entry point. One is when no
handler applies after all: the fast path's check also flags non-Tensor
arguments, which _maybe_handle_torch_function ignores. The other is when
the OpOverload is gone.

One difference remains. When every handler returns NotImplemented, the
TypeError names the op by the OpOverload's __module__ and __name__
("torch.ops.<ns>.<op>.default"). The C++ entry point names it
"torch.ops<ns>.<op>", without a dot after "ops".

Alternative: making the C++ entry point's handling cheaper, for example by
caching the OpOverload lookup, would also help ops without PyObject
dispatch. But it would keep the pybind11 argument conversion and the extra
hop.

```

It also checks that the caller gets the same result and result type. It
covers a mode, a kwarg, and a subclass with __torch_function__, both as an
argument and inside a Tensor[]. It also checks that a handler's own return
value is passed through, and the TypeError when every handler returns
NotImplemented. With the fast path's kwargs left out of the handoff, the
test fails.

body:

Entering `with torch._C._AutoDispatchBelowAutograd():` costs ~880 ns, and
nearly all of it is pybind11 overhead rather than the guard itself. It's
bound as a pybind11 class (py_context_manager_DEPRECATED), so creating it,
calling __enter__ and __exit__, and destroying it each go through pybind11's
call dispatch and instance bookkeeping. A custom_op's autograd forward
enters it on every call. So does the autograd path of most higher-order ops
(cond, map, scan, while_loop, flex_attention, invoke_subgraph, ...).

It's now a plain C extension type whose object holds the guard. It keeps the
semantics of the binding it replaces:
- creating it takes the guard, so it also works without `with`, as
  test_incorrect_schema_mutation uses it;
- __exit__ releases the guard, and so does destroying the object if
  __exit__ wasn't called;
- __enter__ returns None, and it takes no arguments.
The type can't be subclassed; nothing subclasses it.

Alternatives: a plain-type version of py_context_manager would do the same
for every guard bound that way. This changes only the one used on hot paths.

Test Plan:

```
python -m pytest test/test_python_dispatch.py -k test_auto_dispatch_below_autograd_restores_tls

A custom_op's autograd forward spends ~2.5 us per call just redispatching
below Autograd, in three Python-level steps:
- it masks the keyset with a pybind operator, `keyset &
  _C._after_autograd_keyset` (~650 ns), which creates another pybind
  DispatchKeySet;
- it calls OpOverload.redispatch, a Python layer (~450 ns);
- the PyObject redispatch then converts the keyset back to C++ by calling
  its raw_repr() method.

The PyObject dispatcher now has a third callable, redispatch_below_autograd
(keyset, *args, **kwargs). It does what redispatch(keyset &
_after_autograd_keyset, ...) under _AutoDispatchBelowAutograd does, in C++,
as PythonKernelHolder already does when it skips an Autograd kernel. The
custom op autograd kernel's forward and redispatch_no_grad call it directly
when PyObject dispatch is on, and keep the old code otherwise. forward keeps
its own `with _C._AutoDispatchBelowAutograd()`, because setup_context runs
under it too.

Every redispatch now reads the keyset with a pybind cast instead of calling
raw_repr(), which makes OpOverload.redispatch ~600 ns cheaper for any op. A
first argument that isn't a DispatchKeySet now raises TypeError instead of
AttributeError. The __torch_function__ fallback passes the keyset it
computed (masked, for redispatch_below_autograd) to the C++ redispatch.

Alternatives: an OpOverload.redispatch_below_autograd method would keep the
Python layer this skips. Applying the guard only in C++ and dropping
forward's `with` would leave setup_context outside it.

```

A custom_op called with an input that requires grad spends ~2-8 us per call
filling in default arguments for setup_context. The cost is in
utils.fill_defaults, which walks op._schema.arguments, a pybind property
that builds a new list of Argument objects on every access. fill_defaults
reads it twice per argument, plus each Argument's kwarg_only, name and
default_value. A no-op op with one argument pays ~2 us; one with two
defaulted arguments pays ~8 us.

make_autograd_impl now computes the positional and keyword-only defaults
once, and forward appends the missing ones. The result is the same as
fill_defaults: the positional arguments followed by the defaults of the
omitted ones, and the keyword-only arguments in schema order. A list default
is mutable, and fill_defaults gives each call a new list, so schemas with a
list default still use fill_defaults.

A custom_op's device kernel (backend_impl) spends more time checking the
user function's result than calling the function: about 1 us of a ~2.6 us
no-op call. It redoes work whose answer never changes on every call:
schema._is_view_op() (~175 ns, a pybind call), and building get_module
(~90 ns), which only error messages use. The aliasing check also costs
~560 ns: a Python wrapper around _C._any_output_is_alias_to_input_or_output,
which builds a std::unordered_set (a heap allocation per tensor) and calls
its visitor through std::function.

_make_backend_impl now decides once which check applies (aliasing, inplace,
out, or none for view ops, as before), builds get_module once, and calls the
C++ aliasing check directly. The error text moves to
utils._aliasing_constraint_error, which _c_check_aliasing_constraint (still
used by AOTAutograd) uses too.

_any_output_is_alias_to_input_or_output now collects the storages into
SmallVectors, and sorts and binary-searches them instead of hashing.
Sorting keeps long Tensor lists at O(n log n), where a linear scan, the
simpler choice for the usual few tensors, would be quadratic. Its visitors,
shared with _any_requires_grad, take the lambda as a template parameter
instead of a std::function, and skip copying an empty kwargs dict. It also
accepts a single output without a tuple, so callers no longer build one.

body:

* #202566

Most torch.library.custom_op calls don't use the PyObject dispatch fast path,
and take about twice as long as the ones that do. The fast path only accepts
calls that pass every argument positionally as a Tensor or Tensor[]
(TODO(#187974)). Anything else falls back to the C++ Dispatcher: an int or
float argument, None for a Tensor?, a keyword argument, or an omitted argument
with a default. A no-op custom_op taking (Tensor, int) costs ~6.1 us per call,
against ~2.7 us for one taking just a Tensor.

The fast path has to give the Python kernel exactly what the C++ Dispatcher
would. That converts the arguments to IValues and back
(parseIValuesToPyArgsKwargs). The round trip fills in omitted arguments from
their defaults and converts values to the schema's types. It passes the
positional arguments up to the last one that isn't equal to its default, and
the kwarg-only arguments that aren't equal to their defaults as kwargs.

The fast path now does the same without IValues when no value needs
converting. It places the arguments by position and name, fills in defaults,
and checks that every value already has the Python type the round trip would
produce: an exact int in int64 range for an int or SymInt, an exact float, a
bool, a str, a dtype, layout or device, or an int, float or bool for a Scalar.
For a list type it accepts a list or tuple of those and copies it into a new
list. Anything else, including bad arguments, still falls back, so errors
still come from the C++ Dispatcher. See NOTE [PyObject dispatch argument
normalization].

Omitted arguments are filled in from per-operator default objects that every
call shares. A default list (int[] or float[]) passed to the kernel is copied
each time, as the C++ Dispatcher builds a new list from the IValue on every
call; otherwise a kernel that mutates it would change the default for later
calls. That happens when a call omits a defaulted list but passes a later
positional argument that isn't at its default. Lists are the only mutable
defaults the fast path fills in.

For which arguments go positionally and which as kwargs, the fast path
uses the helper the C++ Dispatcher's side (OperatorArgsKwargsView) uses,
splitPythonKernelArgs, so the two can't drift apart. Whether an argument equals its default is decided the way IValues
compare: same type and equal. For some arguments the default isn't available
as a Python object without converting it (a Device default, for example). A
call that passes or omits such an argument falls back. The per-operator table
(PyObjectDispatchSchema) gains the argument information this needs. C++
kernels called directly from the fast path get the normalized arguments, so
those calls can now include non-Tensor arguments too.

Calls to an operator that only takes Tensors, with all of them passed
positionally, are checked for first and skip all of this. The calls the fast
path already handled are no slower.

One difference is left: for an immutable value such as a float, the kernel
gets the caller's own object, where the C++ Dispatcher would pass an equal
copy. Tensors already worked this way.

Alternative: the fast path could also do conversions itself, such as a str to
a Device, a SymInt or a numpy scalar. That means reproducing
torch::jit::toIValue's rules. Those calls are less common, so this change
falls back to the C++ Dispatcher for them instead.

Test Plan:

```
python -m pytest test/test_custom_ops.py -k test_pyobject_dispatch_normalizes_args
python -m pytest test/test_custom_ops.py -k test_pyobject_dispatch_copies_list_defaults
python -m pytest test/test_custom_ops.py
python -m pytest test/test_python_dispatch.py
python -m pytest test/dynamo/test_misc.py test/export/test_export.py test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py test/inductor/test_compiled_autograd.py test/functorch/test_aotdispatch.py -k custom_op
python -m pytest test/test_autograd.py -k custom
python -m pytest test/functorch/test_eager_transforms.py -k "custom or functionalize"
python -m pytest test/test_fake_tensor.py
python -m pytest test/test_functionalization.py
python -m pytest test/test_proxy_tensor.py
```

test_pyobject_dispatch_normalizes_args defines ops taking int, SymInt, float,
bool, str, Tensor?, Tensor[], Tensor?[], int[], float[], ScalarType?, Layout?,
Device? and Scalar arguments, including kwarg-only and defaulted ones. It makes
47 calls passing arguments positionally, by keyword, omitted, equal to their
defaults and with the wrong type. For each call it checks that the kernel gets
the same args and kwargs (Tensors by identity), or that the call raises the
same error, with the fast path on and off. A second part checks that such calls
really take the fast path: the kernel gets the caller's own float object, which
it doesn't through the C++ Dispatcher. test_pyobject_dispatch_copies_list_defaults
calls an op with a defaulted int[] twice, with a kernel that appends to the
list, and checks that the second call still sees the default. Everything
passes.

in ns:

OperatorArgsKwargsView's constructor works out which of an operator's
arguments the C++ Dispatcher passes to a Python kernel positionally and which
as kwargs: positionally up to the last positional argument that isn't equal
to its default, and as kwargs the kwarg-only arguments that aren't. The next
commit makes the PyObject dispatch fast path pass non-Tensor arguments,
defaults and kwargs to Python kernels itself, and it has to follow exactly
the same rule, or a kernel would see different arguments depending on the
path a call took.

This moves the rule into a helper, splitPythonKernelArgs in python_variable.h,
that takes the schema and an is_default predicate, and makes
OperatorArgsKwargsView use it. There's no behavior change: the scans are the
same, except that the kwarg-only scan starts from the schema's argument
count rather than the argument vector's size. The constructor already
assumed those are equal, since it indexed the schema's arguments with the
vector's size.

Test Plan:

```
python -m pytest test/test_python_dispatch.py -n 8
python -m pytest test/test_custom_ops.py -n 8
```

Both exercise the C++ Dispatcher's calls into Python kernels and
__torch_dispatch__, with positional, defaulted and kwarg-only arguments.

* #202566

When the PyObject dispatch fast path computes a dispatch key set whose
kernel is a C++ kernel, it hands the call back to Python
(OperatorHandle.redispatch_boxed, through pybind), which converts the
arguments, dispatches, and converts the results. That is slower than not
using the fast path at all: for an aten op with only Tensor arguments,
enabling it adds ~0.8-1.7 us per call. Custom ops reach C++ kernels too,
e.g. the Functionalize kernel under torch.func.functionalize, and this cost
is what stops the fast path from being an option for operators whose
kernels are in C++.

For a top-level dispatch the fast path already has all of the operator's
arguments in schema order, so it now converts them to IValues itself
(argumentToIValue, as the Python entry point does), releases the GIL, and
calls OperatorHandle::callBoxed, then converts the results
(createPyObjectForStack). That is the same work as the Python entry point
(invokeOperatorFromPython) minus its argument parsing and __torch_function__
checks, which the fast path has already done. Redispatches don't have all of
the arguments, and keep going through redispatch_boxed. After the Autograd
kernel is skipped for a call that doesn't need grad, the redispatch below
Autograd still has them and calls C++ kernels directly; callBoxed recomputes
the key set, which excludes Autograd under AutoDispatchBelowAutograd.

Alternatives: calling the KernelFunction for the computed key set directly
(redispatchBoxed) would skip recomputing the key set, but callBoxed is what
the Python entry point calls, and it records the call for profilers (the fast
path hands the whole call to the C++ Dispatcher while those are active
anyway). A Dispatcher API that takes a precomputed key set and does
callBoxed's bookkeeping would allow that.

body:
