* #202567
* #202566

For an op that uses the PyObject dispatch fast path, a Python kernel that
returns the wrong type gives the caller a different result than the C++
Dispatcher would. The fast path returns whatever the kernel returned, while
the C++ Dispatcher converts the return value to IValues and back
(pushPyOutToStack, createPyObjectForStack), which raises for a value of the
wrong type and normalizes the rest: it turns a list into a tuple for
multiple returns, a tuple into a list for a Tensor[] return, and an int into
a float for a float return. So today a kernel that returns 3 for an op
returning Tensor raises through the C++ Dispatcher but hands the caller the
int through the fast path, and one that returns a list for an op with two
Tensor returns hands the caller a list instead of a tuple.

The fast path now normalizes a Python kernel's return value the same way. If
the value already is what the round trip would produce (a Tensor for a
Tensor return, an exact int for an int, a tuple of those for multiple
returns, ...), it is returned as is; a Tensor[] return is copied into a new
list, as the round trip does. Otherwise it runs that exact round trip, so the
result and any error are the same as from the C++ Dispatcher. The return
types come from a per-operator table built when the fast path is set up
(PyObjectDispatchSchema), and the common single-Tensor return is checked
first. The table covers every return type, but the fast path is still only
enabled for ops whose returns are all Tensors; the next commit lifts that.

The one difference left is identity: for an immutable return value that is
already of the right type (a tuple, float, or str), the caller gets the
kernel's own object rather than an equal copy. Tuples of Tensors already
worked this way.

Test Plan:

```
python -m pytest test/test_custom_ops.py -k normalizes_results
python -m pytest test/test_custom_ops.py
```

test_pyobject_dispatch_normalizes_results runs kernels returning both
well-typed and badly typed values for ops returning Tensor and (Tensor,
Tensor), and checks that the caller gets the same types and values (Tensors
by identity) and the same errors with the fast path on and off. Without the
normalization it fails: the op returning Tensor whose kernel returns 3
raises through the C++ Dispatcher and returns the int through the fast path.

Ops with a single Tensor return are no slower: calling the fast-path callable
directly costs 157-168 ns (158-160 ns before), minimum over 30 rounds of 50k
calls, three runs per build.

title: [custom_op] Skip the Autograd kernel when no input requires grad
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* #202588
* #202587

* #202569
* #202568
* #202567
* #202566

Every torch.library.custom_op call runs its Python Autograd kernel
(autograd_impl), even when grad mode is off or no input requires grad, and in
that case the kernel only redispatches below Autograd (redispatch_no_grad).
That hop is most of the call: for a no-op op it costs ~4.4 us of ~7.1 us on
the PyObject dispatch fast path, and ~6.5 us on the C++ Dispatcher path,
where calling a Python kernel also means acquiring the GIL and converting the
arguments to Python and back.

Library.impl gains a private _skip_if_no_grad keyword, passed to the
dispatcher binding and stored on the PythonKernelHolder. It declares that the
kernel only redispatches below Autograd when grad mode is off or no input
requires grad, so both entry points can do that themselves:
PythonKernelHolder::operator() checks the IValues before acquiring the GIL,
and the PyObject fast path checks the PyObjects. Either way they enter
AutoDispatchBelowAutograd and redispatch with keyset & after_autograd_keyset,
which is what redispatch_no_grad does. custom_op registers its Autograd
kernel with the flag. The check is at least as strict as autograd_impl's (it
also looks at kwargs and at Tensors inside lists), so whenever it skips the
kernel, autograd_impl would have taken its no-grad branch. The flag is only
accepted for Autograd keys.

Alternatives: marking the kernel function with an attribute that the holder
looks for works too, but the contract is easier to see as an explicit
registration option. Making it a property of KernelFunction in the core
Dispatcher would cover C++ Autograd kernels as well, but those already make
this decision cheaply. Not registering an Autograd kernel for ops without
register_autograd would change what happens when such an op is
differentiated.

Test Plan:

```
python -m pytest test/test_custom_ops.py -k "test_skip_autograd_kernel_if_no_grad or test_custom_op_kernel_runs_below_autograd_without_grad"
python -m pytest test/test_custom_ops.py
python -m pytest test/test_python_dispatch.py
python -m pytest test/dynamo/test_misc.py test/export/test_export.py test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py test/inductor/test_compiled_autograd.py test/functorch/test_aotdispatch.py -k custom_op
python -m pytest test/test_autograd.py -k custom
```

test_skip_autograd_kernel_if_no_grad checks, with PyObject dispatch on and
off, that an Autograd kernel registered with the flag doesn't run for inputs
that don't require grad (or under no_grad), does run when a Tensor or a
Tensor in a list requires grad, and that the flag is rejected for other
keys; with the flag off, the kernel runs on every call.
test_custom_op_kernel_runs_below_autograd_without_grad checks that a
custom_op kernel using a captured parameter that requires grad still returns
a Tensor that doesn't, i.e. the kernel runs under AutoDispatchBelowAutograd
as before. Everything passes.

Perf: the same no-op custom ops registered with and without the flag in one
process, interleaved, median of 20 rounds of 10k calls, two runs:

```

title: [RecordFunction] Skip the per-call callback check when no callbacks exist
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #202572

Every top-level operator call (Dispatcher::call and Dispatcher::callBoxed)
calls at::getStepCallbacksUnlessEmpty to decide whether to record the call
for the profiler or other observers. In a process with no callbacks
registered, which is the usual case, that still costs an out-of-line call, a
thread-local lookup of the callback cache, an atomic load of the global
callback version, and a decrement of the per-thread sampling countdown, only
to find that nothing is listening. For a no-op operator that is ~8 ns of a
~46 ns dispatch.

getStepCallbacksUnlessEmpty is now inline and first does a relaxed load of
at::detail::num_callback_sources, returning nullopt when it is zero;
otherwise it calls the previous implementation
(detail::getStepCallbacksUnlessEmptySlow), so behavior with callbacks
registered is unchanged. The counter is the number of global callbacks plus
one per thread that has thread-local callbacks. GlobalCallbackManager
updates it when callbacks are added, removed, or cleared. Each thread's
LocalCallbackManager counts itself while its thread-local list is non-empty,
updating on addCallback, removeCallback, clearCallbacks, and setTLS (which is
how thread-local callbacks reach other threads through ThreadLocalState), and
uncounts itself when the thread exits. The count can be too high (e.g.
disabled callbacks), which only means taking the slow path, but never too low.
The load is relaxed: a callback registered on another thread is seen on a
later call, as with the version check the slow path already relies on.
cmake/prioritized_text.txt now lists getStepCallbacksUnlessEmptySlow in place
of getStepCallbacksUnlessEmpty, which is no longer emitted out of line.

Alternatives: a cheaper check could also be a thread-local flag, but a
thread-local lookup across shared libraries is a large part of what this
avoids. Keeping getStepCallbacksUnlessEmpty out of line and adding a separate
inline function would keep its exported symbol for C++ extensions built
against older headers, but every caller would have to switch; PyTorch doesn't
keep C++ ABI compatibility across versions.

Test Plan:

```

body:

Several C++ paths that run on every call copy the at::Tensor they get from
THPVariable_Unpack only to read from it: `auto t = THPVariable_Unpack(obj)`
drops the reference that THPVariable_Unpack returns. Each copy costs ~70-90 ns
here, an intrusive refcount increment and decrement plus the PyObject
preservation bookkeeping on the TensorImpl. The tensor is owned by the Python
object, which the caller keeps alive for the whole call, and none of these
sites keep or mutate the tensor, so a const reference is enough.

The sites are the tensor visitor behind torch._C._any_requires_grad and
torch._C._any_output_is_alias_to_input_or_output, which run on every
torch.library.custom_op call (from its Autograd kernel and its aliasing check;
the visitor's callback now takes const at::Tensor&); torch._C._increment_version,
which runs on every call of a custom op with mutates_args;
TensorPropertyGuardAccessor in Dynamo's guards, checked on every call of a
compiled function that has size/stride/storage-offset guards; and
getPointerFast in Inductor's fast Triton launcher, run for every tensor
argument of every launch.

The same pattern is left alone where it's cold (Tensor.tolist,
`tensor[idx] = tensor`, guard construction) or needs an owned tensor
(indexing, the tensor constructor), and in torch/csrc/mps/Module.cpp, which I
couldn't build. pybind's type_caster<at::Tensor> also copies every tensor
argument of pybind-bound functions; avoiding that needs a different caster
design and isn't part of this change.

body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* #202588
* #202587

* #202584

* #202572
* #202571
* #202570
* __->__ #202569
* #202568
* #202567
* #202566

Every custom op kernel call spends ~830 ns in the layers that keep Dynamo out
of the kernel, ~10% of a no-op op's ~8 us eager call. register_kernel stored
`torch._disable_dynamo(wrapped_fn)`, so a call went through _disable_dynamo's
lazy-import shim, then DisableContext._fn, then wrapped_fn (which checks
set_kernel_enabled), and only then the kernel, each layer forwarding
`*args, **kwargs`.

The shim exists so torch internals can apply the decorator without importing
torch._dynamo while torch is being imported (some custom ops are defined
then), but it stays in the call path after its first call. Now the kernel's
entry in _backend_fns is a stub whose first call imports Dynamo, builds the
wrapper and replaces itself, so later calls reach the wrapper directly. The
set_kernel_enabled check moves into backend_impl, which removes wrapped_fn; a
disabled kernel runs a separately wrapped init fn.

To make that wrapper take the kernel's own parameters without duplicating
Dynamo's logic, DisableContext's wrapper is now generated from one template,
_DISABLE_WRAPPER_TEMPLATE, which is the former body of DisableContext._fn.
DisableContext instantiates it with `*args, **kwargs` (compiled once and
cached); _disabled_wrapper(fn, explicit_signature=True) instantiates it with
fn's parameters via signature_forwarding_code (cached per parameter list).
custom_op calls _disabled_wrapper rather than DisableContext so that a
torch.compile'd kernel isn't unwrapped by innermost_fn. The generated code
looks up set_eval_frame and the other helpers as module globals at call time,
as before, so they can still be patched (test_repros patches
_maybe_set_eval_frame); if fn has a parameter that would shadow one of them it
gets the generic wrapper. The generated code's filename is under torch/, so
Dynamo skips its frames as it did DisableContext._fn's, and linecache shows
its source in tracebacks. Review the template and _disabled_wrapper in
eval_frame.py first, then _kernel_stub and backend_impl in custom_ops.py.

This keeps the Dynamo guard on kernels. #187619 removed it and was reverted
for test_to_nn_LinearCrossEntropyLoss_swap_True_set_grad_False_cuda_float32,
which passes here.

Two visible changes: tracebacks through a disabled function show the
generated frame (`eval_frame.py<disable wrapper(*args, **kwargs)>`,
`return _dynamo_fn(*args, **kwargs)`) instead of eval_frame.py's
`return fn(*args, **kwargs)`, and a custom op kernel error message names the
module as torch._dynamo.eval_frame instead of torch._library.custom_ops (the
kernel's own module would be better; neither is today).

Alternatives: a second copy of the hot path for custom_op would leave
DisableContext untouched, but the two would have to be kept in sync by hand.
Generating a wrapper on every disable() call would cost an exec per
decoration; the generic wrapper is compiled once instead.

body:

* __->__ #202568
* #202567
* #202566

Calling a torch.library.custom_op with a keyword argument costs ~4 us more
than calling it positionally. CustomOpDef.__call__ forwards `*args, **kwargs`
to the OpOverload, and the PyObject dispatch fast path (#187949) falls back to
the C++ dispatcher whenever a call has kwargs. For a no-op op on a devserver,
`f(x, x1=y)` took ~12.9 us, against ~8.8 us positionally.

When the schema is inferred from the function, the decorator now builds a
CustomOpDef subclass whose __call__ is generated from the function's signature,
e.g. `def __call__(_opdef, x, n=<default>): return _opdef._opoverload(x, n)`.
It passes positional parameters positionally, filling in the function's own
default values, so keyword calls stay on the fast path. Python looks up
__call__ on the type, so each op gets its own subclass, and the decorator
instantiates it directly: reassigning __class__ after construction would slow
every attribute lookup on the CustomOpDef, which the call path makes ~10 times.
Positional calls are no faster in a measurable way.

Two details keep Dynamo's behavior unchanged. The generated code is compiled
with this file's filename, at CustomOpDef.__call__'s line numbers, because
Dynamo picks trace rules by filename: code from "<string>" counts as user code,
which Dynamo also compiles as a standalone frame, so a graph break inside the
op call was counted twice (test_data_dependent_compile). Tracebacks then point
at the generic `return self._opoverload(...)` line. And while Dynamo is tracing
the decorator itself (an op defined inside a compiled function), it keeps the
plain CustomOpDef, because Dynamo can't trace the type() call and would fall
back to eager for the whole function
(test_custom_op_defined_inside_without_fake_hard_errors). torch.compiler is
looked up with getattr because some custom ops are defined while torch is
still being imported.

Ops with an explicit schema=, including triton_op, keep the generic __call__,
since the function's signature need not match the schema.

The code that turns a signature into a parameter list and call arguments is
torch/_library/utils.py:signature_forwarding_code, so other generated
forwarders can share it.

Normalizing kwargs inside the C fast path instead would also help callers that
use torch.ops.<ns>.<op>.default directly; that is complementary and still
worth doing. Filling in defaults doesn't help calls that omit a non-Tensor
default yet, because the fast path still rejects non-Tensor arguments.

```

python -m pytest test/dynamo/test_misc.py test/export/test_export.py test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py test/inductor/test_compiled_autograd.py -k custom_op

title: [PyObject dispatch] Record ops for the profiler again
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #202567
* #202572

Ops dispatched through the PyObject fast path, which includes every
torch.library.custom_op since #187949, are missing from torch.profiler traces.
The fast path calls Python kernels directly and never reaches
Dispatcher::callBoxed, which is where the C++ Dispatcher records each call
(RecordFunction) for profilers and other observers.

The fast path now hands the call to the C++ Dispatcher whenever a
RecordFunction callback could run for an operator call on this thread. A new
inline function, at::hasCallbacksForScope(RecordScope::FUNCTION), checks that.
Like getStepCallbacksUnlessEmpty, it first reads the callback counter that the
previous commit adds (at::detail::num_callback_sources), so with no callbacks
registered the check is one relaxed load. Otherwise it reads the per-thread
callback cache that callBoxed's check also reads. That skips callbacks for
other scopes and callbacks turned off with enableRecordFunction(false), without
taking a lock. Redispatches don't check, as the C++ Dispatcher doesn't record
them either. The check doesn't sample callbacks: callBoxed's own check
(at::getStepCallbacksUnlessEmpty) does, so a sampled callback still sees each
call with its probability p. Using that sampling check here as well would
sample twice, recording such calls with probability p^2.

Alternative: the existing at::hasCallbacks() would need no new function. But it
locks the global callback mutex and copies the global callback list on every
call (~40 ns of a ~160 ns call), and it counts callbacks for every scope.

The cost is that while such a callback is registered, calls that could take the
fast path go through the C++ Dispatcher instead, even if the callback samples
rarely. Recording in the fast path itself would avoid that, but it needs the
Dispatcher's runRecordFunction and IValue inputs when a callback asks for them;
that's left for a follow-up.

```

title: [bugfix][custom_op] Run each device's own kernel when registering several at once
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* #202588
* #202587
* #202586
* #202585
* #202584

* #202571
* #202570
* #202569
* #202568
* #202567
* __->__ #202566

When a custom op registers kernels for several device types in one call
(custom_op(..., device_types=("cpu", "cuda")) or
register_kernel(("cpu", "cuda"))), every one of those devices runs the
function registered for the last device type, and is disabled whenever that
one is. So a later register_kernel("cpu") has no effect on CPU, which keeps
running the "cuda" function, and set_kernel_enabled("cuda", False) also
disables the CPU kernel.

The cause is that register_kernel defines two closures inside its loop over
the device types, and both look up device_type in the enclosing scope each
time they run: the dispatcher kernel (backend_impl), which picks the function
to call from _backend_fns, and the wrapper stored there (wrapped_fn), which
checks whether the kernel is disabled. Python closures capture the variable,
not its value, so once the loop has finished every one of them sees the last
device type. Registering the same function for all of them hides this until
a device gets a different one.

Both are now built by methods, _make_backend_impl(device_type) and
_make_backend_fn(device_type, fn), so each has its own device_type; their
bodies are unchanged. Binding the value with a default argument instead would
add a parameter to functions that are called with the operator's own
arguments.

Test Plan:

```
python -m pytest test/test_custom_ops.py -k test_multi_types_register_kernel_for_one
python -m pytest test/test_custom_ops.py
```

test_multi_types_register_kernel_for_one checks both halves. It registers an
op for CPU and CUDA, replaces the CPU kernel, and checks that CPU calls use
the new kernel, that disabling CUDA doesn't affect them, and that disabling
CPU falls back to the original function. Then it registers one function for
CPU and CUDA at once and checks that disabling CUDA doesn't change CPU
calls, while disabling CPU falls back to the op's original function. It runs
without a GPU. Before this change it fails on the first check (the CPU call
returns x + 1 instead of x + 2); with only the dispatcher-kernel half of the
fix, it fails on the second part (disabling CUDA also disables CPU). All of
test_custom_ops.py passes.

title: [FakeTensor] Build plain constructor outputs without the dispatch cache
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* #202564
* #202563
* #202562
* #202561
* __->__ #202560
* #202559
* #202558
* #202557
* #202556
* #202555
* #202554
* #202553
* #202552

Under FakeTensorMode, torch.empty_like(x) costs ~56 us, about the same as
torch.add, though all it has to produce is a new tensor with x's shape, dtype
and device. Every builtin op goes through the dispatch cache, and a cache hit
first builds a key from every property of every input (~17 us here), only to
find an entry that amounts to "a contiguous tensor with x's metadata". The
general path, used on a miss, is worse (~240 us): it runs the generic checks
and then empty_like's decomposition. Building the output directly takes ~11
us. These ops are common in the fake impls of custom ops, which always run,
so a custom op whose fake impl calls empty_like pays this on every call.

FakeTensorMode.dispatch now checks fast_constructor_impls (in fake_impls.py)
before the cache. Its entries cover the like constructors (empty_like,
zeros_like, ones_like, full_like, rand_like, randn_like), the new_* methods
(new_empty, new_zeros, new_ones, new_full), and empty.memory_format,
empty_strided, zeros and ones. Each builds a meta tensor of the right size,
dtype and strides under in_kernel_invocation_manager and wraps it in a
FakeTensor, as the cache does on a hit. Each returns NotImplemented, leaving
the op to the cache and general path, for anything whose result could differ
from that plain tensor: inputs that aren't this mode's FakeTensors, constant
FakeTensors (constant propagation), symbolic shapes, layouts other than
strided, preserve_format on a non-contiguous input (which keeps its strides),
pin_memory or unexpected kwargs, sizes or fill values that aren't plain
numbers, rand_like/randn_like of a non-floating dtype (which raises today),
and propagate_real_tensors. torch.full is left out: without a dtype its
output dtype depends on the fill value. With cache crosschecking enabled,
these outputs are crosschecked against the general path like cache hits.

test_cache_aten_index counted a cache miss for the new_empty that index's
fake impl makes its output with; that no longer goes through the cache.

Test Plan:

```
python -m pytest test/test_fake_tensor.py -k test_fast_constructors_match_general_path

python -m pytest test/test_decomp.py -n 16 -k "zeros or empty or ones or full or like or new_"
```

test_fast_constructors_match_general_path runs each fast path on a set of
handled inputs and checks that its output, and the output of dispatching the
op normally, match what the cache and general path produce (metadata including
strides, storage size and device, and the dispatch key set) without touching

body:

Reading a property of a Tensor subclass instance, such as a FakeTensor's dtype
or an nn.Parameter's shape, costs ~150-200 ns more than on a plain Tensor,
almost all of it in checking whether the subclass overrides
__torch_function__. That check (has_torch_function_attr), and the matching
__torch_dispatch__ check, call PyObject_FastGetAttrString, which on Python
3.13+ passes the C string to PyObject_GetOptionalAttrString. That makes a new
str object on every call, and CPython's type attribute cache matches names by
identity, so the lookup misses the cache every time and walks the MRO; the
instance dict lookup also has to hash the new string.

Both checks now keep their name as a static interned string, the pattern
already used elsewhere in torch/csrc, and look it up through a new
PyObject_FastGetAttr that takes a Python string, so the lookup hits the cache.
The lookup is otherwise the same, instance attributes included.

in_kernel_invocation_manager costs ~3.8 us, and FakeTensorMode enters it on
every cache hit, as well as for every meta kernel it runs. It is a
@contextmanager generator that enters two pybind guard objects,
_DisableTorchDispatch and _PreserveDispatchKeyGuard, each ~1 us to create,
enter and exit, and then calls _set_meta_in_tls_dispatch_include.

members disable torch dispatch and then save the TLS dispatch keys, and its
constructor adds Meta to the include set, so on exit it restores the same
state in the same order the two guards did. in_kernel_invocation_manager
becomes a class with __enter__ and __exit__ around it, keeping its name and
how it's called (every caller uses it in a `with` statement). The TLS include
and exclude sets inside and after it match the old implementation's, also when
it's entered inside another exclude guard.

title: [FakeTensor] Make constructing a FakeTensor cheaper
body:
Stack from [ghstack](<url>) (oldest at bottom):
* #202564
* #202563
* #202562
* #202561
* #202560
* #202559
* #202558
* #202557
* #202556
* __->__ #202555
* #202554
* #202553
* #202552

Constructing a FakeTensor costs ~14 us, most of it bookkeeping rather than the
tensor itself. It's the largest single piece of a FakeTensorMode cache hit,
which builds a new FakeTensor for its output. FakeTensor.__new__ initializes
each of its five SymNumberMemoDescriptor memos to None, and each descriptor
__set__ formats three attribute names with f-strings and sets all three
attributes, ~0.8 us per memo. __new__ also pops the ~15 ignored state names
from **state even when it is empty, resolves the device through a list
comprehension over three candidates, and then sets fake_device through its
property, which normalizes the already normalized device a second time.

The descriptor now computes its attribute names once in __set_name__ and
gives the owning class a None default for the memo. An unset memo then reads
as None without the tensor storing anything: __get__ returns None before it
reads the version and epoch attributes. __new__ drops the memo
initialization, skips the ignored state handling when there is no state,
normalizes the device directly when `device` is the only one given, sets
_fake_device itself, and checks elem.is_meta instead of reading
elem.device.type. A new FakeTensor's __dict__ no longer holds the memo, version
and epoch entries until a memo is set; reconstructing a FakeTensor from its
__dict__ already ignored them.

FakeTensor(mode, meta_tensor, device) goes from 14.3 to 5.8 us.

[dynamo] Guard sourced OpOverload attributes (#200472)

# Pre-approved PR

Go through the following checklist

- [x] Passes lint (`spin fixlint`)
- [x] Added/updated tests
- [ ] Updated documentation (if applicable)
- [ ] Included benchmark results (for PRs impacting perf)

---

## Supported by

Supported by @williamwen42

## BC-breaking?

> AI-assisted assessment: No intended public API compatibility break.

## Summary (human written only)

The overall goal is to remove as many raw VT constructions as possible, but sometimes the raw VT construction makes sense.

## Agent details (if applicable)

> AI-assisted summary, prepared for human review:
>
> TorchInGraphFunctionVariable attribute lookup directly constructed sourced
> OpOverload members, so it did not install the BUILTIN_MATCH guard needed to
> invalidate the cache when an overload attribute was rebound. Route already-
> classified non-property sourced members through create_with_source, which adds
> that guard without repeating VariableBuilder classification.
>
> Exact property getters keep the previous unguarded construction: guarding their
> result would resolve the source by calling the getter again. A real-user-code

No

With the CK BLAS preference, fp16/fp64 GEMMs returned garbage, addmm dropped the bias, and unsupported shapes raised; this makes CK hand any call it cannot do to the default BLAS backend (hipBLASLt where preferred) and enables the fp16 instances on gfx9.

message:
Profiler with modules warn explicit (#202437)

**Problem**

#192808 deprecated the profiler's `with_modules` option, but the warning only fires when the option is `True`. Code that passes `with_modules=False` gets no warning, yet it will break with a `TypeError` once the argument is removed. Such callers are common: HuggingFace accelerate passes the option, as `False` by default, every time it builds a profiler, and torchbench and tritonbench forward it from their profiling options.

**Fix**

`with_modules` now defaults to `None` in `torch.profiler.profile`, `_KinetoProfile`, and `torch.autograd.profiler.profile`. Any other value warns. The message now tells callers to stop passing the argument.

For `torch.profiler.profile` users, the check now runs in `_KinetoProfile.__init__`, with a stacklevel that reaches the caller. Previously it fired only when profiling started, inside the autograd profiler that `prepare_trace` builds, and pointed at a line in torch. `prepare_trace` now sets that profiler's `with_modules` after constructing it, so the warning doesn't repeat. `torch.autograd.profiler.profile.__init__` keeps its own check for direct users.

`torch.autograd.profiler_legacy.profile` is left alone. The whole class is already deprecated, and the legacy profiler never read the flag.

We also explicitly add that the deprecation started in 2.15.

**Test Plan**

`test_with_modules_deprecated` now covers both `True` and `False`.

```
python test/profiler/test_profiler.py -k with_modules -k module_hierarchy -v
python test/profiler/test_profiler.py
```

Compile-time Triton autotuning must preserve the runtime argument contract when sample inputs are reused. Clone mutated tensors with their original strides so scalar stride arguments continue to describe the actual allocations.

[ROCm][kineto] Wait for in-flight kernel dispatch records when stopping (#202758)

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Fixes #200903
Fixes #200382
Fixes #200246

Fixes #200401
Fixes #199891
Fixes #199893

Supported by @jeffdaily

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

The torch.profiler for ROCm was sometimes missing GPU kernel events because it wasn't waiting for them to arrive when stopping profiling.

## Agent details (if applicable)

My agent came up with this analysis, but I've read and approved it.

**Problem.** Short `torch.profiler` sessions on ROCm often come back with no GPU kernel events. This is what fails the copy-dispatch tests in `test_torch.py` (the DISABLED issues above), and it also hits CUDA-graph replays. Root cause and reproducer: ROCm/TheRock#9008.

**Cause.** rocprofiler-sdk writes the KERNEL_DISPATCH buffer record from its HSA completion handler, which can run after `hipDeviceSynchronize()` has returned. `RocprofLogger::stopLogging()` flushed once without waiting, so the record arrived in the next session's flush and was dropped there as out of range. rocprofiler-sdk 1.4.2 makes this much more frequent (ROCm/rocm-systems#14378), but it also happens with 1.4.1 under load.

**Change.** A KERNEL_DISPATCH callback tracing service (ENQUEUE operation) records the `dispatch_id` of every kernel dispatched while the session is active, including each kernel of a graph launch and runtime-internal blits; `buffer_callback` removes it when the dispatch record arrives. `stopLogging()` re-flushes every 50 us until none are pending, bounded by the new kineto config key `ROCPROF_DISPATCH_RECORD_WAIT_MSECS` (default 20; 0 restores the old behaviour), and warns how many records it gave up on (for the first 10 stops in a process). message:
[profiler] Keep the files Kineto writes next to a compressed trace export (#202449) (#202449)

Summary:

When the output path of `export_chrome_trace` ends in `.gz` or `.zst`, the
profiler writes the Chrome JSON into a temporary directory, compresses it to
the output path, and then deletes the directory. Only the JSON is copied out,
so any other file that Kineto wrote next to it is deleted with the directory.
An uncompressed export keeps those files, because Kineto writes them straight
into the output directory.

The `NamedTemporaryFile` in `/tmp` that this path used before it gained zstd
support had the same effect: the other files stayed in `/tmp` under a random
name.

This change names the temporary JSON after the output path without the
compression suffix, and moves every other file in the temporary directory to
the output directory. A `foo.json.gz` or `foo.json.zst` export now keeps the
same sibling files that a `foo.json` export gives. A build that writes only
the JSON sees no change.

- Stale cache: I think the biggest concern would be hitting a stale cache entry. The cache is owned by subgraph tracer, so I don't believe we need to worry about file edits duing tracing or using a stale cache from an old compile call any more than framesummary's linecache call.
- Potential cache lookup slowdown: There is a potential for code to have few cache hits.

## Summary (human written only)

As part of the thrust to identify areas of potential self-improving compiler, this PR shows the first identified speedup of such an agent. The bottleneck identified was the time spent formatting stack_trace information on the fx nodes. While we need to preserve the trace for downstream consumers (backends), we can cache the stacks which gains us an advantage in models where we loop over hidden layers (as in [llama transformers](<url>)) or simply single lines which emit multiple fx_nodes which will likely always be beneficial.

message:
[precompile] Autotune Triton kernels at compile time during a capture (#202255)

**Problem.** A training capture compiles backward kernels that no captured batch runs. Those Triton kernels never autotune down to one config, so freezing the runtime cache refuses them with `launcher_count_not_one` and the whole capture fails.

**Fix.** The capture turns on Inductor's compile-time autotuning (`triton.autotune_at_compile_time`), the same way `standalone_compile` does, so every kernel is tuned while its graph lowers, whether or not a captured call runs it. It also turns any nonzero `triton.multi_kernel` off, with a warning naming the value, since a multi-kernel picks its sub-kernel when the loaded module runs and the artifact does not record that config. The overrides come from one shared `_frozen_kernel_config()`, applied only when the capture's backend is `"inductor"` (an eager-backend capture lowers no kernels, so it keeps the ambient Triton config and logs no warning), and a `MakeFxTracer` capture lowers under them too. It fixes two pre-existing Inductor bugs the forced flag would expose: under `triton.autotune_at_compile_time` the Python wrapper emitted multi-kernel defs only into the compile-time autotune block, so a module raised `NameError` on `multi_kernel_N`; and a kernel inside a user stream context (`with torch.cuda.stream(s):`) referenced `raw_stream` in the compile-time autotune block without defining it there, a `NameError`.

**Summary.** A precompile capture lowers each backward together with its forward, so it compiles Triton kernels for backwards that no captured call runs, and generated Triton kernels normally tune only on their first launch. Those kernels keep every candidate config, freezing the runtime cache refuses them with `launcher_count_not_one`, and the capture fails; leaving them out is not an option because replay loads each backward eagerly under `no_compilation()`. message:
[precompile] Record torch prim/helper op modules and warn at capture about lazy and unrecorded ops (#202259)

**Problem.** An artifact imports the modules that register its custom ops before it runs and checks the ops are registered (the two commits below), but for some ops a capture finds no such module, and for some of torch's own ops it found none either. Those artifacts then fail on another host at `load` with a `PrecompileError`, and nothing told the user at capture.

message:
[MPS] Add adaptive_avg_pool3d (#201754)

adaptive_avg_pool3d (and `interpolate(mode="area")` on 5D inputs, which calls it) was not implemented on MPS.

It reuses the 2D implementation from the previous PR instead of adding 3D copies, so this change is host-side only. All the Metal kernels already handle 3 pooling dims: the forward is the existing `avg_pool` kernel (or `adaptive_avg_pool_simd` for large windows), and the backward is the scale + gather pair. On the host, the adaptive avg forward/backward templates and entry-point checks are parametrized by pooling_dims, and the 2D and 3D ops are thin wrappers around them. Both keep the `_i32`/`_i64` index-type selection.

Unlike 2D, divisible sizes do not take a shortcut: MPS avg_pool3d runs the same Metal kernel, so the forward is equally fast. avg_pool3d_backward is ~1.3x faster for divisible sizes, but it relies on atomics and is therefore nondeterministic, while the gather kernel is not.

## Human Note

self explanatory

## Agent note

`install_nccl4py` ran `pip install nccl4py==0.5.0` at the start of the
`distributed`, `h100_distributed` and single-GPU distributed (`default`
config) test runs. Its dependency `cuda-core` is not in the images, so each of

show `Successfully installed cuda-core-1.2.2 nccl4py-0.5.0` on the CUDA,
ROCm and CPU distributed jobs.

This moves nccl4py into requirements-ci, pinned at 0.5.0 like the test-time
install it replaces (NCCLCollConfig first appeared in 0.5), and drops the
test-time install. Its dependency cuda-core is not pinned, like the other
transitive dependencies in requirements-ci, so it is resolved when the image
is built rather than on every test run.

The marker restricts it to Linux x86_64/aarch64 with Python < 3.15, the only
platforms with nccl4py wheels. That also keeps it out of the macOS, Windows
and s390x jobs, which install requirements-ci at test time.

message:
[ROCm][kineto] Fix segfault at exit with a profiler session still open (#202665)

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Related: #199973 (found while testing it)

Supported by @jeffdaily

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

The torch.profiler for ROCm could segfault at process exit if a profiling session was still running, because it used thread-local state that had already been destroyed.

## Agent details (if applicable)

My agent came up with this analysis, but I've read and approved it.

**Problem.** A process that exits while a `torch.profiler` session with GPU activity is still running can segfault on ROCm. On gfx90a with hipBLASLt it crashes on every exit; on other archs and on the rocBLAS path it depends on what is left in freed memory (`MALLOC_PERTURB_=165` makes those crash too).

**Cause.** `exit()` destroys the main thread's thread_locals before the static destructors of rocBLAS and hipBLASLt run. Those destructors call `hipModuleUnload`, which rocprofiler-sdk still traces, so `RocprofLogger::api_callback` indexes its destroyed `thread_local` timestamp map. Per-thread-buffer mode and the correlation-id stacks touch destroyed thread_locals the same way.

**Change.** `api_callback` keeps the ENTER timestamp in the SDK's per-call `user_data`, which rocprofiler-sdk retains from the ENTER to the EXIT phase of one call, so the map is gone (and with it a hash insert and erase per traced HIP call). The remaining per-thread state (correlation-id stacks and the per-thread buffer) moves into one `thread_local ThreadState` whose destructor sets a trivially destructible `t_threadExiting` flag before its members are destroyed; once set, `api_callback` and the correlation push/pop return early and rows go to the shared buffer. The HIP calls dropped this way are those a thread makes after its kineto state is gone: for the main thread that is inside `exit()`, where no session can collect them; a worker thread exiting during a session loses its last ...

message:
ubuntu-cross-riscv: fetch zlib from GitHub releases (robustness follow-up to #175237) (#189382)

Refs #175193. Robustness follow-up to #175237.

## Scope (read first)

This does **not** address the primary action item on #175193 -- per @malfet, that is separating non-standard/experimental docker builds into their own workflow so they do not block mainstream x86/aarch64 builds. This PR only removes the fragile download URL that caused the original breakage, and is safe to take or leave independently of that larger effort. Happy to take on the workflow-separation work separately if wanted.

## Root cause

The `ubuntu-cross-riscv` image fetches zlib from `<url>}.tar.gz`, but zlib.net only hosts the *current* release. When a new zlib ships, the pinned `ZLIB_VERSION` tarball disappears from that URL and the build fails with a 404. That is what happened originally (1.3.1 removed after 1.3.2 released); #175237 fixed it by bumping the pinned version, but the next zlib release will 404 the same way.

## Change

Fetch from `github.com/madler/zlib/releases`, which retains every tagged release permanently, so a pinned version never disappears. This also makes zlib consistent with how this same Dockerfile already fetches `libffi` and `xz` (both use `github.com/.../releases/download`).

## Test plan

Vendor URL is fragile, release URL is durable:
```
curl -sIL <url>  # 404
curl -sIL <url>  # 200
curl -sIL <url>  # 200
```
Built this Dockerfile (`--target final`) with the change on a reproducible x86 runner; the image builds through the zlib layer and to completion:
```
docker buildx build --target final -f .ci/docker/ubuntu-cross-riscv/Dockerfile .ci/docker
```

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

cuBLAS handle creation can fail even when PyTorch's allocator holds reclaimable cached memory. This fix adds retry logic on `CUBLAS_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED`. It releases unused memory and reattempts to create a handle. This allows recovery when releasing memory frees enough space.

>

>
> Tests passed with native, `cudaMallocAsync`, and expandable-segment allocators.

dynamo: Fix branching on non-constant truthiness in generic_jump (#202375)

The fallback branch of `generic_jump` called `truth_fn(result)` where
`result` is the `VariableTracker` returned by `generic_is_true`, not a
bool. A `VariableTracker` object is always truthy, so whenever the
truthiness of the branched-on value was not folded to a constant
earlier in `generic_jump`, `if x:` / `y if x else z` always took the
same branch.

This silently produced wrong results for e.g. `range` (once automatic
dynamic makes its bounds symbolic on recompile), `types.MappingProxyType`
and `dict.keys()` inputs, including through `operator.truth`, whose
polyfill branches on its argument. For the latter two even the first
compile with an empty value took the "true" branch.

The fix evaluates the result the same way the `UserDefinedObjectVariable`
branch above already does: `evaluate_expr()` for a `SymNodeVariable`

message:
[cuspy] Keep the timing and trace metadata the chrome export has in .pftrace (#202249)

The .pftrace export drops two things the chrome export of the same window
keeps, so tools cannot reproduce chrome-trace results from it:

- GPU render stages were clamped to the next op's start on their lane, which
  cut real overlap short (e.g. PDL, graph-replay timestamps). The clamp is
  removed: every stage keeps its exact CUPTI duration.
- The chrome export's top-level fields (distributedInfo, deviceProperties,
  baseTimeNanoseconds, ...) are now written as ChromeMetadata entries
  (name + json_value), so process-group membership survives. traceName is
  written as the chrome export sets it (trace_name, else the output path),
  replacing the CPU input's own traceName.

Display change: Perfetto does not nest GPU render stages; a stage that
overlaps another on its lane goes on an extra track with the same lane
name. The spanning GPU annotation already sat on its own track, and the
clamp kept all of a lane's kernels on one more. Without it, a lane shows
one track per level of overlap, so lanes with overlapping ops get extra
rows. Checked with trace_processor: overlapping stages import with exact
durations, no import errors, and nothing dropped.

The .pftrace tests' protobuf scanner is now shared at module level instead
of copied into each test.

Test plan:
`python test/profiler/test_cuspy.py -k pftrace`
The new `test_pftrace_keeps_overlap_and_chrome_metadata` runs the native
encoder on two overlapping kernels on one lane and a CPU trace carrying
distributedInfo and its own traceName, then decodes the protobuf and checks
both kernels keep their exact durations, the ChromeMetadata entries, and
that traceName is the export's trace_name.

message:
[fx] Resolve lazy imports with FX's patches reverted when scanning for autowrap targets (#202252)

**Problem.** torchrec's train pipeline FX-traces the whole model when the pipeline starts. On an interpreter with PEP 690-style lazy imports, that trace runs the body of a lazily imported module while FX's patches are applied, and a body that calls `torch.jit.script` fails with `RuntimeError: Unknown type name 'JaggedTensor'`.

**Fix.** When `symbolic_trace` reads the globals of a scope it scans for autowrap or `torch.fx.wrap` targets, it resolves the lazy imports among them with every enclosing trace's patches reverted and FX's tracing flag cleared, and a `Tracer` constructed inside another trace does the same for its `autowrap_modules`. Lazy globals read by any other code during the trace, and the dispatch modes `make_fx` has active, are not covered.

**Summary.** FX's autowrap scan (`_autowrap_check`) reads every global of a scope while the trace's patches are applied, and under PEP 690-style lazy imports reading an unresolved name runs that module's body right there. When the body calls `torch.jit.script`, TorchScript compiles FX's patched wrapper against `torch/fx/_symbolic_trace.py`'s globals and fails, so any job whose setup FX-traces such a model dies before training starts. This PR resolves the lazy names of the scanned scopes through a new `_resolve_lazy_imports`, which reverts the patches of the current trace and of every trace it is nested in and clears FX's tracing flag before reading them. To support that, `_maybe_revert_all_patches` becomes re-entrant, and `_patch_wrapped_functions` repeats until a resolved body registers no new wraps. Detection relies on `importlib.is_lazy_import`, which only PEP 690-style forks such as Cinder provide, so on stock CPython everything except the re-entrancy change is a no-op.

[precompile] A Dynamo artifact imports the modules that register its custom ops (#202258)

**Problem.** A Dynamo precompile artifact imports the entry function's module but not the modules that register the custom ops its graphs call, so replay of a function that only calls `torch.ops.<ns>.<op>` fails with `AttributeError: '_OpNamespace' '<ns>' object has no attribute '<op>'`.

**Summary.** A Dynamo capture compiles one backend graph per frame and per graph break, and its artifact serves only the backends it keeps, but before this change it never imported the modules that register the custom ops those graphs call. Replay then failed with an `AttributeError` on `torch.ops.<ns>.<op>` unless the user had imported the registering module first. The capture now records the ops of every backend graph, of Inductor's forward and backward code, and of each graph break (every torch op on the stack of the instruction Dynamo breaks on, for any break reason, plus the op fake tensors failed on; where Dynamo cannot resume after the break, only that op and not the rest of the frame), and the artifact imports the registering modules and checks the ops right after the driver's version checks, refusing a served module that is not importable (and, in the standalone driver, one that is `__main__`) before the op check. message:
[MPS] Add `linalg.eig` and `linalg.eigvals` support (#201244)

Co-authored by Claude

I wrote some notes and a Python implementation of the QR algorithm here: [link](<url>)

This PR adds `linalg.eig` and `linalg.eigvals`. Floating point inputs are promoted to complex at the beginning because a real input can have complex eigenvalues/vectors. It would be possible to avoid this promotion and use algorithms specifically designed for real inputs, which would likely be more performant, but we don't do this, to limit code size.

The details of the algorithms used are described in `Note [linalg.eig for MPS]` and other comments throughout the PR. To give a simplified overview, eigenvalue decomposition is implemented in the following steps:

1. The input matrix is balanced to decrease error in the computed eigenvalues

2. The matrix is reduced to Hessenberg form using a series of householder reflector matrices.

3. Perform QR iteration on the Hessenberg matrix to convert it to an upper triangular matrix `T`. We avoid computing the full QR decomposition and instead use an [implicit QR algorithm](<url>), where each iteration applies a series of Givens rotations, the first of which applies a Wilkinson shift, and the remaining of which implement a bulge chasing algorithm, so that each iteration produces a similar Hessenberg matrix with smaller subdiagonal values. Since the output `T` is triangular and only similarity transformations were applied, the eigenvalues of the input are found on the diagonal entries of `T`.

Eigenvectors are calculated in the following steps:

1. Call `linalg_householder_product` to compute the product `P` of the householder reflectors that were applied to the input matrix.

2. During QR iteration, apply all of the Givens rotations to `P`, to produce `U`, the Schur vectors of the input, which describe all of the transformations that were applied to the balance input during Hessenberg reduction and QR iteration.

message:
[MPS] Use native fp8 MPP matmul for _scaled_mm_v2 on macOS 27 (#202545)

The existing `_scaled_mm_v2` kernels decode every fp8 element to half in threadgroup memory before multiplying, which caps them at ~3.6 TFLOPS on M5 Pro, about 5x slower than dequantizing both operands and calling bf16 `mm`. Metal 4.1 (macOS 27 SDK) adds native fp8 formats, and MetalPerformancePrimitives `matmul2d` accepts `metal_fp8_e4m3_format` operands directly. Its e4m3 encoding matches `torch.float8_e4m3fn` bit-for-bit (checked over all 256 patterns and for saturating float->fp8 conversion).

This adds a third layer to the bundled-metallib scheme from #197529: shaders in `METAL_41_SHADERS` (currently only ScaledMM) are additionally compiled with `-std=metal4.1 -mmacos-version-min=27.0` into `kernels_41.metallib`, embedded as the `metal_41` section, and `BundledShaderLibrary` checks it before `metal_40` when `has_metal_4_1()` holds. `cmake/Metal.cmake` probes the toolchain by compiling an fp8 MPP matmul.

The new `scaled_mm_native` kernel runs a single 64x64-tile MPP matmul over all of K straight from the fp8 operands, so it uses the default multiply mode and needs no zeroed accumulator. Its epilogue (scales and bias) is shared with `scaled_mm_mpp` through `scaled_mm_store_accum`. It is used when both operands are K-contiguous (row-major A, column-major B, the layout cuBLASLt requires) and leading strides fit int32; M <= 4 still uses the few-rows kernel and other layouts the existing kernels. `relaxed_precision` is off, since enabling it gave no speedup.

N = K = 4096, tensorwise scaling, bf16 output, M5 Pro:

| M | before | after | dequant + mm | bf16 mm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | 1409 us | 316 us | 931 us | 325 us |
| 1024 | 9342 us | 1312 us | 1931 us | 1327 us |
| 4096 | 51661 us | 4531 us | 5674 us | 4640 us |
| 2048 x 11008 | 64029 us | 6005 us | 7440 us | 5881 us |

Only tested on M5 Pro; behavior on M1-M4 under macOS 27 is unverified.

[c10d] Move FakeProcessGroup from C++ to a Python PyBackend (#202141)

`FakeProcessGroup` is a test-only backend, but its C++ implementation meant every semantic change needed a C++ rebuild. With `dist.BackendBase` subclassable from Python, it can live in Python.

Design: `torch/distributed/_backends/fake.py` reimplements `FakeProcessGroup` and `FakeProcessGroup.Options` on `dist.BackendBase` with the same semantics. It is registered through the `torch.distributed.backends` entry point (with a built-in fallback), so `init_process_group("fake")` no longer requires importing a testing module. `torch/testing/_internal/distributed/fake_pg.py` stays as a re-exporting shim, and `torch._C._distributed_c10d.FakeProcessGroup` stays as a lazy alias for downstream users. The C++ class is removed; `FakeWork` remains. `_ProcessGroupWrapper` (DEBUG=DETAIL) now keeps Python backend objects alive, as `_register_backend` does.

Fix stale symbolic-shape cache results after value ranges are narrowed. (#202505)

Summary:
Previously, _refine_ranges cleared only the static-evaluation cache. (manually also!)
the contract is to clear automatically by updating version counter !

Cached results in simplify and _simplify_floor_div could remain stale, and range updates through other paths could also leave static-evaluation results stale. (callers to _update_var_to_range that do not go through _refine_ranges).

Track actual range changes in the existing cache-version mechanism and remove the one-off clear. This consistently invalidates all version-aware caches while preserving cache hits when the stored range is unchanged.

message:
[AOTI][XPU] Support weight_use_caching_allocator on XPU (#201813)

**Failure:** `test_update_user_managed_buffer_xpu` (`AOTInductorTestABICompatibleGpu` / `AOTInductorTestDualWrapper`) fails on some XPU CI hosts with `AssertionError: -68702699520 not greater than -68702699520`.

**Why:** `aot_inductor.weight_use_caching_allocator` is silently ignored on XPU: the `USE_XPU` branch of `RAII_gpuMalloc` always uses `sycl::malloc_device`, and the XPU shim has no caching-allocator entry point. AOTI constant buffers therefore bypass the XPU caching allocator and are invisible to `torch.xpu.memory_allocated`, so the test falls back to the driver query `mem_get_info`, which on some hosts reports `free == total` regardless of allocations.

**Fix:** Add `aoti_torch_xpu_caching_allocator_raw_alloc` / `_raw_delete` to the XPU shim (backed by `c10::xpu::XPUCachingAllocator`, versioned 2.16.0), and use them in the `USE_XPU` branch of `RAII_gpuMalloc` when `AOT_INDUCTOR_USE_CACHING_ALLOCATOR` is defined, mirroring CUDA. The test now enables the config on every GPU and measures with `memory_allocated` instead of `mem_get_info`.

Fixes intel/torch-xpu-ops#5484.

[decomp] Support matmul folding for zero-copy non-contiguous views in torch.compile (#197100)

## Issue

Fixes #197083

## Summary

The Python `matmul` decomposition did not use the same stride check as native `matmul`. It rejected some non-contiguous inputs that can be reshaped without a copy. As a result, `torch.compile` kept the `bmm` path and performed an extra layout copy.

This change uses `_compute_stride` for the view check. It also checks `tensor2.mT` when the right-hand input has more dimensions, matching native `matmul`.

## Test Plan

- Added tests for:
  - zero-copy folding with size-1 dimensions;
  - padded non-contiguous strides;
  - layouts that cannot be folded;
  - the higher-rank right-hand-side path using `mT`.
- `python -m py_compile torch/_decomp/decompositions.py test/test_decomp.py`
- `lintrunner --take FLAKE8,RUFF,PYFMT torch/_decomp/decompositions.py test/test_decomp.py`
- `git diff --check`

The full PyTorch test suite was not run because this source checkout does not have a local PyTorch build.

## Benchmark

Environment:

- PyTorch: `2.10.0+cu128`
- GPU: NVIDIA A100
- dtype: `float16`
- Backend: `torch.compile(inductor)`

The following standalone example reproduces the compiled path. Change `B`, `S`, `K`, and `N` to profile other shapes.  The example below uses `B=384, S=8192, K=N=4096`. `x[:, :K].unsqueeze(1)` creates the non-contiguous input with stride `(S, K, 1)`.

message:
[Feature Refactoring] Support PrivateUse1 backends in capturable optimizer detection (#200484)

Related to [#200596](<url>)

## Summary

Update `OptimizerVariable._safe_to_set_capturable` in Dynamo to recognize
PrivateUse1 backends as capturable-supported devices, so that `torch.compile`
injects `capturable=True` into the traced param_groups for these accelerators.

## Motivation

The capturable device check in `_safe_to_set_capturable` was hardcoded to
`p.is_cuda or p.is_xpu`, which excludes every PrivateUse1 backend. This
diverges from the runtime optimizer device list and from eager execution.
This is part of the broader effort to make PyTorch third-party backend
friendly for PrivateUse1.

## Approach

Replace the hardcoded `p.is_cuda or p.is_xpu` predicate with
`_get_capturable_supported_devices()`, the same authoritative device list the
runtime optimizers use. This covers CUDA/XPU as before, picks up the
registered PrivateUse1 backend name (the main motivation of this PR), and
additionally includes HPU and XLA. The HPU/XLA inclusion is an intentional
scope expansion, not a regression: Dynamo should agree with the runtime
optimizer device list instead of maintaining a parallel hardcoded set.

## Notes

- `test_capturable_predicate_covers_runtime_devices` is CPU-runnable and
  locks the full device list (every device returned by
  `_get_capturable_supported_devices(supports_xla=True)` plus `cpu`/`mps`
  negatives), so the intentional HPU/XLA scope expansion is enforced by test.
- `test_capturable_optim_on_privateuse1` exercises the eager PrivateUse1
  optimizer path and directly asserts the predicate for the PrivateUse1 device
  only. Compiled-initialization device placement (asserting `state[p]["step"]`
  lands on the accelerator) is not covered because it depends on the foreach
  meta/fake kernels accepting device scalars; this is tracked in [#202205](<url>).
- No public API or signature changes; the fix is confined to Dynamo's
  optimizer variable tracking.

message:
[bugfix][custom_op] Run each device's own kernel when registering several at once (#202566)

When a custom op registers kernels for several device types in one call
(custom_op(..., device_types=("cpu", "cuda")) or
register_kernel(("cpu", "cuda"))), every one of those devices runs the
function registered for the last device type, and is disabled whenever that
one is. So a later register_kernel("cpu") has no effect on CPU, which keeps
running the "cuda" function, and set_kernel_enabled("cuda", False) also
disables the CPU kernel.

The cause is that register_kernel defines two closures inside its loop over
the device types, and both look up device_type in the enclosing scope each
time they run: the dispatcher kernel (backend_impl), which picks the function
to call from _backend_fns, and the wrapper stored there (wrapped_fn), which
checks whether the kernel is disabled. Python closures capture the variable,
not its value, so once the loop has finished every one of them sees the last
device type. Registering the same function for all of them hides this until
a device gets a different one.

Both are now built by methods, _make_backend_impl(device_type) and
_make_backend_fn(device_type, fn), so each has its own device_type; their
bodies are unchanged. Binding the value with a default argument instead would
add a parameter to functions that are called with the operator's own
arguments.

op for CPU and CUDA, replaces the CPU kernel, and checks that CPU calls use
the new kernel, that disabling CUDA doesn't affect them, and that disabling
CPU falls back to the original function. Then it registers one function for

message:
[dynamo] Preserve product inputs when repeat is zero (#201609)

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Fixes #201276

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

here's the fix i implemented for #201276

## Agent details (if applicable)

AI-generated analysis:

`ItertoolsVariable` handles `itertools.product` by unpacking every input iterable and then calling `itertools.product(*seqs, repeat=r)` on the unpacked values. With `repeat=0`, CPython returns a single empty tuple without converting (and so without consuming) any input, but Dynamo had already unpacked them, so iterator inputs were exhausted and a later `next()` on them returned the default. The inputs are now only unpacked when `repeat` is not 0.

```python
import itertools
import torch

def fn(x):
  values = iter([7, 8])
  list(itertools.product(values, repeat=0))
  return x + next(values, -1)

x = torch.tensor(0)
print(fn(x), torch.compile(fn, backend="eager", fullgraph=True)(x))
```

| | Without compile | `torch.compile` (eager / aot_eager) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before | `tensor(7)` | `tensor(-1)` |
| After | `tensor(7)` | `tensor(7)` |

Test: `test_itertools_product_zero_repeat_preserves_inputs` in `test/dynamo/test_functions.py`, parametrized over the `eager` and `aot_eager` backends. On the 2026-10-16 nightly it fails (2 failed); with this change `pytest test/dynamo/test_functions.py -k itertools_product` passes (6 passed).

message:
[ci] Install fsspec in the CI images (#202400)

## Human Note

self explanatory

## Agent note

fsspec is the only one of torch's runtime dependencies that is not in
`.ci/docker/requirements-ci.txt`. Only the images that run `install_onnx.sh`
get it by accident (through transformers), so on the others, when a test job
installs the freshly built wheel
(`pip install dist/*.whl[opt-einsum]` in `_linux-test.yml`, the TSAN branch of
`test.sh`, and the ROCm/XPU `docker exec` equivalents), pip downloads whatever
fsspec release is newest at that moment. Every other dependency of the wheel
is already satisfied by the image.

In the most recent completed `pull`, `trunk`, `periodic`, `inductor`,
`torchtitan`, `operator_microbenchmark` and `attention_op_microbenchmark` runs
on main, 56 of about 130 distinct Linux test configs logged
`Successfully installed fsspec-2026.9.0 ...` at test time: dynamo, CPU, CUDA,
aarch64, ROCm and microbenchmark jobs.

This adds it to requirements-ci without a version, like the image's other
loosely specified packages. The version is then chosen when the image is
built and upgrades together with the image, instead of whenever a new release
appears.

Authored with an AI assistant (Claude).

## Test Plan

```
for spec in "3.11 x86_64-manylinux_2_28" "3.12 aarch64-manylinux_2_28" \
  "3.14 x86_64-manylinux_2_28" "3.15 x86_64-manylinux_2_28" \
  "3.12 aarch64-apple-darwin" "3.12 x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"; do
  set -- $spec
  uv pip compile --quiet --python-version $1 --python-platform $2 .ci/docker/requirements-ci.txt | grep fsspec
done
```

All resolve (`fsspec==2026.9.0` today), and nothing else in the resolution
changes. The new docker images are built by ciflow/docker on this PR. After
that, the "Install the wheel" step on Linux test jobs should no longer list
fsspec under `Successfully installed`.

message:
[test] Fix storage copy GIL test heartbeat on Windows (#201833)

Fixes <url>
Supported by @jeffdaily

## Summary

`test_storage_copy_releases_gil_during_blocking_cuda_to_cpu` (added in #200489) fails on Windows with `3 not greater than or equal to 5`.

The heartbeat thread used `stop.wait(0.001)`. On Windows a timed wait is rounded up to the ~15.6 ms system timer tick, so the heartbeat ticks only ~3-5 times during the 50 ms GPU sleep even when the GIL is released, and the test cannot tell a released GIL from a held one.

This PR uses `time.sleep(0.001)` for the heartbeat (~1 ms on Windows since Python 3.11) and lengthens the GPU sleep to 200 ms, which keeps 12+ ticks even where the timer is still 15.6 ms (Python 3.10 on Windows). The assertion is unchanged.

## Test plan

Windows 11, gfx1201, ROCm nightly. Heartbeats during a 50/200 ms block with the GIL held (`ctypes.PyDLL` `Sleep`) vs released (`ctypes.WinDLL` `Sleep`), 20 runs each:

| Python | Heartbeat, window | GIL held | GIL released |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.11-3.13 | `stop.wait(0.001)`, 50 ms (before) | 1 | 3-5 |
| 3.10 | `time.sleep(0.001)`, 200 ms | 1 | 12-14 |
| 3.11 | `time.sleep(0.001)`, 200 ms (after) | 1 | 133-188 |

The updated `count_heartbeats` run against real copies: `Tensor.copy_` (releases the GIL) gets 44-48 heartbeats and passes; `UntypedStorage.copy_` from a build without #200489 (holds the GIL) gets 1 and fails, as intended.

message:
[precompile] An artifact imports the modules that register its custom ops (#202257)

**Problem.** A precompile artifact's compiled graph calls `torch.ops.<ns>.<op>` directly, but nothing on the replay path imports the module that registers that op, so a fresh serving process fails with `AttributeError: '_OpNamespace' '<ns>' object has no attribute '<op>'`.

**Fix.** A make_fx artifact (eager and inductor backends) now records the custom ops it calls, the modules that register them, the kernels they had at capture and, by op and dispatch key, the modules whose kernel overrode another one; at load it imports those modules on a best-effort basis and then checks the ops and kernels themselves, raising a `PrecompileError` that names whatever is still missing, any overriding module that failed to import, and any overriding kernel that is no longer the active one.

**Summary.** Before this PR an artifact that called a custom op relied on something else having imported the op's defining module, which replay on a fresh rank (and PEP 690-style lazy imports) never does. The artifact now carries `CUSTOM_OP_MODULES`, `CUSTOM_OPS`, `CUSTOM_OP_KERNELS` and `CUSTOM_OP_OVERRIDE_MODULES`, and section 0, the driver function `_import_custom_op_modules` emitted ahead of the graph code, imports each module, catching any exception. Because a defining module is only a guess (it may not be the registering one, and some ops have no module at all), the load check is on the ops: each schema must be found and each kernel recorded at capture must still be registered, and for each entry of `CUSTOM_OP_OVERRIDE_MODULES` (`{op: {key: module}}`, a kernel the graph ran that replaced another kernel for the same key) the module must also import and its kernel must still be the active one, registered from that module's file, since the replaced kernel would otherwise run in its place unseen by the kernel check. If anything is missing, an overriding module failed to import or an overriding kernel was repla ...

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Part of #168567

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

This PR adds an int4mm implementation for ROCm WMMA hardware.  The CDNA implementation had been woven into the existing CUDA implementation with #ifdef spaghetti and the new WMMA implementation made it worse, so I've separated out the ROCm code into its own section of int4mm.cu.  CUDA's implementation is unchanged from main and stands on its own, separate from ROCm's.  Both are now maintainable separately.

## Agent details (if applicable)

> int4mm.cu's ROCm tinygemm is MFMA with a hard-coded wave size of 64, so `_weight_int4pack_mm` and `_convert_weight_to_int4pack` reject RDNA and gfx1250 and `test__weight_int4pack_mm` is skipped there. This adds a wave32 WMMA path: `wmma_f32_16x16x16_bf16` on gfx11 and gfx12, and `wmma_f32_16x16x32_bf16` on gfx1250 (two k-tiles per instruction). Lane layouts were measured with probes on each family. The packed-weight shape is unchanged on every arch.
>
> int4mm.cu now has a shared prelude and two self-contained halves: CUDA under `#if !defined(USE_ROCM)`, whose text is identical to main's after resolving `USE_ROCM`, and ROCm under `#else`. In the ROCm half each family is a trait struct (`RocmMmaCdna`, `RocmMmaGfx11`, `RocmMmaGfx12`, `RocmMmaGfx1250`) chosen once by `using RocmMma = ...`, so the loaders, kernel and pack kernel have no per-arch conditionals. The ROCm half uses HIP type names, so hipify leaves it untouched.
>
> It also replaces the ROCm dequant's inline `asm volatile("v_and_or_b32 ...")` with plain C. LLVM's hazard recognizer does not see inline asm, and on gfx1250 the asm overwrote a preceding WMMA's A registers with no wait states, giving wrong, run-to-run varying results for k >= 128. With plain C the compiler inserts the required waits.

[ROCm] Make test_conv_cuda_graph_new_shape deterministic (#202451)

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Follow-up to #201481 (author has write access).

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

Test-only follow-up to #201481: pin the new graph-capture conv test to deterministic MIOpen solvers so it stops failing on the ROCm preview image. Details below.

## Agent details (if applicable)

`test_conv_cuda_graph_new_shape` (from #201481) fails on the rocm-preview mi350 job for its transposed fp16 variants. Only `grad_weight` differs, and it is not the capture: replaying the same graph twice gives different results, and so do two eager calls. From ROCm 10.2 (MIOpen 3.6.2), MIOpen's default config for these small fp16 weight-gradient convs is the global split-K variant of `ConvAsmImplicitGemmGTCDynamicWrwXdlopsNHWC`, whose reduction order is not fixed; ROCm 10.1 picked a non-split config of the same solver, which happened to be exact. The test compares two runs of a conv it never asked to be deterministic, at the fp16 default tolerance.

Passing `deterministic=True` to `cudnn.flags` makes MIOpen use a deterministic solver (CK `ConvHipImplicitGemmGroupWrwXdlops`), so replay, eager immediate and eager Find agree bit for bit. The capture failure #201481 fixes does not depend on deterministic, so the test still catches it. Loosening the tolerance instead would need about atol 0.2 for fp16 `grad_weight`.

Test Plan: on MI355X (gfx950), at the same commit, ROCm 10.2.0a20261014 and 10.3.0a20261027 fail 3 of 12 variants before this change and pass 12/12 after (3 runs each); ROCm 10.1 passes both before and after; against a torch without #201481 the changed test fails with the capture error.
```
python test/nn/test_convolution.py -k test_conv_cuda_graph_new_shape -v
```

[ROCm] Sort a copy of bool inputs instead of normalizing them in place (#202517)

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Fixes #202005

Supported by @jeffdaily

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

On ROCm, sorting a bool tensor that was expanded along a dimension (a common pattern for block masks) raised an internal-overlap error instead of sorting. The ROCm-only workaround for non-standard bools wrote into the input tensor; it now sorts a normalized copy, so the input is left alone and expanded inputs work.

## Agent details (if applicable)

Problem: `x = row[None, :].expand(64, n)` with a bool `row`; `x.sort()` / `x.argsort()` on ROCm raise "more than one element of the written-to tensor refers to a single memory location". CPU, CUDA, uint8 and `.contiguous()` inputs work.

Cause: the ROCm block in `sort_cuda_kernel` added by #147459 normalizes non-standard bools with `self.copy_(self.to(at::kByte))`, an in-place write into the caller's input, which fails for overlapping memory (and mutates a const input).

Change: on ROCm, bool inputs are sorted from `self.view(at::kByte).ne(0)`, a standard-bool copy built from the raw bytes (one kernel, and a non-standard bool is never loaded as `bool`). New `test_sort_expanded_bool` covers the small in-place sort and the segmented sort paths, stable and unstable; on ROCm the expanded input also holds non-standard bools (CUDA sort does not normalize them, per sort's OpInfo).

Test plan (done with Claude, MI250X): the issue repro and the new test fail before and pass after; `test_sort_and_select.py` 223 passed, 0 failed; the `test_non_standard_bool_values` tests for sort, argsort and msort pass (6/6).
```
python test/test_sort_and_select.py -k test_sort_expanded_bool
python test/test_sort_and_select.py
python test/test_ops.py -k "*test_non_standard_bool_values*sort*"
```

message:
[ROCm] Do not pass /usr/include to HIP extension builds (#202518)

## Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Fixes #202007

Supported by @jeffdaily

## BC-breaking?

No

## Summary (human written only)

On Linux distros that install ROCm under /usr (Fedora), every HIP C++ extension build failed in libstdc++ headers because cpp_extension passed `-isystem /usr/include`. The HIP branch now skips /usr/include the same way the CUDA branch already does.

## Agent details (if applicable)

Problem: with `ROCM_HOME=/usr`, `torch.utils.cpp_extension.include_paths("cuda")` returns `/usr/include`, which reaches both the host and hipcc compiles as `-isystem /usr/include`. That reorders the system include chain, so libstdc++'s `#include_next <stdlib.h>` / `<math.h>` fail.

Cause: the HIP branch of `include_paths()` appends `_join_rocm_home('include')` unconditionally; the CUDA branch below it already skips `/usr/include` ("gcc doesn't like having /usr/include passed explicitly").

Change: the same guard for the HIP branch. New `TestCppExtensionImport.test_hip_include_paths_skip_usr_include` mocks `IS_HIP_EXTENSION` and `ROCM_HOME=/usr` and checks that `/usr/include` is not returned.

Test plan (done with Claude, MI250X, GCC 13.3): the new test fails before and passes after; `test_cpp_extensions_jit.py` 34 passed, 0 failed (12 environmental skips), including the HIP JIT extension builds, which still get the ROCm SDK include path.

```

[CI] Disable BuildKit provenance for CI images (#202609)

## Summary (human written only)

This default option increases the number of entries on ECR to 3x for each image as each push will now accompany by an index and an attestation. None are needed, we didn't use them on CI in the past.

```
pytorch-linux-jammy-py3.12-clang21-e5ceb251...  (tag)
└── image index  sha256:676abc...  the tagged object; just a list of the two below
  ├── amd64 image  sha256:71af64...  the real image: 85 layers, ~1.8 GB
  └── attestation  sha256:c40071...  564 B manifest -> one 1.3 KB file (provenance)
```

## Agent details (if applicable)

Since docker-builds moved to remote BuildKit (#184664), every CI image is pushed with a provenance attestation. That makes each tag take 3 images in the `pytorch/ci-image` ECR repo instead of 1. With ~650 new images a day, the repo hit ECR's 100000-image limit on 2026-10-29 and pushes started failing (e.g. #202400). I pruned old images to unblock it, but it would fill up again in ~2 months.

Nothing uses the attestation, so this turns it off. Each tag is then 1 image. #202402 separately stops re-pushing tags that already exist.

[CODEOWNERS] Require rule handles to be on their block's owner line (#202091)

The previous PR records one `# owner:` list per label block but lets an
active rule name people who aren't on it. This has the taxonomy lint require
every handle on an active rule to also appear on its block's owner line, so an
owner list can't silently miss someone who reviews the area's code.

Three existing rules notify people who aren't owners of their block. Rather
than turn those notifications into ownership claims, they are recorded as
explicit exceptions in `REVIEWERS_NOT_OWNERS` in
`scripts/codeowners/check_taxonomy.py`, and the rest of the file is enforced:

- `/test/functorch/test_aotdispatch.py`: Chillee, ezyang (block `module: aotdispatch`)
- `/torch/_export/serde/schema.py`: SherlockNoMad (block `oncall: export`)
- `/torch/fx/proxy.py`: zou3519 (block `module: fx`, owner `none`)

`find_ownership_errors` gains two checks. "Reviewers missing from owner lists"
reports any handle on an active rule in a labeled block that is neither on the
block's owner line nor an exception, compared case-insensitively. "Unneeded
reviewer exceptions" reports an exception that no longer applies: the handle
became an owner, left the rule, or the rule was removed or renamed. So the list
can only shrink, and a stale entry can't later exempt a new rule unreviewed.
Exception handles are compared case-insensitively like everything else. Rules above a
section's first `# label:` line have no owner line and aren't checked.
`TaxonomyPattern` gains a `reviewers` field holding the rule's own handles, and
the header's description of owner lines states the rule. Since this is the
first check to read a rule's block owners, `parse_codeowners` now takes them
only from the owner line directly under the label line; a misplaced owner line
is reported and otherwise ignored.

No owner line changes and no behavior change: only header comments change, so
GitHub review requests and the `owners.py` output are the same.

## Summary (human written only)

Follow-up to #179704. Since the reentrant backward got an explicit grad, the child graph runs to completion, and the engine doesn't cancel it when the parent errors, so `test_reentrant_parent_error_on_cpu` raced the child accumulating into `t2` before the `assertIsNone` checks. It has been failing intermittently on ROCm MI300 and MI350 as recently as 2026-10-21. This holds the child with a hook on its root until the parent error is raised, then waits for the child to return and checks that the parent didn't run the rest of its graph (`t3.grad` and `t1.grad` stay `None`). The hook and the wait both have a timeout so the test fails instead of hanging the shard.

message:
[inductor] Keep a clone whose storage offset differs from its source in `remove_noop_ops` (#202409)

Summary:
`remove_noop_ops` replaces a no-op node with its source when `same_tensor_meta` matches, and it skipped the storage offset in that comparison for every no-op. A non-view no-op such as `clone` produces a tensor with its own storage at offset 0. Erasing one whose source sits at a nonzero storage offset changes what a user that depends on storage placement observes:

- `as_strided`. Its storage offset is relative to the storage. `x[1:].clone().as_strided((4, 16), (16, 1), 0)` reads the clone from its start. With the clone erased, it reads the source's storage from offset 0, which is different data. This happens for graph inputs and for intermediates that are realized as buffers.
- User-defined Triton kernels. A launcher may clone a tensor whose base is not 16-byte aligned so that a TMA descriptor, built on the host or in the kernel, gets an aligned base. With the clone erased, the descriptor gets the misaligned source; host-side creation fails with "base must be 16-byte aligned".

A non-view no-op now has to match its source's storage offset to be erased only when it has such a user: `as_strided`, or any argument of `triton_kernel_wrapper_functional`. User-defined kernels are opaque, so all of their arguments count. Users are followed through views that share the node's storage, including the outputs of multi-output views such as `split` and `unbind`. This is a denylist: custom ops and extern fallback kernels are intentionally not included.

Left out on purpose:
- `as_strided_scatter`: its lowering, like eager, clones the input before it applies `as_strided`, so the input's storage offset is never observed.
- `sym_storage_offset`: Dynamo graph-breaks on or specializes `storage_offset()` for clone-derived tensors, so it does not reach this pass on them.
- `triton_kernel_wrapper_mutation`: mutation wrappers are created by `decompose_triton_kernel_wrapper_function ...
