title: Validate delegated node IDs and builtin operator codes in optional_debug_tools
body:
## Summary

`GetNodeDelegationMetadata` in `tensorflow/lite/optional_debug_tools.cc` indexes `is_node_delegated` and `replaced_by_node` directly using entries from `nodes_to_replace` without checking null delegate parameter pointers or verifying that each node ID lies within `[0, subgraph.nodes_size())`. Out-of-range delegated node IDs write past the metadata vectors.

In addition, `PrintInterpreterState` indexes `EnumNamesBuiltinOperator()` directly with `builtin_code` without checking `[BuiltinOperator_MIN, BuiltinOperator_MAX]`, reading out of bounds when inspecting registrations with negative or unknown operator codes, and dereferences `nodes_to_replace` in the execution-plan delegate summary without null checks.

Add pointer and index bounds checks in `GetNodeDelegationMetadata` and the execution-plan delegate summary, and fall back to `"(invalid)"` when `builtin_code` lies outside `[BuiltinOperator_MIN, BuiltinOperator_MAX]`.

## Testing

- Unfiltered Release (`-c opt`) `//tensorflow/lite:optional_debug_tools_test`: 5 tests passed
- Unfiltered AddressSanitizer `//tensorflow/lite:optional_debug_tools_test`: 5 tests passed
- The unpatched control and two isolated guard-removal controls failed on the expected heap and global out-of-bounds accesses

This change was prepared with automated assistance and reviewed and tested by the submitter.

title: Validate joined string lengths and non-positive portable quantization sizes in Lite
body:
## Summary

`AddJoinedString` in `tensorflow/lite/string_util.cc` subtracts one from `strings.size()` when empty, accumulates `size_t` lengths into a signed 32-bit `int` without checking `max_length_`, and invokes `memcpy` on zero-length segments in an empty buffer. Joining an empty list can underflow the separator calculation, and joining segments whose combined length exceeds `max_length_` or wraps 32-bit signed `int` can under-size `data_` before copying.

In addition, `PortableSymmetricQuantizeFloats` and `PortableAsymmetricQuantizeFloats` in `tensorflow/lite/kernels/internal/reference/portable_tensor_utils.cc` and `tensorflow/compiler/mlir/lite/quantization/lite/toco_legacy/portable_tensor_utils.cc` dereference `std::minmax_element` iterators or zero-fill output buffers without checking `size <= 0`.

Guard `AddJoinedString` for empty lists, enforce `max_length_` using checked `size_t` arithmetic consistent with `AddString`, skip zero-length `memcpy` calls, and return neutral scale and offset defaults when `size <= 0` across the portable float quantization helpers.

## Testing

- Unfiltered Release (`-c opt`) `//tensorflow/lite:string_util_test` and `//tensorflow/lite/kernels/internal:per_channel_quantize_test`
- Unfiltered global Clang AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer `//tensorflow/lite:string_util_test` and `//tensorflow/lite/kernels/internal:per_channel_quantize_test`
- Verified `bazel build //tensorflow/compiler/mlir/lite/quantization/lite/toco_legacy:portable_tensor_utils` in both configurations for synchronized `PortableSymmetricQuantizeFloats` definitions

This change was prepared with automated assistance and reviewed and tested by the submitter.

title: kernels/gather_nd: use int64_t offsets in GatherSliceOpKernel
body:
Promote `offset` and `loc_offset` in `GatherSliceOpKernel` from `Index` to `int64_t` to match the 64-bit types of `batch_strides`, `slice_size`, `i`, and `loc`, avoiding redundant int64-to-int32 narrowing when `Index` is `int32`.

**Before:**
```cpp
Index offset = 0;
...
const Index loc_offset = i - loc * slice_size;
```

**After:**
```cpp
int64_t offset = 0;
...
const int64_t loc_offset = i - loc * slice_size;
```

`batch_strides[j]` is `int64_t`; `i` and `loc` were already promoted to `int64_t` in 7c7fdefb932. This change makes `offset` and `loc_offset` consistent with the rest of the kernel's 64-bit index types.

Remove `@org_xprof` C++ dependencies from TensorFlow profiler targets.

TensorFlow profiler targets previously pulled in `@org_xprof//xprof/...` C++ targets, which caused OSS TensorFlow builds to compile XProf C++ sources against XLA/TSL headers and required patching `@org_xprof` C++ files in `tensorflow/third_party/xprof/xprof.patch` whenever XLA/TSL APIs changed.

- Remove unused `#include` headers and build dependencies on `@org_xprof//xprof/convert/...` from `_pywrap_profiler` in `tensorflow/python/profiler/internal/profiler_wrapper.cc`.
- Call `tsl::profiler::ValidateHostPortPair` and `tsl::profiler::Monitor` directly in `_pywrap_profiler_plugin` and remove the legacy `xspace_to_tools_data` and `xspace_to_tools_data_from_byte_string` bindings, removing the dependency on `@org_xprof//xprof/pywrap:profiler_plugin_impl`.

title: Fix periodic hann_window and hamming_window for odd lengths
body:
Fixes #129743

### Problem

`tf.signal.hann_window` and `tf.signal.hamming_window` return the symmetric window for odd `window_length` even when `periodic=True`, which is the default. For example, `hann_window(5)` gives `[0, .5, 1, .5, 0]` instead of `[0, .345, .905, .905, .345]`. Because `tf.signal.stft` uses `hann_window` by default, an odd `frame_length` gives spectra that differ from SciPy, librosa and PyTorch, and from TensorFlow's own `tf.raw_ops.AudioSpectrogram`: a max abs difference of 0.89 on the repro in the issue, compared with 3e-7 for an even length. The window also loses its constant overlap-add property, e.g. N = 9 with a hop of 3.

### Change

In `_raised_cosine_window`, divide by `window_length + periodic - 1` for every length, instead of `window_length + periodic * even - 1`. A periodic window of length N is then the first N points of the symmetric window of length N + 1, for both odd and even N. This is how `scipy.signal.get_window`, `torch.hann_window` and `GetPeriodicHann` in `core/kernels/spectrogram.cc` define it. Even lengths and symmetric windows are unchanged. Length 1 keeps its existing special case.

Tests:
- `window_ops_test._scipy_raised_cosine` copied SciPy 0.14's windows, which had the same odd-length behavior. It now extends and truncates for every length, as current SciPy does.
- `spectral_ops_test._np_hann_periodic_window` returned a symmetric window for odd lengths. It is now the standard periodic Hann.
- New `test_periodic_window_odd_length` checks Hann and Hamming at lengths 3, 5, 9 and 31, with both a static length and one only known at run time.

### Testing

I don't have a Bazel build. I ran the changed test files with Python against the TF 2.21.0 macOS arm64 wheel, with this PR's `window_ops.py` copied in:

- `window_ops_test.py`: 453 tests OK (1 skipped).
- `spectral_ops_test.py`: 70 tests OK (1 skipped). For this run I also copied master's `reconstruction_ops.py` into the wheel and left out `test_inverse_stft_rejects_zero_frame_length`. That test needs kernel validation that is on master but not in the 2.21 binary, and it aborts there with or without this change.
- The updated tests against the old `window_ops.py`: 68 failures in `window_ops_test` (odd-length periodic cases) and 8 in `spectral_ops_test` (`test_stft_and_inverse_stft` with frame lengths 25 and 23). So the tests catch the bug.
- `pylint --rcfile=tensorflow/tools/ci_build/pylintrc` on the three Python files: no new messages.

I did not test on GPU or TFLite. The TFLite `window_ops_test` only uses length 10, so it is unaffected.

### Notes

This changes numerical output for `hann_window`/`hamming_window` with an odd length and `periodic=True`, and for `stft`/`inverse_stft` with the default window and an odd `frame_length`. I added a `RELEASE.md` entry. `inverse_stft_window_fn` derives its window from the forward window, so `stft` → `inverse_stft` round trips still reconstruct the signal. Anyone who needs the old values can pass `periodic=False`.

title: widen key/value_index to int64 in InitializeTableFromTextFile
body:
InitializeTableFromTextFile takes key_index and value_index as int32_t, but the InitializeTableFromTextFile and ...V2 ops read those attrs into int64 and only require them to be >= -2. A column index above INT32_MAX passes that check and is then truncated to a negative int32 inside the helper. Because it is not one of the -1 or -2 sentinels, it slips past the column-count check (max(key_index, value_index) + 1 stays small) and reaches tokens[index] on the split line, reading the token vector out of bounds. A crafted value such as 2**31 narrows to INT32_MIN and segfaults.

Widening both indices to int64_t carries the real value through to the existing column-count guard, so an oversize index is rejected with the same InvalidArgument the op already raises for an index past the last column rather than wrapping negative. The narrowing lived only at this helper's signature; the attr plumbing and the line iterator are already int64, so valid indices are unchanged and only the three declarations move. Added a regression test next to the existing invalid-index coverage.

title: Keep float64 and complex NumPy inputs in matrix_rank and lu_*
body:
Fixes #129739.

`matrix_rank`, `lu_solve`, `lu_matrix_inverse` and `lu_reconstruct` convert their matrix with `dtype_hint=dtypes.float32`. The hint is there so lists and integer inputs become float32, but `convert_to_tensor` also applies it to NumPy arrays whenever the cast is possible:

```python
x = np.diag([1.0, 1e-9])
tf.linalg.matrix_rank(x)  # 1  (float32 SVD and tolerance)
tf.linalg.matrix_rank(tf.constant(x))  # 2

z = np.array([[1, 1j], [1j, -1]])  # rank 1
tf.linalg.matrix_rank(z)  # 2, rank of the real part

lu, perm = tf.linalg.lu(complex_matrix)
tf.linalg.lu_reconstruct(lu.numpy(), perm.numpy())  # float32, real parts only
```

I added a small `_convert_with_float32_hint` helper that skips the hint when the value already has a float64 or complex dtype, and used it in the four places. Everything else is converted exactly as before. I compared outputs before and after for Python float and int lists, float16/float32/float64/int64/complex128 NumPy arrays, and float32/float64 tensors: only the float64 and complex NumPy rows change. For `matrix_rank` a complex NumPy input now raises the same `TypeError` as a complex tensor already does, instead of silently using the real part.

I kept this to the four functions that use the float32 hint in `linalg_impl.py` rather than changing `convert_to_tensor`, since its hint behavior is documented and changing it would reach far beyond these functions.

### Testing

- `MatrixRankNumpyInputTest`: float64 NumPy input keeps the 1e-9 singular value, complex NumPy input raises `TypeError`.
- `LUNumpyInputTest`: `lu_reconstruct`, `lu_matrix_inverse` and `lu_solve` keep float64 and complex128 for NumPy inputs and match NumPy to 1e-10.

Both run in graph and eager mode. They fail on tf-nightly 2.23.0-dev20261028 and pass with the patched `linalg_impl.py` dropped into that install. The whole `linalg_ops_test.py` passes with the patch (883 tests). pylint with `tensorflow/tools/ci_build/pylintrc` reports nothing on the changed lines. CPU only (arm64 macOS).

title: Support half and bfloat16 images in resize gradients
body:
Fixes #129737.

Two resize gradients don't handle half/bfloat16 images, which breaks mixed precision training for models that resize inside the graph:

- `tf.image.resize(..., antialias=True)` and the lanczos/gaussian/mitchellcubic methods go through `ScaleAndTranslate`. The forward op takes half, bfloat16 and double images, but `ScaleAndTranslateGrad` is `T: {float}` for both `grads` and `original_image`, so backprop raises `InvalidArgumentError` for every dtype except float32.
- `method="bicubic"` returns a `None` gradient for half and bfloat16 images with no error, because `ResizeBicubicGrad` only has float/double kernels and the Python gradient skips other dtypes.

Both grad kernels only read the shape of `original_image`, so the fix stays in `image_grad.py`: pass the image as float32 where the kernel needs it and cast the result back to the image's dtype, which is what `ResizeBilinearGrad` already returns. For float32 (and float64 for bicubic) the casts are no-ops, so the existing paths don't change. Integer images still get `None`, as before.

I went with the Python-side cast instead of adding 16-bit kernels for the two grad ops since it's a much smaller change and the gradient is computed in float32 either way (the forward op's output is float32).

### Testing

- `ScaleAndTranslateOpTestBase.testGradsForNonFloat32Images`: half, bfloat16 and float64 gradients for lanczos3/gaussian/mitchellcubic, with and without antialias, have the input's dtype and match the float32 gradient.
- `ResizeBicubicOpTestBase.testGradForHalfAndBfloat16`: same check for bicubic.

Both fail on tf-nightly 2.23.0-dev20261028 (the first with the `ScaleAndTranslateGrad` error, the second because the gradient is `None`) and pass with the patched `image_grad.py` dropped into that install. The whole `image_grad_test.py` passes with the patch (78 tests), and so do the resize test classes in `image_ops_test.py`. I also checked the float64 bicubic and lanczos3 gradients against numeric Jacobians, `tf.function`, graph-mode `tf.gradients` for half, and that uint8 still returns `None`. pylint with `tensorflow/tools/ci_build/pylintrc` is clean on the changed lines. CPU only (arm64 macOS).

title: Fix tf.experimental.numpy repeat negative-repeats validation with NumPy's ValueError
body:
`np.repeat` raises `ValueError` before any computation when `repeats` contains a negative entry, with a distinct message for a scalar and for a sequence of entries:

```
>>> np.repeat([1, 2], -1)
ValueError: negative dimensions are not allowed

>>> np.repeat([1, 2], [-1, 2])
ValueError: repeats may not contain negative values.

>>> np.repeat([[1, 2], [3, 4]], [2, -1], axis=1)
ValueError: repeats may not contain negative values.
```

The tf-numpy wrapper instead reached the backend Tile kernel, which fails with a confusing `InvalidArgumentError`:

```
InvalidArgumentError: Expected multiples[1] >= 0, but got -1 [Op:Tile] ...
```

Validate the Python/NumPy `repeats` value up front and raise NumPy's exact `ValueError` messages (both forms). A Tensor `repeats` keeps the previous behavior, since the check only inspects the Python value — consistent with the other Python-side validations in `numpy_ops` (e.g. `pad`).

Tests: `testRepeat` gains the scalar negative case, a mixed `[2, -1]` entry sequence, and a negative entry against an axis, each asserting NumPy's exact message.

Signed-off-by: Kaivalya Singh <<email>>

title: Add tf.experimental.numpy diff prepend/append support with NumPy semantics
body:
NumPy's `np.diff` accepts optional `prepend`/`append` values that are added along `axis` before the differences run:

```
>>> np.diff(np.array([1, 2, 3]), prepend=0)
array([1, 1, 1])

>>> np.diff(np.array([1, 2, 3]), append=5)
array([1, 1, 2])
```

The tf-numpy wrapper lacked both parameters entirely: `tnp.diff(a, prepend=0)` raises `TypeError: diff() got an unexpected keyword argument 'prepend'`.

Mirror NumPy's implementation in `np_math_ops.diff`:

- A scalar (0-d) `prepend`/`append` is broadcast to length 1 along `axis` and all other dimensions of `a` (NumPy's `_broadcast_to` on `shape` with `shape[axis] = 1`) and concatenated once, before the `n` differences run.
- An array `prepend`/`append` is concatenated as-is; when both shapes are statically known, a dimension mismatch outside `axis` raises NumPy's exact `ValueError: all the input array dimensions except for the concatenation axis must match exactly` instead of the backend's `InvalidArgumentError`.
- The two sides are promoted to a shared dtype with `np_utils.result_type` before concatenating, like NumPy's concatenate promotes (e.g. `np.diff(int32, prepend=1.5)` yields float64).
- Boolean inputs keep the boolean (`!=`) difference semantics when the promoted dtype is still boolean.

Tests extend `testDiff`: scalar `prepend`/`append` (including `n=2` with both boundaries), array `prepend` with `axis=0` and array `append` with `axis=1` matched against `np.diff`, the mixed-dtype promotion case, the boolean-boundary case, and a mismatch outside `axis` raising NumPy's ValueError.

Signed-off-by: Kaivalya Singh <<email>>

title: Fix tf.experimental.numpy flipud/fliplr rank validation with NumPy's ValueError
body:
`np.flipud` requires an input of rank >= 1 and `np.fliplr` one of rank >= 2, raising `ValueError` before any computation:

```
>>> np.flipud(np.array(5))
ValueError: Input must be >= 1-d.
>>> np.fliplr(np.array(5))
ValueError: Input must be >= 2-d.
>>> np.fliplr(np.arange(3))
ValueError: Input must be >= 2-d.
```

The tf-numpy wrappers instead handed every input to the backend reverse kernel, which fails with a confusing out-of-range axis `InvalidArgumentError` for a too-low rank (`flip(m, 0)`/`flip(m, 1)` with an out-of-range axis for the input's rank), e.g. `ValueError`-worthy inputs produced `errors_impl.InvalidArgumentError: Dimension size must be Positive or 0` / range errors from the C++ kernel.

Validate the statically-known input rank up front and raise NumPy's exact `ValueError` messages; an input of unknown rank keeps the previous behavior (consistent with the other statically-known-rank validations in `numpy_ops`, e.g. `repeat`).

Tests: a new `testFlipudFliplrMinimumRank` covers the ValueError for scalar and rank-1 inputs, valid ranks keep working by matching `np.flipud`/`np.fliplr`, and an unknown-rank `tf.function` keeps the previous behavior. The `testFlip` assertion that expected the backend `InvalidArgumentError` for `fliplr` on a rank-1 input is updated to expect NumPy's `ValueError`.

Signed-off-by: Kaivalya Singh <<email>>

title: Avoid overflow in convert_image_dtype with half and wide int types
body:
Fixes #129731.

For float -> int, `convert_image_dtype` multiplies by `dtype.max + 0.5` in the image's own float type. When that type can't represent the constant it rounds up to `dtype.max + 1` or more, and 1.0 then scales to one past the integer range:

```python
c = tf.image.convert_image_dtype
c(tf.constant([0., .5, 1.], tf.bfloat16), tf.uint8)  # [0, 128, 0]  scale = 256
c(tf.constant([0., .5, 1.], tf.float16), tf.int16)  # [0, 16384, -32768]  scale = 32768
c(tf.constant([0., .5, 1.], tf.float16), tf.uint16)  # [0, 65535, 65535]  scale = inf
c(tf.constant([0, 65535], tf.uint16), tf.float16)  # [0, inf]
```

float32 -> int32/uint32 and float64 -> int64 have the same rounding (2**31, 2**32, 2**63), so 1.0 overflows the cast there too, which is undefined and is what #60078 ran into on Windows.

The fix only kicks in when the scale would round up. In that case half and bfloat16 images are scaled in float32 (which holds `dtype.max + 0.5` exactly for 8 and 16 bit targets), and the scale is capped at the largest value below `dtype.max + 1` in the compute type, so 1.0 always stays in range. For int32 and wider targets that means 1.0 maps to the largest float32/float64 below 2**31 etc., e.g. 2147483520 for int32. This is the same nudging `saturate_cast` already does for its clamp limits. For int -> float, when the integer max doesn't fit in the target (uint16 and wider into half), the multiply happens in float32 and only the result in [-1, 1] is cast down.

I kept the common paths untouched on purpose. Comparing old and new outputs over every half/bfloat16 value in [-1, 1], 300k float32/float64 values, and integer ranges for each dtype pair (with and without `saturate`), all 50 combinations that weren't overflowing (float32 -> uint8, half -> uint8, bfloat16 -> int8, int8 -> half, uint8 -> float32, ...) give bit-identical results. Only the overflowing pairs change. The output op name is unchanged in graph mode.

### Testing

Added three tests to `ConvertImageTest` covering half/bfloat16 -> uint8/int16/uint16, float -> int32/uint32/int64 (including -1.0 and `saturate=True`), and uint16/int32/int64 -> half. All three fail on tf-nightly 2.23.0-dev20261028 and pass with the patched `image_ops_impl.py` dropped into that install. I also ran the whole `image_ops_test.py` both ways: the patched run has no failures beyond the unpatched baseline (the only differences are the three new tests, and the decode tests that need Bazel testdata error out in both runs). pylint with `tensorflow/tools/ci_build/pylintrc` is clean on the changed lines. I only tested on CPU (arm64 macOS); the change is Python-level dtype logic with no new ops.

title: Add a `!tfl.blockwise_quant` element type for N-D blockwise quantization.
body:
Add a `!tfl.blockwise_quant` element type for N-D blockwise quantization.

`BlockwiseQuantization.block_shape` in the schema describes a tensor tiled into
blocks of an arbitrary N-D shape, with one scale (and optional zero point) per
block. `!quant.uniform` cannot express this, so add a TFL dialect type that
mirrors it:

  !tfl.blockwise_quant<i4 -> f32, block_shape = [1, 32],
  scales = dense<...> : tensor<64x2xf32>,
  zero_points = dense<...> : tensor<64x2xi8>>

Scales and zero points are held as `ElementsAttr`s, so they can be backed by
resource blobs, and their element types are independent of the storage and
expressed types. A parameter tensor may have extent 1 on any axis to broadcast
across that axis.

`tfl.pseudo_qconst` and `tfl.dequantize` accept the new type, and their
verifiers check that the parameters are shaped like the block grid. Nothing
produces the type yet.

title: Reset XNNPACK weight cache build steps on every exit path.
body:
Reset XNNPACK weight cache build steps on every exit path.

`WeightCacheBuilder` never freed its staging `data_` buffer between
build steps, leaving it allocated at the size of the largest packed
weight for the lifetime of the cache. `StopBuildStep` also returns early
when a step wrote nothing (such as a subgraph whose weights were all
cache hits), skipping the `is_build_step_` reset, and a failed
`StartBuildStep` left `is_build_step_` set as well.

Use `ScopeGuard` so both functions end the step on every return and free
the staging buffer whenever a step ends. To keep failed steps safe to
continue or restart, validate fingerprints and file writes in `Append`
before recording entries in `schema_`, and clear stale `schema_` entries
in `StartBuildStep` when the header has no buffer list yet.

title: Match TF kernels in XLA stateless_uniform and stateless_normal on CPU and GPU
body:
Fixes #121243

## Problem

Under `jit_compile=True`, `tf.random.stateless_uniform` and `tf.random.stateless_normal` return different values from eager and graph mode for the same seed on CPU. Comparing each stage of the XLA lowering with the TF kernels on TF 2.21:

| Stage | TF kernels vs XLA |
| --- | --- |
| Key and counter from a non-negative int32 seed | identical |
| Key and counter from a negative int32 seed, or an int64 seed | different |
| Raw Philox bits for the same key and counter | identical |
| Uniform values for the same key and counter | identical for half, different for bfloat16, float and double |
| Normal values for the same key and counter | different |

Three things differ:

- **Bits to floats:** the TF kernels build a half, bfloat16 or float value from the low 10, 7 or 23 bits of a 32-bit Philox word, and a double from the low 20 bits of one word and all 32 bits of the next (`Uint16ToHalf`, `Uint16ToGfloat16`, `Uint32ToFloat` and `Uint64ToDouble` in `xla/tsl/lib/random/random_distributions.h`). `xla::UniformFloatingPointDistribution` follows `Uint16ToHalf` for half, but takes the high bits for float and double, and the XLA kernels build bfloat16 values by truncating a float. For the float32 word `0x4337a926`, the TF kernel returns 0.43485 and XLA returns 0.26257.
- **Box-Muller pairing:** the TF normal kernels (`BoxMullerFloat`, `BoxMullerDouble`) transform consecutive pairs of uniform values and write the two results next to each other. `xla::NormalFloatingPointDistribution` pairs the first half of the values with the second half. For bfloat16, XLA also truncated the float result where the TF kernel rounds it.
- **Seeds:** `GenerateKey` sign-extends int32 seeds and uses all 64 bits of int64 seeds. On XLA, `GetU64FromS32Seeds` and `ScramblePhiloxKey` zero-extend int32 seeds and keep only the low 32 bits of int64 seeds.

The July change that added `MixSeedsForEagerCompatibility` (from #121416) only touched the V1 kernels in `stateless_random_ops.cc`, which `tf.random.stateless_*` doesn't use, and those still converted bits with `xla::UniformFloatingPointDistribution`.

## Fix

The changes are all in tf2xla. `xla/hlo/builder/lib/prng.cc`, which JAX also uses, is unchanged.

- `EagerCompatibleUniformDistribution` and `EagerCompatibleNormalDistribution` in `random_ops_util.cc` build values from Philox bits the way the TF kernels do. Each half, bfloat16 or float value comes from one 32-bit word and each double from one 64-bit word (two consecutive 32-bit words). Box-Muller runs on consecutive pairs, and half and bfloat16 normals are computed in float and rounded.
- `StatelessRandomUniformV2` and `StatelessRandomNormalV2` use them when the algorithm is Philox, the only one the TF kernels implement. `StatelessRandomUniform` and `StatelessRandomNormal` use them on the CPU and GPU XLA devices, which are the devices where those kernels use Philox.
- `MixSeedsForEagerCompatibility` moves from `stateless_random_ops.cc` to `random_ops_util.cc` and widens seeds to 64 bits like `GenerateKey`. On CPU and GPU, `StatelessRandomGetKeyCounter` and `StatelessRandomGetKeyCounterAlg` now use it in place of `ScramblePhiloxKey`.

Other algorithms and devices keep the current code, including TPU, where the default is not Philox. The truncated normal, integer, multinomial and other stateless kernels are unchanged, since their XLA algorithms differ from the TF kernels' in more than the bit conversion.

## Behavior differences

- **Values:** on CPU and GPU, `stateless_uniform` and `stateless_normal` under XLA now return the TF kernels' values instead of their current ones. Keys and counters change only for negative seeds and for int64 seeds outside the int32 range. For those seeds the other stateless ops change too. The V1 ops already mixed seeds this way on every device, so on other devices they change only for negative seeds.
- **Docs:** the note #121252 added to the docstrings is still accurate for TPU and for the other ops, so I left it as is. I can update the `stateless_uniform` and `stateless_normal` ones if you'd like.
- **Speed:** CPU timings for `[1024, 32000]` with the key and counter passed in, median of 15 runs, range over two runs:

| op | dtype | TF 2.21 (ms) | this PR (ms) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| uniform | float16 | 44.0 to 47.5 | 46.0 to 47.0 |
| uniform | bfloat16 | 46.9 to 50.6 | 46.2 to 48.6 |
| uniform | float32 | 46.3 to 47.5 | 49.7 to 52.1 |
| uniform | float64 | 35.0 to 35.6 | 35.4 to 35.6 |
| normal | float16 | 85.6 to 90.2 | 96.7 to 105.6 |
| normal | bfloat16 | 82.7 to 85.1 | 81.9 to 84.1 |
| normal | float32 | 100.7 to 105.0 | 102.1 to 105.6 |
| normal | float64 | 118.6 to 121.1 | 127.7 to 130.1 |

Float16 normals are now computed in float, like the TF kernel. End to end, `tf.function(jit_compile=True)` around `tf.random.stateless_uniform([1024, 32000], seed)` takes 1286 to 1336 ms for float32 on TF 2.21 and 35 ms with this PR. Float64 takes 35 ms on both. On TF 2.21, the float32 path only gets slow when the `ScramblePhiloxKey` key derivation is in the same computation as the bit generator. I haven't looked into why.

## Testing

New tests in `tensorflow/compiler/tests/stateless_random_ops_test.py`, skipped on TPU:

- `testGetKeyCounterMatchesTfKernel` compares `stateless_random_get_key_counter` on XLA with the TF kernel. It covers int32 and int64 seeds, including negative seeds and seeds outside the int32 range.
- `testMatchesTfKernel` compares the V2 ops (`stateless.stateless_random_uniform` and `stateless_random_normal`, with the default `alg` and with `alg='philox'`) and the V1 ops (`gen_stateless_random_ops`) with the TF kernels. It runs each float type for the shapes `[]`, `[0]` and `[3, 7]` and the seeds `[1, 2]`, `[0, 0]`, `[-1, 7]` and `[123456, -5]`. It checks exact equality for uniform and `assertAllCloseAccordingToType` for normal.

I built the tf2xla V1 and V2 stateless kernels and `random_ops_util` from master and from this branch as custom ops against TF 2.21, together with TF's CPU kernels for the same ops. Then I ran the test files on `XLA_CPU` with the ops routed to each build:

| Test file | master | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `compiler/tests/stateless_random_ops_test.py` | 24 of the 25 new tests fail; the other 132 pass | all 156 pass (11 skipped on both) |
| `python/kernel_tests/random/stateless_random_ops_test.py` | 498 pass, 1 fails | same |

The new test that passes on master is `testMatchesTfKernel_uniform_philox_float16`. XLA already converts half values like `Uint16ToHalf`, and with an explicit `alg='philox'` the key and counter come from `_philox_scramble_seed` in Python rather than from `StatelessRandomGetKeyCounter`.

The one failure in the second file, `testThreefryKeyCounterShape`, happens on both builds. It checks a later change to `python/ops/random_ops_util.py` that TF 2.21 doesn't have. That file also checks that the V1 and V2 ops agree, which still holds.

For the algorithms that keep the current code, `StatelessRandomUniformV2` and `StatelessRandomNormalV2` with ThreeFry return the same values as master for all four float types and the shapes `[]`, `[0]`, `[7]` and `[3, 5]`.

A broader comparison with the TF kernels covered all four float types, the V1 and V2 ops, and shapes `[2, 2]`, `[1001]`, `[3, 5, 7]`, `[1]` and `[]`. It used seeds `[1, 2]`, `[0, 0]`, `[-1, 7]`, `[123456, -5]` and `[2**31 - 1, -2**31]`:

| | master | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Key and counter (also int64 seed `[2**40 + 3, -2**35]`) | different for 4 of 6 seeds | identical |
| Uniform | different for bfloat16, float and double, and for half with negative seeds | identical |
| Normal, max abs difference | up to 5.9 | 2.4e-4 (float16), 2.0e-3 (bfloat16), 1.5e-6 (float32), 0 (float64) |

The float16 and bfloat16 differences are one unit in the last place.

title: Enable TFLITE_SINGLE_ROUNDING by default in TFLite.
body:
Enable TFLITE_SINGLE_ROUNDING by default in TFLite.

TFLite's scalar `MultiplyByQuantizedMultiplier` defaulted to legacy `gemmlowp` double rounding while `ruy` GEMM kernels already use single rounding unconditionally, causing 1-ULP off-by-one discrepancies (~1.8% of requantization inputs) between reference/scalar paths and `ruy`.

Preserve `gemmlowp` double rounding in legacy `uint8_t` reference and `optimized_ops` kernels so they remain consistent with their `gemmlowp`/NEON implementations, migrate negative-shift callers in `leaky_relu.h` to the two-argument `MultiplyByQuantizedMultiplier` overload, and include `<cstdlib>` in MLIR Lite `compatibility_macros.h` for `abort()`.

title: reject per-tensor operand with per-axis output in UniformQuantizedAdd
body: UniformQuantizedAdd requantizes both operands to the output scale before adding them, and to do that it reuses output_quantization_axis together with the output_scales and output_zero_points buffers. Those three are only checked against the broadcasted output shape, but the requantize step applies the axis to each operand, whose rank and dimension sizes can differ from the output under broadcasting. When the output is per-axis quantized while an operand is left per-tensor, that mismatch takes the per-channel requantize path over the smaller operand: a per-tensor rhs with a lower rank than the output walks output.dim_size(axis) of the operand and reads the scale and zero-point buffers past their end while writing the per-channel multiplier temporaries out of bounds, and a per-tensor lhs instead falls back to the per-tensor path and aborts on the single-element check inside Tensor::scalar(). I ran into it while fuzzing the op with mixed quantization axes through tf.raw_ops. The kernel only supports all-per-tensor or all-per-axis (aligned) configurations, which the existing axis-match checks already assume, so the fix rejects a per-axis output unless both operands are per-axis as well, right next to those checks. I added two regression tests covering the per-tensor lhs and per-tensor rhs cases alongside the existing error-path test.

title: Fix Win32 file mapping handle ownership and cleanup in MMapHandle.
body:
Fix Win32 file mapping handle ownership and cleanup in MMapHandle.

`swap(MMapHandle&, MMapHandle&)` exchanged the size, offsets, and data
pointer without swapping the Win32 `file_mapping_` handle used by move
construction and move assignment, causing a moved-to handle to close a
stale mapping handle in `UnMap()` and leak the active one.

`MMapHandle::UnMap()` also only closed `file_mapping_` when `data_` was
non-null and never reset it to `nullptr`, leaking the mapping handle if
`CreateFileMappingA` succeeded before `MapViewOfFile` failed. Close and
clear `file_mapping_` independently of `data_`.

title: Return zero from XLA SqrtGrad, RsqrtGrad and ReciprocalGrad when the upstream gradient is zero
body:
Fixes #118674

## Problem

Under `jit_compile=True`, the gradient of `tf.where(x > 0, tf.sqrt(x), 0)` is NaN at `x <= 0`, while eager and graph mode return 0. The cause isn't the `Select` gradient: graph mode without XLA builds the same gradient graph and returns 0. The difference is in the gradient kernels of the guarded op:

- The TF CPU/GPU kernels for `SqrtGrad`, `RsqrtGrad` and `ReciprocalGrad` (`scalar_sqrt_gradient_op`, `scalar_rsqrt_gradient_op` and `scalar_inverse_gradient_op` in `tensorflow/core/kernels/cwise_ops_gradients.h`) return 0 wherever the upstream gradient `dy` is 0.
- The tf2xla kernels in `tensorflow/compiler/tf2xla/kernels/binary_ops.cc` apply the gradient formula directly.

The branch that `tf.where` doesn't select gets a zero gradient. At `x = 0`, `SqrtGrad` then computes `0 * 0.5 / sqrt(0)`, which is NaN in the XLA kernel and 0 in the TF kernel. `Rsqrt` and `Reciprocal` behave the same way, since their outputs are inf at 0, and so does any NaN output such as `sqrt(-1)`.

Calling the kernels directly with `dy = 0` on TF 2.21:

| op | `y` | TF CPU | XLA |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sqrt_grad` | `[0, nan, inf]` | `[0, 0, 0]` | `[nan, nan, 0]` |
| `rsqrt_grad` | `[0, nan, inf]` | `[0, 0, 0]` | `[-0, nan, nan]` |
| `reciprocal_grad` | `[0, nan, inf]` | `[0, 0, 0]` | `[-0, nan, nan]` |

## Fix

`UnaryGradImpl` takes the gradient computed by the existing formula and selects 0 wherever `dy` is 0, matching the TF kernels. The three formulas are unchanged. It first broadcasts `dy` with `XlaBinaryOp::Broadcast`, like `DivNoNanImpl` and `MulNoNanImpl` in the same file, so the predicate has the output's shape when the XLA kernel broadcasts its inputs.

## Behavior differences

Only elements where `dy` is 0 change. They are now 0, as in the TF kernels, where XLA previously returned NaN, 0 or `-0` depending on `y`. Elements with a nonzero `dy` are computed as before.

The MLIR patterns `LowerSqrtGradOp` and `LowerRsqrtGradOp` in `tensorflow/compiler/mlir/tensorflow/transforms/lower_tf.td` use the same formulas. `SqrtGrad` and `RsqrtGrad` are on the MLIR bridge's tf2xla-preferred list, so I left those patterns as they are. I can update them here as well if you'd like.

## Testing

New `BinaryOpsTest.testUnaryGradOpsWithZeroUpstreamGradient` in `tensorflow/compiler/tests/binary_ops_test.py` runs the three ops with `y = [0, inf, nan, 4]` and `dy = [0, 0, 0, 5]` for every float and complex type.

I built the three kernels from master and from this branch as custom XLA ops against TF 2.21. Then I ran `binary_ops_test.py` on `XLA_CPU` with `gen_math_ops.reciprocal_grad`, `rsqrt_grad` and `sqrt_grad` routed to each build:

| Kernel | New test | `testFloatOps`, `testComplexOps` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| master | fails: `reciprocal_grad` returns `[-0, nan, nan, -80]` | pass |
| this PR | passes | pass |

I also ran every test in the file in its own process, with the three ops routed to this branch's kernels and with TF 2.21's own kernels. The new test is the only one whose result differs. 39 tests pass on both. 11 fail on both because the file tests fixes that are on master but not in TF 2.21, and `testDynamicDimensionLongerThanStaticOne` fails or crashes at random on both. None of these 12 call the three ops.

The repro from the issue, end to end with `jit_compile=True` and `x = [-1, 0, 1, 4]`:

| Pattern | master | this PR |

title: Load OpenCL extension functions in CLDevice constructor.
body:
Load OpenCL extension functions in CLDevice constructor.

Previously, `LoadOpenCLFunctionExtensions()` was only called inside `CreateDefaultGPUDevice()`. When an application initialized the OpenCL environment with a caller-supplied `cl_device_id` via `InferenceEnvironmentOptions::device`, extension function pointers such as `clCreateCommandBufferKHR` remained null even when the device reported support for `cl_khr_command_buffer`, causing a null function pointer dereference during command buffer creation.

Move `LoadOpenCLFunctionExtensions()` into the `CLDevice(cl_device_id, cl_platform_id)` constructor so extension functions are loaded regardless of how the device is created, and guard `cl_khr_command_buffer` usage in `InferenceContext` with a `clCreateCommandBufferKHR != nullptr` check.

title: Cap FixedLengthRecordDataset read buffers at the file size
body:
Fixes #113159

## Problem

`tf.data.FixedLengthRecordDataset` sizes every read buffer from `buffer_size` alone, whatever the size of the file. With the reproducer from the issue (an 80-byte file and `buffer_size=sys.maxsize - 8`), `io::InputBuffer` runs `new char[buffer_size]`, which throws `std::bad_alloc` and aborts the process. GZIP and ZLIB files abort the same way in the `ZlibInputStream` constructor. Restoring an iterator from a checkpoint aborts too, because both iterators create their buffers again in `RestoreInternal`.

## Fix

`Dataset::ReadBufferSize(file_size)` returns `min(buffer_size_, file_size)`, clamped to `[1, INT_MAX]`, and every read buffer now uses it:

- `UncompressedIterator`: the `InputBuffer` in `GetNextInternal` and `RestoreInternal`.
- `CompressedIterator`: the input and output buffers of `ZlibInputStream` in `GetNextInternal` and `RestoreInternal`. Both call sites now look up the file size with `GetFileSize`, which the uncompressed iterator already does for every file.

An input buffer larger than the file is never filled. The output buffer only sets how many decompressed bytes each `inflate` call writes. `ZlibInputStream::ReadNBytes` keeps inflating until the read is satisfied, so any positive size returns the same bytes; the existing tests already use a 10-byte buffer with 3-byte records.

`io::InputBuffer` stores its size as an `int`, and `ZlibInputStream` reads its input with an `int` byte count, so a buffer larger than `INT_MAX` fails for files of 2 GiB or more. The 1-byte minimum lets `ZlibInputStream` read a file that reports a size of 0 but has data, which it can't do with an empty input buffer.

The `BufferedInputStream` branch in `CompressedIterator` is unreachable, since `MakeIteratorInternal` only creates that iterator for GZIP and ZLIB, so I left it as is.

## Behavior differences

- **Memory:** a `buffer_size` larger than a file no longer allocates `buffer_size` bytes for that file, and no buffer is larger than `INT_MAX` bytes.
- **Compressed files:** each GZIP or ZLIB file costs one extra `GetFileSize` call when it is opened or restored.
- **Inflate step size:** for a compressed file smaller than `buffer_size`, each `inflate` call writes at most the compressed file size. At zlib's maximum compression ratio (64 MiB of zeros compressed to 63 KiB, read as 65,536 records of 1 KiB), reads took 542 to 555 ms with this change and 540 to 545 ms on master, with both the default and a 1 MiB `buffer_size`.

## Testing

New tests in `tensorflow/python/data/kernel_tests/fixed_length_record_dataset_test.py`:

- `FixedLengthRecordDatasetTest.testBufferSizeLargerThanFile` reads uncompressed, GZIP and ZLIB files with `buffer_size=2**63 - 1`.
- `FixedLengthRecordDatasetCheckpointTest.testBufferSizeLargerThanFile` runs the checkpoint verify functions over the same three file types. To support it, `_build_dataset` now passes `compression_type` and `buffer_size` through to the dataset. It already accepted `compression_type` but ignored it.

I built the kernel from master and from this branch as custom ops against TF 2.21. Then I ran the test file with `readers.FixedLengthRecordDataset` routed to each build:

| Kernel | Test file | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| master | this PR | aborts with `std::bad_alloc` in the new tests |
| this PR | this PR | 127 tests pass (69 TF1 variants skipped) |
| this PR without the two `RestoreInternal` changes | this PR | the checkpoint test aborts with `std::bad_alloc` in both the uncompressed and the compressed restore path |
| master and this PR | master | 55 tests pass on both |

I also ran a differential check on the master and patched builds. It covers 150 reads and mid-stream checkpoint restores:

- File types: uncompressed, GZIP and ZLIB.
- File contents: normal, empty, header and footer only, a body that is not a multiple of the record length, and 1000-byte records.
- Buffer sizes: 1, 7, 10, the default and 1 MiB.

Both builds returned identical records and errors, including for 0-byte files.

I also read 2.5 GiB files with `buffer_size=sys.maxsize` and 1 MiB records. With the `INT_MAX` cap, an uncompressed file reads and restores from a mid-stream checkpoint correctly, and a GZIP file returns all 2,560 records. Without the cap, the uncompressed file aborts with `std::bad_alloc` and the GZIP file returns no records.

Related: #113160. #126869 also bounds these buffers, as part of a broader change that covers `num_parallel_reads` as well. This PR only addresses the `buffer_size` abort.

title: [LiteRT converter] Don't fold reshapes around a dot_general whose LHS reshape raises the rank.

[LiteRT converter] Don't fold reshapes around a dot_general whose LHS reshape raises the rank.
END_PUBLIC

`RemoveReshapeAroundDotGeneral` (`-mhlo-optimize`) splits the input of the

title: Fix illegal memory read on GPU for sub-32-bit atomic CAS operations
body:
### Description
Fixes #129577.

#### Root Cause
In GPU device code (`tensorflow/core/util/gpu_device_functions.h`), atomic operations on sub-32-bit types (`Eigen::half`, `Eigen::bfloat16`) rely on `GpuAtomicCasHelper`. Because GPU hardware/PTX only supports 32-bit and 64-bit `atomicCAS`, sub-32-bit atomics are emulated by reading the enclosing 4-byte-aligned 32-bit word (`ptr & ~0x3`), updating the target 16-bit half, and executing a 32-bit `atomicCAS`.

When a 16-bit element is at a 4-byte-aligned boundary (e.g., `intptr & 0x2 == 0`) and is the **last element of an odd-length buffer** (e.g. 3 elements of `float16` = 6 bytes allocation, where the last element is at byte offset 4):
- The 32-bit read starting at offset 4 reads bytes 4–7.
- For allocations using direct allocators like `TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR=cuda_malloc`, bytes 6–7 are past the end of the allocation (size 6 bytes).
- This results in an out-of-bounds illegal memory read flagged by compute-sanitizer:
  ```
  ========= Invalid __global__ read of size 4 bytes =========
  ========= Address 0x7ff115000804 is out of bounds
  ========= and is inside the nearest allocation at 0x7ff115000800 of size 6 bytes
  ```

#### Solution
1. **`TypedAllocator::AllocationBytes`**: In `tensorflow/core/framework/typed_allocator.h`, ensure tensor memory allocations for sub-32-bit types (`sizeof(T) < sizeof(uint32_t)`) are padded to the next multiple of `sizeof(uint32_t)` (4 bytes), with overflow safety. For a 3-element `float16` tensor, 8 bytes are allocated instead of 6 bytes (at most 2 bytes overhead), safely backing the 32-bit CAS load.
2. **`ScopedAllocatorMgr`**: In `tensorflow/core/common_runtime/scoped_allocator_mgr.cc`, ensure precalculated field sizes in `ScopedAllocator` match the padded allocation size for sub-32-bit types.
3. **Documentation**: Documented the 4-byte allocation contract in `gpu_device_functions.h`.
4. **Unit Tests**: Added `CPUAllocatorTest.AllocationBytesPadding` in `tensorflow/core/framework/allocator_test.cc` verifying padding behavior for 8-bit, 16-bit, and >= 32-bit types.

title: Add an optional non-blocking per-device execution limiter for IFRT serving.
body:
Add an optional non-blocking per-device execution limiter for IFRT serving.

We serve some models on a server, and when a burst of concurrent requests hits a shared TPU, `IfrtServingExecutable` copies every request's inputs and outputs into TPU HBM and queues execution on the device, even though a single TPU chip does one model inference at a time. Waiting requests pile up transient input and output buffers in HBM simultaneously WITHOUT improving throughput, causing our HBM to spike!

The alternative of blocking caller threads (on a semaphore) is unsafe because IFRT async execution runs on TFRT's non-blocking work queue. Blocking starves downstream callbacks.

To bound HBM usage, let callers cap the number of in-flight requests per device (the requests for which inputs and outputs are allocated HBM). Note that this differs from the number of enqueued requests — enqueued requests have their inputs stored on the CPU host while waiting. For a single-chip use case, a cap of 2 keeps one running inference and one staged execution in HBM.

Introduce `IfrtAsyncExecutionLimiter` and wire an optional `IfrtAsyncExecutionLimiter*` through `IfrtModelContext` and `IfrtServingExecutable` (default `nullptr` disables limiting). Sharing a single limiter instance across co-hosted models lets them share the same per-device concurrency cap.
Each request still reserves its target device upfront so load trackers count queued work, but waits to stage inputs in HBM until it holds a `Permit` for its device(s) (acquired in sorted device-ID order for multi-device programs to avoid deadlocks). When a device is at capacity, excess requests wait asynchronously in a per-device FIFO queue on the host (via a future). Thus, no threads are blocked! And no HBM is allocated for their inputs and outputs.

For use cases that don't use the flag (default value of 0), this change is a no-op.

title: kernels/training_ops: guard SparseApply* GPU/CPU ops against int32 index overflow
body:
## Problem

Five CUDA kernels in `tensorflow/core/kernels/training_ops_gpu.cu.cc` compute a flat destination index as:

```cpp
Tindex param_index = param_row * col_size + (grad_index % col_size);
```

where `Tindex` may be `int32_t`. All five are explicitly instantiated for `int32_t` on `DEVICE_GPU`. When `var.dim_size(0)` exceeds `INT32_MAX`, a valid `param_row` near the top of the range causes the multiplication to overflow signed int32, wrap to a large negative value, and after sign-extension to 64 bits the GPU kernel reads/writes memory outside the allocated buffer.

Secondary hazard: `const Tindex N = indices.dim_size(0)` silently truncates `indices.dim_size(0)` before any bounds check when `indices.dim_size(0) > INT32_MAX`, and on GPU `grad.NumElements()` can exceed the 32-bit GPU launch limit when indices contain duplicate rows.

Affected kernels (lines in `training_ops_gpu.cu.cc`):

| Line | Kernel |
|------|--------|
| 50 | `SparseApplyAdagradKernel` |
| 89 | `SparseApplyProximalAdagradKernel` |
| 132 | `SparseApplyFtrlKernel` |
| 236 | `SparseApplyKerasMomentumKernel` |
| 816 | `SparseApplyAdadeltaKernel` |

## Fix

Replace the six per-op guards with a shared helper `ValidateSparseApplyIndexRange<Device, Tindex>` called **before** `const Tindex N = indices.dim_size(0)` in all six `Compute()` methods.

The helper:
- Always checks `var.dim_size(0)` and `indices.dim_size(0)` fit in `Tindex`. 
-  CPU workloads where `var.NumElements() > INT32_MAX` but `var.dim_size(0) <= INT32_MAX` (wide embedding tables) continue to work.
- On GPU only, additionally checks `var.NumElements() <= Tindex::max()` and `grad.NumElements() <= INT32_MAX` (GPU launch limit).

Also adds `#include <cstdint>` and `#include <limits>` and a unit test `testSparseApplyOpsRejectIndexOverflow` using a zero-element `[2147483648, 0]` shape to avoid large allocations in CI.

title: [TF] Fix unaligned complex scalar access in ROCm GpuSparse wrappers
body:
[TF] Fix unaligned complex scalar access in ROCm GpuSparse wrappers

In `rocm_sparse.cc`, host scalar parameters (`alpha`, `beta`) are passed by address to hipSPARSE routines via `AsHipComplex` (or as `const void*` in `hipsparseSpMM_bufferSize` / `hipsparseSpMM`). In ROCm, `hipFloatComplex` (`float2`) and `hipDoubleComplex` (`double2`) inherit from `HIP_vector_base<T, 2>`, which is declared with `alignas(2 * sizeof(T))` (8-byte alignment for `complex64`, 16-byte alignment for `complex128`) and backed by a native vector type, whereas `std::complex<T>` only guarantees `alignof(T)` (4-byte and 8-byte alignment, respectively).

Copy `*alpha` and `*beta` into `alignas(sizeof(Scalar))` local variables inside `CsrmmImpl`, `GpuSparse::SpMMBufferSize`, `GpuSparse::SpMM`, `CsrmvImpl`, `CsrgeamBufferSizeExtImpl`, and `Csrgeam2Impl` in `rocm_sparse.cc` so the host scalar addresses handed to hipSPARSE satisfy the `hipFloatComplex` / `hipDoubleComplex` alignment requirement.

title: Fix USE_PYWRAP_RULES parsing and missing TSL header exports.
body:
Fix USE_PYWRAP_RULES parsing and missing TSL header exports.

In `python_version.bzl`, `bool(os.environ.get("USE_PYWRAP_RULES", False))` evaluates non-empty strings such as `"0"` or `"false"` to `True`, preventing `USE_PYWRAP_RULES` from being disabled via environment variable. title: Eliminate redundant copies in DecodeCompressed.
body:
Eliminate redundant copies in DecodeCompressed.

`DecodeCompressed` runs on high-throughput input pipelines, where copying tensor payloads across ops wastes CPU cycles and allocator bandwidth on every batch.

For uncompressed inputs, the op now forwards the input tensor directly to the output instead of allocating a new tensor and deep-copying each string. This turns passthrough into a constant-time zero-copy handoff, cutting 16 MiB batch CPU time from 2.39 ms to ~63 ns (a 51% to 99.997% reduction across payload sizes).

For ZLIB and GZIP streams, chunk reads now yield unowned string views directly into the input tensor rather than staging bytes in temporary strings, speeding up multi-chunk decompression by up to 22.6% (and throughput by up to 29.1%).

title: Fix shape, index, and division bounds in Grappler ArithmeticOptimizer
body:
## Summary

Add defensive shape, index, and division checks across five rewrite stages in `tensorflow/core/grappler/optimizers/arithmetic_optimizer.cc`:

1. **`RemoveIdentityTranspose`**: validate `b[i] >= 0` and `static_cast<size_t>(b[i]) < a.size()` before indexing `a[static_cast<size_t>(b[i])]`.
2. **`HoistCWiseUnaryChainsStage` (`FirstNInputsAreUnique`)**: compute `start = node.op() == "Concat" ? 1 : 0` first and require `n >= 0 && n <= node.input_size() - start`.
3. **`ReplaceMulWithBroadcastByTile`**: return `absl::OkStatus()` when `input_dim == 0` before computing `output_dim / input_dim`, preserving negative symbolic unknown dimensions.
4. **`ReplacePackWithTileReshape`**: check `NumNonControlInputs(*input) > 1` on the current chain cursor, validate `input_shape` and `output_shape` via `PartialTensorShape::BuildPartialTensorShape` before checking `IsFullyDefined()`, and reject out-of-range axes, negative `N` with a distinct error message, and `int32_t` dimension or multiplicity overflow.
5. **`ConvertPowStage`**: return `absl::OkStatus()` when `pow.NumElements() == 0`.

The two Pack regression subcases fetch an `Identity` named `output`, leaving the outer `Pack` eligible for rewriting. The 332-fan-in comments describe rejection specifically for `p7`, and the shape-validation comment reflects `BuildPartialTensorShape`.

The remaining positive-control test is named `ValidTransposeAndConcatHoistControlsSucceed`, and the shape-boundary comment uses `return early` with the requested wording.

## Verification

- Built and ran the complete, unfiltered `//tensorflow/core/grappler/optimizers:arithmetic_optimizer_test_cpu` target: all 108 tests passed in Release (`-c opt`) and ASan+UBSan (`-fsanitize=address,undefined` with `-fno-sanitize-recover=all` and `TF_ENABLE_ONEDNN_OPTS=0`), with test-result caching disabled and no sanitizer diagnostics.
- `git diff --check` passed.

This change was prepared with automated assistance. These results cover the current revision.

title: Validate Grappler function and loop optimizer attribute and port bounds
body:
Grappler should reject invalid loop attributes and leave unsupported function calls and loop predicates unchanged.

This change validates indirect call `Tin` and `Tout` at the entry of `SpecializeFunction`, before constructing a specialized function or rewriting its call site. It checks the attribute types and counts against the caller inputs and target function signature without allocating temporary type vectors. Call-site updates use the caller's existing local `NodeDef`.

For loop invariant motion, `parallel_iterations` must be an integer in the range `1..INT_MAX` before the node is changed. Output ports are checked before indexing the inferred output types, and an omitted `is_constant` attribute is handled safely.

Dead-branch removal checks missing and control-only fanins, resolves port-qualified inputs, and skips control inputs in all three zero-iteration-loop input scans. Constant predicates and operands share safe tensor extraction. Evaluated predicates must be scalar booleans, and evaluated outputs are released on every return path. Malformed constant Switch predicates produce a `VLOG(3)` message.

The tests cover invalid iteration counts and attribute types, preservation of `parallel_iterations = 10`, indirect-call signature mismatches and cached specializations, malformed and non-scalar constants, and missing, control, and port-qualified inputs. The loop optimizer and both test targets declare their direct Abseil status dependencies.

Validation: the complete, unfiltered `//tensorflow/core/grappler/optimizers:loop_optimizer_test` and `//tensorflow/core/grappler/optimizers:function_optimizer_test` suites pass in both Release (`-c opt`) and ASan+UBSan configurations, with test-result caching disabled. Each configuration runs both generated test variants: 21 loop tests and 31 function tests per variant, 104 passing test executions total. No ASan or UBSan error reports were produced. These were CPU builds; the `_gpu` target names do not imply GPU execution.

title: Tie graph-mode custom gradient registrations to their graph's lifetime
body:
Fixes #129615.

## Problem
In graph mode, `@tf.custom_gradient` registers a `CustomGradient-<uid>` function in the global gradient registry and never removes it. That function captures forward tensors, so every traced `FuncGraph` that used a custom gradient, with all its ops and tensors, stays alive for the life of the process. Repeatedly training Keras models with `run_eagerly=False` leaks two graphs per model.

## Fix
- The graph that contains the custom-gradient `IdentityN` op now owns the gradient function, in a new `Graph._custom_gradient_functions` dict.
- The registry keeps only a small forwarder that holds a weak reference to the graph and looks the function up by name.
- `weakref.finalize` removes the registry entry once the graph is garbage collected.
- The forward pass is unchanged: no `_override_gradient_function` and no change around `identity_n`. So it cannot conflict with `GradientTape` or `ForwardAccumulator`, which was the problem in #129616.
- SavedModel export still works, because the forwarder does not depend on `op.graph`.

## Tests
Added to `CustomGradientTest` in `gradients_test.py`:
- `testCustomGradientRegistrationReleasedWithGraph`
- `testCustomGradientRegistrationReleasedWithFunction`
- `testCustomGradientForwardAccumulatorInFunction`

The two lifetime tests fail without the fix and pass with it. Against TF 2.21, with this patch applied to the installed `custom_gradient.py` and `ops.py`, all `CustomGradientTest` tests and SavedModel `test_custom_gradients*` tests pass.

Results from the issue's reproduction script (30 models):

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Retained FuncGraphs | +60 | 0 |
| Retained Operations | +26,160 | 0 |
| CustomGradient registry entries | +60 | 0 |

title: PR #51563: [ROCm] Support contiguous sub-communicators in the MORI collectives backend
body:
PR #51563: [ROCm] Support contiguous sub-communicators in the MORI collectives backend

Imported from GitHub PR <url>

## Summary

The MORI backend used to accept only the full global clique with an identity
rank-to-PE mapping. Any collective over a subset of devices was rejected, for
example `replica_groups={{0,1},{2,3}}` or a collective-permute whose connected
components form smaller cliques.

This PR adds support for sub-communicators whose ranks map to a **contiguous**
PE range (`rank i -> PE base + i`), such as `{3,4,5}`. Arbitrary mappings such
as `{0,2,7}` are still rejected with a clear error.

It also repins MORI to `xla-pin-20261024`, which provides the matching
facade-side support.

## Changes

### `xla/backends/gpu/collectives/mori_communicator.{h,cc}`

- Each `MoriCommunicator` now owns its own `CollectivesFacade` instance, created
  through `CollectivesFacade::Get(rank, num_ranks, rank_to_pe)`. Previously it
  held a non-owning pointer to the per-device singleton.
- `CollectivesFacade::Get` validates the mapping. It requires the PEs to be
  contiguous, to fit within the node's LSA team, and to match this device's PE.
  If any of these fail, `Create` returns `InvalidArgument` with the rank and the
  full `rank_to_pe` mapping.
- The old full-world/identity-mapping checks and the cached `rank_` and
  `num_ranks_` are gone. `NumRanks()`, `CurrentRank()`, `ToString()` and the
  all-to-all buffer-count check now read the communicator-local rank and size
  from the facade.
- The unused `MoriCollectives*` back-pointer and the `friend` declaration are
  removed, and `Create` no longer takes the parent collectives.

### `xla/backends/gpu/collectives/mori_collectives.cc`

- Updated to the new MORI API: `CollectivesFacade::Create(comm, pool_size,
  max_staging)` no longer takes `rank`/`nranks`, and
  `MoriCommunicator::Create` no longer takes the parent collectives.
- `rank_to_pe` is still built from the clique key's global device ids. A
  comment now notes the contiguity requirement.

### `third_party/roc_mori/workspace.bzl`

- Repinned from `xla-pin-20261015` (`4330cd96`) to `xla-pin-20261024`
  (`994a8c88`).

## Limitations

- Only contiguous PE ranges within a single node (LSA team) are supported.

title: Fix ArgMax/ArgMin reading int64 axis incorrectly on big-endian (s390x)
body:
ArgOp::Compute reads the dimension tensor unconditionally as **int32**. For a Tidx=int64 axis on big-endian, scalar<int32_t>() reads the **high** 32 bits of the 8-byte buffer, causing the axis value to be silently **misread** and the op to reduce the wrong dimension.

Wrapped the dimension read in a __BYTE_ORDER__ guard. On big-endian, dispatch on dimension.dtype() and use scalar<int64_t>() for DT_INT64. On little-endian the preprocessor keeps the original line untouched — no change to compiled output on x86.

title: Store Fusion Explorer graphs and metadata directly in the zipapp.
body:
Store Fusion Explorer graphs and metadata directly in the zipapp.

`--xla_dump_fusion_visualization` previously built a temporary SQLite database on disk (`fusions.db`), compressed each unique DOT graph with GZIP before inserting it as a BLOB, memory-mapped the database file, and DEFLATE-compressed it a second time into the output `.pyz` zipapp, only for `viewer_server.py` to unpack `fusions.db` back to a temporary directory on startup. That pulled the entire SQLite library (~1.90 MB stripped) into binaries linking `hlo_graph_dumper` solely to index an append-only list of frames and integer-keyed DOT graphs.

Write `metadata.json` and `graphs/<i>.dot` directly into `tsl::io::ZipWriter` in `xla/service/hlo_graph_dumper.cc` and serve them directly from `zipfile.ZipFile` in `xla/service/fusion_explorer/viewer_server.py`, dropping the SQLite dependency. Packaging is ~1.3x faster on multi-step fusion traces by avoiding temporary database file I/O and double compression, and viewer startup is ~2.3x faster with lower disk and memory overhead because `viewer.html` and `metadata.json` are read once in memory while individual DOT graphs are read on demand without extracting a database file.

title: Accept bool input in tf.experimental.numpy real, conj, isreal and iscomplex
body:
The functions for getting the real part of a complex number (`isreal`, `iscomplex`, `real`, `conj`) raise an exception when fed with boolean inputs via the `tensorflow.experimental.numpy` import:

```python
import tensorflow.experimental.numpy as tnp
tnp.isreal([True, False])  # TypeError: Cannot convert 0 to EagerTensor of dtype bool (NumPy: [True, True])
tnp.iscomplex([True, False])  # TypeError: Cannot convert 0 to EagerTensor of dtype bool (NumPy: [False, False])
tnp.real([True, False])  # TypeError: input must be a numeric tensor (NumPy: [True, False])
tnp.conj([True, False])  # TypeError: Expected numeric or variant tensor (NumPy: [1, 0])
```

`tnp.conjugate` fails with the same error as `tnp.conj`.

### Reason

The `real` and `conj` are direct aliases of `math_ops.real` and `math_ops.conj`, which don't accept bool tensors. The `isreal` and `iscomplex` functions perform checks of the type `imag(x) == 0` and `imag(x) != 0`. With bool values, `imag` returns a bool array and comparison of this array with 0 raises an exception unless NumPy methods on `Tensor` is used (which is not the case when just importing tensorflow).

### Fix

The `real` and `conj` functions now return boolean inputs untouched, as is done for integers and floats (note that `conj` keeps the dtype of the bool, unlike NumPy returning `[1, 0]` int arrays). `conjugate` now calls `conj`. If `isreal` and `iscomplex` are called, they now check the dtype of the input value, doing the existing check on complex inputs, and returning `[True, True]` and `[False, False]` arrays on the others (as NumPy implementation).

### Testing

- Add `[True, False]` to `testReal` and `testImag` in `np_array_ops_test.py`.
- `testComplexPartsOfBool` added to `np_math_ops_no_numpy_methods_test.py`, which is where this test is placed because the other test files import with NumPy methods on `Tensor` and mask the `isreal`/`iscomplex` error.
- Tested that `testReal` and `testComplexPartsOfBool` fail without this patch and pass with it.
- Run all test suites for numpy_ops before/after the patch (including `tests/np_test.py` and `np_interop_test` with CUDA). All tests give the same output except for two updated tests (`testRoll` fails before and after because of the local nightly build being older than master).

title: The TFLite slim model importer, the TFLite StableHLO pipeline and the ODX pipeline run `vhlo-legalize-to-stablehlo` directly. That pass only accepts VHLO ops at the current version. Producers such as JAX serialize for older consumers, so their artifacts can hold older op versions. These readers then ...
body:
The TFLite slim model importer, the TFLite StableHLO pipeline and the ODX pipeline run `vhlo-legalize-to-stablehlo` directly. That pass only accepts VHLO ops at the current version. Producers such as JAX serialize for older consumers, so their artifacts can hold older op versions. These readers then fail with "failed to legalize operation 'vhlo.<op>_vN'" whenever an op gets a new VHLO version.

Use `createStablehloDeserializePipeline` instead. It runs `vhlo-to-version` to the current version before legalizing, as StableHLO's own deserializer and XLA do. Programs already at the current version are unaffected.

title: fix(sparse): validate input dtypes in tf.sparse.cross (closes #118198)
body:
## Problem
When non-integer, non-string tensors (such as floating-point tensors with `inf` or `NaN` values) are passed to `tf.sparse.cross` or `tf.sparse.cross_hashed`, the function produces inconsistent and corrupted categorical string tokens across CPU and GPU devices (e.g. `b'-9223372036854775808_X_5'` on CPU vs `b'9223372036854775807_X_5'` on GPU) due to undefined integer casting behavior.

## Root Cause
In `tensorflow/python/ops/sparse_ops.py` (`_sparse_cross_internal` and `_sparse_cross_internal_v2`), inputs were checked only with `if values[i].dtype != dtypes.string:` and blindly cast to `dtypes.int64` via `math_ops.cast`. Because `dtype.is_integer` was not checked, floating-point tensors bypassed the expected categorical type restriction and underwent undefined integer casting. Furthermore, an error message in `_sparse_cross_internal` incorrectly stated `"All inputs must be SparseTensors"` instead of `"All inputs must be Tensor or SparseTensor."`.

## Solution
1. **Shared Input Validation Helper (`sparse_ops.py`)**:
  - Added `_validate_sparse_cross_inputs(inputs, op_name)` shared between `_sparse_cross_internal_v2` and `_sparse_cross_internal`.

title: Validate row partitions before ragged tensor output calculations
body:
## Summary

This change validates the inputs of `RaggedTensorToTensorBaseOp::Compute` (`tensorflow/core/kernels/ragged_tensor_to_tensor_op.cc`) before any output shape or index calculation consumes them:

- `Compute` first requires a ragged rank of at least 1, exactly one partition tensor per configured partition type, a scalar `FIRST_DIM_SIZE`, and a vector for every other partition type. It then requires `values` to have rank at least 1 before it reads `values.dim_size(0)`.
- `ValidateRowSplits` checks every `ROW_SPLITS` partition before `GetMaxWidthRowSplit` or `CalculateOutputIndexRowSplit` uses it: the tensor must be nonempty, start at 0, and be nondecreasing, compared before any subtraction.
- Before the output is allocated, the last value of the innermost `ROW_SPLITS` must not exceed `values.dim_size(0)`, with the same `Row partition size (...) exceeds the number of values (...)` message as the existing check after index construction. An outer `ROW_SPLITS` followed by another `ROW_SPLITS` must end at `next.size() - 1`. The values length is held as `int64_t`.
- `CalculateOutputIndexValueRowID` rejects a first `VALUE_ROWIDS` entry that is negative or not less than the parent size, comparing in the signed index type.
- `GetFirstDimensionSize` rejects a negative `FIRST_DIM_SIZE` and keeps its own scalar and vector shape checks for `FIRST_DIM_SIZE` and a first `ROW_SPLITS`.
- The empty-split checks that `ValidateRowSplits` makes redundant are removed, `CalculateOutputIndexRowSplit` documents its precondition, split loops use `Eigen::Index`, `Tensor` handles are bound as `const Tensor&`, and `<cstdint>` is included.

## Verification

- `ragged_tensor_to_tensor_op_test.cc` adds a valid `ROW_SPLITS` control and negative tests for: non-zero, non-monotonic, and empty `ROW_SPLITS` (first, outer, and inner partitions); negative and out-of-range first `VALUE_ROWIDS`; negative and non-scalar `FIRST_DIM_SIZE`; non-vector first `ROW_SPLITS`, inner `ROW_SPLITS`, and `VALUE_ROWIDS`; a short partition list; scalar `values`; nested `ROW_SPLITS` count mismatches; and innermost and nested split endpoints beyond the values length, including `int64_t{1} << 62`. Every added test runs with both `int32` and `int64` row partitions.
- `bazel test //tensorflow/core/kernels:ragged_tensor_to_tensor_op_test` passes on the final tree (all 34 tests).
- With the same tests, removing the new endpoint and count checks from `Compute` fails `RowSplitLastValueBoundedBeforeIndexCalculation`, `NestedRowSplitLastValueBounded`, and `NestedRowSplitPartitionSizesMustMatch` (the `int64_t{1} << 62` cases throw from `vector::reserve`), and removing the `values` rank check fails `ScalarValuesRejected`. The kernel at a8814c11 fails 9 of the added tests and aborts on `ShortPartitionListRejected`.

title: Validate begin, end, and strides dtype compatibility in ValidateStridedSliceOp
body:
## Summary

`ValidateStridedSliceOp` in `tensorflow/core/util/strided_slice_op.cc` dispatches `BuildDenseSpec` based on `strides_tensor.dtype()` (`DT_INT32`, `DT_INT64`, or `DT_INT16`), and `BuildDenseSpec` then reads `begin_tensor` and `end_tensor` using that same template type `T` without verifying that `begin_tensor` and `end_tensor` have the same `dtype()` as `strides_tensor`. When `begin_tensor` or `end_tensor` has a different integer type than `strides_tensor` (for example `DT_INT64` vs `DT_INT32`), accessing `begin_tensor` or `end_tensor` as `T` triggers a fatal type check failure instead of returning `absl::InvalidArgumentError`. In addition, an unsupported `strides_tensor.dtype()` previously reached `LOG(FATAL)` instead of returning an error `absl::Status`.

## Fix

- In `ValidateStridedSliceOp` (`tensorflow/core/util/strided_slice_op.cc`), validate that `strides_tensor.dtype()` is one of `DT_INT16`, `DT_INT32`, or `DT_INT64`, and that any non-null `begin_tensor` and `end_tensor` have the same `dtype()` as `strides_tensor` before calling `BuildDenseSpec`.
- Replace the `LOG(FATAL)` fallback in `ValidateStridedSliceOp` with `absl::InvalidArgumentError`.
- Add unit tests in `tensorflow/core/util/strided_slice_op_test.cc`:
  - `ValidateStridedSliceOpTest.MatchingInt64BeginEndStridesSucceeds`
  - `ValidateStridedSliceOpTest.RejectsMismatchedOrInvalidDtypes`

title: Correct reduce_variance for rounding error in the mean
body:
Fixes #117286

## Problem

`tf.math.reduce_variance` and `tf.math.reduce_std` compute `mean((x - mean)**2)`. Any rounding error in the mean shifts every deviation by the same amount, and squaring adds that shift to the variance. Under `jit_compile=True`, XLA turns the division by the element count into a multiplication by its reciprocal, so for `[1e10, 1e10, 1e10]` in float32 the mean comes out one ulp high and the variance is 1048576 instead of 0. The same formula also loses accuracy in eager mode when the data has a large offset.

`tf.nn.moments` had the same problem and was fixed in #125560. These two functions still use the old formula.

## Fix

- In `_reduce_variance_in_stable_dtype`, which both functions share, subtract the squared mean of the deviations, `mean(d**2) - mean(d)**2` with `d = x - mean`. This is the formula `tf.nn.moments` uses on master. For complex inputs it is `mean(|d|**2) - |mean(d)|**2`.
- Clamp the result at zero, as `tf.nn.moments` does.

Behavior differences:

- **Overflow-scale inputs:** for identical values large enough that both terms overflow (`[1e38] * 3` in float32, `[1e307] * 3` in float64), the result under XLA is NaN instead of inf. `tf.nn.moments` on master behaves the same way.
- **Cost:** the extra reduction adds one more pass over the input. On CPU, float32 `[4096, 4096]` with `axis=1` went from 2.6 ms to 3.9 ms in a graph and from 2.9 ms to 4.9 ms under XLA.

## Testing

`testReduceVarAndStdIdenticalLargeValues` mirrors `MomentsTest.testIdenticalLargeValues`. It covers rows of identical values in float16, bfloat16, float32, float64, complex64 and complex128, with both signs and both `keepdims` settings, calling the functions directly, through `tf.function`, and with `jit_compile=True`. `math_ops_test` now sets `xla_enabled = True` so the XLA leg runs. On master the test fails in graph and eager mode: under XLA the variance is 67108864 for `7.5e10` in float32 and 134217728 for `7.5e10+7.5e10j` in complex64. With this change it passes.

Results, on CPU (macOS arm64) with TF 2.21.0 and master's or this branch's version of the three functions loaded into `math_ops`:

| Input, `axis=1` | Master, eager | Master, XLA | This PR, eager | This PR, XLA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `[1e10] * 3` float32, variance / std | 0 / 0 | 1048576 / 1024 | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |
| `[1e15] * 3` float32, variance / std | 0 / 0 | 4.5e15 / 6.7e7 | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |
| `N(1e3, 0.01)`, shape `[1000, 64]`, `axis=0`, max rel. error vs float64 | 7.2e-4 | 2.8e-3 | 1.1e-7 | 2.8e-7 |
| `N(1e4, 1)`, shape `[64, 1000]`, max rel. error vs float64 | 2.5e-6 | 2.4e-5 | 5.4e-7 | 3.8e-7 |

- **Unchanged:** errors on zero-offset data, complex results, gradients (max difference 7e-18 in float64), NaN and inf inputs, and the docstring examples.
- **Other suites:** the rest of `math_ops_test` and `weak_tensor_math_ops_test` show no new failures.

Related: #118179, #125560

title: Release graph-mode custom gradients together with their graph
body:
Fixes #129615

## Problem

In graph mode (including `tf.function` tracing), every `@tf.custom_gradient` call registers its gradient function in the global gradient registry under a unique `CustomGradient-<uid>` name, and nothing ever removes that entry. The registered function closes over the user's `grad_fn`, which usually captures forward tensors (as in the `tf.custom_gradient` docstring examples), so every traced `FuncGraph` that used a custom gradient stays alive for the rest of the process. Repeatedly building and discarding models or `tf.function`s therefore grows memory without bound, even after `clear_session()` and `gc.collect()`.

#109334 removed one of these captures (`result`), which is enough for the Keras workload in the issue, but the registry entries still accumulate and any `grad_fn` that uses a forward tensor still pins its graph.

## Fix

- The gradient function is attached to the `IdentityN` op through the graph's existing gradient function override (`Operation._gradient_function`, the same hook `control_flow_util_v2` and SavedModel loading use), so the graph owns it and it is released together with the graph.
- The `CustomGradient-<uid>` registry entry and the `_gradient_op_type` attr are kept, because SavedModel export looks up custom gradients by that name (`_trace_gradient_functions` in `save.py`). The registered function now holds only a weak reference, and a `weakref.finalize` removes the entry once the gradient function is collected.
- If code keeps a reference to the registered function and calls it after the graph is gone, it raises a `LookupError` naming the gradient.
- The inputs are converted to tensors once, and the `IdentityN` op is created with tape recording stopped. `Graph._override_gradient_function` cannot be nested, and a `ForwardAccumulator` inside a `tf.function` would otherwise call a function (which sets its own override) while recording the op. `record_operation` still records the custom gradient for tapes and accumulators.

Gradient computation itself is unchanged: `ops.get_gradient_function` already checks `op._gradient_function` before the registry, and it returns the same wrapper that used to be registered.

Behavior differences:

- **Imported graph copies:** if a copy of the graph is imported elsewhere (for example from a `GraphDef`) and its gradient is requested after the original graph has been collected, the lookup now fails with the usual "No gradient defined" error instead of reusing the old gradient function. That function usually refers to tensors of the collected graph, so this case did not work in general before either.
- **Forward mode in `tf.function`:** a `ForwardAccumulator` now takes the JVP of a custom gradient function from its `grad_fn`, as `GradientTape` does for the VJP. Before, the `IdentityN` op was recorded with its pass-through gradient first and the accumulator kept that JVP, so it differentiated the forward computation. Eager mode still does. For `x * x` with a `grad_fn` of `100 * dy` at `x = 3`, the JVP inside a `tf.function` goes from 6.0 to 100.0, and stays 6.0 in eager mode.

## Testing

Added `CustomGradientTest.testCustomGradientReleasedWithGraph` in `gradients_test.py`: it builds a custom gradient whose `grad_fn` uses a forward tensor, checks the gradient value and that the registry entry exists, then drops the graph and checks that the graph is collected, the registry entry is gone, and a previously looked-up registered function raises `LookupError`. It fails on master (the graph stays alive) and passes with this change.

Added `CustomGradientTest.testCustomGradientForwardAccumulatorInFunction`: it runs a `ForwardAccumulator` and a `GradientTape` around a custom gradient inside a `tf.function` and checks the value, JVP and gradient. It fails with an `AssertionError` from `_override_gradient_function` without the recording change and passes with it.

Verified against pip TensorFlow 2.21 with the patched `custom_gradient.py` loaded over the installed module (CPU, macOS):

- `gradients_test.py`: 115 tests; the only failure, `testHessianNameScope`, also fails without this change.
- SavedModel custom gradient round trips (`load_test.py`, all 9 `*custom_gradient*` cases): pass.
- `while_v2_test`, `record_test`, `gradient_checker_v2_test`, `check_numerics_callback_test`, `mirrored_variable_test`, `loss_scale_optimizer_test`, and the custom gradient tests in `resource_variable_ops_test`: pass.
- `backprop_test`, `forwardprop_test`, `control_flow_ops_test`: identical results with and without this change (the failures there come from master-only tests running on 2.21).

The reproduction script from the issue (30 Keras models, `run_eagerly=False`):

| | FuncGraph | Operation | SymbolicTensor | `CustomGradient-*` entries |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.21 | +60 | +26,160 | +24,780 | +60 |
| master | +0 | +0 | +0 | +60 |
| this PR | +0 | +0 | +0 | +0 |

A `tf.function` retraced 10 times around a custom gradient whose `grad_fn` uses its input retains 10 `FuncGraph`s on master and none with this change.

Related: #80895, #97697

title: Override disable_padding to false for priority-aware batch scheduler.
body:
Override disable_padding to false for priority-aware batch scheduler.

When `enable_priority_aware_batch_scheduler` is enabled, `disable_padding` is not supported: leaving `disable_padding` set to `true` causes `ApplyBatchPaddingPolicy` and `RoundToLowestAllowedBatchSize` to bypass `allowed_batch_sizes` rounding and padding.

Override `disable_padding` to `false` with a `LOG(WARNING)` in `BatchResourceBase::GetBatcherQueueOptions` and `SharedBatchScheduler::AddQueue` when `enable_priority_aware_batch_scheduler` is `true`, matching how other unsupported queue options are rewritten.

title: Reject partial single-slice checkpoints in TensorSliceReader::GetTensor
body:
## Summary

`TensorSliceReader::GetTensor` (`tensorflow/core/util/tensor_slice_reader.cc:236-263`) rejects multi-slice checkpoints when `tss->Slices().size() > 1` (`Sliced checkpoints are not supported`), but when `tss->Slices().size() == 1` it assumes the sole stored `TensorSlice` covers the full tensor `shape`. If a checkpoint file contains only a single partial slice (for example `0,2:-` for a `[4, 5]` tensor), `GetTensor` allocates a full `tensorflow::Tensor` of `shape` via `tensorflow::Tensor::BuildTensor`, copies only the partial slice into the output buffer, and returns `absl::OkStatus()` with the remaining tensor elements left uninitialized.

This change validates `slice.SliceTensorShape(shape, &slice_shape)` and verifies `slice_shape.IsSameSize(shape)` in `TensorSliceReader::GetTensor` before allocating the output tensor, returning `absl::UnimplementedError("Sliced checkpoints are not supported")` when the single slice does not cover the full tensor shape.

## Validation

Added unit tests in `tensorflow/core/util/tensor_slice_reader_test.cc`:
- `TensorSliceReaderTest.GetTensorFullSliceControlSucceeds`
- `TensorSliceReaderTest.GetTensorRejectsSinglePartialSlice`
