title: Fix shape and attribute validation in Grappler `ShapeOptimizer`
body:
### Summary

Add attribute, fanin, and integer range checks in `ShapeOptimizer::Optimize` (`tensorflow/core/grappler/optimizers/shape_optimizer.cc`):

1. **Missing `T` attribute in `is_int`**:
  - `is_int` previously called `node.attr().at("T").type()`. `node.attr()` is a protobuf map, and its `at()` fails a CHECK and aborts the process when the key is missing, so a `Prod` or `Div` node without a `"T"` attribute aborted the optimizer.
  - Use `node.attr().find("T")` and treat a node without `"T"` as not an integer node.

2. **`Shape` -> `Prod` -> `Size` rewrite**:
  - Skip a `Shape` node when its input 0 has no regular fanin (`shape_input.node == nullptr || shape_input.port_id < 0`), for example when a control input sits in that slot. The rewrite copies `input(0)` of the `Shape` node into the new `Size` node.
  - Rewrite a `Prod` fanout only when the `Shape` output feeds input 0 of the `Prod` (`fanout.port_id != 0` is skipped), `is_int(*fanout.node)` holds, and `NumNonControlInputs(*fanout.node) == 2`. Without the input 0 check, a `Prod(data, Shape(x))` that uses the shape as its reduction indices was rewritten into `Size(x)`, which drops `data`.
  - Skip the rewrite when input 1 of the `Prod` has no regular fanin (`reduce_indices.node == nullptr || reduce_indices.port_id < 0`) instead of dereferencing `reduce_indices.node`.

3. **`Div` -> `Const` size-ratio rewrite**:
  - Check `is_int(node)` before rewriting a `Div` node.
  - Skip a `Div` when either data input has no regular fanin (`input1.port_id < 0` or `input2.port_id < 0`), for example `Div(["^size_x", "size_y"])`.
  - For `DT_INT32`, skip the rewrite when the 64-bit `ComputeSizeRatio(shape1, shape2)` result exceeds `std::numeric_limits<int32_t>::max()`, instead of truncating it into `int_val`. `DT_INT64` results are still folded into `int64_val`.

### Tests

Added to `tensorflow/core/grappler/optimizers/shape_optimizer_test.cc`:

- `ShapeOptimizerTest.DoesNotOptimizeShapeAsProdReductionInput`: `Prod(data, Shape(x))` with a rank-1 `x` stays a `Prod` with its inputs unchanged and evaluates to the same value.
- `ShapeOptimizerTest.OptimizeStaticSizeRatioAtAndAboveInt32Limit`: an int32 ratio of `2147483647` folds to a `Const`, an int32 ratio of `2^31` stays a `Div`, and an int64 ratio of `2^31` folds to a `Const` with `int64_val(0) == 2^31`.
- `ShapeOptimizerTest.HandlesMalformedProdInputs`: a `Prod` whose second input is a control input (`^x`) stays a `Prod`.
- `ShapeOptimizerTest.HandlesControlInputInDivDataSlot`: an int32 `Div` with a control input in data slot 0 (`^size_x`) stays a `Div` with its inputs unchanged. Both `Size` nodes read a `Const` with a static shape, and the test then optimizes the same graph with two data inputs on that `Div` and expects a `Const` with value 1, which shows that the graph is otherwise eligible for folding.
- `ShapeOptimizerTest.HandlesMissingIntegerTypeAttributes`: a separate graph with a `Prod` and a `Div` that have no `"T"` attribute returns `kAborted` with an empty output, and the test checks that both nodes are in the input graph.

### Verification

Built with Bazel (`-c opt`, Linux x86_64, no GPU present) and ran `bazel test //tensorflow/core/grappler/optimizers:shape_optimizer_test_cpu //tensorflow/core/grappler/optimizers:shape_optimizer_test_gpu --test_output=all`:

- With this change: 8 of 8 tests pass in each target.
- With the same tests and `shape_optimizer.cc` from the PR base: `DoesNotOptimizeShapeAsProdReductionInput` (the `Prod` is rewritten to `Size` with input `x`), `OptimizeStaticSizeRatioAtAndAboveInt32Limit`, and `HandlesMalformedProdInputs` fail, and the run ends at `HandlesControlInputInDivDataSlot`, which also fails, so `HandlesMissingIntegerTypeAttributes` does not run.
- With this change except the `Div` input port check: the first six tests pass and `HandlesControlInputInDivDataSlot` fails.

title: Fix/issue 128986 Disable fast min/max by default on CPU to follow IEEE 754 signed zero semantics
body:
## Problem
Fixes #128986

When reducing or computing elementwise minimum / maximum on floating point values with XLA on CPU, `tf.reduce_min([0.0, -0.0])` returns `+0.0` instead of `-0.0`, whereas eager execution and GPU XLA return `-0.0`.

IEEE 754-2019 minimum semantics require `-0.0` when comparing `+0.0` and `-0.0`.

## Root cause
In `third_party/xla/xla/debug_options_flags.cc`, `opts.set_xla_cpu_enable_fast_min_max(true)` was enabled by default on CPU (unlike GPU which defaults to `false`). When enabled, floating point min/max is lowered via `FCmpULE` / `FCmpUGE` with select (`llvm_util.cc`). Because `+0.0 == -0.0` in standard float comparison, `+0.0 <= -0.0` evaluates to `true` and selects `+0.0`.

## Fix
1. Set `opts.set_xla_cpu_enable_fast_min_max(false)` by default on CPU in `third_party/xla/xla/debug_options_flags.cc` (matching GPU default), with explanatory comment and updated flag help text.
2. Added parameter-based unit tests for signed-zero preservation under default CPU debug options in `third_party/xla/xla/tests/fmax_fmin_test.cc` and `third_party/xla/xla/tests/reduce_test.cc`.

## Testing
- Verified test suite passes:
  ```bash
  bazel test @xla//xla/tests:fmax_fmin_test @xla//xla/tests:reduce_test
  ```

title: Fix/issue 128477 Fix tensor-width-dependent signed zeros in tf.math.maximum and minimum
body:
## Problem
Fixes #128477

Maximum and Minimum keep the first operand on ties, including `+0.0` vs `-0.0`, like `std::max`/`std::min`, `np.maximum`/`np.minimum`, XLA and the Maximum/Minimum gradients (`x >= y`, `x <= y`). Eigen backends do not agree on that tie (NEON FMAX and GPU fmaxf return `+0.0`), so results could depend on tensor width and platform.

### Fix
Defined `tf_scalar_max_op` and `tf_scalar_min_op` in `tensorflow/core/kernels/cwise_ops.h`:
- Uses compare+select (`a < b ? b : a` for maximum, `b < a ? b : a` for minimum) on both scalar and packet paths, with `pcmp_eq(b, b)` NaN guards in `packetOp`.
- Integers have no NaN or signed zero and use Eigen directly via `IsInteger = NumTraits<T>::IsInteger` specialization.
- Maximum and Minimum functors in `tensorflow::functor` now use `tf_scalar_max_op` and `tf_scalar_min_op`.

### Testing
- Added `testSignedZeroWidthConsistency` across widths `(1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 9, 16, 17, 33)` and dtypes `float16`, `bfloat16`, `float32`, `float64`.
- Added `testNaNPropagationWidths` CPU NaN width-sweep test across widths `(1, 4, 7, 8, 9, 16, 17, 33)` for `float16`, `float32`, and `float64`, verifying `+NaN` first operand preserves signbit 0.

title: Fix adjust_saturation turning pixels gray when the hue rounds to 1.0
body:
Fixes #129605.

`adjust_saturation` turned a red pixel gray (or black at scale 2) when its blue channel was a few ulps above its green channel. The hue of such a pixel is a tiny negative number, and `rgb_to_hsv` wraps it with `hh + 1`, which rounds to exactly `1.0f`. `hsv_to_rgb` then computes `h_category = 6`, which its `switch` does not handle, so the pixel lost all chroma. This change wraps a hue of 1.0 to 0, which is the same angle.

The GPU kernel has the same rounding: `rgb2hsv_cuda` computes `(6 - tiny) / 6 == 1.0f`, and `hsv2rgb_cuda` matches no sector for `h * 6 == 6`. It gets the same one-line wrap. I could not run the GPU kernel.

`AdjustSaturationTest.testHueJustBelowZero` runs `[0.8, 0.1, 0.10000001]` and `[1.0, 0.0, 1e-7]` at scales 0.5 and 2.0 and compares with the existing `colorsys` reference.

I don't have a full TensorFlow build, so I compiled the CPU kernel before and after this change as custom ops against tf-nightly 2.23.0-dev20261026 (GCC 15.2, Ubuntu 26.04 on WSL2) and compared them:
- the new test's cases fail before (gray, black) and pass after;
- the uint8 expectations of `testHalfSaturation` and `testTwiceSaturation` are unchanged;
- on random images in the styles of `testAdjustRandomSaturation` (all random, two channels equal), plus 4,000 pixels built to sit on the wrap, at seven scales from 0 to 5 (224,000 pixel outputs): 8,316 outputs changed, all of them from wrong to matching `colorsys` within the test's tolerance. None got worse; 49 outputs were outside that tolerance before this change and are unchanged by it.

title: Fix/issue 127820 Document signed integer division overflow wraparound contract and prevent UBSan overflow
body:
## Problem
Fixes #127820

When evaluating signed integer division with `int_min / -1` (e.g., `tf.math.floordiv`, `tf.raw_ops.TruncateDiv`, `tf.raw_ops.FloorDiv`, `tf.raw_ops.Div`), the operation returns the signed integer minimum value (`INT_MIN`) due to two's complement integer overflow wraparound (which avoids a SIGFPE hardware divide exception on CPU and matches GPU / hardware semantics).

However, this signed integer division overflow contract was not explicitly documented in the API definitions and docstrings, leading to ambiguity for users regarding whether `int_min / -1` raises an exception or wraps around. Additionally, `safe_div_or_mod_op` in `cwise_ops.h` performed signed negation on `INT_MIN` which triggered undefined behavior sanitizer (UBSan).

### Root cause
1. In `cwise_ops.h`, `safe_div_or_mod_op` explicitly handled `INT_MIN / -1` to avoid FPE by overflowing `a`, but the signed negation `-safe_a` on `INT_MIN` represents signed overflow in C++.
2. The behavior of signed integer division overflow (modular wraparound to `INT_MIN`) was not explicitly documented in `FloorDiv`, `TruncateDiv`, `Div`, or `tf.math.floordiv`.

### Fix
1. Documented the signed integer division overflow wraparound contract in `api_def_FloorDiv.pbtxt`, `api_def_TruncateDiv.pbtxt`, `api_def_Div.pbtxt`, `tf_generated_ops.td`, and `tf.math.floordiv` docstring.
2. Updated `safe_div_or_mod_op` in `cwise_ops.h` to evaluate `DivOrMod()(safe_a, T(1))` on `INT_MIN / -1`, preventing signed integer negation overflow UB while maintaining two's complement wraparound.
3. Added unit tests in `division_future_test.py` and `division_past_test.py` covering `INT_MIN / -1` for `int8`, `int16`, `int32`, and `int64` across `floordiv`, `truncate_div`, `floor_div`, `div`, `floor_mod`, and `truncate_mod`.

### Testing
- Added `testSignedIntegerDivisionOverflow` to `division_future_test.py` and `division_past_test.py` running in both graph and eager modes.

title: Fix AvgPool3D graph-mode shape inference for empty VALID outputs
body:
## Problem
Fixes #113322 (the remaining `AvgPool3D` part)

On a VALID-padded pool whose window is slightly larger than a known input dimension, eager execution returns an empty output, while graph mode (`tf.function`) fails during shape inference:

```python
import tensorflow as tf

@tf.function
def f(x):
  return tf.nn.avg_pool3d(x, ksize=4, strides=4, padding="VALID")

x = tf.zeros([1, 3, 3, 3, 2])
print(tf.nn.avg_pool3d(x, 4, 4, "VALID").shape)  # eager: (1, 0, 0, 0, 2)
f(x)  # ValueError: Negative dimension size caused by subtracting 4 from 3 ... AvgPool3D
```

#127941 fixed this for `AvgPool` (and so `avg_pool1d`/`avg_pool2d`, including the `NCW` case from the issue). On a current `tf-nightly` (2.23.0-dev20261026) that case now returns `(4, 10, 0)` in both modes. `AvgPool3D` still uses `Pool3DShape` and has the original bug.

## Root cause
`AvgPool3D` is registered with `Pool3DShape`, which calls `GetWindowedOutputSizeFromDims` for every spatial dimension. That helper does `input - window` and so reports a negative dimension, while the runtime kernel computes the output size with signed division and yields 0.

## Fix
Add `AvgPool3DShape`, which shares the `Pool3DShape` implementation (now `Pool3DShapeImpl`) and applies the same empty-output rule as `AvgPoolShape`: for VALID padding, a known input dimension smaller than the window gives an output size of 0 when `window - input < 2 * stride`. Larger windows still raise the negative-dimension error.

Per the follow-up in #127941 ("Limit empty-output shape inference to average pooling"), the behavior is scoped to `AvgPool3D` only. `Pool3DShape` is unchanged, so `MaxPool3D`, `MaxPool3DGradGrad` and the `_Mkl*Pool3D` ops behave as before.

## Testing
- `common_shape_fns_test` (new `AvgPool3DShapeTest`): empty output for NDHWC and NCDHW, partially empty output, negative error for oversized windows, unchanged output for windows that fit, and `MaxPool3D` still rejecting oversized windows.
  - `bazel test //tensorflow/core/framework:common_shape_fns_test` passes. With the `AvgPool3D` registration reverted to `Pool3DShape`, the test fails.
- `pooling_ops_3d_test.py`: `testAvgPool3dValidEmptyOutput` (graph and eager), `testAvgPool3dValidEmptyOutputInTfFunction`, and `testAvgPool3dValidNegativeOutput`.
  - **Not run locally.** The full TensorFlow build for the Python target failed on this macOS machine in the XNNPACK `arm64_sme2.cc` compile (Apple clang 15 lacks SME attribute support). The file compiles with `py_compile`. Relying on CI for these tests.

## Not changed
`MaxPool`/`MaxPool3D` and `Conv` still report a negative dimension in graph mode for this case. They are tracked separately (for example #129497) and left out here to keep this change scoped to the average-pooling behavior agreed in #127941.

title: check flat_values size in RaggedTensorToVariantGradient concat
body: The gradient op for RaggedTensorToVariant allocates its output from the dense_values_shape input and then concatenates the flat_values carried by the encoded variant gradients into that buffer. Those two sizes come from independent inputs and nothing ties them together: dense_values_shape sizes the output, while the variants decide how many elements get copied. ConcatCPU copies each piece in full, and its single-row fast path never compares the running total against the output size, so a declared output smaller than the real data gets written past its end. I hit this with a two-variant gradient carrying 1000 floats against a dense_values_shape of [1], which overflows the one-element output on the heap; the mirror case, where the sum is smaller than the output, leaves the tail uninitialized and returns leaked heap contents. The check lives in the concat branch of RaggedTensorToVariantGradientOp::Compute, right before the copy, and requires the summed flat_values size to equal dense_values_shape.num_elements(). I kept it in the kernel so neither the overflow nor the uninitialized read can reach ConcatCPU, and added a regression test next to the existing gradient error-path tests.

title: lite: ensure HADAMARD_ROTATION resizes its output to match the input tensor
body:
`HADAMARD_ROTATION`'s `Eval()` always copies the entire input buffer into the output buffer before rotating it in place, so the two tensors must have identical size -- but `Prepare()` never established or checked that, leaving the output's shape/allocation independently determined by whatever shape the model declares for it.

This adds an explicit `context->ResizeTensor()` call in `Prepare()`, following the same convention used by other same-shape TFLite ops (e.g. `GenericPrepare` in `activations.cc`).

**Testing:** added a regression test (`OutputShapeMismatchIsCorrectedByPrepare` in `hadamard_rotation_test.cc`) that declares a deliberately mismatched, small output shape and verifies `Prepare()` now resizes it to match the input before `Invoke()` is ever called. All tensors involved are tiny, so this doesn't require any unusual test resources. Existing parameterized tests already only exercise matching input/output shapes, so their behavior is unchanged.

title: lite: guard against integer overflow when FlatSize() sizes memcpy/memset calls
body:
A handful of TFLite kernels compute a memcpy/memset length directly from `RuntimeShape::FlatSize()`, which returns `int` and does not check for overflow (the header itself documents this: "Use CheckedFlatSize instead in non-hot-path code"). For tensor dimensions whose product exceeds `INT32_MAX`, the resulting wrapped `int`, once implicitly converted to `size_t` for the multiply, can become a very large length argument.

This switches the five affected call sites to `RuntimeShape::CheckedFlatSize()`, which already exists for exactly this purpose and already has its own overflow-rejection unit tests in `runtime_shape_test.cc` (`TestCheckedFlatSizeRejectsOverflow`, `TestCheckedFlatSizeRejectsNegativeDim`):

- `tensorflow/lite/kernels/dynamic_update_slice.cc`
- `tensorflow/lite/kernels/internal/optimized/optimized_ops.h` (2 call sites)
- `tensorflow/lite/kernels/internal/reference/reference_ops.h`
- `tensorflow/lite/kernels/perception/max_unpooling_2d.cc`

`DynamicUpdateSlice()` now returns `TfLiteStatus` so `Eval()` can reject the op if the check fails, instead of silently producing a corrupted length. The other four sites are inside shared `void`-returning reference/optimized template helpers with no `TfLiteContext` available to report an error, so the fix there skips the (otherwise meaningless) zero-fill on overflow rather than passing an unchecked length to `memcpy`/`memset`.

**Testing:** `CheckedFlatSize()` itself is already covered by existing tests, so this change relies on an already-verified primitive rather than introducing new overflow-detection logic. I did not add a new end-to-end kernel test reproducing the overflow through these call sites, because doing so through the normal `SingleOpModel`/`AllocateTensors()` test harness would require constructing a tensor with more than 2^31 elements, i.e. an actual multi-gigabyte allocation in the test itself -- not a reasonable thing to add to the unit test suite. Behavior for all shapes that don't overflow is unchanged.

title: Reject Bincount sizes near INT32_MAX on GPU
body:
Fixes #129575

On GPU, Bincount and DenseBincount use CUB’s histogram to count. CUB does its bin math with 32-bit ints and adds up to 1024 to the number of bins. When size is within 1024 of INT32_MAX, that overflows and the histogram kernels access memory out of bounds.

This PR:

returns an error on GPU when size is above INT32_MAX - 1024, before the output is allocated;
returns an error when the input has more than INT32_MAX values, since CUB also takes the input length as an int.

Test: test_size_too_large_for_gpu_histogram checks that size 2**31 - 2 gets an error on GPU.

title: Pass the channel group count to the NCHW_VECT_C MaxPool kernel
body:
Fixes #129587

MaxPoolV2 on a qint8 NCHW_VECT_C input on GPU passed `params.depth` (single channels) to `MaxPoolForwardNoMaskKernel_NCHW_VECT_C`, which expects the number of 4-channel groups. The kernel ran 4 times as many threads as the output has elements, and the extra threads indexed past the end of the input and the output. This passes `params.depth / 4`.

The existing NCHW_VECT_C tests cover this path. Under compute-sanitizer, `testMaxPoolSamePaddingPacket4_37` in `pooling_ops_test_gpu` reports 12 out-of-bounds reads in `MaxPoolForwardNoMaskKernel_NCHW_VECT_C` before this change and 0 errors after.

title: Fix host memory input allocation attributes in SingleThreadedExecutor
body:
Fix host memory input allocation attributes in SingleThreadedExecutor

In `SingleThreadedExecutorImpl::Initialize`, `input_alloc_attrs_` was previously populated only from `kernels_[i].output_locations[j]`. Because `SingleThreadedExecutorImpl` inlines `Arg` nodes without creating `ArgOp` kernels and also omitted `const_tensor_kernels_[i].output_locations`, any kernel input fed by an `Arg` node (or `ConstTensorKernel`) received a default-constructed `AllocatorAttributes` in `input_alloc_attrs_` with `on_host() == false`.

When `tf.raw_ops.For` executes on GPU in eager mode, its body function uses `SINGLE_THREADED_EXECUTOR`, and `EnsureMemoryTypes` inserts a `_HostSend` / `_Recv` pair when the host-memory `int32` loop index `_Arg` feeds a GPU kernel (such as `Cast` to `float32`). Because `ctx->input_alloc_attr(0).on_host()` on `_HostSend` was `false`, `SameWorkerRecvDone` treated the host-allocated loop counter as device memory and attempted a device-to-device DMA copy (`AsynchronousMemcpyD2D`) from a CPU heap pointer, aborting with `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE`.

Populate `input_alloc_attrs_` from `op_kernel->input_memory_types()[j] == HOST_MEMORY` (which covers `Arg` inputs) and merge `kernels_[i].output_alloc_attrs[j]` and `const_tensor_kernels_[i].output_alloc_attr`.

title: [TF] Fix unaligned complex128 scalar access in GPU SparseMatrixAdd and GpuSparse wrappers
body:
[TF] Fix unaligned complex128 scalar access in GPU SparseMatrixAdd and GpuSparse wrappers

In `functor::CSRSparseMatrixAdd<GPUDevice, T>`, `CSRSparseMatrixMatMul<GPUDevice, T>`, `CSRSparseMatrixMatVec<GPUDevice, T>`, and `GpuSparse` (`cuda_sparse.cc`), host scalar parameters (`alpha`, `beta`, `one`) are passed by address to cuSPARSE routines, which treat them as `const cuDoubleComplex*` when `T = complex128` (`std::complex<double>`).

Because `cuDoubleComplex` (`double2`) is declared with 16-byte alignment (`__builtin_align__(16)`) while `std::complex<double>` only has 8-byte alignment, unaligned 8-byte stack or static addresses can cause cuSPARSE routines (such as `cusparseZcsrgeam2_bufferSizeExt` / `cusparseZcsrgeam2`) to fault with `SIGSEGV` (`SI_KERNEL` general protection fault on unaligned 16-byte vector load).

Align host scalars to `sizeof(T)` in `add_op.cc`, `mat_mul_op.h`, and `cuda_sparse.cc` (`one_ptr`, `SpGEMM_*`, and the `GpuSparse` wrapper implementations `CsrmmImpl`, `SpMMBufferSize`, `SpMM`, `CsrmvImpl`, `CsrmvExImpl`, `SpMVImpl`, `Csrgeam2Impl`, and `CsrgeamBufferSizeExtImpl`) so that `complex128` scalars always satisfy the 16-byte alignment requirement of `cuDoubleComplex`.

title: Finish SharedBatchScheduler split-failed tasks and track BatchTask outstanding items per task.
body:
Finish SharedBatchScheduler split-failed tasks and track BatchTask outstanding items per task.

In `SharedBatchScheduler`, finish tasks via `FinishTask` when lazy task splitting fails in `PriorityTaskQueue::RemoveTask` or `Queue::PadOpenBatchWithLowPriorityTasks`, and notify `empty_notification_` if `ScheduleBatch()` drains the queue without producing a batch. In `BatchResourceBase`, track `num_outstanding_batched_items_` per `BatchTask` (transferring accounting across `SplitInputTask` subtasks) so items are released exactly once whether a task enters `ProcessBatchCallBack` (including `unbatched_tasks`), fails `Schedule()`, or finishes directly in the scheduler.

title: [TF2XLA] Restrict RealDiv XLA kernel and MLIR legalization to float and complex types
body:
[TF2XLA] Restrict RealDiv XLA kernel and MLIR legalization to float and complex types

`RealDiv` includes integer types in its `REGISTER_OP` definition (`BINARY_MORE()`), which cannot be removed due to OpDef backwards compatibility, but standard CPU/GPU kernels only register `RealDiv` for floating-point and complex types (`float`, `half`, `double`, `bfloat16`, `complex64`, `complex128`).

Previously, `RealDiv` was registered in `tf2xla/kernels/binary_ops.cc` via `XLA_MAKE_BINARY` without a `TypeConstraint`, and in MLIR TF-to-XLA / StableHLO legalization (`legalize_tf_patterns.td`) via `DirectBinaryPat` without a tensor element type constraint. As a result, XLA compiled `RealDiv` on integer tensors by lowering it to `xla::Div` / `chlo.broadcast_divide`, silently performing truncating integer division instead of rejecting integer dtypes like eager and graph execution.

Restrict the XLA `RealDiv` kernel registration to `kFloatAndComplexTypes` and constrain the MLIR `TF_RealDivOp` legalization patterns to `TF_FpOrComplexTensor`.

RELNOTES: XLA (including TPU) now rejects tf.raw_ops.RealDiv on integer
inputs, matching TF CPU/GPU. Use tf.math.truediv, tf.math.floordiv or
tf.truncatediv instead.

title: Validate axis, slice bounds, mask shifts, and TensorArray inputs in Grappler ConstantFolding
body:
## Summary

This change validates input shapes, ranks, dtypes, masks, and bounds before Grappler simplifies `ReverseV2`, `Slice`, and `StridedSlice` or materializes `TensorArraySizeV3` in `tensorflow/core/grappler/optimizers/constant_folding.cc`:

1. `SimplifyStridedSlice`: Validate input arity; read `new_axis_mask`, `shrink_axis_mask`, `begin_mask`, `end_mask`, and `ellipsis_mask` via `GetNodeAttr` into `int32_t` and skip the node if any read fails or if `new_axis_mask` or `shrink_axis_mask` is nonzero; require a known input rank with `rank < 1024` and every dimension known; reject multi-bit `ellipsis_mask` values; require `begin`, `end`, and `strides` to be non-control 1-D `DT_INT32` or `DT_INT64` constants with matching dtypes and element counts and fewer than 32 sparse specifications (`strides.NumElements() < 32`); reject `non_ellipsis_specs > rank`; map dense dimensions directly to sparse indices across explicit and implicit ellipses; read `begin`, `end`, and `strides` values as `int64_t`; and test mask bits with 32-bit unsigned shifts (`1U << i`, with `i < 32`).
2. `MaterializeShapes`: Materialize `TensorArraySizeV3` only when it has exactly two non-control inputs (`NumNonControlInputs(*node) == 2`), input 0 reads output port 0, and input 1 is a regular input whose node exists; when the producer of input 0 is a `TensorArrayV3` (`array->op() == "TensorArrayV3"`) whose `size` input reads output port 0; and when `dynamic_size`, if present, decodes as a bool through `GetNodeAttr` and is false. Then decode the `size` constant into a default-constructed `Tensor`, require both declared and decoded dtypes to be `DT_INT32`, and require a positive scalar (`value.dims() == 0` and `size > 0`).
3. `SimplifySlice`: Validate input arity and known rank, require `begin` and `size` to be non-control 1-D `DT_INT32` or `DT_INT64` constants with matching dtypes and element counts equal to input rank, and compare `size` against an input dimension only when that dimension is nonnegative (or `size == -1`).
4. `RemoveReverse`: Validate input arity and known rank (`shape.dim_size() <= 8`), verify that `axis` is a non-control 1-D `DT_INT32` or `DT_INT64` constant, range-check each axis entry before canonicalization, and reject duplicate canonical axes.

## Testing

Ran `//tensorflow/core/grappler/optimizers:constant_folding_test` (`86/86` passing on a CPU build; `MulConvPushDownTest_Conv2D_NCHW_VectorLikeConst` is compiled only under `GOOGLE_CUDA || TENSORFLOW_USE_ROCM`), including unit tests in `tensorflow/core/grappler/optimizers/constant_folding_test.cc` covering:
- `ConstantFoldingTest.SimplifyStridedSliceInt64AndHighRankMaskBounds`
- `ConstantFoldingTest.ReverseRankZeroAndOutOfBoundsAxisSkipped`
- `ConstantFoldingTest.MaterializeShapesAndSimplifySliceRankAndElementBounds`
- `ConstantFoldingTest.StridedSliceValidSparseEllipsisMapping`
- `ConstantFoldingTest.ReverseValidScalarAndRankEight`
- `ConstantFoldingTest.SliceValidSymbolicDimensionWithInt64Size`
- `ConstantFoldingTest.TensorArrayPositiveScalarSizeMaterialization`
- `ConstantFoldingTest.SliceAndReverseWithUnknownRankRemainUnchanged`
- `ConstantFoldingTest.<blob>`

- `ConstantFoldingTest.TensorArraySizeDynamicOrMalformedDynamicSize`

title: Let cross-trainer cache workers answer skip when no element is ready.
body:
Let cross-trainer cache workers answer skip when no element is ready.

Without the cross-trainer cache, a tf.data service worker with no element ready answers a `GetElement` request with `skip` when the client allows it, and the client moves the request to another worker. `CachingTaskRunner` ignores `allow_skip` and always waits until the input pipeline produces the trainer's next element. A client sends at most one request per worker and at most `max_outstanding_requests` in total, so when there are more workers than that (for example 240 workers and 100 requests), a request waiting on one slow worker cannot read elements that other workers already have ready.

Answer `skip` from `CachingTaskRunner` when the request allows it, the trainer's next element is not in the cache, and the worker has not produced it yet. A skipped request returns no element and does not move the trainer's position in the cache, so no data is lost or repeated. Errors, such as a cancelled cache or an input pipeline error, are still returned. As without the cache, the check is best effort: if a concurrent request with the same trainer ID takes the element first, the request waits for the next one.

This changes behavior for every job that uses the cross-trainer cache. When no worker has an element ready, each client thread now gets up to 5 × (number of workers) `skip` answers in a row, for example 1,200 with 240 workers, before it falls back to a blocking request. Jobs without the cache already behave this way.

title: Track end-to-end batch latency and model-level TPU cost in BatchStats.
body:
Track end-to-end batch latency and model-level TPU cost in BatchStats.

`BatchSizeStats` previously tracked only per-batch-size `tpu_cost` when TPU cost measurements were present, while neither `BatchSizeStats` nor `ModelBatchStats` recorded end-to-end batch processing latency or model-level TPU cost. Downstream batch thread sizing and in-process telemetry require comparing end-to-end batch execution latency (including host tensor concatenation and output splitting) against accelerator execution duration both per batch size and across the model.

Add `batch_latency()` `CostTracker` accessors (and `const` overloads) to `BatchSizeStats` and `ModelBatchStats`, along with model-level `tpu_cost()` accessors on `ModelBatchStats`. Measure wall-clock batch processing duration in `BatchResourceBase::ProcessFuncBatch` and `BatchResourceBase::ProcessBatch` and pass it to `SplitBatchCostsAndRecordMetrics` to populate per-batch-size and model-level `batch_latency` and `tpu_cost` statistics.

title: Grow global SharedBatchScheduler thread pools to the maximum requested.
body:
Grow global SharedBatchScheduler thread pools to the maximum requested.

When `SharedBatchScheduler::Create()` is called with `use_global_scheduler = true`, all callers in the process share a single `SharedBatchScheduler` instance. Previously, only the `Options` from the first `Create()` call initialized `batch_threads_` and `warmup_threads_`, ignoring larger thread counts requested by subsequent callers. If an initial caller created the global scheduler with fewer batch threads or zero warmup threads, later models requesting higher concurrency or dedicated warmup threads remained constrained to the initial pool sizes.

Add `MaybeGrowThreads()` and invoke it on each `Create()` call when `use_global_scheduler = true` so `batch_threads_` and `warmup_threads_` grow monotonically to the largest `num_batch_threads` and `num_warmup_batch_threads` requested. When `warmup_threads_` transitions from empty to non-empty, enable the warmup queue on all existing queues via `Queue::EnableWarmupQueue()`. Guard `batch_threads_`, `warmup_threads_`, and `enable_warmup_queue_` with `mu_`, and move thread vectors into local variables under `mu_` before joining in `~SharedBatchScheduler()`.

title: Cap concurrent in-flight regular batches per queue in SharedBatchScheduler.
body:
Cap concurrent in-flight regular batches per queue in SharedBatchScheduler.

When multiple queues share a pool of batch threads, a single queue with a burst of traffic can occupy all batch threads or exceed the concurrency level that its downstream execution can efficiently support. Supporting shared thread pool sizing across multiple queues requires bounding how many regular batches any individual queue may have in flight at once without starving other queues or blocking warmup requests.

Add an opt-in `max_in_flight_batches` option to `SharedBatchScheduler::QueueOptions` (defaulting to 0, which preserves the existing unlimited behavior). When set to a positive value, `internal::Queue` declines to schedule additional regular batches once `num_batches_being_processed_` reaches `max_in_flight_batches`, and notifies the scheduler as soon as an in-flight batch completes if another batch is ready to run. Track warmup batches separately in `num_warmup_batches_being_processed_` via `ProcessWarmupBatch` so warmup threads and regular batch threads do not interfere with each other's in-flight accounting.

title: Fix tf.signal.kaiser_window for window_length=0.
body:
<!-- Title: Fix tf.signal.kaiser_window for window_length=0 -->

`tf.signal.kaiser_window` built its sample positions with a float `range` from `-(window_length - 1) / 2` to `(window_length - 1) / 2 + 0.1`. For `window_length=0` the start (0.5) exceeds the limit (-0.4), so the `Range` op raises `InvalidArgumentError`, both eagerly and inside a `tf.function` with a dynamic length. `np.kaiser(0, beta)` and the other `tf.signal` windows return an empty window.

This change derives the positions from `range(window_length)` minus the half length, so there are always exactly `window_length` samples. The values for every other length are unchanged.

Reproduction on tf-nightly:

```python
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf

print(np.kaiser(0, 12.0))  # []
print(tf.signal.hann_window(0).numpy())  # []
tf.signal.kaiser_window(0)  # InvalidArgumentError: Requires start <= limit when delta > 0: 0.5/-0.4 [Op:Range]
```

Testing:

- Added `test_kaiser_window_zero_length` to `window_ops_test.py`, covering a static and a `tf.function` dynamic length for float16, float32 and float64. It fails before this change and passes after.
- The full `window_ops_test.py` passes (437 tests, graph and eager modes), including the constant-folding test.
- `pylint --rcfile=tensorflow/tools/ci_build/pylintrc` scores 10.00/10 on both files.

The change was written with AI models under my direction. I reviewed it myself, and the testing above was run before opening this PR.

title: Fix int16 overflow in GatherNd with 32768 or more index tuples
body:
Addresses #129561.

DoGatherNd checks the number of index tuples (N_big) against std::numeric_limits<int>::max(), but then recomputes it as Index N_result. With int16 indices and 32768 or more index tuples, N_result overflows: the kernel either skips the gather and returns its uninitialized output buffer (when N_result <= 0), or fails the CHECK in Tensor::shaped and aborts the process (when N_result > 0).

Reject such inputs with an InvalidArgumentError, as the kernel already does for params whose number of elements does not fit the index type. Computing N_result in 64 bits instead would not be enough, because the CPU functor also addresses index tuples with Index. The new check never triggers for int32 or int64 indices.

title: check values count against indices in StagingMap::put
body: StagingMap::put only validates that the indices tensor is strictly ordered and each index is within dtypes_, never that the number of staged values equals the number of indices. tf.raw_ops.MapStage with four indices but a single value tensor stores an OptionalTuple of size 1 while the indices address slots 0..3, so a following MapUnstage or MapPeek indexes the stored tuple out of bounds, reading a garbage std::optional<Tensor> and then moving/resetting it (heap out-of-bounds read and write, SIGSEGV on tf 2.21); the incomplete-insert path reads (*tuple)[i] past the end for the same reason. Reject the count mismatch in put so both MapStage and OrderedMapStage fail with InvalidArgumentError, and add regression tests for both ops.

title: [XLA] Add unified AI agent PR preparation guidelines in AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and GEMINI.md.
body:
[XLA] Add unified AI agent PR preparation guidelines in AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and GEMINI.md.

**Status quo**
The root `AGENTS.md` in `openxla/xla` contains only a short pointer to `xla/AGENTS.md`, and the repository root lacks `CLAUDE.md` and `GEMINI.md` files. Meanwhile, OpenXLA team members maintain separate review, readability, compatibility, and PR preparation skills covering C++17 constraints, `#ifdef` avoidance, GPU AOT compatibility, CUDA runtime version checks, CPU ABI stability, compiler phase invariants, and unit testing standards.

**Why**
Contributors use different AI coding assistants (OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, and Gemini CLI) to author and prepare XLA Pull Requests. Providing a single, identical, comprehensive instruction set across `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and `GEMINI.md` in the OpenXLA root ensures every agent applies the team's review and PR preparation standards before a PR is opened.

**Design choices**
- Aggregate the OpenXLA team's review, readability, compiler architecture, compatibility, and testing skills into `third_party/xla/AGENTS.md`.
- Replicate the exact same content into `third_party/xla/CLAUDE.md` and `third_party/xla/GEMINI.md` so all three files remain byte-for-byte identical.
- Register `CLAUDE.md` and `GEMINI.md` in `_XLA_TOP_LEVEL_FILES` in `third_party/xla/common.bara.sky` so Copybara exports all three files to the root of `openxla/xla`.

**Compromises**
- Keeping `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and `GEMINI.md` as three identical files introduces file duplication at the repository root, because GitHub and agent CLIs do not universally follow symlinks or cross-file include directives across tools.

**Alternatives**
- Symlinking `CLAUDE.md` and `GEMINI.md` to `AGENTS.md` was rejected because Copybara and several agent CLIs expect regular files rather than symlinks.

body:
### Summary
Fixes a source build failure in TensorFlow 2.21.0 caused by an LLVM archive checksum mismatch.

### Problem
When building TensorFlow 2.21 from source, Bazel attempts to download the LLVM archive pinned at commit `909041e4802c4b9a2223ca04099f35bf1dbbd460`:
1. The mirror at `storage.googleapis.com/mirror.tensorflow.org/...` returns `404 Not Found`.
2. The GitHub fallback returns an archive with SHA256 `<blob>`.
3. Bazel fails because `workspace.bzl` expects `<blob>`.

GitHub regenerated git archive tarballs following hash abbreviation adjustments, changing the archive checksum while leaving code contents identical.

### Solution
Update `LLVM_SHA256` in `third_party/xla/third_party/llvm/workspace.bzl` to `<blob>`.

Fixes #129543.

title: PR #51286: [XLA:GPU] Enable topk_special_floats_test on ROCm by encoding a plain float total-order key
body:
PR #51286: [XLA:GPU] Enable topk_special_floats_test on ROCm by encoding a plain float total-order key

Imported from GitHub PR <url>


📝 Summary of Changes
`topk_special_floats_test` expects `+0` to rank above `-0`. On ROCm the large shapes are rewritten to rocprim, and rocprim's float radix sort treats `+0` and `-0` as equal, so the returned index is wrong. CUDA still uses the float key, and its existing skip stays.
**What we change:**
- `SortComputationAnalysis` records `is_total_order` (`compare->order() == ComparisonOrder::kTotal`).
- The key is encoded only when the device is ROCm, the key type has a negative zero, the comparator is a plain compare (`kDefaultOrder`, not the NumPy-order or weak-order pattern), and `order=TOTAL`. `OrderedIntegralFromFloat` bitcasts the key to a signed integer of the same width and XORs negative values with the signed maximum. This is the map `ComparisonExpander` uses. It is its own inverse, so `FloatFromOrderedIntegral` applies it again and bitcasts back to the float after the sort.
- F16 and BF16 keys become S16, F32 becomes S32, and F64 becomes S64. The keys-only kernel is `CubSortKeys` for `int16_t`, `int32_t`, or `int64_t`. Among float keys, pair sorts are rewritten only for F32, so an encoded pair key is S32, which the pair kernel already accepts.
- Which sorts are rewritten does not change. The deviceless scratch-size lookup is keyed by byte width, and that width is unchanged. The encode and decode add elementwise ops before and after the sort, only for ROCm total-order float sorts that are already rewritten to rocprim.
- The replacement is built in one place, as suggested in review. For non-NumPy sorts, custom-call element 0 is the sorted key (decoded when it was encoded) and element 1 is the values. `PairInOperandOrder` restores operand order when the key was operand 1. `UnpackResultPair` is removed. New instructions are created through the sort, so they keep its metadata.
- `FloatTotalOrder` checks the original keys-only case, `f32[1000]` descending: the rocprim key is S32 on ROCm and F32 on CUDA. `SortTotalOrder` covers f16, bf16, f32, and f64, both directions, on `[16,128]`, and compares the result with the interpreter. `FloatTotalOrderPairKeyAtOperand0` and `FloatTotalOrderPairKeyAtOperand1` check both operand orders with `AMDMI210DeviceInfo`. `FloatTotalOrderSpecialValues` executes +0, -0, both infinities, and both NaNs on ROCm and skips on CUDA.
- `topk_special_floats_test` is enabled on ROCm. The NVIDIA skip for batch == 1, n >= 4096, k > 16 (b/572311831) stays.
Unchanged: CUDA still sorts the float key (#50426). NumPy-order and non-total compares are not encoded. Sorts that are not rewritten to rocprim stay on their existing path.

🎯 Justification
Enable more unit test on ROCm.

🚀 Kind of Contribution
🧪 Tests

title: Read Linux CPU RSS from /proc/self/smaps_rollup in TFLite memory_info.
body:
Read Linux CPU RSS from /proc/self/smaps_rollup in TFLite memory_info.

On Mali GPUs (`mali_kbase`), driver-allocated native GPU pages are added to the
process's `mm->rss_stat[MM_FILEPAGES]` counter, inflating `/proc/<pid>/status`
`VmRSS`/`VmHWM` and `getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss` with unmapped GPU memory.
Other GPU drivers track unmapped GPU allocations outside `mm->rss_stat`, causing
inconsistent CPU memory footprint reporting across devices when GPU delegates
are used.

Update `GetMemoryUsage()` on Linux to read VMA-backed `Rss:` from
`/proc/self/smaps_rollup` (falling back to `rusage::ru_maxrss` if unavailable)
so `mem_footprint_kb` and `private_footprint_bytes` consistently report CPU
memory across all devices.

message:
Allow clearing scheduling group annotations on non-async instructions.

When XLA cannot schedule every instruction in a `_scheduling_group_id` group at once (for example, when an in-order async queue adds a dependency on another in-flight operation during scheduling), `DefaultSchedulerCore::ScheduleAnnotation` clears the group annotation on the remaining unscheduled instructions so they can be scheduled normally later.

Previously, `ScheduleAnnotation` asserted that any remaining unscheduled instruction in the group was an `async-start` or `async-done`. However, `LegalizeSchedulingAnnotations` can propagate a group ID onto intermediate non-async instructions (such as a `bitcast` between two dependent collectives in the same group). When the downstream collective start is deferred, those upstream non-async instructions also remain unscheduled and hit the `RET_CHECK` failure.

Remove the async-only `RET_CHECK` when clearing annotations on unscheduled instructions in `ScheduleAnnotation`, and add a unit test in `xla/service/latency_hiding_scheduler_test.cc` covering a propagated `bitcast` inside a partially scheduled group.

message:
PR #50868: [XLA] Fix HLO parser crash when the wrapped op of a sugared async-start fails to parse

Imported from GitHub PR <url>

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #49227.

Parsing a sugared async start like `call-start(), to_apply={%nope}` segfaults instead of returning a parse error. `CreateAsyncWrappedComputation` returns a null `HloComputation*` when the wrapped instruction fails to parse, and that null gets assigned into `std::optional<HloComputation*> async_computation`. Assigning a pointer engages the optional, so the `if (!async_computation)` check never fires and the null computation reaches `HloInstruction::CreateAsyncStart`, where the `HloAsyncStartInstruction` constructor dereferences it.

This regressed in 8bc8533fb6 (the refactor that introduced `CreateAsyncWrappedComputation`); before that the code checked the raw root pointer. The fix keeps the result in a local pointer and returns early when it is null, same as before the refactor. Any sugared `*-start` op was affected, for example `custom-call-start()` without `custom_call_target` crashed the same way.

## 🎯 Justification

Malformed HLO text should produce an `INVALID_ARGUMENT` status, not kill the process. `run_hlo_module`, `hlo-opt` and every test that parses HLO go through this code.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

Two tests in `hlo_parser_test.cc`: `DesugarParsingTest_CallStart_InvalidToApply` (the input from the issue) and `DesugarParsingTest_CustomCallStart_MissingTarget` (different wrapped op, different failure). Both segfault at HEAD and pass with the fix.

```
bazel test //xla/hlo/parser:hlo_parser_test
```

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

None needed, the change is in the parser error path only.

message:
Reset XNNPACK weight cache build steps on every exit path.

`WeightCacheBuilder` never freed its staging `data_` buffer between
build steps, leaving it allocated at the size of the largest packed
weight for the lifetime of the cache. `StopBuildStep` also returns early
when a step wrote nothing (such as a subgraph whose weights were all
cache hits), skipping the `is_build_step_` reset, and a failed
`StartBuildStep` left `is_build_step_` set as well.

Use `ScopeGuard` so both functions end the step on every return and free
the staging buffer whenever a step ends. To keep failed steps safe to
continue or restart, validate fingerprints and file writes in `Append`
before recording entries in `schema_`, and clear stale `schema_` entries
in `StartBuildStep` when the header has no buffer list yet.

message:
PR #47800: [XLA] Clamp out-of-bound set-dimension-size sizes in the HLO evaluator

Imported from GitHub PR <url>

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #47368.

`HloEvaluator::HandleSetDimensionSize` passes the raw runtime value of the
size operand straight into `MutableLiteralBase::SetDynamicSize`. Nothing
validates that value against the dimension bound, so a size larger than the
bound trips the fatal `CHECK_GE(bound, size)` in `literal.cc` and aborts the
whole process, and a negative size is silently stored and aborts later in
`LiteralBase::ToStatic` (`Shape::set_dimensions` CHECK). On the Interpreter
platform the evaluator executes the module directly, so a program whose
set-dimension-size size operand comes from input data can kill the process,
which is how the fuzzed module in the issue crashes `run_hlo_module`.

This change clamps the size to [0, bound] in `HandleSetDimensionSize` before
storing it. The evaluator is the only place a runtime program value becomes a
literal dynamic size, so this single site covers the crash class. In-contract
programs are unaffected (the clamp is the identity for sizes in [0, bound]).

Clamping (rather than erroring) matches the direction of #46625, which gives
the compiled CPU path the same [0, bound] clamp where the dynamic padder
materializes dynamic tensors, and keeps interpreter-vs-backend comparisons in
`run_hlo_module` executable for such modules (CPU/GPU execute them without
complaint today). Note that `get-dimension-size` still observes the raw size
value: it forwards the size-producing instruction's result, mirroring how the
dynamic padder forwards the raw size tensor on compiled backends, so only the
literal's stored dynamic size is clamped.

## 🎯 Justification

An out-of-contract runtime value in input data must not be able to abort the
process. The CHECKs themselves guard correct internal invariants (the literal
data buffer is sized to the bound); the evaluator is the boundary layer that
has to enforce the contract on pro ...

message:
PR #48160: [XLA:CPU] Fix crash when a sort comparator calls nested computations

Imported from GitHub PR <url>

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #47366.

Compiling a sort whose comparator contains a computation-calling op (reduce, reduce-window, map) crashes the CPU thunk emitter with `map_util.h:50 Check failed: it != collection.end() Map key not found`. `IrEmitter2::EmitSortComparator` emits the comparator directly with `EmitComputation`, so the computations the comparator transitively calls (for example a reduce's reducer) are never emitted, and the later `FindOrDie(emitted_functions_, ...)` lookup in `IrEmitter::EmitThreadLocalCall` dies.

This change pre-emits the comparator's transitively called computations through `IrEmitter::EmitNestedComputation` before emitting the comparator, the same way the other kernel emit paths already do (`IrEmitter2::EmitFusionHostKernel`, `ElementalKernelEmitter::ThreadLocalCallbackFactory`, `ComputationKernelEmitter`). `EmitNestedComputation` handles recursion and deduplicates through `emitted_functions_`, so comparators without called computations are unaffected.

## 🎯 Justification

The input is valid HLO: reduce/map inside a sort comparator is legal and the same modules run fine on the interpreter. The gap exists since the sort thunk emitter was introduced; simple elementwise comparators never hit it. With this change the reported module and several variants (reduce, reduce-window, map in the comparator) compile and run, and ordering-valid comparators match the interpreter reference.

message:
PR #46783: [XLA] Simplify binary concatenate of a repeated operand to a broadcast

Imported from GitHub PR <url>

#ai-generated

`HandleConcatenate` returns early for a two-operand concatenate whose operands are not a broadcasted scalar. That early return sits above the `Concat(X, X, ...)` to broadcast-of-reshape rewrite, so the rewrite fires for three or more operands and never for exactly two.

This is issue #26780. The five-operand form is simplified:

```
ENTRY main {
  x = s8[2,1,4] parameter(0)
  ROOT concat = s8[2,5,4] concatenate(x, x, x, x, x), dimensions={1}
}
```

while the two-operand form is left alone:

```
ENTRY main {
  x = s8[3,1,4] parameter(0)
  ROOT concat = s8[3,2,4] concatenate(x, x), dimensions={1}
}
```

A concatenate materializes its result, a broadcast of a reshape does not and fuses into its consumer, so the two-operand case pays for a copy that the three-or-more case avoids. Doubling a degenerate dimension is a common shape after a reshape or an expand_dims, so the gap is easy to hit.

The fix guards the concat-to-pad rewrite with its scalar-broadcast condition instead of returning from the function, so the two-operand case falls through to the existing degenerate-dimension check. Precedence is unchanged: a two-operand concatenate with a broadcasted scalar operand still becomes a pad. Most of the diff is the reindentation that guard causes.

Verification: I did not build XLA for this change, so the argument is by reading. The new `BinaryConcatToBroadcast` test mirrors the existing `ConcatToBroadcast` test with two operands instead of six, and the touched lines are clang-format clean.

message:
PR #46793: [XLA] Support bit-width-changing bitcast-convert in the dynamic padder

Imported from GitHub PR <url>

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #45967.

The dynamic padder failed with "Unimplemented padding for instruction:
bitcast-convert" whenever a bit-width-changing bitcast-convert consumed an
operand with a dynamic dimension. Same-width bitcast-converts already worked
through the elementwise early-exit in ChooseIdentityValue, but the
width-changing form is not elementwise (its shape changes), so it fell
through to the unimplemented default.

Padding data reinterprets to padding data under a bitcast, and the dimension
the op adds or removes is always the static innermost one, so no identity
value is needed. This adds kBitcastConvert to the group of ops that return
nullptr from ChooseIdentityValue. Dynamic dimension inference already
propagates the dynamic dimensions correctly for both directions (it routes
bitcast-convert through the index-preserving elementwise passthrough, and
pre-existing dimensions keep their indices in both the widening and the
narrowing form).

The repro from the issue is tf.bitcast applied to the output of tf.where:
where produces s64[<=16,1], and the int64 to float32 bitcast makes
f32[<=16,1,2], which then failed to compile.

One hole is closed on the way: shape inference checked only the bound of the
minor dimension consumed by a narrowing bitcast-convert, so a dynamic minor
dimension (for example f32[10,<=2] to s64[10]) was accepted, and with the
padder fix such an ill-defined program would have compiled and produced
garbage instead of failing. InferBitcastConvertShape now rejects a dynamic
consumed minor dimension explicitly.

## 🎯 Justification

Eager TF executes the where + bitcast graph fine; XLA refused to compile it.
The graph is well defined for any runtime size, so this is a missing case in
the dynamic padder, not a semantic limitation.

message:
PR #49899: [XLA:CPU] Do not offload reduce-window with base dilation to YNNPACK

Imported from GitHub PR <url>

## 📝 Summary of Changes

`IsReduceLikeOpSupportedByYnn` checked `base_dilation` only for window dimensions with `size > 1` or `stride > 1`. A dimension with window size 1 and stride 1 but `base_dilation = 2` passed the check, and `DefineReduceWindowOp` in the YNNPACK emitter never looks at base dilation, so it computed the undilated reduction and wrote it into the (larger) dilated output buffer. Silent wrong result, no error.

This change moves the base dilation check in front of the `size > 1 || stride > 1` block so it applies to every window dimension. Such reduce-windows now stay on the regular CPU emitter, which handles base dilation correctly. The window dilation and window reversal checks stay where they were, both are no-ops on a size 1 window.

## 🎯 Justification

Fixes #48714. `LIBRARY_FUSION_TYPE_REDUCE` is enabled by default, so any CPU `reduce-window` with `lhs_dilate` on a size 1 / stride 1 dimension and at least 4096 elements returned wrong values. Reachable from plain `lax.reduce_window(..., base_dilation=...)` in JAX.

message:
PR #50406: [GPU] Preserve memory-space annotations in dynamic-slice fusions

Imported from GitHub PR <url>

This fixes a case where dynamic-slice fusion can leave an FFI call’s buffers in ordinary memory even though the call requests collective (symmetric) memory, `S(7)`.

Consider this structure, with a 128-element `input` and 256-element `weights` and `destination` buffers. These are schematic HLO excerpts; the attribute names and indices are exact:

```text
tile = slice(weights, [128:256])
tmp = custom_call(input, tile),
  frontend_attributes={operands_memory_spaces="{0:7}",
  results_memory_spaces="{0:7}"}
out = dynamic_update_slice(destination, tmp, 128)
```

The call requests collective memory for `input` and its result. Fusion replaces the temporary slices with views into their backing buffers:

```text
fused(p0_weights, p1_input, p2_destination) {
  tile = slice(p0_weights, [128:256])
  tmp = custom_call(p1_input, tile),
  frontend_attributes={operands_memory_spaces="{0:7}",
  results_memory_spaces="{0:7}"}
  return dynamic_update_slice(p2_destination, tmp, 128)
}
```

Previously, the requirements remained only on the inner call, where allocation and boundary-copy analysis could miss them:

```text
out = fusion(weights, input, destination), calls=fused
```

This change puts the corresponding requirements on the outer fusion:

```text
out = fusion(weights, input, destination), calls=fused,
  frontend_attributes={operands_memory_spaces="{1:7,2:7}",
  results_memory_spaces="{0:7}"}
```

The call’s operand `0` becomes fusion operand `1`. The destination at operand `2` also needs collective memory because the FFI now writes directly into its slice. `weights` stays in ordinary memory. Entry-boundary copies preserve ordinary-memory inputs and outputs where required.

The rewrite also preserves explicit input/output aliases. For example:

```text

On NVIDIA GPUs where `ConvertFloatNvidiaPass` is enabled (`(ptx >= 78 && cc >= 90) || (ptx >= 81 && cc >= 89)` for `f8E4M3FN` and `f8E5M2`, and `ptx >= 86 && cc >= 100` for `f4E2M1FN`), `RewriteTruncFPattern` in `xla/backends/gpu/codegen/emitters/transforms/convert_float_nvidia.cc` rewrites every `arith.truncf` to `f8E4M3FN`, `f8E5M2`, or `f4E2M1FN` by first converting any non-`f16` source to `f32` via `ConvertToF32` (`arith.truncf ... : f64 to f32`) and then emitting the NVVM `f32 -> f8/f4` conversion intrinsic (`cvt.rn.f32.f64` followed by `cvt.rn.satfinite.e4m3x2.f32` / `e5m2x2.f32` / `e2m1x2.f32`). The overflow fix-up (`FixInfinityConversionValue`) also tests the `f32`-rounded value.

Because every rounding midpoint of `f8E4M3FN`, `f8E5M2`, and `f4E2M1FN` (and the overflow thresholds of `f8E4M3FN` and `f8E5M2`) is an exact `f32` value with an even significand, `f64` inputs that lie within half an `f32` ulp past an `f8`/`f4` midpoint or threshold are first rounded onto the midpoint in `f32` and then rounded the wrong way by the second tie-to-even step (compare `openxla/xla#42731`, which fixed the analogous `f64/f32 -> f16 -> f8` double rounding on `XLA:CPU`):

|---|---|---|---|
| `1 + 2^-4 + 2^-30` | `f8e4m3fn` | `1.0` | `1.125` |
| `464 + 2^-20` | `f8e4m3fn` | `448.0` | `NaN` (overflow) |
| `2^-10 + 2^-40` | `f8e4m3fn` | `0.0` | `0.001953125` (`2^-9`) |
| `1 + 2^-3 + 2^-30` | `f8e5m2` | `1.0` | `1.25` |
| `61440 - 2^-10` | `f8e5m2` | `inf` | `57344.0` |
| `2^-17 + 2^-47` | `f8e5m2` | `0.0` | `1.52587890625e-05` (`2^-16`) |

message:
Reject partial single-slice checkpoints in TensorSliceReader::GetTensor

## Summary

`TensorSliceReader::GetTensor` (`tensorflow/core/util/tensor_slice_reader.cc:236-263`) rejects multi-slice checkpoints when `tss->Slices().size() > 1` (`Sliced checkpoints are not supported`), but when `tss->Slices().size() == 1` it assumes the sole stored `TensorSlice` covers the full tensor `shape`. If a checkpoint file contains only a single partial slice (for example `0,2:-` for a `[4, 5]` tensor), `GetTensor` allocates a full `tensorflow::Tensor` of `shape` via `tensorflow::Tensor::BuildTensor`, copies only the partial slice into the output buffer, and returns `absl::OkStatus()` with the remaining tensor elements left uninitialized.

This change validates `slice.SliceTensorShape(shape, &slice_shape)` and verifies `slice_shape.IsSameSize(shape)` in `TensorSliceReader::GetTensor` before allocating the output tensor, returning `absl::UnimplementedError("Sliced checkpoints are not supported")` when the single slice does not cover the full tensor shape.

## Validation

Added unit tests in `tensorflow/core/util/tensor_slice_reader_test.cc`:
- `TensorSliceReaderTest.GetTensorFullSliceControlSucceeds`
- `TensorSliceReaderTest.GetTensorRejectsSinglePartialSlice`

message:
Avoid per-element IteratorContext copies in FlatMapDatasetOp.

Every output element call to `GetNextInternal` and `SkipInternal` in `FlatMapDatasetOp` previously constructed a nested `IteratorContext` via `MakeNestedIteratorContext(ctx)` and merged `nested_ctx.checkpoint()` into `ctx->checkpoint()`, while input element advancement heap-allocated `std::make_unique<IteratorContext>(*ctx)` and merged into `input_ckpt_`. Copying `IteratorContext` on every element copies `IteratorContext::Params` (including six `std::shared_ptr`s with atomic reference-count updates, `std::function` objects, the `split_providers` vector, and `data_service_address`) and initializes four `absl::flat_hash_map`/`set` tables inside `MemoryCheckpoint`, even though `MergeCheckpoint` is a no-op when `!ctx->symbolic_checkpoint()` and `MakeNestedIteratorContext` is an identity copy when `ctx->split_providers().empty()`.

Introduce a private `NestedIteratorContext` helper class on `FlatMapDatasetOp::Dataset::Iterator` (mirroring `IteratorContextWithIndexMapper`) that lazily constructs a child `IteratorContext` inside `std::optional<IteratorContext>` only when symbolic checkpointing is enabled or split providers must be stripped for a sub-iterator, and otherwise returns `ctx` directly. Use `NestedIteratorContext` in `GetNextInternal` and `SkipInternal` for both `current_element_iterator_` and `input_impl_`, and stack-allocate `IteratorContext` in `RestoreCurrentElementIteratorSymbolic`. This reduces `FlatMapDataset` `GetNext` CPU time by 8.2% (+9.0% throughput) and `Skip` CPU time by 6.4% (+6.9% throughput).

message:
[Mosaic] Replace and erase original op before running downgrade rules in RunSerde.

Previously, `RunSerde` passed `new_op` to `downgrade_rules` before replacing uses of `op` with `new_op` and erasing `op`. As a result, `new_op` had no uses during the downgrade rule (preventing downgrade rules from inserting post-processing ops that consume `new_op`), and setting `was_erased = true` in a downgrade rule would leave the unmangled `op` behind.

Replace `op`'s uses with `new_op` and erase `op` before invoking `downgrade_rules`, and split `SerdeRuleType` into `UpgradeRuleType` and `DowngradeRuleType` (removing the unused `bool&` parameter from downgrade rules). Bump `JAX_IFRT_VERSION_NUMBER` to 82 so that Mosaic GPU picks the matching rule types.

Keep `SerdeRuleType` and a `RunSerde` overload that takes `SerdeRuleType` downgrade rules as deprecated aliases, so that JAX versions that predate this change still build.

message:
[XLA:GPU] Add layout-aware CudnnScaledDotRewriter.

Add a pass that rewrites kScaledDot with K-minor physical layouts into
__cudnn$fusion, with inline scale padding and swizzling. The pass gives
kScaledDot the same flow as kDot: a library rewrite of unfused ops after
GemmFusion, instead of an in-place change of __triton_gemm in the autotuner.
It also lets the autotuner compare Triton and cuDNN through fission.
A later change wires it after GemmFusion and into the autotuner.

The pass pads the scales only along the contracting dimension, so the fused
scaled dot needs no slices. It skips M or N that is not a multiple of 128,
and shapes that cuDNN rejects: K that is not 16-byte aligned, and MXFP4 with
an M-minor output. It runs only on SM 10.0, where a B200 test checks that
every accepted shape compiles.

message:
Lower ApproxTopK fallback to unstable sort on CPU and GPU.

`ApproxTopK` on TPU already aggregates candidates using an unstable sort (`is_stable=false`), whereas `ApproxTopKFallback` on CPU and GPU previously forced `is_stable=true`. On XLA:GPU, requiring stability routed `approx_top_k` through a 64-bit key/index bit-packing adapter rather than dispatching directly to the native unstable `select_k` kernel.

`is_stable=true` was set in July 2026 as a workaround because lowering `approx_top_k` with `is_stable=false` exposed an XLA:GPU layout assignment bug where non-default operand layouts (such as `{0, 1}` propagated from an upstream `all-gather`) were passed into `__gpu$TopK` and the RAFT `select_k` kernel, which require contiguous default (`{1, 0}`) input layout. Now that `GpuLayoutAssignment` explicitly constrains `__gpu$TopK` operands to default layout, `approx_top_k` can safely lower with `is_stable=false`.

Switch `ApproxTopKFallback` to emit `is_stable=false`, aligning CPU and GPU semantics with TPU and allowing XLA:GPU to dispatch `approx_top_k` directly to RAFT `select_k` without U64 packing and unpacking overhead.

message:
PR #51852: [XLA:GPU] Match exact 16-bit rounded constants in GemmRewriter's BcastConstScalarNear

Imported from GitHub PR <url>

#ai-generated

## Status quo

In `xla/backends/gpu/transforms/gemm_rewriter.cc`, the approximate-GELU pattern in `HandleMultiply` matches the constants `sqrt(2/pi)` (`0.7978845608`) and `0.044715` with `BcastConstScalarNear` before calling `FuseGeluActivation` to rewrite the activation into cuBLASLt's `GELU` / `BIAS_GELU` epilogue (or their `_AUX` variants). `BcastConstScalarNear` uses the relative tolerance predicate:

```cpp
return std::abs(*actual - expected) < (std::abs(*actual + expected) * epsilon);
```

with `epsilon = 128 * std::numeric_limits<T>::epsilon()`.

## Why

- For `BF16`, `std::numeric_limits<bfloat16>::epsilon()` is `2^-7`, so `epsilon = 1.0`. The predicate becomes `|a - e| < |a + e|`, which in exact arithmetic holds for every positive `a` (and in `double` holds for every positive `bf16` value in `[2^-54, 2^53]` for `c1` and `[2^-58, 2^49]` for `c2`, i.e., 13,697 of the 32,512 positive normal `bf16` values).
- For `F16`, `std::numeric_limits<Eigen::half>::epsilon()` is `2^-10`, so `epsilon = 0.125`, accepting any constant in `(7/9, 9/7)` of the expected value (`-22%` to `+29%`, i.e., 804 `f16` values for `c1` and 744 for `c2`).

As a result, when a `bf16` or `f16` matmul goes through `GemmRewriter` (for example with `--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false`; from reading `gpu_compiler.cc` this should also be the default path on CUDA GPUs older than Ampere (not tested)), any user-written activation of the form `y * 0.5 * (1 + tanh(c1 * (y + c2 * y^3)))` is replaced by cuBLASLt's `GELU` / `BIAS_GELU` epilogue (or their `_AUX` variants) for any positive `bf16` constants `c1` and `c2` in the ranges above (for example `c1 = 2, c2 = 0.5`), and for `f16` constants within `-22%` / `+29%` of the GELU constants (for example `c2 = 0.05`, as in `ApproxGeluActivationWrongConstant`), which ignores `c1` and `c2` and computes standard approx ...

message:
[XLA:GPU] Check all instructions against register limits in indexing cost model. This massively saves on compile-time of E2E models at almost no cost on performance.

Previously, we only checked fusion boundary instructions (roots and fusion operands) and `iota` instructions. This change checks all instructions in the tiled computation: keep the `0.4 * registers_per_block_limit()` threshold for roots, fusion operands, and `iota`s, and check intermediate instructions inside the fusion against the full `registers_per_block_limit()` without the `0.4` factor (to be more relaxed).

This issue was surfaced on a `input -> broadcast -> reduce` case, where the intermediate broadcast isn't checked, yet it now requires more registers than the fusion boundaries, causing heavy spilling on certain configurations.

message:
Avoid temporary allocations and double validation in ShapeUtil.

`ShapeUtil::MakeValidatedShape(PrimitiveType, absl::Span<const int64_t>)`
previously called `MakeDynamicDimensions(dimensions)`, which heap-allocated and
populated a temporary `std::vector<bool>` on every shape construction solely to
pass `dimension == Shape::kUnboundedSize` into the `std::vector<bool>` overload
while also omitting `minor_to_major->reserve(ndims)`. In addition,
`ShapeUtil::MakeValidatedShapeWithDescendingLayout` allocated a temporary
`std::vector<int64_t>`, filled it via `std::iota`, and called
`MakeValidatedShapeWithLayoutInternal`, which first constructed and validated
the shape with a default descending layout via `MakeValidatedShape`, then
overwrote `*shape.mutable_layout()` with a second `LayoutUtil::MakeLayout`
construction and ran `ShapeUtil::ValidateShape` a second time.

Introduce `MakeValidatedShapeImpl` in `xla/shape_util.cc` to evaluate
`d == Shape::kUnboundedSize` inline when `dynamic_dimensions` is null, reserve
`minor_to_major` capacity up front, and optionally skip default layout
population when called from `MakeValidatedShapeWithLayoutInternal` (which now
validates only the newly attached layout via
`LayoutUtil::ValidateLayoutInShape`). Delegate
`MakeValidatedShapeWithDescendingLayout` directly to `MakeValidatedShape` after
rejecting non-array `PrimitiveType` values.

message:
When Nsight Systems or Nsight Compute holds the CUPTI subscriber slot, `cuptiSubscribe` returns `CUPTI_ERROR_MULTIPLE_SUBSCRIBERS_NOT_SUPPORTED` (or `CUPTI_ERROR_MAX_LIMIT_REACHED`). Previously, `CuptiErrorManager` disabled CUPTI process-wide on this error, `CuptiTracer::EnableApiTracing` set `api_tracing_enabled_` before `PrepareSubscriberForSession` succeeded, and `CuptiTracer::Disable` unconditionally dereferenced uninitialized state.

Handle external CUPTI subscriber conflicts per session:

- Allow `CUPTI_ERROR_MAX_LIMIT_REACHED` and `CUPTI_ERROR_MULTIPLE_SUBSCRIBERS_NOT_SUPPORTED` in `CuptiErrorManager::Subscribe` without disabling CUPTI, and document the static-CUPTI `SubscribeV2` fallback contract.
- Call `PrepareCallbackStart()` after `PrepareSubscriberForSession()` in `CuptiTracer::EnableApiTracing()`, clear subscriber state, log a warning, and return `absl::UnavailableError` (callers with `raise_error_on_start_failure = true` now receive `absl::StatusCode::kUnavailable` instead of `kInternal`).
- Set `need_root_access_ = true` in `PrepareSubscriberForSession()` on `CUPTI_ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_PRIVILEGES`.
- Extract `CuptiTracer::ResetSessionState()` to deduplicate session-state teardown on `Enable()` failure and `Disable()`.

message:
PR #51084: [XLA:CPU] Gate embedded HLO proto when loading executables

Imported from GitHub PR <url>

📝 Summary of Changes
- Make CPU AOT executable loading respect xla_embed_ir_in_executable instead of attaching an HloProto unconditionally.
- Use the serialized module configuration for the parameterless LoadExecutable() overload and the provided DebugOptions for  the configurable overload.
- Share executable-loading logic through LoadExecutableImpl(bool).
- Strip literal payloads from embedded protos while preserving literal shapes for memory analysis.
- Preserve full protos when HLO snapshot dumping is enabled.

Resolves #50471

🎯 Justification
Deserialized CPU executables currently retain an additional HloProto containing copies of the optimized HLO module and buffer assignment, even when xla_embed_ir_in_executable is disabled.

This causes loaded executables to consume substantially more resident memory than equivalent executables compiled in-process. It particularly affects services that serialize compiled executables and restore many of them during startup.

The change aligns the deserialization path with the normal compilation path by retaining the additional proto only when requested. Snapshot dumping continues to receive a full proto so that existing snapshot behavior for loaded executables is preserved.

🚀 Kind of Contribution
🐛 Bug Fix, ⚡️ Performance Improvement,

📊 Benchmark (for Performance Improvements)

- no embedded proto under the default configuration;

- an embedded proto when the option is explicitly enabled;
- propagation of the option through the serialized module configuration;
- removal of literal payloads while preserving literal shapes;
- preservation of full literal payloads when HLO snapshot dumping is enabled.

message:
[XLA:GPU] Disallow sub-byte vector types in VectorizeLoadsAndStoresPass

`LowerTensorsPass` lowers `vector.transfer_read` and `vector.transfer_write` to
byte-addressed `llvm.getelementptr` operations without sub-byte bit shifting or
masking. Vectorizing sub-byte accesses whose total vector bit-width is less
than 8 bits (such as `vector<2xi2>` when unroll factor is 2) therefore loses
the 4-bit offset within a byte for odd pairs.

Require `vector_bit_width >= 8` in `GetVectorType` so sub-byte accesses that do
not span at least a full byte remain scalar and use the bit-shift/masking path
in `RewriteTensorExtract` and `RewriteTensorInsert`.

Also remove dead `i1` vector handling in `LowerTensorsPass` and its synthetic
tests, since `PRED`, `S1`, and `U1` tensors are lowered to `tensor<...xi8>` up
front.

Fixes <url>

[XLA] Make HloPassOptions::Get return std::optional.

Replace `Get<T>(key, default_value)` with `Get<T>(key)`, which returns
`std::nullopt` for an unset option. Unset and default values are distinct both

A type mismatch now leaves the option unconsumed, and `CheckAllConsumed()`

message:
Populate Layout minor_to_major dimensions in-place in LayoutUtil.

`LayoutUtil::MakeDescendingLayout` and `LayoutUtil::MakeAscendingLayout`
previously allocated and populated a temporary `std::vector<int64_t>` before
calling `LayoutUtil::MakeLayout`, which then copied elements one by one via
`add_minor_to_major`. Because `Layout` stores `minor_to_major` in a
`DimensionVector` (`absl::InlinedVector<int64_t, 6>`), constructing a temporary
`std::vector<int64_t>` incurred an unnecessary heap allocation and copy on
every call.

Delegate `LayoutUtil::MakeDescendingLayout` directly to
`CreateDefaultLayoutForRank`, which resizes and populates the `DimensionVector`
in-place, and update `LayoutUtil::MakeAscendingLayout` and
`LayoutUtil::MakeLayout` in `xla/layout_util.cc` to resize or assign
`layout.mutable_minor_to_major()` directly without intermediate
`std::vector<int64_t>` allocations.

message:
PR #51351: [ROCm] Keep scaled-dot composites native through custom partitioning

Imported from GitHub PR <url>

When `jax.nn.scaled_matmul` runs under JAX custom partitioning on more than one device, the per-device body returned by the partition callback contains an `xla.scaled_dot` composite (on ROCm, `scaled_matmul` lowers through `lax.scaled_dot`). That composite never reaches `CompositeRewriter`: the pre-SPMD run of the pass is over by the time the callback creates it, and the callback path destroys the composite on its way into the partitioned module.

### Changes
- `CloneWithNewOperands` keeps `is_composite` on a cloned call.
- `custom_partition_callback.cc`: the callback's `CallInliner` preserves `xla.scaled_dot`, and the `composite` attributes are restored after `SpmdBuilder` derives the clone from the custom call.
- `gpu_compiler.cc`: `CompositeRewriter` runs again at the end of the SPMD pipeline, so composites created during partitioning take the same path as those rewritten before it.
- `composite_rewriter.cc`: the new `kScaledDot` keeps the call's metadata; after SPMD there is no enclosing call whose inlining would propagate an `op_name` (test added).

### Tests
- `hlo_instruction_test`, `composite_rewriter_test`, `call_inliner_test` pass.
-  end to end with MaxText on MI350X (2 to 8 GPUs, DP/FSDP/TP), all MX GEMMs compile to native `scaled-dot`, single-device HLO and loss unchanged.

[XLA:GPU][NFC] Deduplicate A2A+GEMM and GEMM+A2A splitting in WindowedEinsumHandler.

Extract `WindowedEinsumVisitor::SplitA2aGemmAlongContractingDim` in `xla/backends/gpu/transforms/windowed_einsum_handler.cc` to share the contracting-dimension splitting logic between `HandleDot` (A2A+GEMM) and `HandleAllToAll` (GEMM+A2A).

The two implementations were identical except for:
- Which instruction is the root of the pattern (`dot` for A2A+GEMM vs. `a2a` for GEMM+A2A), used for the output buffer shape and final `ReplaceInstruction` call.
- Which LHS tensor is sliced in each split (`a2a->mutable_operand(0)` for A2A+GEMM vs. `dot->mutable_operand(0)` for GEMM+A2A).
- The shape and ordering of the per-split `all-to-all` and `dot` instructions (`all-to-all` with `lhs_slice_shape` followed by `dot` for A2A+GEMM vs. `dot` followed by `all-to-all` with `a2a->shape()` for GEMM+A2A).

message:
Check all operand uses before sharing buffers

When an instruction reads a value through several positions (e.g. `x` and `bitcast(x)`) or through several operands (e.g. `fusion(x, x)`), all of them are backed by the same buffer. But `BufferAssigner::LiveRangeInterferes` allowed the user to reuse that buffer if any consumed position allowed it, and `HeapSimulator::RunComputation` only checked the defining position. So an in-place fusion could overwrite elements of its input before reading them through the bitcast.

Therefore this change adds `HloDataflowAnalysis::CanShareOperandValueBufferWithUser`, which requires every use of the operand value by the user to allow sharing, and uses it in both places. This is the same per-use check that copy insertion already does. Also:

1. `CanShareOperandBufferWithUser` checks all fusion parameters that correspond to the operand, rejects the `GetInPlaceInputOutputPairs` fast-path when the same operand is also passed in another operand position (unless disjoint read/write regions are annotated), and checks internal uses of an in-place fusion parameter before sharing buffers.
2. `DoesNotUseOperandBuffer` checks all uses of the operand value at a loop fusion instead of returning early on the first dead fusion parameter.
3. `GpuAliasInfo` checks the paths from all fusion parameters that correspond to the operand (including internal ops consuming a parameter twice, per-path `DynamicSlice` tracking, `"dynamic_slice_fusion"` custom fusions, variadic scatter output indices, and non-elementwise multi-output fusion roots), since its hint takes precedence over the generic fusion logic.
4. `NVPTXAliasInfo` rejects in-place `all-reduce` and `collective-broadcast` when the same operand appears more than once.

message:
PR #50988: [XLA:GPU] Splat scalar operands in Triton atomics lowering

Imported from GitHub PR <url>

#ai-generated

Fixes <url>

## Summary of changes

Splat scalar `value` and `expected` operands to the pointer tensor shape before
creating `tt.extern_elementwise` in `LowerAtomicWriteOp` and
`LowerAtomicSpinWaitOp`. Scalar-pointer operations retain scalar operands.

Update the atomic-write and atomic-spin-wait FileCheck expectations, including
64-pointer masked cases that check the scalar splat and mask forwarding. Add a
full-pipeline regression test for a 64-rank block barrier, atomic write and
atomic spin-wait with `num-warps=1`, and remove the incorrect automatic-broadcast
comments.

## Justification

Small one-shot all-reduces over 64 devices can fail during Triton-to-LLVM
lowering with:

```text
size mismatch when packing elements for LLVM struct expected 2 but got 1
```

The block barrier passes a tensor of signal pointers and a scalar signal value
to the atomics lowering. With 64 ranks and one warp, each thread owns two
pointers, but the unsplatted scalar contributes only one value. Splatting the
value gives each pointer a corresponding operand without disabling the
collective kernel or changing its selection policy.

This was observed while compiling MaxText Llama 3.1 405B training on 64 GB200
GPUs. Thanks to @ksew1 for reporting the failure and identifying the block-barrier
atomics mechanism in #50877.

## Kind of contribution

Bug fix with regression coverage.

## Regression coverage

The atomics tests check both the scalar-to-tensor splat and the unchanged mask
operand. `triton_xla_atomics_pipeline.mlir` reaches LLVM through
`--triton-xla-pipeline='target=10.0 num-warps=1'`, covering the block barrier
and both unmasked atomic operations at 64 ranks.

Mask forwarding is checked at the atomics rewrite level. A separate existing
mask-type mismatch in the CUDA extern-atomics lowering prevents an `i1`-masked
case from completing the full pipeline.

message:
[TF2XLA] Restrict RealDiv XLA kernel and MLIR legalization to float and complex types

`RealDiv` includes integer types in its `REGISTER_OP` definition (`BINARY_MORE()`), which cannot be removed due to OpDef backwards compatibility, but standard CPU/GPU kernels only register `RealDiv` for floating-point and complex types (`float`, `half`, `double`, `bfloat16`, `complex64`, `complex128`).

Previously, `RealDiv` was registered in `tf2xla/kernels/binary_ops.cc` via `XLA_MAKE_BINARY` without a `TypeConstraint`, and in MLIR TF-to-XLA / StableHLO legalization (`legalize_tf_patterns.td`) via `DirectBinaryPat` without a tensor element type constraint. As a result, XLA compiled `RealDiv` on integer tensors by lowering it to `xla::Div` / `chlo.broadcast_divide`, silently performing truncating integer division instead of rejecting integer dtypes like eager and graph execution.

Restrict the XLA `RealDiv` kernel registration to `kFloatAndComplexTypes` and constrain the MLIR `TF_RealDivOp` legalization patterns to `TF_FpOrComplexTensor`.

RELNOTES: XLA (including TPU) now rejects tf.raw_ops.RealDiv on integer
inputs, matching TF CPU/GPU. Use tf.math.truediv, tf.math.floordiv or
tf.truncatediv instead.
