title: [Flight] Write rows as strings to object-mode Node destinations
body:
React's Node stream config [encodes each row](<url>) into a 4 KB `Uint8Array` and writes the array when it fills. Only a string over about 1365 characters (`length * 3 > 4096`) is [written as a string](<url>), because it might not fit the view.

Since vercel/next.js#100142, Next pipes Flight into an object-mode stream, and both of its consumers want strings. `createFromNodeStream` [parses a string chunk directly](<url>). The writer of the inline `__next_f` script escapes strings straight into the script. Rows under the threshold still arrive as bytes, so both consumers decode them: `TextDecoder` per row in the reader, `Buffer#toString` in the writer. For those rows, the string React built is encoded, then decoded twice, to get the same string back.

On Next canary today the stream is byte mode, and this PR changes nothing there.

## Change

`beginWriting` records whether `destination.writableObjectMode` is set. If it is, `writeStringChunk` [keeps strings as strings](<url>): it appends each one to a pending string and writes that once it passes the threshold the view uses, so the destination receives about as many writes as before. A string over the threshold is written alone, as before. Binary chunks (typed array rows) still go through the view. Strings and views are flushed in write order.

A text row is `id:T<byteLength>,` followed by the text, and the reader [takes the text to be the whole chunk](<url>), so the text must not be joined with other rows. `flushCompletedChunks` writes it with the new [`writeStandaloneChunkAndReturn`](<url>), which flushes what is pending and writes the chunk on its own. The other stream configs implement it as `writeChunk`.

A byte-mode destination takes the old path.

## Numbers

`sandbox-bench`, with Next at the head of vercel/next.js#100142 (`82e818977a`) in both arms. React is this change (`deeee8f8ee`, the head commit without the test) against its base on `main` (`ab0d927f53`). 16 fresh VMs per experiment, each running both arms twice, interleaved. Cells are the 95% range across VMs. Bold is p < 0.01, a plain range is p < 0.05, and "no change" means the range includes zero.

The change only touches rows under the threshold, so it depends on how many of those a page has. `/blog` is mostly long rows and barely moves. `/dashboard` has many short rows.

| Route | Median latency, 1 client | Median latency, 8 clients | Throughput, 8 clients |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `/dashboard` | no change | **−11% to −4%** | **+5% to +16%** |
| `/docs` | **−4% to −1%** | no change | no change |
| `/blog` | no change | no change | no change |

Streaming routes from `bench/basic-app`. `/streaming/bulk` has 384-byte rows, `/streaming/chunkstorm` 1 KB strings, `/streaming/heavy` 240 boundaries with a 3 KB string prop and a 1.5 KB text node each, `/streaming/heavy-unicode` the same with one non-Latin-1 character in each string.

| Route | Median latency, 1 client | TTFB, 1 client | Throughput, 8 clients |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `/streaming/bulk` | **−9% to −2%** | **−9% to −2%** | no change |
| `/streaming/chunkstorm` | **−5% to −1%** | **−6% to −2%** | no change |
| `/streaming/heavy` | **−6% to −2%** | **−8% to −3%** | +0% to +8% |
| `/streaming/heavy-unicode` | **−6% to −1%** | **−7% to −2%** | **+4% to +11%** |

Flight bytes are identical between arms on every route. In CPU profiles of the app routes, `Buffer#toString` and `decodeUTF8` go to zero; `encodeInto` is down about a tenth, and the rest of it is Fizz encoding the HTML.

<details>
<summary>All cells</summary>

Change with 95% range across the 16 VMs of each experiment. Bold is p < 0.01; a plain range is p < 0.05; "no change" means the range includes zero.

| Route | Median latency, 1 client | TTFB, 1 client | Median latency, 8 clients | Throughput, 8 clients |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `/dashboard` | no change (−6.4 to +2.0) | no change (−10.0 to +5.4) | **−7.7% (−11.4 to −4.0)** | **+10.4% (+5.1 to +15.7)** |
| `/docs` | **−2.6% (−4.3 to −0.9)** | **−2.5% (−4.2 to −0.8)** | no change (−7.7 to +1.7) | no change (−0.9 to +11.5) |
| `/blog` | no change (−3.4 to 0.0) | no change (−3.2 to +0.2) | no change (−2.2 to +8.8) | no change (−4.2 to +6.0) |
| `/streaming/bulk` | **−5.1% (−8.5 to −1.7)** | **−5.6% (−9.2 to −2.0)** | no change (−7.5 to +3.9) | no change (−0.8 to +8.6) |
| `/streaming/chunkstorm` | **−3.2% (−5.3 to −1.1)** | **−3.9% (−6.1 to −1.7)** | no change (−6.7 to +2.5) | no change (−1.2 to +8.2) |
| `/streaming/heavy` | **−4.0% (−6.4 to −1.6)** | **−5.2% (−7.5 to −2.9)** | no change (−6.6 to +2.4) | +3.9% (+0.1 to +7.7) |
| `/streaming/heavy-unicode` | **−3.4% (−5.7 to −1.1)** | **−4.2% (−6.9 to −1.5)** | **−5.8% (−8.9 to −2.7)** | **+7.0% (+3.5 to +10.5)** |

</details>

## Output is unchanged

- **Payload.** The new test renders the same model to an object-mode and a byte-mode destination and checks the two payloads are equal. In the bench, Flight bytes are identical between arms on every route.
- **Text rows.** The test checks that a 2000-character string arrives as a chunk of its own and that `createFromNodeStream` parses the string chunks as written.
- **Lone surrogates.** A byte-mode destination replaces them with U+FFFD as it encodes. An object-mode destination receives the string as written, and a consumer that encodes elsewhere has to do the same replacement itself. Next [does](<url>).

<details>
<summary>Verification</summary>

- `ReactFlightDOMNode-test.js` (react-server-dom-webpack): 39 passed, dev and prod. The existing tests already pipe into an object-mode `PassThrough`, so they run through the new path; the new test checks the chunk shapes.
- CI is green on this branch.
- Bench cells: `react-37944-realistic` (`/blog,/dashboard,/docs`) and `react-37944-stress` (the four streaming routes).

</details>

title: [Flight] Fill reply references early and complete chunks that wait on each other together
body:
Fixes Flight replies that decode collections with placeholders or never resolve when a Server Function is bound to its own container. These are the reply decoder failures found by #37940. This applies the reference completion changes from #37938 to `ReactFlightReplyServer`, which decodes values sent by `encodeReply`.

For example, passing this Set through `encodeReply` and `decodeReply` currently produces a Set containing `null`:

```js
const set = new Set();
set.add(set);
```

The encoder writes the Set's entries in a separate part. The entries refer back to the model that holds the Set, so each chunk waits for the other. The old cycle handling breaks that wait by handing out a partially filled value. Constructing a Set from an array whose entry is still `null` copies the placeholder; filling the array later does not repair the Set.

## How the Set now completes

The decoder reserves an empty Set before its entries are ready. That gives the reference in the entries array an object to point to. Once that entry is filled, it can be added to the reserved Set.

Neither assignment initializes a chunk. The model still waits for the entries chunk, and the entries chunk still waits for the model. The cycle check groups them and examines their other dependencies. When all their fields are filled and nothing outside the group is pending, it initializes both chunks before notifying consumers. The delivered Set now contains itself.

If the Set also contains a value whose module is loading, that dependency keeps the group blocked. A failure still rejects it through the reference's failure listener. Maps use the same reservation mechanism, with construction also waiting for the key and value fields of each entry pair.

This is the same split between filling a reference and releasing its dependency described in #37938, including waiting for a placeholder encountered along a path and using the selected waits between groups to find cycles without repeated graph walks.

## Adapting the change to replies

The reply decoder caches a chunk for each Server Function metadata object. That chunk now has a handler whose reference reads the bound arguments. Once the argument fields and module are ready, the reference constructs the function and fills the chunk's value. A container holding the function can therefore refer back through its arguments and participate in cycle completion. Waiting on the arguments through a Promise previously hid that dependency from the cycle check.

Typed arrays arrive as Blobs whose bytes must be read asynchronously. That read now resolves a chunk, and the receiving field waits on it through an initialization reference. A failed read rejects the reference.

The port also carries the reply decoder's accounting and validation through the new paths:

- Arrays selected by a reference count against the receiving model's array limit. A Blob's bytes count when its buffer is read.
- Collection initializers record which collection consumed them. Another reference to that collection can reuse it; a different collection or an iterator cannot consume the same initializer.
- Early path traversal applies the existing property and Server Reference guards. Plain forward references remain invalid, and temporary references keep their existing registration.

Replies contain no elements, Lazy nodes or DEV debug information, so those parts of #37938 are unnecessary here.

## FormData ids

The reply fuzz also found an independent FormData bug. References use hexadecimal ids, but FormData entry names use decimal ids. At id 10, the decoder looked under `a` while the encoder wrote under `10`, so the entries were lost. The decoder now parses the reference id before constructing the entry prefix.

## Reviewing and testing

The first commits extract handler and reference helpers, reserve collections, expose bound-argument dependencies, and record the handler's chunk and references. The [core commit](<url>) adds early filling and cycle completion. The [last commit](<url>) fixes FormData ids.

Focused tests cover self-containing Sets and Maps, binding a Server Function to its containing array after the module loads, and FormData after more than nine outlined values. The eight known reply reader cases and the generated reply graphs are enabled here. The streamed array that contains itself remains skipped until the encoder fix in #37950; the generator's other exclusions are lifted by the corresponding fixes later in the stack.

Lint and the default fuzz seeds pass at this PR's head, with the fuzz run in both DEV and production.

title: [Flight] Run the reader fuzz against the reply decoder
body:
`ReactFlightReplyServer` decodes replies (`encodeReply` on the client, `decodeReply` on the server) with its own copy of the client's reader. Same design, same obligations, so the fuzz should run against it too. This adds a `reply` host next to `node` and `edge` (<url>). The checks don't change; only the transport does.

## What's different about the reply host

The client encodes the graph with `encodeReply` and the server decodes it with `decodeReplyFromAsyncIterable`. The entries of the reply arrive in packets of a few at a time, and server function modules load one by one, so those are the events the test releases in random order.

A reply can't carry client references, elements, server components or Error values. A client reference in a graph becomes a server function with no bound arguments; the generator leaves the other kinds out, and a known case that needs one doesn't run on the reply host.

`encodeReply` waits for every Promise and stream before it produces the body, so the writer-side events all happen before decoding starts. Only reader-side events are left to shuffle.

## What it found

The decoder has the bugs the client had before #37938:

- A Set or Map that contains itself decodes with `null` in its own place.
- A server function bound to arguments that include its own container never arrives.

Those cases are `it.skip` on the reply host and its random graphs stay skipped; #37941 fixes them. A streamed array that contains itself fails on the encoder side instead (`JSON.stringify` has no name for the back-reference); that one is fixed at the top of the stack.

title: [Flight] Fix three writer bugs found by the reader fuzz
body:
Three writer bugs the fuzz turned up, all in how the writer refers to something it has already written once. Each has a focused test; the first also un-skips its fuzz case and lets server components into the random graphs, and the third lets the large binary leaf in.

## A shared server component blocks its model (<url>)

In DEV, a server component that isn't at the root of its task gets outlined into a task of its own so its debug info has a row to go to. `createTask` registers the element under the new task's ID. If the same element shows up a second time, the writer emits a plain reference to that row, and the model holding it can't resolve until the component has rendered. Prod refers to the first occurrence's slot instead, which holds a lazy node, so the model resolves right away.

Now, when the outlined task doesn't complete synchronously, the element gets registered as a lazy reference, which is what the first occurrence got anyway. In DEV this costs one WeakMap lookup per outlined component that suspended.

Prod has the same bug in one place: when a row grows past the size limit, the element on it is deferred to a row of its own and written lazily, but stays registered under that row's plain id. A second occurrence then makes its model wait for the render, and fail if the render throws. The deferred element is registered as a lazy reference too, and so is an element that `outlineModel` outlines into a row of its own, which in DEV is how an Error's cause is written.

## Debug info eats iterators (<url>)

On Node in DEV, the writer describes an awaited value for debug info before it serializes the model that holds it. `renderDebugModel` turned every iterable into an array with `Array.from`, which for a sync iterator reads it to the end. The model then got an empty iterator.

Now only iterables are expanded. An iterator itself falls through to the generic object description. Same work `Array.from` was already doing, minus draining the iterator. The fuzz reaches it through a Promise that resolves to an iterator; that case and the unit test cover it.

## A large typed array held twice (<url>)

The writer didn't record where it wrote a typed array or an ArrayBuffer, so a second holder got the bytes written again. On Edge, a chunk larger than the writer's 4KB view is enqueued into the destination as is, and a byte stream destination takes the buffer with it, so the second write had an empty view to write from: two stream items holding the same 5000-byte array arrived with the second one empty. The array is now registered under its row when it is first written, like a Promise, so a later holder refers to that row.

title: [Flight] Fill references early and complete chunks that wait on each other together
body:
Fixes Flight responses that deliver unfinished values or never resolve when their rows depend on each other. The reader fuzz in #37936 found both: shared element props can be delivered with `null` in fields that are still loading, and a Set containing itself or a Server Function bound to its containing array can stay blocked forever.

This replaces the cycle handling in `ReactFlightClient.js`. The client will fill references as soon as the objects they point to exist, keep waiting for those objects' contents, and complete chunks that wait on each other together.

## How the client works today

Flight sends values in numbered rows. A row can contain a reference to another row's value (`"$4"`) or to a property inside it (`"$0:items:2"`). The client represents each row with a **chunk**. Initializing that chunk makes its value available to `then` callbacks, rendering and stream reads.

Parsing a model row creates its objects and arrays, but some references may still be waiting for another row or a module. Those fields get `null` placeholders. An **initialization handler** holds the parsed value and counts its outstanding dependencies. When a referenced chunk initializes, the client fills the corresponding field and decrements the count. At zero, the receiving chunk initializes too.

That makes a cycle of references a cycle of waits. It can happen even without a cycle in the application's data:

```js
const value = {theme: 'dark'};
renderToReadableStream({fn: read.bind(null, value), value});
```

The writer puts `value` in the model row. The bound arguments arrive in a separate row and refer to it there. When the receiving environment loads the real Server Function, it must bind those arguments before it can fill `fn`. The model waits for the function, the function waits for its arguments, and the arguments wait for the model.

The existing `resolveBlockedCycle` tries to break these waits by searching backward through listeners. When it finds a cycle, it fulfills a reference with the target row's current value and releases that dependency. But the target can still have fields waiting for unrelated inputs. Releasing the dependency can let a consumer observe those placeholders. Other cycles, including ones through bound arguments, are not visible to that search and never finish.

## What changes

### Fill the argument from the model while both chunks are blocked

In the example, parsing the two rows leaves the reader with objects like these:

```js
const model = {fn: null, value: {theme: 'dark'}};
const args = [null]; // The entry refers to model.value.
```

The missing `fn` does not prevent the reader from reaching `model.value`. The new code can follow that reference and fill the argument immediately:

```js
args[0] = model.value;
```

Neither chunk has initialized. The arguments chunk still waits for the model chunk, so filling the argument cannot expose the unfinished model to a consumer. It also keeps listening for failure: if the model fails later, the arguments fail too.

This is the split between `fulfillReference`, which follows the path and fills the field, and `releaseReference`, which drops the dependency when the referenced chunk initializes. Previously, filling the field also released the dependency.

A path can itself encounter a field that is still a placeholder. The response now indexes pending fields by object and key, so the reference can wait for that particular field and resume there when it is filled. It does not have to wait for the whole chunk or traverse the selected object's contents.

### Bind the function once its argument fields are filled

Now `args[0]` holds the object that should be bound. Once the function's module has loaded, the reader can do the equivalent of:

```js
model.fn = read.bind(null, args[0]);
```

`bind` copies the values in the arguments array, so every entry must be filled before it runs. It does not read the contents of the object in `args[0]`: those can still be loading, because the bound function holds that object and later writes will update it. The chunks remain blocked until those contents are ready.

To make this possible, the wait for bound arguments is now an ordinary initialization reference with a constructor attached. It can read the parsed arguments array and wait for its fields and the module. It also records the model's dependency on the arguments chunk, which was previously hidden inside a Promise wait and invisible to cycle detection.

### Complete the two chunks together

Both assignments are now done, but the dependency counts still say that the model waits for the arguments and the arguments wait for the model. Neither count can reach zero on its own.

The new `checkBlockedCycle` groups these two handlers and checks their remaining dependencies. In this example, their fields are filled, the module has loaded, and the only remaining waits are on each other. It marks both chunks initialized before waking any listeners. The response can now resolve with `fn` bound to `{theme: 'dark'}`.

If `value` also contained a field waiting for another module, that dependency would keep the group blocked. The function could already be bound, but the response would still wait for that field. If the module failed, the existing failure listeners would reject the chunks. Finding a cycle does not release its waits on anything outside the cycle.

### Give a collection an object to refer back to

Sets and Maps need the same protection against copying placeholders. Their constructors wait for the input array's entries to be filled; a Map also waits for the fields of each entry pair. They can then copy those values without walking the contents of the objects they contain.

A collection that contains itself needs one more step. For example, the writer emits a self-containing Set as:

```text
1:["$0"]
0:"$W1"
```

Row 0 constructs a Set from row 1, whose only entry refers back to row 0. Waiting to create the Set until its entry is filled would leave the entry with nothing to point to.

The reader now reserves an empty Set while parsing row 0. Once that parse ends, it can put the Set into row 1's entry, then add that entry to the Set. Both chunks still wait on each other, just as in the bound-function example. With the entry installed and no outside dependency, they initialize together. Maps use the same reservation mechanism.

## Finding cycles without repeated graph walks

Each handler records its outstanding references and the chunk it will initialize. After a parse or listener delivery finishes, the check examines those references. A reference whose field is unfilled, or whose target has not arrived or finished parsing, stops the check. Filling or releasing that reference schedules another check.

A filled reference into another parsed, blocked chunk records a wait on that chunk's group. If the recorded waits lead back to the checking group, the groups on that loop merge. The check continues over their other references. A group completes only when all its reference fields are filled, its remaining references lead back into itself, and it has no other work outstanding.

Each group keeps all its dependencies and selects one to drive its next check. A failure from any dependency still rejects it immediately. The selected waits form a forest, maintained as a link-cut tree. Finding its root tells the check whether a wait closes a cycle, without walking a long chain for every listener. Finding a root, linking and cutting each cost O(log n) amortized. The path around a cycle is walked when its groups merge, and the smaller groups' handler and reference lists move into the largest group.

## Other changes needed for early filling

Paths can cross a Lazy wrapper that the client inserted around an unfinished element. Such a path continues into the parsed element and records a dependency on its chunk. Holding the Lazy wrapper itself, or holding a Promise, still lets the surrounding model finish independently of what is behind it.

DEV debug information also contains references. Its pending entries now belong to the handler that will expose them. Debug information from incomplete chunks is transferred at completion so it does not collide with reserved entries or miss data that arrives later. An Error's `cause` and `errors` are revived into the Error itself, so a delayed reference updates the property the application receives.

## Reviewing and testing

The commits first extract handler and reference helpers, then reserve collections and expose bound-argument dependencies, then prepare handler and debug bookkeeping. The [core commit](<url>) introduces early filling and the new cycle check. The [last commit](<url>) enables the generated graphs, with exclusions for writer bugs fixed later in the stack.

Focused Edge and Browser tests cover self-containing Sets and Maps, functions bound to their containing arrays, shared props with pending contents, paths through suspended elements, and cycles exposed through separate Promises. The thirteen known reader cases and the generated graphs pass on both client hosts in DEV and production.

Read-time probes remain within noise of main on a 20,000-node model with 200 modules resolving individually, and on fifty Promises, stream items, Sets or Map selections sharing an 80,000-object tree while a module is pending.

title: [Flight] Fix six stream bugs found by the reader fuzz
body:
Six stream bugs the fuzz turned up. They're independent of each other and of the reader change in #37938; they're in this stack because the fuzz is what found them. The reply decoder (`decodeReply` on the server) has its own copy of the client's stream controller, so where it has the same bug the same commit fixes both. Each bug has a focused test in the Edge suites except the unhandled rejections, which has its fuzz case.

## Closing before a queued item (<url>)

When a stream item's import was still loading, the item sat in a queue. If the server closed the stream in the meantime, the client closed its side immediately and the queued item never came out. Close now waits for the queue to drain. The reply decoder cleared its queue one item too early in the same way, when the item ahead of a blocked one resolved, and gets the same fix; there the blocked item waits on a server reference's module.

## Byte streams detaching the transport buffer (<url>)

When a byte-stream row ended exactly at the end of a transport chunk, the client enqueued a view into that chunk to avoid a copy, reasoning that nothing else would read the chunk again. Enqueueing into a byte stream detaches the view's buffer. On Node the transport chunk is usually a slice of a pooled Buffer that other chunks share, and pooled buffers can't be detached at all, so this either threw or emptied the chunks that followed. The client now skips the copy only when the chunk is its whole buffer.

## Items arriving after cancel (<url>)

The server doesn't know when a consumer calls `reader.cancel()`, so rows for that stream keep coming. The client enqueued them into the canceled stream, which throws, and the throw took down the rest of the response. The controller now remembers the cancellation and drops them. The reply decoder gets the same fix for entries that arrive after the decoding side canceled.

## Unhandled rejections in DEV when an item fails (<url>)

In DEV, a chunk's `then()` runs its callbacks through a native Promise so that `await` picks them up. The stream code calls `then()` with only a resolve callback in four places, meaning "ignore the error", but the wrapper Promise then rejects with nobody handling it. A stream item whose module fails to load left five unhandled rejections behind. The wrapper now gets an ignoring reject handler when the caller gave none.

## A BYOB read left waiting at the end of a byte stream (<url>)

A byte stream read with `getReader({mode: 'byob'})` never finished when the close row arrived in a later transport chunk than the last bytes. By then the consumer's next read was already waiting, and `controller.close()` does not settle a waiting BYOB read; the Streams spec leaves that to the source, which has to answer the pending request with `byobRequest.respond(0)`. The existing BYOB tests passed because the close row shared a chunk with the data, so the queue drained into the read first. Both readers now respond to the pending request after closing.

Each of the first five turns its fuzz case back on: `two stream items each waiting on a module`, `byte stream read with a BYOB reader`, `stream canceled while the writer is still producing`, `stream item with a failing module`, `byte stream closed while a read is waiting`.

## A typed array emptied by a byte stream in the same chunk (<url>)

A typed array row that fits inside one transport chunk is handed out as a view of the chunk's buffer, not a copy. When a byte-stream row ended the same chunk, the client enqueued that row as a view too, which detaches the buffer, and the typed array that had already been delivered went empty. The byte-stream row is now copied when a typed array row was read out of the chunk before it. Test: `keeps a typed array intact when a byte stream row ends the same transport chunk`.

title: [Flight] Add reader fuzz tests
body:
Adds a fuzz test for the Flight client.

The client is supposed to hand a value to the application once everything inside it has arrived. When the data contains cycles, or two places share the same value, and modules load and Promises resolve in an unlucky order, this may go wrong in two ways:

- the value may get delivered too early, with `null` where a module or a nested object will later go
- or it may never get delivered, because two things end up waiting for each other.

It is hard to guess which orders are unlucky, so this test tries random ones.

The test builds a random graph of values, streams it through the real server and client, decides when each module loads, Promise resolves, stream item arrives and component renders, and after every one of those steps checks that the client has delivered exactly the values whose inputs have all arrived, with the right contents. A value the writer sent together with another, because the two share something, may arrive with it and fail with it; what a value was sent with is the writer's choice, so the test allows either.

## How it works

A case is a graph of named nodes. A node can be:

-  a leaf (a primitive, including `undefined` and `Infinity`, a Date, typed arrays of several kinds, one larger than a packet, a Blob, FormData, a client reference that loads or fails to load, an Error, an AggregateError)
- a container that is whole only once its contents are (an array, an object, one of them with colons in its keys, a Set, a Map, a sync iterator, a function's bound arguments, an element's props, a Fragment)
- or a handle whose contents arrive later (a Promise, a stream, an async iterable, a server component).

The generator creates one of each leaf and a few empty containers, then applies random moves: put a node into a container, make a container hold itself or another, wrap a node in a handle, bind a function to two nodes, alias an element's props, make a module or a Promise or a component fail. Targets are drawn from all nodes so far, which is where cycles and sharing come from.

Each graph runs several times, with the events shuffled, the bytes cut into packets at random places, and the consumer attaching at a different point (before the first packet, after the first flush, after all events, after EOF). The seed comes from `FUZZ_TEST_SEED`, which the hourly fuzz workflow sets. A normal `yarn test` run uses four seeds; `FLIGHT_FUZZ_CASES=128` runs the full sweep.

## What a failure looks like

A random graph that fails on main, with the nodes that don't matter here left out:

```
Replay with FUZZ_TEST_SEED=default:6 FLIGHT_FUZZ_CASES=1 -t "graph seed=default:6 demand=early variant=0"
To work on it, paste this next to the generated graphs and run it with -t pasted:
```
```js
it('pasted', () =>
  runGraph({
  nodes: {
  value2: {value: null},
  date0: {date: 1700000036932},
  set0: {set: ['iterator0', 'set0', 'map0', 'error0', 'host0', 'array0']},
  map2: {map: [['date0', 'date0'], ['set0', 'value2']]},
  // ... 20 more nodes
  },
  roots: {entry: 'map2', other: 'object0'},
  rootPromise: true,
  afterEof: true,
  events: ['load component0 body', 'load module1', 'load element0', 'load module0', /* ... */],
  packetSizes: [6, 20, 1054],
  yieldBetweenPackets: false,
  demand: 'early',
  }),
);
```
```
Error: after evaluate module0: root.entry.key1.member1: expected a Set of 6, received null
```

To reduce, paste the test and delete nodes until it stops failing. For example, the above may reduce to:

```js
it('pasted', () =>
  runGraph({
  nodes: {
  value2: {value: null},
  set0: {set: ['set0']},
  map2: {map: [['set0', 'value2']]},
  },
  roots: {entry: 'map2', other: 'map2'},
  }),
);
```

```
Error: after the first packets: root.entry.key0.member0: expected a Set of 1, received null
```

Cases worth keeping are added to the file as a plain `it` under a name, like `it('Set containing itself', () => runGraph({...}))`. In this PR, there are 31 known bad ones, so we check them in and keep them as regression tests for fixes up the stack.

## What fails today

This checkin actually skips most tests (both random and known) because they need fixes up the stack.

Next PRs will unskip those.

Reader, fixed in #37938:
- an element's props object referenced from elsewhere in the model is delivered with `null` for the props still loading
- a Set or Map that contains itself never resolves
- a server function bound to arguments that include its own container never resolves
- a bound argument that also appears elsewhere in the response never resolves, with no cycle in the data; this is why the random graphs are skipped here
- in DEV, an Error's `cause` that arrives after the Error stays `null`

Reader streams, fixed in #37937:
- a stream closed while its last item still waits on a module closes before the item comes out; the reply decoder has the same bug
- a byte stream read from a pooled Node Buffer detaches the shared buffer
- a stream the consumer canceled throws when more rows arrive
- in DEV, a stream item that fails leaves five unhandled rejections behind
- a byte stream read with a BYOB reader never ends when the close row arrives in a later packet than the last bytes
- a typed array delivered as a view of a transport chunk is emptied when a byte stream row at the end of the same chunk is enqueued

Writer, fixed in #37939:
- in DEV, a suspended server component used twice makes its model wait for the render
- in DEV on Node, debug info drains a sync iterator that a Promise resolves to before the model is written
- an element deferred to its own row because the row grew too big makes a later occurrence's model wait for its render
- on Edge, a typed array larger than the writer's buffer that is held in two places arrives empty the second time

Reply decoder, fixed in #37941 after #37940 runs the test against it:
- the Set, Map and bound-function cases above
- a FormData value written after nine or more other outlined values is lost

Writer, fixed in #37950:
- a streamed array that contains itself overflows the writer's stack
- a stream held in two places is read twice, which locks it
- in DEV, an Error whose cause is itself overflows the writer's stack
- in DEV, an Error whose cause is a suspended server component makes a model that holds the component wait for its render
- a stream inside a stream item that another place also holds is read twice (reply encoder)

Both sides, fixed in #37952:
- a value under a property name with a colon is not deduped, and a cycle through one overflows the writer's stack
- an object key whose value is `undefined` is dropped

title: [Fizz] Keep the leading newline of <pre> content that is not a single string
body:
## Summary The HTML parser drops a newline that directly follows `
` or ``, so Fizz writes an extra `\n` when the content starts with one. It only checks a single string child (a TODO in the same function notes this), so when the content is an array or a component, its leading newline is eaten by the parser and hydration fails:

```js
const code = '\nconst x = 1;\n';
function Code() {
  return code;
}


{code}{' '}



```

For the first one `renderToString` emits `
\nconst x = 1;\n 
`, the parsed text is `const x = 1;\n `, and `hydrateRoot` reports "Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client". Same for the second. `
{code}
` is fine. Measured on 19.3.1 and 19.3.0-canary-a6792708-20261019.

This adds `startsWithNewline`, which looks at the first piece of output in `children`: strings, numbers and bigints are checked directly, empty values are skipped, arrays are searched in order, and a host element counts as not starting with a newline, except hoistable `title`/`meta`/`link`/`style`/`script`, which may not render in place. For anything else (components, fragments, lazy and so on) the answer is unknown. Fizz now writes the extra newline when the content starts with one or when it can't tell, since a newline right after `
` is always dropped by the parser. Host-element children such as `
…
` produce the same markup as before.

## How did you test this change?

- Two `itRenders` cases in `ReactDOMServerIntegrationElements-test.js`: `
{'\nHello'}{' world'}
` and `
`. On main they fail in the server string, server stream and hydration modes; with this change they pass.
- `yarn test "ReactDOMServer|ReactDOMFizz|ReactDOMFloat|ReactServerRendering"`: 45 suites, 2380 passed, 1 skipped, and the same with `--prod`. `yarn test -r=stable ReactDOMServerIntegrationElements`: 346 passed.
- `yarn flow dom-node`, `yarn linc` and prettier pass.

title: [Fiber] Fix useActionState dispatching a stale action after switching back to a previous action
body:
## Summary

When the action passed to `useActionState` changes from A to B and then back to A, dispatching still runs B.

`updateActionStateImpl` checks whether a new action was passed by comparing it with `actionQueueHook.memoizedState`. When they differ, it schedules a passive effect that sets `actionQueue.action`. It never writes the new action back to `memoizedState`, though, and `updateWorkInProgressHook` clones `memoizedState` from the current hook. So the comparison is always made against the action from mount:

1. Mount with A: `memoizedState = A`, `actionQueue.action = A`
2. Render with B: `B !== A`, so the effect sets `actionQueue.action = B`. `memoizedState` stays A.
3. Render with A: `A !== A` is false, so nothing is scheduled. `actionQueue.action` stays B.

This can happen in real apps that switch between two stable actions, for example a mode toggle, and the form then submits through the wrong action.

The fix:

- Always store the current action on the hook, and compare against the **committed** hook (`currentHook.memoizedState`) rather than the work-in-progress one, like `updateEffectImpl` does. Comparing against the work-in-progress hook would lose the effect when the component renders again in the same pass (StrictMode double render, render phase updates, Suspense replay), since the second pass would see the action as unchanged.
- Push the effect on every render, with `HookHasEffect` only when the action changed. Otherwise, if the action changes while inside a hidden `<Activity>`, the effect never runs while hidden and is no longer in the effect list when it is revealed, so reconnecting passive effects would not apply the new action. Today this case only works because the buggy comparison keeps re-pushing the effect.

## How did you test this change?

Added three tests to `ReactDOMForm-test.js`:

- switching A → B → A and dispatching runs A
- changing A → B inside `<StrictMode>` and dispatching runs B
- changing A → B while hidden in an `<Activity>`, then revealing and dispatching, runs B

| | A → B → A | StrictMode | hidden Activity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `main` | fails (runs B) | passes | passes |
| first commit only (write to the work-in-progress hook) | passes | fails (runs A) | fails (runs A) |
| this PR | passes | passes | passes |

Ran:

- `yarn test` (experimental), `yarn test --prod`, `yarn test -r=stable` and `yarn test -r=stable --prod` for `ReactDOMForm ReactDOMFizzForm ReactHooksInspectionIntegration ReactFlightDOMForm ReactHooks Activity profilingCache`: all pass.

title: [Experiment] Flight Result as a map of Server Component expansions
body:
Experiment.

## Today

A framework that server-renders a page with Server Components renders the RSC payload to a stream, tees it, sends one copy to the browser, and parses the other copy back into React elements so that Fizz can render the HTML from it. The server serializes the payload and then parses its own output. On Next's bench app the parse is about 17% of the CPU per request.

## What this adds

`renderToResult(model)` returns a Result without running anything:

```js
type Result = {
  model,  // the model you passed in, untouched
  tasks: WeakMap<ReactElement, Task>, // one per Server Component element, created on first use
  context,  // cache(), cacheSignal(), useId() and hints for this render
};

type Task = {
  status: 'pending' | 'fulfilled' | 'rejected',
  value,  // what the component returned
  then,  // a Task is a thenable, so a consumer can suspend on it
};
```

Two kinds of consumers read a Result.

The existing serializers, `renderToPipeableStream(result)`, `renderToReadableStream(result)` and `prerender(result)`, produce the same stream they produce from the model. When they reach a Server Component element, they look it up in `tasks` instead of calling the component.

`createFromResult(result)` is new. It walks the model in the same process and hands Fizz the tree it would have gotten from parsing the stream: Server Component elements become their task's value, Client Component elements become lazy references into the SSR module graph, and plain data is passed through by identity, without copying.

## How a render goes

```js
async function Page() {
  const posts = await getPosts();
  return <PostList posts={posts} />; // PostList is a Client Component
}

const result = renderToResult(<Page />);
```

Nothing has run yet. Fizz starts reading with `createFromResult`, reaches `<Page />`, and asks the Result for its task. There is none, so the Result creates one and runs `Page` under its context. `Page` awaits, so the task is pending; the reader gives Fizz a lazy for it and Fizz suspends. When `Page` returns, the task is fulfilled with `<PostList posts={...}>`, and Fizz continues with an element whose type is a lazy over the `PostList` module and whose `posts` is the same array.

Then the framework starts `renderToPipeableStream(result)` for the browser. The serializer reaches `<Page />`, finds the fulfilled task, and writes a row for `<PostList posts={...}>`. `Page` ran once.

The reader follows the serializer's rules: it keys elements the way the serializer keys them, rejects the values the serializer rejects with the same messages, and treats a Server Component element as its own row, so a bad value inside one fails that element and not the whole tree.

The previous attempt (#37807) rendered the whole model up front into a separate graph and serialized that with a second serializer. Building the graph cost about as much as the parse it replaced, and GC time went up 68%. This version builds nothing up front: the only state is `tasks`, consumers read the model as it is, and the serializer is the existing one with one lookup added.

## What the Result owns

Anything that can only happen once belongs to the Result, not to a consumer:

- A Server Component runs once.
- A stream or iterator inside the model is read once and replayed to each consumer.
- An error is reported once; the consumers share its digest.
- `renderToResult(model, {signal})` aborts every consumer when the signal aborts.
- `cacheSignal()` ends when the Result is aborted or when its last consumer is done. A consumer can still start after that.

There are entry points for webpack, turbopack, parcel and esm, on Node and Edge.

## Tests

The Flight DOM test suite runs a second time with every render going through a Result (91 tests; the 5 that depend on debug info inside a Server Component are skipped).

A fuzz test generates random models and checks that rendering directly, serializing a Result, reading it in process, and prerendering it all produce the same values and the same Fizz HTML. It runs 40 seeds per CI run and new seeds in the hourly fuzz job; 1000 seeds pass in production mode. Some scenarios load client modules asynchronously, so the code that re-reads a value after a module finishes loading is covered too.

## Benchmark

vercel/next.js#100498 on the sandbox, 16 VM boots, Node streams, against the canary this is based on. Bold means p < 0.01 across boots, with the 95% interval; "n.s." means no measurable difference.

| route | clients | throughput | median latency | TTFB |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| /dashboard | 1 | **+12.8% ±4.7** | **−9.9% ±3.7** | **−22.2% ±8.1** |
| /dashboard | 8 | **+15.4% ±10.0** | n.s. | n.s. |
| /docs | 1 | **+11.9% ±4.7** | **−8.7% ±3.8** | **−11.0% ±3.6** |
| /docs | 8 | **+15.1% ±5.7** | **−11.8% ±5.4** | **−12.8% ±5.6** |
| /blog | 1 | n.s. | n.s. | n.s. |
| /blog | 8 | n.s. | n.s. | n.s. |

/dashboard and /docs stream. On the stream path Fizz has to wait whenever the Flight chunk it needs hasn't been parsed yet, so it writes a placeholder and fills it in later. With the Result it never waits for a chunk, so the shell goes out as soon as it is rendered. That is the TTFB drop. Under load, other requests use the time that was spent waiting, so it shows up as throughput instead.

/blog sends 830KB of plain data (about 35k small objects) to one Client Component. Reading that data in process costs about the same as parsing it did, and serializing it is most of the request either way, so there is no difference on that route.

The stream path itself is unchanged: on the flight-ssr-bench fixture (Fizz and Flight+Fizz, Node and web streams, sync and async, in process and behind an HTTP server at 1 and 10 connections) no cell moves.

## Not done

Debug info (owner stacks, console replay) for Server Components that a Result ran.

title: [Flight] Skip revival for models without protocol strings
body:
JSON.parse already produces the final value when a model has no Flight tokens and no key the reviver removes. Skip the recursive revival when the input contains no dollar sign, no backslash, and no `__proto__` spelling. Escaped tokens and keys keep the existing path.

A 1.9MB model of 20,000 plain objects parses in 12ms instead of 24ms.

title: [Fiber] Track non-extensible thenables in a side table instead of crashing
body:
## Summary

`trackUsedThenable` tracks a thenable by attaching `status`/`value`/`reason` expandos to it:

```js
pendingThenable.status = 'pending'; // throws on non-extensible objects
```

If the thenable doesn't accept new properties — e.g. a promise passed through `Object.freeze`, or a thenable shared out of an immutable cache — that write throws `TypeError: Cannot add property status, object is not extensible` from inside React and the render fails.

This is a follow-up to #37796, which skipped the DEV-only `_debugInfo` instrumentation for non-extensible thenables but left this one. Unlike the debug info, this write happens in **production too**, so `use(Object.freeze(promise))` crashed in both dev and prod:

```
TypeError: Cannot add property status, object is not extensible
  at trackUsedThenable (packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberThenable.js:281)
```

## Fix

Non-extensible thenables are tracked in a `WeakMap` side table keyed by the thenable itself. That keeps exactly the same semantics as the expando: `use` can unwrap the value synchronously once it resolved, and the entry is collected with the thenable. Extensible thenables (the overwhelmingly common case) take the existing path and never touch the side table — the only added cost there is one `Object.isExtensible` call in the uncached-thenable branch.

## How did you test this change?

Two new regression tests in `ReactUse-test.js` — a frozen promise that resolves and one that rejects. Both fail on `main` with the `TypeError` above and pass with this change.

- `ReactUse-test.js` in dev and `--prod`: 53 tests each
- `ReactSuspense-test.internal.js`, `ReactLazy-test.internal.js`, `ReactSuspenseWithNoopRenderer.js`
- `flow check` (dom-node config), eslint, prettier: clean

title: [Flight] Complete models by their reachable fields, with a reader fuzz suite
body:
## Problem

A reference into another model waited for that model's whole chunk. When two models referenced each other, `resolveBlockedCycle` broke the cycle by handing one side the other's value as it was at that moment, placeholders included, and the receiving chunk initialized with those placeholders exposed to its callbacks. The simplest case is an element's props object referenced again from the same model:

```js
const element = <Widget data={data} payload={payload} />;
data.alias = element.props; // written as "$0:element:props"
```

`response.then(value => value.props.payload)` observes `null` while `payload`'s module is still loading. A Set that contains itself and a Server Function bound to its own container deadlocked for the same reason.

## Approach

Two things the chunk status used to conflate are separated:

- A model has an **identity** as soon as its reviver returns, even while references inside it are outstanding. References select from the identity.
- A model is **complete** when nothing reachable from its value is still a placeholder. Public callbacks wait for completion.

Every reference records the field it fills, so a path selecting through a placeholder waits for that field rather than its chunk. When a reference is fulfilled out of an incomplete model, the owning chunk walks the selected value once, takes a dependency on each pending field it reaches, and walks a field's value when that field is installed. Constructors (Set, Map, Blob, FormData, iterators) wait for their input slots to be installed; Sets and Maps are allocated before their entries arrive so that back-references land on the final identity. Server Functions bind once their module has loaded and every argument slot is installed, instead of `Promise.all` over the arguments chunk.

Lazy nodes and Promises remain delivery boundaries, as before.

## Fuzz suite

`ReactFlightReaderFuzz-test.js` renders generated value graphs with the real writer, reads them with the public client on both hosts, and releases the events the client waits for (packets, module loads, Promise resolutions, stream items) one at a time in random orders. After each event it checks that every value whose inputs have all arrived has been delivered, that nothing was delivered before its inputs arrived, that delivered values equal the server's, and that they still do once everything has settled.

The expectations come from the source graph and the record of released events only. `contents` is the one definition of what a value contains; which events a value needs, when it is owed, which values a failure reaches and which values are compared all derive from it. Known gaps are listed by what has to change, and a failure in any other shape is a regression. With every skip removed, 140 of 272 cases fail on `main` in development and 127 in production.

## Commits

Each commit passes Flow, lint, the Flight suites in development and production, and the fuzz suite with its skips as of that commit.

**Fuzz suite**

1. **Add reader fuzz tests** — the suite, with the random graphs and the reader gaps skipped.
2. **Wait for queued stream items before closing** — stream close ordering, with a regression test.

**Groundwork**

3. **Extract initialization handler allocation** — refactor, no behavior change.
4. **Extract reference installation and listener registration** — refactor, no behavior change.
5. **Wait on pending fields when selecting a path** — `_pendingFields`; a path through a placeholder waits for the field.
6. **Flatten the status switch in getOutlinedModel** — refactor, no behavior change.
7. **Defer debug info from an incomplete chunk until the receiver completes** — DEV bookkeeping needed once references are fulfilled early.
8. **Run constructors once their input slots are installed** — the inputs phase for Set/Map/Blob/FormData/iterators; reserved collections.

**The reader change**

9. **Complete models by their reachable fields, not by chunk** — `_identities`, the completeness walk, `resolveBlockedCycle` removed. Enables the cyclic shapes in the fuzz suite.
10. **Bind Server Functions once their argument slots are installed** — enables the bound-function shapes and the generated graphs.
11. **Fail a constructor as soon as a nested input fails** — failure subscriptions for constructor inputs.

**Independent reader fixes**

12. **Skip revival for models without protocol strings** — plain-JSON fast path (24ms → 12ms on a 1.9MB model).
13. **Copy byte stream chunks that share their transport buffer** — enqueueing a view into a pooled Node Buffer threw or emptied the chunks that followed.
14. **Stop enqueueing into a stream the consumer canceled** — rows arriving after `reader.cancel()` threw and took down the response.

## Behavior changes

- A field unaffected by a failure elsewhere in its model can now be selected successfully. The test `rejects a value that waits on a row that fails to parse` (from #37542) asserted the opposite; it is replaced by `keeps a selected field available when its containing model rejects`. Row layout is the writer's choice, so the old coupling was accidental.
- In DEV, the slow debug channel test reads the first paragraph through its Lazy node, since the element's row can now complete before the element's own props do.

## Cost

A WeakMap entry per outstanding reference, and one walk per consuming chunk of a value selected out of a model that has not completed; a constructor built from such a value walks its inputs once more for failures. No walk happens for models whose references all resolve to complete chunks. On a 20,000-node tree with 200 client references loading one at a time, parsing takes the same time as `main` (27ms). Selecting that whole tree out of an incomplete Map row takes 95ms against 27ms on `main`: two walks of 80,000 objects.

## Writer gaps (skipped)

- In DEV, a suspended server component that occurs twice is outlined and its second occurrence is written as a direct reference to the outlined row, so the model holding it waits for the component to render. Prod refers to the first occurrence's slot and gets the lazy node.
- In DEV on Node, `renderDebugModel` runs `Array.from` on sync iterators while describing an awaited value, consuming them before the model is written.
- A streamed array that contains itself overflows the writer's stack: stream items are written without a reference of their own, so a cycle inside one has no name. Giving object items an identity is a protocol decision.

title: Ensure unique `useId` values in large trees
body:
## Summary

Fixes #37911
Closes <url> (uses `slice()` which always allocates a new string)

When the tree position id exceeds 30 bits, `pushTreeContext` splits the low bits into a base 32 overflow string. The chunk is always a whole number of 5 bit groups, but `toString(32)` drops leading zero characters, erasing the boundary between the overflow digits and the remaining digits. Two structurally different tree positions could then serialize to the same id.

We now pad the overflow chunk with `padStart(numberOfOverflowBits / 5, '0')`. `padStart` short-circuits when the chunk is already full width, so the common case allocates nothing extra (it also beats a sentinel-bit plus `slice(1)` approach, which always allocates for these short strings).

- added test

title: Ensure unique `useId` values in large trees
body:
## Summary

When a tree id gets longer than 30 bits, `pushTreeContext` moves the low bits into the `overflow` string with `toString(32)`. That drops leading zeros, so a chunk like `00101` turns into `5` instead of `05`, and the boundary between the overflow chunks and the rest of the id is lost. Two different positions in the tree can then end up with the same id, like `_R_bqlala_` in the issue.

The fix sets a leading 1 bit before calling `toString(32)` and slices that character off, so every chunk keeps its full width. Fiber has the same code in `pushTreeId`, so I changed it too to keep hydration ids matching.

Fixes #37911

- added test

title: Add a test for the Children helper warning when a Map is passed
body:
## Summary

Adds a regression test for the DEV warning that the `React.Children` helpers emit when they are given a `Map`.

`React.Children.map` traverses its input through `mapIntoArray`, and when the children are a `Map` it logs `'Using Maps as children is not supported. Use an array of keyed ReactElements instead.'` (`packages/react/src/ReactChildren.js`). That code path had no test coverage:

- The only existing test that asserts this message is in `packages/react-dom/src/__tests__/ReactMultiChild-test.js`, which covers the **reconciler** path in `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactChildFiber.js`. That one is emitted via `console.error` with a component stack, whereas the `React.Children` one is emitted via `console.warn` with no stack, from a different module — they are not the same code path.
- Jest coverage for `packages/react/src/ReactChildren.js` (running `ReactChildren-test.js`) reports the warning branch as uncovered.

This PR is **test-only**: no production code is changed.

## How did you test this change?

```bash
cd packages/react
CI=1 yarn test packages/react/src/__tests__/ReactChildren-test.js
```

Before: `42 passed`.
After: **`43 passed, 43 total`** — 1 new test, no regressions in the existing `Children.map` / `forEach` / `toArray` / `count` cases.

I also confirmed the new test is not vacuous by temporarily breaking the source: guarding the warning behind `false &&` in `ReactChildren.js` makes exactly this test fail

```
✕ warns when a Map is passed to Children.map
  Expected warning was not recorded.
Tests:  1 failed, 42 passed, 43 total
```

while all 42 pre-existing tests still pass. The source was then restored byte-for-byte (sha256 verified before mutating and after restoring).

title: Warn in DEV when useMemo's first argument is not a function
body:
## Summary

Fixes #16589.

`useMemo` with a non-function first argument fails with a `TypeError` that leaks an internal parameter name:

```js
useMemo(5, []);
// TypeError: nextCreate is not a function
```

Nothing points at the call site, and `nextCreate` is not a name the user has ever seen. This adds a DEV warning that reports what was received, with a component stack pointing at the offending component.

**The throwing semantics are unchanged on every path that previously worked** — the same `TypeError` is still thrown, from the same place, at the same time. Nothing is converted into a custom `Error`, and no existing assertion changes.

This mirrors how a non-function argument to `useImperativeHandle` has been handled for years (`ReactFiberHooks.js`), down to the message shape, the `__DEV__` guard, and being placed in both the mount and update paths:

```js
if (__DEV__) {
  if (typeof create !== 'function') {
  console.error(
  'Expected useImperativeHandle() second argument to be a function ' +
  'that creates a handle. Instead received: %s.',
  // $FlowFixMe[invalid-compare]
  create !== null ? typeof create : 'null',
  );
  }
}
```

The check is added to `mountMemo`/`updateMemo` rather than to the dispatcher, following the same precedent, so it does not change what throws: when the deps are unchanged the memoized value is reused and the argument is never called, so that path warns without throwing.

**On "a type system would catch this":** it does when the types are precise, but not in plain JavaScript, not when the value is typed `any` (untyped third-party data, `JSON.parse`, a loosely typed ref) where narrowing never applies, and not when a value is moved into the factory position during a refactor. The warning fires only on a path that is already broken, so it costs nothing when the code is correct.

## How did you test this change?

Three cases added to `packages/react-reconciler/src/__tests__/ReactHooks-test.internal.js`:

1. `useMemo(5, [])` still rejects with the original `TypeError` **and** logs the new warning with a component stack — i.e. the red-before/green-after is only about the missing readable message, not about the throw.
2. A valid `useMemo(() => 42, [])` logs nothing.
3. Mounting with a valid factory and then updating to a non-function **with unchanged deps** warns and does **not** throw. This pins the placement decision above: the argument is never called on that path.

```bash
cd packages/react-reconciler
CI=1 yarn test __tests__/ReactHooks-test.internal.js
# Before: 72 passed
# After:  75 passed, 75 total
```

Full reconciler suite: `react-reconciler/src/__tests__/` — 77 suites, 1150 passed, 0 failed. `yarn test --prod` over the same scenarios shows no behaviour change, since the warning is `__DEV__`-only. `yarn prettier-check`, `yarn linc` and `yarn flow dom-node` all pass.

One note on the number of warnings: when the render throws, React retries it and the DEV warning is emitted on each attempt, so a throwing render logs it twice. That is existing behaviour of hook DEV checks rather than something this change introduces — the existing `useImperativeHandle` check reports the same number of times in the same situations — so it is asserted as-is rather than special-cased.

title: [eslint-plugin-react-hooks] Treat static primitive constants as stable in exhaustive-deps
[DOM] Keep React's own resource links when clearing the Document on a root's first commit
body:
## Summary

When a root renders into `document`, its first commit runs `clearContainerSparingly`. That keeps `<script>`, `<style>` and `<link rel="stylesheet">`, but removes every other `<link>`, including the `<link rel="preload" as="style">` React itself inserted moments earlier for a stylesheet resource.

The stylesheet resource still points at that preload (`resource.state.preload`). If the preload hasn't loaded yet when it's removed, the browser aborts the request and no `load` or `error` event ever fires. A Suspense boundary that later reveals that stylesheet then waits on the detached node until `SUSPENSEY_STYLESHEET_TIMEOUT` (60s). Until then the user sees the fallback, or nothing.

Next.js hits this on every page that calls `notFound()`: it serves an empty `<html id="__next_error__">` shell and client-renders the not-found tree with `createRoot(document)` (vercel/next.js#99287). On a production site we measured 3 of 60 cold loads blank for the full 60s. Every stuck load showed the CSS preload going `net::ERR_ABORTED` at the moment of the clear.

The fix makes `clearContainerSparingly` keep links React marked as hoistable. `clearHead` already makes this check, so React-owned resource links now survive both clearing paths. At the time of the root clear, hoistable instances owned by fibers haven't been placed yet (that happens in the mutation phase). So a marked `<link>` here is one of React's own resource elements (a preload, preconnect or similar), not a leftover from the tree being thrown away.

Four existing tests encoded the old behaviour: they asserted React's preload was gone after a client render into `document`. They now expect the preload to stay next to its stylesheet, which is what already happens for roots rendered into a container. One of them carried a comment attributing the missing preloads to the head singleton remount. That comment was wrong: `clearHead` keeps hoistables, and the `baz` preload inserted after the first commit survives the remount in that same test. I removed the comment.

## How did you test this change?

New test in `ReactDOMFloat-test.js`: a root on `document` renders a stylesheet resource inside a Suspense boundary that is still blocked on data. The fallback commits, which clears the document. Then the data resolves and the boundary waits on the stylesheet.

- Without the fix, the preload is gone after the first commit. With that assertion removed, the test fails at `loadPreloads(['route.css'])` because there's no preload left in the document to load, and the boundary stays on `loading...` until the 60s timeout.
- With the fix, the preload loads, the stylesheet is inserted, and the content reveals once it loads.

```
yarn test packages/react-dom/src/__tests__/ReactDOMFloat-test.js  # 143 passed, 1 skipped
yarn test -r=stable packages/react-dom/src/__tests__/ReactDOMFloat-test.js  # 143 passed, 1 skipped
yarn test --prod packages/react-dom/src/__tests__/ReactDOMFloat-test.js  # 143 passed, 1 skipped
yarn test packages/react-dom  # 4264 passed
yarn test -r=stable packages/react-dom  # 4261 passed
yarn flow dom-node  # no errors
prettier --check / eslint on both files  # clean
```

The only failures in the full `packages/react-dom` runs are `[GATED, SHOULD FAIL]` cases in `ReactDOMServerPartialHydration-test.internal.js`. They fail identically on `main` without this change.

We also applied the same one-line change as a `pnpm patch` to the react-dom builds bundled with `<email>`. In a `next build && next start` production build of our site, both stylesheet preloads are still in `<head>` once a `notFound()` page has rendered (unpatched: 0), and 0 of 100 loads were blank.

title: Fix state preservation when resolving lazy components
body:
## Summary

Fix state loss when switching from a resolved `React.lazy` component to its underlying component type.

## Problem

When a lazy component resolves, React's Fiber stores both the original lazy wrapper in `elementType` and the resolved component in `type`.

During a subsequent render, if the application replaces the lazy component with its resolved component type, reconciliation does not recognize the existing Fiber as compatible with the new element. React therefore remounts the component instead of reusing its existing Fiber, causing local state to be lost.

For example, a component rendered through `lazy(() => import('./Counter'))` may lose its state when the application subsequently renders `Counter` directly, even though both refer to the same underlying component.

The issue affects two reconciliation paths:
- A single child reconciled by `reconcileSingleElement`.
- Children in an array reconciled by `updateElement`.

## Solution

Extend the existing lazy-component compatibility checks to handle the reverse transition: an existing lazy Fiber whose resolved `type` matches the incoming element type.

The new checks verify that:
1. The existing Fiber's `elementType` is an object.
2. Its `$$typeof` identifies it as a `REACT_LAZY_TYPE`.
3. Its resolved `type` matches the incoming `elementType`.

When these conditions hold, React can reuse the existing Fiber and preserve the component's state instead of remounting it.

## Implementation

**`packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactChildFiber.js`**

- **`updateElement`**: Adds the reverse compatibility check for existing lazy Fibers encountered during array-child reconciliation.
- **`reconcileSingleElement`**: Adds the equivalent check for single-element reconciliation.

These changes complement the existing checks that handle an incoming lazy element whose resolved component type matches the current Fiber.

**`packages/react-reconciler/src/__tests__/ReactLazy-test.internal.js`**

- Adds a regression test verifying that state is preserved when switching from a resolved lazy component to its underlying component type.

## Testing

- Ran `corepack yarn test ReactLazy-test.internal` — **42 tests passed**.
- Verified that the new single-child regression test fails without the implementation change and passes with it.

**Not yet verified:** production-mode tests, formatting, lint, and Flow checks.

Array-child regression coverage has not yet been added explicitly.

title: [Fizz] Fix truncated prerender output under backpressure
body:
An aborted prerender can finish all tasks while partial output remains queued. If a Node stream applies backpressure, Fizz can close it before it flushes the remaining boundaries. This bug predates #37876 and also affects initial prerenders.

Fizz now waits for `partialBoundaries` to empty before it closes the destination. The regression test forces backpressure with `highWaterMark: 1` and verifies that `push()` returns `false`. Without the fix, the stream emits the first boundary's partial content and closes before it emits the second's.

title: Fix TypeError in CheckStringCoercion typeName() for null-prototype objects in DEV
body:
## Summary

Fixes #37881

In development mode (`__DEV__`), `typeName(value)` in `packages/shared/CheckStringCoercion.js` constructs a human-readable diagnostic type string when a prop, key, attribute, or style value throws during string coercion (`'' + value`).

Currently, `typeName(value)` accesses `(value as any).constructor.name`:
```javascript
const type =
  (hasToStringTag && (value as any)[Symbol.toStringTag]) ||
  (value as any).constructor.name ||
  'Object';
```

When `value` is created without a prototype (e.g. `Object.create(null)` or `{ __proto__: null }`), `(value as any).constructor` is `undefined`. Accessing `.name` on `undefined` causes an unhandled runtime error:
```
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')
  at typeName (packages/shared/CheckStringCoercion.js)
```
This crashes React's internal DEV helper before React can log the diagnostic error message and troubleshooting recommendations.

This PR safely checks for `constructor` existence before accessing `.name`:
```javascript
const constructor = (value as any).constructor;
const type =
  (hasToStringTag && (value as any)[Symbol.toStringTag]) ||
  (constructor && constructor.name) ||
  'Object';
```
When `constructor` is `undefined` or null, it gracefully falls back to `'Object'`.

## How did you test this change?

- Added a regression test in `packages/react-dom/src/__tests__/ReactIdentity-test.js` verifying that passing a null-prototype object with a throwing `valueOf` does not crash `typeName()`, properly prints the diagnostic error message (`The provided key is an unsupported type Object. This value must be coerced to a string before using it here.`), and throws the expected coercion exception.

title: [rust-compiler] Fix Unicode diagnostic underline positions
body:
## Summary Fixes #37897 The experimental Rust Babel adapter misaligns diagnostic underlines after non-ASCII characters and can make underlines too long for multiline ranges. The formatter treats Babel’s UTF-16 source columns as UTF-8 byte offsets. To reproduce, compile this component with the adapter configured to use `panicThreshold: 'all_errors'`: ```jsx function App(props) { const text = "café"; props.value = text; return

{props.value}

; } ``` The props-mutation error is expected, but the Rust adapter places the underline on the space before `props`: ```text > 5 | const text = "café"; props.value = text; | ^^^^^ value cannot be modified ``` This change measures marker spacing and multiline lengths in UTF-16 code units to match Babel. Tab handling and ASCII behavior remain unchanged. ## How did you test this change? From the repository root on the PR branch, with Rust installed: ```bash cd compiler cargo test -p react_compiler_diagnostics code_frame::tests cargo test -p react_compiler_diagnostics ``` Both new regression tests failed with the original formatter and passed with the fix. All 9 diagnostics tests passed. Coverage includes ASCII, accented text, CJK characters, emoji, combining marks, tabs, and multiline ranges.
