message:
[react-devtools] Keep console specifiers literal when no argument is supplied (#36930)

`formatConsoleArguments` in

`packages/react-devtools-shared/src/backend/utils/formatConsoleArguments.js`
is used by the DevTools backend (via `hook.js`) to inline `console.*`
printf-style substitutions after stripping React's appended component
stack.
For `%s`/`%d`/`%i`/`%f` it consumes the next argument with
`args.splice(argumentsPointer, 1)` and formats the result.

When a format string has more specifiers than arguments, `splice`
returns an
empty array, so `arg` is `undefined` and the specifier is rendered as
text:
`%s` becomes `"undefined"`, and `%d`/`%i`/`%f` become `"NaN"`.

```js
formatConsoleArguments('%s %s', 'the');
// before: ['the undefined']
// after:  ['the %s']
```

Browsers and Node's `util.format` leave an unmatched specifier as a
literal
(`console.log('%s %s', 'a')` prints `a %s`; `console.log('%d')` prints
`%d`).
So a message like `console.warn('value: %s')` was shown in DevTools as
`value: undefined` instead of `value: %s`.

This guards each of the `%d`/`%i`, `%f`, and `%s` cases on argument
availability (`argumentsPointer >= args.length`): when nothing is left
to
consume it keeps the specifier text and does not splice, mirroring the
existing trailing-`%` handling added in #36852. An explicitly passed
`undefined`/`null` argument is unchanged and still renders as
`undefined`/`null`, since a value is present at that position (the
`formats nullish values` test still passes).

  expect(formatConsoleArguments('%s %i', 'value')).toEqual(['value %i']);

message:
[react-devtools] substitute %i and %f in console format strings (#36929)

`formatConsoleArgumentsToSingleString` in
`packages/react-devtools-shared/src/backend/utils/index.js`
inlines `console.*` printf-style substitutions into a single string.
That string is
used both as the dedup key and as the displayed text for per-component
warnings/errors.

The `switch` that consumes the captured flag handles `s`, `d`, `i`, and
`f`, and the
function's own header comment says it "Implements s, d, i and f
placeholders". But
the substitution regex only captured `[jds]`:

```js
const REGEXP = /(%?)(%([jds]))/g;
```

So `%i` and `%f` were never matched. The `case 'i'` and `case 'f'` arms
were dead
code: the specifier was emitted literally and its argument was never
consumed. Worse,
because the unmatched specifier does not shift its argument, every
following specifier
in the same format string then binds to the wrong argument (a cascading
off-by-one
over the remaining args).

`%i` and `%f` are standard console integer/float specifiers (Node
`util.format` and
browsers both support them), so this affected common log formats. The
fix adds `i`
and `f` to the regex class so the existing switch arms run:

```js
const REGEXP = /(%?)(%([jdisf]))/g;
```

This is a one-character-class change that reconciles the regex with the
switch and
the header comment. The pre-existing behavior that `%j` is matched but
has no
`case` (so it falls through unchanged) is intentionally left as-is; it
is out of
scope for this fix.

## How did you test this change?

Added three regression tests to the existing
`formatConsoleArgumentsToSingleString`
describe block in
`packages/react-devtools-shared/src/__tests__/utils-test.js`:

- `formatConsoleArgumentsToSingleString('%i', 3.14)` -> `'3'`
- `formatConsoleArgumentsToSingleString('%f', 3.5)` -> `'3.5'`
- `formatConsoleArgumentsToSingleString('a %i b %s', 7, 'x')` -> `'a 7 b
x'` (locks
  in argument alignment)

message:
[Fizz] Guard the shell-error callbacks instead of nulling them out on the request (#36916)

Follow-up to #36903

The previous change stopped `onAllReady` from firing after a fatal shell
error by assigning `noop` to `request.onAllReady` inside `fatalError`.
This mutated a completion callback on the request as a side channel,
mirroring the existing `request.onShellError = noop` in `completeShell`.
This refactor removes both noop assignments and instead guards the calls
at the point where they would happen, so the callbacks on the request
stay the ones the caller passed in.

For `onAllReady`, `erroredTask` now returns right after `fatalError` in
the root (`boundary === null`) case, so it no longer falls through to
the `allPendingTasks === 0` check that calls `completeAll`. This matches
the sibling `finishAbortedTask`, which already returns after a fatal
root error. Later task completions cannot reach `completeAll` either,
because `performWork` bails out once the request status is past `OPEN`.

For `onShellError`, `fatalError` now decides whether to call it based on
the same condition that governed the assignment: the shell is complete
exactly when `request.pendingRootTasks === 0`, and `completeShell` only
runs at that point, so guarding the call is equivalent to the previous
nulling out. `onFatalError` still always fires because the error is
always fatal to the request.

This is a behavior-preserving refactor of the fix landed in #36903; the
tests added there continue to pass unchanged.

Contributing to CPython
-----------------------

For more complete instructions on contributing to CPython development,
see the `Developer Guide`_.

.. _Developer Guide: <url>

Using Python
------------

Installable Python kits, and information about using Python, are available at
`python.org`_.

.. _python.org: <url>

Build Instructions
------------------

On Unix, Linux, BSD, macOS, and Cygwin::

  ./configure
  make
  make test
  sudo make install

This will install Python as ``python3``.

You can pass many options to the configure script; run ``./configure --help``
to find out more.  On macOS case-insensitive file systems and on Cygwin,
the executable is called ``python.exe``; elsewhere it's just ``python``.

Building a complete Python installation requires the use of various
additional third-party libraries, depending on your build platform and
configure options.  Not all standard library modules are buildable or
usable on all platforms.  Refer to the
`Install dependencies <<url>>`_
section of the `Developer Guide`_ for current detailed information on
dependencies for various Linux distributions and macOS.

On macOS, there are additional configure and build options related
to macOS framework and universal builds.  Refer to `Mac/README.rst
<<url>>`_.

On Windows, see `PCbuild/readme.txt
<<url>>`_.

To build Windows packages, see `PC/layout/README.md
<<url>>`_.

If you wish, you can create a subdirectory and invoke configure from there.
For example::

  mkdir debug
  cd debug
  ../configure --with-pydebug
  make
  make test

(This will fail if you *also* built at the top-level directory.  You should do
a ``make clean`` at the top-level first.)

To get an optimized build of Python, run ``configure --enable-optimizations``
before you run ``make``.  This sets the default make targets up to enable
Profile Guided Optimization (PGO) and may be used to auto-enable Link Time
Optimization (LTO) on some platforms.  For more details, see the sections
below.

Profile Guided Optimization
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

PGO takes advantage of recent versions of the GCC or Clang compilers.  If used,
either via ``configure --enable-optimizations`` or by manually running
``make profile-opt`` regardless of configure flags, the optimized build
process will perform the following steps:

The entire Python directory is cleaned of temporary files that may have
resulted from a previous compilation.

An instrumented version of the interpreter is built, using suitable compiler
flags for each flavor. Note that this is just an intermediary step.  The
binary resulting from this step is not good for real-life workloads as it has
profiling instructions embedded inside.

After the instrumented interpreter is built, the Makefile will run a training
workload.  This is necessary in order to profile the interpreter's execution.
Note also that any output, both stdout and stderr, that may appear at this step
is suppressed.

The final step is to build the actual interpreter, using the information
collected from the instrumented one.  The end result will be a Python binary
that is optimized; suitable for distribution or production installation.


Link Time Optimization
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Enabled via configure's ``--with-lto`` flag.  LTO takes advantage of the
ability of recent compiler toolchains to optimize across the otherwise
arbitrary ``.o`` file boundary when building final executables or shared
libraries for additional performance gains.


What's New
----------

We have a comprehensive overview of the changes in the `What's new in Python
3.16 <<url>>`_ document.  For a more
detailed change log, read `Misc/NEWS
<<url>>`_, but a full
accounting of changes can only be gleaned from the `commit history
<<url>>`_.

If you want to install multiple versions of Python, see the section below
entitled "Installing multiple versions".


Documentation
-------------

`Documentation for Python 3.16 <<url>>`_ is online,
updated daily.

It can also be downloaded in many formats for faster access.  The documentation
is downloadable in HTML, EPUB, and reStructuredText formats; the latter version
is primarily for documentation authors, translators, and people with special
formatting requirements.

For information about building Python's documentation, refer to `Doc/README.rst
<<url>>`_.


Testing
-------

To test the interpreter, type ``make test`` in the top-level directory.  The
test set produces some output.  You can generally ignore the messages about
skipped tests due to optional features which can't be imported.  If a message
is printed about a failed test or a traceback or core dump is produced,
something is wrong.

By default, tests are prevented from overusing resources like disk space and
memory.  To enable these tests, run ``make buildbottest``.

If any tests fail, you can re-run the failing test(s) in verbose mode.  For
example, if ``test_os`` and ``test_gdb`` failed, you can run::

  make test TESTOPTS="-v test_os test_gdb"

If the failure persists and appears to be a problem with Python rather than
your environment, you can `file a bug report
<<url>>`_ and include relevant output from
that command to show the issue.

See `Running & Writing Tests <<url>>`_
for more on running tests.

Installing multiple versions
----------------------------

On Unix and Mac systems if you intend to install multiple versions of Python
using the same installation prefix (``--prefix`` argument to the configure
script) you must take care that your primary python executable is not
overwritten by the installation of a different version.  All files and
directories installed using ``make altinstall`` contain the major and minor
version and can thus live side-by-side.  ``make install`` also creates
``${prefix}/bin/python3`` which refers to ``${prefix}/bin/python3.X``.  If you
intend to install multiple versions using the same prefix you must decide which
version (if any) is your "primary" version.  Install that version using
``make install``.  Install all other versions using ``make altinstall``.

For example, if you want to install Python 2.7, 3.6, and 3.15 with 3.15 being the
primary version, you would execute ``make install`` in your 3.15 build directory
and ``make altinstall`` in the others.

title: ctypes array cache can return distinct types when types are created concurrently
body:
### Bug report

On the free-threaded build, this fails with `TypeError: expected c_int_Array_1 instance instead of c_int_Array_1`:

```python
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from ctypes import c_int
from threading import Barrier

barrier = Barrier(8)

def make_type(n):
  barrier.wait()
  return c_int * n

with ThreadPoolExecutor(8) as pool:
  for n in range(1, 1001):
  types = list(pool.map(make_type, [n] * 8))
  for t in types:
  types[0].from_param(t())
```

It passes on the GIL-enabled build because there isn't an opportunity for a GIL thread switch.

If I instead create a type that has a Python hook, I can deterministically trigger the same race on the GIL-enabled build as well:

```python
import ctypes
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from threading import Barrier

barrier = Barrier(2)

class Meta(type(ctypes.c_int)):
  def __set_name__(cls, owner, name):
  barrier.wait(timeout=5)

class C(ctypes.c_int, metaclass=Meta):
  pass

with ThreadPoolExecutor(2) as pool:
  a, b = pool.map(lambda _: C * 100, range(2))

print(a is b)
a.from_param(b())
```

This second script prints `False` and then `TypeError: expected C_Array_100 instance instead of C_Array_100` on both builds, because defining `__set_name__` makes python code run after the cache miss on the array type cache during creation of the array class.

I think the fix is to rewrite how `PyCArrayType_from_ctype` uses the `array_cache`: <url>

The current implementation has a check-then-insert TOCTOU bug.

I found this looking at the root cause of <url> See also #127945.

title: asyncio: SSL transport raises AttributeError after close() in connection_lost()
body:
# Bug report

If a protocol closes its SSL transport in `connection_lost()`, which is a common pattern, later calls on the transport fail:

```python
import asyncio
from test.test_asyncio import utils as tu

class Proto(asyncio.Protocol):
  def connection_made(self, tr):
  self.tr = tr
  def connection_lost(self, exc):
  self.tr.close()
  self.lost.set_result(None)

async def main():
  async def handler(reader, writer):
  writer.close()
  srv = await asyncio.start_server(handler, '127.0.0.1', 0,
  ssl=tu.simple_server_sslcontext())
  port = srv.sockets[0].getsockname()[1]
  loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
  proto = Proto()
  proto.lost = loop.create_future()
  tr, _ = await loop.create_connection(
  lambda: proto, '127.0.0.1', port, ssl=tu.simple_client_sslcontext())
  await proto.lost
  tr.write(b'x')  # AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute '_write_appdata'
  srv.close()

asyncio.run(main())
```

`set_protocol()`, `get_write_buffer_size()` and `get_extra_info()` fail the same way. Plain TCP transports don't have this problem.

It also breaks the `loop.sendfile()` fallback over SSL: if the peer disconnects mid-transfer, `restore()` calls `set_protocol()` and raises `AttributeError` instead of the expected connection error.

The cause is in `_SSLProtocolTransport.close()`. When it's called on a transport already marked closed, it sets `_ssl_protocol = None`. That was added in gh-98539 so the transport doesn't keep the SSL context alive, but it leaves the transport unusable.

Affects 3.11 and later.

title: Docs: change functools.Placeholder import alias
body:
### Documentation

The `functools.partial()` [docs](<url>) has the following example for using `Placeholder` with `partial()`:

```python
from functools import partial, Placeholder as _
remove = partial(str.replace, _, _, '')
message = 'Hello, dear dear world!'
remove(message, ' dear')

remove_dear = partial(remove, _, ' dear')
remove_dear(message)

remove_first_dear = partial(remove_dear, _, 1)
remove_first_dear(message)
```

The import alias `import Placeholder as _` seems to be bad practice, as the underscore could easily conflict with temporary loop variables or a text translation function, both of which are usually named `_`.

I suggest using `_P` instead, which is also pretty convenient.

title: concurrent.interpreters Queue truncates fractional timeouts with int() (and accepts negative fractional timeouts)
body:
### Bug report

### Bug description

The cross-interpreter `Queue` returned by
`concurrent.interpreters.create_queue()` documents `queue.Queue` semantics
for its `put()`/`get()` timeouts — the docs say that if *timeout* is a
positive number "it blocks at most *timeout* seconds"
([Doc/library/concurrent.interpreters.rst](<url>)).
However, both methods convert the timeout with `int(timeout)` before
computing the deadline (`Lib/concurrent/interpreters/_queues.py`), which
truncates fractional timeouts and defeats the negative-timeout check:

```python
import time
from concurrent import interpreters

q = interpreters.create_queue()

def timed(fn, label):
  start = time.monotonic()
  try:
  fn()
  except Exception as e:
  print(f"{label}: raised {type(e).__name__} "
  f"after {time.monotonic() - start:.2f}s")
  else:
  print(f"{label}: returned after {time.monotonic() - start:.2f}s")

timed(lambda: q.get(timeout=0.5),  "get(timeout=0.5)")
timed(lambda: q.get(timeout=1.9),  "get(timeout=1.9)")
timed(lambda: q.get(timeout=-0.5), "get(timeout=-0.5)")
```

Output on 3.16.0a1+ (main @ 83fe630):

```
get(timeout=0.5):  raised QueueEmpty after 0.00s  # expected: ~0.50s
get(timeout=1.9):  raised QueueEmpty after 1.01s  # expected: ~1.90s
get(timeout=-0.5): raised QueueEmpty after 0.00s  # expected: ValueError
```

`put()` on a full queue behaves the same way. For comparison,
`queue.Queue.get(timeout=0.5)` waits the full 0.50s and
`queue.Queue.get(timeout=-0.5)` raises
`ValueError: 'timeout' must be a non-negative number` immediately.

The truncation also explains why the existing tests did not catch this:
they use `timeout=0.1`, which truncates to 0 and still raises, just
0.1s too early.

Two knock-on effects of the `int()` conversion: `timeout='1'` is silently
accepted (stdlib raises `TypeError` from the `< 0` comparison), and
`timeout=float('inf')` / `float('nan')` leak `int()`'s
`OverflowError` / `ValueError` with messages about integer conversion
rather than anything timeout-related.

### Expected behaviour

Fractional timeouts are honoured like `queue.Queue`: the call blocks for
approximately the requested duration; any negative timeout (including
fractional ones such as `-0.5`) raises `ValueError` before waiting;
`timeout=0` remains a non-blocking poll.

I have a fix and regression tests ready and will open a PR.

### CPython versions tested on

CPython main (3.16.0a1+dev, 83fe630), built locally on Linux x86-64.

3.16

_No response_

title: annotationlib.ForwardRef.evaluate() ignores explicit globals/locals when the reference holds a closure cell
body:
### Bug report

### Bug description

When a `ForwardRef` obtained from `annotationlib.get_annotations(...,
format=Format.FORWARDREF)` refers to a single name from an enclosing
function scope, it stores the value in a closure cell (`__cell__`).
`ForwardRef.evaluate()` returns that cell value immediately, before
looking at the `globals` and `locals` arguments — so explicitly passed
namespaces are silently ignored:

```python
from annotationlib import Format, ForwardRef, get_annotations

def outer():
  def inner(a: x):
  pass
  fr = get_annotations(inner, format=Format.FORWARDREF)["a"]
  x = 99
  return fr

fr = outer()
print(fr.evaluate())  # 99 (correct)
print(fr.evaluate(locals={"x": 42}))  # 99  ← expected 42
print(fr.evaluate(globals={"x": 43}))  # 99  ← expected 43

# A plain ForwardRef without a cell honours the explicit namespaces:
print(ForwardRef("x").evaluate(locals={"x": 42}))  # 42
```

This is inconsistent with every other resolution path in the same
method: for a plain `ForwardRef`, and for references holding multiple
cells (a dict of cells), explicitly passed `locals` win over the
captured scope. Only the single-cell path flips the precedence.

The documented contract points the other way as well:
`ForwardRef.evaluate()` documents that "The arguments to this method
can be used to provide bindings for names that would otherwise be
undefined" and that "*globals* and *locals* are passed to `eval()`,
representing the global and local namespaces in which the name is
evaluated" (`Doc/library/annotationlib.rst`).

Expected behaviour: explicitly passed `globals`/`locals` take
precedence over the closure cell, as they do on the other paths; the
cell value is used as a fallback when the name is not provided
explicitly (and when no namespaces are passed at all, behaviour is
unchanged).

I have a fix and regression tests ready and will open a PR.

- CPython main (3.16.0a1+dev, 83fe630), built locally; `annotationlib`
  was added in 3.14, and the single-cell shortcut in
  `ForwardRef.evaluate()` is present there in the same form.

title: _pydecimal loses companion signal flags when a signal is trapped
body:
### Bug report

### Bug description

The pure-Python `decimal` implementation (`_pydecimal`) does not set the
context flags of companion conditions when an operation's result is
delivered through a trapped signal. The C implementation (`_decimal`,
libmpdec) records the full set of conditions in the context flags before
raising the trapped exception.

Minimal example — an overflowing multiplication signals `Overflow`,
`Inexact` and `Rounded`; `Overflow` is trapped (as it is in the default
context):

```python
import _decimal as C
import _pydecimal as P

def probe(module):
  ctx = module.Context(prec=9, Emin=-999, Emax=999)
  ctx.clear_flags()
  try:
  ctx.multiply(module.Decimal('1E+800'), module.Decimal('1E+800'))
  except module.Overflow:
  pass
  return sorted(s.__name__ for s, v in ctx.flags.items() if v)

print("C _decimal:  ", probe(C))
print("P _pydecimal:", probe(P))
```

Output (verified on CPython 3.12 and on a 3.16 build):

```
C _decimal:  ['Inexact', 'Overflow', 'Rounded']
P _pydecimal: ['Overflow']  # Inexact and Rounded are lost
```

The same loss occurs for every operation that signals several conditions
at once whenever any of them is trapped, e.g.:

| Case (single trap) | `_decimal` flags after the exception | `_pydecimal` flags |
|---|---|---|
| `divide(1, 3)`, trap `Inexact` | `Inexact, Rounded` | `Inexact` |
| `divide(1E-999, 1E+10)`, trap `Underflow` | `Clamped, Inexact, Rounded, Subnormal, Underflow` | `Underflow` |
| `divide(1E-999, 1E+10)`, trap `Subnormal` | `Clamped, Inexact, Rounded, Subnormal, Underflow` | `Subnormal, Underflow` |
| `divmod(5, 0)`, trap `DivisionByZero` | `DivisionByZero, InvalidOperation` | `DivisionByZero` |
| `quantize(1.23, 1E+995)` with `clamp=1`, trap `Inexact` | `Clamped, Inexact, Rounded` | `Inexact` |

With no traps enabled the two implementations agree exactly.

### Expected vs actual

Per the documentation (`Doc/library/decimal.rst`, "Signals"): *"For each
signal there is a flag and a trap enabler. When a signal is encountered,
its flag is set to one, then, if the trap enabler is set to one, an
exception is raised."* An overflowing operation *encounters* `Inexact`
and `Rounded` — both implementations set those flags whenever `Overflow`
is not trapped — so the flags should be set regardless of whether some
other signal is trapped. The two implementations are interchangeable
backends of the same module, so code that catches the exception and then
inspects `context.flags` (a documented monitoring pattern) must observe
the same state with either backend.

Root cause: in `Lib/_pydecimal.py`, `Context._raise_error()` sets one
signal's flag and raises immediately when that signal is trapped.
Operations signal companion conditions through *sequential* `_raise_error`
calls (e.g. `Decimal._fix` signals `Overflow`, then `Inexact`, then
`Rounded`), so a trapped signal makes the remaining calls unreachable.

Note that *which* exception is raised is correct in both implementations
(the precedence order established by bpo-8567); only the flag state left
behind differs. This is also why the existing test suite does not catch
it: the decTest driver disables the traps of the expected conditions for
its flag comparisons, and the extended error tests assert only the
exception type, never the resulting flags.

title: logging: Logger.setLevel() and logging.disable() are O(number of loggers)
body:
### Bug report

Every `Logger.setLevel()` and `logging.disable()` call goes through `Manager._clear_cache()`, which walks the whole `loggerDict` and clears each logger's `isEnabledFor` cache, even the ones that never cached anything. So setting the level on N loggers one by one is quadratic. That shows up in apps or test suites with thousands of loggers (one per module/plugin/connection) that get configured individually.

```python
import logging, time

for n in (1000, 2000, 4000, 8000):
  logging.root.manager.loggerDict.clear()
  loggers = [logging.getLogger(f"app.mod{i}") for i in range(n)]
  for lg in loggers:
  lg.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG)
  t = time.perf_counter()
  for lg in loggers:
  lg.setLevel(logging.INFO)
  print(f"{n:5d} loggers: {time.perf_counter() - t:.3f} s")
```

On 3.14.7 this gives about 0.23 s at 2000 loggers, 0.89 s at 4000 and 4.4 s at 8000 (each doubling is about 4x).

A fix is to have the manager remember which loggers actually have something in their cache (a `WeakSet` filled on the `isEnabledFor` cache-miss path, which already holds the lock) and only clear those. The cache-hit path doesn't change. I have a patch ready and can open a PR.

title: Skip the `__bytes__` lookup in bytes() for exact bytes and int
body:
### Feature or enhancement

Since 3.11 added `bytes.__bytes__` (gh-68422), `bytes(b)` for an exact `bytes` looks up `__bytes__`, creates a bound method and calls it, only to get `b` back. For an exact `int` the lookup always misses, because int has no
`__bytes__`.

Both types are immutable, so `bytes_new_impl()` can check for them first:
- return an exact `bytes` argument directly, as `PyObject_Bytes()` and `PyBytes_FromObject()` already do;
- skip the lookup for an exact `int`.

Subclasses, including `bool`, still look up `__bytes__`, so there's no behaviour change.

That makes `bytes(b)` about 2.2x faster, a bytes subclass `Sub(b)` about 1.4x, and `bytes(16)` about 1.1x. Other `bytes()` calls and the controls are unchanged (pyperf, PGO+LTO).

<details><summary>Benchmark script</summary>

```python
import pyperf

runner = pyperf.Runner()
for stmt in ["bytes(b)", "bytes(16)", "bytes(ba)", "bytes(mv)", "bytes(l)",
  "bytes(s, 'ascii')", "bytes(hb)", "Sub(b)", "bytes()",
  "len(l)", "l[0]", "x + 1", "str(x)"]:
  runner.timeit(stmt, stmt,
  "b = b'abcdefghijklmnop'; ba = bytearray(b); mv = memoryview(b); "
  "l = list(range(16)); s = 'abcdefghijklmnop'; x = 12345\n"
  "class Sub(bytes): pass\n"
  "class HB:\n  def __bytes__(self): return b\n"
  "hb = HB()")
```

</details>

title: ChainMap reverse union bypasses missing-key lookup semantics
body:
### Bug report

Reverse union can replace the value exposed by its right-hand `ChainMap` with a different value from an underlying mapping.

```python
from collections import ChainMap, Counter

chain = ChainMap(Counter(), {"x": 5})
print(chain["x"])  # 0
print(dict(chain))  # {'x': 0}
print(dict({"x": 99} | chain))  # {'x': 5}, expected {'x': 0}
```

`Counter.__missing__` returns zero, so the first mapping successfully handles the lookup. That shadowing behavior is intentional, as discussed in #117576 and #93432. The discrepancy here is specifically the reverse union, which bypasses the values exposed by the right operand.

`ChainMap.__ror__` updates a dictionary from each underlying mapping in reverse order. That combines stored entries rather than obtaining values through `ChainMap.__getitem__`. In contrast, `dict(chain)` and `dict.update(chain)` preserve the view's lookup semantics. The existing `test_union_operators` test also expects `(d | cm).maps == [d | dict(cm)]` for dictionary-backed chains.

The proposed fix updates the result from the `ChainMap` itself. It preserves key order and the returned class, while using normal per-key lookups. Defaulting mappings can therefore have their usual read side effects.

Suggested priority is P3. The incorrect result requires a chain with specialized lookup semantics and a reverse union.

### Duplicate search

Searched open and closed issues and PRs for `ChainMap` and combinations with `Counter`, `__ror__`, `union`, `defaultdict`, `__missing__`, and `merge`. Reviewed the PEP 584 issue #80325, the implementation and review discussion in #18832, and the related lookup reports #117576 and #93432. I did not locate a report of this reverse-union discrepancy. The original implementation discussion considered updating from the view but discussed efficiency rather than this value mismatch.

### CPython versions tested on

The unchanged `Lib/collections/__init__.py` from main commit `7515b64aa7231e8a8cf5271155829a208d789583` was loaded directly on Python 3.15.0b2 on Windows. This is a test of the exact module source, not a native build of that main commit.

A native CPython 3.16.0a1+dev build from fix commit `aa591236ad337499fe80e90e6ad28178c81a8367` was also tested on Ubuntu 24.04. With the original baseline collections module restored, the minimal reproduction and both new regression tests fail for the expected values. Restoring the fixed module makes them pass. Ten runs of the five selected test modules, with hash seeds 1 through 10, each report 286 cases, 284 passes, two skips, and no failures or errors. Both new tests are present and pass in every run. [Native build and validation logs](<url>).

### Tool assistance

AI tools assisted the investigation, patch, and tests. The reproduction, lookup contract, related reports, and proposed diff were reviewed before submission.

title: checksharedmods fails on non-glibc cross builds (host interpreter gets target LD_LIBRARY_PATH)
body:
### Bug report

Cross-compiling 3.15 for a musl target (glibc build machine) fails in `make` at the `checksharedmods` target:

```
nativepython3: error while loading shared libraries: libc.so: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
make: *** [Makefile:1801: checksharedmods] Error 127
```

The rule runs the build python under `RUNSHARED`:

```
@$(RUNSHARED) $(PYTHON_FOR_BUILD) $(srcdir)/Tools/build/check_extension_modules.py
```

In a cross build `PYTHON_FOR_BUILD` is the host interpreter (from `--with-build-python`) but `RUNSHARED` points `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` at the target's build dir, so the host interpreter gets the target libraries. On glibc->glibc nobody notices, but with a musl target the glibc host binary can't load the musl `libc.so` and dies before Python even starts.

This started with #141926 / GH-141958, which dropped the old

```sh
if test "$cross_compiling" = yes; then
  RUNSHARED=
fi
```

That PR was about getting PGO to work under emulation, but `checksharedmods` runs in the normal `build_all` path even without PGO, so now every non-emulated cross build to a different libc breaks here.

As far as I can tell `check_extension_modules.py` doesn't actually need the target libs on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` when cross-compiling — it already takes the cross path (via `_PYTHON_HOST_PLATFORM`) and only checks that the module files exist, it doesn't import them.

Putting the `cross_compiling` RUNSHARED reset back makes the build work again. Would it make sense to restore it, or to only use `RUNSHARED` for the build-python when a `HOSTRUNNER` is set?

body:
### Feature or enhancement

After <url> the usage of `STORE_FAST_LOAD_FAST` as almost none. It should either be removed or replaced with `STORE_FAST_LOAD_FAST_BORROW`. 

Opcode counts for all code objects from compiling the 2071 files of `Lib/` (nested code objects included, `CACHE` entries excluded):

| Opcode | main (2e1666f1f24) |  PR which adds STORE_FAST_LOAD_FAST_BORROW|
|---|---|---|
| `STORE_FAST_LOAD_FAST` | 66 | 0 |
| `STORE_FAST_LOAD_FAST_BORROW` | 0 | 1,997 |
| `STORE_FAST` | 152,996 | 151,065 |
| `LOAD_FAST_BORROW` | 539,756 | 538,149 |
| `LOAD_FAST` (strong) | 20,858 | 20,924 |
| `LOAD_FAST_BORROW_LOAD_FAST_BORROW` | 46,070 | 45,875 |
| `STORE_FAST_STORE_FAST` | 12,069 | 12,069 |
| all instructions | 5,147,291 | 5,145,554 |

As long as superinstructions are limited to single lines, there are not many cases where we will have a `STORE_FAST_LOAD_FAST`. Some benchmarks:

| Benchmark (5,000 elements) | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `[x for x in lst]` | 32.0 us | 29.5 us: 1.08x faster |
| `[x + 1 for x in lst]` | 73.1 us | 68.4 us: 1.07x faster |
| `[x.real for x in lst]` | 97.7 us | 89.2 us: 1.10x faster |
| `for i in range(5000): i` | 36.6 us | 34.1 us: 1.07x faster |

Callgrind on the first benchmark: 131.7 vs 122.8 instructions per iteration. From the benchmarks only the second and third make sense in real-world code. The first and the last do not. In the pystats of the pyperformance suite the pair is about 0.08% of all executed instructions (94% of them directly after a `FOR_ITER`).

<details>
<summary>Scripts used for the opcode counts and the benchmark</summary>

```python
"""Compile every .py under LIBDIR with the running interpreter and count opcodes.
Usage: python -I count_opcodes.py LIBDIR"""
import collections, dis, json, os, sys

libdir = sys.argv[1]
CACHE = dis.opmap['CACHE']
counts = collections.Counter()

def walk(co):
  for i in range(0, len(co.co_code), 2):
  op = co.co_code[i]
  if op != CACHE:
  counts[dis.opname[op]] += 1
  for c in co.co_consts:
  if isinstance(c, type(co)):
  walk(c)

for root, dirs, files in os.walk(libdir):
  for f in sorted(files):
  if f.endswith('.py'):
  p = os.path.join(root, f)
  try:
  with open(p, 'rb') as fh:
  co = compile(fh.read(), p, 'exec')
  except (SyntaxError, ValueError):
  continue
  walk(co)

print(json.dumps({'total': sum(counts.values()), 'counts': counts}, sort_keys=True))
```

```python
import sys, timeit
lst = list(range(5000))
def ident(it): return [x for x in it]
def plus(it): return [x + 1 for x in it]
def attr(it): return [x.real for x in it]
def rng(n):
  for i in range(n): i
cases = [("[x for x in lst]", lambda: ident(lst)), ("[x + 1 for x in lst]", lambda: plus(lst)),
  ("[x.real for x in lst]", lambda: attr(lst)), ("for i in range(5000): i", lambda: rng(5000))]
print(sys.version.split()[0])
for name, fn in cases:
  best = min(timeit.repeat(fn, number=500, repeat=21)) / 500 * 1e6
  print(f"  {name:28s} {best:7.1f} us")
```

</details>

body:
### Documentation

The docstring for `os.path.normcase` on Posix is `Normalize case of pathname.  Has no effect under Posix` and the [documentation](<url>) says "On other operating systems, return the path unchanged."

title: `fnmatch.filter` and `filterfalse` work with pathlikes only on non-Posix platforms
body:
`fnmatch.filter` contains a check:

```
  if os.path is posixpath:
  # normcase on posix is NOP. Optimize it away from the loop.
```

It calls `normcase` on the paths to be filtered only on non-Posix platforms.

The check dates from 2001 and the comment was probably true then. But nowadays, `os.path.normcase` does do something even on Posix: it normalizes path-like objects into strs or bytes.

So on MacOS I get:

```
>>> import fnmatch
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> fnmatch.filter([Path("hi")], "hi")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-2>", line 1, in <module>
  fnmatch.filter([Path("hi")], "hi")
  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/Users/jelle/py/cpython/Lib/fnmatch.py", line 61, in filter
  if match(name):
  ~~~~~^^^^^^
TypeError: expected string or bytes-like object, got 'PosixPath'
```

But this will work on Windows.

I think this is should be fixed for two reasons:
- It's an unnecessary difference in behavior between platforms. Python should work the same across OSes as much as possible, and there's no good reason for the behavior to differ here.
- In general, we want path-related functions to accept path-like objects (PEP 519)

However, we've generally treated PEP 519 changes as new features, so let's change this on main only.

Discovered in python/typeshed#16647

title: `test_is_python_process_non_python_subprocess` always times out when `sleep` is a multicall binary (Alpine/BusyBox, RHEL UBI9)
body:
### Bug report

### Bug description:

The fix for gh-159534 (GH-160028, backported to 3.15 in GH-160080) makes `test_is_python_process_non_python_subprocess` fail every time on systems where `sleep` is provided by a multicall binary. That includes the Alpine buildbots, where the original gh-159534 failure was found:

```
FAIL: test_is_python_process_non_python_subprocess (test.test_profiling.test_sampling_profiler.test_children.TestIsPythonProcess.test_is_python_process_non_python_subprocess)
Test that a non-Python subprocess is not detected as Python.
----------------------------------------
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../Lib/test/test_profiling/test_sampling_profiler/test_children.py", line 628, in test_is_python_process_non_python_subprocess
  _wait_for_process_exec(proc, "sleep", SHORT_TIMEOUT)
  File ".../Lib/test/test_profiling/test_sampling_profiler/test_children.py", line 91, in _wait_for_process_exec
  for _ in sleeping_retry(timeout, max_delay=0.1):
  File ".../Lib/test/support/__init__.py", line 2779, in sleeping_retry
  for _ in busy_retry(timeout, err_msg, error=error):
  File ".../Lib/test/support/__init__.py", line 2749, in busy_retry
  raise AssertionError(msg)
AssertionError: timeout (45.1 seconds)
```

#### Buildbots

AMD64 Alpine Linux NoGIL 3.x:
- [build 3444](<url>) (before GH-160028): the original intermittent failure, `True is not false`.
- [build 3445](<url>) (first build with GH-160028): `timeout (45.1 seconds)`. Every build since fails the same way, e.g. [build 3523](<url>).

AMD64 Alpine Linux 3.15:
- [build 800](<url>) (before GH-160080): only `test_lazy_import` fails.
- [build 815](<url>) (first build with GH-160080) and every build since, including [build 851](<url>) just before v3.15.2 was tagged: this test fails too.

This failure is separate from the `test_lazy_import` crash on Alpine (gh-159535). The Alpine builders will stay red after that crash is fixed.

#### Cause

The new `_wait_for_process_exec()` helper waits until `os.path.basename(os.readlink(f"/proc/{pid}/exe")) == "sleep"`. When `sleep` is a multicall binary, `/proc/{pid}/exe` points to the multicall binary instead:

| System | `/usr/bin/sleep` or `/bin/sleep` | `/proc/{pid}/exe` of a running `sleep` |
|---|---|---|
| Alpine 3.24 (BusyBox) | symlink to `/bin/busybox` | `/bin/busybox` |
| RHEL UBI9 (`coreutils-single`, the image default) | shebang script `#!/usr/bin/coreutils --coreutils-prog-shebang=sleep` | `/usr/bin/coreutils` |
| RHEL UBI9 after `dnf swap coreutils-single coreutils` | regular binary | `/usr/bin/sleep` |

The condition never becomes true, so the test always times out.

Reproducer, tested in `python:3-alpine` and `registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi`:

```python
import os, subprocess, time
proc = subprocess.Popen(["sleep", "10"])
time.sleep(0.5)
print(os.readlink(f"/proc/{proc.pid}/exe"))
proc.kill()
```

### Suggested fix

The helper only needs to know that the child has called `exec()`. The program name doesn't matter. Before `exec()`, the forked child's `/proc/{pid}/exe` is the parent's Python executable, so wait until it differs from the parent's:

```diff
-def _wait_for_process_exec(proc, name, timeout):
+def _wait_for_process_exec(proc, timeout):
  # Wait until a child process calls exec() to replace the forked process
-  # executable. Raise AssertionError on timeout.
+  # executable. Don't check the executable name: it can be a multicall
+  # binary such as /bin/busybox. Raise AssertionError on timeout.
+  parent_exe = os.readlink("/proc/self/exe")
  for _ in sleeping_retry(timeout, max_delay=0.1):
  exe = os.readlink(f"/proc/{proc.pid}/exe")
-  if os.path.basename(exe) == name:
+  if exe != parent_exe:
  break
```

```diff
-  _wait_for_process_exec(proc, "sleep", SHORT_TIMEOUT)
+  _wait_for_process_exec(proc, SHORT_TIMEOUT)
```

I tested this check with the reproducer on Alpine (BusyBox) and on UBI9 with both `coreutils-single` and `coreutils`. It detects the `exec()` in all three cases, while the current name check fails on Alpine and on UBI9 with `coreutils-single`.

title: Emscripten: Remove obsolete `pthread_getattr_np` workaround in `ceval.c`
body:
### Bug report

### Description

The workaround in `Python/ceval.c` was introduced to address a broken `pthread_getattr_np()` implementation in Emscripten versions prior to 4.0.6 (GH-130396, #131088).

The existing comment explicitly describes it as temporary:

```c
#if defined(__EMSCRIPTEN__)

// Temporary workaround to make `pthread_getattr_np` work on Emscripten.
// Emscripten 4.0.6 will contain a fix:
// <url>
```

However, the workaround is still enabled for all Emscripten versions because it only checks `__EMSCRIPTEN__`, regardless of the toolchain version.

The upstream fix was included in Emscripten 4.0.6, and CPython now uses Emscripten 6.0.13 (`Platforms/emscripten/config.toml`).

Therefore, this workaround appears to be obsolete and could potentially be removed, allowing CPython to use Emscripten's native `pthread_getattr_np()` implementation.

The removal should be verified against the current Emscripten toolchain to ensure that stack boundary detection and recursion protection continue to work correctly.

title: Keep PyLong "x_divrem" inner loop carry in 64 bits
body:
### Feature or enhancement

This is a split issue from <url> which focus on the improvement of longobject `x_divrem` inner loop.

The inner loop `x_divrem`:
```
/* subtract q*w0[0:size_w] from vk[0:size_w+1] */
zhi = 0;
for (i = 0; i < size_w; ++i) {
  /* invariants: -PyLong_BASE <= -q <= zhi <= 0;
  -PyLong_BASE * q <= z < PyLong_BASE */
  z = (sdigit)vk[i] + zhi - (stwodigits)q * (stwodigits)w0[i];
  vk[i] = (digit)z & PyLong_MASK;
  zhi = (sdigit)Py_ARITHMETIC_RIGHT_SHIFT(stwodigits, z, PyLong_SHIFT);
}
```

`zhi`, the loop-carried borrow in Knuth Algorithm D, was stored as an `sdigit (32-bit int)` and then widened to 64-bit `stwodigits` on the next iteration. That extra conversion sat on the critical chain which is strong latency bounded:
```
  ldr  w0, [x12, x2, lsl #2]
  ldr  w1, [x27, x2, lsl #2]
  add  w0, w3, w0  // critical chain
  sxtw  x0, w0  // critical chain (32 -> 64)
  umsubl  x0, w1, w14, x0  // critical chain
  and  w1, w0, #0x3fffffff
  str  w1, [x12, x2, lsl #2]
  asr  x0, x0, #30  // critical chain
  mov  w3, w0  // critical chain (64 -> 32)
```
Store `zhi` as stwodigits instead to save the type conversions. Invaddition, the compiler can then compute `vk[i] - q*w0[i]` at first and only then add the carried borrow, so this computation no longer depends on `zhi`:
```
  ldr  w4, [x3, x1, lsl #2]
  ldr  w0, [x28, x1, lsl #2]
  umsubl  x0, w0, w13, x4
  add  x2, x0, x2  // critical chain
  and  w4, w2, #0x3fffffff
  str  w4, [x3, x1, lsl #2]
  asr  x2, x2, #30  // critical chain
```
The loop-carried chain shrinks to two instructions. Knuth invariants are unchanged, so quotients and remainders are the same. The `pidigits` benchmark improves about 8% on x86-64 and about 12% on AArch64.

The detailed performance data will be pasted later.

title: Thread.start() retains an unstarted thread when an audit hook raises BaseException
body:
### Bug report

`Thread.start()` leaves a thread in `_limbo` when the native-start audit hook raises `KeyboardInterrupt` or `SystemExit`. No OS thread was created, but `threading.enumerate()` keeps returning the thread. Raising `RuntimeError` from the same hook already cleans up correctly.

```python
import sys
import threading

def refuse(event, args):
  if event == "_thread.start_joinable_thread":
  raise KeyboardInterrupt

sys.addaudithook(refuse)
thread = threading.Thread()
try:
  thread.start()
except KeyboardInterrupt:
  pass

print(thread._os_thread_handle.ident)  # 0: no OS thread was created
print(thread.is_alive())  # False
print(thread in threading.enumerate())  # True
```

I expect the failed thread to be removed from the registry. [`threading.enumerate()` excludes threads that have not started](<url>).

The native-start call is wrapped in `except Exception`, which misses these exceptions. Cleanup must also distinguish refusal from an exception arriving as the native call returns after creating an OS thread; that thread still needs its registration.

This differs from #140746 and #153776, where an OS thread is created and then fails during bootstrap. The earlier cleanup in #51730 covers `ThreadError`.

title: tarfile filter="data" behavior slightly loosened after gh-160097
body:
### Bug report

gh-160097 gave tar_filter a check that data_filter already had. In moving the check, the condition changed. It was "the member's resolved path equals the destination". It is now "the member's normalised name is ." 

A symlink or hard-link member can still reach the destination, and now passes filter="data", in three ways:

* `../dest`;
* `s/.` after an earlier member `s -> .`, which needs no knowledge of the destination;
* `../E`, where `E` is an _existing_ symlink outside the destination that points at it.

vs before:

* `extract()` and `extractall()` may raise `RecursionError` where they raised `OutsideDestinationError`.
* The extraction completes and changes the destination directory's own permissions.
* A symlink outside the destination that points at it is deleted or replaced. That includes the symlink through which the caller named the destination.

### reproducer

common code used be the scenarios below:

```python
import io, os, tarfile, tempfile

def archive(*members):  # (name, type, linkname, mode, data)
  buf = io.BytesIO()
  with tarfile.open(fileobj=buf, mode="w") as tf:
  for name, type, linkname, mode, data in members:
  info = tarfile.TarInfo(name)
  info.type, info.linkname, info.mode, info.size = type, linkname, mode, len(data)
  tf.addfile(info, io.BytesIO(data))
  buf.seek(0)
  return tarfile.open(fileobj=buf)
```

1. RecursionError vs prior OutsideDestinationError

```python
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as box:
  os.mkdir(box + "/dest")
  with archive(("../dest", tarfile.SYMTYPE, "dest", 0o777, b"")) as tf:
  tf.extractall(box + "/dest", filter="data")
```

2. link destination permissions

```python
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as box:
  os.mkdir(box + "/dest", 0o700)
  with archive(("d", tarfile.DIRTYPE, "", 0o755, b""),
  ("s", tarfile.SYMTYPE, ".", 0o777, b""),
  ("s/.", tarfile.LNKTYPE, "d", 0o777, b"")) as tf:
  tf.extractall(box + "/dest", filter="data")
  print("destination mode:", oct(os.stat(box + "/dest").st_mode & 0o7777))
```

that was previously an OutsideDestinationError, now it changes the mode of the destination.  security regression, this one lets any destination path be targeted.

3. symlink outside destination

```python
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as box:
  os.mkdir(box + "/real")
  os.symlink("real", box + "/current")
  with archive(("first.txt", tarfile.REGTYPE, "", 0o644, b"1"),
  ("../current", tarfile.SYMTYPE, "real", 0o777, b""),
  ("later.txt", tarfile.REGTYPE, "", 0o644, b"2")) as tf:
  tf.extractall(box + "/current", filter="data")
  print("current is a symlink:", os.path.islink(box + "/current"))
  print("current/:", os.listdir(box + "/current"), " real/:", os.listdir(box + "/real"))
```

That should've been an OutsideDestinationError, now it mucks with things outside... security regression, but requires a pre-existing symlink to target.

### Fix thoughts

Minimal: put the five removed lines in tarfile from <url> back while keeping the six new ones?

Broader: judge a link member by where the link is made (ie: did the tarfile extraction write it), resolving the parent directory only.

3.13, CPython main branch

### Operating systems tested on:

Linux

title: Update `list()` to use the existing freelist
body:
### Feature or enhancement `list_vectorcall()` currently allocates with `PyType_GenericAlloc()` so `list()` and `list(iterable)` always allocate new. `[]` and `PyList_New()` reuse an object when possible from the existing list freelist instead. Can reuse the freelist in the `tp_vectorcall` slot which only applies for the exact type. I found this while profiling builtin constructor calls with callgrind (instructions per function). For `list(t)`, about a third of the cost was `PyType_GenericAlloc()` plus the matching malloc/free, which `[]` never pays. Microbenchmarks (pyperf, PGO+LTO, Linux x86-64, interleaved A/B, main vs patch): | Benchmark | main | patch | |-----------|:-------:|:---------------------:| | list() | 21.2 ns | 15.3 ns: 1.38x faster | | list(d) | 36.1 ns | 27.4 ns: 1.32x faster | | list(t) | 30.3 ns | 23.9 ns: 1.27x faster | | list(l) | 32.0 ns | 25.7 ns: 1.24x faster | | list(r) | 43.6 ns | 36.0 ns: 1.21x faster | Untouched controls (`[]`, a `list` subclass, `x + 1`, `len(l)`, `l[0]`, `tuple(l)`) stay within the A/A noise (≤ 1.07x).
Benchmark script ```python import pyperf runner = pyperf.Runner() for stmt in ["list()", "list(t)", "list(l)", "list(r)", "list(d)", "L(t)", "[]", "len(l)", "l[0]", "x + 1", "tuple(l)"]: runner.timeit(stmt, stmt, "t = (1, 2, 3); l = [1, 2, 3]; r = range(3); d = dict.fromkeys(t); x = 12345\n" "class L(list): pass") ``` ```sh ./python bm_list.py --affinity=10-13 -o main.json # on main ./python bm_list.py --affinity=10-13 -o patch.json # on the patch python -m pyperf compare_to main.json patch.json --table -G ``` Runs were interleaved (main, patch, main, patch) on PGO+LTO builds.
pystats: list() now hits the freelist Object counters for 100,000 executions (stats enabled only around the loop): | statement | main: allocations / from freelist | patch: allocations / from freelist | |---|---|---| | `list()` | 100,001 / 98,978 | 1 / 198,978 | | `list(t)` | 200,001 / 98,978 | 100,001 / 198,978 | | `[]` | 1 / 198,978 | 1 / 198,978 | After warm-up, every `list()` object comes from the freelist, as with `[]`. The remaining allocation in `list(t)` is the item array.
- The list freelist was added in 2004 by gh-40215.. - `list_vectorcall()` was added in GH-18928 and kept using the existing generic alloc. ### Has this already been discussed elsewhere? title: JIT stop_tracing dispatches a stale ENTER_EXECUTOR after the executor is invalidated
body:
`label(stop_tracing)` snapshots `opcode` before `stop_tracing_and_jit()` and then `DISPATCH_GOTO_NON_TRACING()` jumps to that saved opcode. The call can invalidate the executor that the sampled `ENTER_EXECUTOR` points at, restore the original instruction, and store `NULL` in its `co_executors` slot. The dispatch still calls `_PyJIT_Entry(NULL)`.

This is on 3.15.1, 3.15.2, and `main` (checked 2026-10-28). It needs `--with-tail-call-interp` and `--enable-experimental-jit`. The tail-call `DISPATCH_GOTO_NON_TRACING()` macro does not re-read the instruction; it tail-calls `instruction_funcptr_handler_table[opcode]`.

## What the crash looks like

`_PyJIT_Entry+0x20` is `call *jit_code(%r12)` with the executor pointer NULL. The tier-1 handler is `ENTER_EXECUTOR` with oparg 0. The code unit in memory has already been restored (in the crash below, `JUMP_BACKWARD` oparg 25) and `co_executors->executors[0]` is NULL.

The Python frame in the reliable crash is a normal generator expression, `JarStruct.__init__.<locals>.<genexpr>` in Firefox's `python/mozbuild/mozpack/mozjar.py`:

```python
self.size_fields = set(
  t for t in self.STRUCT.values() if t not in JarStruct.TYPE_MAPPING
)
```

That expression is valid. The same script completes with `PYTHON_JIT=0`.

## Why the instruction changes inside the call

`stop_tracing` is only reached from `ENTER_EXECUTOR` while `IS_JIT_TRACING()` is true and `_PyJit_EnterExecutorShouldStopTracing(og_opcode)` is false. That helper returns true only for `RESUME_CHECK_JIT`. Otherwise `next_instr` stays on the `ENTER_EXECUTOR` instruction and control goes to `stop_tracing` with oparg still the executor index.

`stop_tracing_and_jit()` calls `_PyOptimizer_Optimize()`. While optimizing, the tracer drops recorded values. One of those is a bound method whose `self` is an unclosed buffered file (`Py_XDECREF` on a uop operand with `HAS_RECORDS_VALUE_FLAG`). `meth_dealloc` drops the last reference to the file, the finalizer emits `ResourceWarning`, and `setup_context()` in `Python/_warnings.c` does `PyDict_SetItem(globals, "__warningregistry__", registry)` on the current frame's globals.

Those globals are watched. `globals_watcher_callback()` calls `_Py_Executors_InvalidateDependency()`. `executor_invalidate()` restores `_PyOpcode_Deopt[vm_data.opcode]` and `vm_data.oparg` into the code unit and stores NULL in the executor slot.

A hardware watchpoint on the genexpr's code unit, armed on entry to `_TAIL_CALL_stop_tracing` while the word was `ENTER_EXECUTOR`, caught exactly those writes before the segfault:

1. low 16 bits become the restored opcode
2. the word becomes `JUMP_BACKWARD` / oparg 25
3. `executors[0]` becomes NULL

The backtrace of the first write is `executor_invalidate` ← `_Py_Executors_InvalidateDependency` ← `globals_watcher_callback` ← `PyDict_SetItem` ← `do_warn` ← `PyErr_ResourceWarning` ← `fileio_dealloc_warn` ← buffered close/finalize ← `meth_dealloc` ← `_PyOptimizer_Optimize` ← `_TAIL_CALL_stop_tracing`.

`TRACE_RECORD`'s full path is not affected: it calls `stop_tracing_and_jit()` and then `DISPATCH()`, and `DISPATCH()` re-reads. The cold-exit path in `_COLD_EXIT` calls `_Py_ExecutorDetach()` and then `GOTO_TIER_ONE(target)`, which also re-reads. The stale snapshot is specific to `label(stop_tracing)`.

`insert_executor()` detaches and immediately stores the new executor, so a completed replace does not leave a NULL slot. The NULL slot here is a pure invalidation.

## Fix

Re-read after `stop_tracing_and_jit()` returns, before dispatching. Only the low byte of oparg lives in the code unit; `ENTER_EXECUTOR`'s own deopt already uses `(oparg & ~255) | executor->vm_data.oparg` for that reason.

```c
label(stop_tracing) {
#if _Py_TIER2
  assert(IS_JIT_TRACING());
  int opcode = next_instr->op.code;
  _PyJit_translate_single_bytecode_to_trace(tstate, frame, NULL, _EXIT_TRACE);
  LEAVE_TRACING();
  int err = stop_tracing_and_jit(tstate, frame);
  ERROR_IF(err < 0);
  /* stop_tracing_and_jit() can drop the last reference to a
  temporary and run a finalizer. A ResourceWarning then writes
  __warningregistry__ into a watched globals dict, and
  executor_invalidate() restores this instruction and clears its
  executor slot. Dispatching the ENTER_EXECUTOR opcode sampled
  above calls _PyJIT_Entry(NULL). Keep any EXTENDED_ARG bits
  already accumulated in oparg; only the low byte lives in the
  code unit. */
  opcode = next_instr->op.code;
  oparg = (oparg & ~255) | next_instr->op.arg;
  DISPATCH_GOTO_NON_TRACING();
#else
  Py_FatalError("JIT label executed in non-jit build.");
#endif
}
```

`Tools/cases_generator/tier1_generator.py` emits the two assignments into `Python/generated_cases.c.h` and drops the comment. Both files need to change. If the instruction is still `ENTER_EXECUTOR` (nothing invalidated it, or a new executor was inserted), the low byte is the executor index and the handler masks with `oparg & 255`.

A NULL check inside `ENTER_EXECUTOR` would only hide this. The handler should not be entered once the slot has been cleared.

## Reproducer

CPython 3.15.1 built with `--with-tail-call-interp --enable-experimental-jit --enable-optimizations` (clang, NDEBUG). `PYTHON_JIT` defaults to on. `-X jit=0` does not disable this build's JIT; `PYTHON_JIT=0` does.

The reliable trigger is Firefox 158 `toolkit/mozapps/installer/packager.py --minify` against a dist tree, which reaches the genexpr above after a few missing-manifest warnings. With the JIT on, the process dies in `_PyJIT_Entry` during that genexpr. Tight loops, `set(genexpr)` repeated tens of thousands of times, and a standalone `JarWriter` did not hit the window: the finalizer has to run inside `_PyOptimizer_Optimize` while the sampled instruction is an `ENTER_EXECUTOR` whose executor depends on the frame's globals.

A 3.15.2 interpreter with the re-read above, built with the tail-call interpreter and the experimental JIT, runs that same packager to completion, including under `PYTHON_JIT_STRESS=1`. The unpatched system interpreter still segfaults on the same script.

## Versions

- 3.15.1 and 3.15.2: the `stop_tracing` label is identical, and the 3.15.2 tarball has no JIT change that avoids this
- `main` at 2026-10-28: the same label, still without the re-read
- Linux x86_64

```python
# the crashing frame, not a reduced repro
self.size_fields = set(
  t for t in self.STRUCT.values() if t not in JarStruct.TYPE_MAPPING
)
```

title: Pure-Python datetime.fromisoformat() accepts a trailing date-time separator
body:
### Bug report

Title: Pure-Python `datetime.fromisoformat()` accepts a trailing date-time separator

# Bug report

### Bug description:

The pure-Python `datetime.fromisoformat()` (`Lib/_pydatetime.py`) accepts a string that ends with the date-time separator and has no time after it, and returns midnight. The C implementation raises `ValueError`:

```python
>>> import datetime, _pydatetime
>>> datetime.datetime.fromisoformat('2009-04-19T')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Invalid isoformat string: '2009-04-19T'
>>> _pydatetime.datetime.fromisoformat('2009-04-19T')
datetime.datetime(2009, 4, 19, 0, 0)
>>> _pydatetime.datetime.fromisoformat('2009-04-19 ')
datetime.datetime(2009, 4, 19, 0, 0)
```

The same happens with basic and week dates (`'20090419T'`, `'2009-W16-7T'`).

`fromisoformat()` splits the string at the separator and then only parses the time part `if tstr:`, so an empty time part makes it fall back to the date-only path. The C version (`datetime_fromisoformat()`) only takes the date-only path when nothing follows the date (`len > separator_location`) and otherwise passes the empty time to the time parser, which rejects it.

This matters for PyPy and other implementations that use `_pydatetime`.

title: zipfile reads only the first frame of a multi-frame Zstandard member
body:
# Bug report

### Bug description:

`zipfile` decodes a Zstandard (method 93) member with a single `compression.zstd.ZstdDecompressor`, and `ZipExtFile._read1()` treats the decompressor's `eof` as the end of the member. A zstd stream may consist of several concatenated frames ([RFC 8878, section 3.1](<url>)), and multi-threaded or streaming compressors (`zstd -T0`, `pzstd`, any writer that flushes frames) produce exactly that. For such a member `zipfile` returns only the first frame's output, and the CRC check then raises `BadZipFile`. `zstd.decompress()` and `ZstdFile` both handle the same bytes correctly.

```python
import io
import struct
import zipfile
import zlib
from compression import zstd

part1 = b"first frame " * 1000
part2 = b"second frame " * 1000
payload = part1 + part2
member_data = zstd.compress(part1) + zstd.compress(part2)  # two frames
assert zstd.decompress(member_data) == payload

# Store the two-frame stream, then relabel the member as method 93 with the
# CRC and size of the decompressed payload.
buf = io.BytesIO()
with zipfile.ZipFile(buf, "w") as zf:
  zf.writestr(zipfile.ZipInfo("data.bin"), member_data)  # ZIP_STORED
raw = bytearray(buf.getvalue())
crc = zlib.crc32(payload)
cd = raw.rindex(b"PK\x01\x02")
for method, crc_off, size_off in ((8, 14, 22), (cd + 10, cd + 16, cd + 24)):
  struct.pack_into("<H", raw, method, zipfile.ZIP_ZSTANDARD)
  struct.pack_into("<L", raw, crc_off, crc)
  struct.pack_into("<L", raw, size_off, len(payload))

with zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(bytes(raw))) as zf:
  print(zf.testzip())  # 'data.bin'
  zf.read("data.bin")  # zipfile.BadZipFile: Bad CRC-32 for file 'data.bin'
```

Output on 3.14.4, 3.15.0a8 and main (19270d3):

```
data.bin
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
zipfile.BadZipFile: Bad CRC-32 for file 'data.bin'
```

We hit this with real archives whose members were written by a multi-threaded zstd encoder, and currently decode method-93 members with our own frame loop instead of `zipfile`.

**Proposed fix:** in `ZipExtFile._read1()`, when the zstd decompressor reaches the end of a frame and the member still has compressed input (`unused_data`, or `_compress_left > 0`), continue with a new `ZstdDecompressor`. Bytes that do not parse as a frame then raise `ZstdError`, and a truncated last frame still fails the CRC check. I have a PR with tests ready.

One question for maintainers: once the declared `file_size` has been produced, `_read1()` stops reading, so bytes after the last frame inside the member's `compress_size` are never examined. That matches how the other methods behave today (a deflate stream followed by junk is also accepted), so the PR keeps it. Should trailing data inside the member be an error for zstd, or for all methods? Happy to follow up either way.

_Disclosure: this issue was drafted by Claude (Anthropic's AI assistant, via Claude Code) on behalf of @HipHoff, who approved filing it and takes responsibility for it. The repro above was run on CPython 3.14.4, 3.15.0a8 and a local debug build of main._

title: _sre: out-of-bounds read in the SRE code validator for IN opcode with skip < 2
body:
### Crash report

`_sre.compile()` validates the raw code list it gets. For the `IN` opcode, the validator reads out of bounds when the `skip` operand is `0` or `1`.

Found with a fuzzer.

```python
import _sre
_sre.compile("x", 0, [13, 0, 1], 0, {}, ())
```

The code list is `[SRE_OP_IN, skip=0, SRE_OP_SUCCESS]` (`13` is `SRE_OP_IN`, `1` is `SRE_OP_SUCCESS`).

```
==19==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x50d400012c80 (pc 0x555b6ecddef2 bp 0x7fff9102de70 sp 0x7fff9102de10 T0)
==19==The signal is caused by a READ memory access.
  #0 in _validate_inner Modules/_sre/sre.c:2218:30
  #1 in _validate_outer Modules/_sre/sre.c:2461:12
  #2 in _validate Modules/_sre/sre.c:2467:9
  #3 in _sre_compile_impl Modules/_sre/sre.c:1849:10
  #4 in _sre_compile Modules/_sre/clinic/sre.c.h:1147:20
  ...

SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV Modules/_sre/sre.c:2218:30 in _validate_inner
==19==ABORTING
```

The crash is the `code[skip-2]` read in the `SRE_OP_IN` branch of `_validate_inner()`. The code is:

<url>

```c
GET_SKIP;
/* Stop 1 before the end; we check the FAILURE below */
if (_validate_charset(code, code+skip-2))
  FAIL;
if (code[skip-2] != SRE_OP_FAILURE)
  FAIL;
code += skip-1;
```

`GET_SKIP` checks only that `skip` is not too big (not past the end of the code). It does not check that `skip` is too small. When `skip` is 0 or 1, `skip - 2` is a wrong index, so `code[skip-2]` reads out of bounds.

I did not find a way to reproduce this with the public `re` module. It looks like its compiler always emits `skip >= 2` for `IN`.

A possible fix is to reject `skip < 2` right after `GET_SKIP`:

```c
GET_SKIP;
if (skip < 2)
  FAIL;
```

title: io.TextIOWrapper.tell() can read past its snapshot buffer after seek() past a carriage return
body:
### Bug report

`io.TextIOWrapper.tell()` can compute a skip larger than its snapshot buffer after `seek()` to a position that follows a carriage return. with universal newlines the decoder keeps a pending `\r`, so the seek cookie has `chars_to_skip > 0`; `seek()` replays the input chunk into a new snapshot but leaves the bytes-per-char ratio from the previous `read()`. `tell()` then multiplies that stale ratio by `chars_to_skip`. on a debug build the assertion in `_io_TextIOWrapper_tell_impl` fires:

```python
import io

f = io.TextIOWrapper(io.BytesIO(b"one\rtwo\rthree\r"), encoding="utf-8")
f.read(4)
pos = f.tell()
f.read(1)
f.seek(pos)
f.read(1)
print(f.tell())
```

```
Assertion failed: (skip_bytes <= PyBytes_GET_SIZE(next_input)), function _io_TextIOWrapper_tell_impl, file textio.c, line 2987.
```

release builds do not assert. the oversized length is handed to the decoder, which reads past the bytes object, so `tell()` can fail on valid input. on 3.13.13 and 3.14.7:

```python
import io

data = ('ab\r' + '\u20ac' * 15).encode()
f = io.TextIOWrapper(io.BytesIO(data), encoding='utf-8')
f.read(3)
pos = f.tell()
f.read(1)
f.seek(pos)
f.read(1)
f.tell()
```

```
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x82 in position 4: invalid start byte
```

`_pyio.TextIOWrapper` fails the same assertion, and under `python -O` it returns a position one character too far: after the seek it reads `'o\nthree\n'` where `'wo\nthree\n'` is expected.

setting the ratio from the replayed chunk in `seek()`, as `_read_chunk()` does, fixes both implementations.

title: symtable: repr() of a Symbol raises TypeError under -X lazy_imports=all
body:
# Bug report

### Bug description:

With `-X lazy_imports=all`, `repr()` of a `symtable.Symbol` raises `TypeError`:

```python
import symtable
top = symtable.symtable('x = 1', '<string>', 'exec')
print(top.get_symbols())
```

```
$ ./python -X lazy_imports=all repro.py
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "repro.py", line 3, in <module>
  print(top.get_symbols())
  ~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "Lib/symtable.py", line 264, in __repr__
  flags_str = '|'.join(self._flags_str())
  File "Lib/symtable.py", line 272, in _flags_str
  if self.__flags & flagvalue == flagvalue:
  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for &: 'int' and 'lazy_import'
```

Without the option it prints `[<symbol 'x': LOCAL, DEF_LOCAL>]`.

`Lib/symtable.py` builds its `_flags` and `_scopes_value_to_name` tables from `globals()`: <url>

With `lazy_imports=all`, the `from _symtable import ...` at the top of the module is lazy, so `globals()` holds `lazy_import` objects instead of the integer constants. `_flags` breaks `repr()` as above, and once that is fixed, `_scopes_value_to_name` still makes the scope print as `1` instead of `LOCAL`.

This is the `test_symtable` failure mentioned in gh-149640, and why `test_symtable` is in `Lib/test/lazy_imports_all_exclude.txt`. The 3.15 branch has the same code.

Possible fix: take the values from the `_symtable` module (for example `getattr(_symtable, name)`) instead of from `globals()`. With that, `test_symtable` passes with and without `-X lazy_imports=all` and can come off the exclusion list. I can open a PR if this sounds right.

title: Pure-Python `timedelta` loses precision with large float arguments
body:
# Bug report

### Bug description:

The pure-Python `timedelta` (`Lib/_pydatetime.py`) gives a different result than the C one when a large float is passed for `weeks`, `hours`, `minutes` or `milliseconds`:

```python
>>> import datetime, _pydatetime
>>> datetime.timedelta(weeks=12345678.9)
datetime.timedelta(days=86419752, seconds=25920, microseconds=225)
>>> _pydatetime.timedelta(weeks=12345678.9)
datetime.timedelta(days=86419752, seconds=25919, microseconds=999743)
```

The C result is the correct one: the float is exactly 12345678.90000000037252902984619140625 weeks, which is 86419752 days, 7:12:00.000225 after rounding. Smaller values are affected too, for example `timedelta(weeks=100000.1)` is off by 2 µs and `timedelta(hours=10000000.1)` by 1 µs.

`_pydatetime` first adds the arguments together with float arithmetic (`days += weeks*7`, `seconds += minutes*60 + hours*3600`, `microseconds += milliseconds*1000`), so the sub-second part is already rounded away before it gets split off. The C version (`accum()` in `_datetimemodule.c`) converts the integer part of each argument exactly and only sums the leftover fractional microseconds as a float. That is also what the docs describe ("the fractional microseconds left over from all arguments are combined and their sum is rounded...").

I found this by comparing the two implementations on random inputs. With arguments up to about 1e7, around 1 in 5 results were different, by up to ~2.5 ms.

I'd like to send a PR that makes `_pydatetime` use the same approach as the C code.

title: compile: double free of pc->fail_pop in codegen_pattern_or on allocation failure with nested or-pattern
body:
When an allocation fails while compiling a match statement whose or-pattern contains another or-pattern, `codegen_pattern_or` frees `pc->fail_pop` and `codegen_match` then frees it again, so `compile()` crashes instead of raising `MemoryError`.

The failure is injected with the test-only `_testcapi.call_with_nomemory`:

```python
import ast, _testcapi
tree = ast.parse('def f(x):\n match x:\n  case [1|2] | 3: pass\n')
for off in range(1500):
  held = None
  held = [[] for _ in range(128)]  # refill/empty the list freelist so PyList_New in codegen really allocates
  try:
  _testcapi.call_with_nomemory(off, off + 1, compile, tree, 'a.py', 'exec')
  except (MemoryError, SyntaxError):
  pass
print('survived')
```

Saved as `input.py` and run on an ASan build that includes `_testcapi`:

```
python input.py
```

Output:

```
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x503000002988
READ of size 1 at 0x503000002988 thread T0
  #0 in _PyMem_DebugCheckAddress Objects/obmalloc.c:3351
  #4 in PyMem_Free Objects/obmalloc.c:1292
  #5 in codegen_match Python/codegen.c:6775
...
freed by thread T0 here:
  #5 in PyMem_Free Objects/obmalloc.c:1292
  #6 in codegen_pattern_or Python/codegen.c:6573
```

Every injected failure should surface as `MemoryError` from `compile()`, with the pointer freed once, and the script should print `survived`.

Found at commit 3646ea571f3d8290806a3029d555b179f8be1539. It still reproduces at 3acc941f2b72 (latest upstream checked): ASan heap-use-after-free in the checking build, and the release build segfaults (exit code 139). `case (1|2) | 3`, where the inner or-pattern is not inside a sequence pattern, survives.

Looks like in the inner `codegen_pattern_or`, `old_pc = *pc` copies the outer `fail_pop` array, and if the first `PyList_New(0)` in the loop fails, `goto error` runs before `pc->fail_pop = NULL`. The error block then frees `old_pc.fail_pop` while `pc->fail_pop` still points to it, and `codegen_match` frees it again.

Found with an LLM-based testing tool; I used Claude to reduce it and look for the cause.

title: codeobject: == on code objects takes exponential time in scope nesting depth (30 nested classes still running after 120 s)
body:
Comparing two equal code objects with `==` takes time that doubles with each level of nested class or def scope, so a 30-deep nest is still running after 2 minutes.

```python
import ast
depth = 30
source = ''.join(' ' * d + 'class C%d:\n' % d for d in range(depth)) + ' ' * depth + 'pass\n'
tree = ast.parse(source)
a = compile(tree, 'f.py', 'exec'); b = compile(tree, 'f.py', 'exec')
print(a == b)
```

Saved as `input.py` and run with `python input.py`, it printed nothing within 120 s and was killed by `timeout` (exit 124). With smaller `depth`, `a == b` on a release build took about 0.3 s at depth 16, 3.6 s at 20 and 14 s at 22 (the host was heavily loaded, so only the factor of about 2 per level matters).

It should print `True` promptly, since the two code objects come from the same tree and are equal, with time roughly linear in the nesting depth.

Found at commit 3646ea571f3d8290806a3029d555b179f8be1539; it still reproduces at 3acc941f2b72 (latest upstream, release build: killed at the timeout). Both the checking build (ASan/UBSan) and the release build hang the same way, with no assertion or sanitizer report. Nested `def`s and annotated class bodies show the same growth.

Looks like `code_richcompare` in Objects/codeobject.c compares `_PyCode_ConstantKey(co_consts)`. For a tuple the key is the pair `(tuple_of_item_keys, original_tuple)`, so comparing two keys recurses into each nested code object twice (once through the item keys, once through the original tuple), which doubles the work per level.

Related: #101346 ("The hash and equals methods of code objects are large, complex and unnecessary").

The deep nesting comes from a generated test, not from a real program.

Found with an LLM-based testing tool; I used Claude to reduce it and look for the cause.

title: `subprocess.run()` can warn that a child is still running after killing it on Ctrl-C
body:
### Bug report

Run this on Linux or MacOS and press Ctrl-C while `sleep` is running. `start_new_session=True` keeps the child from receiving the terminal's SIGINT.

```sh
python3 -Wd -c 'import subprocess; subprocess.run(["sleep", "60"], start_new_session=True)'
```

After the expected `KeyboardInterrupt` traceback, Python prints an additional warning.

```text
ResourceWarning: subprocess 9 is still running
```

I would expect `run()` to take care of reaping the child it killed. The caller never gets a `Popen` object to wait on. In a separate run I used `os.waitid()` with `WNOWAIT` inside the `KeyboardInterrupt` handler and confirmed that the child had already died from SIGKILL before the warning was emitted.

It looks like `Popen.wait()` uses its 250 ms grace period after SIGINT. When that expires, `run()` calls `kill()` and reraises, relying on `Popen.__exit__()` to wait. But the `KeyboardInterrupt` branch in `__exit__()` skips the wait once the grace period has been used. Then `__del__()` sees `returncode is None` and warns before polling. [`run()` exception handler](<url>) · [`Popen` cleanup](<url>) · [Original rationale for the grace period](<url>)

Reproduced on Linux with CPython 3.14.8, 3.15.0, and a 3.16 development build, and on MacOS with 3.12 and a 3.16 dev build.

title: gh-71986: Fix the base64 and bz2 codec incremental decoders
body:
The `base64_codec` incremental decoder decoded every chunk on its own, so splitting the input inside a group of four base64 characters failed:

```pycon
>>> b"".join(codecs.iterdecode([b"AA", b"AA\r\n"], "base64"))
binascii.Error: Incorrect padding
```

It now subclasses `codecs.BufferedIncrementalDecoder` and decodes only complete groups of four alphabet characters, keeping the rest until the next call (or `final=True`). Bytes outside the alphabet (newlines, `=`) are not counted, since `binascii.a2b_base64()` ignores them in non-strict mode, so the joined output matches decoding the whole input at once.

The `bz2_codec` incremental decoder returned `''` (a `str`) when called after the end of the compressed data; it now returns `b''`.

Martin Panter attached a patch to the original bpo issue in 2016. This is a new implementation against current main: that patch counted `=` as a data character, which no longer matches `a2b_base64()` (`b"AA=AA="` decodes, but its first four characters `b"AA=A"` don't).

I used Claude Code to write this change.

title: gh-83055: Reserve freed asyncio.Queue slots for woken putters
body:
When the queue is full, `get_nowait()` pops a waiting putter and wakes it, but the freed slot stays open until that putter resumes. A later `put()` (fast path) or `put_nowait()` can take it; the woken putter then finds the queue full and is re-appended to the *end* of `_putters`, so items are put out of order and a waiter can be starved.

This PR reserves the freed slot for the woken putter:

* `get_nowait()` increments `_reserved` when it wakes a putter; `full()` counts reserved slots (`qsize() + _reserved >= maxsize`).
* The woken putter releases its reservation right before `put_nowait()`; if it is cancelled after being woken it passes the reservation to the next putter.
* `shutdown()` clears the counter.

This is the same idea `asyncio.Semaphore` uses for fairness (taking the value on the waiter's behalf). Compared to the earlier attempt (gh-112501):

* no new exceptions; `full() is False` still guarantees `put_nowait()` succeeds;
* O(1), no scanning of done futures;
* unreserved free slots remain usable, so Serhiy's example (two `get_nowait()` with one waiting putter, then `put_nowait()`) succeeds.

Behaviour change: `full()` may be `True` while `qsize() < maxsize`, for as long as a woken putter has not resumed. Documented in `full()`/`put()`.

Getters are left as is: the issue is about the order items enter the queue, and reserving items would change the meaning of `empty()`.

title: gh-160964: Keep asyncio SSL transport usable after close on lost connection
body:
Closing an SSL transport that is already marked closed, for example from the protocol's `connection_lost()`, used to detach it from its `SSLProtocol` by setting `_ssl_protocol = None` (added in gh-98539). After that, `write()`, `set_protocol()`, `get_write_buffer_size()` and `get_extra_info()` raised `AttributeError`. The `loop.sendfile()` fallback hits this in `restore()` when the peer disconnects mid-transfer.

The transport now keeps its protocol. Instead, `SSLProtocol._release_ssl()` drops the SSL object, the context and their `ssl_object`/`sslcontext` extra info, which is what the detaching was meant to achieve. If the TLS shutdown is still in progress (for example when the peer started it, so the app's first `close()` already lands in that branch), the release waits until `connection_lost()`.

A single `close()` behaves as before, so the app can still read `get_extra_info('ssl_object')` in its `connection_lost()`.

Tests: two new unit tests in `test_sslproto`; both fail on `main`. The existing `test_ssl.test_create_connection_memory_leak` still passes, and `test_asyncio` and `test_ssl` pass on Linux.

title: gh-137549: Handle BaseExceptionGroup in asyncio.Timeout.__aexit__
