title: gh-160948: Fix annotationlib.ForwardRef.evaluate() ignoring explicit globals/locals for closure-cell references
body:
## Summary

`ForwardRef.evaluate()` had an early return for references holding a
single closure cell (`__cell__` is a `CellType`) that ran before any
namespace handling. As a result, explicitly passed `globals`/`locals`
were silently ignored for such references, while every other path in
the same method (plain references, dict-of-cells references) gives
explicit namespaces precedence over the captured scope.

## Fix

In `Lib/annotationlib.py` (`ForwardRef.evaluate`):

- The single-cell shortcut now only applies when neither `globals`
  nor `locals` was passed, preserving the existing fast path and
  behaviour for the common no-argument call.
- In the plain-identifier resolution branch, the cell value is
  consulted after `locals` and `globals` (and before `builtins`,
  matching normal scope order), so it acts as a fallback when an
  explicitly passed namespace does not provide the name. An empty
  cell (`ValueError`) falls through exactly as before.

No other paths are changed: the dict-of-cells and `__extra_names__`
handling, type-parameter injection, and the non-identifier `eval`
path are untouched.

## Tests

Two regression tests in `Lib/test/test_annotationlib.py`
(`TestForwardRefClass`):

- `test_evaluate_cell_with_explicit_namespaces` — explicit `locals`
  and `globals` win over the cell (locals over globals when both are
  given, in both VALUE and FORWARDREF formats); the cell remains the
  fallback when the name is absent from the explicit namespaces.
- `test_evaluate_empty_cell_with_explicit_namespaces` — an emptied
  cell still raises `NameError` with no arguments, explicit namespaces
  are consulted, and a refilled cell resumes its fallback role without
  overriding explicit namespaces.

Both tests fail on the unmodified code and pass with this change.

Results (local build of main @ 83fe630):

- `test_annotationlib`: 123 tests run — SUCCESS (121 pre-existing +
  2 new).
- `test_typing`: SUCCESS.
- `test_inspect`: 1 failure in
  `test_details_option_with_package`, which also fails on the
  unmodified tree in this environment (it compares `inspect` CLI
  output containing stdlib file paths); unrelated to this change.

Fixes gh-160948.

*Disclosure: this change was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author, who takes responsibility for it.*

title: gh-160949: Fix concurrent.interpreters Queue truncating fractional timeouts
body:
### Summary

`Queue.put()` and `Queue.get()` in
`Lib/concurrent/interpreters/_queues.py` converted the timeout with
`int(timeout)` before computing the polling deadline. That truncated
fractional timeouts (`0.5` behaved as `0`, `1.9` as `1`) and defeated the
negative check (`-0.5` became `0`, so `QueueEmpty`/`QueueFull` was raised
instead of `ValueError`), contradicting the documented
"blocks at most *timeout* seconds" semantics shared with `queue.Queue`.

### Fix

Drop the `int()` conversion in both methods so the deadline
(`time.monotonic() + timeout`) uses the timeout as given, and check
`timeout < 0` on the original value. The error message now matches
`queue.Queue` ("'timeout' must be a non-negative number"; the old message
was also an f-string with no placeholder). The polling architecture
(10 ms `_delay` loop against an absolute monotonic deadline) is
unchanged. This also makes `timeout='1'` raise `TypeError` from the
comparison, exactly like `queue.Queue`.

One deliberate judgement call: `timeout=float('inf')` previously raised
`OverflowError` from `int()`; it now simply never reaches its deadline
(equivalent to blocking indefinitely). `float('nan')` behaves the same
way. Neither matches `queue.Queue` exactly (it raises incidentally from
`threading` internals), but no documented contract covers non-finite
timeouts; happy to add explicit validation if maintainers prefer.

### Tests

New tests in `Lib/test/test_interpreters/test_queues.py`
(`TestQueueOps`):

- `test_get_timeout_fractional` / `test_put_timeout_fractional` — a 0.5s
  timeout on an empty/full queue blocks for 0.4–2s (bounds chosen to
  fail on the truncated behaviour, ~0.0s, while staying CI-safe).
- `test_timeout_negative` — `timeout=-0.5` raises `ValueError` for both
  `get()` and `put()`.
- `test_timeout_zero` — `timeout=0` stays a non-blocking poll.

The fractional/negative tests fail on unpatched main and pass with the
fix. Full results with the fix:

- `test_interpreters.test_queues`: 34 tests, OK
- `test_interpreters test__interpreters`: 251 run, 11 skipped, SUCCESS

Fixes gh-160949.

*Disclosure: this change was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author, who takes responsibility for it.*

title: gh-160945: Fix _pydecimal losing companion signal flags when a signal is trapped
body:
`_pydecimal` lost the flags of companion conditions when an operation
signalled several conditions and one of them was trapped:
`Context._raise_error()` set one signal's flag and raised at once, so
the calls signalling the remaining conditions never ran. `_decimal`
records all conditions in the context status before raising. The
exception raised is unchanged; only the flags are now complete.

`Context._defer_traps()` defers a trapped exception raised inside the
block until the block exits; `_raise_error` still sets every flag and
returns the default response. The sequential multi-signal sequences in
`Decimal._fix`, `__divmod__`, `__pow__`, `quantize`,
`to_integral_exact` and `next_toward` are wrapped in it.

Tests: new `ContextFlags.test_trapped_signal_sets_companion_flags`,
covering trapped Overflow, Inexact, Underflow, Subnormal and
DivisionByZero. It runs against both implementations, fails on
`_pydecimal` without this change, and `test_decimal` passes (596
tests).

Differential fuzzing against `_decimal` (5,793 seeded cases) matched
results, exceptions and flags everywhere except 6 cases of a separate
pre-existing difference: with `clamp=1` and a zero quotient,
`__divmod__` does not finalise the quotient in `_pydecimal`, so
`Clamped` is not signalled. Not addressed here.

title: gh-87613: AC VC add support for *args and use it for zip
body:
Argument Clinic `@vectorcall` generation accepted `*args` parameters but the generated code expected an argument tuple. The first commit uses the fastcall form to parse the args array making it work right.

`zip` previously hand coded argument parsing and had no vectorcall. Argument error messages are unchanged except for unknown keywords: `zip(strict=1, x=2)` now reports "got an unexpected keyword argument 'x'" instead of "takes at most 1 keyword argument (2 given)".  The docstring gains a summary line; `__text_signature__` is unchanged.

pyperf microbenchmark (PGO+LTO, run serially):

| Benchmark  | base  | zip  |
|------------------------|:-------:|:---------------------:|
| zip(a, b, strict=True) | 118 ns  | 61.5 ns: 1.92x faster |
| zip(a, b)  | 64.9 ns | 53.1 ns: 1.22x faster |
| zip(a)  | 55.0 ns | 47.1 ns: 1.17x faster |
| list(zip(a, b))  | 123 ns  | 113 ns: 1.09x faster  |
| zip()  | 27.4 ns | 25.7 ns: 1.07x faster |
| Sub(a, b)  | 71.5 ns | 70.6 ns: 1.01x faster |

Benchmark hidden because not significant (1): `zip.__new__`

Benchmark code:

```python
import pyperf

runner = pyperf.Runner()
setup = "a = (1, 2, 3); b = [4, 5, 6]"
for stmt in ["zip()", "zip(a)", "zip(a, b)", "zip(a, b, strict=True)",
  "list(zip(a, b))"]:
  runner.timeit(stmt, stmt, setup)
runner.timeit('zip.`__new__`', 'new(zip, a, b)', setup + '; new = zip.__new__')
runner.timeit('Sub(a, b)', 'S(a, b)', setup + '\nclass S(zip): pass')
```

title: gh-160787: Reap the killed child in subprocess.run() on KeyboardInterrupt
body:
I found that subprocess.run() had a cleanup issue when Ctrl-C (KeyboardInterrupt) occurred. The child process was correctly killed, but it was not being reaped. run() relied on Popen.__exit__() for cleanup, but __exit__() intentionally skips waiting for the child during KeyboardInterrupt. As a result, Python could emit a misleading ResourceWarning saying the subprocess was still running even though it had already been terminated.

To fix this, I updated Lib/subprocess.py so that run() explicitly reaps the child process immediately after killing it. I used a bounded wait of up to 1 second to ensure the cleanup happens without violating CPython's requirement that Ctrl-C handling must not block indefinitely.

I also added a regression test, test_run_keyboardinterrupt_reaps_killed_child, in Lib/test/test_subprocess.py. The test simulates a KeyboardInterrupt during subprocess.run() and verifies that the child process has been collected by checking that it receives an exit status. The test fails before the fix and passes afterward.

Finally, I added a NEWS entry documenting the bug fix, while leaving the existing Ctrl-C tests unchanged to ensure no existing behavior was affected.

### AI assistance

> I used Claude Code (an AI assistant) to investigate and draft this change; I reviewed it and can explain it.
>
> **Root cause.** On an exception, `run()` kills the child and relies on `Popen.__exit__()` to wait. After a `KeyboardInterrupt`, `__exit__()` skips the wait once the SIGINT grace period was used (`_sigint_wait_secs == 0`), so the killed child is never reaped and `__del__()` warns before it polls.
>
> **Fix.** `run()` reaps the killed child with `process._wait(timeout=1)`. A plain `process.wait()` would block indefinitely and break the bpo-25942 guarantee that `test_run_keyboardinterrupt_no_kill` checks ("no open-ended wait() after the first"). `_wait()` is used rather than `wait()` because `wait()` adds its own SIGINT grace period, which no longer applies to a child that was just killed. `__exit__()` uses `_wait()` the same way.
>
> **Tests.** New `test_run_keyboardinterrupt_reaps_killed_child`: it fails without the change ("unexpectedly None") and passes with it. The existing `*keyboardinterrupt*` tests pass unchanged. A real-signal repro (timer sends SIGINT to the parent, `start_new_session=True` child) emitted the ResourceWarning 3/3 times before the fix and 0/5 after.
>
> ```
> ./python -m test test_subprocess -m "*keyboardinterrupt*"  # 4 tests OK
> ./python -m test test_subprocess -j4  # 372 run, OK
> make patchcheck  # NEWS entry present, clean
> ```
>
> Tested on Linux (WSL2), CPython main at ef1fce0a69 (3.16.0a1+).

title: gh-89290: Add notes to the exception for an unmarshallable object
body:
Add notes to the `ValueError` raised by `marshal.dumps()` for an unsupported object.

The notes follow pickle's convention: one note per enclosing level, innermost first, with the same wording for container items, dict values and set elements.

3 differences with pickle: 
- a failing dict key gets a note, pickle leaves it unannotated;
- a failing slice field is named directly (start, stop, step), pickle reports a tuple index inside the reconstructor arguments;
- code object fields are identified by name, qualified name, file and line, pickle rejects code objects.

current:
```pycon
>>> import marshal
>>> class MyStr(str): pass
... marshal.dumps(compile("def f(): pass", MyStr("foo.py"), "exec"))
... 
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-1>", line 2, in <module>
  marshal.dumps(compile("def f(): pass", MyStr("foo.py"), "exec"))
  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
ValueError: cannot marshal MyStr objects
```

with notes:
```pycon
>>> import marshal
>>> class MyStr(str): pass
... 
>>> marshal.dumps(compile("def f(): pass", MyStr("foo.py"), "exec"))
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-2>", line 1, in <module>
  marshal.dumps(compile("def f(): pass", MyStr("foo.py"), "exec"))
  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
ValueError: cannot marshal MyStr objects
when marshalling co_filename of code object f (foo.py, line 1)
when marshalling tuple item 0
when marshalling co_consts of code object <module> (foo.py, line 1)
```

New tests cover every container type, slice field and code object field.

title: gh-160936: Make logging setLevel() and disable() cost O(cached loggers)
body:
`Logger.setLevel()` and `logging.disable()` call `Manager._clear_cache()`, which walks every logger in `loggerDict` to clear its `isEnabledFor` cache, whether or not it has cached anything. Setting levels on N loggers one at a time is O(N^2):

```
  before  after
1000 loggers  0.392 s  0.007 s
2000 loggers  1.562 s  0.014 s
4000 loggers  6.255 s  0.028 s
8000 loggers  24.787 s  0.057 s
```

(debug build of main, script from the issue)

The manager now keeps a `WeakSet` of loggers that have populated their cache. `isEnabledFor` adds itself on the cache-miss path, inside the lock it already takes, so the hot cache-hit path is untouched. `_clear_cache` only visits those loggers, and still only clears ones that are registered in `loggerDict` under their name, same rule as before.

`test_logging` passes; the existing `test_caching` covers the invalidation behaviour.

title: gh-160931: Speed up bytes construction from exact bytes and int
body:
Since 3.11 added `bytes.__bytes__`, bytes(b) for an exact bytes binds and calls that method only to get b back.  Return an exact bytes argument directly, like PyObject_Bytes() and PyBytes_FromObject() do, and skip the lookup, which always misses, for an exact int.

How bytes(x) resolves is unchanged: both types are immutable, so the skipped lookup and call could only ever produce the same result, and subclasses, including bool, still look up `__bytes__` first.  These cases just get there faster.

Could inline the PyLong as another `if` but that makes a bigger diff and the runtime is very close to just adding the `!PyLong_CheckExact` case.

pyperf, PGO+LTO, interleaved A/B on 19270d3bbb5 (A/A spread <= 1.05x):

| Benchmark  | main  | patch  |
|-------------------|:-------:|:---------------------:|
| bytes(b)  | 28.5 ns | 12.8 ns: 2.22x faster |
| Sub(b)  | 51.7 ns | 36.0 ns: 1.44x faster |
| bytes(16)  | 23.5 ns | 21.0 ns: 1.12x faster |
| bytes(hb)  | 38.7 ns | 38.0 ns: 1.02x faster |
| bytes(s, 'ascii') | 26.5 ns | 27.1 ns: 1.02x slower |
| bytes()  | 10.7 ns | 11.1 ns: 1.03x slower |

Not significant: bytes(ba), bytes(l), bytes(mv).  The small slowdowns (1.02-1.03x) are within the noise on my machine.

  import pyperf

  runner = pyperf.Runner()
  for stmt in ["bytes(b)", "bytes(16)", "bytes(ba)", "bytes(mv)", "bytes(l)",
  "bytes(s, 'ascii')", "bytes(hb)", "Sub(b)", "bytes()"]:
  runner.timeit(stmt, stmt,
  "b = b'abcdefghijklmnop'; ba = bytearray(b); mv = memoryview(b); "
  "l = list(range(16)); s = 'abcdefghijklmnop'\n"
  "class Sub(bytes): pass\n"
  "class HB:\n  def __bytes__(self): return b\n"
  "hb = HB()")

title: gh-71448: Support extension in BytesIO.truncate
body:
`BytesIO.truncate()` past the end now zero-fills, as `IOBase.truncate()` documents. A buffer shared with the caller (initial bytes, `getvalue()`) is unshared first, so the caller's bytes are never written.

To support this, `resize_buffer_lock_held()` is split into `realloc_buffer_lock_held()` (exact size) and `prepare_write_lock_held()` (private, overallocated).

`_pyio.StringIO` also extends now, via `_pyio.BytesIO`; the C `StringIO` does not. `_pyio.StringIO` and `_io.StringIO` already differ in truncate units (code points vs UTF-8 bytes). For now leaving that gap.

title: gh-160929: Preserve ChainMap lookup values in reverse unions
body:
## Why

`dict | ChainMap` can replace a value exposed by the right-hand mapping with a deeper map's stored value. For example, `ChainMap(Counter(), {'x': 5})['x']` is `0`, but its reverse union returned `5`.

## What changed

- Update the result from the `ChainMap` view so its lookup semantics determine the values.
- Cover `Counter` and `defaultdict`, including collisions, key order, and the original maps' state.
- Add a NEWS entry.

## Scope

The change is limited to reverse union and its regression tests.

## Tradeoffs

The union now performs per-key chain lookups, as `dict(chain)` does. Long disjoint chains can require quadratic lookup work. Default factories can run and insert missing keys, as they do when reading the same `ChainMap` directly.

## Verification

- Built native CPython 3.16.0a1+dev on Ubuntu 24.04. Both regression tests fail against the original module and pass with the fix; the minimal reproduction changes from the wrong `5` to the expected `0`.
- Ran `test_collections test_userdict test_userlist test_userstring test_numeric_tower` with ten hash seeds. Each pass reports 286 tests, 284 passes, two skips, and zero failures or errors. Both new tests are present and pass in every run. [Native validation and results](<url>).
- Repository lint, `make patchcheck`, and `git diff --check` pass. [Lint result](<url>). [Contribution checklist result](<url>).

## Illustrated explanation

The first `Counter()` layer returns `0` for the missing key. The old reverse union copied the deeper stored `5`; the fix preserves the value returned by the `ChainMap` view.

![Illustrated ChainMap reverse union: the empty Counter returns zero for missing x; the old merge copies five from a deeper layer, while the corrected union reads through the view and preserves zero.](<url>)

[Accessible text explanation and validation notes](<url>). The illustration is supplemental; it is hosted outside this source patch.

Fixes #160929.

AI tools assisted the investigation, patch, tests, and supplemental illustration. I have personally reviewed the AI-assisted material in this PR.

title: gh-160561: Fix race in test_socket testFromFdError
body:
`testFromFdError` (added in gh-160579) compares the process-wide fd count before and after a few rejected `socket.fromfd()` calls. In `BasicTCPTest`/`BasicTCPTest2` the client thread runs concurrently and closes its socket in `clientTearDown()`; if that happens between the two `fd_count()` calls the test fails with `AssertionError: 6 != 7`. This was seen on the TSan (free-threading) job, e.g. <url>

Wait on `self.done` (set at the end of `clientTearDown()`) before the first count, as `check_shutdown()` already does.

Verified by forcing the race (delaying the client thread and `fromfd()`): the old test fails with the same off-by-one, the new one passes. `test_socket` passes.

Needs backport to 3.15 and 3.14 together with gh-160579.

title: gh-160429: Ignore ConnectionResetError from shutdown() when closing proactor sockets
body:
On Windows, if the peer resets the connection after sending FIN, `sock.shutdown(SHUT_RDWR)` in `_ProactorBasePipeTransport._call_connection_lost()` raises `ConnectionResetError` (WinError 10054). The rest of the cleanup is skipped: the socket stays open, the transport is never detached from its server, and `Server.wait_closed()` never returns.

The connection is already gone at that point, so the reset is ignored, the same way `_loop_reading()` and `_loop_writing()` already treat `ConnectionResetError` as a normal end of the connection. Other `shutdown()` errors propagate as before.

Reproduced with real sockets on Windows 11 against a debug build of main: the server writes a response, the client half-closes without reading it, then closes, which sends a RST. Without the fix, 10 of 10 runs left the socket open (the debug build reports it as an unclosed-socket `ResourceWarning`) and `wait_closed()` hung; with the fix, 10 of 10 cleaned up. The added test uses a mocked socket, like `test_call_connection_lost`. `test_asyncio` passes on the same build.

gh-160600 was an earlier draft for this issue, closed by its author before review.

title: gh-160873: Remove obsolete pthread_getattr_np workaround
body:
Emscripten 6.0.1 deprecated `-sUSE_PTHREADS` and `-sMEMORY64` in favor of the standard `-pthread` and `-m64` flags (emscripten-core/emscripten#27025). With the currently pinned Emscripten 6.0.10, both emit a `-Wdeprecated` warning at link time:

  emcc: warning: USE_PTHREADS is deprecated (prefer the standard -pthread flag). [-Wdeprecated]
  emcc: warning: MEMORY64 is deprecated (prefer the standard -m64 or --target=wasm64 flags). [-Wdeprecated]

This PR switches `configure.ac` to the standard flags:

- `--enable-wasm-pthreads`: `-sUSE_PTHREADS` → `-pthread` in `LDFLAGS_NODIST`. The existing `-pthread` in `CFLAGS_NODIST` is not passed to the link step, so the linker flag is still needed.
- `wasm64-*-emscripten`: `-sMEMORY64=1` → `-m64` in `CFLAGS` and `LDFLAGS`.
- `Platforms/emscripten/README.md` is updated to match.

I've also removed the Emscripten-specific `NDOTDOTS = 48` workaround from `test_glob_dotdot` in `Lib/test/test_pathlib/test_pathlib.py`. Its comment says it can be removed once emscripten-core/emscripten#24591 is merged. That PR (don't return ELOOP on a path with many `..` components) was merged in June 2025 and should be in 4.0.11 and later, well below the pinned 6.0.10. The test now uses `NDOTDOTS = 50` on all platforms.

title: gh-149584: `_remote_debugging`: Read stack chunks directly instead of through the page cache
body:
`process_single_stack_chunk` would read the chunk with `_Py_RemoteDebug_ReadRemoteMemory` instead of going through the page cache. Reading chunks through the page cache doesn't really do anything:

 * on Linux pages are 4KB, so it goes straight to `process_vm_readv`
 * on macOS the chunk is exactly one page, the sampler keeps its own cache and nothing else in the sample reads that page, so all the paged read adds is a retry after the first `KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS`

That retry can only succeed after the target has mapped a new chunk at the same address, so the sampler ends up parsing a chunk that is not the one the thread state pointed at. `Invalid stack chunk size 0` is the symptom (a live chunk never has size 0):

```bash
maurycy@gimel cpython-rd-base (main 312222f) % sudo dtrace -q -Z -x dynvarsize=64m -n '
  pid$target:_remote_debugging*:copy_stack_chunks:entry { self->in_copy = 1; self->fails = 0; }
  pid$target:_remote_debugging*:copy_stack_chunks:return /self->in_copy/ { @per_copy[self->fails] = count(); self->in_copy = 0; }
  pid$target::mach_vm_read_overwrite:entry /self->in_copy/ { self->addr = arg1; }
  pid$target::mach_vm_read_overwrite:return /self->in_copy && self->addr/ { @kr[arg1] = count(); self->fails += arg1 != 0; self->addr = 0; }
  END { printa("  chunk read kr=%d: %@d\n", @kr); printa("  copies with %d failed reads: %@d\n", @per_copy); }' \
  -c "./python.exe repro_chunk_retry.py 5000"
  chunk read kr=1: 954
  chunk read kr=0: 10607
  copies with 2 failed reads: 315
  copies with 1 failed reads: 324
  copies with 0 failed reads: 4361
```

324 copies got `KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS` and then a successful read of the same address a few microseconds later.

`deep_recursion` oracle target at 100kHz, `cache_frames=True`, 3s:

| error | main | direct chunk read |
|---|---|---|
| chunk read failed (`size 16384`, `kern_return_t 1`) | 41575 | 35592 |
| frame read failed (`size 88`, `kern_return_t 1`) | 24037 | 37221 |
| Incomplete sample: did not reach base frame | 8659 | 7027 |
| Invalid stack chunk size 0 | 669 | 17 |
| total failed samples | 74940 (25.0%) | 79857 (26.6%) |

On Linux `perf stat` counts the same number of `process_vm_readv` calls with both builds.  The retried reads are reported as the original read failure now, so the error rate goes up on Oracle.

Not newsworthy IMO. I don't know how to create a not racy test here.

Context: I've found this one while reviving <url> and investigating some Oracle numbers when aliasing.

title: gh-160789: Fix double free in codegen_pattern_or() on MemoryError
body:
`codegen_pattern_or` copies `*pc` into `old_pc` and frees `old_pc.fail_pop` on its error path, so from that point it owns the caller's `fail_pop` array. The loop only cleared `pc->fail_pop` after the first `PyList_New(0)`. If that allocation failed, `pc->fail_pop` still pointed at the array the error path had just freed, and `codegen_match` freed it again.

The fix moves the two lines that reset `pc->fail_pop` and `pc->fail_pop_size` above the `PyList_New(0)` call. On later iterations they are already NULL and 0 after `emit_and_reset_fail_pop`, so only the first iteration's error path changes.

Only a nested or-pattern reaches it, because the outer `fail_pop` is NULL at the top of a case. That is why `case (1|2) | 3` survives and `case [1|2] | 3` does not: the sequence pattern has already allocated `fail_pop` when the inner or-pattern starts.

With a `--with-pydebug` build on macOS, the reproducer from the issue dies at injected allocation 82 on main with the debug allocator's bad pad bytes report and a segfault. With the change it prints `survived`. I also ran the same loop over `{"k": 1|2} | 3`, `C(1|2) | 3`, `[1|2] | [3|4]`, `[a, (1|2)] | [a, 3]`, `[[1|2] | 3] | 4` and `(1|2) | 3`, and all of them now raise `MemoryError` cleanly.

Testing:

- New `test_nested_or_pattern_allocation_failure` in `test_compile`, next to the gh-158241 test and in the same subprocess shape. It fails on main with `Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault` and passes with the fix.
- `test_patma test_compile test_ast test_syntax test_dis test_peepholer test_compiler_codegen`: 1191 run, 7 skipped, 0 failures.
- `test_patma -R 3:3` is clean.
- `make patchcheck` and `ruff check` on `Lib/test/test_compile.py` are clean.

An alternative is to clear `pc->fail_pop` once, straight after `old_pc = *pc`, but the loop resets it on every iteration anyway, so moving the existing lines up keeps the diff to a reorder.

title: gh-160864: Clean up refused native thread starts
body:
Fixes #160864.

Remove a thread from `_limbo` when the native-start call refuses creation with a `BaseException`, including `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`. The original exception still propagates.

Check the native handle before cleanup. An exception can arrive as the native call returns after creating an OS thread; that thread must keep its registration until bootstrap consumes it. The handle check runs only on the exceptional path.

Tests exercise real audit-hook refusal for `RuntimeError`, `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`, plus a profiler interruption immediately after native creation. The latter checks that the child still completes without bootstrap errors.

This leaves context initialization and child-bootstrap failures outside the scope of this fix. Related work in #140746 and #153776 addresses failures after OS-thread creation.

Validation:

- Both focused tests pass. Original code fails the two new audit-refusal cases; an unconditional `BaseException` cleanup fails the post-native test with a child-bootstrap `KeyError`.
- The full debug-build suite ran 52,062 tests, with 4 failures and 2,873 skips. The failures are `test_chown_gid` and three pathlib `test_glob_dotdot` assertions; all four reproduce with original `threading.py`. Threading, thread pools and subprocess tests pass, as do the multiprocessing modules that ran.
- Pinned pre-commit hooks pass on both Python files. Sphinx lint passes on the NEWS text.

All four changed executable lines were profiled, including both guard outcomes. The successful path executes the same 60 Python instructions. Timing on the busy macOS host was noisy: normal-start CPU medians rose 3.3% initially and 0.4% in one bounded follow-up; wall medians rose 50.1% and 3.5%. I am not claiming a speedup. Refused-start CPU medians were 2.858 to 2.807 microseconds for `RuntimeError`, 2.657 to 2.897 for `KeyboardInterrupt`, and 2.564 to 2.914 for `SystemExit`; the latter two now perform cleanup that the baseline omits.

After 1,000 real audit-hook refusals, the baseline retained 1,000 thread objects and the fix retained none. Tracemalloc recorded 2,449,950 versus 88,960 current bytes, including the harness's weak-reference bookkeeping.

AI tools helped investigate the failure, prepare the patch and tests, and run the checks.

For example, `HeaderRegistry()('Subject', '=?utf-8?b?YQ?=')` decodes to `'a'` but
reports no `InvalidBase64PaddingDefect` through its public `defects` attribute.

Propagate those defects and avoid repeated sibling-list concatenation in the
existing collector. Keep defect order, duplicate object identity, and empty-tree
behavior. The existing parameterized tests now check decoding, defects, and
folding for both `Subject` and custom headers.

This omission also appears in [catalog item 34b](<url>).
The collector is listed in #136063, alongside the active parser work in #152521
and #152710. Neither PR currently implements these two changes; this is a small
fix in the same area, with that prior work acknowledged.

Validation on macOS arm64, CPython 3.16 debug:

- `./python.exe -m test test_email test_mailbox test_smtplib`: 2,305 tests, 5 skips.
- `make patchcheck` and the applicable pinned pre-commit hooks pass.

- The full 561-module run completed with local failures in `test_chown_gid`,

title: gh-160852: Re-read the bytecode after JIT stop_tracing
body:
Fixes the crash in gh-160852.

`label(stop_tracing)` samples `opcode` before `stop_tracing_and_jit()` and then `DISPATCH_GOTO_NON_TRACING()` uses that snapshot. The tail-call macro does not re-read the instruction. `stop_tracing_and_jit()` can drop the last reference to a bound method of an unclosed buffered file. The `ResourceWarning` writes `__warningregistry__` into the current frame's watched globals, `executor_invalidate()` restores the original bytecode and stores `NULL` in the executor slot, and the stale `ENTER_EXECUTOR` calls `_PyJIT_Entry(NULL)`.

Re-read the opcode and the low byte of `oparg` after optimize. `EXTENDED_ARG` bits already accumulated in `oparg` stay in place, matching the deopt in `ENTER_EXECUTOR` (`(oparg & ~255) | saved_arg`). `Tools/cases_generator/tier1_generator.py` emits those two assignments into `Python/generated_cases.c.h`.

I verified the same change on 3.15.2, built with `--with-tail-call-interp --enable-experimental-jit`. The unpatched 3.15.1 interpreter segfaults in `_PyJIT_Entry` while Firefox's `packager.py --minify` evaluates `JarStruct.__init__.<locals>.<genexpr>`. The patched interpreter finishes that run, including with `PYTHON_JIT_STRESS=1`. I do not have a small standalone repro: the finalizer has to run inside `_PyOptimizer_Optimize` while the sampled instruction is an `ENTER_EXECUTOR` whose executor depends on the frame's globals.

title: gh-109564: asyncio: drop connections accepted by a closed server
body:
If `Server.close()` runs after a connection was accepted but before its transport is created, `Server._attach()` hits `assert self._sockets is not None`. The selector loop reports the `AssertionError` to the exception handler, and the half-built transport later raises `TypeError` from `__del__` (`Server._wakeup()` with `_waiters` already `None`). On the proactor loop the exception escapes the accept callback and the accepted socket leaks.

Both accept paths now close such a connection quietly before the transport is created. SSL connections go through the same path.

The regression test closes the server from the protocol factory, which forces this ordering deterministically on both selector and proactor loops. It fails without the fix on Linux and Windows.

This overlaps with #154861, which guards only the selector path.

title: gh-160788: Fix exponential time in code object comparison
body:
`code_richcompare()` compared `_PyCode_ConstantKey(co_consts)`. For a tuple, that key is the pair `(item_keys, tuple)`, so comparing two keys compares each nested code object twice: once through its item key, which is the code object itself, and once through the original tuple. That doubles the work at every level of nesting.

This compares the keys of the constants one by one instead. The result is the same: equal item keys already imply equal items, so comparing the original tuple again never changed the result.

With the reproducer from the issue on a debug build, depth 20 took 3.0 s on main and depth 30 didn't finish. With this change, depth 30 takes under 1 ms.

Tests:
- `test_code_equality_nested`: the 30-deep reproducer. It hangs on main.
- `test_code_equality_uses_consts`: checks that the comparison still tells apart `0.0`, `-0.0`, `0`, `False`, `(0.0,)` and an extra constant. It passes on main and with this change.

title: gh-158646: Fix race in test_shutdown_corrupted_ssl_sends_close_notify
body:
The server side of `test_shutdown_corrupted_ssl_sends_close_notify` called `unwrap()` right after corrupting the client's TLS stream, which sent its own close_notify to a client that was about to close its socket. That turned the client's close into a TCP reset. Linux still delivers data queued before a reset, but Windows discards it, so the server's read failed with `WinError 10054` (sometimes `10053`) even though the client had sent close_notify correctly. The asyncio code is fine; the test was racy.

Fix: the server now waits for the client's close_notify with `recv()` (which returns `b''` on a clean TLS EOF) before calling `unwrap()`. A ragged EOF without close_notify still makes `unwrap()` raise `SSLError`, so the test keeps catching the gh-98078 regression (verified by temporarily removing the gh-98078 send in `sslproto.py`).

Verified on a Windows 11 x64 debug build:

| Run | Result |
|---|---|
| Unmodified test, 100 iterations × Selector + Proactor | 16 server-thread exceptions, 1 unittest failure |
| Fixed test, 300 iterations × Selector + Proactor | 0 failures |
| Full `test_asyncio.test_sslproto` on Windows and Linux | pass |

title: gh-160842: Read every frame of a multi-frame Zstandard zipfile member
body:
A zstd stream may consist of several concatenated frames (RFC 8878, section 3.1), which multi-threaded and streaming compressors produce. `ZipExtFile._read1()` used the decompressor's `eof` as the end of the member, so it returned only the first frame and then failed the CRC check.

When the zstd decompressor reaches the end of a frame and compressed input remains (`unused_data`, or `_compress_left > 0`), `_read1()` now continues with a new `ZstdDecompressor`. The member ends when the compressed input is exhausted on a frame boundary, or when the declared `file_size` has been produced, as before.

Failure behaviour:
- bytes between frames that are not a valid frame raise `ZstdError`;
- a truncated last frame still produces short output and fails the CRC check with `BadZipFile`.

The other methods are unchanged. The repack scan in `_scan_data_descriptor_no_sig_by_decompression()` still stops at the first frame. For a multi-frame member written with a data descriptor and no signature, the size check there rejects the candidate, so the result is the same as before this PR.

Tests: `ZstdMultipleFramesTests` in `test_zipfile/test_core.py` covers two frames read in several chunk sizes, 49 small frames, garbage between frames, and a truncated last frame. Without the fix, three of the four fail. `./python.exe -m test test_zipfile` passes on a macOS debug build of main. That build had no zlib, so the zlib-dependent tests were skipped.

The issue asks one question: should trailing bytes after the last frame, inside `compress_size`, be an error? This PR leaves that as it is for every method.

_Disclosure: this PR was authored by Claude (Anthropic's AI assistant, via Claude Code) on behalf of @HipHoff, who takes responsibility for the change. It is a draft until he has reviewed it and signed the CLA._

title: gh-57945: Document exceptions not wrapped by urlopen()
body:
The `urlopen()` documentation says only that it raises `URLError` on protocol errors. In practice, exceptions raised while reading or parsing the HTTP response come from `http.client` without being wrapped. These include:

- `http.client.HTTPException` subclasses such as `BadStatusLine`. These are not `OSError` subclasses, so even `except OSError` misses them.
- `OSError` subclasses such as `TimeoutError` (the server doesn't respond within *timeout*) and `RemoteDisconnected`.

`ValueError` is also raised for a URL with no scheme.

This happens because `AbstractHTTPHandler.do_open()` wraps `OSError` in `URLError` only around `h.request()`, not around `h.getresponse()`.

Earlier discussion on the issue (Antoine Pitrou, Martin Panter) and the related issues gh-53069, gh-66986 and gh-69819 settled on documenting this rather than adding more wrapping, which would break existing code. This PR changes only the documentation.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](<url>)


---- 

Helpful reproducer for this.

```python
import socket, threading, time, urllib.request, urllib.error

def serve(reply, delay=0):
  s = socket.socket(); s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0)); s.listen(1)
  def run():
  c, _ = s.accept(); c.recv(65536)
  time.sleep(delay)
  if reply is not None: c.sendall(reply)
  time.sleep(0.5); c.close(); s.close()
  threading.Thread(target=run, daemon=True).start()
  return f"<url>)[1]}/"

cases = {
  "read timeout during getresponse": (None, 2, 0.5),
  "bad status line":  (b"GARBAGE\r\n\r\n", 0, 5),
  "invalid status code":  (b"HTTP/1.1 1000 OK\r\n\r\n", 0, 5),
  "empty reply (RemoteDisconnected)":(b"", 0, 5),
  "too many headers":  (b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n" + b"X: y\r\n"*200 + b"\r\n", 0, 5),
}
for name, (reply, delay, tmo) in cases.items():
  url = serve(reply, delay)
  try:
  urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=tmo).read()
  print(f"{name:36} -> no error")
  except Exception as e:
  print(f"{name:36} -> {type(e).__module__}.{type(e).__qualname__}"
  f"  isURLError={isinstance(e, urllib.error.URLError)}  isOSError={isinstance(e, OSError)}")
# connection refused (connect phase) and bad scheme/value
for name, url in [("connection refused", "<url>"), ("unknown scheme", "foo://x"), ("no scheme", "example.com")]:
  try: urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=2)
  except Exception as e:
  print(f"{name:36} -> {type(e).__module__}.{type(e).__qualname__}  isURLError={isinstance(e, urllib.error.URLError)}")
```

too many headers  -> http.client.HTTPException  isURLError=False  isOSError=False

title: gh-59515: Support multiple challenges in urllib Digest Auth
body:
`HTTPDigestAuthHandler` and `ProxyDigestAuthHandler` only looked at the first `WWW-Authenticate` / `Proxy-Authenticate` header and took its first word as the scheme. As a result:

* A Digest challenge was ignored if a Basic challenge came first, in the same header or in an earlier one.

* An unsupported scheme listed first (for example `Kerberos, Basic realm="x"`) raised `ValueError`. Because the Digest handler runs before the Basic handler, that also blocked `HTTPBasicAuthHandler`.

This PR changes only `AbstractDigestAuthHandler`.
`AbstractBasicAuthHandler` already handles multiple challenges since GH-18284 and is not modified.

* `http_error_auth_reqed()` now reads all headers (`get_all()`) and uses the first Digest challenge found. It raises `ValueError` only when neither Digest nor Basic is offered; otherwise it returns `None` so the next handler can try.

* A new private `_parse_challenges()` splits a header into challenges per RFC 9110 §11.6.1. A comma-separated element that starts with a word not followed by `=` begins a new challenge. Its quote/escape handling matches `parse_http_list()`. It makes a single linear pass with no regex.

* `retry_http_digest_auth()` is unchanged. It receives the original text of the Digest challenge, so escapes are not processed twice. For a single-challenge header the string is the same as before.

title: gh-160773: Fix use-after-free in OSError.__str__
body:
Fixes #160773 

`OSError.__str__` passed borrowed references to its attributes (`errno`, `strerror`, `filename`, `filename2`, and `winerror` on Windows) to `PyUnicode_FromFormat`. Formatting one attribute with `%S`/`%R` can run arbitrary Python code. If that code modifies another attribute, the object being formatted can be freed while still in use.

The fix now take strong references to the attributes before formatting and release them afterwards.

Added a regression test which cover the `filename` and `filename -> filename2` formats.

Tested on linux (Ubuntu 26.04).

title: gh-160749: Correct documentation of tp_alloc and tp_free inheritance for heap types
body:
Fixes gh-160749

Summary of Changes

Clarify the inheritance and default documentation for the tp_alloc and tp_free slots in Doc/c-api/typeobj.rst.

The documentation previously stated that heap subtypes do not inherit tp_alloc or tp_free, and that for heap subtypes, tp_alloc is always set to PyType_GenericAlloc() and tp_free defaults to a generic deallocator.

However, heap types also include types created through C API functions such as PyType_FromSpec and PyType_FromMetaclass. For these types, if Py_tp_alloc or Py_tp_free is omitted from the specification slots, the corresponding slot is inherited from the base type through inherit_slots in Objects/typeobject.c. If the base type defines a custom allocator or deallocator, the C API heap subtype can inherit that custom implementation.

The exception applies to subtypes created using Python’s class statement or the type() constructor, which are handled by type_new_alloc. In these cases, tp_alloc and tp_free are explicitly initialized to PyType_GenericAlloc and PyObject_GC_Del, respectively.

Changes Made

* PyTypeObject.tp_alloc: Clarified that subtypes inherit this slot from the base type, defaulting to PyType_GenericAlloc when inherited from object. Documented the exception for subtypes created using the class statement or type().
* PyTypeObject.tp_free: Clarified that subtypes inherit this slot from the base type, subject to garbage collection compatibility rules. Documented the exception for subtypes created using the class statement or type().
* Default sections: Updated the documentation for both slots to distinguish between types created through Python’s class statement or type() constructor and other subtypes, including static types and C API heap types created through PyType_FromSpec.

Testing

Documentation-only change. No code changes or additional tests are included.

title: gh-160814: Fix out-of-bounds read in the SRE code validator for IN with skip < 2
body:
The `IN` opcode branch of `_validate_inner()` reads `code[skip-2]` without checking that `skip >= 2`. `skip` is unsigned, so for `skip` of 0 or 1 the index `skip - 2` wraps to a huge value and the read goes out of bounds, crashing the interpreter.

This is reachable only by passing hand-crafted bytecode to `_sre.compile()`; the public `re` compiler always emits `skip >= 2` for `IN`.

title: gh-160811: fix TextIOWrapper.tell() after seek() past a carriage return
body:
`seek()` to a cookie with `chars_to_skip > 0` replays the input chunk into a new snapshot but kept the bytes-per-char ratio from the previous `_read_chunk()`, so `tell()` could compute a skip larger than the snapshot.  the C implementation then read past the bytes object, and `_pyio` returned a position one character too far.  this sets the ratio from the replayed chunk in both implementations, the same way `_read_chunk()` does, and adds a regression test for the C and pure-Python classes.  backports to 3.14 and 3.13 need the test moved to `Lib/test/test_io.py`.

title: gh-160806: Fix precision loss in pure-Python `timedelta` with large float arguments
body:
`_pydatetime.timedelta()` added its float arguments together before splitting off the fractional part, so large values lost their sub-second part (`timedelta(weeks=12345678.9)` was off by 482 µs).

It now sums the microseconds the same way as the C implementation: the integer part of each argument exactly, and only the leftover fractional microseconds as a float, rounded half to even at the end. This also replaces the old step-by-step normalisation, which is much longer.

Since the arguments are now handled one by one in the same order as in C, `inf`/`nan` arguments also raise the same exception type as the C version (for example `timedelta(days=inf, seconds=nan)` raised `OverflowError` instead of `ValueError`).

Integer arguments are converted with `int()` first, so int subclasses with odd `__mul__`/`__divmod__` (`test_issue31752`) still work.

title: [3.14] gh-159652: Fix import lock leak when the C stack is nearly exhausted (GH-159660)
body:
When an import failed with a stack overflow RecursionError, releasing the import locks on the error path could itself raise RecursionError, because the cleanup runs in a new C frame. This left the global import lock or a module lock held forever, and later imports in other threads blocked indefinitely.

_imp.acquire_lock() now raises RecursionError when there is not enough stack left to release the lock. importlib calls it before taking any import lock, so this covers the per-module locks too. The module lock weakref callback skips cleanup in that case instead of
reporting an unraisable exception.
(cherry picked from commit 926b0bf3110bf86550ef248cf911e24fc123ec64)

Co-authored-by: Cary Hawkins <<email>>

_imp.acquire_lock() now raises RecursionError when there is not enough stack left to release the lock. importlib calls it before taking any import lock, so this covers the per-module locks too. The module lock weakref callback skips cleanup in that case instead of
reporting an unraisable exception.

Fixes gh-41668.

### Summary of Changes
When decompressing truncated gzip archives or streams ending unexpectedly before the trailer, \
eadall()\ and \decompress()\ raised \EOFError\ while discarding all decompressed blocks accumulated prior to the EOF.

title: gh-40889: Fix email.utils.parseaddr on multiple intermediate route hops
body:
Fixes gh-40889.

### Summary of Changes
When \ mail.utils.parseaddr\ parses addresses containing obsolete route syntax with multiple hops (e.g. \<@hop1.org,@hop2.org:<email>>\), the parser fails on the comma delimiter and falls through into treating it as an invalid addrspec. This patch adds comma handling to \getrouteaddr()\ in \Lib/email/_parseaddr.py\ so that multi-hop route addresses resolve cleanly to the target mailbox. Regression tests added to \Lib/test/test_email/test_email.py\ and news entry added.

title: gh-160766: Handle nested annotated and generic aliases that contain forward references in annotations
body:
This adds another special case to `_Stringifier.__convert_to_ast` to handle `types.GenericAlias` and `typing.Annotated` similar to the handling of list, set, tuple, dict that constructs the ast to rebuild the `GenericAlias` or `Annotated` object.

This is to prevent the `ForwardRef` objects from becoming "hidden" inside the `GenericAlias` or `Annotated` objects.

For `GenericAlias` an `ast.Call` node is created to reconstruct the `GenericAlias` as there's no guarantee it was created through subscripting. The call is converted back to subscript format when evaluating the `ForwardRef` in `STRING` format in order to match the repr of `GenericAlias` objects.

For `Annotated`, subscripting is used. Are there any other types that need to be handled?

```python
from annotationlib import get_annotations, Format

class X:
  a: Y[list[Z]]

# Get annotations here to get the ForwardRef
anno = get_annotations(X, format=Format.FORWARDREF)['a']

class Y[T]:
  pass

class Z:
  pass

print(anno.evaluate(format=Format.STRING))
print(anno.evaluate(format=Format.VALUE))
```

Main:
```python
Y[list[ForwardRef('Z', is_class=True, owner=<class '__main__.X'>)]]
__main__.Y[list[ForwardRef('Z', is_class=True, owner=<class '__main__.X'>)]]
```

PR:
```python
Y[list[Z]]
__main__.Y[list[__main__.Z]]
```

body:
Like `xgettext`, `pygettext` now prints `pygettext: no input file given` and exits with status 1 when no input file is given, instead of silently writing a header-only `messages.pot`.

This covers the first case in the issue only. As discussed there, the no-messages case keeps its current behaviour (an empty template is valid).

When URL result objects (`SplitResult`, `ParseResult`, `DefragResult`, etc.) are instantiated directly rather than returned from `urlsplit()` or `urlparse()`, their `_keep_empty` attribute is not set.

title: gh-158500: Reject trailing characters in date.fromisoformat()
body:
`date.fromisoformat()` accepts strings of length 7, 8 or 10, but neither parser checks that it read the whole string. A 10-character string without a `-` after the year goes down the basic-format path, which reads `YYYYMMDD` (or `YYYYWwwD`) and returns, ignoring the last two characters. So a truncated or mistyped timestamp turns into a plausible but wrong date:

```pycon
>>> from datetime import date
>>> date.fromisoformat('2020010112')  # e.g. a YYYYMMDDHH stamp
datetime.date(2020, 1, 1)
>>> date.fromisoformat('2020W011xx')
datetime.date(2019, 12, 30)
>>> date.fromisoformat('20200101é')  # C only: 9 characters, but 10 bytes in UTF-8
datetime.date(2020, 1, 1)
```

With this change, all three raise `ValueError: Invalid isoformat string`, as `datetime.fromisoformat()` already does for the same input.

The fix checks that the parser stopped exactly at the end of the date, in both `parse_isoformat_date()` in C and `_parse_isoformat_date()` in `_pydatetime`. `datetime.fromisoformat()` uses the same function for its date part, but there the date always ends at the separator for valid strings. I compared the C module before and after on ~300k fuzzed strings: only `date.fromisoformat()` results changed (all from accepted to rejected), and `datetime.fromisoformat()` results did not change at all.

While adding the tests I found that the pure-Python `datetime.fromisoformat()` has a similar problem. It skipped time parsing whenever the time part was empty, so a date followed by any single character was accepted:

```pycon
>>> import _pydatetime
>>> _pydatetime.datetime.fromisoformat('2020-01-01T')
datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0)
>>> _pydatetime.datetime.fromisoformat('2021-01-071')
datetime.datetime(2021, 1, 7, 0, 0)
```

The C implementation already rejects these. It now parses the time whenever something follows the date, the same as C. It's the same "didn't consume the whole input" bug, so I kept it here, but I'm happy to split it out if you'd prefer.

Tests are added to `test_fromisoformat_fails` and `test_fromisoformat_fails_datetime`, so they run against both implementations.

title: gh-160719: Define _Py_STDC_VERSION in pyport.h
body:
`pyport.h` uses `_Py_STDC_VERSION` to pick `_Py_thread_local`, `_Py_NULL` and `_Py_TYPEOF`, but the macro is defined in `pymacro.h`, which `Python.h` includes after `pyport.h`. So those C11/C23 branches are never taken. This moves the definition into `pyport.h`.

Macro values with `#include "Python.h"` (`cc -E -dM`):

| Compiler | Macro | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| gcc 13, `-std=c11` | `_Py_thread_local` | `__thread` | `_Thread_local` |
| clang 18, `-std=c23` | `_Py_NULL` | `NULL` | `nullptr` |
| clang 18, `-std=c23` | `_Py_TYPEOF(expr)` | `__typeof__(expr)` | `typeof(expr)` |

`./python -m test test_cext -u cpu` passes on Linux (the MSVC-only test is skipped).

This doesn't touch the inverted `static_assert` fallback condition in `pymacro.h`, which gh-160705 already fixes.

title: gh-160347: Guard async generator awaitables against concurrent entry
body:
Fixes #160347.

The INIT-to-ITER transition is visible before the first throw into the generator finishes. A concurrent call on the same awaitable can then resume the generator without delivering the pending exception. A losing call can also clear `ag_running_async` and close the shared awaitable after receiving "async generator already executing", leaving the original operation unable to continue. That state corruption also occurs with same-thread reentry on GIL builds and affects `asend()`.

Guard each `send()`, `throw()`, and `close()` call on ASend and AThrow, including the `am_send` path. An overlapping call raises the existing `ValueError` before touching the awaitable's state. The guard is released when the call yields or returns; `ag_running_async` still excludes other awaitables while the owning operation is suspended.

These guards replace the old awaitable-state CAS transitions. The two byte fields fit existing padding, with no object-size increase in either build tested.

The regression tests cover same-thread reentry, direct `await`, and Event-coordinated concurrent calls. They check that the original awaitable remains usable, retains ownership across suspension, completes cleanup, and still rejects reuse after closing. All 21 subcases fail against the original free-threaded build and pass with this patch. The 12 applicable serial/direct-await subcases also fail before the fix on a GIL build.

### Validation

Linux x86-64, GCC 13.3:

- Free-threaded debug build: 3,418 tests run, 25 skipped, no failures. Two Windows-only test modules were skipped.
- GIL release build: 404 tests passed.
- Targeted `-R 3:3` checks: no reference leaks.
- Ruff 0.15.17, sphinx-lint 1.0.2, `patchcheck.py`, and `git diff --check` passed.

```sh
# Free-threaded debug build
./python -m test -j2 test_asyncgen test_free_threading.test_async_generators test_coroutines test_generators test_yield_from test_asyncio test_contextlib

# GIL release build
./python -m test -j2 test_asyncgen test_coroutines test_generators test_yield_from test_contextlib

# Reference leaks
./python -m test -R 3:3 -m '*awaitable_reentrant*' -m '*concurrent_shared_awaitable_resume' test_asyncgen test_free_threading.test_async_generators
```

Small interleaved microbenchmarks were too variable on this host to establish a reliable timing delta.

body:

* Pass the cached `' '` and `'\n'` strings for the default `sep` and `end` directly, instead of converting them from C strings with `PyFile_WriteString()`, which runs `strlen()` and the UTF-8 decoder on every call to get back the same cached string.

`write()` receives the same calls as before. Benchmarks are in the issue: 1.20x faster geometric mean across 8 cases, 5 faster (1.12x to 1.66x) and 3 not significant.

Developed with the help of AI: Claude Opus 5.5.

title: gh-130662: Remove unnecessary plus sign from news entry
body:
Remove leading plus sign added in #132549 from NEWS entry.

Ultimately, the leading plus sign may cause Sphinx warning if a translator doesn't write ```+:class:`~decimal.Decimal` ``` like the original like:

```
build/NEWS:8698: WARNING: inconsistent cross-references in translated message. original: ['`~decimal.Decimal`'], translated: [':class:`~decimal.Decimal`'] [i18n.inconsistent_references]
```

See Brazilian Portuguese translation for instance. Notice how the original message (msgid) has a plus sign write before the class role and the translation message (msgstr) doesn't, which caused the above warning:

```
#: ../NEWS:8672
msgid ":gh:`130662`: +Accept leading zeros in precision and width fields for +:"class:`~decimal.Decimal` formatting, for example ``format(Decimal(1.25), '.016f')``."
msgstr ":gh:`130662`: Aceita zeros à esquerda em campos de precisão e largura para formatação :class:`~decimal.Decimal`, por exemplo ``format(Decimal(1.25), '.016f')``."
```

The Sphinx warning was spotted in <url> browsing the pt-br count.

message:
gh-158646: Fix race in test_shutdown_corrupted_ssl_sends_close_notify (#160848)

The server called unwrap() right after corrupting the client's TLS
stream, which sent its own close_notify to a client that was about to
close its socket.  That turned the client's close into a TCP reset, and
on Windows a reset discards the client's close_notify that is still
unread, so the server failed with WinError 10054 (or 10053).

Wait for the client's close_notify with recv() before calling unwrap().
A ragged EOF without close_notify still makes unwrap() raise SSLError,
so the test keeps catching the gh-98078 regression.

message:
gh-159652: Fix import lock leak when the C stack is nearly exhausted (GH-159660)

When an import failed with a stack overflow RecursionError, releasing the import locks on the error path could itself raise RecursionError, because the cleanup runs in a new C frame. This left the global import lock or a module lock held forever, and later imports in other threads blocked indefinitely.

_imp.acquire_lock() now raises RecursionError when there is not enough stack left to release the lock. importlib calls it before taking any import lock, so this covers the per-module locks too. The module lock weakref callback skips cleanup in that case instead of
reporting an unraisable exception.

message:
gh-159963: Don't hold parent package import locks while a submodule executes (GH-159965)

Since gh-83065 (3.15.0), the first import of pkg.mod kept pkg's module
lock until pkg/mod.py had finished executing.  Threads that needed only
the finished pkg stayed blocked for that long, and concurrent first
imports could raise _DeadlockError or a spurious "partially initialized
module" ImportError, or hang, with no import cycle involved.

Parent packages are now imported, or waited for if another thread is
initializing them, before the submodule's module lock is taken, so only
that lock is held while the submodule executes.  The lock ordering
deadlock fixed by gh-83065 stays fixed.

importlib.import_module() now returns the partially initialized module
in a circular import split across threads, as the import statement
already did, instead of raising _DeadlockError.  That was long-standing
behavior rather than part of the 3.15.0 regression.
author: Gregory P. Smith

gh-159739: Keep sqlite3 cursor metadata and factories valid during queries (#160403)

A cursor exposed its description tuple before filling in all the columns, so an allocation failure or a reader on a free-threaded build could encounter an unset tuple entry. An allocation failure could also clear lastrowid and crash the next execute. Build new metadata before replacing the old values and synchronize reads and writes. Keep a strong reference to each row or text factory while it is called so replacing the factory during a fetch cannot destroy an active callable.
author: Jelle Zijlstra

message:
gh-159739: Keep text I/O state valid across reentrant callbacks (#160398)

A raw read can reinitialize a TextIOWrapper as write-only, and codec callbacks or finalizers can release an encoder, decoder, or decoded chunk while a read or write still needs it. This can crash the interpreter. Check that a decoder is still available after reading, keep codecs alive across calls, and read the chunk length before transferring ownership. Also recheck StringIO after converting the truncate size because __index__() can close the stream.

message:
gh-160040: Distrust compromised eMudhra intermediate CA keys (CVE-2026-115557) (GH-160042)

The ssl module now rejects TLS certificate chains that contain any of a set of
compromised eMudhra intermediate CA keys.  This is an extraordinary measure and
a last line of defense: removing trust is primarily the job of the platform root
store, and the built-in denylist only blocks connections while that update has
not yet reached the OS, a container image, or a bundled trust store in various
Python packages.  Entries are added to the denylist only under a very high
threshold.

The denylist matches on the public key (the SHA-256 digest of the RFC-5280
SubjectPublicKeyInfo), so it also covers the cross-signed certificates that
reuse one of the distrusted keys.

gh-160388: Load the copied library in the deleted-mapping test (#160396)

The deleted-`libpython` mapping test uses `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` to load a temporary copy of the library. On glibc, an interpreter's `DT_RPATH` can take precedence and load a different copy, so the test fails because the temporary copy was not mapped. gh-159739: Preserve CJK codec state across chunk boundaries and callbacks (#160400)

The HZ encoder can consume a tilde after writing only its first escape byte. A split ISO-2022 escape can exceed the incremental decoder’s pending buffer, and a reset can leave the previous character set selected. Keep the native codec table and the active encoder error policy alive so replacing their Python owners cannot leave a codec using freed memory.

A character data callback can disable buffering or remove the next event handler during a flush. message:
Clarify TLS 1.3 behavior of the SSLContext PSK callbacks (GH-160159)

Under TLS 1.3 a PSK is only offered and may be declined, and both sides
fall back to certificate authentication when one is available, so
CERT_NONE leaves the server unauthenticated and a zero length PSK does
not reject the connection.  Drop CERT_NONE from the example and the PSK
tests.

A callback that raises is treated like one returning a zero length PSK,
so under TLS 1.3 it also falls back to certificate authentication.  A
server with a certificate loaded declines even a matching PSK with
OpenSSL's default TLS 1.3 cipher suite order, which selects a SHA-384
suite.  Mention checking session_reused as the client side alternative
to not using CERT_NONE.
author: Gregory P. Smith

message:
gh-106045: Keep searching from venv home when the resolved base executable has no stdlib (#160123)

GH-156483 made `getpath` locate a venv's base installation relative to the *resolved* base executable instead of the `home` key in `pyvenv.cfg`. When the resolved executable lives outside the installation tree (e.g. a launcher binary symlinked into it), nothing is found there and discovery falls back to the compiled-in `PREFIX`. The venv then either fails to start or silently runs with another installation's standard library.

This PR:

- Keeps GH-156483's behavior when the resolved executable's directory locates a standard library (`pybuilddir.txt`, the stdlib zip, or `os.py`). Otherwise it keeps searching from `home`, as before GH-156483.
- In that fallback case, still searches the resolved executable's directory for `lib-dynload` when determining `exec_prefix`: after `prefix`, before `home` and the compiled-in `EXEC_PREFIX`. Layouts with a separate exec prefix (e.g. `./configure --exec-prefix`) then keep loading extension modules from the right place, and a stale `lib-dynload` near the `home` symlink can't take precedence over the one beside the resolved executable.

The tests added by GH-156483 pass unchanged. Three new `test_getpath` cases cover the launcher-outside-the-installation and separate-exec-prefix layouts, and a misleading `lib-dynload` near `home`; each fails without this change.

<details>
<summary>Reproducer</summary>

On `main` (0a86a34), with a plain `./configure --prefix=$HOME/py-under-test && make && make install`:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# Usage: venv-home-repro.sh <installed-prefix> <X.Y>
set -eu
PREFIX=$1; VER=$2
W=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir -p "$W/runtime/bin" "$W/runtime/lib" "$W/launcher"
cp -R "$PREFIX/lib/python$VER" "$W/runtime/lib/"
cp "$PREFIX/bin/python$VER" "$W/launcher/python3"
ln -s "$W/launcher/python3" "$W/runtime/bin/python3"
PYTHONHOME="$W/runtime" "$W/runtime/bin/python3" -m venv --without-pip "$W/venv"
grep '^home' "$W/venv/pyvenv.cfg"
echo ...
author: Itamar Oren

a mismatched closing bracket pop the brace that opened an f-string
replacement field, which the f-string state relies on. In `f'{]a'`, this
triggered an assertion failure in _PyLexer_scan_string.

Check the replacement field brace in both modes.
author: Lysandros Nikolaou

message: gh-132414: Make invalid command-line options visible in the error message (GH-157921)
author: Vasiliy Kiryanov

message:
gh-159739: Preserve ctypes base metadata when cloning fails (#160174)

When creating a ctypes structure subclass, cloning its layout initially copied pointers to buffers owned by the base class. If a later allocation failed, cleaning up the subclass could free those buffers, leaving the base with invalid metadata and potentially causing a crash. Detach the owned pointers until their copies have been allocated. Backport to 3.15 and 3.14.
author: Jelle Zijlstra

message:
gh-159739: Hold the codec registry lock while unregistering (#160168)

Concurrent calls to codecs.unregister() can shrink the search path between its length check and indexed lookup in a free-threaded build. The lookup then returns NULL and an unconditional decref crashes the interpreter; hold the registry mutex across the scan and removal. Also reported in gh-157078. Backport to 3.15 and 3.14.
author: Jelle Zijlstra

message:
gh-159739: Allocate thread-local state before constructing the object (#160166)

If allocating a thread-local object’s internal dictionary or watchdog set fails, a subclass finalizer can run with that state missing. Accessing a thread-local attribute then dereferences the missing state and crashes; allocate both containers before creating the object. Backport to 3.15 and 3.14.
author: Jelle Zijlstra

message:
gh-159739: Keep SimpleQueue valid after buffer allocation fails (#160165)

If allocating a SimpleQueue buffer fails, the partially constructed object reports nonzero capacity despite having no storage. A subclass finalizer that calls put() then writes through a NULL pointer and crashes; publish the capacity only after allocation succeeds. Backport to 3.15 and 3.14.
author: Jelle Zijlstra

message:
gh-159739: Skip context watchers cleared during notification (#160164)

A context watcher callback can clear a later watcher while a context-switch notification is being dispatched. The dispatcher still uses its earlier snapshot of active watchers, so it calls a NULL callback and crashes; check that each callback is still registered before invoking it. Backport to 3.15 and 3.14.
author: Jelle Zijlstra

title: Binary size regression on MSP430
body:
A large binary size regression appeared between nightly-2026-10-22 and nightly-2026-10-23 on the MSP430 target, increasing binary size by ~40%, from 23KiB to 33KiB. It persists on the latest nightly-2026-10-29 toolchain.
While running CI for the [msp430-hal](<url>) project, I noticed some examples suddenly failing to link due to insufficient space on the target device. For example, building [spi_nb.rs](<url>):
```
cd device_examples/msp430fr2355
cargo +nightly-2026-10-22 build --example spi_nb
```
Analyzing the generated binary shows it's about 23KiB:
```
$ msp430-elf-size -A target/msp430-none-elf/debug/examples/spi_nb
target/msp430-none-elf/debug/examples/spi_nb  :
section  size  addr
.defmt  3  1
.vector_table  92  65444
.text  9530  32768
.rodata  14100  42300
.bss  2  8192
.data  0  8194
```

But the same example built with `cargo +nightly-2026-10-23 build --example spi_nb` produces a binary that's too large to fit in program memory: `region 'ROM' overflowed by 548 bytes`. 
If we modify the memory.x file to pretend to have more space than we actually do, we can see the generated binary would have been about 33KiB:

```
$ msp430-elf-size -A target/msp430-none-elf/debug/examples/spi_nb
target/msp430-none-elf/debug/examples/spi_nb  :
section  size  addr
.defmt  3  1
.vector_table  92  65444
.text  15590  12288 <--- significantly bigger
.rodata  17596  27880 <--- bigger
.bss  2  8192
.data  0  8194
```

Removing the possibly fallible `.unwrap()`s on lines 52 and 58 makes the regression disappear (also reducing the binary size to practically nothing), so I presume this is related to unwrapping an Err variant, and string parsing during a panic.

If you want to replicate this, you will need to download the [msp430-hal](<url>) repo, install the [MSP430-GCC](<url>) toolchain, then the rust toolchains (and rust-src): 
```
rustup install nightly-2026-10-22
rustup component add rust-src --toolchain nightly-2026-10-22-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
rustup install nightly-2026-10-23
rustup component add rust-src --toolchain nightly-2026-10-23-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
```
You can then cd into the `device_examples/msp430fr2355` folder and build the examples.

### Code `a/src/lib.rs`: ```rust #![feature(generic_const_items, gca_const_items, gca_macroless_args, gca_min_const_items)] #![expect(incomplete_features)] pub struct S(H); pub const P: usize = N; impl S { pub fn f(_: [u8; P::]) {} } ``` `b/src/lib.rs` (depends on `a`): ```rust pub type X = a::S; ``` ``` cargo +nightly doc -p b ``` `cargo build` and `cargo doc -p a` succeed. Only documenting `b` crashes.

title: Where-clauses on associated types are not checked for well-formedness
body:
I tried this code:

```rust
pub struct NC<T: Copy>(pub T);

pub trait Tr {
  type A where NC<String>: Sized;
}
```

**Expected:** E0277 (`String: Copy` is not satisfied, required by `NC`). The same clause on a method in the same trait gives exactly that

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `String: Copy` is not satisfied
4 |  fn a() where NC<String>: Sized;
  |  ^^^^^ the trait `Copy` is not implemented for `String`
```

**Actual:** compiles, under both solvers, on nightly-2026-10-29 and on stable 1.99.0.

title: Function with lifetime bounds using `const { try_as_dyn }` causes ICE

Without mir-opt: [comment]().
Original version with mir-opt (mir-opt only caused const-eval to run through GVN, and made this easier to hit in practice through Inline) ### Code ```Rust #![feature(try_as_dyn)] pub fn emit_gc_shared_sections<'a: 'static>() { // any lifetime bound will do here, e.g. 'a, 'b: 'a _ = core::any::try_as_dyn::<_, dyn core::any::Any>(&()); // any valid call to try_as_dyn will do here } ``` Compile with `rustc --crate-type=lib -O repro.rs`. title: Unsoundness due to user-provided `Pattern` impl returning an incorrect `Searcher`
What to do with pre-expansion linting?
body:
# Background

Rust has pre-expansion linting: Linting that works on AST nodes before macro expansion. 
At the moment, rustc has 2 pre-expansion lints: `KEYWORD_IDENTS_2018`, and `KEYWORD_IDENTS_2024`.
Clippy has 5: `DEPRECATED_CFG_ATTR`, `DEPRECATED_CLIPPY_CFG_ATTR`, `NON_MINIMAL_CFG`, `UNNECESSARY_CLIPPY_CFG`, `NONSTANDARD_MACRO_BRACES`.

Pre-expansion linting, as the name suggests, happens before expansion.
So it can emit lints in code that is configured out:
```rust
#[cfg(false)]
fn gen() {} //~ ERROR `gen` is a keyword in the 2024 edition
```

Even lint attributes work when they're configured out!
For example:
```rust
#[cfg(false)]
#[warn(keyword_idents_2024)] // works!
fn gen() {} //~ WARN `gen` is a keyword in the 2024 edition
```

# Question 1: Should invalid lint attributes that are configured out emit errors?

So clearly, lint attributes that are configured out have semantic meaning. Invalid ones usually don't emit any errors though:
```rust
#[cfg(false)]
#[allow] // OK
#[allow[wut]] // OK
#[allow(expect)] // OK
#[allow(({!}))] // OK
#[allow[helix::<ub>]] // OK
fn test() { }
```

However, in the specific case when a meta item representing a lint is given arguments, errors are emitted:
```rust
#[cfg(false)]
#[allow(lint(arguments_not_allowed_here))] //~ ERROR malformed lint attribute input
fn test() { }
```

**Proposal 1: Invalid lint attributes that are configured out should never emit errors**
So the example above should compile. This makes the lint attribute consistent with other attributes, which also don't emit errors when configured out:
```rust
#[cfg(false)]
#[inline{INVALID}] // OK
fn test() { }
```

# Question 2: Should lint attributes that are configured out even have effect?

Currently, lint attributes that are configured out still have a semantic meaning.
This is strange, since nowhere else in Rust does something that is configured out have a semantic meaning.

**Proposal 2: Lint attributes that are configured out should not have effect**

To be clear, we should still emit lints in code that is configured out. 
We are only saying that lint attributes that are configured out should not have effect on how lints are emitted.
```rust
#[deny(keyword_idents_2024)]  // This does have effect, it is not configured out!
mod meow {
  #[cfg(false)]
  #[warn(keyword_idents_2024)] // This currently has effect, we propose that it shouldn't!
  fn gen() {}
}
```

title: `as_chunks_mut` loop vectorizes worse than the equivalent `chunks_exact_mut` loop (x86-64, small constant trip count)
body:
Clippy's `chunks_exact_to_as_chunks` lint suggests replacing `chunks_exact(N)` with `as_chunks::<N>()`. Following it in a hex encoder made a hot path slower. The two functions below write the same bytes, but on the default x86-64 target the `as_chunks_mut` one is about 15% slower: LLVM's loop vectorizer interleaves it by 2, which leaves the last 4 of its 20 iterations as scalar code.

I tried this code (`rustc -C opt-level=3 --crate-type=lib --emit=asm`):

```rust
#[inline(always)]
fn hex_digit(nibble: u8) -> u8 {
  let d = nibble & 0x0F;
  d + b'0' + if d > 9 { 39 } else { 0 }
}

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub fn encode_chunks_exact(bytes: &[u8; 20], out: &mut [u8; 40]) {
  for (pair, &b) in out.chunks_exact_mut(2).zip(bytes) {
  if let [h, l] = pair {
  *h = hex_digit(b >> 4);
  *l = hex_digit(b);
  }
  }
}

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub fn encode_as_chunks(bytes: &[u8; 20], out: &mut [u8; 40]) {
  for ([h, l], &b) in out.as_chunks_mut::<2>().0.iter_mut().zip(bytes) {
  *h = hex_digit(b >> 4);
  *l = hex_digit(b);
  }
}
```

I expected to see this happen: the same machine code for both. That is what happens with `-C target-cpu=x86-64-v3` or higher, and with a trivial loop body (`*h = b >> 4; *l = b & 0xF;`): LLVM merges the two functions.

Instead, this happened:

| | instructions (SIMD) | time per call (Ryzen 9 9950X, best of 9) |
|---|---|---|
| `encode_chunks_exact` | 91 (90) | 3.82 ns |
| `encode_as_chunks` | 137 (71) | 4.37 ns (+14%) |

With `-C remark=all -C debuginfo=1`:

```text
encode_chunks_exact:
  loop-vectorize (analysis): the cost-model indicates that interleaving is not beneficial
  loop-vectorize (success): vectorized loop (vectorization width: 4, interleaved count: 1)
  loop-unroll (success): completely unrolled vectorized loop with 5 iterations
encode_as_chunks:
  loop-vectorize (success): vectorized loop (vectorization width: 4, interleaved count: 2)
  loop-unroll (success): completely unrolled vectorized loop with 2 iterations
  loop-unroll (success): completely unrolled epilogue loop with 4 iterations
```

### Why, as far as I can tell

The IR entering `LoopVectorizePass` is the same for both functions except for the store address (names as in `repro.ll` below):

```llvm
; encode_chunks_exact
%off = shl nuw nsw i64 %i, 1
%dst = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %out, i64 %off

; encode_as_chunks
%dst = getelementptr inbounds nuw [2 x i8], ptr %out, i64 %i
```

The vectorizer interleaves a loop whose cost is below `-small-loop-cost` (default 20). Bisecting that flag (`-C llvm-args=-small-loop-cost=N`) puts the `chunks_exact_mut` loop's cost at 20 and the `as_chunks_mut` loop's at 19: `encode_as_chunks` gets IC 1 at N ≤ 19, and `encode_chunks_exact` gets IC 2 at N ≥ 21. So one instruction, the `shl`, decides it. With a constant trip count of 20, VF 4 × IC 2 = 8 does not divide it, and 4 iterations are left to scalar code. It looks like the interleave count is chosen without weighing the scalar remainder it creates for a small constant trip count.

The same choice helps when the trip count is not known. The loops over slices of run-time length (in the repro below) get VF 8 with IC 1 and IC 2 the same way, and there `as_chunks_mut` is faster: 3.61 vs 4.96 ns at 20 bytes, equal at 4,096 bytes. On aarch64 the `as_chunks_mut` loop is instead fully unrolled and SLP-vectorized (43 instructions against 34).

### Standalone LLVM reproducer

The two loops as they enter the vectorizer, cleaned up (`opt` from rustc 1.99.1's `llvm-tools`, LLVM 23.1.1):

```console
$ opt -passes=loop-vectorize -pass-remarks=loop-vectorize -pass-remarks-analysis=loop-vectorize -disable-output repro.ll
remark: <unknown>:0:0: the cost-model indicates that interleaving is not beneficial
remark: <unknown>:0:0: vectorized loop (vectorization width: 4, interleaved count: 1)
remark: <unknown>:0:0: vectorized loop (vectorization width: 4, interleaved count: 2)
$ opt -passes=loop-vectorize -pass-remarks=loop-vectorize -small-loop-cost=19 -disable-output repro.ll
remark: <unknown>:0:0: vectorized loop (vectorization width: 4, interleaved count: 1)
remark: <unknown>:0:0: vectorized loop (vectorization width: 4, interleaved count: 1)
```

`opt -passes='default<O3>'` followed by `llc -O3` turns it into 91 and 139 instructions.

<details><summary>repro.ll</summary>

```llvm
; Two loops that differ only in how the store address is computed (from rustc 1.99.1's IR
; just before LoopVectorizePass). LV interleaves the second by 2 (loop cost 19 < the
; default -small-loop-cost of 20) but not the first (cost 20: the extra shl). With a
; constant trip count of 20, VF 4 x IC 2 = 8 leaves a 4-iteration scalar remainder.
;
;  opt -passes=loop-vectorize -pass-remarks=loop-vectorize \
;  -pass-remarks-analysis=loop-vectorize -disable-output repro.ll

target datalayout = "e-m:e-p270:32:32-p271:32:32-p272:64:64-i64:64-i128:128-f80:128-n8:16:32:64-S128"
target triple = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"

; out.chunks_exact_mut(2): the offset is an explicit shl.
define void @chunks_exact(ptr noalias readonly captures(none) dereferenceable(20) %bytes, ptr noalias writeonly captures(none) dereferenceable(40) %out) {
entry:
  br label %loop

loop:
  %i = phi i64 [ 0, %entry ], [ %i.next, %loop ]
  %i.next = add nuw nsw i64 %i, 1
  %off = shl nuw nsw i64 %i, 1
  %dst = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %out, i64 %off
  %src = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %bytes, i64 %i
  %b = load i8, ptr %src, align 1
  %hi = lshr i8 %b, 4
  %hi.0 = or disjoint i8 %hi, 48
  %hi.c = icmp ugt i8 %b, -97
  %hi.adj = select i1 %hi.c, i8 39, i8 0
  %hi.d = add nuw nsw i8 %hi.0, %hi.adj
  store i8 %hi.d, ptr %dst, align 1
  %lo = and i8 %b, 15
  %lo.0 = or disjoint i8 %lo, 48
  %lo.c = icmp samesign ugt i8 %lo, 9
  %lo.adj = select i1 %lo.c, i8 39, i8 0
  %lo.d = add nuw nsw i8 %lo.0, %lo.adj
  %dst1 = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %dst, i64 1
  store i8 %lo.d, ptr %dst1, align 1
  %done = icmp eq i64 %i.next, 20
  br i1 %done, label %exit, label %loop

exit:
  ret void
}

; out.as_chunks_mut::<2>(): the scale is in the GEP's element type.
define void @as_chunks(ptr noalias readonly captures(none) dereferenceable(20) %bytes, ptr noalias writeonly captures(none) dereferenceable(40) %out) {
entry:
  br label %loop

loop:
  %i = phi i64 [ 0, %entry ], [ %i.next, %loop ]
  %i.next = add nuw nsw i64 %i, 1
  %dst = getelementptr inbounds nuw [2 x i8], ptr %out, i64 %i
  %src = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %bytes, i64 %i
  %b = load i8, ptr %src, align 1

f32::powi on Windows returns incorrect sign on Windows
body: Calling `powi` with a large odd exponent returns an incorrect sign on Windows. With the following code: ```rust println!("{}", (-1.0f32).powi(16_777_217)); println!("{}", (-1.0f64).powi(16_777_217)); ``` Both calls should return `-1`, but the `f32` version instead returns `1`. `powi` does specify that precision is non-deterministic, but this seems to go beyond just a minor change in precision into a mathematically incorrect result so I'm not sure it's intended. ### Meta I can confirm this changed in rustc 1.45 just like but that issue was about minor precision differences, not a completely wrong result. `rustc --version --verbose`: ``` rustc 1.99.0 (b940084d7 2026-09-28) binary: rustc commit-hash: b940084d7eb6a299eb4bfeb8e34901bc051e7ac4 commit-date: 2026-09-28 host: x86_64-pc-windows-msvc release: 1.99.0 LLVM version: 23.1.1 ```
