small_sort_network never terminates for zero-sized types at len >= 18 (latent, unreachable via public sort APIs)
body:
`small_sort_network` (`library/core/src/slice/sort/shared/smallsort.rs`) does not terminate for a zero-sized `T` when `len >= 18`. This is **latent**: every current caller returns early for ZSTs, so it is not reachable through the public sort APIs today. Filing it so the assumption is recorded (or asserted) before a future caller relies on it.

### Why it loops

For `len >= 18` (`no_merge == false`) the region loop ([L338](<url>)–[L361](<url>)) sorts the left half, then moves `region` to the right half and repeats until `region.as_ptr() != v_base`:

```rust
if region.as_ptr() != v_base {
  break;
}
// SAFETY: The right side of `v` based on `len_div_2` is guaranteed in-bounds.
unsafe { region = slice::from_raw_parts_mut(v_base.add(len_div_2), len - len_div_2) };
```

For a ZST, `v_base.add(len_div_2) == v_base`, so the right-half region starts at `v_base` again, the `break` is never taken, and the loop runs forever.

ZSTs do take this route: `()` is `Copy` + `Freeze` with `size_of == 0`, so `has_efficient_in_place_swap::<()>()` holds and `<() as UnstableSmallSortTypeImpl>::small_sort` dispatches to `small_sort_network`.

### Why it is unreachable today

`slice::sort::stable::sort`, `slice::sort::unstable::sort` and `slice::sort::select::partition_at_index` all return early when `T::IS_ZST`, and the quicksort/driftsort paths that call `small_sort` are only reached through them.

### Evidence

Found while verifying the smallsort module with Kani (Challenge 8 of [model-checking/verify-rust-std](<url>)), whose `library/` matches this code. A harness calling `<() as UnstableSmallSortTypeImpl>::small_sort` on `[(); 18]`, with `sort9_optimal`, `sort13_optimal` and `insertion_sort_shift_left` stubbed out as no-ops (they cannot change a ZST slice; the loop's pointer logic does not depend on them), fails the unwinding assertion of this loop at `unwind(12)` and never reaches the code after the call. The same route with `u8` leaves the loop after two iterations and verifies. The `[(); 17]` case (`no_merge`) returns normally.

### Possible fix

A `debug_assert!(!T::IS_ZST)` (or an early `return` for ZSTs) at the top of `small_sort_network`, or a note in the `UnstableSmallSortTypeImpl` docs that ZSTs must be filtered by the caller.

title: msan makes `noundef` an ABI attribute, breaking Rust ABI promises
body:
LLVM function attributes are usually not ABI-relevant, any exception needs to be explicitly documented. msan breaks that by making `noundef` an ABI attribute. This is incompatible with Rust semantics where we want to consider `i32` and `MaybeUninit<i32>` to be ABI-compatible types (and we document as much). It also causes ABI issues for the hidden return pointer, see <url>

I think ideally this would be fixed upstream. If that's not possible, we should probably just entirely stop emitting `noundef` for msan builds to avoid this issue.

Not sure whom to ping for sanitizer problems... @rcvalle maybe?
Cc @nikic

title: CoerceShared reborrow emits an out-of-bounds copy
body:
I tried this code (): ```rust #![feature(reborrow)] use core::marker::{CoerceShared, PhantomData, Reborrow}; struct Source<'a> { data: [u8; 1], marker: PhantomData<&'a ()>, } impl Reborrow for Source<'_> {} #[repr(align(256))] #[derive(Copy, Clone)] struct Target<'a> { data: [u8; 1], marker: PhantomData<&'a ()>, } impl<'a> CoerceShared> for Source<'a> {} fn main() { let source = Source { data: [1], marker: PhantomData }; let view: Target<'_> = source; assert_eq!(view.data, [1]); println!("{} {}", core::mem::size_of_val(&source), core::mem::size_of_val(&view)); } ``` I expected to see this happen: No ASAN error Instead, this happened (-Zsanitizer=address): ```sh ==2==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow on address 0x77a9b10f02c1 at pc 0x59764cb46c9c bp 0x7ffde9a286f0 sp 0x7ffde9a27eb0 ``` ### Meta `rustc --version --verbose`: ``` rustc 1.101.0-nightly (76456a688 2026-10-25) binary: rustc commit-hash: 76456a688bc0ed897fa23a677d4ddb5b3fdb575a commit-date: 2026-10-25 host: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu release: 1.101.0-nightly ```

title: BPF: Bump CPU to v4 to enable 64-bit atomics
body:
BPF does have atomic instructions, but the LLVM BPF backend only selects the 64-bit atomic load/store patterns (including relaxed, which lower to plain loads/stores) when the subtarget has `load-acq-store-rel`, and that flag is set only for `cpu = "v4"` in `initSubtargetFeatures`.

With the default v1/generic CPU, the 64-bit `AtomicPtr` load/store used by `core::io::Error` fails to compile at ISel with `Cannot select: ... AtomicLoad`.

Targeting v4 also enables the rest of the v4 ISA (`alu32`, `jmp32`, `ldsx`, `movsx`, `bswap`, `sdiv_smod`, `gotol`, `storeimm`, `gotox`), which matches modern eBPF VMs and is what the existing `bpf-types.rs` inline-asm test already assumes (it passes `-C target_feature=+alu32` and uses w-regs).

Different instructions from the v4 instruction set became available in different Linux kernel versions, notably:

- Immediate store (`ST_IMM`): v5.3.
- 32-bit ALU/JMP (`alu32`/`jmp32`, also in v3): v5.3.
- Load with sign extension (`ldsx`): v5.6.
- Move with sign extension (`movsx`): v5.11.
- Endianness conversion (`bswap`): v5.12.
- Signed division/modulo: v5.13.
- Long-form jumps (`gotol`): v5.14.
- Indirect jump (`gotox` / `may_goto`): v6.9.
- load-acquire / store-release (`LDAX` / `STAX`): v6.15.

Kernel 6.15 or newer are already adopted by many Linux distributions.

The oldest kernel supported by <url> ecosystem is 5.10. Emitting instructions unsupported by that kernel can be avoided by not using `core::io::Error` and other parts of core that can potentially use unsupported atomics.

This problem was unnoticed before, because BPF target (currently) emits bitcode, and bpf-linker is a bitcode linker, that lowers bitcode to BPF bytecode after unused code is removed.

<url> proposes making BPF target emit BPF binaries. That requires ability to build entire core library. This change partially fixes the issue.

Code in this change is generated by (an open-weight and self-hosted) LLM, it was agreed on in the Zulip thread [0], where @nagisa volunteered as a reviewer.

title: dec2flt: round f16 subnormal ties to even in the Eisel-Lemire path
body:
## Problem Parsing an `f16` value that lies exactly halfway between two subnormals rounds up instead of to even. ```rust let x: f16 = "0.0000000298023223876953125".parse().unwrap(); // exactly 2^-25 assert_eq!(x.to_bits(), 0); // fails: got 1 (the smallest subnormal, 2^-24) ``` 2^-25 is the midpoint between `0` and the smallest subnormal `2^-24`. Under round-half-to-even it must become `0`. The same thing happens for every odd multiple of 2^-25 in the subnormal range. ## Cause In `compute_float` (`library/core/src/num/imp/dec2flt/lemire.rs`), the subnormal branch rounds with `mantissa += mantissa & 1`, which is round-half-up. The ties-to-even check only exists on the normal path, and it is gated on `MIN_EXPONENT_ROUND_TO_EVEN..=MAX_EXPONENT_ROUND_TO_EVEN`, which is `-4..=23` for `f16`. That range does not cover subnormals. For `f16` this case actually reaches the Eisel-Lemire fast path. 2^-25 = 5^25 × 10^-25, so it parses as `w = 5^25` (which fits in a `u64`) with `q = -25`. For `f32` and `f64`, subnormal ties need far more digits than fit in `w`, so they take the slow path and are unaffected. ## Fix Before rounding a subnormal, check for an exact halfway case using the same exactness test as the normal path (`lo <= 1`, the round bit set, and all truncated bits zero). If the kept mantissa is even, clear the round bit so the value rounds down. The exponent bound is `q >= -27`. An exact tie needs `w` to be divisible by `5^-q`, and `w < 2^64` limits `-q` to at most 27. This is the same bound as the existing `inside_safe_exponent` check. Subnormal values never have a positive `q`, so no upper bound is needed. ## Tests Added `f16_subnormal_ties_round_to_even` in `library/coretests/tests/num/dec2flt/mod.rs`. It checks the first nine subnormal ties, (2k+1)·2^-25, which must round to the even neighbour `2k`. Each value is also tested with six trailing zeros appended, which gives it more than 19 significant digits.
Before the fix: the new test fails ``` $ ./x test library/coretests --test-args f16_subnormal_ties_round_to_even running 1 tests num::dec2flt::f16_subnormal_ties_round_to_even ... title: Error when parsing implausibly large float strings
body:
This proposes that dec2flt error on very large decimal character string inputs (2^50 bytes) rather than claim to process them correctly.

Context: In an attempted lean formalization of the the correctness of the behavior of the dec2flt libary these bugs were discovered:
<url>
<url>

They concern parsing and overflow problems that can occur with large inputs.

The pull request rust-lang/rust#164331 proposes fixes for these problems but still doesn't handle some physically enormous (exabyte scale) inputs.  Although the code could be changed to handle these, the added complexity seems like it may not be worth it in favor of just refusing on these huge inputs, as suggested/considered in <url>

With this change, together with PR rust-lang/rust#164331, the code would work on all inputs.

(Without rust-lang/rust#164331, there are inputs of size around 65KiB that are also incorrect)

2^58 would actually suffice here; 2^50 is still enormous and may make it easier to reason when reading.

Note: these PRs are generated in response to a project Lean-formalizing the correctness of the dec2flt library using an LLM based autoformalization system; LLMs were used to write code but not commit messages, comments, etc.

I wrote changes introduced by this single commit by hand. I used an LLM to ideate about changes, and also to review the code before submitting. I used both gpt6/astra and claude 5.5/opus as assistants.

## What

A potential fix for <url> and a follow-up for <url>

Here we introduce a dedicated script to free disk space on macOS Github runners. We do minimal changes to invoke this script accordingly from the CI Workflow.

The new script works by deleting iOS simulator instance files and runtimes. I assumed these components are not needed and therefore, safe to delete.

I ran a few related experiments [in this repo](<url>). For `macos-26` this script reclaims ~ 120GB of space. That repo also tests most of `free-disk-space-mac.sh` behavior.

I added a waiting logic after `xcrun simctl runtime delete all` (which runs asyncly) because in general this command finishes fast (less than 30 seconds) and the script can correctly calculate how much disk space was freed afterwards. 

I did not try to replicate the same funcionality available in the existing Linux couterpart of this script, e.g. earlier finishing if some amount of space is already available. I assume that can be a follow-up.

<!-- homu-ignore:end -->

We did not yet have a way to use reflection data for enum's at runtime. This adds a method to query the current `VariantId` give no type information except the `TypeId`. We do this in two steps:
1. get the Discriminant given no information about the type at runtime
2. map the Discriminant to a VariantId

To do 1) we need to generate code for the specific type. Specifically we need to generate `std::mem::discriminant`. Emitting a _function ptr_ during const-eval is enough to get a monomorphized version of that generated. To get 2) we have an intrinsic that returns a list of `VariantId` to `Discriminant` mapping. Getting the discriminant then looking it up in the mapping is packaged into a single function which is what the user actually calls.

Since we have a lot of enum usage in rust the performance of this matters a lot. The current approach is suboptimal, the mapping is done through a linear scan and may not optimize out nicely. I suggest we put some effort in optimizing this _after_ we are sure this will be the API.

This change works around an issue in sccache when handling PGO file names for msvc parameters when calling clang-cl. 
The original issue is that any changes to the PGO profile data files will not cause a sccache miss for the relevant binaries when rebuilding for optimization, and instead will pull the cached obj files, skipping any prof data changes. 

This works by adding the profdata file contents directly to the hash for relevant targets using a SCCACHE_EXTRAFILES additional setting. 

When the sccache issue is resolved and in use with Rust, this change can be safely reverted.

title: std: use `_exit` for `process::exit`
body:
Fixes <url>
Fixes <url>
Fixes <url>

This fixes three issues related to `process::exit` at once: C's `exit` is not MT-safe, and there is no entirely sound way to make it so, and it calls destructors for TLS variables (and C++ static variables) that may be currently in use, leading to double-frees and similar undefined behaviour. The POSIX-defined `_exit` function on the other hand immediately terminates the process without running any handlers and hence does not have any of these problems, so this PR switches `process::exit` to use it instead of `exit`.

While skipping `atexit` handlers is a bit unfortunate, it shouldn't come as that big a surprise to users of `process::exit`; that function is already documented not to perform any stack cleanup. It's a change in behaviour, though, so this will need FCP.

title: De-inline interned span ops
body:
Interned spans are rare, and interned lookups are complex, involving TLS lookups and locking. This commit moves them out of line from `Interned::data` (affecting several `Span` operations), plus `Span::is_dummy`, `Span::parent`. This makes them match `Span::new_ordered`, which already has the interned case out of line.

This reduces rustc binary size and is a very small perf win.

title: Reform `feature(ergonomic_clones)`
body:
Tracking issue: <url>

It seems like the mood in the lang team is that they are no longer motivated to champion this feature in its current form: <url>

I still like it, though. I believe that, with some tweaks, it can serve as a useful complement to `move` expressions. This PR is my proposal to the lang team to pick this feature up and reform it for continued experimentation.

### Changes in this PR

- `use ||` closures and `async use {}` blocks are no longer a thing.
- `.use` aborts on panic, instead of triggering UB.
- `$expr.use` requires `$expr`'s type to implement `Copy` or `UseCloned`.
- `.use` in a normal, non-`move` closure now has special capturing behavior. To elaborate:

Within a closure, `.use` on a captured place results in a special by-use capture mode. Captures with this mode are cloned both when the closure is created, as well as every time the closure is run. In other words, `|| x.use` is essentially equivalent to `|| move(x.clone()).clone()`. This allows the closure to implement `Fn()` without borrowing from the stack frame of its parent.

The clone on closure construction happens only once, even if the capture is `.use`d several times within the closure body. For example, `|| { x.use; x.use }` clones only once on construction, and twice each time the closure is run. (The naïve desugaring in terms of `move` expressions would clone twice on construction.)

The by-use capture mode is considered to have the lowest priority among all other capture modes. For example, the following closures do not clone on construction: `|| { x.use; x }`, `|| { x.use; &x }`.

By-use capturing also supports edition 2021 precise capturing. For example:

```rust
struct Foo<'a> {
  field: &'a (bool, i32),
}

fn foo(f: Foo) {
  // This closure captures `foo.field.0` once by value.
  // (N.B.: The naïve `move` expressions desugaring would capture twice)
  let closure = || {
  let a = foo.field.0.use;
  let b = foo.field.0.use;
  }
}
```
---

title: Propagate block coldness across unwind edges and mark cold callsites
body:
During MIR codegen, `find_cold_blocks` identifies basic blocks that end in `Unreachable` or call a `#[cold]` function and propagates coldness backward to predecessor blocks when all of their successors are cold. However, `Terminator::successors` includes `is_cleanup` landingpad edges on unwinding `Call` terminators. Because shared cleanup landingpads are also reachable from hot callsites and are not marked cold, any intermediate block on a panic path that makes an unwinding call (such as `core::fmt::Argument::new_display` or `core::fmt::Arguments::new` before `panic_fmt`) fails to be marked cold. In addition, `rustc_codegen_ssa` only used `cold_blocks` to attach `unlikely` branch weights to `SwitchInt` terminators and never marked calls inside cold non-cleanup blocks with the LLVM `cold` callsite attribute.

This PR filters out `is_cleanup` successors when propagating coldness backward in `find_cold_blocks` and adds `BuilderMethods::apply_attrs_to_cold_callsite` in `rustc_codegen_ssa` and `rustc_codegen_llvm` and invoke it from `TerminatorCodegenHelper::do_call`.

body:

- Follow-up to <url>
---
<!-- homu-ignore:end -->

This commit changes the type of LLVM module references from `&'ll Module` to a newtype struct `Module<'ll>` with an invariant lifetime brand, similar to the previous migration from `&'ll Context` to `Context<'ll>`.

As before, `&'ll Module` being covariant in `'ll` is unsound, so switching to an invariant lifetime should help to ensure that contexts and modules are used coherently.

There should be no change to compiler output.

title: skip max_repr_align in Layout::eq_abi
body:
We don't have to compare all fields of `Layout`. Some of them are irrelevant most of the time, only some special callconv adjustments use them. Given that we compare both `PassMode` and `Layout`, we will notice those differences in `PassMode` comparison. Comparing them also in `Layout` is too strict as the values can differ without actually resulting in a different ABI. For instance, `max_repr_align: Some(1)`  is effectively the same as `max_repr_align: None`.

title: Drop array elements in order after a partial move
body:
When an array may have been partially moved out by an array pattern, drop elaboration splits it into
kept indices and dropped subslices, but then built the drop ladder over those pieces in reverse. So
`let a = [D(1), D(2)]; if false { let [_x, _] = a; }` dropped 2 before 1. The reversal came in with
rust-lang/rust#109008; before that the ladder went first to last, which is what the Reference says.

This removes the `.rev()` and adds a run-pass test. Two existing drop-order tests
(`if-let-guards.rs`, `or-pattern-drop-order.rs`) were asserting the reversed order, so I fixed their expectations.

Fixes rust-lang/rust#164809

AI was used to write tests for this. I reviewed the changes myself. Thanks

title: Keep comments inside parens when suggesting to remove unused delims
body:
When there's a comment between a paren and the inner expression, `unused_parens` suggests removing
it along with the paren, and with line breaks the spans cover the whole block. This points at the
delimiters only in that case, and only removes the delimiter on a side that has a comment.

Fixes rust-lang/rust#164722

FYI, tests are written with the help of AI. I reviewed and they are working as expected. Thanks

title: Suggest `gca!` for path const args that use generic params
body:
Fixes rust-lang/rust#164999

When a const arg is just a path like `Self::N` and the gca features are on, the error now suggests wrapping it in `gca!` instead of telling you to make a `type const` item:

```
help: consider wrapping `Self::N` in the `gca!` macro
  |
8 -  fn foo() -> [u8; Self::N];
8 +  fn foo() -> [u8; gca!(Self::N)];
```

It only fires when both `gca_min_const_items` and `gca_const_items` are enabled (with just the min feature the wrapped form still errors), and it skips `const { .. }` blocks, non-path expressions, macro spans, and inherent assoc consts, since `gca!` doesn't help there yet. Those keep the old help.

This PR serves as a follow-up PR of PR rust-lang/rust#163488, which distinguish experimental/internal features in rustdoc. This PR provides a solution to fix compile error that exists in rust-lang/rust#163488 and adds some test cases.

The solution is adding an internal API check in `librustdoc/html/render/mod.rs`. This check contains the same criteria used in <url> , but only checks the name of the feature. The reason not to check whether this feature is in `self.enabled_features` is: I think we only generate HTML tags and warnings about internal features, and we don't care whether this feature is enabled.

Another solution is adding a new check method in `rustc_feature/src/unstable.rs`, which performs the check. For example, adding this function in `rustc_feature/src/unstable.rs`:

```rust
pub fn is_internal_feature(feature: &Symbol) -> bool {
  let name = feature.as_str();
  name == "core_intrinsics" || name.ends_with("_internal") || name.ends_with("_internals")
}
```

So we can use `is_internal_feature` in `rustdoc` to check whether this feature is internal. I think this is a better way because `rustc_feature` and `rustdoc` share the same check.

I use the LLM to help me understand how to write test cases, because this is my first time writing test case for rustdoc. All the test cases are writen by myself and all are passed.

title: Support `NonNull` pointers as `asm!` input operands
body:
Currently the `asm!` macro supports raw (thin) pointers as operands, and references as input operands. As discussed in [Zulip](<url>), it seems reasonable to extend support to fundamental types with the same ABI as raw pointers. This commit adds support for (thin) `NonNull` pointer inputs. The reason for not allowing `NonNull` _outputs_ is that the `asm!` code has no way to explicitly assert that the safety invariant of `NonNull` is preserved.

Support for `Box<T>` and `Optional<NonNull<T>>` seems a bit more debatable, so that's left as future work (which might require more than a FCP).

title: Keep known_panics_lint values across single-predecessor assert edges
body:
KnownPanicsLint drops values of locals that are assigned more than once at the end of each block.
With overflow checks on, `x >>= n` puts an assert before the shift, so the shift ends up in the next
block and the lint loses `x` right there. This keeps visiting into the assert/goto target when it has
only one predecessor, and clears those locals once that chain ends.

Same applies to `/=` and `%=` (div-by-zero assert), which were missed even with `-O`.

Fixes rust-lang/rust#164191

# Stabilization report

## Summary

Zmmul is the integer multiplication subset of the RISC-V `M` extension. It enables LLVM to lower multiplications to the "MUL, MULH, MULHU, MULHSU, and (for RV64 only) MULW"[^1] instructions, while keeping divisions implemented in software.

This is useful for constrained embedded applications where multiplication operations are important enough for performance to warrant a hardware implementation, but division is rarely ever performed and so the extra cost of a hardware divider cannot be justified.

Using the `m` target feature could result in undefined behaviour by lowering to unimplemented division instructions, but excluding it leads to noticeably worse performance because hardware multiplication can't be used. `Zmmul` fixes this problem by enabling only multiplication.

[^1]: Spec: <url>

Tracking issue:

- None

Reference PRs:

- <url> (MISA vs. target features)
- <url> (stabilize Zmmul)

### What is stabilized

`-Ctarget-feature=+zmmul` can now be passed without a warning. `#[cfg(target_feature = "zmmul")]` and `#[target_feature(enable = "zmmul")]` are accepted.

## Feedback

### Nightly use

This has been in use at $INTERNSHIP for our `riscv32i-unknown-none-elf` embedded project for a few months now and works as expected: LLVM lowers to multiplication instructions but not division instructions.

### Coverage

There is currently no test coverage in rust-lang/rust. Given that this is just forwarded to LLVM, I think it's fair to put the test burden on LLVM and not rustc.

### Tool changes

- [x] rust-analyzer
  - Thanks to the recent addition of a target feature auto-sync, we don't need to worry about this

## Type system, opsem

### Sound by default?

Code with this target feature enabled is sound unless it is executed in an environment where integer multiplication instructions are not available. See some of the discussion in <url> about whether M implies Zmmul and the guidelines around the `misa` register for more details on this.

It is the responsibility of the user to guarantee that the instructions are implemented.

## History

- The target feature was implemented in <url> where it was discussed that stabilization after a few weeks/months would be okay

title: teach Const::Unevaluated to handle direct consts
body:
Lots of theorizing and discussion has happened here. Here's some words: One such writeup of the issue was done by me in this comment, for some background context: <url> - one solution is to lower references to direct-rhs const items in MIR to `Const::Unevaluated` rather than `Const::Ty` (as they are fundamentally sourced from regular values rather than the type system, which is what `Const::Unevaluated` vs `Const::Ty` means). One particular way to do that is to intercept const eval at a very particular point: where we have just resolved the instance, but still have access to the unresolved instance, due to adding support for evaluating resolved projected items being vaguely annoying (certainly possible to do so, just difficult and annoying to maintain from a tech debt point of view). An example of an alternative implementation would be to add support to the trait solver for resolved projections, and instead intercept const eval within e.g. `eval_to_const_value_raw` or `eval_to_allocation_raw`

This PR explicitly only addresses direct consts in `ExprKind::NamedConst`. It does NOT address direct consts in patterns, in `simd_swizzle`, or `#[const_continue]`, all of which use `const_eval_resolve_for_typeck`.

This visualizer handles wide pointers to `?Sized` types, e.g.

```
struct S {
  a: u8,
  b: [i16]
}
```

These were undecidable not too long ago, but we [now have enough information to reliably visualize these properly](<url>).

lldb 23 added the ability for an `SBValue` object to acquire its parent, which is very helpful for this so we can retrieve the length. Prior to lldb 22, the best option we have is to store a reference to the parent wide pointer within python itself and retrieve them in the child's visualizer (this happens via `WidePtrSyntheticProvider.WIDE_PTR_BY_UNSIZED_CHILD_ID`. I know it's maybe a bit hack-y, but this is semi-canonical and CodeLLDB did it pretty extensively in their visualizers). Using that method, we are thankfully able to get identical output between lldb 22 and 23.

As a note, this visualizer *does not* work for MSVC at the moment because [LLDB pretends zero-sized fields in PDB debug info don't exist](<url>) =)

body:
In `check_expr_lit`, if we have an integer literal and the expected type is an integer type var, we currently create a new type var that is later unified with the expected one. Only one ui test is changed, for the better:

Given how simple the change is, I think it's worthwhile.

title: uefi: clamp TCP4 receive length to the provided buffer size
body:
Fixes rust-lang/rust#164946

On UEFI, `TcpStream::read` returned whatever length the network driver reported after a
receive completed, without checking it against the size of the buffer we passed in. A buggy
driver that over-reports would make `read` claim more bytes than the buffer holds, and
callers like `read_to_end` would then treat memory past the buffer as initialized.

This passes the total buffer length into `read_inner` (from both `read` and `read_vectored`)
and returns `min(data_length, max_len)`. Returning an error instead of clamping would also
work; happy to switch if you'd prefer that.

Checked with `x check library --target x86_64-unknown-uefi`; I couldn't test it at runtime
since that needs a misbehaving UEFI network driver.

title: uefi: roll back env changes when `start_image` fails
body:
Fixes rust-lang/rust#164949

On UEFI, `process::output` applies the child's environment changes to the process-global UEFI environment and rolls them back after `start_image`. If `start_image` returned an error, the `?` returned early before the rollback ran, so the child's variables (notably `path`, which later `resolve_program` lookups depend on) leaked permanently into the parent.

This keeps the `start_image` result, restores the environment unconditionally, and only then propagates the error.

Tested with `./x check library --target x86_64-unknown-uefi`, `./x fmt --check` and `./x test tidy`. I have not run it on UEFI hardware or under QEMU.

cc @dvdhrm @nicholasbishop (UEFI target maintainers)

title: Avoid stdlib's `impl Hash for Discriminant` for stable hashing
body:
<!-- homu-ignore:start -->
*[View all comments](<url>)*
<!-- homu-ignore:end -->

<!-- homu-ignore:start -->
- Part of <url>
- Follow-up to <url>
---
<!-- homu-ignore:end -->

Of all the different ways we currently leak compiler/stdlib details into stable hashes, relying on `Discriminant::hash` seems high on the list of ones that could cause actual problems in the future.

This PR therefore removes `impl StableHash for Discriminant`, and replaces it with an explicit negative impl as a roadblock to anyone who might unknowingly try to reintroduce the problem.

To make this work, `#[derive(StableHash)]` now invents its own fake discriminant based on the syntactic ordering of enum variants. That should keep the hash values consistent across compiler stages.

In places where we were hashing Discriminant manually, this PR introduces explicit “tag” enums as seen in <url>

---

This change necessarily perturbs the hashes included in legacy-symbol-mangling symbols, as demonstrated in the re-blessed tests. This should be fine, as I believe the exact hash values are considered unstable anyway and have changed in the past.

body:
Delay diagnostics related to async-await in 2015 edition, and keep a list of their spans. If there are enough of them, emit a single diagnostic telling users that they are very likely in the wrong edition. Otherwise, emit the original diagnostics at the bottom of the diagnostic list.

```
error: `async`/`await` is not permitted in Rust 2015 edition
  --> $DIR/edition-deny-async-fns-2015.rs:3:1
  |
LL | async fn foo() {}
  | ^^^^^
...
LL | fn baz() { async fn foo() {} }
  |  ^^^^^
LL |
LL | async fn async_baz() {
  | ^^^^^
LL |  async fn bar() {}
  |  ^^^^^
...
LL |  async fn foo() {}
  |  ^^^^^
  |
  = note: ...and 4 other places
  = help: to use `async`/`await`, switch to Rust 2018 or later by passing `--edition 2024 to `rustc`
  = note: for more on editions, read <<url>>
```

This is a maximalist potential approach to fix rust-lang/rust#90849.

title: borrowck: Explain implicit object lifetimes in static calls
body:
Fixes rust-lang/rust#162882

With `&dyn Error`, the object lifetime defaults to the borrow's lifetime. Calling `is` needs a `'static` object, but E0521 points at the borrow and makes it look like the reference has to be `'static` too. Adding `+ 'static` to the object is enough for the example in the issue.

This suggests `&(dyn Error + 'static)` for the parameter and explains the implicit lifetime in the same help message, as requested in the issue. I think keeping the reason next to the edit makes the fix much easier to understand. When the trait's bounds supply the lifetime, the message explains that too.

I kept the suggestion to arguments passed directly from parameters. The checks also look at the callee's bounds and the lifetimes in trait arguments, to avoid suggesting an object bound when the borrow itself needs to be `'static` or those trait lifetimes don't match. If the edit would make an elided return lifetime ambiguous, the diagnostic gives a note instead.

Rollup merge of #165066 - RalfJung:abi-ice, r=oli-obk

skip max_repr_align in Layout::eq_abi

We don't have to compare all fields of `Layout`. Some of them are irrelevant most of the time, only some special callconv adjustments use them. message:
Rollup merge of #164315 - folkertdev:complex-powerpc32, r=beetrees

make powerpc `Complex` ABI GCC-compatible

tracking issue: <url>

The first commit gets the coercions right, but breaks down once the available registers are close to exhausted. GCC never splits a complex value across registers and the stack: when a complex value only partially fits, the remaining GPRs are consumed and the whole complex value (and any subsequent arguments) are passed via the stack.

This means we need an accurate accounting of the number of GPRs that have been consumed so far, so that we can emit padding to consume the remaining GPRs when a value needs to be passed on the stack. I've tried my best at that in commit 2, testing equivalence empirically with GCC.

Rather than getting the GCC algorithm right, instead we make a second pass over the arguments, and deduce the number of GPRs from the `PassMode` that the first pass determined for each argument. That seems to do the trick.

message:
Rollup merge of #164924 - beetrees:no-ssa-type-kind, r=bjorn3

Remove `TypeKind` from `rustc_codegen_ssa`

`TypeKind` is a very LLVM-shaped enum (e.g. there is a single `TypeKind::Integer` but multiple variants for floats because that's what LLVM does) - other backends (e.g. `rustc_codegen_gcc`) usually don't have a single call to get the required information and have to check for each variant individually, even though most callers only care if a type is one or at most a few variants. This PR removes `TypeKind` and `cx.type_kind()` from `rustc_codegen_ssa`, replacing them with `Option`-returning methods `int_width`, `float_type` and `vector_element_type_and_length`.

cc @antoyo for `rustc_codegen_gcc`

Rollup merge of #164766 - fmease:cta-migration-mvp, r=petrochenkov

Unstably introduce MVP edition migration lint `unmarked_unchecked_type_aliases` together with bikeshed attribute `#[rustc_unchecked_type_alias]`

Quoting from <url>

> *Migration lints* are used to migrate projects from one edition to the next.
They are implemented with a `MachineApplicable` suggestion which
will rewrite code so that it will **successfully compile in both the previous and the next
edition**.

However, as it stands we can't just stabilize feature `checked_type_aliases` in the next edition because it would break the world (in the next edition); generally speaking, arbitrary implicitly unchecked type aliases (i.e., what we have today on stable) can't just become checked type aliases without breakage. E.g.,

* the RHS could be ill-formed (most likely diverging const exprs, dyn-incompatible trait refs or unmet projection bounds) in which case the alias could obviously never be migrated as is (this is not a theoretical point; see crater run in <url> for example).
* rather unlikely but the user could be ignoring lint `type_alias_bounds` and be writing explicit bounds which would now be enforced at usage sites which could lead to local or downstream breakages (i.e., a major change wrt. SemVer)
* more likely, implicit `Sized` bounds would now be enforced at usage sites which could lead to local or downstream breakages
* the type alias could be private & used in a public item signature which would now trigger lint `private_interfaces` which might be set to `deny` or stricter leading to (soft) breakage

Therefore, there *must* be a mechanism to define unchecked type aliases in the next edition / under feature `checked_type_aliases`. This mechanism could then be used by the edition migration lint for (unchecked) type aliases that cannot be turned into a checked one without breaking the local crate or downstream consumers thereof. Of course, the lint should try to avoid that mechanism where poss ...

message:
Rollup merge of #164953 - Zalathar:discriminant, r=oli-obk

Avoid stdlib's `impl Hash for Discriminant` for stable hashing

Of all the different ways we currently leak compiler/stdlib details into stable hashes, relying on `Discriminant::hash` seems high on the list of ones that could cause actual problems in the future.

This PR therefore removes `impl StableHash for Discriminant`, and replaces it with an explicit negative impl as a roadblock to anyone who might unknowingly try to reintroduce the problem.

To make this work, `#[derive(StableHash)]` now invents its own fake discriminant based on the syntactic ordering of enum variants. That should keep the hash values consistent across compiler stages.

In places where we were hashing Discriminant manually, this PR introduces explicit “tag” enums as seen in <url>

---

This change necessarily perturbs the hashes included in legacy-symbol-mangling symbols, as demonstrated in the re-blessed tests. This should be fine, as I believe the exact hash values are considered unstable anyway and have changed in the past.

message:
Remove `AttrTokenStream` and `AttrTokenTree`

They are like `TokenStream` and `TokenTree`, but with the additional
`AttrTokenTree::AttrsTarget` variant that stores the attributes and
tokens for an attribute target.

This duplication is annoying, and also leads to some inefficiencies
when we have to produce an `AttrTokenStream` only to then convert it to
a `TokenStream`.

The new `LazyAttrTokenStreamInner::to_token_stream_with` takes a
`configure` closure. This closure is passed through various layers down
to `make_token_trees`, where it controls cfg expansion. Callers that
don't do expansion pass a trivial `keep_all` closure.
`try_configure_tokens` passes a non-trivial `configure` closure.

Overall this change makes the code shorter and slightly improves compile
times. One minor behavioural change on an error case: if parse recovery
finishes with an unmatched opening delimiter, `make_token_trees` drops
the caller's preceding trees; the old code kept them. This is obscure
and no existing tests hit it.

The next commit will rename `LazyAttrTokenStream` to `LazyTokenStream`.
It's a separate commit because it is uninteresting churn.

message:
Rollup merge of #164811 - GauravPawar101:fix-issue-164621, r=mejrs

fix: Prevent ICE when comparing EII impl against generic declaration

## Summary

Added a guard in compare_eii_function_types and check_no_generics to skip signature comparison when the EII declaration has type/const parameters.

## Problem

An EII declaration with type parameters ```rust (e.g., #[eii(foo)] fn bar<T>()) ``` triggers error E0044 -> "externally implementable items may not have type parameters". Even aftre the compiler continued analysis and called  to compare the implementation's signature against the declaration's. This comparison generated a `TypeError` containing the decl's `ty::Param(T)`, and the error reporter subsequently tried to look up parameter T in the implementation's generics that werent' there, this caused an ICE:
index out of bounds: the len is 0 but the index is 0

## Fix

Added an early return guard

## Tested variatns

- Generic declaration only
- Generic impl only
- Generic declaration + impl (ICE case)
- No generics (original reproducer)

Closes rust-lang/rust#164621

message:
Rollup merge of #159580 - Unique-Usman:ua/cfg, r=petrochenkov

Reject cfg on expressions that cannot be safely removed

## Change description

This PR changes how `#[cfg]` behaves in expression positions where removing the expression would result in invalid syntax.

For example:

```rust
let _ = 1 + #[cfg(unix)] 2;
```

This currently works on Unix because the condition is `true`, but becomes invalid on non-Unix targets when the expression is removed.

The proposed change rejects `cfg` in these positions regardless of whether the condition is `true` or `false`. The goal is to avoid code whose validity depends on the target and to make the behavior more predictable as `stmt_expr_attributes` is stabilized.

## Summary of the discussion

@petrochenkov pointed out that this differs from the usual token-based model for macros: `#[cfg(true)] expr` produces `expr`, while `#[cfg(false)] expr` produces no tokens. From that perspective, only the latter naturally results in an error.

On the other hand, @estebank pointed out that these cases are easy to introduce accidentally and may only be discovered when the code is compiled for another target. This becomes more important with the stabilization of expression attributes.

We also discussed that this is technically a breaking change, since some currently accepted code such as `#[cfg(true)]` inside a macro invocation would stop compiling (<url>). The conclusion was that this is effectively closing a stability hole, and the amount of affected code is expected to be very small.

The current implementation also uses `RemoveNodeNotSupported` for these cases and adds coverage for both `#[cfg(true)]` and `#[cfg(false)]`.

message:
Rollup merge of #164787 - Zalathar:llref, r=hanna-kruppe

cg_llvm: Use an invariant lifetime brand for LLVM contexts

This PR changes the type of LLVM context references from `&'ll Context` to `&'ll Context<'ll>`, introducing an invariant lifetime brand.

The current usage of `&'ll Context` is not sound, because covariance in `'ll` allows different contexts to be mixed in ways that the underlying bindings are not prepared to handle.

(Most of the time, mixing contexts is unlikely to happen by accident, but switching to a more-sound API is good maintenance hygiene for these complex bindings.)

In most code there is no practical difference between `&'ll Context<'ll>` and `&Context<'ll>`, but when storing the context in structures (e.g. SCx) it is helpful to be able to avoid an extra lifetime.

---

A big chunk of the migration was done via a regex replace of `Context` with `Context<'ll>`, and then manually chasing down any resultant/remaining errors. I have tried to manually check each of the changes multiple times, forwards and backwards, but this is a pretty tedious process so hopefully I did catch everything that shouldn't be there.

I intend to migrate various other related types as well, but just Context on its own is quite a lot to review already.

There should be no change to compiler output.

message:
Rollup merge of #164856 - Kobzol:expect-test, r=Mark-Simulacrum

Switch from `insta` to `expect-test` in bootstrap

While I like `insta` a bit more for snapshot tests, it has a disadvantage that it requires installing a separate binary (`cargo insta`) for blessing *inline* snapshot tests. That is not very intuitive for people who need to bless inline bootstrap snapshots, and then realize that `x test bootstrap --bless` does nothing.

This PR switches from `insta` to `expect-test`, which allows updating inline snapshots via an environment variable while running `cargo test`, without requiring a separate binary. `expect-test` is a `rust-lang` (well, `rust-analyzer`) [repository](<url>), so we should be good there, and it even removes two `dev` dependencies from bootstrap.

Changing the inline snapshots was a bit non-trivial to do with a regex (at least in my IDE) because we have to switch the argument order, which is not that simple across multiple lines. So I decided to try <url> I used an LLM to propose the initial rewrite rule, and then modified it slightly and ran `ast-grep` to update the code. The applied rule was this:
```yaml
id: insta-to-expect-test
language: rust
rule:
  pattern: insta::assert_snapshot!($$$ARGS)
transform:
  LHS:
  replace:
  source: $$$ARGS
  replace: '(?s)^(?<lhs>.*?),\s*@(?<rhs>.*?)\s*,?\s*$'
  by: '${lhs}'
  RHS:
  replace:
  source: $$$ARGS
  replace: '(?s)^(?<lhs>.*?),\s*@(?<rhs>.*?)\s*,?\s*$'
  by: '${rhs}'
fix: expect_test::expect![[$RHS]].assert_eq(&$LHS)
```

You can test it in the `ast-grep` [playground](<url>).

I used double brackets because it formatted better (IMO) with `x fmt`. Most of the diff comes from the this mechanical change. I split it into a separate commit for easier review.

I tried to replicate the disk snapshots as closely as possible, by even including the source file path in them, though I think it is not very useful. There are some newline changes in a few tests, I didn't feel like it is worth fixing those.

message:
Rollup merge of #164103 - Dnreikronos:trait_solver_resolve_region_vars, r=BoxyUwU

trait solver: Resolve region vars before eager placeholder handling

Region vars can already have known values in the unification table while the stored constraint still contains the vars. `max_universe` looks through the table, but `PlaceholderReplacer` sees the stored terms. In Boxy's nested binder case, that leaves an alias constraint ambiguous even after equating its regions.

I used `deeply_resolve_via_unification_table` at the start of eager handling for each universe. That leaves only the current universe's placeholder to bind and lets the result match the actual assumption on the outer binder. Unknown vars stay unknown.

The test DSL needed a small equality operation, `'a2 = 'a`, to reach this state. The paired outlives constraints in the original example go straight into solver storage and don't populate the table on current main. I added the version with real table equalities, plus a chained-var case. Both adjusted cases fail when the resolution call is removed and pass with it.

I think keeping this separate makes rust-lang/rust#157984 easier to review. The broader equality and subtyping work stays there.

assumptions_on_binders: Test mixed ambiguous ORs

Follow up to rust-lang/rust#162442. Boxy pointed out that one got superseded by rust-lang/rust#162935, and yeah, once adwin's PR removes `propagate_ambiguity` there's nothing left for my code change to do. The test still covers a case nothing else does though, so this just moves the test over.

The idea is an OR where one side is an alias outlives with a non-lifetime binder, which ends up ambiguous, and the other side is something we can prove from the root assumptions. That should hold no matter which order the OR is in. I also kept the cases that should still error, an AND where the ambiguous part is still required and an OR where every side is ambiguous. adwin mentioned in rust-lang/rust#162935 they weren't sure what to do with the non-lifetime binder ambiguity yet, so I think it's nice to have something pinning down how it behaves today.

It provides a more principled and type-safe way to extract and process

message:
Add an early return to `instantiate_and_apply_query_response`

If the response is an identity, and there are no external constraints,
and the response var kinds match the canonical goal var kinds, this
function is a no-op.
author: Nicholas Nethercote

message:
Introduce `IsIdentity` type

`Response` has `is_identity` and `is_identity_modulo_regions` methods.
These are reasonably hot and traverse the response's `var_values` in
very similar ways. This commit merges these two methods into a single
method that returns a new three-value enum `IsIdentity`. It also
pre-computes that `IsIdentity` for each response and stores it in the
new `Response::var_values_is_identity` field.

This is a perf win because it avoids repeated traversals.
author: Nicholas Nethercote

message:
Special-case canonical bound vars in `unify_query_var_values`

This avoids a lot of calls to `instantiate_value`.
author: Nicholas Nethercote

message:
Optimize `unify_query_var_values`

Both `unify_query_var_values` call sites are preceded by a call to
`instantiate_value` on the `var_values`. If instantiation changes any of
the elements we end up interning an entirely new list, through
`fold_list`.

This commit changes things so that `unify_query_var_values` does
instantiation on individual elements as it iterates, and avoids having
to intern an entire list. This changes the caching behaviour in some
cases, but overall it's a perf win.
author: Nicholas Nethercote

message:
Instantiate a response in pieces

In `instantiate_and_apply_query_response`, instantiate the two
instantiatable parts of the response separately. This requires adding a
new method `instantiate_value` to `SolverDelegate` (r-a will need
updating separately) and making a function of the same name in
`rustc_infer` public.

Do a similar thing for `State` in `instantiate_canonical_state`.

This is equivalent behaviour that will enable further changes in
subsequent commits.

message:
Rollup merge of #164958 - Web4everyone32:uefi-env-rollback-on-spawn-failure, r=joboet

uefi: roll back env changes when `start_image` fails

Fixes rust-lang/rust#164949

On UEFI, `process::output` applies the child's environment changes to the process-global UEFI environment and rolls them back after `start_image`. If `start_image` returned an error, the `?` returned early before the rollback ran, so the child's variables (notably `path`, which later `resolve_program` lookups depend on) leaked permanently into the parent.

This keeps the `start_image` result, restores the environment unconditionally, and only then propagates the error.

Tested with `./x check library --target x86_64-unknown-uefi`, `./x fmt --check` and `./x test tidy`. I have not run it on UEFI hardware or under QEMU.

cc @dvdhrm @nicholasbishop (UEFI target maintainers)

**scikit-learn** is a Python module for machine learning built on top of
SciPy and is distributed under the 3-Clause BSD license.

The project was started in 2007 by David Cournapeau as a Google Summer
of Code project, and since then many volunteers have contributed. See
the `About us <<url>>`__ page
for a list of core contributors.

It is currently maintained by a community of contributors, with volunteers but also `support from several
organisations <<url>>`__.

Website: <url>

Installation
------------

Dependencies
~~~~~~~~~~~~

scikit-learn requires:

- Python (>= |PythonMinVersion|)
- NumPy (>= |NumPyMinVersion|)
- SciPy (>= |SciPyMinVersion|)
- Narwhals (>= |NarwhalsMinVersion|)
- joblib (>= |JoblibMinVersion|)
- threadpoolctl (>= |ThreadpoolctlMinVersion|)

=======

Scikit-learn plotting capabilities (i.e., functions start with ``plot_`` and
classes end with ``Display``) require Matplotlib (>= |MatplotlibMinVersion|).
For running the examples Matplotlib >= |MatplotlibMinVersion| is required.
A few examples require scikit-image >= |Scikit-ImageMinVersion|, a few examples
require pandas >= |PandasMinVersion|, some examples require seaborn >=
|SeabornMinVersion| and Plotly >= |PlotlyMinVersion|.

User installation
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

If you already have a working installation of NumPy and SciPy,
the easiest way to install scikit-learn is using ``pip``::

  pip install -U scikit-learn

or ``conda``::

  conda install -c conda-forge scikit-learn

The documentation includes more detailed `installation instructions <<url>>`_.


Changelog
---------

See the `changelog <<url>>`__
for a history of notable changes to scikit-learn.

Development
-----------

We welcome new contributors of all experience levels. The scikit-learn
community goals are to be helpful, welcoming, and effective. The
`Development Guide <<url>>`_
has detailed information about contributing code, documentation, tests, and
more. We've included some basic information in this README.

Source code
~~~~~~~~~~~

You can check the latest sources with the command::

  git clone <url>

Contributing

`Contributing guide
<<url>>`_.

Testing
~~~~~~~

title: CI Pin all GitHub Actions to full commit SHAs
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

### TL;DR

1. Replace every external `uses: owner/repo@<tag>` with `owner/repo@<40-character SHA> # vX.Y.Z`, using the SHA of that exact release.
2. Update them with `.github/dependabot.yml` with a `cooldown` period.

-----

#34006 lists "Hash-pin all github actions used in the `publish_pypi.yml` and `wheels.yml` workflows". This issue proposes extending that to every workflow. 

Pinning all the actions follows the comment in #29180, written down in `.github/dependabot.yml`: hash-pin release-critical actions "This strategy may be generalized to all other github actions in the future." 

After this, we could add [zizmor](<url>) to the pre-commit, as it clears the `unpinned-uses` findings (mentioned in #34006). This can be discussed on a separate issue. 

### Current state

[SPEC 8](<url>), which scikit-learn endorses, requires full-SHA pinning for release workflows. But it doesn't discourage pinning elsewhere.

<details>
<summary>On `main` there are 17 actions not pinned to a SHA (69 references)</summary>

| Action | References |
|---|---|
| `actions/checkout` | 27 |
| `actions/setup-python` | 15 |
| `actions/upload-artifact` | 5 |
| `actions/download-artifact` | 4 |
| `conda-incubator/setup-miniconda` | 3 |
| `thomasjpfan/labeler` | 2 |
| `codecov/codecov-action` | 2 |
| `actions/cache` | 2 |
| `scientific-python/circleci-artifacts-redirector-action` | 1 |
| `scientific-python/action-towncrier-changelog` | 1 |
| `re-actors/alls-green` (branch `release/v1`) | 1 |
| `peter-evans/create-pull-request` | 1 |
| `github/codeql-action/init` | 1 |
| `github/codeql-action/autobuild` | 1 |
| `github/codeql-action/analyze` | 1 |
| `andymckay/labeler` | 1 |
| `actions-ecosystem/action-remove-labels` | 1 |

</details>

### Dependabot 

In #34006, @betatim recalled a concern that full pinning could make `Dependabot` stop working. 
But `Dependabot` already updates both the SHA and the `# vX.Y.Z` comment as @AnneBeyer noted (#33917). She also found that a known `Dependabot` bug can leave the version comment out of sync with the SHA (dependabot/dependabot-core#8011). However, "it is annoying but not critical" (Olivier's comment this on #34006 as well). 

We could discuss the details about `Dependabot` updates if people agree first on SHA pinning all the actions. 

### Other projects

PyPI and CPython pin every action this way, including GitHub's own `actions/*`, and Dependabot keeps the pins current:

- **PyPI** ([pypi/warehouse](<url>)): Dependabot runs daily with a 7-day cooldown. pypi/warehouse#20202 bumps `actions/checkout` 6.0.3 → 7.0.0 in all five workflows that use it, and pypi/warehouse#20780 shows the SHA and the version comment being replaced together.
- **CPython** ([python/cpython](<url>)): Dependabot runs quarterly with a 14-day cooldown, puts all actions in one group, and has a separate entry for each maintenance branch. python/cpython#159106 is a recent example.

### Why all workflows

A tag can be moved to a different commit by whoever controls the action's repository, or by someone who has compromised it. The workflow then runs the new code without any change in this repository. A commit SHA always refers to the same code.

---

title: LinearDiscriminantAnalysis: "svd" and "lsqr"/"eigen" solvers disagree when priors differ from class proportions
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm a senior data scientist and I use scikit-learn regularly for classification and modelling work. I found this while checking that the three LDA solvers give the same results as the closed-form Gaussian model. I used AI tools to help me investigate and write this report, and I reproduced the bug myself on main.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When `priors` differs from the class proportions in `y`, `LinearDiscriminantAnalysis` gives different `predict_proba` and `predict` results depending on the solver.

The cause is how the within-class covariance is weighted:
- `solver="svd"` (the default) weights each class covariance by its sample count: `sum_k (n_k / n) * C_k`.
- `solver="lsqr"` and `solver="eigen"` weight by the priors: `sum_k prior_k * C_k`, which is also how `covariance_` is documented. With `store_covariance=True`, the svd solver reports this prior-weighted `covariance_` but does not predict with it.

With `priors=None` the two weightings are identical, so the solvers agree.

Impact: setting balanced priors on imbalanced data is a common use of `priors`. Then the predictions depend on the solver, and switching solver (e.g. to use shrinkage, which "svd" does not support) silently changes them. In the example below, about 15% of the predicted labels change.

#33626 already made the solvers agree for the default priors; this is the case it does not cover.

Which weighting is intended? Weighting by class counts is the maximum likelihood estimate of the shared covariance (the priors then only enter through the log(prior_k) term), while the documentation of `covariance_` describes prior weighting.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
# 200 vs 20 samples, classes with different spread
X = np.vstack([rng.randn(200, 2) * [1.0, 0.3], rng.randn(20, 2) * [0.3, 2.0] + [1.5, 0.5]])
y = np.repeat([0, 1], [200, 20])
X_test = rng.uniform(-3, 3, size=(2000, 2))

lda = {
  solver: LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(
  solver=solver, priors=[0.5, 0.5], store_covariance=True
  ).fit(X, y)
  for solver in ["svd", "lsqr", "eigen"]
}
proba = {s: m.predict_proba(X_test) for s, m in lda.items()}
pred = {s: m.predict(X_test) for s, m in lda.items()}

print("same covariance_ for svd and lsqr:", np.allclose(lda["svd"].covariance_, lda["lsqr"].covariance_))
print("max |proba svd - proba lsqr|:", np.abs(proba["svd"] - proba["lsqr"]).max())
print("max |proba eigen - proba lsqr|:", np.abs(proba["eigen"] - proba["lsqr"]).max())
print("labels differing, svd vs lsqr:", (pred["svd"] != pred["lsqr"]).mean())
```

### Expected Results

All three solvers give the same probabilities and labels (up to floating point error), as they do with `priors=None`.

### Actual Results

```
same covariance_ for svd and lsqr: True
max |proba svd - proba lsqr|: 0.7918808064805439
max |proba eigen - proba lsqr|: 4.440892098500626e-16
labels differing, svd vs lsqr: 0.1455
```

### Versions

```shell
System:
  python: 3.13.17 (tags/v3.13.17:64e080d, Oct 21 2026, 14:08:53) [MSC v.1944 64 bit (AMD64)]
executable: C:\Users\DELL\Desktop\me\github_contrib\sklearn_issue_fix\.venv\Scripts\python.exe
  machine: Windows-11-10.0.26200-SP0

Python dependencies:
  sklearn: 1.10.dev0
  pip: 26.2.2
  setuptools: None
  numpy: 2.5.4
  scipy: 1.18.1
  Cython: 3.2.5
  pandas: None
  matplotlib: None

threadpoolctl: 3.7.0

Built with OpenMP: True

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I'd like to work on this once a maintainer confirms which behaviour is intended. Two possible fixes:

A. Keep prior weighting (matches the docs and the lsqr/eigen solvers): in `_solve_svd`, scale the centered samples of class k by `sqrt(prior_k / n_k)` instead of `sqrt(1 / n_samples)`. This is a ~4 line change. I have it working locally with a regression test, and results with `priors=None` are unchanged.

B. Use class-count weighting everywhere (the maximum likelihood estimate): change `_class_cov` so "lsqr"/"eigen" weight by `n_k / n`, and update the documentation of `covariance_`.

I'll wait for the issue to be triaged before opening a PR.

title: Should `move_estimator_to` refuse unfitted inputs?
body:

> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

Currently, one can use `move_estimator_to` on inputs before they are fitted, in which case it doesn't really do anything meaningful, and the objects are still fittable afterwards as if the function had not been called.

But since an unfitted estimator has no state to be moved, I think it would make sense to throw an error if the estimator requires fitting and the function is called on an unfitted object like that, just like methods like `.predict()` would do.

title: RFC Array API support for `KMeans` and its `"kmeans++"` inititialization
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

I prototyped some array API support for `KMeans` with the help of a coding agent. I did that by iteratively running experiments and logging results in an HTML journal maintained in an branch of an external repo that I dedicate to de-novo experiments:

- <url>

The descriptions of the repo has an up to date detailed summary of what was explored. There are even more details with experimentation results and plots in the [agent's managed journal](<url>) but the journal entries are iterative and therefore harder to interpret than the high level summary in the linked PR's description.

### Main results

- on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU, a generic array API implementation of kmeans++ and Lloyd iterations can be competitive with cuML and both can be much faster (up to 7x) than the best CPU implementation on that AWS host;
- the same array API code on CPU is not competitive with our existing Cython implementation and even less so when taking optimizations proposed by @cakedev0 (in particular <url>) into account;
- I also explored Torch- and CuPy-specific optimizations on top of the generic array API code path: those can improve performance a bit for some cases (large numbers of clusters) with moderate added complexity.

### My take

- I think I would be in favor of expanding our KMeans class to include a array API codepath for non-NumPy inputs, in particular to leverage the capabilities non-CPU devices.
- I don't think it's worth bothering with the Torch and CuPy specific codepaths in a first PR. Making a decision about backend specific array API code branches should be discussed in follow-up issues and PRs if people feel the need for them.
- I think we should keep the Cython codepath for the CPU case. It means that we will have a bit of code duplication to maintain but I think it's ok. It's similar to what we have for the Cython/array API optimized loss module used by linear models with array API support.
- I observed that CuPy is a bit slower than PyTorch CUDA (1.1x to 2.x slower depending on the data and number of clusters).

### Limitations

I have not experimented with the multiple GPU setting. I think the "scalable-kmeans++" init of cuML would make it harder for a simple array API implementation to be competitive in that more advanced setting.

title: BUG: metrics.auc returns incorrect areas for decreasing unsigned coordinates and fails monotonicity validation
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I’m Saurav Singla, a Head of Data Science working on machine learning and model evaluation.

While investigating metric correctness with AI assistance, I found that `sklearn.metrics.auc` can silently return an incorrect area when decreasing x-coordinates are stored as unsigned integers. The investigation reproduced this behavior in scikit-learn 1.7.2, 1.8.0, and 1.9.1. Equivalent floating-point inputs produce the expected result.

I’m reporting this because decreasing coordinates are explicitly supported by the documentation, and unsigned inputs also appear to bypass the monotonicity check. I could not find an existing scikit-learn issue describing this specific behavior. I’ve included a minimal reproducer and environment details below.


### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`sklearn.metrics.auc` silently computes incorrect areas when decreasing x-coordinates are stored as unsigned integers, although decreasing coordinates are explicitly supported by its documentation.

For example, with `x = np.array([2, 1, 0], dtype=np.uint8)` and `y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0])`, the expected area is `1.0`, but `auc(x, y)` returns `255.0` without a warning. Converting the same coordinates to `float64`, or reversing both arrays, returns `1.0`.

Unsigned inputs also bypass monotonicity validation: `x = np.array([0, 2, 1], dtype=np.uint8)` returns a numeric result, whereas the equivalent floating-point input raises `ValueError`.

I encountered this during a targeted investigation of metric correctness with AI assistance, rather than through a production incident. I care about evaluation results being consistent across equivalent numeric representations. For users passing unsigned coordinate arrays directly to `auc`, the behavior can silently corrupt reported areas and allow invalid curves through validation.

The behavior was reproduced in scikit-learn 1.7.2, 1.8.0, and 1.9.1. This report concerns direct calls to `auc`; it does not demonstrate a problem with ordinary `roc_auc_score` usage.


### Steps/Code to Reproduce

import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.metrics import auc

print("scikit-learn:", sklearn.__version__)

y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0])

# Valid decreasing coordinates: all three results should be 1.0.
x = np.array([2, 1, 0], dtype=np.uint8)
print("Unsigned:", auc(x, y))  # 255.0
print("Float:", auc(x.astype(np.float64), y))  # 1.0
print("Reversed:", auc(x[::-1], y[::-1]))  # 1.0

# Non-monotonic coordinates: both calls should raise ValueError.
for dtype in (np.uint8, np.float64):
  x = np.array([0, 2, 1], dtype=dtype)
  try:
  print(f"{dtype.__name__}, non-monotonic:", auc(x, y))
  except ValueError:
  print(f"{dtype.__name__}, non-monotonic: ValueError")

### Expected Results

For the valid decreasing coordinates, all three representations should return `1.0`. Converting the coordinates from unsigned integers to floats, or reversing both arrays, should not change the area.

For the non-monotonic coordinates `[0, 2, 1]`, both unsigned integer and floating-point inputs should raise `ValueError`.

Expected output, excluding the version line:

```text
Unsigned: 1.0
Float: 1.0
Reversed: 1.0
uint8, non-monotonic: ValueError
float64, non-monotonic: ValueError
```


### Actual Results

Observed output on scikit-learn 1.9.1:

```text
scikit-learn: 1.9.1
Unsigned: 255.0
Float: 1.0
Reversed: 1.0
uint8, non-monotonic: 128.5
float64, non-monotonic: ValueError
```

The decreasing unsigned coordinates produce `255.0` instead of `1.0`. The non-monotonic unsigned coordinates return `128.5` instead of raising `ValueError`.

Both incorrect unsigned-input results are returned silently, without a warning or exception, so there is no traceback for the reported failures. The `ValueError` for the floating-point control is expected and caught by the reproducer.

The same results were also reproduced on scikit-learn 1.7.2 and 1.8.0, using NumPy 2.3.5 and SciPy 1.17.0.


### Versions

```shell
System:
  python: 3.12.14 (main, Aug 25 2026, 14:00:49) [Clang 22.1.3 ]
executable: /opt/codex/runtimes/codex-primary-runtime/dependencies/python/bin/python
  machine: Linux-6.18.55-x86_64-with-glibc2.39

Python dependencies:

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I would be interested in working on a PR after maintainers confirm and triage the issue, with AI assistance disclosed.

The apparent root cause is that `auc` uses `np.diff(x)` to determine direction and validate monotonicity. For unsigned inputs, decreasing differences wrap to positive values, so these checks fail. The subsequent trapezoidal integration also performs subtraction on the unsigned coordinates.

A possible fix would:

* Determine monotonicity and direction using direct comparisons between adjacent coordinates, avoiding subtraction.
* Ensure coordinate differences used for integration are computed safely.
* Add regression tests for decreasing and non-monotonic inputs across unsigned integer types, with signed integer and floating-point controls.

The dtype strategy needs care: blindly converting `uint64` to `int64` can overflow, while converting to `float64` can lose precision for large integers. I would discuss the preferred handling with maintainers before implementing it.

I will wait for triage before opening a PR.

title: Categorical trees: error message and docstring state the wrong limit for categorical_features
body:
### Describe the bug

With the new native categorical support in trees (#33354, #33972, forests in #34832), the input values get ordinal-encoded internally before validation, so the raw category values can be anything (negative, non-integer, > 255). The real limit is on the **number** of distinct categories, and it's 256 (not 255) with `splitter="best"`.

But the docstring and error message still describe the older "codes must already be in [0, 255]" design:

- the `categorical_features` docstring (`DecisionTreeClassifier`, `DecisionTreeRegressor` and the forests) says "at most 255 unique categories", but 256 work fine (all 256 predicted correctly, also with missing values present)
- with 257+ categories the error says `Values for categorical features should be integers in [0, 255]. Found 256.` even when my values are e.g. `1000..1256`. The `256` is the internal encoded max (`n_cats - 1`), not something from my data, so the message points at the wrong problem
- same wording for `splitter="random"`: `integers in [0, 16777215]`

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

# 1. values outside [0, 255], negative and non-integer values are all accepted
X = np.array([[-1.0], [0.5], [300.0], [2000.0]] * 10)
y = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0] * 10)
tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(categorical_features=[0]).fit(X, y)
print(tree.predict([[-1.0], [0.5], [300.0], [2000.0]]))

# 2. 256 unique categories are accepted (docstring says at most 255)
X = np.arange(256, dtype=float).reshape(-1, 1)
DecisionTreeRegressor(categorical_features=[0]).fit(X, np.arange(256.0))
print("256 categories: fitted")

# 3. 257 unique categories: the error talks about the value range
X = np.arange(1000, 1257, dtype=float).reshape(-1, 1)
DecisionTreeRegressor(categorical_features=[0]).fit(X, np.arange(257.0))
```

### Expected Results

- the docstring states the real limit (256 categories with `splitter="best"`)
- the error describes the actual problem, e.g. `Categorical feature 0 has 257 categories, but at most 256 are supported with splitter="best".`

### Actual Results

```
[1. 2. 3. 4.]
256 categories: fitted
ValueError: Values for categorical features should be integers in [0, 255]. Found 256.
```

### Additional context

I think this comes from the first version of #33354, where the codes had to be "contiguous integers in [0, 255]". The ordinal encoding was added later, but the message and docstring weren't updated. #35181 moves this check but keeps the same message, so cc @cakedev0. Happy to open a PR for it, either after #35181 or folded into it, whichever you prefer.

### Versions

```
sklearn: 1.10.dev0 (nightly wheel, main @ 59106029d)
python: 3.12.4, Windows 11
numpy: 2.6.0.dev0, scipy: 2.0.0.dev0, pandas: 3.2.0.dev0
narwhals: 2.27.1, joblib: 1.6.0, threadpoolctl: 3.7.0
```

_Disclosure: I used Claude Code to help with the investigation._

title: `move_estimator_to` could check for array API compatibility
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

Currently, `move_estimator_to` will happily accept any estimator and silently move its public attributes to the requested namespace regardless of whether the resulting output will be usable or not.

Currently, there is a tag for array API support, but it appears to be based on whether `.fit()` will work only, while it is possible to successfully move and call prediction methods on cases that were fitted with parameters not covered by array API.

For instance, this works:
```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

from sklearn import set_config
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(20, 3))
y = rng.standard_normal(size=X.shape[0])

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = LinearRegression(positive=True).fit(X, y)

import array_api_strict
from sklearn.utils._array_api import get_namespace_and_device, move_to, move_estimator_to
xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(array_api_strict.zeros(1))
model_moved = move_estimator_to(model, xp=xp, device=device)
X_moved = move_to(X, xp=xp, device=device)

model_moved.predict(X_moved)
```
```
Array([-0.14719218,  0.27491875,
  0.15094873,  0.00518319,
  -0.24659107,  0.47541943,
  0.08403356,  0.47856467,
  -0.0745007 ,  0.10200964,
  -0.42983405, -0.14796583,
  0.55067349,  0.21196237,
  -0.07794093, -0.04677004,
  -0.26202396, -0.01739524,
  -0.21785575,  0.04422776], dtype=array_api_strict.float64)
```

Even though the tag declares it not so:
```python
from sklearn.base import get_tags
get_tags(model_moved).array_api_support
```
```
False
```

However, this will not work and the user will not find out until they try to use the result:
```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

from sklearn import set_config
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(20, 3))
y = rng.integers(2, size=X.shape[0])

from sklearn.svm import SVC
model = SVC().fit(X, y)

import array_api_strict
from sklearn.utils._array_api import get_namespace_and_device, move_to, move_estimator_to
xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(array_api_strict.zeros(1))
model_moved = move_estimator_to(model, xp=xp, device=device)
```
```python
X_moved = move_to(X, xp=xp, device=device)
model_moved.predict(X_moved)
```
```
TypeError: 'dtype' must be a dtype, not a <class 'type'>
```

title: PERF Utilize all cores in the face of uneven workloads
body: > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](), and in particular the sections for [new contributors]() and the ["Needs triage"]() label. In some cases sklearn breaks up work using `gen_even_slices()`. The typical number of slices is `n_jobs`. Here's an example from KNeighbors: ```python chunked_results = Parallel(n_jobs, prefer="threads")( delayed(self._tree.query)(X[s], n_neighbors, return_distance) for s in gen_even_slices(X.shape[0], n_jobs) ) ``` If each slice takes the exact amount of time, this is fine. ## The problem ### Uneven workloads mean reduced parallelism However, what happens if one slice takes longer to process? Since there is one slice per thread, the other threads will sit idle. That means effective parallelism is lower than requested parallelism. And in fact this happens with KNeighbors in some cases. Here's a sample profile, visualized as a timeline ([original]()). **Notice how most of the worker threads just sit idle towards the end, waiting for one or two of the threads to finish:** ### The solution: smaller chunks of work If you split up the input array into a larger number of smaller chunks, e.g. `n_jobs * 30`, you end up with much smaller holes of idleness at the end. That means higher effective parallelism. And then as long as the number of chunks isn't too large to start hitting the overhead of scheduling a task, you end up with faster results. ## Places where this might be the case If workload times are exactly proportional to input size, splitting up into more slices isn't necessary. So each case would need to be benchmarked separately. I'm pretty sure KNeighbors benefits, at minimum. ``` sklearn/decomposition/_lda.py 463: for idx_slice in gen_even_slices(X.shape[0], n_jobs) sklearn/decomposition/_dict_learning.py 444: slices = list(gen_even_slices(n_samples, effective_n_jobs(n_jobs))) sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py 1970: for s in gen_even_slices(_num_samples(Y), effective_n_jobs(n_jobs)) sklearn/neighbors/_base.py 912: for s in gen_even_slices(X.shape[0], n_jobs) 1269: for s in gen_even_slices(X.shape[0], n_jobs) ```
