title: RFC Maintainer Quality of Life improvement project
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

### Foreword

I am opening this to a few ideas I have in the back of my mind. Any kind of comments, feed-back, suggestions or help on this would be more than welcome!

The pain points this issue is trying to address are not well-defined and multi-factorial, but my hope is that we can identify smaller problems that can be addressed and that contribute to maintaining the project being a more pleasant experience.

As an example of super useful automation, the rule to auto-close PRs fixing an issue which has "Needs Triage" label <url> by @virchan. We need more of this kind of things!

I am completely aware that some problems are on the human interaction side and can not be fixed by technological means. I am also well aware of the caveat of working on automation for the sake of automation and forgetting that it should help making the project more maintainable. If I put an idea below it's because I thought about it a bit and think it's worth doing it. Of course, you may disagree with me, and I would be happy to hear your objections!

cc @scikit-learn/core-devs @scikit-learn/contributor-experience-team 

### Add a few automated labels to make it easier to filter issues

In an ideal world GitHub would have this kind of features built-in but it doesn't 😓, trust me I double-checked 😉.

- PR diff size labels: #35142. PR diff size is an imperfect but good enough proxy to estimate how much time/energy a PR takes to review/merge. It's complementary to the "Quick review" label that is set manually.
- TODO number of approval labels. I envisage a label `review:one-approval`, `review:two-approvals`. One tweak would be that Contributor Experience Team members approvals are counted. Optionally a `review:ongoing` as soon as someone did a review, so that we can try to remember to follow-up.
- TODO contributor type of labels: `first-time-contributor`, `early-contributor` (less than 10 PRs merged), `seasoned-contributor` (more than 10 PR merged), `team-member`. This would be convenient to be able to filter between different modes of reviews rather than going to the default PR page, being driven by notifications, or other semi-random factors ...

One useful follow-up once we have these labels is to create additional [Views](<url>) to use them more easily.

### Add profile information to issue/PRs automatically to help dealing with automated accounts

see [comment for vibe-check](<url>): rough consensus on this.

The first thing is to show a summary of the profile information. We can discuss later about acting on it, like auto-closing the issue/PR, blocking the account, but let's first start by making the info easily accessible.

Tools that already exist:

- **AgentScan** they have an action used by plenty of "popular" projects, like [Node.js](<url>), [StoryBook](<url>), [Vite](<url>). This is the first thing I use these days to do a [user scan](<url>). There is also a [scikit-learn repo scan](<url>) but less useful. In my experience, AgentScan is a bit too "nice" in the sense that I have seen accounts labeled as "organic", although it was a clear block for me, like 5-10 PRs opened in unrelated repos in the same day or so. 
- **[Anti slop](<url>)**: used by "popular" projects like [HuggingFace Transformers](<url>) see [automated comment](<url>). It's more a list of "simple rules" to check to avoid common patterns.
- **gh-profiler**: nice little tool but a bit limited. This is where I got the idea from showing the profile info in issues/PRs. For completeness, I opened an issue about tweaking the gh-profiler format and didn't get any reply so far [^1] <url>

[^1]: which is completely fine of course, we are all busy open-source maintainers

### Miscellaneous and not fully decided ideas

- rule for duplicate PRs: see [comment](<url>) for quick vibe-check

- rule to have early contributors (less than 10 PRs merged) open an issue before opening a PR? This adds a bit of latency in the system which I think is a good thing, even if it is a bit sad in a way that we have to do it ... see [comment](<url>) for quick vibe-check (not really a consensus yet)

title: Add `reliability_curve` and `ReliabilityDisplay` for regressors
body:
> [!WARNING]

### Introduce yourself

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I'd like to move forward with adding a reliability curve and display class for regressors.
This has been agreed upon as a follow-up topic in <url> (I don't intend to address the `reliability_error` part here, which will be a topic of its own, but I think the curve and display can be added independent of that).
It was also previously noted as desirable to have in B.1. in issue <url>

This can then also be used in [this example](<url>).

As discussed with @ogrisel, it could also be extended to support quantile regression, possibly implemented as a `kwarg` variation in a follow-up, which can then be used to simplify <url>

### Describe your proposed solution

I would start with implementing `reliability_curve` and `ReliabilityDisplay` for mean regression, similar to the calibration counterparts we already have for classification.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

There will be overlap with the calibration counterparts, but as was already discussed in <url> `calibration_curve` (and `CalibrationDisplay`) are classifier specific and 
>retro-fitting it to accommodate regressions would make the signature a little funky

so <url> suggested to use separate implementations and the `reliability` terminology for the regression case.

### Additional context

@lorentzenchr's [model-diagnostics](<url>) implements `plot_reliability_diagram` using isotonic regression, which has also been proposed for classification in #23132 and #23824. From what I understand, this can also be used as `strategy` for regression. I'd start from the recently updated default values of `calibration_curve` (`n_bins=cube_root` and `startegy=quantile`), and leave this as a follow-up.

title: HistGradientBoostingClassifier: multiclass training loss diverges at default hyperparameters (LightGBM/XGBoost at equivalent settings do not)
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

### Describe the bug

On Covertype, `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` with **every hyperparameter at its default** (only `max_iter=200, early_stopping=False, random_state=0` set) reaches a minimum *training* log-loss of 0.418 at iteration 55, and then **rises**: 1.08 at iteration 100, 1.93 at 200. 87 of the 200 iterations increase the training loss, and leaf values reach 2.2e4. The fit is deterministic (a second fit is bit-identical) and gives identical numbers on aarch64 (AWS Graviton4) and x86. On the full dataset with `max_leaf_nodes=255` it goes 0.200 at iteration 40 → 0.817 at 100, with leaves reaching 5.7e4.

LightGBM 4.7.0 and XGBoost 3.4.2, configured through scikit-learn's own `get_equivalent_estimator` (l2 = 0; XGBoost's learning rate doubled for its 2p(1−p) hessian), decrease monotonically on the same rows, to 0.16 and 0.15.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_covtype
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import log_loss

X, y = fetch_covtype(return_X_y=True)
idx = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(y))[:20000]
X, y = X[idx, :10], y[idx]  # 10 numeric features, 7 classes

m = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=200, early_stopping=False, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
for k, p in enumerate(m.staged_predict_proba(X), 1):
  if k in (25, 50, 55, 100, 200):
  print(k, round(log_loss(y, p, labels=m.classes_), 4))
```

The exact script that produced the numbers here (it also does the parameter sweep and the LightGBM/XGBoost comparison) is [hgb_repro.py](<url>), and [hgb-repro.log](<url>) is its output (scikit-learn 1.9.1, numpy 2.5).

### Expected Results

Training loss that does not increase for dozens of iterations at default settings, as with LightGBM/XGBoost at equivalent settings.

### Actual Results

`25: 0.4847, 50: 0.4380, (min 0.4180 @ 55), 100: 1.0845, 200: 1.9335`

### What makes it go away (one change at a time)

- **Fixes it:** `l2_regularization` ≥ 0.01; `min_hessian_to_split` ≥ 0.01 (patched into `TreeGrower`, as it isn't an estimator parameter); `learning_rate=0.05`; a zero baseline instead of the log class priors; **`min_samples_leaf=1`**.
- **Does not fix it:** `max_leaf_nodes` 7, 15 or 255 (255 is worst); `min_samples_leaf` 5 or 100; `min_hessian_to_split=0.002`. `learning_rate=0.2` makes it worse.

At `min_samples_leaf=1`, sklearn and LightGBM agree (0.155 vs 0.152 at iteration 200). At 5 and 20, only sklearn diverges. A likely reason: LightGBM checks `min_data_in_leaf` against bin counts *estimated from hessians* (`cnt_factor = num_data / sum_hessian` in `feature_histogram.hpp`), while sklearn uses true counts. sklearn can therefore build ~20–40-row leaves whose hessian sum is barely above `min_hessian_to_split=1e-3`. In the first rising iteration (20), one such leaf has 34 rows, G = 2.0, H = 1.05e-3 and a step of −191. That is my reading of the evidence, not a verified root cause.

With the default `early_stopping='auto'`, the fit stops at `n_iter_=11` (training loss 0.64), with leaf values already at 1.9e3.

Possible remedies: a documentation note on `l2_regularization`/`min_samples_leaf` for multiclass; a small non-zero default `l2_regularization` (XGBoost defaults to `lambda=1`); or exposing `min_hessian_to_split`.

### Versions

scikit-learn 1.9.1, numpy 2.5.4, scipy 1.18.1, Python 3.14 (conda-forge), on linux-aarch64 and linux-64. Results are identical on both.

title: NeighborhoodComponentsAnalysis.fit rejects string class labels on main
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

### Introduce yourself

I use NeighborhoodComponentsAnalysis as a supervised projection in front of a KNeighborsClassifier, with class labels that are strings. I ran my pipeline against the development branch and it stopped fitting.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

On main, `NeighborhoodComponentsAnalysis.fit` raises a `ValueError` as soon as `y` holds string labels, whether `y` is a NumPy string array, a plain Python list of strings or an object array. Integer labels still work. On the released 1.9.1 the same calls fit without error, so this is a regression on main that has not reached a release yet. String labels are a normal input for a supervised estimator, and anyone with a `NeighborhoodComponentsAnalysis` + `KNeighborsClassifier` pipeline on string classes will get this error once the change ships.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np

from sklearn.neighbors import NeighborhoodComponentsAnalysis

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X = rng.rand(10, 2)
cases = {
  "int labels": np.arange(10) % 2,
  "str ndarray": np.array(["a", "b"] * 5),
  "str list": ["a", "b"] * 5,
  "object ndarray": np.array(["a", "b"] * 5, dtype=object),
}

for name, y in cases.items():
  try:
  NeighborhoodComponentsAnalysis(max_iter=2).fit(X, y)
  observed = "fit ok"
  except Exception as exc:
  observed = f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"
  print(f"{name:15s} observed: {observed}")
  print(f"{'':15s} expected: fit ok")
```

### Expected Results

All four cases fit, as they do on 1.9.1:

```
int labels  observed: fit ok
str ndarray  observed: fit ok
str list  observed: fit ok
object ndarray  observed: fit ok
```

### Actual Results

On main (85593ca7a0):

```
int labels  observed: fit ok
  expected: fit ok
str ndarray  observed: ValueError: dtype='numeric' is not compatible with arrays of bytes/strings.Convert your data to numeric values explicitly instead.
  expected: fit ok
str list  observed: ValueError: dtype='numeric' is not compatible with arrays of bytes/strings.Convert your data to numeric values explicitly instead.
  expected: fit ok
object ndarray  observed: ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'a'
  expected: fit ok
```

### Versions

```shell
System:
  python: 3.12.3 (main, Aug 31 2026, 10:18:26) [GCC 13.3.0]
executable: <venv>/bin/python
  machine: Linux-7.1.5-76070105-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.39

Python dependencies:
  sklearn: 1.9.1
  pip: None
  setuptools: None
  numpy: 2.5.4
  scipy: 1.18.1
  Cython: None
  pandas: 3.0.6
  matplotlib: None
  joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.7.0
  narwhals: 2.27.1

Built with OpenMP: True
```

OS: Pop!_OS 24.04 LTS. This environment is the 1.9.1 wheel with `sklearn/neighbors/_nca.py` replaced by the file from main at 85593ca7a0, which is the only file involved; the unmodified 1.9.1 wheel gives "fit ok" in all four cases.

### Interest in fixing the bug

The cause is the input validation in `fit` (`sklearn/neighbors/_nca.py` lines 243-251 at 85593ca7a0), changed in #34122. It now calls `validate_data(..., validate_separately=(...))`, and that branch validates `y` with `check_array(y, input_name="y", accept_sparse=False, ensure_2d=False)` (`sklearn/utils/validation.py` line 3048), which keeps the default `dtype="numeric"` (line 734) and so rejects string arrays (lines 1072-1076). Before #34122 the call was `validate_data(self, X, y, ensure_min_samples=2)`, which sends `y` through `_check_y` and `column_or_1d` with `dtype=None`; the code right after validation already calls `check_classification_targets(y)` and `LabelEncoder().fit_transform(y)`, so non-numeric labels are expected there. `test_nca.py` has no test fitting on string labels, and the common string-label classifier check does not run on a transformer, which is why the test suite still passes.

The smallest fix is to add `"dtype": None` to the `y` dict passed to `validate_separately`. A test fitting NCA on `str` and on `object` labels, checking that the result matches the integer-label fit, would keep this from coming back. I am happy to open a PR with the fix and the test.

title: Temperature calibration gives wrong probabilities when labels are not 0..k-1
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

### Introduce yourself

I calibrate multiclass models with `CalibratedClassifierCV` and tried the new temperature scaling method on a dataset whose classes are coded 1, 2 and 3. The probabilities looked off compared to sigmoid calibration, so I compared against the same data with the labels shifted to start at 0.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With `method="temperature"`, `CalibratedClassifierCV.fit` only label-encodes `y` when its first element is a `str`. Integer labels that are not already `0..n_classes-1` (for example 1/2, -1/1 or 1/2/3) are passed to the temperature fit as raw class indices. The fitted temperatures are then wrong and `predict_proba` changes when the classes are only renamed. There is no error or warning. With labels 1/2 every fold's `beta_` lands on the lower bound of the search, exp(-10), which flattens the calibrated probabilities. String labels give exactly the same result as 0/1, so the bug only affects integer labels outside `0..n_classes-1`. This happens with both `ensemble=True` and `ensemble=False`, and on 1.8 and 1.9, so released versions are affected.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np

from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression


def fit_temperature(X, y, ensemble):
  clf = CalibratedClassifierCV(
  LogisticRegression(), method="temperature", cv=3, ensemble=ensemble
  ).fit(X, y)
  betas = [float(c.calibrators[0].beta_) for c in clf.calibrated_classifiers_]
  return np.round(betas, 6), clf.predict_proba(X)


X, y = make_classification(n_samples=60, n_features=4, random_state=0)
X3, y3 = make_classification(
  n_samples=60, n_features=4, n_informative=3, n_redundant=1, n_classes=3, random_state=0
)
problems = {
  "binary": (X, y, {"1/2": y + 1, "-1/1": 2 * y - 1, "str": np.array(["a", "b"])[y]}),
  "3-class": (X3, y3, {"1/2/3": y3 + 1, "str": np.array(["a", "b", "c"])[y3]}),
}

for problem, (Xp, y0, relabelled) in problems.items():
  for ensemble in (True, False):
  ref_betas, ref_proba = fit_temperature(Xp, y0, ensemble)
  print(f"{problem}, ensemble={ensemble}, labels 0..k-1: beta_ = {ref_betas}")
  for name, yr in relabelled.items():
  betas, proba = fit_temperature(Xp, yr, ensemble)
  same = np.allclose(proba, ref_proba)
  print(f"  labels {name:6s}: beta_ = {betas}")
  print(f"  predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed {same}, expected True")
print(f"exp(-10) = {np.exp(-10):.6f} (lower bound of the beta search)")
```

### Expected Results

Renaming the classes should not change the calibration: for every relabelling, `beta_` should match the `0..k-1` fit and `predict_proba` should be equal to it (`True` on every line), as it already is for string labels.

### Actual Results

```
binary, ensemble=True, labels 0..k-1: beta_ = [0.740325 0.383557 0.434524]
  labels 1/2  : beta_ = [4.5e-05 4.5e-05 4.5e-05]
  predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed False, expected True
  labels -1/1  : beta_ = [4.500000e-05 1.823720e-01 1.619173e+00]
  predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed False, expected True
  labels str  : beta_ = [0.740325 0.383557 0.434524]
  predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed True, expected True
binary, ensemble=False, labels 0..k-1: beta_ = [0.468948]
  labels 1/2  : beta_ = [4.5e-05]
  predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed False, expected True
  labels -1/1  : beta_ = [0.192596]
  predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed False, expected True
  labels str  : beta_ = [0.468948]
  predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed True, expected True
3-class, ensemble=True, labels 0..k-1: beta_ = [0.878013 0.526881 1.740861]
  labels 1/2/3 : beta_ = [4.500e-05 4.500e-05 5.229e-02]
  predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed False, expected True
  labels str  : beta_ = [0.878013 0.526881 1.740861]
  predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed True, expected True
3-class, ensemble=False, labels 0..k-1: beta_ = [0.842258]
  labels 1/2/3 : beta_ = [4.5e-05]
  predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed False, expected True
  labels str  : beta_ = [0.842258]
  predict_proba equal to 0..k-1 result: observed True, expected True
exp(-10) = 0.000045 (lower bound of the beta search)
```

### Versions

```shell
System:
  python: 3.12.3 (main, Aug 31 2026, 10:18:26) [GCC 13.3.0]
executable: <venv>/bin/python
  machine: Linux-7.1.5-76070105-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.39

Python dependencies:
  sklearn: 1.9.1
  pip: None
  setuptools: None
  numpy: 2.5.4
  scipy: 1.18.1
  Cython: None
  pandas: 3.0.6
  matplotlib: None
  joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.7.0
  narwhals: 2.27.1

Built with OpenMP: True
```

OS: Pop!_OS 24.04 LTS. The same code is on main.

### Interest in fixing the bug

The guard is in `CalibratedClassifierCV.fit` (`sklearn/calibration.py` lines 483-487 at 85593ca7a0, line 377 in 1.9.1): `if self.method == "temperature" and isinstance(y[0], str): y = label_encoder_.transform(y=y)`. Temperature scaling came in with #31068 and the guard was last changed in #32246. For integer labels `y` reaches `_TemperatureScaling.fit` unencoded, where `labels = column_or_1d(y, dtype=dtype_)` (line 1205) goes into `HalfMultinomialLoss`. The loss uses the label directly as a column index, `k = int(y_true[i])` and then `raw_prediction[i, k]` (`sklearn/_loss/_loss.pyx.tp` lines 1271-1272). With labels 1/2 the positive class indexes column 2 of a two-column row, and -1 indexes before the row. The extension is built with `wraparound=False` and bounds checks off (`sklearn/meson.build` line 186), so these indices read outside the row instead of raising.

The fix I would propose is to encode `y` whenever `self.method == "temperature"`, dropping the `isinstance(y[0], str)` condition. I tried that change locally on 1.9.1, and `predict_proba` then matches the `0..k-1` result for all the relabellings above with both `ensemble` values. A regression test could check that `predict_proba` does not change when the labels are shifted or remapped, for `ensemble=True` and `ensemble=False`. I am happy to open a PR with the fix and the test.

title: IterativeImputer(keep_empty_features=True) modifies the input array in place
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

### Introduce yourself

I use scikit-learn for tabular modelling and use `IterativeImputer` with `keep_empty_features=True` so that the output keeps the input's columns.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With `keep_empty_features=True`, `IterativeImputer.fit_transform` and `transform` write into the array I pass in. For a Fortran-ordered float64 array with an all-missing column, that column in my own array is replaced by zeros after the call, so later code that looks at the original data no longer sees the missing values. For a pandas DataFrame the same write hits a read-only view of the frame's data, so `fit_transform` raises `ValueError: assignment destination is read-only` on any float frame, even one without an empty column. With `keep_empty_features=False` both inputs work and are left unchanged.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer  # noqa: F401
from sklearn.impute import IterativeImputer

# 1. F-ordered float64 array with an all-missing column is modified in place.
X = np.asfortranarray(
  [[1.0, np.nan, 3.0], [4.0, np.nan, np.nan], [7.0, np.nan, 9.0], [2.0, np.nan, 5.0]]
)
X_before = X.copy()
IterativeImputer(keep_empty_features=True, max_iter=2).fit_transform(X)
print("fit_transform: input column 1 before:", X_before[:, 1].tolist())
print("fit_transform: input column 1 after: ", X[:, 1].tolist())
print("fit_transform: input unchanged:", np.array_equal(X, X_before, equal_nan=True),
  "(expected True)")

imp = IterativeImputer(keep_empty_features=True, max_iter=2).fit(X_before.copy(order="F"))
X_new = X_before.copy(order="F")
imp.transform(X_new)
print("transform: input unchanged:", np.array_equal(X_new, X_before, equal_nan=True),
  "(expected True)")

# 2. A pandas DataFrame, here without any empty column, fails because the
# array is a read-only view of the frame's data.
df = pd.DataFrame(
  {"x0": [1.0, 2.0, np.nan, 4.0, 5.0], "x1": [2.0, 1.0, 3.0, 5.0, 4.0]}
)
print("DataFrame, keep_empty_features=False:",
  IterativeImputer(keep_empty_features=False, max_iter=2).fit_transform(df).shape)
try:
  out = IterativeImputer(keep_empty_features=True, max_iter=2).fit_transform(df)
  print("DataFrame, keep_empty_features=True:", out.shape)
except Exception as exc:
  print("DataFrame, keep_empty_features=True: observed", type(exc).__name__ + ":", exc)
print("DataFrame, keep_empty_features=True: expected an imputed (5, 2) array")
```

### Expected Results

The input is never modified, and the DataFrame is imputed as it is with `keep_empty_features=False`:

```
fit_transform: input unchanged: True
transform: input unchanged: True
DataFrame, keep_empty_features=True: (5, 2)
```

### Actual Results

```
fit_transform: input column 1 before: [nan, nan, nan, nan]
fit_transform: input column 1 after:  [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
fit_transform: input unchanged: False (expected True)
transform: input unchanged: False (expected True)
DataFrame, keep_empty_features=False: (5, 2)
DataFrame, keep_empty_features=True: observed ValueError: assignment destination is read-only
DataFrame, keep_empty_features=True: expected an imputed (5, 2) array
```

  File "<venv>/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/impute/_iterative.py", line 773, in fit_transform

  File "<venv>/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/impute/_iterative.py", line 666, in _initial_imputation

title: Multimetric scoring mixes up scorers that differ only in pos_label
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

### Introduce yourself

I use scikit-learn for binary classification work and evaluate models with `cross_validate` and `GridSearchCV` using several scorers at once.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When a `scoring` dict contains two scorers that use the same response method but different `pos_label`, for example average precision for class 0 and for class 1, the second scorer silently receives the response computed for the first scorer's `pos_label`. Its scores are wrong, with no error or warning. Scored alone, the same scorer gives the right value. This affects `cross_validate` and anything else that builds a multimetric scorer, such as `GridSearchCV` with a `scoring` dict and a `refit` choice based on those scores. It happens with both `response_method="predict_proba"` and `response_method="decision_function"`.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, make_scorer
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X = rng.randn(60, 3)
y = (X[:, 0] + 0.5 * rng.randn(60) > 0).astype(int)

for response_method in ("predict_proba", "decision_function"):
  ap_neg = make_scorer(
  average_precision_score, response_method=response_method, pos_label=0
  )
  ap_pos = make_scorer(
  average_precision_score, response_method=response_method, pos_label=1
  )
  clf = LogisticRegression()

  alone = cross_validate(clf, X, y, cv=3, scoring={"ap_pos": ap_pos})
  both = cross_validate(clf, X, y, cv=3, scoring={"ap_neg": ap_neg, "ap_pos": ap_pos})

  print(response_method)
  print("  expected test_ap_pos (ap_pos alone):  ", np.round(alone["test_ap_pos"], 3))
  print("  observed test_ap_pos (with ap_neg too):", np.round(both["test_ap_pos"], 3))
  print("  test_ap_neg:", np.round(both["test_ap_neg"], 3))
```

### Expected Results

`test_ap_pos` is the same whether `ap_pos` is the only scorer or is evaluated together with `ap_neg`:

```
expected test_ap_pos (ap_pos alone):  [0.901 0.965 0.932]
```

### Actual Results

```
predict_proba
  expected test_ap_pos (ap_pos alone):  [0.901 0.965 0.932]
  observed test_ap_pos (with ap_neg too): [0.456 0.379 0.391]
  test_ap_neg: [0.811 0.944 0.893]
decision_function
  expected test_ap_pos (ap_pos alone):  [0.901 0.965 0.932]
  observed test_ap_pos (with ap_neg too): [0.456 0.379 0.391]
  test_ap_neg: [0.811 0.944 0.893]
```

With `ap_neg` in the same dict, `test_ap_pos` drops from about 0.93 to about 0.4 in every fold, for both response methods.

### Versions

```shell

executable: <venv>/bin/python
  machine: Linux-7.1.5-76070105-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.39

```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The cause is `_cached_call` in `sklearn/metrics/_scorer.py` at 85593ca7a0, lines 92-104. The multimetric cache is keyed on the response method name only, but the value it stores is the output of `_get_response_values(..., pos_label=pos_label)`, which is already specific to `pos_label`: the `predict_proba` column for that class, or `decision_function` with its sign flipped when `pos_label` is the first class. `_Scorer._score` passes each scorer's own `pos_label` (lines 461-466), and `_use_cache` (line 195) enables the cache exactly when two scorers share a response method, so the second scorer gets the first scorer's output. Before #26037 (1.3.0) the cache held the raw method output and each scorer selected its own column afterwards, so this looks like a regression from that change. No test in `sklearn/metrics/tests/test_score_objects.py` combines two scorers that differ only in `pos_label`.

A fix is to key the cache on the pair `(response_method, pos_label)`, or to cache the raw response and apply the `pos_label` selection per scorer after the lookup. I would add a test with two scorers that differ only in `pos_label`, for `predict_proba` and `decision_function`. I am happy to open a PR for this.

title: OrdinalEncoder.inverse_transform swaps infrequent and missing values
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

### Introduce yourself

I use scikit-learn for tabular modelling and rely on `OrdinalEncoder` with `min_frequency` on columns that also contain missing values.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

For a feature that has both infrequent categories and missing values, `OrdinalEncoder.inverse_transform` decodes the infrequent rows to NaN and the missing rows to `"infrequent_sklearn"`. `transform` is correct, so the round trip silently swaps the two groups with no error or warning. Anything that decodes encoded data back to the original labels, for example to report or inspect predictions per category, gets the wrong labels for those rows.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np

from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder

# One feature with two frequent categories, one infrequent category and
# two missing values.
X = np.array(["a"] * 5 + ["b"] * 5 + ["c"] + [np.nan] * 2, dtype=object).reshape(-1, 1)

enc = OrdinalEncoder(min_frequency=2).fit(X)
print("categories_:", enc.categories_[0].tolist())
print("infrequent_categories_:", enc.infrequent_categories_[0].tolist())

Xt = enc.transform(X)
print("transform, last 3 rows:", Xt[-3:, 0].tolist())

X_inv = enc.inverse_transform(Xt)
print("observed inverse_transform, last 3 rows:", X_inv[-3:, 0].tolist())
print("expected inverse_transform, last 3 rows:", ["infrequent_sklearn", np.nan, np.nan])
```

### Expected Results

The infrequent row decodes to `"infrequent_sklearn"` and the two missing rows decode to NaN:

```
expected inverse_transform, last 3 rows: ['infrequent_sklearn', nan, nan]
```

### Actual Results

```
categories_: ['a', 'b', 'c', nan]
infrequent_categories_: ['c']
transform, last 3 rows: [2.0, nan, nan]
observed inverse_transform, last 3 rows: [nan, 'infrequent_sklearn', 'infrequent_sklearn']
expected inverse_transform, last 3 rows: ['infrequent_sklearn', nan, nan]
```

`transform` gives the codes 2, NaN, NaN as expected, but `inverse_transform` returns NaN for the `c` row and `infrequent_sklearn` for both missing rows.

### Versions

```shell

executable: <venv>/bin/python
  machine: Linux-7.1.5-76070105-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.39

  filepath: <venv>/lib/python3.12/site-packages/scipy.libs/libscipy_openblas-5f890258.so
  version: 0.3.31.dev

  version: 0.3.34.106.0
threading_layer: pthreads
  architecture: Haswell
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The cause is in `sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py` at 85593ca7a0, lines 1640-1658. `inverse_transform` first writes the missing index (3 here, the position of NaN in `categories_[0]`) into the missing rows at line 1643, then computes the infrequent code at line 1650 as `len(categories) - len(infrequent_indices[i])`. `len(categories)` counts the NaN category, but `_fit_infrequent_category_mapping` (lines 369-415) removes the missing category before building the mapping, so `transform` uses one code fewer. Here `inverse_transform` expects the infrequent code to be 3, which is exactly the missing index, so the missing rows are flagged as infrequent and the real infrequent code 2 is decoded through the filtered `categories`, whose last entry is NaN. This logic dates from #25677 (1.3.0) and is the same on 1.9.1. `test_ordinal_encoder_missing_appears_infrequent` in `sklearn/preprocessing/tests/test_encoders.py` only checks `transform`.

A fix is to take the infrequent code from the fitted mapping (`self._default_to_infrequent_mappings[i].max()`, or subtract one when `i in self._missing_indices`) and make sure missing rows still decode to NaN after `categories` is filtered. I would add an `inverse_transform` round trip to the missing-and-infrequent test. I am happy to open a PR for this.

_No response_

Related to <url>

When an estimator sets `feature_names_in_`, which happens whenever a DataFrame is passed to them for instance, the resulting estimator will not be movable to namespaces that do not support string arrays.

import torch

title: BUG: MinMaxScaler and MaxAbsScaler partial_fit produce NaN statistics after an all-NaN batch
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I’m Rugved, an AI Engineer Intern and machine-learning practitioner. I use scikit-learn for preprocessing, model training, evaluation, and practical machine-learning projects.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

While investigating incremental preprocessing with missing values, I found that `MinMaxScaler.partial_fit()` and `MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit()` can discard valid statistics learned from earlier batches.

If a feature contains valid values in one batch but only NaN values in a later batch, the later batch replaces the feature's accumulated statistics with NaN.

This affects users processing large or streaming datasets in batches. A batch with no valid observations for a feature should not invalidate statistics already learned for that feature. Currently, subsequent transformations of finite values in that feature also produce NaN.

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler, MaxAbsScaler

print("scikit-learn:", sklearn.__version__)

A = np.array([
  [1.0, 10.0],
  [3.0, 20.0],
])

B = np.array([
  [np.nan, 30.0],
  [np.nan, 40.0],
])

X = np.vstack([A, B])

for cls in (MinMaxScaler, MaxAbsScaler):
  batch_scaler = cls().fit(X)

  incremental_scaler = cls().partial_fit(A)
  incremental_scaler.partial_fit(B)

  print(f"\n{cls.__name__}")

  for attr in ("data_min_", "data_max_", "max_abs_", "scale_"):
  if hasattr(incremental_scaler, attr):
  print(f"{attr}: {getattr(incremental_scaler, attr)}")

  print(
  "Incremental transform:",
  incremental_scaler.transform([[2.0, 25.0]])
  )

  print(
  "Batch-fit transform:",
  batch_scaler.transform([[2.0, 25.0]])
  )
```

### Expected Results

The all-NaN values in the first feature of the second batch should be treated as missing and ignored during the incremental update.

Previously learned valid statistics should be preserved. The incremental results should match fitting on the combined dataset.

For the example above:

```text
MinMaxScaler:
data_min_: [1. 10.]
data_max_: [3. 40.]
scale_: [0.5  0.03333333]
Incremental transform: [[0.5 0.5]]

MaxAbsScaler:
max_abs_: [ 3. 40.]
scale_: [ 3. 40.]
Incremental transform: [[0.66666667 0.625]]
```

Finite input values should not be transformed to NaN merely because a later batch contains no valid observations for that feature.

### Actual Results

The second `partial_fit` call completes without raising an exception, but it corrupts the statistics for the first feature.

Observed output with scikit-learn 1.6.1:

```text
MinMaxScaler
data_min_: [nan 10.]
data_max_: [nan 40.]
scale_: [  nan 0.03333333]
Incremental transform: [[nan 0.5]]
Batch-fit transform: [[0.5 0.5]]

MaxAbsScaler
max_abs_: [nan 40.]
scale_: [nan 40.]
Incremental transform: [[  nan 0.625]]
Batch-fit transform: [[0.66666667 0.625  ]]
```

The update also emits:

```text
RuntimeWarning: All-NaN slice encountered
```

No exception is raised, but finite values in the affected feature are transformed to NaN.

### Versions

- Python: 3.12.13
- scikit-learn: 1.6.1
- NumPy: 2.0.2
- SciPy: 1.16.3
- Runtime: Linux x86_64

### Additional Context

The documentation for both scalers states that NaNs are treated as missing values and disregarded during fitting.

A related issue involving the same pattern in `StandardScaler.partial_fit()` is [#35070](<url>).

### Interest in Fixing the Bug

Yes, I would be interested in working on a PR if the issue is confirmed and triaged by the maintainers.

The apparent root cause is in the incremental aggregation logic. For an all-NaN feature, the per-batch statistic is NaN:

- `MinMaxScaler` computes `nanmin` and `nanmax`, which return NaN for an all-NaN feature.
- `MaxAbsScaler` computes the maximum absolute value, which also returns NaN for an all-NaN feature.

During subsequent `partial_fit` calls, these NaN batch statistics are merged with the previously stored statistics using ordinary minimum/maximum operations. Those operations propagate NaN and overwrite valid statistics.

A possible fix would be to merge statistics while treating a NaN batch statistic as “no new observation”:

- If the previous statistic is valid and the new batch statistic is NaN, preserve the previous value.
- If the previous statistic is NaN and the new batch statistic is valid, use the new value.
- If both values are NaN, preserve NaN because no valid observation has been seen.

I would add regression tests covering both scalers, including comparisons between incremental fitting and fitting on the combined dataset. I would wait for maintainer feedback on the intended behavior and edge cases before opening a PR.

title: `TargetEncoder.fit_transform` raises `KeyError: 'groups'` when metadata routing is enabled and no `groups` are passed
body:
### Introduce yourself

Dear all,
I am a professor of applied math at École polytechnique, very close to the Turing build, so important for the scikit-learn community. I use scikit-learn mainly for teaching, as the ones doing the hard jobs are now my students.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With `enable_metadata_routing=True`, `TargetEncoder.fit_transform(X, y)` raises `KeyError: 'groups'` when it is called without `groups`. This is the common case. It also happens inside a `ColumnTransformer` or a `Pipeline`, so any pipeline that contains a `TargetEncoder` fails as soon as routing is switched on globally. The bug does not depend on the CV splitter: the default `cv=5` and `StratifiedKFold(...)` both fail.

The cause is in `sklearn/preprocessing/_target_encoder.py` (line 366 in 1.9.1, unchanged on `main`):

```python
if _routing_enabled():
  if params["groups"] is not None:
  X, y, params["groups"] = indexable(X, y, params["groups"])
  routed_params = process_routing(self, "fit_transform", **params)
```

`params` only contains the metadata that were actually passed, so `params["groups"]` fails when no `groups` are given.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.preprocessing import TargetEncoder

sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.choice(["a", "b", "c"], size=(100, 1))
y = rng.integers(0, 2, size=100)

TargetEncoder().fit_transform(X, y)
```

### Expected Results

No error. The cross-fitted encoding should be the same as with routing disabled, since there is no metadata to route.

### Actual Results

```
  File ".../sklearn/preprocessing/_target_encoder.py", line 366, in fit_transform
  if params["groups"] is not None:
  ~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^
KeyError: 'groups'
```

### Versions

  if params["groups"] is not None:
```
by

```
in File ".../sklearn/preprocessing/_target_encoder.py", line 366.

title: BUG: HistGradientBoosting merges distinct values at upward-rounded midpoints
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi! I'm a machine learning developer. I use scikit-learn regularly for building predictive models and data analysis.

While researching how tree-based models handle highly separable datasets, I noticed an unexpected drop in accuracy in a specific edge case. I dug into the source code to understand why the model was failing to learn the separation and managed to trace it down to this specific floating-point rounding tie in the binning logic.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

There is a floating-point precision flaw in the HistGradientBoosting binning logic. When the algorithm computes the arithmetic midpoint between two very close, distinct floating-point values, the finite midpoint can round upward to equal the upper data value.

Because the threshold comparison is upper-inclusive (<= threshold), both distinct values are incorrectly lumped into the exact same bin. This prevents perfectly separable targets from being learned by the model.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Here is a minimal reproducer where 20 zeros and 20 ones are perfectly separable, but the model completely fails to distinguish them and predicts 0.5 for everything due to the midpoint rounding tie:
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor

# Create distinct values separated by a tiny margin
x_base = np.array([1, 2], dtype=np.float64)
x_transformed = 1 + (2**-52) * x_base

# Repeat to satisfy default min_samples_leaf=20
X = np.repeat(x_transformed, 20).reshape(-1, 1)
y = np.repeat([0, 1], 20)

# One boosting step with learning_rate=1 should perfectly separate this
model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=1, learning_rate=1.0)
model.fit(X, y)

print("Predictions:", model.predict(X))
```
### Expected Results

The distinct values should be separated into different bins, allowing the tree to split them and predict [0, 1] accurately.

### Actual Results

The midpoint rounds to the upper value, placing both sets of data into bin 0. The model predicts 0.5 for all samples.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.1 and current main
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I am interested in fixing this.

Root cause and strategy: The root cause is that the arithmetic midpoint of two adjacent distinct floats can round upward to precisely equal the upper float. Because the threshold split uses <=, both values are assigned to the same bin. The strategy for the fix is to detect when the computed finite midpoint equals the upper bound and in that specific case, replace the threshold with the lower bound. This mathematically guarantees the values are separated.

I already have a C-level patch and a suite of 84 regression tests prepared locally that successfully implements this strategy. I will wait for this issue to be triaged, but I am ready to open a PR for this as soon as the team approves.

Disclosure: An AI assistant helped me isolate the binary64 rounding mechanism that causes this failure. I have manually verified the math and the failure.

title: `move_estimator_to` should not move `classes_`
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When fitting a classifier like `LogisticRegression` under array API, the `classes_` attribute is determined from `y`, keeping its namespace and device.

However, when an already fitted model is moved through `move_estimator_to`, the `classes_` attribute is also moved, resulting in something different than if the estimator was originally fitted to the namespace that's being moved into, and which doesn't really make sense since the classes do not need to follow the types of 'X' or coefficients.

import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

from sklearn import set_config
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)

from sklearn.utils._array_api import move_to, move_estimator_to, get_namespace_and_device

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)

A NumPy array.

title: RFC Deprecate the `pre_dispatch` parameter
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

`pre_dispatch` is exposed by `GridSearchCV`, `RandomizedSearchCV`, `cross_validate`, `cross_val_score`, `cross_val_predict`, `learning_curve`, `validation_curve`, `LearningCurveDisplay.from_estimator` and `ValidationCurveDisplay.from_estimator`. I couldn't find a case where setting it helps with today's joblib, and I think we should deprecate it.

### Why it was added

It was added to `GridSearchCV` in 2011 to bound memory usage. At that time, joblib pickled `X` into every task sent to the pool, so dispatching all the (candidate, split) tasks at once meant one copy of `X` per task. That's no longer the case:

- joblib memmaps large arrays (including the ones inside DataFrames and sparse matrices);
- loky only pickles a task when it enters a call queue of `n_workers + 1` items. Queued tasks stay in the parent and only reference the data.

Our default (`"2*n_jobs"`) is also joblib's default, so dropping the parameter changes nothing for users who don't set it. The same parameter was already removed from `CalibratedClassifierCV` (#18030), and @ogrisel questioned its usefulness on memory in #23108.

The docstring is also wrong in several ways:

- It says `None` dispatches everything, but parameter validation rejects `None` (`"all"` works).
- It says an int gives "the exact number of total jobs that are spawned", but joblib counts batches, and with `batch_size="auto"` a batch can hold many tasks.
- It recommends dispatching everything for "lightweight and fast-running jobs". I couldn't measure any gain from that, and it's the only setting that hurts in the benchmarks below.

### Benchmarks

I tried cases where one could expect the knob to matter: large dense arrays with the loky and threading backends, data that joblib can't memmap (a polars DataFrame, a list of strings for a text pipeline), and an estimator with a large constructor parameter. `GridSearchCV` with `n_jobs=8`, Intel Core Ultra 5 225H (14 cores), Python 3.13, joblib 1.6.0, one run each. Each cell is fit time / parent peak RSS increase / peak PSS increase summed over the parent and the workers:

| case | `"n_jobs"` | `"2*n_jobs"` (default) | `"all"` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Ridge`, 200k x 100 float64 array, loky | 11.5s / 29MB / 3.1GB | 10.8s / 29MB / 3.1GB | 10.6s / 29MB / 3.2GB |
| same, threading backend | 15.1s / 2.35GB / 2.35GB | 14.7s / 2.35GB / 2.35GB | 14.9s / 2.35GB / 2.35GB |
| `Ridge`, same data as a polars DataFrame | 113s / 700MB / 2.7GB | 130s / 700MB / 2.5GB | 115s / 700MB / 2.6GB |
| `TfidfVectorizer` + `LogisticRegression`, 300k documents as a list of str | 107s / 81MB / 2.1GB | 104s / 81MB / 2.2GB | 104s / 82MB / 2.2GB |
| `TfidfVectorizer(vocabulary=<1M terms>)` + `LogisticRegression` | 201s / 640MB / 5.9GB | 178s / 901MB / 6.0GB | 199s / 3.2GB / 8.4GB |

The size of the data doesn't change anything, memmappable or not. The last case is the only one where the setting matters. `clone` deep-copies constructor parameters that aren't estimators, and `"all"` keeps one copy per task alive in the parent (~27 MB each here). The default already bounds that.

With many fast tasks (2000 candidates x 5 folds of ~1 ms on iris), `"all"` isn't faster either: 4.6 s vs 4.4 s for the default. Those timings exclude the callback context overhead reported in #35104, which makes `"all"` much worse (290 s).

<details>
<summary>Benchmark script</summary>

```python
"""Does GridSearchCV's ``pre_dispatch`` still bound memory (or help speed)?

Each (case, pre_dispatch) pair runs in a fresh Python process so that loky
workers are not reused across runs. A sampler thread polls the memory of the
whole process tree (parent + loky workers) during ``fit``:

- parent_rss: peak RSS increase of the parent process (where not-yet-dispatched
  tasks and their arguments live);
- tree_pss: peak PSS increase summed over the tree (PSS splits shared pages,
  e.g. memmaps, between processes so they are not counted once per worker).

Usage: python benchmarks/bench_pre_dispatch.py [case ...]
"""

import json
import subprocess
import sys
import threading
import time

N_JOBS = 8
PRE_DISPATCHES = ["n_jobs", "2*n_jobs", "all"]


def make_case(name):
  import numpy as np

  from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
  from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, Ridge
  from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
  from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

  rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

  def text_data(n_docs, n_words=40, vocab_size=50_000):
  words = np.array([f"w{i}" for i in range(vocab_size)])
  tokens = words[rng.zipf(1.3, size=(n_docs, n_words)) % vocab_size]
  X = [" ".join(row) for row in tokens]
  y = rng.integers(0, 2, n_docs)
  return X, y

  if name in ("numpy", "numpy_threading", "polars"):
  # 200k x 100 float64 = 160 MB, 40 candidates x 5 folds = 200 tasks
  X = rng.standard_normal((200_000, 100))
  y = X @ rng.standard_normal(100) + rng.standard_normal(200_000)
  if name == "polars":
  import polars as pl

  X = pl.DataFrame(X, schema=[f"f{i}" for i in range(X.shape[1])])
  grid = {"alpha": np.logspace(-3, 3, 40)}
  return Ridge(), grid, X, y

  if name == "text":
  # list of str: not memmappable, pickled for every task sent to a worker
  X, y = text_data(300_000)
  grid = {"logisticregression__C": np.logspace(-3, 3, 20)}
  est = make_pipeline(TfidfVectorizer(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=50))
  return est, grid, X, y

  if name == "big_param":
  # Fixed 1M-term vocabulary passed as a constructor parameter: clone
  # deep-copies it for every task.
  X, y = text_data(20_000)
  vocab = {f"w{i}": i for i in range(50_000)}
  vocab.update({f"term_{i}": 50_000 + i for i in range(950_000)})
  grid = {"logisticregression__C": np.logspace(-3, 3, 20)}
  est = make_pipeline(
  TfidfVectorizer(vocabulary=vocab), LogisticRegression(max_iter=50)
  )
  return est, grid, X, y

  if name == "tiny_tasks":
  # 2000 candidates x 5 folds of ~1 ms fits: the case the docstring says
  # pre_dispatch="all" is for
  from sklearn.datasets import load_iris

  X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
  grid = {"max_depth": range(1, 21), "random_state": range(100)}
  return DecisionTreeClassifier(), grid, X, y

  raise ValueError(name)


def tree_memory(proc):
  """Return (parent RSS, sum of PSS over the process tree), in bytes."""
  import psutil

  rss = proc.memory_info().rss
  pss = 0
  for p in [proc, *proc.children(recursive=True)]:
  try:
  pss += p.memory_full_info().pss
  except psutil.Error:
  pass
  return rss, pss


def run_one(case, pre_dispatch):
  import psutil
  from joblib import parallel_config

  from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

  est, grid, X, y = make_case(case)
  backend = "threading" if case == "numpy_threading" else "loky"

  proc = psutil.Process()
  base_rss, base_pss = tree_memory(proc)
  peak = [0, 0]
  stop = threading.Event()

  def sample():
  while not stop.is_set():
  rss, pss = tree_memory(proc)
  peak[0] = max(peak[0], rss - base_rss)
  peak[1] = max(peak[1], pss - base_pss)
  time.sleep(0.02)

  sampler = threading.Thread(target=sample)
  sampler.start()
  tic = time.perf_counter()
  with parallel_config(backend=backend):
  GridSearchCV(
  est, grid, cv=5, n_jobs=N_JOBS, pre_dispatch=pre_dispatch, refit=False
  ).fit(X, y)
  elapsed = time.perf_counter() - tic
  stop.set()
  sampler.join()
  return {
  "case": case,
  "pre_dispatch": pre_dispatch,
  "time_s": round(elapsed, 2),
  "parent_rss_mb": round(peak[0] / 1e6),
  "tree_pss_mb": round(peak[1] / 1e6),
  }


def main():
  if len(sys.argv) == 4 and sys.argv[1] == "--worker":
  print(json.dumps(run_one(sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3])))
  return

  cases = sys.argv[1:] or [
  "numpy",
  "numpy_threading",
  "polars",
  "text",
  "big_param",
  "tiny_tasks",
  ]
  print(f"{'case':<16} {'pre_dispatch':<10} {'time':>7} {'parent':>8} {'tree':>8}")
  for case in cases:
  for pre_dispatch in PRE_DISPATCHES:
  out = subprocess.run(
  [sys.executable, __file__, "--worker", case, pre_dispatch],
  capture_output=True,
  text=True,
  )
  if out.returncode:
  print(case, pre_dispatch, "FAILED\n", out.stderr[-2000:])
  continue
  r = json.loads(out.stdout.strip().splitlines()[-1])
  print(
  f"{case:<16} {pre_dispatch:<10} {r['time_s']:>6}s "
  f"{r['parent_rss_mb']:>6}MB {r['tree_pss_mb']:>6}MB",
  flush=True,
  )


if __name__ == "__main__":
  main()
```

</details>

### Proposal

Deprecate `pre_dispatch` in all the functions and classes above in 1.10 and remove it in 1.12. joblib's default applies afterwards.

The alternative is to keep it and fix the docstring. I'd prefer not to: it's API surface on 9 public entry points for a knob with no measured benefit. If a real need shows up later, I think the right place for it is `joblib.parallel_config`, as @thomasjpfan suggested in #23108 (it doesn't accept `pre_dispatch` today).

Is there a workload where setting `pre_dispatch` helps that I missed?

title: BUG `GridSearchCV(n_jobs=8)` is 10x to 50x slower than in 1.8 on many small tasks: every task pickles the whole callback context tree
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Since the callbacks API (#33322), a parallel `GridSearchCV` with many cheap fits is much slower than in 1.8. On a 2000-candidate grid on iris (10k fits of ~1 ms), `n_jobs=8` takes ~3 s on 1.8.0 but 100-150 s on 1.9.1 and 24-67 s on main. That's much slower than `n_jobs=1` (~9 s). No callback is registered.

`BaseSearchCV.fit` creates one `CallbackContext` per (candidate, split) up front and passes one to each `_fit_and_score` task. `subcontext` registers the child in the parent's `_children_map` and sets `child.parent`, so pickling one task's context pickles its parent and every sibling. The pickled task grows linearly with the number of tasks: ~50 KB per task for 500 tasks, ~420 KB per task for 5000 tasks (measured on main by pickling the `delayed` arguments `BaseSearchCV.fit` builds).

joblib pickles each batch separately, so the total pickling work is roughly (number of batches) x (number of tasks). Auto-batching hides part of it because a batch shares the pickle memo. With `pre_dispatch="all"` (batches of one task) and `refit=False`, the search takes 290 s on main, and 4.6 s with the contexts left out of the tasks.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import time

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
param_grid = {"max_depth": range(1, 21), "random_state": range(100)}  # 2000 candidates

for n_jobs in [1, 8]:
  search = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(), param_grid, cv=5, n_jobs=n_jobs)
  tic = time.perf_counter()
  search.fit(X, y)
  print(f"n_jobs={n_jobs}: {time.perf_counter() - tic:.1f}s")
```

### Expected Results

Same as 1.8.0:

```
n_jobs=1: 8.7s
n_jobs=8: 3.1s
```

### Actual Results

1.9.1:

```
n_jobs=1: 10.9s
n_jobs=8: 105.9s
```

`n_jobs=8` varies a lot between runs: 100.6 s, 105.9 s and 151.1 s on 1.9.1, and 23.8 s, 31.9 s and 67.2 s on main. 1.8.0 is stable at 3.0-3.1 s. Intel Core Ultra 5 225H (14 cores), same Python and joblib for all three.

### Versions

```shell
System:
  python: 3.13.14 (main, Jun 23 2026, 15:18:27) [Clang 22.1.3 ]
  machine: Linux-6.17.0-1032-oem-x86_64-with-glibc2.39

Python dependencies:
  sklearn: 1.9.1
  numpy: 2.5.3
  scipy: 1.18.1
  joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.7.0
  narwhals: 2.26.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

No

title: Allow infinite values in X for IsotonicRegression
body:
> [!WARNING]

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

We use Isotonic regression to calibrate scores on a log-odds / log-likelihood-ratio scale. On such scales, the extreme values are naturally +inf / -inf (e.g., probabilities of exactly 0 or 1). IsotonicRegression.fit currently rejects these inputs:
```
import numpy as np
from sklearn.isotonic import IsotonicRegression

ir = IsotonicRegression()
ir.fit([0.0, 1.0, np.inf], [0.0, 0.5, 1.0])
# ValueError: Input X contains infinity or a value too large for dtype('float64')
```

However, the algorithm itself can support `inf` values without a problem. The Error is raised by `check_array`, which has `ensure_all_finite=False`.

### Describe your proposed solution

Relax the validation in `check_array` to allow for `(-)inf`, but add a check for NaNs (e.g. `np.any(np.isnan(X))`) that raises a ValueError.

_No response_

title: META: lock contention can make thread-parallel code collapse on many-core machines (free-threading)
body:
On free-threaded Python, a lock that many threads take at the same time can make thread-parallel code collapse on a machine with hundreds of cores, while the same code looks fine on a laptop. I hit this with random forests. I'm opening this issue to share what I found, discuss how to avoid it in scikit-learn, and track the related work.

#### How I got here

As you might know, I'm benchmarking scikit-learn on several machines, one of them is a 2 x 86-core Xeon 6787P (344 hardware threads).

On this machine, random forests fitted with 344 threads (what you get with `n_jobs=-1`) were often slower on free-threaded 3.14 than with the GIL (median 0.45x over 31 representative benchmark cases). For instance, the reproducer below takes ~3s with the GIL and ~12s free-threaded.

With gdb, I first found most threads parked on CPython's `LOAD_GLOBAL` specialization lock (python/cpython#152075, fixed on CPython `main`).

Then I saw the same collapse on other locks, taken once per tree:

- the `sys.modules` lookups of function-level imports and the `lru_cache` behind `inspect.getattr_static`, both from narwhals' dataframe checks in `check_array`;
- the `warnings` module lock, taken by the per-task warning filters handling of `sklearn.utils.parallel`.

The slowdown always appeared suddenly past a few tens of threads. This comes from CPython's locks (python/cpython#158901): once a thread has waited more than 1 ms, each lock acquisition costs a thread wake-up, so the waits get longer and the lock never gets back to the fast path. On a 14 or 16-core laptop this threshold is barely reached, so nothing shows.

#### Reproducer

```python
import time

from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.ensemble import ExtraTreesClassifier

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=100_000, n_features=20, random_state=0)
clf = ExtraTreesClassifier(n_estimators=688, n_jobs=-1, random_state=0)
tic = time.perf_counter()
clf.fit(X, y)
print(f"fit: {time.perf_counter() - tic:.2f} s")
```

Fit time on the 2 x 86-core Xeon 6787P, 3 runs, one fresh process per run:

| | GIL (3.14.7) | free-threaded (3.14.7t) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main` (6ad9bb9ed6) | 2.2 to 3.3 s | 12.3 to 13.0 s |
| cakedev0/scikit-learn#19 | 1.7 to 1.9 s | 0.70 to 0.74 s |

#### What fixed it for forests

cakedev0/scikit-learn#19 makes the reproducer 17x faster free-threaded:

- Trees are fitted with a thread pool that starts its threads lazily, one per task (`ThreadPoolExecutor`, through the `_parallel_thread_map` of #34914). The threads start a bit apart, so they rarely take the same lock at the same time. joblib's threading backend starts all its workers before dispatching, so they run the same code in lockstep. With the GIL it's the opposite: starting the workers first is faster, so the thread pool does that only when the GIL is enabled.
- Trees don't validate again the inputs already validated by the forest (`check_input=False` no longer calls `check_array` per tree).
- `sklearn.utils.parallel` no longer resets the warning filters in each task (now in its own issue and PR: #35089, #35090). This also fixes a race on GIL Python with threads: the user's warning filters could be silently lost, and spurious "`delayed` should be used with `Parallel`" warnings raised.

#### What to watch for

Code that runs in many threads at the same time should avoid process-wide locks in each task. The ones I found:

- `warnings.catch_warnings()` and changes of the warning filters;
- `functools.lru_cache`'d functions (cache hits included), including stdlib ones like `inspect.getattr_static`;
- `import` statements inside functions;
- `isinstance` checks against an ABC, true or false, including `scipy.sparse.issparse` (`isinstance(x, SparseABC)`): the ABC's caches are sets shared by all threads, and each lookup takes the set's lock. So every `issparse(ndarray)` call from every thread goes through one `PyMutex`;
- input validation (`check_array` and its narwhals checks): validate once, before the parallel loop.

Benchmarks on 16 cores can hide a 10x to 100x collapse. Close to the threshold, timings are also bimodal (4.8 to 9.6 s for the same fit at 344 threads), so repeats are needed.

Note for benchmarks: measure warm fits too (several fits in one process), not only fresh processes. On free-threaded Python, the `LOAD_GLOBAL` specialization contention is paid by the first fit only: on `main`, the reproducer's first fit takes 10 to 12 s, the next ones ~4 s.

Thread-based parallelism in scikit-learn today: forests (`fit`, `predict`, `apply`, `decision_path`), `IsolationForest`, `neighbors` queries, `pairwise_distances`, SGD one-vs-all, coordinate descent paths, HGB binning, and `LogisticRegression` free-threaded.

#### Tracking

Upstream:

- [ ] `LOAD_GLOBAL` specialization contention: python/cpython#152075 (fixed on CPython `main`, backported to 3.14 in python/cpython#158904, 3.15 backport in python/cpython#158905)
- [ ] `PyMutex` fair handoff makes contention collapse: python/cpython#158901
- [ ] joblib's threading backend overhead: joblib/joblib#1830
- [ ] narwhals' dataframe checks contend (mostly `inspect.getattr_static`): not reported yet, depends on python/cpython#158901
- [ ] `issparse` contends on the ABC cache of `SparseABC`: not reported yet. Seen with gdb on `test_partial_dependence_non_null_weight_idx` with `--parallel-threads 14` (all but one thread waiting in `issparse` from `Tree.apply`), once the `warnings` lock contention was removed. A fast path in `issparse` for exact types (scipy) or lock-free ABC cache lookups (CPython) would avoid it

title: BUG: thread-based `Parallel` can corrupt the process-wide warning filters
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](<url>), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](<url>) and the ["Needs triage"](<url>) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

On Python without context-aware warnings (every GIL build, and free-threaded 3.13), `sklearn.utils.parallel.Parallel` with a thread-based backend can corrupt the process-wide warning filters. The user's own filters can be silently lost, and spurious "`sklearn.utils.parallel.delayed` should be used with `sklearn.utils.parallel.Parallel`" warnings are raised.

To propagate the caller's warning filters to joblib workers (#30380), every task runs:

```python
with warnings.catch_warnings():  # save the global filter list, swap in a copy
  warnings.resetwarnings()  # empty it
  for f in captured_filters:  # re-add the caller's filters one by one
  warnings.filterwarnings(...)
  return func(*args, **kwargs)
# on exit: restore the saved list
```

Without context-aware warnings, `warnings.filters` is one list shared by the whole process, and `catch_warnings` isn't thread-safe (the Python docs say so). With threads, tasks enter and exit these blocks out of order:

1. Thread 1 enters: it saves the user's list (L0), the global becomes a copy (L1), and it starts emptying and refilling L1.
2. Thread 2 enters while L1 is half-refilled: it saves L1, the global becomes L2.
3. Thread 1 exits and restores L0.
4. Thread 2 exits and restores L1: the half-reset copy.

A task's `resetwarnings()` can also run while the global list is the very list captured by `Parallel` (after another thread restored it), and empty it: the next tasks then see no filters and raise the warning above.

It needs a thread switch at the wrong moment, so it's rare with the default switch interval (5 ms) and a few threads. It's more frequent with many threads, with `catch_warnings` calls inside the tasks (`check_array` and `get_params` do that), and when tests run in several threads at once: I think this is the intermittent failure of #32631 on free-threaded 3.13, xfailed in #33320.

On free-threaded 3.14 (context-aware warnings) there is no race, but the same code takes the `warnings` module lock in every task, which makes many threads queue on it.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import sys
import warnings

from sklearn.utils.parallel import Parallel, delayed

sys.setswitchinterval(1e-5)  # makes the race frequent

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="my filter")
n_before = len(warnings.filters)
for _ in range(3):
  Parallel(n_jobs=32, prefer="threads")(delayed(int)() for _ in range(200))

my_filter_kept = any(f[1] is not None and f[1].pattern == "my filter" for f in warnings.filters)
print(f"{n_before} -> {len(warnings.filters)} filters, my filter kept: {my_filter_kept}")
```

### Expected Results

```
11 -> 11 filters, my filter kept: True
```

and no warning.

### Actual Results

On every run (3 runs, GIL 3.14.7, 344-thread machine):

```
11 -> 0 filters, my filter kept: False
```

and 88 to 172 spurious warnings per run:

```
sklearn/utils/parallel.py:144: UserWarning: `sklearn.utils.parallel.delayed` should be used with `sklearn.utils.parallel.Parallel` to make it possible to propagate the scikit-learn configuration of the current thread to the joblib workers.
```

On a 14-core laptop (GIL 3.14.6) it happens as well, for instance `11 -> 4 filters` with hundreds of warnings.

title: BUG fix sparse QuantileTransformer subsampling
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #34857.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

This PR fixes sparse `QuantileTransformer` subsampling when `ignore_implicit_zeros=False`.

Previously, the implementation scaled the number of sampled non-zero values by the column density. For a very sparse feature, `subsample=10_000` could therefore retain only a small number of non-zero observations. The resulting quantiles were noisy and could distort the transformed distribution.

The implementation now samples up to `subsample` non-zero values directly and uses weighted percentiles to represent the exact number of implicit zeros. This preserves the zero mass without materializing an array proportional to the number of input rows. Existing behavior is preserved for `ignore_implicit_zeros=True` and for columns that do not require subsampling.

A regression test uses a very sparse column with 100,000 rows and verifies that the subsampled quantiles remain close to the full-data quantiles. The test fails with the previous density-scaled sampling logic.

A changelog entry was added at `doc/whats_new/upcoming_changes/sklearn.preprocessing/35274.fix.rst`.

Validation:

- `git diff --check` — passed.
- `python -m compileall -q sklearn\\preprocessing\\_data.py sklearn\\preprocessing\\tests\\test_data.py` — passed.
- Standalone weighted-percentile validation — passed; the new calculation is within the regression tolerance and the previous algorithm is not.
- GitHub CI: all required checks passed, including lint, CodeQL, documentation, analysis, changelog, and unit-test checks. Eight optional checks were skipped.
- Local targeted pytest execution was blocked because the scikit-learn C extension was not built.
- Local editable build was blocked by the available MSVC compiler, which could not compile the extension target.

title: FIX Use a callable refit in successive halving searches
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

None. Related: #25151 removed the check that `refit` is a bool, #30990 documented `refit=callable` for the halving searches, #34250 made `cv_results_` the last iteration only.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

The halving searches accept a callable `refit`, and their docstring says it returns `best_index_` given `cv_results_` and that `best_score_` is then not available. The callable is never called: `BaseSuccessiveHalving._select_best_index` overrides the `BaseSearchCV` method and ignores `refit`, so the best-scoring candidate of the last iteration is always selected and `best_score_` is set.

```python
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.experimental import enable_halving_search_cv  # noqa
from sklearn.model_selection import HalvingGridSearchCV
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

def refit(cv_results):
  print("refit called")
  return 0

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=400, random_state=0)
search = HalvingGridSearchCV(
  DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0),
  {"max_depth": range(1, 10)},
  refit=refit,
  random_state=0,
).fit(X, y)
# "refit called" is never printed, and search.best_score_ is set
```

With this change, a callable `refit` is passed the results of the last iteration, i.e. the final `cv_results_`, and returns an index into them. This matches the docstring, where `best_index_` indexes `cv_results_`, and since #34250 `cv_results_` only holds the last iteration. Earlier iterations used fewer resources, so their candidates are not comparable anyway. The returned index is validated by `BaseSearchCV._select_best_index`, then shifted back to an index into all the results so that `best_params_` and the refit use the right candidate. `best_score_` is no longer set in that case, as documented and as in `GridSearchCV`.

`_trim_cv_results_to_last_iter` now returns the offset of the last iteration instead of taking `best_index`, so that `_select_best_index` and `fit` can both use it.

Tests: `test_refit_callable` checks that the callable is called once with the final `cv_results_`, that `best_index_` and `best_params_` follow its choice, that `best_score_` is not set, and that an index past the last iteration raises `IndexError`. `test_select_best_index` gets a callable case. Both fail on `main`. `sklearn/model_selection` passes (689 passed).

#### Introduce yourself

Hi, I'm a ML Engineer and PhD Student, working mainly with Spiking Neural Networks and Neuromorphic Computing!

#### AI usage disclosure

I used AI assistance for:
- Test generation
- Research and understanding

#### Any other comments?

To review: callables that rely on all iterations, e.g. by returning an index into `all_cv_results_`, now get an `IndexError`. They had no effect before, since the callable was never called.

title: FIX metrics.auc calculation and monotonicity validation for unsigned coordinates
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
Fixes #35224

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
In `sklearn.metrics.auc`, monotonicity and direction were evaluated using `dx = np.diff(x)` directly on the input coordinate array. When `x` has an unsigned integer dtype (`np.uint8`, `np.uint16`, `np.uint32`, `np.uint64`), subtracting adjacent decreasing elements underflows (e.g. `uint64(1) - uint64(2) == 18446744073709551615`).

Because unsigned numbers cannot be negative, `np.any(dx < 0)` was unconditionally `False`, which:
1. Erroneously classified decreasing coordinates as increasing (`direction = 1`).
2. Failed to raise `ValueError("x is neither increasing nor decreasing")` when non-monotonic unsigned arrays were passed.
3. Passed underflowed differences into `trapezoid(y, x)`, causing it to compute an astronomical area ($7.378 \times 10^{19}$ instead of $4.0$).

This PR casts unsigned integer coordinates to `np.float64` (`if np.issubdtype(x.dtype, np.unsignedinteger): x = x.astype(np.float64)`) before computing differences and trapezoid integration. It also adds a parametrized regression test suite across all unsigned integer widths (`uint8` through `uint64`), asserts that non-monotonic unsigned arrays properly raise `ValueError`, and adds the upcoming changelog entry.

#### Introduce yourself
I am a software engineering contributor working with scientific computing and numerical tooling in Python. I investigated this numerical underflow issue in `sklearn.metrics.auc` and verified the fix against the regression tests.

#### Any other comments?
All existing AUC unit tests pass without regressions.
