title: FIX: prevent overflow in _incremental_mean_and_var
body:
Towards #5602.

#### What does this implement/fix? 

`StandardScaler.partial_fit` keeps the cumulative sum of the samples
(`last_sum = last_mean * last_sample_count`) to update the running mean.
On long streams or on values with a large magnitude, this sum overflows
to `inf`, and the mean becomes `inf`.

The fix keeps the cumulative-sum formula of the mean when it produces
finite results (it is more precise), and falls back to the delta-based
update of Chan, Golub and LeVeque (1979) when it does not:

```
delta = new_mean - last_mean
updated_mean = last_mean + delta * new_count / total_count
```

The delta-based formula is algebraically equivalent to the
cumulative-sum one, but it never reconstructs the sum. The fallback is
declared in the docstring of `_incremental_mean_and_var`.

The patch is written against the array API (`xp`, not `np`), so it keeps
working on the non-NumPy backends that `_incremental_mean_and_var`
already supports. The device is passed explicitly to every `xp.asarray`
and `xp.where`, so backends that are strict about device consistency
(such as `array_api_strict`) work.

#### Why this approach

Three previous attempts were closed:

- #11549 fixed only the mean with a delta-based update and left the
  variance cross-term untouched. It was closed as incomplete.
- #34664 and #34874 proposed the delta-based formula for both mean and
  variance, but did not distinguish between the cumulative-sum path
  (precise, used when it does not overflow) and the delta-based path
  (safe, used when it does).

This PR reuses the parallel Welford / Chan-Golub-LeVeque accumulator
that my library, Dense-Armor, already runs in production in
`dense_armor/utility/stats/moments.py`. The formula is Eq. 2.1b of
STAN-CS-79-773, page 4.

The choice that distinguishes this PR from the previous three:

- It fixes the **mean** overflow without losing precision on normal
  inputs, by keeping the cumulative-sum path when it is safe.
- It does **not** touch the variance. The variance overflow is a
  separate bug (see Scope) and it is not addressed here. Previous
  attempts tried to fix both at once and ended up either incomplete or
  out of scope in a way that was not declared.

#### Scope

- The **mean overflow** is fixed and covered by
  `test_incremental_mean_and_var_large_values_no_overflow`.
- The **`with_std=False` path** is fixed and covered by
  `test_incremental_mean_and_var_with_std_false_overflow`.
- The **variance overflow** is **not** part of this PR. At constant
  data and `1.79e301`, `new_unnormalized_variance = sum((X - T) ** 2) - correction ** 2 / n`
  overflows to `inf - inf = nan` at the very first iteration, before
  any merge can run. A delta-based merge cannot fix a `nan` produced
  upstream. Fixing the variance overflow requires a separate change to
  how `new_unnormalized_variance` is computed, which is out of scope
  here.

#### Tests

Two non-regression tests in `sklearn/utils/tests/test_extmath.py`:

| Test | What it checks |
|---|---|
| `test_incremental_mean_and_var_large_values_no_overflow` | The reproducer. On `main`, the mean is `inf`. With the fix, it is finite and matches `fit()` within `1e-10`. |
| `test_incremental_mean_and_var_with_std_false_overflow` | `with_std=False` at `1.79e301`. Only the mean fallback fires, no variance path. |

The first test fails on `main` (the mean is `inf`) and passes on this
branch.

Full suite:

```
$ pytest sklearn/utils/tests/test_extmath.py -q
263 passed, 45 skipped
```

The array API test for `StandardScaler` with sample weights also passes
with `array_api_strict`, including on a non-default device.

#### Changelog

The changelog fragment is in
`doc/whats_new/upcoming_changes/sklearn.utils/35250.fix.rst`:

```rst
- |Fix| :meth:`preprocessing.StandardScaler.partial_fit` no longer produces
  ``inf`` for the mean on long streams or on values with a large magnitude.
  The mean is now updated with the delta-based formula of Chan, Golub and
  LeVeque (1979) when the cumulative-sum formula would overflow.
  By :user:`tatopenn-cell`
```

#### AI usage disclosure

AI assistance was used for: code generation, research and understanding
(reading issue #5602 and the STAN-CS-79-773 report of Chan, Golub and
LeVeque), test generation. The author reviewed every line, ran the tests
locally, and can explain every change. The delta-based update is
Eq. 2.1b of Chan, Golub, LeVeque (1979), page 4 of STAN-CS-79-773. The
author is a human who opened this PR manually and will engage with the
reviewers on GitHub.

#### Pre-existing issues not addressed

Four pre-existing ruff errors in `extmath.py` (lines 568, 775, 908,
998) and two pre-existing mypy errors (scipy stubs, Cython extension)
are not introduced by this PR and are left untouched to keep the diff
in scope.

#### Any other comments?

The case study of the issue, with the paper reference (STAN-CS-79-773,
Eq. 2.1a and 2.1b at page 4), the numbers, and the pytest failure on
`main`, is at:
<url>

Tagging @lorentzenchr and @EdenRochmanSharabi for review.

title: FIX: prevent overflow in _incremental_mean_and_var
body:
Fixes #5602.

### What does this implement/fix?

`StandardScaler.partial_fit` keeps the cumulative sum of the samples
(`last_sum = last_mean * last_sample_count`) and the cross-term of the
variance. Both overflow on long streams or on values with a large
magnitude, and the mean becomes `inf`.

The fix keeps the cumulative-sum formula when it does not overflow
(it is more precise), and falls back to the delta-based update of Chan,
Golub and LeVeque (1979) when the cumulative sum overflows:

~~~
delta = new_mean - last_mean
updated_mean = last_mean + delta * new_count / total_count
updated_m2 = last_m2 + new_m2 + delta**2 * last_count * new_count / total_count
~~~

The formula is algebraically equivalent to the cumulative-sum one, but it
never reconstructs the sum. This is a deliberate deviation from a pure
replacement: a pure replacement of the mean formula with the delta-based
one loses precision on `test_incremental_variance_numerical_stability`.
The fallback is declared in the docstring of `_incremental_mean_and_var`.

The previous attempt (#11549) fixed the mean but left the variance
cross-term untouched, which is why it was closed. This PR fixes both.

The patch is written against the array API (`xp`), not `np`, so it keeps
working on the non-NumPy backends that `_incremental_mean_and_var` already
supports.

Two non-regression tests in `sklearn/utils/tests/test_extmath.py`:

- `test_incremental_mean_and_var_large_values_no_overflow`: the
  reproducer of the issue. On `main`, the mean becomes `inf`. With the

- `test_incremental_mean_and_var_constant_values`: constant data has

The first test fails on `main` (the mean is `inf`) and passes on this

title: Fix Pipeline.score routing sample_weight when it is None
body:
With `enable_metadata_routing=True`, `Pipeline.score` passes `sample_weight` to `process_routing` unconditionally. When the final estimator does not request `sample_weight` for `score` (a pipeline ending in `StackingRegressor`, for example), routing validation raises a `TypeError`, so a plain `pipe.score(X, y)` fails:

```python
import sklearn
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
from sklearn.ensemble import StackingRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)
X, y = make_regression(random_state=0)
pipe = make_pipeline(StackingRegressor([("lr", LinearRegression())])).fit(X, y)
pipe.score(X, y)  # TypeError: Pipeline.score got unexpected argument(s) {'sample_weight'}
```

The non-routing branch in the same method already guards with `if sample_weight is not None`, so this just mirrors that guard in the routing branch. `validate_metadata` only rejects parameters no child object requested, so a requested-but-absent `sample_weight` still resolves to the callee default.

Adds a regression test based on the reproducer from the issue.

Fixes #35195

title: PERF Extract more KNeighbors prediction parallelism by using smaller chunks
body:
This is part of addressing #35184.

With large chunks, one worker thread that takes longer can cause all the other worker threads to sit around idle doing nothing. This therefore uses smaller chunks with threading.

With Loky and with smaller number of samples this makes things worse, so this is not done in those cases.

No AI.

### Benchmark - 8 cores, free-threaded Python 3.14

Once you hit 10,000 samples, if threading backend is used, this increases the number of chunks, allowing for speedups. 10,000 is neutral speed wise, the actual improvements kick in at higher number of samples, somewhere in between 10,000 and 100,000. Certainly 100,000 has a meaningful improvement, 4-5% speedup. Not amazing, but it's free performance.

The thresholds as you can see are empirically chosen.

Also note there is some noise, there is no reason for Loky backend to be faster since it doesn't change anything.

|--|--|--|--|--|--|

title: FIX Preserve distinct multi-output labels in resample
body:
`resample(..., stratify=y)` joined each row of a two-dimensional target into a space-separated string. Distinct rows such as `("a b", "c")` and `("a", "b c")` therefore became the same class, breaking stratified resampling — a reproduction with four rows returned two copies of one label.

- What: encode multi-output label rows as tuple representations instead of space-joined strings, so values containing spaces cannot collide.
- Why: self-discovered defect — space-joining is not an injective encoding for label rows.
- Tests: added a regression test with space-containing label values.
- Verified: reproduction before fix showed 1 distinct label, after fix 2 as expected; `sklearn/utils/tests/test_indexing.py` 130 passed; `git diff --check` clean. No open PR addresses this.

title: FIX clamp max_samples to non-zero weights when sampling without replacement
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #34673. The regression was introduced by #31414 (first released in 1.8.0).

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

Since #31414, `_generate_bagging_indices` draws sample indices with `np.random.choice(..., p=normalized_sample_weight)`. With `bootstrap=False` (sampling without replacement), numpy requires `size` to be at most the number of non-zero entries in `p`, so any `sample_weight` containing zeros makes `BaggingClassifier`, `BaggingRegressor`, and `IsolationForest` (on its defaults: `bootstrap=False`, `max_samples="auto"`) fail with:

```
ValueError: Fewer non-zero entries in p than size
```

For datasets of 256 samples or fewer, a single zero weight is enough to crash `IsolationForest`. Zero weights are the documented way to exclude observations from a fit, and with sampling without replacement those samples can never be drawn anyway, so the right behavior is to cap the number of draws at the number of non-zero weights. This makes the fit equivalent to dropping the zero-weighted rows by hand, which is what users currently have to do as a workaround.

Changes:
- `sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py`: clamp `max_samples` to `np.count_nonzero(sample_weight)` in `BaseBagging._fit` when sampling without replacement.
- `sklearn/ensemble/_iforest.py`: same clamp in `IsolationForest.fit`, applied before `max_samples_` and `max_depth` are derived so the fitted attributes stay consistent with the actual draw size.
- Extended `test_draw_indices_using_sample_weight` with a `bootstrap=False` parametrization (fails on main with `ValueError: Fewer non-zero entries in p than size`) and added non-regression tests, including the all-zero weights case which keeps raising the existing informative `ValueError` from `_check_sample_weight`.

All-zero `sample_weight` is untouched: it is already rejected by `_check_sample_weight` before this code path.

Verified locally on a scikit-learn 1.9.1 install: the new/extended tests fail on the unpatched release (9 failed) and pass with the patch (35 passed); `IsolationForest` and `BaggingClassifier` from the issue reproduction now fit successfully.

Areas that deserve careful review:
- whether the clamp belongs before the derivation of `max_depth` in `IsolationForest.fit` (I kept `max_samples_`, `max_depth`, and the actual draw consistent with each other);
- whether fitting should instead warn more loudly that zero-weight rows are excluded. I chose not to add a new warning because excluding zero-weight rows is the intended semantics, but happy to add one mirroring the Bagging `bootstrap=True` recommendation if preferred.

#### Introduce yourself

I use scikit-learn for applied ML work. This contribution came from a review pass over the ensemble code after noticing that zero-weighted rows, a common way to exclude observations, crashed forest fitting on default settings since 1.8.

title: Avoid Windows Conda shell-init failure in CI
body:
The Windows x64 job failed during Conda setup: `conda init --all` encountered a permissions error before the build began.

- **Windows setup:** Skip automatic Conda initialization on Windows while preserving it on other runners.
- **Bash activation:** Source Conda’s shell hook in `~/.bash_profile` for the existing `bash -l` steps.

```yaml
run-init: ${{ runner.os != 'Windows' }}

- name: Initialize conda for bash
  if: runner.os == 'Windows' && startsWith(env.DISTRIB, 'conda')
  shell: bash
  run: echo 'source "$CONDA/etc/profile.d/conda.sh"' >> ~/.bash_profile
```

body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes the Pyodide build broken by #35198.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

#35198 bumped cibuildwheel from v3.4.1 to v4.3.3 in `emscripten.yml`. This workflow does not set `CIBW_BUILD`, so it builds whatever cibuildwheel selects by default, and the bump changed that selection:

- before (v3.4.1): cp312 and cp313
- after (v4.3.3): cp313, cp314 and cp315

**cp315** uses the prerelease Pyodide xbuildenv `315.0.0a2`, which has no scipy wheel. pip then tries to build scipy from source and fails with `Dependency "OpenBLAS" not found`. Since the merge of #35198, the nightly build for Pyodide fails this way ([build log](<url>)). cp315 is selected by default because CPython 3.15 is a stable release **but its default Pyodide is still an alpha**. This PR skips it with `CIBW_SKIP: "cp315-*"`.

**cp312** (Pyodide 0.27) is not built anymore: it is an opt-in `pyodide-eol` target in cibuildwheel v4, and I didn't enable it.

I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation
- Research and understanding (finding the failing target in the CI logs)

#### Any other comments?

Building scipy from source can never work in this job (it needs OpenBLAS and Fortran compiled for WASM), so we could set `PIP_ONLY_BINARY: "numpy,scipy"` in the cibuildwheel step. A missing wheel would then fail right away with `No matching distribution found for scipy` which would have made the failure in #35198 easier to understand. WDYT?

title: ENH Add support for asymmetric callable pairwise distances
body:
## Summary

This PR proposes support for asymmetric callable distance functions in `sklearn.metrics.pairwise_distances`, addressing #13403.

Currently, callable metrics are assumed to be symmetric during single-threaded execution. This can produce incorrect results for asymmetric measures such as KL divergence.

The proposed change introduces `assume_symmetric=True`, preserving existing default behavior while allowing users to explicitly request independent computation of each ordered pair with `assume_symmetric=False`.

## Changes

- Add the `assume_symmetric` parameter to `pairwise_distances`.
- Update `_pairwise_callable` to compute directional distances when symmetry is not assumed.
- Add parameter validation and documentation.
- Add regression tests for asymmetric metrics, parallel execution, default behavior, and compatibility with built-in metrics.

## Testing

Ran:

```bash
python -m pytest sklearn/metrics/tests/test_pairwise.py -q
```

Results: **291 passed, 302 skipped, 2 xfailed.**

Formatting and whitespace checks also passed.

## Open design questions

1. Adding `assume_symmetric` as a public argument can conflict with an existing callable metric that accepts a keyword with the same name.
2. Existing parallel execution can produce asymmetric results even with the default setting, whereas single-threaded execution assumes symmetry. This proposal preserves that behavior.

I would appreciate maintainer feedback on the proposed API before finalizing the implementation.

This pull request includes code written with the assistance of AI.
I have personally reviewed the AI-assisted implementation, tests, and changes.

title: DOC Explain when to use the Calinski-Harabasz index vs the Silhouette…
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Towards #8647. The previous attempt, #34432, added a gallery example and was closed because the gallery is saturated (#27151), so this PR only touches the user guide.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

The issue says it is unclear when to use `calinski_harabasz_score` and how it compares with `silhouette_score`. It also asks whether the score has limits and whether it scales with the number of samples. This adds those answers to the existing Advantages and Drawbacks lists:

- **Advantages:** the cost is linear in `n_samples`, while the Silhouette Coefficient uses all pairwise distances and its cost is quadratic.
- **Drawbacks:** the score has no upper bound and grows with `n_samples` for the same distribution, so it is only meaningful when comparing clusterings of the same dataset.
- **Drawbacks:** the score is based on squared Euclidean distances to the centers, while the Silhouette Coefficient accepts any metric.

I checked each claim with `make_blobs` (3 centers):

|---|---|---|
| `n_samples=300` | 772.8 | 0.612 |
| `n_samples=3000`, same distribution | 8512.5 | 0.633 |
| `n_samples=30000`, same distribution | 83798.2 | 0.631 |
| `n_samples=300`, centers 20× further apart | 329803.9 | 0.982 |

title: ENH Mention ngram_range in CountVectorizer empty vocabulary error
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #33981. Supersedes #34302 and #33987, which were closed while the issue was still waiting for triage.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

If every document is shorter than the lower bound of `ngram_range`, `CountVectorizer.fit` (and `TfidfVectorizer.fit`) raises `empty vocabulary; perhaps the documents only contain stop words`, which points at the wrong cause. As suggested by @jeremiedbb in the issue, the message now also mentions `ngram_range`:

  CountVectorizer(analyzer="char", ngram_range=(2, 4)).fit(["a", "b"])
  # Before: ValueError: empty vocabulary; perhaps the documents only contain stop words
  # After:  ValueError: empty vocabulary; perhaps the documents only contain stop words,
  #  or every document has fewer than 2 characters, the lower bound of ngram_range=(2, 4)

The hint is added only when `ngram_range` can actually cause the empty vocabulary:
- `ngram_range[0] > 1`. With a lower bound of 1, any token produces a unigram.
- `analyzer` is `"word"` (the unit is "tokens") or `"char"` (the unit is "characters").
- It is not added for `"char_wb"`, which pads each word with spaces and always emits at least one n-gram per word. It is also not added for a callable `analyzer`, which ignores `ngram_range`.

The original sentence is kept unchanged as a prefix, so existing code matching on it keeps working.

Tests:
- `test_countvectorizer_empty_vocabulary_ngram_range` checks the hint for the `"char"` and `"word"` analyzers. Both cases fail on `main` and pass with this change.
- `test_countvectorizer_empty_vocabulary_no_ngram_range_hint` checks that no hint is added when `ngram_range` is not the cause: stop words with `ngram_range=(1, 2)`, and `"char_wb"` on blank documents.

**Points for review:**
- For `analyzer="char"`, the stop-words clause is still shown even though stop words never apply with that analyzer. I kept it to avoid changing the existing prefix; it could be dropped for char analyzers.

title: ENH Minimum norm solution for the newton-cholesky GLM solver, alternative to #34339
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Alternative to #34339. This branch is #34339 (by @lorentzenchr) merged with main, plus the fixes below, so it also contains the commits of #34339. See my comments there for the context.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

It keeps the eigendecomposition fallback of #34339 in `inner_solve`, and changes how `finalize` computes the minimum norm solution:

1. **No n_samples x n_samples matrix.** `scipy.linalg.null_space` does a full SVD of `[X, 1]`, with U of shape (n_samples, n_samples): 80 GB for 100k samples. The null space is now computed from the eigendecomposition of the weighted Gram matrix `[X, 1]' diag(sw) [X, 1]`, of shape (n_dof, n_dof), which costs about one Hessian evaluation.
2. **Sparse X.** `finalize` raised `ValueError: zero-dimensional arrays cannot be concatenated` for a sparse X with collinear features (newton-cholesky accepts CSR/CSC). On main, those fits fall back to lbfgs and work.
3. **Penalized fits are not projected.** #34339 also projected penalized fits that raised a `LinAlgWarning` (e.g. `alpha=1e-17` with a full one-hot encoding), which moves them away from the penalized optimum. Their solution is unique, so the projection now only runs for `alpha=0`.
4. **The intercept is not part of the norm**, as for `LinearRegression` (centering) and as the limit of the L2 penalty for `alpha -> 0`, which never penalizes the intercept (see #25948). With the intercept in the norm, the coefficients depend on the units of y: for a Poisson fit on a full one-hot encoding, fitting `1000 * y` instead of `y` changed every dummy coefficient. Now only the intercept changes, by `log(1000)`.
5. **Zero sample weights are equivalent to removing samples.** The null space of `[X, 1]` ignored `sample_weight`, so zero-weight rows could hide the collinearity of the other rows.
6. **Singular Hessians that LAPACK does not flag.** `finalize` only projected after `scipy.linalg.solve` raised a `LinAlgWarning`, but it doesn't always do so for an exactly singular Hessian: 21 out of 100 fits in [the example from my comment on #34339](<url>), which are then not the minimum norm solution for either convention. With this PR, all 100 fits warn and return the minimum norm solution, with the intercept out of the norm. `finalize` now checks the eigenvalues of the Hessian for every unpenalized fit. That's one `eigvalsh` of shape (n_dof, n_dof) per fit: ~0.1% of the fit time with 50 features, ~1.5% with 300, ~10% with 1000 (laptop). Penalized fits don't pay it.
7. **One `LinAlgWarning` per fit**, raised in `finalize`: the rank of X when it is rank deficient (and the minimum norm solution was returned), otherwise the "ill-conditioned Hessian" message of #34339 if `inner_solve` met one. Before, whether you got a warning for a rank deficient X depended on LAPACK.

Also:
- `test_logistic_regression_solvers_multiclass_unpenalized` looped over a `set` and called `pytest.xfail` when reaching newton-cd-gram, so the solvers after it in hash order were never checked and the test always reported XFAIL.
- The `alpha` docstrings said X "must have full column rank" for `alpha=0`. They now say the solution is only unique in that case, and the newton-cholesky docs say when the minimum norm solution is returned.
- New tests: the minimum norm solution and its single warning for a full one-hot encoding (dense and sparse, including the singular Hessians LAPACK misses), zero sample weights, and the single warning for multiclass.

Not changed: multiclass (follow-up, as agreed in #34339), and the absolute `max_eval <= sqrt(eps)` threshold of the eigendecomposition fallback.

title: PRF Reduce Lloyd's thread buffers after the parallel region
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

I found this while looking at why scikit-learn-intelex is much faster than scikit-learn on `KMeans` in [scikit-learn-benchmarks](<url>): on an Intel Xeon 6787P (2 x 86 cores), Lloyd iterations stop scaling at ~16 threads.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

Current implementation has three costs per Lloyd iteration that grow with the number of threads:
- at the end of the parallel region, every thread adds its buffers (`n_clusters * n_features` values) to the result under an `omp_set_lock`. The pairwise distances reductions already use a similar pattern with the `parallel_on_Y` strategy.
- the chunks are passed as memoryview slices (`X[start:end]`, ...). Slicing can raise, so Cython wraps the whole `with nogil, parallel():` block in `PyGILState_Ensure()` / `PyGILState_Release()`: all the threads take the GIL one after the other at the start and at the end of each iteration. 
- every thread `calloc`s its buffers at each iteration. Above glibc's mmap threshold (32 MiB, e.g. sparse data with many features), they are new mappings each time, and their page faults dominate the iteration. For dense data, this is usually negligible.

This PR:
- Avoids the lock by summing the thread buffers after the parallel region, without lock.
- Avoids the memoryview slicing by passing the chunks as `start` / `end` indices instead of slices, in Lloyd and in other places.
- Allocates the thread buffers once per fit, in `_kmeans_single_lloyd` (`_alloc_thread_buffers`: one row per thread, aligned and padded to cache lines), and passes them to each Lloyd iteration. The reduction zeroes the buffers for the next iteration, but only the cache lines that hold a non-zero value: the pages that a thread never writes to stay unmapped, as after a `calloc`.

The pairwise distances reductions already use this pattern with the `parallel_on_Y` strategy (`_argkmin.pyx.tp`: heaps allocated in each thread, indexed by `omp_get_thread_num()`, merged after the parallel region in a `prange` over samples without locks).

Some notes:
- The reduction order is now fixed (by thread index), so for a given number of threads the result doesn't depend on the order in which the threads got the lock anymore.
- The buffers of the centers aren't allocated anymore when the centers are not updated (predict).
- Sparse with 1 thread, GCC 13 builds can be up to ~12% slower than main (Core Ultra X7 358H, 20newsgroups and RCV1): the inner loop over the non-zeros reloads the pointer to the centers from the stack at each iteration (register pressure). With GCC 16 (Xeon 6787P) and clang (M2), it's on par with main or faster. Computing the dot products with 2 centers per loop over the non-zeros removes this, but it brings nothing with threads, so I left it out.

#### AI usage disclosure

I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation, A/B testing several approaches/variants: I've dug deeply into this final version but not in all the things the AI tested.
- Test generation
- Research and understanding (profiling)

The main things I trust:
- existing tests, and the new test against a NumPy implementation
- my benchmarks
- from the code, it's easy to believe this removes serial costs

#### Benchmarks

See <url> 34 KMeans cases (sift, nytimes, fashion_mnist, road_network and CIFAR-10, plus 20newsgroups and RCV1 as CSR matrices), in float32 and float64, with `init="random"` and up to 100 Lloyd iterations, 5 runs per case. Dashboards: [intel-xeon](<url>), [intel-laptop](<url>).

title: DOC Clarify probability density and log-likelihood in KernelDensity
body:
#### Referenced Issues/PRs

Fixes #16939

#### What does this implement/fix? Describe your changes.

This PR addresses the ambiguity in the return values of the **KernelDensity.score_samples( )** and **KernelDensity.score( )** methods and their relations to probability density, log-density, and log-likelihood.

As discussed in issue #16939, the negative log-density values returned by the score_samples method could be mistaken for negative probabilities.

A probability density function (PDF) is not a probability; rather, it is a non-negative function that integrates to 1 over the domain of the random variable of interest. Because the PDF can take values greater than 1, its logarithm can be positive or negative.

The changes proposed in this PR attempt to resolve the issues raised in issue #16939 in three places:

• In the docstring of KernelDensity.score_samples(): clarifying that the method returns the log-density of the query samples, which can indeed be positive or negative;

• In the docstring of KernelDensity.score(): clarifying that the method returns the total log-likelihood, i.e. the sum of the log-densities returned by score_samples();

• In the density estimation user guide (doc/modules/density.rst): updating the density expression and clarifying the notions of probability density and log-density.

By addressing the conflation between the log-density values for individual samples and the total log-likelihood for all samples, this PR attempts to improve the interpretability and usability of the KDE API.

title: PERF Speed up Euclidean and Manhattan distance metrics
body:
By using instruction-level parallelism, it's possible to speed these up nicely. Specifically, having two accumulators means more instructions that aren't dependent on each other.

Note that this changes the outputs slightly, because floating point addition isn't associative. Since the current code already chose not to use one of the various algorithms that minimizes summing error, that didn't seem like a problem.

For the KNeighborsClassifier benchmark I used (see below), IPC according to `perf stat` was:

* Before on `main`: 3.0
* In this PR: 3.6

No AI.

## `KNeighbors` benchmark results

Slightly slower on smaller n_features, but also there's a lot of noise. Significantly faster on higher n_features.

| Baseline time (secs) | PR time (secs) | Metric | Algorithm | n_features |
|--|--|--|--|--|
| 0.066 | 0.065 | euclidean | ball_tree | 5 |
| 0.018 | 0.020 | euclidean | kd_tree | 5 |
| 0.060 | 0.067 | manhattan | ball_tree | 5 |
| 0.023 | 0.022 | manhattan | kd_tree | 5 |
| 1.634 | 1.215 | euclidean | ball_tree | 50 |
| 1.036 | 0.786 | euclidean | kd_tree | 50 |
| 1.767 | 1.441 | manhattan | ball_tree | 50 |
| 1.965 | 1.536 | manhattan | kd_tree | 50 |

Benchmark code:

<details>

```python
from time import time
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from joblib import parallel_backend


def run():
  backends = ["threading"]  # , "loky"]
  sample = 20_000
  algorithmns = ["ball_tree", "kd_tree"]
  metrics = ["euclidean", "manhattan"]
  classifications = [
  dict(n_features=5, n_informative=3, n_redundant=2),
  dict(n_features=50, n_informative=15, n_redundant=5),
  ]
  print("| Time (secs) | Samples | Metric | Algorithm | Backend |")
  print("|-|-|-|-|-|")
  for classification in classifications:
  X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20_000, random_state=3, **classification)
  for metric in metrics:
  for algorithmn in algorithmns:
  for backend in backends:
  with parallel_backend(backend=backend, n_jobs=8):
  X_test, y_test = make_classification(
  n_samples=sample, random_state=3, **classification
  )
  start = time()
  for _ in range(5):
  model = KNeighborsClassifier(
  algorithm=algorithmn, metric=metric, n_jobs=-1
  )
  model.fit(X, y)
  model.predict(X_test)
  end = time()
  result = (end - start) / 5
  print(
  f"| {result:.3f} | {sample} | {metric} | {algorithmn} | {backend} |"
  )


if __name__ == "__main__":
  run()
```

</details>

## Microbenchmark of euclidean distance

I wanted to see what the impact is on different array sizes; the output is `array size: elapsed time`.

For all but arrays of size 1 the optimization seems to help, though much more significantly with larger arrays. So doesn't seem to make things worse in practice.

### `main`

```
  2:  12802 ns
  3:  15523 ns
```

### This PR


### Benchmark code

<details>

I compiled with `PYTHONPATH=build/cp314t/ cythonize -X language_level=3 -X boundscheck=False -X wraparound=False -X initializedcheck=False -X nonecheck=False -X cdivision=True -i metrics_ilp_cython.pyx`

I ran with `python -c "import metrics_ilp_cython; metrics_ilp_cython.benchmark(10_000)"`

```python
from sklearn.utils._typedefs cimport float64_t

from sklearn.metrics._dist_metrics cimport euclidean_rdist64
from time import time_ns
import numpy as np

vec1 = np.array([i + 0.01 for i in range(100)])
vec2 = np.array([i + 0.02 for i in range(100)])
```

title: PRF Split HGB early stopping data after binning
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Third part of the split of #35162. Independent of the other parts, based on main.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

With early stopping on the internal validation split, HGB used to split X, then bin both parts. Now it splits the sample indices, bins X once (the bin mapper is fitted on the training samples only, via a new `sample_indices` parameter of `_BinMapper.fit`) and then splits the binned data.

This avoids a float64 copy of X: the binned data is 8 times smaller. This is very beneficial when using HGB under `*SearchCV` as it reduces a lot the risk of OOM when using `n_jobs=-1` (which is very often the best option for speed, but is expensive in memory).

title: MNT Share X validation and categorical encoding between trees, forests and GB
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #35221.

First part of the split of #35162. Follow-up of #34832 (categorical support in forests).

Follow-ups, for now as PRs in my fork on top of this branch (I'll open them here once this one is merged):
- [cakedev0#30](<url>): HGB uses the same helpers, which fixes 3 bugs when a categorical feature is not first.
- [cakedev0#32](<url>): categorical features and missing values in GB.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

Trees, forests and GB now share the same X validation and categorical encoding, in the new `sklearn/tree/_preprocessing.py`.

- **Trees:** validation of X, `y` and `sample_weight` and encoding are done once in `_validate_and_preprocess_input`, then `_fit_validated` builds the tree.
- **Forests and GB:** they reuse `_validate_and_preprocess_input` and call `_fit_validated` directly, so they don't need to know what kind of preprocessing trees do. The trees they fit don't validate `y` and `sample_weight` again. This saves `check_array` calls in each tree, which are costly when many trees are fitted in parallel threads.
- **Encoding:** categorical columns are ordinal-encoded straight into an F-ordered array, in the original column order. No `ColumnTransformer` anymore: it outputs the categorical columns first, so the trees had to copy its output into a second array to restore the column order. Writing each encoded column into its place saves that copy and the `hstack` of the `ColumnTransformer`.
- **Extra trees:** the `criterion="absolute_error"` restriction with categorical features is now only applied with `splitter="best"`. Random categorical splits are evaluated exactly with `absolute_error`: `test_split_impurity` now checks them instead of skipping them. I updated the unreleased changelog entry of #33972.
- **Category limit:** the error for too many categories now gives the feature index and its number of categories, instead of the internal encoded value (#35221). The docstrings now say 256 categories, which is the real limit with `splitter="best"`.

#### AI usage disclosure

I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation (closely guided)
- Test/benchmark generation
- Documentation (changelogs)

#### Benchmarks

Forest fit, on a 2 x 86-core Xeon 6787P (GIL Python 3.14.7, `make_classification` with 100k × 20, 688 trees, median of 9 fits):

| | `n_jobs` | main → this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `ExtraTreesClassifier` | 172 (one socket) | 1.93 → 1.54 s |
| `ExtraTreesClassifier` | 344 | 2.55 → 1.94 s |
| `RandomForestClassifier` | 172 (one socket) | 4.22 → 4.02 s |
| `RandomForestClassifier` | 344 | 7.40 → 6.43 s |

On free-threaded Python, the impact is much bigger on the first fit of a process and then less visible because `check_array` currently takes locks on free-threaded Python and you can get contention, see #35091 for more details (but not really needed to review this PR)

#### Any other comments?

With `check_input=False`, a tree no longer checks that `y` is a valid classification target. This only affects people who bypass validation on purpose.

title: FIX Use "sequential_blas_under_openmp" to limit BLAS under OpenMP
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Closes <url>

Found while working on kmeans++ optimization: since threadpoolctl 3.7, with OpenBLAS's OpenMP threading layer, `limits=1, user_api="blas"` also sets the number of OpenMP threads of the calling thread to 1.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

`ArgKmin.compute` (used by `kneighbors`, `pairwise_distances_argmin`, ...) creates its object inside its BLAS limit, and the constructor reads the number of OpenMP threads with `_openmp_effective_n_threads()`. With OpenBLAS's OpenMP threading layer (the default of conda-forge on macOS) and threadpoolctl 3.7, it gets 1, and the whole k-NN search runs on a single thread.

This PR replaces `limits=1, user_api="blas"` with `limits="sequential_blas_under_openmp"` where needed. threadpoolctl added this option in 3.1 for this use case (<url>): it limits BLAS to 1 thread, except for OpenBLAS with the OpenMP threading layer where it does nothing: inside an OpenMP parallel region, OpenBLAS then uses `blas_omp_threads_local` threads, which is 1 by default ([common_thread.h](<url>)).

Only `ArgKmin` is affected: the other reductions create their object before the BLAS limit, and `KMeans` computes its number of threads in `fit`. Still, I changed them too, so that all the internal limits are the same.

The first commit (dc5a54a4f2) only adds the test, which fails on main in the macOS arm64 conda-forge job (OpenBLAS 0.3.34 with OpenMP threading, threadpoolctl 3.7.0): [CI log](<url>) (`assert [1] == [2]`). I also checked it locally on Linux with conda-forge's OpenBLAS with OpenMP threading: the test fails on main and passes with this PR.

#### AI usage disclosure

I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation
- Test/benchmark generation
- Research and understanding

#### Benchmarks

MacBook Pro M2, conda-forge OpenBLAS 0.3.34 with OpenMP threading (llvm-openmp), 8 threads, best of 3, two runs each, in ABBA order. "3.7 + this PR" is main with threadpoolctl 3.7.0 and `ArgKmin` patched to use `"sequential_blas_under_openmp"`.

| | threadpoolctl 3.6.0 | threadpoolctl 3.7.0 | 3.7.0 + this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kneighbors`, euclidean, 50k x 32, k=5 | 1463 / 1484 ms | 7095 / 7190 ms | 1500 / 1522 ms |
| `kneighbors`, manhattan, 5k queries | 675 / 676 ms | 2784 / 2783 ms | 687 / 692 ms |
| `pairwise_distances_argmin`, 50k vs 1k | 34 / 31 ms | 140 / 139 ms | 31 / 32 ms |

title: perf(PCA): vectorize _assess_dimension for n_components='mle' (~12-31x, output-identical)
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
See also #34618.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
`PCA(n_components="mle")` selects the dimensionality with Minka's method: `_infer_dimension` calls `_assess_dimension` once per candidate rank, and `_assess_dimension` computed its `pa` term with a scalar Python double loop over pairs of features. That is `O(n_features^2)` interpreter-level work per call and `O(n_features^3)` overall.

This replaces the double loop with the equivalent array expression: build the pair terms for `i < rank`, `j > i` (masking the lower triangle) and sum them. Same complexity class, but the work moves out of the Python loop. The mask is created on the same device as the spectrum, so array API inputs on non-default devices work.

Output is unchanged: `n_components_`, `components_` and `explained_variance_` are identical on the datasets I checked (max abs diff `0.0`). The log-likelihood differs only at about 1e-14 from summation order, which does not change the argmax. `test_pca.py` passes, including the array API compliance tests with `array-api-strict` (`SCIPY_ARRAY_API=1`).

`PCA(n_components="mle", svd_solver="full").fit` on low-rank plus noise data:

```
n_features=100:  105 ms ->  9 ms  (~12x)
n_features=300:  3030 ms ->  98 ms  (~31x)
n_features=500: 15060 ms -> 480 ms  (~31x)
```

This is a large constant-factor speedup rather than the lower-complexity reformulation suggested in #34618. It is self-contained and does not prevent that work.

#### Introduce yourself
I mostly work on ML tooling performance. I ran into this while profiling `PCA(n_components="mle")` on wide data, where the selection step was taking several seconds.

title: ENH Share X validation and categorical encoding across trees, forests, GB and HGB
body:
**TL;DR:** this PR removes some code duplication, adds features, fixes bugs, improves performance and moves things towards unifying GB and HGB.

#### Reference Issues/PRs

Follow-up of #34832 (categorical support in forests). First step towards binning support for trees and towards unifying GB and HGB (#27873).

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

Trees, forests, GB and HGB now share the same X validation and categorical encoding, in the new `sklearn/tree/_preprocessing.py`. `_check_categorical_features` is moved there unchanged from `sklearn/utils/validation.py`, with its tests, since `_encode_categorical_features` is its only caller.

- **Trees & forests:** validation of X, `y` and `sample_weight` and encoding are done once in `_validate_and_preprocess_input`, then `_fit_validated` builds the tree. Forests call `_fit_validated` directly, so they don't need to know what kind of preprocessing trees do. Trees fitted by forests and GB don't validate `y` and `sample_weight` again either. This saves `check_array` calls in each tree, which are costly when many trees are fitted in parallel threads, especially on free-threaded Python (see #35091).
- **Encoding:** categorical columns are ordinal-encoded straight into an F-ordered array, in the original column order. No `ColumnTransformer` anymore. This saves time and memory, and fixes bugs in HGB, which moved categorical features first (see below).
- **GB:** uses the same helpers, which adds support for `categorical_features` and for missing values. `predict_stages` now uses the tree's `goes_left`.
- **HGB:** uses the same helpers too, so categorical features are no longer moved first. This fixes 3 bugs when a categorical feature is not the first column: `interaction_cst` applied to the wrong features, `partial_dependence(method="recursion")` computed for the wrong feature, and the cardinality error reporting the wrong feature index.
- **HGB early stopping:** the internal validation split now splits indices, bins X once (bin mapper fitted on the training samples only, via a new `sample_indices` parameter of `_BinMapper.fit`) and then splits the binned data column by column. This avoids a float64 copy of X. Fitted models are bit-identical.

Excluding tests and changelogs: +651 / −754 lines, ~120 of them on each side being the move of `_check_categorical_features`.

#### AI usage disclosure

I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation (closely guided)
- Test/benchmark generation
- Documentation (changelogs)

#### Some small benchmarks

1. HGB fit, early stopping with the internal validation split, 20 iterations:

| n × d | fit time (before → after) | peak RSS above X (before → after) |
|---|---|---|
| 1M × 20 | 0.77 → 0.73 s | 260 → 112 MB |
| 1M × 100 | 2.49 → 2.24 s | 1015 → 261 MB |
| 3M × 50 | 4.12 → 3.90 s | 1498 → 364 MB |


2. Forest fit without the per-tree validation of `y` and `sample_weight`, on a 2 x 86-core Xeon 6787P (GIL Python 3.14.7, `make_classification` with 100k × 20, 688 trees, median of 9 fits):

| | `n_jobs` | before → after |
|---|---|---|
| `ExtraTreesClassifier` | 172 (one socket) | 1.93 → 1.54 s |
| `ExtraTreesClassifier` | 344 | 2.55 → 1.94 s |
| `RandomForestClassifier` | 172 (one socket) | 4.22 → 4.02 s |
| `RandomForestClassifier` | 344 | 7.40 → 6.43 s |

On free-threaded Python, the impact is much bigger on the first fit of a process and then less visible (see #35091 for why).

#### Any other comments?

- With `check_input=False`, a tree no longer checks that `y` is a valid classification target. This only affects people who bypass validation on purpose.
- GB now accepts NaN in any feature, and unknown categories at predict time are treated as missing values (same as trees/forests/HGB).
- `warm_start` is not supported with categorical features in GB, same as forests.
- Possible follow-up: HGB validation doesn't have to force the dtype to float64. It could keep the dtype of the input (maybe just enforce float) and let the bin mapper handle both float32 and float64 (should be straightforward). This would save a copy of X for float32 inputs.

title: FIX Do not modify input in IterativeImputer with keep_empty_features
body:
closes <url>

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

With `keep_empty_features=True`, `IterativeImputer._initial_imputation` set `Xt = X` and then wrote the initial imputation of the empty features into `Xt`. `X` comes from `validate_data` without a copy, so for an F-ordered float64 array the caller's own array was overwritten (all-missing columns became zeros), and for a pandas DataFrame the write hit a read-only view and `fit_transform` raised `ValueError: assignment destination is read-only`, even when no column was empty.

The fix writes into a copy (`Xt = X.copy()`) in the `keep_empty_features` branch. The branch that drops empty features already produced a copy through fancy indexing, so it is unchanged.

I added two tests in `sklearn/impute/tests/test_impute.py`:

- `test_iterative_imputer_keep_empty_features_does_not_modify_input` checks that an F-ordered float64 array with an all-missing column is unchanged after `fit_transform` and after `transform`.
- `test_iterative_imputer_keep_empty_features_dataframe` checks that a float DataFrame is imputed with `keep_empty_features=True` (same result as with `keep_empty_features=False`, since it has no empty column) and that the frame itself is unchanged.

Both tests fail on `main` and pass with the change.

#### Any other comments?

A C-ordered input was not affected because `validate_data` already copies it to F order. The aliasing goes back to #24770 and the in-place write to #29779.

title: FIX OrdinalEncoder.inverse_transform with infrequent and missing values
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
closes <url>

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
For a feature with both infrequent categories and missing values, `OrdinalEncoder.inverse_transform` computed the infrequent code as `len(categories) - len(infrequent_indices[i])`. That count includes the missing category, while `transform` builds its infrequent mapping with the missing category removed, so the expected code was off by one. With a single infrequent category the infrequent and missing rows were swapped silently; with more than one, decoding raised an `IndexError`.

This change reads the infrequent code from the fitted mapping (`_default_to_infrequent_mappings[i].max()`), which is the value `transform` uses. It also moves the replacement of missing values after the categories are filtered down to the frequent ones, and maps them to the last entry of the filtered categories, which is the NaN category.

I extended `test_ordinal_encoder_missing_appears_infrequent` with an `inverse_transform` round trip (two infrequent categories, which raised `IndexError` before), and added `test_ordinal_encoder_inverse_transform_infrequent_and_missing` with one infrequent category and two missing values, which checks that the infrequent row decodes to `"infrequent_sklearn"` and the missing rows to NaN. Both fail on `main` and pass with this change.

#### Any other comments?
`transform` is unchanged. A changelog fragment is included under `sklearn.preprocessing`; its file name needs the pull request number.

title: DOC Fix LogisticRegression C->alpha in user guide on L1-based feature selection
body:
The L1-based feature selection user guide says `C` controls sparsity for both SVMs and logistic regression. The unreleased `LogisticRegression` rename in #32042 (`C` -> `alpha`) makes that wrong for logistic regression.

- **`doc/modules/feature_selection.rst`**: One sentence in the L1-based section is reworded.
  - SVMs: still described by `C`, where a smaller `C` selects fewer features.
  - Logistic regression: now grouped with Lasso under `alpha`, where a higher `alpha` selects fewer features.

```diff
-With SVMs and logistic regression, the parameter C controls the sparsity:
-the smaller C the fewer features selected. With Lasso, the higher the
-alpha parameter, the fewer features selected.
+With SVMs, the parameter C controls the sparsity: the smaller C the fewer
+features selected. With logistic regression and Lasso, the higher the alpha
+parameter, the fewer features selected.
```

- The sentence is hard-wrapped over three source lines, so the diff touches those three lines. The wording change is the single replacement requested.

title: CI Add workflow to label PRs based on diff size
body:
### Motivation

Sometimes, I want to help but also my time/energy budget is kind of low (say 15-30 minutes if we are talking about time). Wouldn't it be nice if there was an easy and quick answer to the question "where could I help?" :stuck_out_tongue_winking_eye:?

No silver bullet, but labeling PR by PR diff size could help a lot I think. This is complementary to the "Quick review" label which needs to be set by a human. I have other ideas on this topic, stay tuned :wink:!

### Implementation

This is using a third-party action <url> that is used by a number "serious" project like [pyrefly](<url>) or [Mozilla Developer Network doc](<url>).

I took the setup from [CodeCarbon workflow](<url>) so it is tested already. For good measure I have also asked an agent to test in on my fork and it seem to work fine, see [summary](<url>).

Here is an [example search](<url>) (XS or S PR diff) if you want to get a feeling how this works in practice.

There is some opportunity for bikeshedding on this [^1], let's collectively try to not do it too much :pray:! I propose we merge a version of this "quickly" and we iterate depending on feed-back.

[^1]: for example, which threshold to pick to decide that a PR is `size/S` vs `size/M`.

### Additional comments

- I pinned the action by hash because this is using `pull_request_target` which has elevated permissions
- I ignore a few generated files for the diff count, i.e. lock files and externals Array API files, let me know if you can think other changes with big diff that we want to ignore
- once merged, this will only update "newly updated" PRs (`opened`+`reopened` `synchronize` means a push in the PR branch). I think this is completely fine and I don't think it's worth trying to label old PRs without activity.

title: PRF Speed up k-means++ initialization
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

I found this while looking at why scikit-learn-intelex is much faster than scikit-learn on `KMeans` in [scikit-learn-benchmarks](<url>): on an Intel Xeon 6787P (2 x 86 cores), the k-means++ init takes 75-97% of the time of `KMeans.fit`.

Related to <url>

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

Current implementation is slow for two reasons:
- for float32 data, `_euclidean_distances` goes through the upcast path: many float64 BLAS calls on small chunks. On sift (1M x 128) with 64 threads, it takes 365 ms vs 2.7 ms for the raw gemm, and it gets slower with more threads.
- for low-dimensional data, the single-threaded numpy passes dominate (~10 ms per step for 350k x 3 samples, while the gemm takes 0.2 ms).

This PR evaluates the candidates of a step in a single OpenMP kernel (`_kmeans_plusplus_trials_dense`). It introduces two units of work:
- the `blocks`: each thread processes exactly one block
- the `chunks`: it's the parallel reduction unit, and it also allows a trick in the candidates sampling which avoids `np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(w * d), r)` which is single-threaded and can dominate when the rest is parallelized.

Each thread does one BLAS call for its block of samples, then adds the squared norms, takes the min with the current closest distances and sums the weighted distances per chunk of 256 samples. The next candidates are sampled from these per-chunk sums (first a chunk, then a sample in that chunk), so there is no cumulative sum over all the samples anymore.

Distances smaller than 1% of `||x||² + ||c||²` (1e-8 in float64) are recomputed directly, to avoid catastrophic cancellation in float32 (this is what the upcast was protecting against: it was added in <url> to fix <url>). In particular, a sample identical to a chosen center gets a zero distance and can't be sampled again: `test_kmeans_plusplus_far_from_origin` fails without this.

Sparse input uses the same sampling and the same recomputation of small distances, so dense and sparse inputs still give the same centers. The candidates are rows of X, so they are sparse too: their dot products with the samples only read the columns of X where they have non-zeros. X is converted to CSC once per call for that (main converts `X.T` at every step, in `X[candidate_ids] @ X.T`).

Some notes:
- For a given `random_state`, the selected centers are not the same as on main, because the cumulative sums used for sampling are different.
- `kmeans_plusplus` now converts X to a C-contiguous float array, so integer input gives float centers (see the docstring example). It also rejects sparse input with 64-bit indices, like the estimators already do (the kernels use 32-bit indices).
- I do one BLAS call per thread rather than one per chunk of samples because many small concurrent BLAS calls scale badly with OpenBLAS (see also <url> for Lloyd).

#### AI usage disclosure

I used AI assistance for:
- Code & Algorithm generation, A/B testing several approaches/variants: I've dug deeply into this final version but not in all the things the AI tested. 
- Test generation
- Research and understanding (profiling)

The main things I trust:
- existing tests
- my benchmarks
- from the code / the algorithm, it's easy to believe this is a good improvement

#### Benchmarks

See the init columns in <url>

Init speed-up ranges from ~1x to 100x depending on the cases. **Typical speed-up is 3x-15x** I'd say.

title: DOC fix soft-threshold and dual objective in Lasso coordinate descent docs
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs None. #### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes. This PR Fixes two formulas in the "Coordinate Descent with Gap Safe Screening Rules" section of `doc/modules/linear_model.rst`: - a) changes the soft-threshold from $\alpha$ to $n_{\mathrm{samples}}\alpha$. The squared-error term is divided by $n_{\mathrm{samples}}$, so multiplying the coordinate objective by that number also scales the penalty. - b) restores the missing factor of two in the dual objective: $D(v) = \frac{1}{2n_{\mathrm{samples}}}(2y^\top v - \|v\|_2^2)$. This makes the duality gap zero at the optimum, as required. Both corrections agree with the local solver source. #### AI usage disclosure Claude Code ( Claude Sonnet 5.5 (high) ) was used which pointed out these errors. Claude Code ( Claude Opus 5.5 (high) ) helped me writing the mathematical explanation for changes a) and b). Codex ( GPT 6.1 sol (xhigh) ) verified the math and reasoning of explanation and output of numerical check. #### Any other comments?

Mathematical reasoning

 Notation: $`n = n_{\text{samples}}`$, $`x_j`$ is column $`j`$ of $`X`$, and $`\|\cdot\|_\infty`$ is the largest absolute entry. Assume $`n`$ is positive, $`\alpha \ge 0`$, and there is no separate intercept.
Explanation of change a (soft-threshold)
Fix every coefficient except $`w_j`$ and let $`\rho = y - X_{-j} w_{-j}`$ be what the other features leave unexplained. The update minimises $`\displaystyle \frac{1}{2n} \|\rho - x_j w_j\|_2^2 + \alpha |w_j| .`$ Multiplying by $`n`$ does not change the minimiser. Expanding the square and dropping terms without $`w_j`$ gives $`\displaystyle \frac{a}{2} w_j^2 - b\, w_j + t\, |w_j|, \qquad a = \|x_j\|_2^2, \quad b = x_j^\top \rho, \quad t = n\alpha .`$ Setting the derivative to zero on each side of zero gives three cases: - $`b`$ larger than $`t`$: $`w_j = (b - t)/a`$. - $`|b| \le t`$: $`w_j = 0`$. - $`b`$ smaller than $`-t`$: $`w_j = (b + t)/a`$. This is soft-thresholding, $`S(z, t) = \text{sign}(z)\max(0, |z| - t)`$, so $`\displaystyle w_j = \frac{S\!\left(x_j^\top \rho,\; n\alpha\right)}{\|x_j\|_2^2} .`$ The threshold is $`n\alpha`$, not $`\alpha`$. Using $`\alpha`$ would solve the same problem with penalty $`\alpha / n`$, which shrinks too little when $`n > 1`$.
Explanation of change b (dual objective)
Introduce $`z = y - Xw`$ and a multiplier $`\lambda`$: $`\displaystyle L(w, z, \lambda) = \frac{1}{2n} \|z\|_2^2 + \alpha \|w\|_1 + \lambda^\top (y - Xw - z).`$ The last term is zero when the constraint holds. Minimising $`L`$ over $`z`$ and $`w`$ separately gives a lower bound on the primal minimum for each $`\lambda`$. - **Over** $`z`$: the minimum is at $`z = n\lambda`$ and equals $`-\frac{n}{2} \|\lambda\|_2^2`$. - **Over** $`w`$: $`\alpha \|w\|_1 - (X^\top \lambda)^\top w`$ has minimum $`0`$ if $`\|X^\top \lambda\|_\infty \le \alpha`$, and is unbounded below otherwise. So the dual problem is $`\displaystyle \max_\lambda \; y^\top \lambda - \frac{n}{2} \|\lambda\|_2^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|X^\top \lambda\|_\infty \le \alpha .`$ The docs use $`v = n\lambda`$. Substituting $`\lambda = v / n`$ gives $`\displaystyle D(v) = \frac{y^\top v}{n} - \frac{\|v\|_2^2}{2n} = \frac{1}{2n} \left( 2\, y^\top v - \|v\|_2^2 \right), \qquad \|X^\top v\|_\infty \le n\alpha .`$ The factor of two appears when both terms are put over the denominator $`2n`$. The old formula, $`\frac{1}{2n}(y^\top v - \|v\|_2^2)`$, halves the linear term. At the optimum $`v^\star = r^\star = y - Xw^\star`$. The Lasso optimality conditions give $`(w^\star)^\top X^\top r^\star = n\alpha \|w^\star\|_1`$, hence $`y^\top r^\star = \|r^\star\|_2^2 + n\alpha \|w^\star\|_1`$ and $`\displaystyle D(r^\star) = \frac{\|r^\star\|_2^2}{2n} + \alpha \|w^\star\|_1 = P(w^\star).`$ The duality gap is therefore zero at the optimum, as it must be. The old formula leaves a positive gap there.
Worked example and numerical check
Take $`X = (1, 1)^\top`$, $`y = (2, 2)^\top`$, $`n = 2`$ and $`\alpha = 0.5`$. Change a gives $`\displaystyle w^\star = \frac{S(4, 1)}{2} = 1.5, \qquad v^\star = y - Xw^\star = (0.5,\, 0.5)^\top .`$ This $`v^\star`$ is feasible, since $`\|X^\top v^\star\|_\infty = 1 = n\alpha`$. Then $`\displaystyle P(w^\star) = \frac{0.5^2 + 0.5^2}{4} + 0.5 \cdot 1.5 = 0.875, \qquad D(v^\star) = \frac{2 \cdot 2 - 0.5}{4} = 0.875 .`$ With the old threshold the update gives $`w = 1.75`$. The old dual formula gives $`0.375`$, a gap of $`0.5`$ at the optimum. Another check: if $`\|X^\top y\|_\infty \le n\alpha`$ then $`w = 0`$ is optimal and $`v = y`$ is feasible. The corrected formula gives $`D(y) = \|y\|_2^2 / (2n) = P(0)`$. The old formula gives $`0`$. The script below runs an independent coordinate descent loop with the $`n\alpha`$ threshold, compares it with `Lasso`, evaluates both dual formulas at $`v^\star = y - Xw^\star`$, checks weak duality on 100 random feasible pairs, and reproduces the worked example. It was run with scikit-learn 1.6.1. ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso rng = np.random.default_rng(0) X = rng.normal(size=(50, 5)) y = X @ np.array([1.5, -1.0, 0.0, 0.5, 0.0]) + rng.normal(size=50) alpha = 0.3 n = X.shape[0] def soft(z, t): return np.sign(z) * max(0.0, abs(z) - t) def primal(w): return np.sum((y - X @ w) ** 2) / (2 * n) + alpha * np.abs(w).sum() def dual(v): # corrected return (2 * y @ v - v @ v) / (2 * n) def dual_old(v): return (y @ v - v @ v) / (2 * n) w = np.zeros(5) for sweep in range(1, 10001): w_prev = w.copy() for j in range(5): rho = y - X @ w + X[:, j] * w[j] w[j] = soft(X[:, j] @ rho, n * alpha) / (X[:, j] @ X[:, j]) if np.max(np.abs(w - w_prev)) < 1e-14: break lasso = Lasso(alpha=alpha, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-14, max_iter=10000).fit(X, y) r = y - X @ w print("sweeps", sweep) print("max |w_cd - w_lasso| :", np.max(np.abs(w - lasso.coef_))) print("P(w*) :", primal(w)) print("D(r*) corrected :", dual(r)) print("D(r*) old :", dual_old(r)) print("dual feasibility slack:", n * alpha - np.max(np.abs(X.T @ r))) ok = True for _ in range(100): w2 = w + rng.normal(scale=0.2, size=5) r2 = y - X @ w2 m = np.max(np.abs(X.T @ r2)) c = 1.0 if m <= n * alpha else n * alpha / m ok &= dual(c * r2) <= primal(w2) + 1e-12 print("weak duality, 100 pairs:", ok) # Worked example: X = (1, 1)^T, y = (2, 2)^T, n = 2, alpha = 0.5 X1, y1, n1, a1 = np.array([[1.0], [1.0]]), np.array([2.0, 2.0]), 2, 0.5 w1 = soft(X1[:, 0] @ y1, n1 * a1) / (X1[:, 0] @ X1[:, 0]) v1 = y1 - X1[:, 0] * w1 print("worked: w*", w1, "v*", v1, "P", np.sum(v1**2) / (2 * n1) + a1 * abs(w1), "D", (2 * y1 @ v1 - v1 @ v1) / (2 * n1), "D_old", (y1 @ v1 - v1 @ v1) / (2 * n1), "sklearn", Lasso(alpha=a1, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-14).fit(X1, y1).coef_) ``` Output: ```text sweeps 15 max |w_cd - w_lasso| : 2.220446049250313e-16 P(w*) : 1.1397166802364513 D(r*) corrected : 1.139716680236452 D(r*) old : 0.20126749426085752 dual feasibility slack: -2.4868995751603507e-14 weak duality, 100 pairs: True worked: w* 1.5 v* [0.5 0.5] P 0.875 D 0.875 D_old 0.375 sklearn [1.5] ``` The coordinate descent loop matches `Lasso` to $`2.2 \times 10^{-16}`$, and $`P(w^\star) = D(v^\star)`$ to within $`10^{-12}`$ (about $`1.1397`$). The old dual formula gives about $`0.2013`$. The negative feasibility slack is rounding error.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

The PR prevents from registering two progress bars to the same estimator (which would result in a bug in the second bar's teardown, see #34744). It is done by adding a `one_per_estimator` class attribute to the `ProgressBar` class. The same attribute can be reused in any callback class that would break if two instances are registered on the same estimator.

It was proposed in the callbacks meeting to allow the two callbacks instances but have the estimator deactivate one. That poses problems if the deactivation mechanism is similar to the one proposed in #34272, as one estimator would deactivate the callback for all other estimators that would also have it registered. The deactivation thus must be only for the specific estimator, and it seems simpler and clearer to me to then just forbid the estimator to hold the two callbacks.

Fixes #35104

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
`CallbackContext` keeps track of the tree structure of the tasks by referencing the context objects of its parent and children tasks. This creates problems of cyclic references of the contexts, and makes it so that unpickling one context requires to unpickle the whole tree, which can introduce a big overhead, as pointed out in #35104.

However, right now the callbacks don't need to access the context objects, they only require the id, task_name and estimator_name of the ancestor tasks of their own task. So this PR removes both the references to the parent and children contexts. 

- Instead of the parent ref, a tuple of ~~named tuples~~ dataclasses (the new class `TaskInfo`) is given as the `task_path` attribute of the callback context, keeping track of the info of each ancestor (task_id, task_name, estimator_name, init_time, source_task_name, source_task_id and sequential_subtasks). 
- Instead of the children ref, only the ids of the children tasks are recorded.

`get_context_path` is removed, but since we have the info of ancestor tasks in `task_path` it is not needed anymore. It was also used to check the `_subestimator_support_warnings` of the root context. In that case, instead of using the attr of the root context, the set is shared across all contexts of the tree.

title: FIX Handle pd.NA in OneHotEncoder and OrdinalEncoder
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #26890

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

When fitting `OneHotEncoder` or `OrdinalEncoder` on a pandas DataFrame containing `pd.NA` in object or string columns, `_extract_missing` in `sklearn/utils/_encode.py` only checked `None` and `is_scalar_nan`, allowing `pd.NA` to remain in `uniques_set`. During Python sorting, comparing `pd.NA` with strings raised:
`TypeError: Encoders require their input argument must be uniformly strings or numbers. Got ['NAType', 'str']`.

Changes:
- In `sklearn/utils/_encode.py`:
  - `_extract_missing`: Include `is_pandas_na` so `pd.NA` is extracted into `missing_values_set` prior to sorting.
  - `_nandict`: Recognize `is_pandas_na` so `transform` maps `pd.NA` to `self.nan_value`.
  - `_get_counts`: Account for `is_pandas_na` when tallying missing counts.
- In `sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py`:
  - Update category validation, drop-value handling, and missing-index tracking in `OneHotEncoder` and `OrdinalEncoder` to recognize `is_pandas_na`.
- In `sklearn/utils/tests/test_encode.py` and `sklearn/preprocessing/tests/test_encoders.py`:

title: FIX HDBSCAN with `cluster_selection_epsilon` crashing on NumPy 2
body:
Fixes #33219

Fitting `HDBSCAN` with `cluster_selection_epsilon` was crashing on NumPy 2 with `TypeError: only 0-dimensional arrays can be converted to Python scalars`.

The epsilon search walks up the condensed tree in `traverse_upwards` (`sklearn/cluster/_hdbscan/_tree.pyx`), and it was assigning the result of a boolean lookup, a size-1 ndarray, straight into a C integer. NumPy 2 no longer converts ndim > 0 arrays to scalars, so the fit blew up as soon as the epsilon search had to climb the tree. The fix indexes the scalar out explicitly (`['parent'][0]` and `['value'][0]`), along the lines of what @betatim suggested in the issue thread.

Repro (crashed before, works now):

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import HDBSCAN

rng = np.random.RandomState(1)
X = np.vstack([rng.normal(0, 0.2, size=(20, 2)), rng.normal(5, 0.2, size=(21, 2))])
HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=5, min_samples=1, allow_single_cluster=True,
  cluster_selection_method="leaf", cluster_selection_epsilon=0.5,
  copy=True).fit_predict(X)
```

Tests:

- Added `test_hdbscan_cluster_selection_epsilon_traverse_upwards` in `sklearn/cluster/tests/test_hdbscan.py`. I confirmed it fails with a TypeError on the unpatched code and passes with the fix.
- Full `sklearn/cluster/tests/test_hdbscan.py`: 145 passed.

title: FIX make Bunch.copy return a Bunch instead of a dict
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
Fixes #27930.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
`Bunch` inherits `dict.copy`, which always returns a plain `dict`, so `Bunch(a=1).copy().a` raises `AttributeError`. `copy.copy(bunch)` already returns a `Bunch`, so the two ways of copying disagree.

This adds a `Bunch.copy` override that returns a `Bunch`. It is still a shallow copy.

Points worth a careful look:

- Keys are copied with `dict.update`, which does not go through `Bunch.__getitem__`, so copying a bunch that holds deprecated keys does not emit their `FutureWarning`.
- The `_deprecated_key_to_warnings` table is copied rather than shared, so deprecated keys still warn on the copy and later `_set_deprecated` calls on one bunch do not affect the other. This differs slightly from the snippet suggested in the issue, which shared the table.

title: FIX resolve midpoint rounding tie in HistGradientBoosting binning
body:
Fixes  #35119
 
In  find_binning_thresholds  ( sklearn.ensemble._hist_gradient_boosting.binning ), when the number of distinct values is less than or equal to  max_bins, bin thresholds are calculated as midpoints of adjacent distinct values.

In IEEE-754 binary64 arithmetic, computing the arithmetic midpoint of two adjacent, distinct floating-point values can round upward to equal the upper data value due to round to the nearest ties to even. Because bin mapping uses upper inclusive comparisons (<= threshold), both values were placed into the same bin, preventing trees from splitting perfectly separable data.

title: Fix: move_estimator_to should not move classes_ attribute
body:
This PR fixes Issue #35109. 

**Reasoning:**
When utilizing `move_estimator_to` to transition estimators to different devices (e.g., CPU to GPU), the recursive `_estimator_with_converted_arrays` method was blindly converting all attributes. This caused problems for the `classes_` array (which often holds string labels that are incompatible with certain target namespaces/devices).

**Changes Made:**
- Added an explicit check to bypass the `classes_` attribute during the recursive conversion in `_estimator_with_converted_arrays`. The attribute is now transferred as-is without device modification.
- Added a non-regression test in `test_array_api.py` to verify this behavior.

Fixes #35109

title: DOC cosine_similarity and cosine_distances behavior for zero vectors
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #15256

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

The cosine is not defined when a vector has a zero norm, but the current docs do not say what scikit-learn returns in that case. `cosine_similarity` returns 0 whenever one of the two vectors is zero, including when the zero vector is compared with itself, so the corresponding diagonal entry is 0 rather than 1 for both dense and sparse input. `cosine_distances` returns 1.0 for those pairs, except that the diagonal is set to 0 when only `X` is provided. title: FIX SVC and OneClassSVM with null sample weights
body:
Closes #25380
Closes #5150

Related: #27763 (stale draft addressing the same issues).

#### What does this implement/fix?

libsvm removes the samples with a null or negative weight before training, but the resulting model was reported as if it had been trained on the original data:

- `support_` indexed the data without the removed samples instead of the data passed to `fit`.
- When all the samples of a class were removed, the model had fewer classes than `classes_`, so `n_support_`, `dual_coef_`, `intercept_` and `predict_proba` had inconsistent shapes (and sparse input raised). Since the model is rebuilt at prediction time with labels `0..n_classes-1`, `predict` could also return the wrong class.

This PR maps the support vector indices back to the original samples and keeps all the classes of the original problem in the model. A class without any retained sample has no support vector, the classifiers involving it are not trained, and it is never predicted: its pairwise decision is constant in favor of the other class, and its `predict_proba` column is 0 while the other classes are estimated as if it were absent.

#### Things to look at

- The `rho = +/-1` convention for untrained pairs in `svm.cpp`; it is what keeps a class without samples from winning votes, both in libsvm and in `decision_function(ovr)`.
- `predict_probability` now runs the pairwise coupling only over classes that have support vectors. It is unchanged when all classes have some.
- Not covered: `LinearSVC` (liblinear) has the same problem with a fully zero-weighted class; this is a separate code path and I left it for a follow-up.

#### Testing

The new tests fail on `main` and pass here. They compare a fit with zero-weighted samples/classes to a fit on the retained samples only (dense and sparse, with class weights and non-consecutive labels). I also ran a randomized comparison and the SVM tests under macOS guard-malloc locally.

title: FIX estimator_html_repr fails on Windows locales with non-UTF-8 default encoding
body:
FIX estimator_html_repr fails on Windows locales with non-UTF-8 default encoding

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

On Windows systems where the default locale encoding is not UTF-8 (e.g. Simplified
Chinese Windows with GBK/cp936), displaying an estimator in Jupyter or VS Code
raises a `UnicodeDecodeError`. This happens because the HTML repr machinery reads
the bundled `estimator.js` asset without specifying an encoding:

```python
with open(str(Path(__file__).parent / "estimator.js"), "r") as f:
  script = f.read()
```

When the system default is GBK, decoding the UTF-8-encoded JS file fails:

```
UnicodeDecodeError: 'gbk' codec can't decode byte 0x94 in position 2952: illegal multibyte sequence
```

Note that the error is raised inside `_repr_mimebundle_`, i.e. *after* `fit()` has
already completed successfully. Users are therefore misled into thinking their
model training failed.

Changes:
- `sklearn/utils/_repr_html/estimator.py`: pass `encoding="utf-8"` to `open()`
  when reading `estimator.js` (and other text assets in the same directory).

Rationale: explicit encodings are consistent with PEP 597's direction, and cost
nothing at runtime since the assets are small and read once per repr. Workarounds
like `PYTHONUTF8=1` or `sklearn.set_config(display='text')` exist but should not
be required for a core display function.

#### Introduce yourself

I'm a quant researcher from China using scikit-learn for machine
learning / time-series projects. I ran into this while doing feature
selection exercises in VS Code's interactive window on Simplified Chinese Windows:
`RFE(...).fit(X, y)` succeeded but the cell output crashed with a UnicodeDecodeError.
That led me to trace it down to `estimator.py` line 563. This is my first
contribution to scikit-learn; happy to adjust as needed.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

title: FIX Don't reset the warning filters in each task of thread-based Parallel
body:
## Stalled for now, see <url>

#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #35089. Also removes the xfail added for #32631 in #33320.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

Tasks that already run with the caller's warning filters no longer reset and refill them:

- Without context-aware warnings (GIL builds, free-threaded 3.13), the filters are process-wide, so that's every task running in the caller's process: worker threads, and `n_jobs=1`. Setting the filters there needs `catch_warnings`, which isn't thread-safe.
- With context-aware warnings, it's the tasks whose context has the caller's filter list: the caller's thread, or a thread that inherited its context (the default on free-threaded 3.14).

To know whether a task runs in the caller's process, `Parallel` stores a module-level `object()` token on each task. A task unpickled in another process (loky, multiprocessing, dask, ...) gets a new object, so it sets the filters as before. I use this rather than the pid because a pid doesn't identify a process across hosts or containers.

Two small related fixes: an empty list of caller filters (e.g. after `warnings.resetwarnings()`) no longer raises the warning about `sklearn.utils.parallel.delayed`, and tasks dispatched by joblib's `Parallel`, whose caller filters are unknown, now keep their filters (they were reset to an empty list).

The new tests fail on `main`, except `test_pickled_task_sets_warning_filters`, which guards the pickled path. With the reproducer of #35089, the filters are now unchanged and no warning is raised. On free-threaded 3.13 with pytest-run-parallel, `test_no_user_warning_with_scoring` emitted the warning in 6 of 8 runs on `main`, and in 0 of 5 runs with the first version of this PR (same code path for these tasks).

#### AI usage disclosure: yes, a lot

#### Any other comments?

Tasks running in the caller's process no longer run inside `catch_warnings`, so they behave like any other code in that process, which changes a few things:

- a task calling `warnings.simplefilter` outside of `catch_warnings` changes the caller's filters (sklearn code always does it inside `catch_warnings`);
- without context-aware warnings, tasks use the current filters, not the ones captured when `Parallel` was called (it matters for a generator output consumed under other filters);
- a warning raised with the same message in each task is shown once instead of once per task, since no `catch_warnings` resets the registry between tasks anymore. sklearn's own warnings look unaffected: a `ConvergenceWarning` in `cross_val_score` is still shown for each fold, because other `catch_warnings` calls in `fit` reset the registry anyway.

What remains is `catch_warnings` itself: it isn't thread-safe with process-wide filters, and sklearn also calls it inside the tasks. The main one is in `check_array`, which turns `ComplexWarning` into an error: with 32 threads calling `check_array`, this `error` filter stays in the global filters for good (3 runs out of 3 on GIL 3.13 and on 3.13t, with plain threads, so with or without this PR). I'll open a separate issue and PR to remove the `catch_warnings` from `check_array`.

Tested on GIL 3.13 and 3.14, and on free-threaded 3.13t and 3.14t (3.14t also with `-X context_aware_warnings=0` and `-X thread_inherit_context=0`).
